articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont parent community has demonstrated incredible ongoing support for our students. Last summer, our school board tapped community member and COVID expert Dr. George Rutherford to discuss safety around school opening (Thank you Dr. Rutherford for your talks to PUSD and LWV). As PUSD started planning for the 2020-2021 school year, Piedmont parents rose up. Our parent health care workers offered to hold Q&A sessions for PUSD staff on COVID transmission and safety practices initially; and most recently, vaccine safety. In preparation for our purple tier waiver application, our advocates appealed to PUSD’s insurer Kaiser Permanente to prioritize teacher testing, meet with the county supervisors’ office to clarify waiver requirements, and introduced PUSD leadership to companies providing teacher/student testing and contact tracing services. With the start of school, parents provided critical tech support for chromebook roll out. We spent countless hours collecting data from other districts, sharing best practices, and campaigning with Alameda County leadership for clear and consistent guidelines for a return to in-person learning. Despite our community’s acute increase in childcare, extracurricular, and supplemental academics expenses, the PEF volunteers worked tirelessly to ultimately fundraise at levels comparable to years pre-pandemic. Parent clubs initiated a mask fundraising with high quality masks donated to teachers, ensuring both student and teacher safety. A single Piedmont mom spearheaded the placement of HEPA filters in the classrooms. During synchronous [learning] time, we provide our children with private, quiet workspace (sometimes in the form of our home office). We have up-ended our work schedules to prevent connectivity issues. For essential workers, our children often had to navigate this process largely on their own as we could not always be home with them to help navigate a new way of learning on-line curricula or offer emotional support during periods of depression from social isolation. Unfortunately, many in our community have needed to provide additional professional mental health support for their children. Many of us reduced hours, delayed a return to the workforce, or passed up on career advancement opportunities. We all work nights and weekends because there is simply no other time. Some have left their jobs. We are all grateful to be in a position to be able to make this choice. Piedmont families, you have fully leaned in, providing time, money, skills, energy, patience and strength. Unfortunately, we cannot relent in supporting our children and their education until PUSD can also rise up.
articles.title: Piedmont community leans In

articles.text: You may have heard about the “Immersive Van Gogh” exhibit coming to San Francisco. This West Coast premiere of a show seen by over 2 million in Paris, is billed as an “immersive” experience, because viewers wander through 300,000 cubic feet of animations, and 60,600 frames of video enhanced by 90,000,000 pixels of light, all digitizing Van Gogh’s creations. The promoters go on to promise that the astonishing scale and breathtaking creativity of the exhibit will allow one to “experience the organic landscapes of Van Gogh’s imagination and journey through his brilliance and madness.” I wonder, would Van Gogh go? It doesn’t seem all that organic if the actual paint and brush strokes are digitized. It makes me wonder whose madness we will actually be journeying through. I was taught that art is best interpreted from the inside out, not the outside in. Our technological culture often works with the premise that understanding and awareness, even meaning, comes at us, rather than emerges from within us. Don’t get me wrong, I definitely want to see this exhibit. I have never experienced 90 million pixels all at once. But I also believe that beauty, inspiration and meaning are spiritual experiences which come from within even if catalyzed from without. If I can’t perceive beauty, no amount of technological bombardment will save me. Perhaps some self-reflection is in order. I know one thing for sure. We have all had our own immersion experiences this year. The “art” in our stories of faith have come alive in new ways, not because the stories have been enhanced but because we have been immersed in some of the struggles these stories were grounded in. There is the world, but there is also our perception of the world. And our perception has changed because we were all cast into the deep end of the experiences of this year. Being in lockdown has resonated with the stories of fearful disciples locking their doors to ward off threats of their own. Immersing ourselves in the stories of racial injustice is changing the way we see the narrative of
articles.title: A year of immersive experiences

articles.text: Editor: It has been more than a year into a global pandemic and more than a year in the rise of brutal attacks on Asians in America. From being gunned down in Atlanta to being beaten on the streets of San Francisco, Asians in America have been and continue to be attacked. Why does that matter? Why would that matter to us here in Piedmont? As residents of Piedmont, we pride ourselves on being educated, on being able to live in safety, on being able to raise kids that will thrive in a world where diversity is now the norm and not the exception. At a time when Asians are under attack in America, it is our goal and responsibility to ensure that Piedmont residents acknowledge what is happening in our country and to take action in our own community. The grandfather who is beaten to death. The mothers murdered. The grandmother who fought back but is left with eyes too injured to see. Those are our daughters, sons, mothers, fathers, siblings, and elders. As Asian Americans, we are wrestling with how to explain these attacks to our children and support them in the trauma they experience. How is it that people would attack us simply because of the color of our skin and the bodies we inhabit? How would you explain that to your own children? We experience the attacks of this month against the backdrop of the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the Japanese Internment Camps during World War II, and the 1982 murder of Vincent Chin. The perpetual message is that we – Asians in America, even those born here – do not belong. Our lives are not of the same value as the lives of our white neighbors. From the irresponsible use of terms like “China Virus” and “Kung Flu” from the powerful seat of the prior president, to the claims in mainstream news that the murder of six Asian women in Atlanta last week was not racially motivated, Asians have been minimized, and erased. I am writing on behalf of members and the board of the Piedmont Asian American Club. Piedmont is a safe place, with supportive schools and organizations like the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. But we feel we can still do a better job educating the community and sharing our unpleasant experiences. Racist interactions that we and our children experience in our schools and with our neighbors show the need to make the message clear: Piedmont is our home, and this is our community. We are here, wanting to make it a better place – together. We all need to call out racism when we see it. This is the work PAAC is doing. Will you join us? Cassindy Chao, co-president Piedmont Asian American Club Catherine Zhang, co-President Mary Geong Robin Wu Lee Chin Phmah Jamie Totsubo The Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) was founded in 1987 with the mission of engaging our schools and community in cultural, educational, and social activities while acting as a forum and resource for Asian American issues in Piedmont. “Congratulations, Dude. The Board has discovered that you’re part of the solution. . .not the problem.”
articles.title: A message from Piedmont Asian American Club

articles.text: Expecting a huge boost in COVID-19 vaccine supply, the state announced on Thursday, March 25 that all Californians ages 16 and up will be able to make vaccination appointments starting on Thursday, April 15. People ages 50 and above will be able to make appointments starting tomorrow, Thursday, April 1. Even with the increased supply, the state expects that the vaccination of Californians who wish to be vaccinated will take several months. “With vaccine supply increasing and by expanding eligibility to more Californians, the light at the end of the tunnel continues to get brighter,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom. “We remain focused on equity as we extend vaccine eligibility to those 50 and over starting April 1, and those 16 and older starting April 15.” Last week, Alameda County opened vaccine eligibility to people aged 16 to 64 years “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk due to complex health conditions,” the county stated. The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found on the County website at: covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines.page People aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. Residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. Over 57 percent of Piedmont’s population, some 4,760 people, has received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of March 29, and almost 40 percent of the City’s residents (est. 3,200) are fully vaccinated, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. Vaccines created by Moderna and Pfizer require two doses administered several weeks apart. A recently approved vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose, but just a few thousand doses of this vaccine have arrived in the county so far. Much more are expected to arrive in the coming days. Piedmont still leads the rest of the cities of Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population, but rates across the county have increased in recent weeks. In all of Alameda County, about 822,000 total doses have been administered and around 24 percent of the county’s population is fully vaccinated. In Oakland, about 39 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 23 percent have been fully vaccinated. President Joe Biden, bolstered by the rising supply rates of the Johnson and Johnson and other vaccines, announced this month that all American adults should be eligible for vaccination by May 1. The state has administered about 17.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 22.4 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 317,000 people per day, a significant increase compared to last week. in Oakland and 13,077 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,401 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide, an increase of 31 in the past seven days. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. pages.text: Wednesday, March 31, 2021 3 COVID NEWS California announces all adults eligible for COVID-19 vaccine on April 15 Eligibility for Californians ages 50 and over opens tomorrow By Barry Eitel Expecting a huge boost in COVID-19 vaccine supply, the state announced on Thursday, March 25 that all Californians ages 16 and up will be able to make vaccination appointments starting on Thursday, April 15. People ages 50 and above will be able to make appointments starting tomorrow, Thursday, April 1. Even with the increased supply, the state expects that the vaccination of Californians who wish to be vaccinated will take several months. “With vaccine supply increasing and by expanding eligibility to more Californians, the light at the end of the tunnel continues to get brighter,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom. “We remain focused on equity as we extend vaccine eligibility to those 50 and over starting April 1, and those 16 and older starting April 15.” Last week, Alameda County opened vaccine eligibility to people aged 16 to 64 years “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk due to complex health conditions,” the county stated. The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found on the County website at: covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines.page People aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. Residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. Over 57 percent of Piedmont’s population, some 4,760 people, has received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of March 29, and almost 40 percent of the City’s residents (est. 3,200) are fully vaccinated, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. Vaccines created by Moderna and Pfizer require two doses administered several weeks apart. A recently approved vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose, but just a few thousand doses of this vaccine have arrived in the county so far. Much more are expected to arrive in the coming days. Piedmont still leads the rest of the cities of Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population, but rates across the county have increased in recent weeks. In all of Alameda County, about 822,000 total doses have been administered and around 24 percent of the county’s population is fully vaccinated. In Oakland, about 39 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 23 percent have been fully vaccinated. President Joe Biden, bolstered by the rising supply rates of the Johnson and Johnson and other vaccines, announced this month that all American adults should be eligible for vaccination by May 1. The state has administered about 17.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 22.4 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. From being gunned down in Atlanta to being beaten on the streets of San Francisco, Asians in America have been and continue to be attacked. Why does that matter? Why would that matter to us here in Piedmont? As residents of Piedmont, we pride ourselves on being educated, on being able to live in safety, on being able to raise kids that will thrive in a world where diversity is now the norm and not the exception. At a time when Asians are under attack in America, it is our goal and responsibility to ensure that Piedmont residents acknowledge what is happening in our country and to take action in our own community. The grandfather who is beaten to death. The mothers murdered. The grandmother who fought back but is left with eyes too injured to see. Those are our daughters, sons, mothers, fathers, siblings, and elders. As Asian Americans, we are wrestling with how to explain these attacks to our children and support them in the trauma they experience. How is it that people would attack us simply because of the color of our skin and the bodies we inhabit? How would you explain that to your own children? We experience the attacks of this month against the backdrop of the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the Japanese Internment Camps during World War II, and the 1982 murder of Vincent Chin. The perpetual message is that we – Asians in America, even those born here – do not belong. Our lives are not of the same value as the lives of our white neighbors. From the irresponsible use of terms like “China Virus” and “Kung Flu” from the powerful seat of the prior president, to the claims in mainstream news that the murder of six Asian women in Atlanta last week was not racially motivated, Asians have been minimized, and erased. I am writing on behalf of members and the board of the Piedmont Asian American Club. Piedmont is a safe place, with supportive schools and organizations like the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. But we feel we can still do a better job educating the community and sharing our unpleasant experiences. Racist interactions that we and our children experience in our schools and with our neighbors show the need to make the message clear: Piedmont is our home, and this is our community. We are here, wanting to make it a better place – together. We all need to call out racism when we see it. This is the work PAAC is doing. Will you join us? articles.text: The current public health crisis has proved that there will always be a need for those who are generous enough to volunteer their time and skills. Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to explore. Thanks to suggestions from residents, the Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers. Alameda County Community Food Bank For 35 years, Alameda County Community Food Bank (ACCFB) has pursued a hunger-free community in Alameda County. ACCFB always has a need for volunteers, but at the moment, their greatest need is for weekday volunteers who can commit to joining the team weekly for full days for at least one month. You can choose to work in weekday food sorting and packaging, volunteer as a market vehicle loader, or in drivethrough distribution. Group reservations are encouraged, so grab a few friends and spend a day giving back. To learn more about volunteering, email volunteer@accfb.org. To learn more about ACCFB’s safety measures and current needs, visit https://www. accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer/. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute volunteers are responsible for keeping Lake Merritt clean. Because of COVID, access to “U-Clean-it” boxes around Lake Merritt are restricted to properly trained volunteers. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the second floor of the Boating Center at 568 Bellevue Avenue, and usually work two to three hours. Training is available from Lake Merritt Institute staff upon request by calling the office at 510-238-2290. Volunteers remove approximately 1,000 to 5,000 pounds of trash from the shores of Lake Merritt every month. Cleanup days are Tuesday at 10:30 a.m., and Saturday at 10 a.m. Numerous members of the Piedmont High Key Club can be found cleaning the lake on any given Saturday. Visit https://lakemerrittinstitute.org/ about-the-institute/ for more information about the organization. Asian Health Services Asian Health Services, located in Oakland, provides health, social, and advocacy services for all regardless of income, insurance status, immigration status, language or culture. The organization provides healthcare to more than 50,000 patients in English and over 14 Asian languages. Volunteers are critical to the center and contribute enormously to patients’ experiences. Opportunities are available in both clinical and non-clinical settings, including: health education, fundraising, language access, and administration. You must complete an online application. For more information, call (510) 986-6830 or email hr@ahschc.org. Visit https://asianhealthservices.org/volunteer-opportunities/ for more information. Project Open Hand Project Open Hand’s mission is to improve health outcomes by providing nutritious meals to the sick and vulnerable in the East Bay. Founded in 1985, the organization provides meals with love to critically ill neighbors and seniors. Each day, volunteers prepare 2,500 nutritious meals, and provide 200 bags of healthy groceries. There is also a need for volunteers, but due to COVID, volunteer shifts can be limited. If you are interested in scheduling a weekly volunteer shift, Project Open Hand asks for a 6-month commitment or 40 hours a semester for students. Contact volunteer@openhand.org with questions or to sign up. Visit https://www.openhand.org/volunteer/volunteer-alameda-county/ individual-alameda-county for more information. East Bay SPCA The East Bay’s oldest animal welfare organization is always in need of volunteers. Volunteering is a wonderful way to improve the lives of animals in the shelter, and a variety of opportunities are available for all ages. East Bay SPCA’s Humane Education programs are tailored for youth volunteers, and sessions are now open for registration. Some examples of potential service projects include making dog treats, assisting with shelter laundry, socializing with animals in the SPCA’s care, and more. Participants will learn about responsible pet care, the medical needs of animals, and pet behavior. Visit https://eastbayspca.org/whatwe-do/humane-education/shelter-scouts/ to sign up for a session. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? Email suggestions to Allyson Aleksey at allysonaaleksey@gmail.com.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 31, 2021 5 Solidarity Wall Continued from page 1 may not be aware of how much the hate violence has impacted our community, how unsafe many of us feel, and how rampant anti-Asian violence has become.” “Anti-Asian hate is so traumatizing and hurtful to our community and to many of us who are devoted citizens of Piedmont, which is our home. Personally, I am incredibly sad that we grew up seeing this hate. It’s unbelievable that now, decades later, it still remains a problem,” said Cassindy Chao-Bierhaus, Co-President of Piedmont Asian American Club. The two organizations created the Solidarity Wall so that Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in Piedmont could feel both support and solidarity from their neighbors, Cheng explained. The groups also wanted to raise awareness to the wider community about the attacks against Asian Americans that have become more frequent in previous months, especially in the Bay Area. “We’ve heard from many Asian American youth that they don’t feel the schools or their peers understand the degree to which Asian Americans have been subjected to racism historically or in the present. We’re hoping to draw attention and spur action on antiAsian hate,” Cheng said. The nationally-observed “Stand With Asians” day was envisioned by Tian He, who was inspired to start this movement following the murder of his friend, a 36-year-old man who was stabbed multiple times in Manhattan’s Chinatown district on February 25. That murder is in addition to a slew of murders, attacks, assaults, and robberies of Asian individuals and Asian-owned businesses, mostly concentrated in New York City, San Francisco, Oakland, and Los Angeles. Last Friday, those who wanted to get involved were asked to create, produce, and post Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) awareness content. Piedmont’s Solidarity Wall served as a community call-to-action. “We’ve heard from community members that the wall has Cassindy Chao (left), Catherine Zhang, Suzy Skugstad, Judy Li, and Alana Zhou stand with signs of support at the Solidarity Wall. On Friday the Solidarity Wall began to accumulate artwork and messages from Piedmont community members in an effort spearheaded by Diana Lee and Irene Cheng. Kids gathered through the weekend at the Exedra to write notes and post signs on the Exedra. One of many posters that appeared at the Exedra. In addition to these colorful graphics with messages such as “We Belong,” people walking by the exedra created their own messages of support for the Asian community and posted them up. Diana Lee (left) co-founder of the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, and Cassindy Chao, co-president of the Piedmont Asian American Club, co-organizers of the pop-up solidarity wall. already sparked many dialogues that may not otherwise have happened, among AAPI community, between AAPI folks and their non-AAPI friends and neighbors, between parents and children, between students and their peers, and between teachers and students. Several community members have mentioned that they found the display poignant and moving, offering a space to reflect and to process what has been happening. We hope the wall spurs further conversation, solidarity, and anti-racism efforts within our community, and beyond,” Cheng said. Residents began adorning the wall as early as 10 a.m. on Friday, March 26, and continued posting signs of support through the weekend. City Councilmember Conna McCarthy, who visited the wall on Friday to place flowers, echoed Cheng’s sentiments. “We’re in a time where everyone’s hearts are breaking because of this kind of violence. Showing up is the first step in taking responsibility for changing it,” she said. “I saw children putting flowers and writing notes, with their mothers and guardians explaining to them why this wall has to be here, and why it’s important. Our community is in a place where we can get together and make a strong statement.” Cheng said that she hopes the dialogue continues, and that Piedmonters will reach out to their Asian American neighbors, check in, and ask how they are doing. Posters produced a powerful message. The Solidarity Wall remained up at the Exedra until Sunday at 5 p.m. when the signs and artwork were taken down and transferred to Piedmont High.

articles.text: Since February, Piedmont parents have advocated for more in-person class time in their appearances at school board meetings, city-wide installation of lawn signs and through independent surveys. Currently, elementary students attend class nine hours a week, high schoolers (taking a full class load) get four hours and 22.5 minutes per week and middle schoolers attend class only two and half hours per week. With vaccinations steadily increasing and COVID cases dwindling (Alameda County is now in the orange tier), the California Department of Public Health’s revised guideline for minimum physical spacing in schools was reduced from six feet to three feet. The health directive stated three feet was “strongly recommended” as a guideline but not required. If other safety measures, like masks and air filters are in place and enforced, under three feet spacing between students is allowed by the state and Alameda County. Piedmont School District began negotiating with its the labor unions representing school administrators, classified staff and teachers on March 24, to expand in-person class time for the remainder of the Spring semester. Including the March 24 bargaining session, the district has held two negotiation sessions with teachers, totaling four and a half hours of negotiation. The content of negotiations, initial positions and statuses of negotiation have not been publicly revealed. At the March 24 school board meeting, dozens of parents called in via Zoom to push for a written confirmation by the district for 100 percent in-class instruction for next fall and an increase now in the spring. The initial discussion on the topic by the board and the ensuing public comment took nearly two and a half hours. “I’m very, very concerned and wonder why it took so long to get teachers back to the negotiating table,” said parent Leslie Santos. “You negotiated the MOU in August; no one anticipated these vaccines as early as December. The vaccines alone should have been an event special enough to start negotiations.” The current MOU created in August and amended in February is still built upon previous Covid guidelines which require six feet of space between students. That guideline has been reduced to three feet between students “We are currently in negotiations. I want to thank APT (teachers union) for coming to the table. I am confident that we will be able to come to agreements that will provide additional time for on-campus instruction, though without sacrificing opportunities for the education for those that choose to remain as Distance Learners,” Booker stated. On March 24, Booker expressed optimism that he would have news of the bargaining developments or even a new tentative agreement to share “early next week.” As of press time, no new developments have been announced. The district intends to call a special board meeting “the second we come up with tentative agreements” Booker said. In addition to coming to terms with teachers, a few logistical items stand in the way of expanding the schedule. The district still needs to conduct a new survey of families to determine who wants in-person and who wants to stay in Distance Learning. Some school sites may need to purchase new furniture (smaller desks). And the district is looking to hire additional teachers to attend to distance learners (primarily at the elementary level). Nine weeks of class remain until the last day of school, June 11.
articles.title: Teachers, school district begin negotiations for in-person class time this spring

articles.text: For some students, working with numbers and equations can be stressful. But basic math skills, like most things in life, can be achieved by anyone by following the most common-sense route: practice. Memorization of the basic math facts is critical to success in math. Memorization is not out. Basic arithmetic skills are useful for recognizing and using patterns in everyday life. Also, memorization of basic facts is necessary for success in test taking. Students who do not know basic arithmetic by memory must laboriously figure out each answer when problem solving. These students run out of time, energy and patience long before completing the test. Instead of focusing on problem-solving techniques, these students spend valuable time and energy figuring out basic math facts. If you notice your child is struggling in mathematics, consider nightly math fact “drills.” This practice is useful for students of all ages and is highly encouraged for children in kindergarten through fourth grade. Find an appropriate operation for your child’s grade level; for example, in kindergarten, students are beginning to memorize addition facts. By fourth grade, multiplication facts should be mastered. Timed tests are given for one minute, during which the student should be writing continuously. Students are expected to know answers instantly. There should be no time to think about or figure out the answer. A child should know that 3 + 4 = 7 as quickly as he or she knows that capital H goes with lower case h. A great online resource that students can work on independently is called Rocket Math. It can be downloaded onto your child’s computer or iPad by visiting play.rocketmath.com. Of course, there is always the tried-and-true option of paper and pencil: simply write a few, single-digit addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division problems for your child to solve. A short, nightly drill is recommended. Find what works best for your child, from flash cards, to computer programs, to writing the facts. At least some written practice is beneficial. Educators, and parents, know that children are motivated by mastery – and practicing basic math facts daily means more success in cumulative problem-solving. Allyson Aleksey is a former 4th grade teacher at a private, accelerated school in Metairie, Louisiana.
articles.title: TIPS FROM A TEACHER In math, memorization is not “out”

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, March 31, 2021 SchOOLs Teachers, school district begin negotiations for in-person class time this spring By Jay Russell Since February, Piedmont parents have advocated for more in-person class time in their appearances at school board meetings, city-wide installation of lawn signs and through independent surveys. Currently, elementary students attend class nine hours a week, high schoolers (taking a full class load) get four hours and 22.5 minutes per week and middle schoolers attend class only two and half hours per week. With vaccinations steadily increasing and COVID cases dwindling (Alameda County is now in the orange tier), the California Department of Public Health’s revised guideline for minimum physical spacing in schools was reduced from six feet to three feet. The health directive stated three feet was “strongly recommended” as a guideline but not required. If other safety measures, like masks and air filters are in place and enforced, under three feet spacing between students is allowed by the state and Alameda County. Piedmont School District began negotiating with its the labor unions representing school administrators, classified staff and teachers on March 24, to expand in-person class time for the remainder of the Spring semester. Including the March 24 bargaining session, the district has held two negotiation sessions with teachers, totaling four and a half hours of negotiation. The content of negotiations, initial positions and statuses of negotiation have not been publicly revealed. At the March 24 school board meeting, dozens of parents called in via Zoom to push for a written confirmation by the district for 100 percent in-class instruction for next fall and an increase now in the spring. The initial discussion on the topic by the board and the ensuing public comment took nearly two and a half hours. “I’m very, very concerned and wonder why it took so long to get teachers back to the negotiating table,” said parent Leslie Santos. “You negotiated the MOU in August; no one anticipated these vaccines as early as December. The vaccines alone should have been an event special enough to start negotiations.” The current MOU created in August and amended in February is still built upon previous Covid guidelines which require six feet of space between students. That guideline has been reduced to three feet between students “We are currently in negotiations. I want to thank APT (teachers union) for coming to the table. I am confident that we will be able to come to agreements that will provide additional time for on-campus instruction, though without sacrificing opportunities for the education for those that choose to remain as Distance Learners,” Booker stated. On March 24, Booker expressed optimism that he would have news of the bargaining developments or even a new tentative agreement to share “early next week.” As of press time, no new developments have been announced. The district intends to call a special board meeting “the second we come up with tentative agreements” Booker said. In addition to coming to terms with teachers, a few logistical items stand in the way of expanding the schedule. The district still needs to conduct a new survey of families to determine who wants in-person and who wants to stay in Distance Learning. Some school sites may need to purchase new furniture (smaller desks). And the district is looking to hire additional teachers to attend to distance learners (primarily at the elementary level). Nine weeks of class remain until the last day of school, June 11. TIPS FROM A TEACHER In math, memorization is not “out” By Allyson Aleksey For some students, working with numbers and equations can be stressful. But basic math skills, like most things in life, can be achieved by anyone by following the most common-sense route: practice. Memorization of the basic math facts is critical to success in math. Memorization is not out. Basic arithmetic skills are useful for recognizing and using patterns in everyday life. Also, memorization of basic facts is necessary for success in test taking. Students who do not know basic arithmetic by memory must laboriously figure out each answer when problem solving. These students run out of time, energy and patience long before completing the test. Instead of focusing on problem-solving techniques, these students spend valuable time and energy figuring out basic math facts. If you notice your child is struggling in mathematics, consider nightly math fact “drills.” This practice is useful for students of all ages and is highly encouraged for children in kindergarten through fourth grade. Find an appropriate operation for your child’s grade level; for example, in kindergarten, students are beginning to memorize addition facts. By fourth grade, multiplication facts should be mastered. Timed tests are given for one minute, during which the student should be writing continuously. Students are expected to know answers instantly. There should be no time to think about or figure out the answer. A child should know that 3 + 4 = 7 as quickly as he or she knows that capital H goes with lower case h. A great online resource that students can work on independently is called Rocket Math. It can be downloaded onto your child’s computer or iPad by visiting play.rocketmath.com. Of course, there is always the tried-and-true option of paper and pencil: simply write a few, single-digit addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division problems for your child to solve. A short, nightly drill is recommended. Find what works best for your child, from flash cards, to computer programs, to writing the facts. At least some written practice is beneficial. Educators, and parents, know that children are motivated by mastery – and practicing basic math facts daily means more success in cumulative problem-solving. Allyson Aleksey is a former 4th grade teacher at a private, accelerated school in Metairie, Louisiana. articles.text: As Piedmont High School’s campus transitions to incorporate a new STEAM building and theater, the question was asked, “What would make it more ideal?” A panel of students, faculty, administration, parents and community members invested hours into deliberating this very question. It was especially noted that while students were performing at remarkably high levels, there certainly was an opportunity for their learning experiences to provide more joy and real-world relevance. Students can too easily view their high school years as only a hoop that must be jumped through, so that one day – perhaps years in the future – they might make a difference in the world and be able to enjoy their contributions to it. Expo has been designed to seize the opportunity to make high school a more joyful and relevant experience. Expo will allow students to apply their knowledge and skills from all of their learning experiences to a problem in which they bring their own passion and interest. For Expo, students will research and analyze a problem of their choosing and persuasively reveal their proposed solution to the world at the culminating Expo event. The manner and form of what students produce for an Expo project is limitless. One might design a tangible object in the STEAM building engineering lab or at home, or the project may be a policy proposal. It could be a book, a song, a computer program, a widget, a business venture, an academic course, an automobile, a sensor, an analyzer, a TED Talk, an Eagle Scout project, or almost anything. It might be geared locally, regionally, nationally or globally. It might completely eradicate a problem, or it might simply serve to contribute in a meaningful way towards mitigation of the problem. All student projects will be revealed at the Expo event on June 4 at 7 p.m., and top tier projects will be highlighted. Judges will identify top tier projects utilizing the rubric included in the Expo Student Guide, available at tinyurl.com/piedmontexpo. It’s important to remember that the Expo project is a standalone work, guided by each individual student’s discretion. Several teachers have incorporated a portion, or even all of their final assessment, as a demonstration of proficiency in standards that could possibly be fully met while students are working on their Expo project. Many student questions are answered in the Student Guide, but clarification is available by e-mailing Mr. Christensen at fchristensen@piedmont.k12. ca.us. Flint Christensen teaches Computer Science at Piedmont High School.

articles.text: Some children push their tongue between their front teeth when swallowing, eating, talking, or while at rest. This is called tongue thrust. It is normal (and protective) for infants to hold their tongues forward when they swallow, but this pattern should stop by the time your child is about 1½ years old. Our tongue stays behind our teeth when we speak, not visible to the listener, with the exception of the “th” sound. However, if your child has a tongue thrust, you may see his tongue when he speaks or eats. Since a tongue thrust can also push your child’s teeth out of place, your child’s dentist may be the first person to tell you that the tongue thrust is causing a problem. Where should our tongue be? The normal posture is to rest the tongue up on the roof of the mouth, about ½ an inch away from the front teeth. Lips should be closed, and teeth slightly apart. Tongue thrust can be caused by a narrowed airway which results in mouth breathing because of allergies or large tonsils. Tongue thrust can be caused by prolonged thumb sucking, or pacifier, bottle or sippy cup use that may change the shape of your child’s jaw, palate and teeth. Tongue thrust can also be due to tongue or lip weakness, or developmental delays. Tongue thrust can be related to a tongue tie. Tongue thrust can also have a Tongue thrusting can lead to many problems. genetic component. The constant improperly placed pressure generated by the tongue thrust can create problems with dental health, speech and the cosmetic appearance of the face over time. We swallow approximately 2,000 times per day with the tongue generating up to 4 pounds of pressure per swallow. Tongue thrust can occur throughout the lifespan. For the infant and very young child, trouble latching, persistent drooling and messy eating may be evident. For the school aged child, dental and speech issues such as a lisp may be noted. Tongue thrust can also cause orthodontic relapse if untreated. In adulthood, sleep disordered breathing, TMJ and facial pain can present. Treatment of tongue thrust usually involves multiple disciplines. Dentists can address the associated oral health issues. Orthodontists can treat the resultant misalignment of the teeth and jaw. While the dentist and orthodontist treat problems which have already occurred, a therapist can correct the tongue thrust problem and the habit at the root of the issue to prevent further complications and promote long term success with your orthodontic investments. Therapy can re-train the muscles of the face and tongue for proper posture at rest, as well as during speech and swallowing. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

(NO PHOTOS) NESA Outstanding Eagle Scout Awards This award, abbreviated “NOESA,” is made by the National Eagle Scout Association on nomination by the Piedmont Council to a volunteer who attained the Eagle rank as a youth and has gone on to perform distinguished service at the local, state or regional level. NOESA recipients have inspired others through their actions and have devoted themselves not only to their profession but also to their avocation and community. Seth Hilton Seth Hilton, the Council’s current president, received his Eagle as a member of a troop in Arroyo Grande, California, and became a nationally recognized lawyer, now with Stoel Rives in San Francisco, where he advises clients on complex regulatory questions and transactions. He became a volunteer in Piedmont when his son entered Cub Scouts and was immediately tapped as the Cubmaster of Pack 3. He has served as an Assistant Scoutmaster of Troop 1 and then as Scoutmaster of Piedmont Troop 3330 for the 2017 National Jamboree. On the Executive Board, he has been Vice President of Cubs, Vice President of Programs, and now serves as President since 2019, using his leadership skills and good humor in abundant measures. He is a consensus builder and inspires all of us to achieve our goals, faithful to the standards and expectations of an Eagle Scout. Rob James A past president of the Piedmont Council, Rob received his Eagle in 1975 as a member of Troop 45 in Salinas. After a latency period of a few decades, he re-entered Scouting along with his son. As an adult Scouter, he has served in almost every role available from Den Leader and Committee Chairman to Board member and Council President. Most recently he served as an Assistant Scoutmaster to the National jamboree in West Virginia in 2017. After graduating from Stanford and Yale, he went to work for Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman, and has remained there for 38 years. In addition to his client work as a partner in the firm’s San Francisco and Houston offices, he is a co-leader of Pillsbury’s Energy and Infrastructure Projects team. Rob is also an author, penning pieces on slide rules, baseball history, and the 1906 San Francisco fire and earthquake. More recently, he published a short book during the pandemic titled “Humanity and the Big Dipper: A history of Our Species in Relation to Seven Stars.” For outstanding service to his community and excellence in his vocation, we are pleased to bestow the NESA Outstanding Eagle Scout Award to Rob James. In addition, Benson acknowledged the 20 Piedmont Scouts who earned their Eagle award, the highest achievement of uniformed Scouts David Ashton, winner of the Piedmont Scout Council’s President’s Award. Katy Kobal earned Piedmont Scouting’s District Award of Merit.

articles.text: Silver Beaver Award – Sue Smegal “Tonight we are pleased to recognize Sue Smegal,” said Benson. . Considered the highest award a local council can present, the Silver Beaver Award was introduced in 1931 as a council-level distinguished service award of the Boy Scouts of America. Recipients of this award are registered Scouters who have made an impact on the lives of youth through outstanding and noteworthy service at the council level. The council is limited to presenting one each year. It is given by every council across the county, and universally respected for it represents dedicated service to others. “Sue has quietly and competently worked behind the scenes for decades. For many years, her service on the Piedmont Council’s Executive Board, Advisory Board, and her continuing service on the Eagle Board of Review has upheld the Council’s mission to support youth and families throughout the community. She chaired three large events for the Piedmont Council, including recognition dinners for Bob Coleman and Gray Cathrall, and the Eagle Scout Celebration in 2010. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. At the top of the essay include the following information: the title, your first and last name, city of residence (must be Piedmont), name of your school, and your current grade. Essays must be typed and double-spaced and submitted in a .pdf format. All entries are to be submitted to lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The deadline is April 17. Winners will be announced on May 1. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community. tel: 510-658-2588 www.piedmontfuneralservices.com 5000 piedmont ave., oakland, ca (fd#2210)

articles.text: Louis XV’s mistress Madame de Pompadour was his most trusted and beloved lover whose death was a great tragedy for the king. History has judged Louis XV as a gentle person, an excellent father, but lacking in confidence and generally weak as a national leader. He had poor financial skills and was not a good war strategist. He did some building, most notably the Ecole Militaire, Place Louis XV (now Place de la Concorde), the Petit Trianon at Versailles and opera theater of the Palace of Versailles; and the Pantheon of Paris. But with hereditary rulers you get what you get. Socially, Louis was shy and inordinately modest, indecisive and hesitant to speak his mind. He was honest, but a penchant for secrecy hobbled him as a negotiator. His most trusted advisor in his later years was Madame de Pompadour, one of his many mistresses, most of them from a much lower societal caste. His reign is not regarded as a particularly successful one. He died of smallpox at age 64 in 1774. Louis had one son, his heir-apparent, or Dauphin, as the French call their “Prince of Wales,” but he preceded his father in death, Three of the Dauphin’s sons would become kings: Louis XVI in 1774, during whose reign the French Revolution broke out in 1789 and then lost his head in 1793; Louis XVIII, the Bourbon restored to the throne after Emperor Napoléon abdicated in 1814; and Charles X, who reigned until the July Revolution of 1830 when he was forcibly deposed. Louis XVI whose father preceded him in death followed Louis XV as the next Bourbon king. Marie Antoinette, the queen of Louis XVI, and the last French queen prior to the French Revolution of 1789.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 31, 2021 11 AMERICANS IN PARIS Continued from page 10 Louis XV reigned from 1715 to his death in 1774. Oil painting by Maurice Quentin de la Tour (French). Criticism arose late in life over his cumulative extravagances; an obsession with royal portraiture and statuary; and the several dozen monuments dedicated to the glory of the king himself. No other French king in history had been more self-celebratory. However, his achievements were monumental, including expansive upgrades to Versailles and Louvre palaces – contributions of permanence and extraordinary beauty, and singularly French. Toward the end of his reign, the Sun King’s shine lost some of its glow: critics gained traction about cost overages and extravagant expenditures; depleted royal coffers; and taxes that fell too heavily on an exhausted populace. Sometime in the 1690s the war gods abandoned Louis, and he ultimately suffered a series of defeats at the hands of England’s greatest general, John Churchill, who Queen Anne rewarded by naming him the First Duke of Marlborough. His greatest victory over the French was the Battle of Blenheim. As the end of Louis’s life, three of his heir-apparent successors – his son, grandson, and elder great-grandson – were all struck down with fatal illnesses within one year. On his deathbed in 1715, Louis advised his remaining great-grandson, the future Louis XV, then five years old, to “lighten the burden on the people and avoid going to war as much as possible,” declaring that war was “the ruin of the peoples.” Aware of his own mistakes and many futile battles, he asked his grandson to be “a peaceful prince.” The boy became king under the regency of his cousin Philippe II, Duke of Orléans. Louis XV reigned for the next 59 years, a span second only to that of Louis XIV, but he did not take his great-grandfather’s advice on war. He began waging war in 1756 on two continents: The Seven Years’ War in Europe where France fought Great Britain and Prussia; and in North America, where France was engaged in the French and Indian War and allied with American natives against the British. France lost in both theaters. In North America, Louis’s empire lost their eastern holdings of Quebec, the Great Lakes and the Ohio Valley to England, and substantial territories overrun by the Brits in the West Indies and India. In Europe, France was forced to cede the Austrian Netherlands to Prussia, all costly and humiliating losses. Louis XV’s mistress Madame de Pompadour was his most trusted and beloved lover whose death was a great tragedy for the king. History has judged Louis XV as a gentle person, an excellent father, but lacking in confidence and generally weak as a national leader. He had poor financial skills and was not a good war strategist. He did some building, most notably the Ecole Militaire, Place Louis XV (now Place de la Concorde), the Petit Trianon at Versailles and opera theater of the Palace of Versailles; and the Pantheon of Paris. But with hereditary rulers you get what you get. Socially, Louis was shy and inordinately modest, indecisive and hesitant to speak his mind. He was honest, but a penchant for secrecy hobbled him as a negotiator. His most trusted advisor in his later years was Madame de Pompadour, one of his many mistresses, most of them from a much lower societal caste. His reign is not regarded as a particularly successful one. He died of smallpox at age 64 in 1774. Louis had one son, his heir-apparent, or Dauphin, as the French call their “Prince of Wales,” but he preceded his father in death, Three of the Dauphin’s sons would become kings: Louis XVI in 1774, during whose reign the French Revolution broke out in 1789 and then lost his head in 1793; Louis XVIII, the Bourbon restored to the throne after Emperor Napoléon abdicated in 1814; and Charles X, who reigned until the July Revolution of 1830 when he was forcibly deposed. NEXT: A teenage marriage: At age 15 Louis XVI was married to 14-year-old Hapsburg Archduchess, Maria Antonia (Marie Antoinette). Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris in September 2019 and now await the promise of normalcy someday post- pandemic. In-house historian Michael Mathews contributed to this column. Louis XVI whose father preceded him in death followed Louis XV as the next Bourbon king. Marie Antoinette, the queen of Louis XVI, and the last French queen prior to the French Revolution of 1789.

articles.text: Photos by Brian Mahany At No. 2 singles, Bridgette McEfee reeled in two victories over the last week, winning 6-2, 6-2 against Carondelet and 6-1, 6-4 against Bishop O’Dowd. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team split its last two matches, defeating Cardondelet 7-2 on Tuesday, March 23, but losing 4-3 to Bishop O’Dowd in a city park in San Leandro last Saturday. “The girls played great in their upset of Carondelet. With Thiel out of state in a tournament, Audrey Edel ran through the Cougars’ No. 1 singles player, Libby Leal, in straight sets 6-4, 6-2. At No. 2, Bridgette McEfee won in straight sets 6-2, 6-2; Bini appeared at No. 4 to win 6-2, 6-0; and Audrey Mahany won 6-4, 6-0 at No. 5. The only losses included Anne Jumper at No. 3 singles in threesets, 2-6, 6-2, 10-8. Talia Blumberg made her varsity debut at No. 6 but fell 6-3, 6-2. In doubles, Amanda Becker and Mara LaForte played at No. 1 to win in three sets, 6-7 (7-3), 6-2, 10-6. At No. 2 Rosie Siemers and Kate Dorman won 6-4, 6-4, and Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro won 6-2, 6-3 at No. 3. articles.text: The Piedmont High boys’ tennis team is off and running to a 5-1 record with a dominant three-match home stand over the last week. Starting on Wednesday, March 24, PHS claimed an 8-1 win over non-league De La Salle and followed wp with onesided wins against league rival Berkeley 6-1 on Thursday, and a shutout of Bishop O’Dowd 7-0 on Saturday. PHS has now won five in a row since losing to non-league opponent Miramonte on March 2. “We’ve only lost two matches out of the last 21. The match was tied 3-3 in the final set before the Highlanders converted three straight points. “After the first set, we had to get into the game and turned it around in the second set. It was 3-all in the third set, then we found that confidence again,” said Maxwell. The Highlanders gained the first win of the afternoon when Berkeley’s No. 2, Faris Hadir, suffering an ankle injury after winning the first set against Sajan Srivastava and had to withdraw from the match. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team nearly upset North Coast Section power California High of San Ramon on Wednesday, March 24 at Witter Field. The Grizzlies, a strong Division 1 team, had its hands full in a 15-12 win over Piedmont. “The game was fantastic even though we lost,” said Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. “We played toe-to-toe with them despite only having 13 players, We were down early but came back to tie. The girls’ played hard and kept up the pace, but we just ran out of steam with around six minutes left.” It was a big night for attacker Caroline Devine with six goals, and classmate Sadie Tschider with four assists. PHS goalie, sophomore Lindsay Kottle, also had a strong performance with nine saves – the top performance in her brief varsity career. “Defense led the way for us. Lindsay made some amazing saves; her clears were spot-on as well,” added Chan. The Grizzlies opened scoring with a pair of goals within the first two minutes before Devine got Piedmont on the board. Cal High led 6-2 before PHS narrowed the gap to 8-7 by halftime. To get there, Devine added a pair of goals with 12:56 and 10:50 left in the first half—making it 6-4. CHS added a seventh with 8:43 left, to which Piedmont’s Katherine Kinne responded with a score two minutes later, 7-5. The Grizzlies made it 8-5 with 2:42 left in the first, but PHS added scores from Tschider after 30 seconds, while Devine pulled it within one, 8-7, with seven seconds left before halftime. In the second half, Piedmont Photos by Todd Marshburn Sophomore Lindsay Kottle made nine saves against Cal High. Caroline Devine had another big game – six goals and two assists – against the Grizzlies. tied the match at 8-8 after just 20 seconds when Tschider found Kinne making a sharp cut toward net for the tying goal. But Cal High scored two goals in the seven minutes it took until Devine found the net again, her fifth, to make it 10-9. Kinne tied up the game, yet again 10-10 with 16:40 left. The Highlanders couldn’t gain the lead after tying it several Sadie Tschider added four assists and two goals. more times. Cal High got its 11th goal with 15:50 left to play. Less than one minute later Charlotte Theut tied it at 11-11. The Grizzlies added their 12th score with 14 minutes left for a 12-11 lead, but Devine, Piedmont’s most dangerous weapon, tied it once again at 12-12 with 12:04 remaining. It was the last time Piedmont scored. With 10:44, Cal High went ahead on a score by Evelyn McMahon—one of her six goals. Then they piled on two more within the final five minutes. Final stats include Devine’s six goals and two assists; Tschider had four assists and two goals; Kinne scored three goals for a hat trick; Theut had a goal and assist. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-3) heads to Newark Memorial today for a 7:00 p.m. match. They play again tomorrow, Thursday, April 1 on the road in Danville in a match with Monte Vista at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont running back Brian Cain had a career day on Saturday, running for 229 yards and four touchdowns against Mt. Eden. Piedmont’s football team traveled to Hayward on Saturday, March 27, where, behind a monster game by sunning back Brian Cain, it obliterated the Mt. Eden Monarchs, 42-7. Cain, a senior, ran for 229 yards and scored four touchdowns. “It was the most rushing yards I’ve ever had. We knew that once we’d get to the second-level of their defense, their larger linebackers wouldn’t be able to chase us down,” said Cain. The Highlanders led 28-7 by halftime, and Cain already had three touchdowns. But it was Piedmont’s defense that quickly figured out the Monarchs’ offense and its mobile quarterback, Alejandro Villanueva, He had more than 20 run attempts, but was held to 70 yards. The Monarchs were coming off a 48-32 win against Newark Memorial where Villanueva was the bulk of their offense. “I didn’t think we’d blow them out like that. We knew that he was a critical piece of their offense. He had big windows to throw against Newark Memorial, and there’s a big difference when you apply pressure,” explained PHS coach Jerome Johnson. Piedmont’s offense plan was to stay on the ground, continuously pounding the defensive line with a healthy mix of carries to the interior line and off the edge. “We knew that they had some bigger players which didn’t really translate well to their speed. Our Offensive Coordinator Jarmar Julian told me to hit the hole and try making something out of it once you turn up field,” said Cain. After forcing a Mt. Eden punt on the opening possession, Piedmont scored on an eight-play series that capped off with a 14-yard touchdown run by Jack Nelson with 4:53 left in the first quarter. Mt. Eden responded with a 58-yard drive to tie the game at 7-7 with 1:17 seconds. Its drive included eight straight carries by its quarterback. But after that, Piedmont’s defense clamped down, limiting the Monarchs to 2-for-9 on third downs and 0-for-2 on fourth downs. Piedmont’s next score came quickly after Ben Marshburn returned the kickoff to the 40-yard line. Cain ran 16 yards off the edge, then an 18-yard carry up the gut to the six-yard line. He finished the drive with a six-yard TD for a 14-7 lead with 18 seconds left in the first quarter. PHS’ next touchdown took just two plays early in the second quarter. Starting at their own 49-yard line, Cain broke a 15-yard run off the right-edge, then followed up with a 36-yard touchdown run, breaking two tackles on his way to the end zone. Piedmont made it 28-7 after converting a 3rd-and-18 with a draw carry to Cain for 25 yards. He hurdled a low tackle attempt and spun off another defender – just part of the Cain power game. He later scored on a five-yard carry with 6:06 left in the half. Nelson got another score for the Highlanders in the third quarter on a 10-yard carry, while Cain scored his fourth touchdown on an 11-yard run in the fourth quarter. Final stats include: Cain’s 25 carries for 229 yards to average 9.16 yards per carry and four touchdowns, to go along with three tackles on defense. Nelson had five carries for 39 yards and two touchdowns. Receiver Ben Marshburn had four receptions for 47 yards and one carry for 19 yards. Defensively, linebacker Jet Moxley had seven total tackles, one for a loss of yards. LB Joe Hempeck also had seven tackles; DL Andy Melian had five total tackles and three tackles for loss; DL Mason Kimball had three tackles and one sack; Nelson had four tackles, one sack, and two tackles for loss. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-0) heads to Berkeley on Friday, April 2 for a 7:00 p.m. game. Jet Moxley (36) had seven total tackles including one for a loss.

articles.text: Tehan Canyon and its seasonal waterfall may be among the lesser known hikes in the East Bay. Nestled in Pleasanton Ridge Regional Park, the portion of land for the trail was purchased within the last three years by East Bay Regional Park District and appears to be early in the development process. Given that the area was opened to the public with little notification, there was no one else on my hike. With the sound of various birds, critters rustling in the shrubbery, and moths being awoken by my arrival, the entire trail had little evidence of being touched by man. To begin your hike, park on Moller Ranch Drive and take the Moller Ranch Trail until you reach an unlocked gate, which will take you off the paved surface and towards the canyon. Moller Ranch Trail takes you along a ridgeline that gives a clear view of Mt. Diablo of Concord to the rolling hills of Del Valle Regional Park and onto Tehan Canyon Road, which is a dirt road that borders some private ranches. Continue down the dirt road for a half mile until you reach a moss covered tree that has a large tank surrounded by a gate on the left. Follow the well-worn path past the tree and venture alongStaff photos This gate marks the start of the trail on the Moller Ranch Trail. Follow the path past this tree to enter Tehan Canyon. A tank surrounded by a gate sits directly to the left. Clovers cover the hillside and floor of the Tehan Canyon Trail. side the creek to enter the canyon. Once entering the canyon, the amount of lush green vegetation surrounding you is breathtaking. Everywhere you look are clovers, ferns, and moss covering every tree and rock in sight. In addition to the abundance of plants, birds of many types were flying and cawing overhead including hawks, pigeons, jays, Ferns shoot out from the hillside in Tehan Canyon. crows, and others I could not identify. While hiking along the creek I was lucky enough to spot a California native red-bellied newt. The marquee attraction of this trail is Tehan Falls, a waterfall that feeds down into the canyon’s creek. However, in spite of recent rains, the waterfall was not active last weekend. Though the 1.5 mile walk toward the falls was easy and at a beginner’s level, reaching the location of the would-be waterfall requires a technical climb up boulders and around trees along the ridge of the creek, making it an advanced course. Despite the absence of water at the waterfall, the profusion of ferns shooting out of the hillside and moss covered boulders was enough to claim a successful day. If you plan to visit the site of the waterfall, be sure to take proper hiking boots and poles for support. Previously published in the Piedmont Post on January 31, 2018. From a hillside in Pleasanton Ridge Regional Park, you can see Mt. Diablo all the way to Del Valle Regional Park in Livermore. A newt spotted near Tehan Canyon Creek.

articles.text: The social impact of COVID-19 on the world of sports continues to take its toll. The California Interscholastic Federation announced recently that they will be adding two new activities to its sports calendar: Birding—Bird Watching, and eSports—online gaming. Both will be added to the CIF’s Season 2 of sports starting on April 17 in order to allow more activities capable of adequate social distancing. “We’ve built a reputation for making strange decisions,” said a CIF executive who was not permitted to speak publicly. “The impact of COVID-19 on California’s prep sports seems ever-lasting and this topic has been on our desk for a while now. We feel that adding Bird Watching provides a competitive route for more students to enjoy the outdoors. Meanwhile, eSports and online gaming leagues are a well-documented growing multi-billion dollar industry. We feel these two activities will enable a demographic of non-athletic students in the larger world of sports.” In a unique breakthrough for CIF-governed prep sports in the state, students signing up for Birding or eSports will be able to compete on other school sports teams at the same time. The initial season of bird watching (birding) will get started on May 8 in conjunction with World Migratory Bird Day and run through the summer until December 31. “It’s a long season said Jason Parrot, but it follows the American Birding Association rules toward accomplishing a “Big Year.” For those not in the know, a Big Year is a challenge amongst birders to identify as many birds as possible by sight or sound within a calendar year. Members of the Class of 2021 will still be eligible to log their Big Year. Per ABA rules, the CIF will start its first full Bird Watching season on January 1, 2022 at 12:00 a.m., going for a full year until 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 31, 2022. “We realize the typical jock may not be into Bird Watching, but students interested in ornithology, biology, and environmental sciences will. Members from graduating classes will still be able to log their numbers and compete as long as their Big Year started during their high school academic career,” said the CIF. Online gaming (eSports) Online gaming will have obvious demand amongst students throughout California from Day 1. With the eSports industry valued at over $150 billion, many colleges like Ohio State, University of Texas, and UC Irvine are reported to be offering degrees in competitive gaming and video game design. In fact, organizations like www.HighSchoolEsportsLeague. com gained accreditation from STEM (Science, Technology, Education, Match), an educational research credentialing firm. They ruled that eSports is a problem-solving, team building exercise and therefore capable of hosting interscholastic competition. It is worth mentioning that Piedmont High is actually among the only schools in Alameda County not signed up for the HighSchoolEsportsLeague. High school programs which compete with PHS are already battling online, including Head-Royce, Skyline, Oakland Military Institute, Miramonte, Alameda, Encinal, San Leandro, Albany, Hayward, Castro Valley, Moreau, and Redwood Christian, according to the official HSEL website. “High Schools throughout California have already formed competitive gaming teams and competing in high-level tournaments; it really was only a matter of time,” said another CIF executive. The CIF’s initial gaming season will get started on May 1 until June 4 with EA Sports’ mainline hits Madden 21 and Fifa 21, while Epic Games’ popular classic, Fortnite, is expected to have multiple divisions. A new slate of games will be planned for the Fall of 2021. None of this is to be taken seriously, even though it is one day ahead of April Fool’s Day.

articles.text: Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) is hosting a live discussion this Saturday, April 3, entitled “Trouble in Mind: an A.C.T. Audience Exchange.” Speakers will discuss Alice Childress’ new play, Trouble in Mind., the first of American Conservatory Theatre’s (A.C.T.) “Out Loud” series featuring play readings of great playwrights from generations past. Childress’ comedy would have been the first play by a Black woman on Broadway if she had “agreed to the producers’ demands to soften its message,” the playwright explained. The forum will begin at 2 p.m. Tickets to the April 3 event are free but must be reserved in advance. articles.text: Opera San Jose will begin streaming “Love and Secrets: a Domestic Trilogy” on April 15, to feature “three tales of passion and yearning, as couples old and young contend with the tumult, joys, and heartache of love.” Wolf-Ferrari’s Il segreto di Susanna, Ned Rorem’s Four Dialogues, and Tom Cipullo’s The Husbands, directed by Tara Branham, all follow the trappings of romantic life. In Il segreto, an innocuous secret threatens a young newlywed couple’s chance at happiness, in a drawing room comedy of errors. It features soprano Vanessa Becerra and baritone Efrain Solis, as well as musicians from the Opera San Jose Orchestra conducted by Joseph Marcheso. Four Dialogues is based on the poetry of Frank O’Hara and is a classic “guy meets girl” tale, marking one couple’s journey Eugene Brancoveanu and Ashley Dixon in Opera San Jose’s production of The Husbands. from love’s first sight to the pages of its bitter end. The roles are sung by soprano Marnie Breckenridge and tenor Carlos Enrique Santelli. The Husbands concludes the trilogy, starring mezzo-soprano Ashley Dixon and baritone Eugene Brancoveanu, conducted by Christopher James Ray. The haunting meditation based on William Carpenter’s prose poem Rain tells the story of departed spouses. To purchase access to the trilogy, visit: https://www.operasj. org/love-and-secrets/.
articles.title: Opera San Jose’s “Love and Secrets: a Domestic Trilogy” begins April 15

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen will curate and conduct a SoundBox program, which will be available to stream on April 15. Salonen’s “Patterns” is the latest installment of the SoundBox series – a popular digital program that San Francisco Symphony has created in response to the current health crisis and subsequent venue closures. The programs offer a “backstage pass” to music curated, conducted, and produced by Symphony members. The maestro will lead members of the orchestra and pianist Elizabeth Dorman in an exploration of minimalist musical structure. Included in the program is Steve Reich’s Clapping Music, Arvo Part’s Spiegel, I’m Speigel, and Terry Riley’s In C. “Patterns” will feature streaming performances of Salonen’s Saltat sobrius, which is built on a piece by the pioneering 12th century French polyphonic composer Perotin. SF Symphony conductor Esa Pekka Salonen. “Patterns build on one another, in a magical and complex dance of design,” Salonen explained. “SounBox Patterns looks to the distant past and cornerstones of musical minimalism to reveal the structure within.” To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphonyplus. org/products/patterns-esa-pekka-salonen.
articles.title: SF Symphony’s Soundbox with Esa-Pekka Salonen on April 15

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony announced on March 14 that its recording of “From the Diary of Anne and Meditations on Rilke” won a 2021 Grammy award in the category of Best Classical Compendium. The album is a recording of Michael Tilson Thomas’ own compositions, featuring Isabel Leonard, Sasha Cooke, and Ryan McKinny as soloists. It was recorded live at Davies Symphony Hall in November 2018 and January 2020 and represents the first San Francisco Symphony media release of MTT’s original compositions. The concept for the album is based on the historic diary kept by Anne Frank during the height of the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. “From the Diary of Anne Frank” was commissioned by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and originally written for Audrey Hepburn, who was a UNICEF ambassador. It received its premiere with MTT and the New World Symphony in 1990. San Francisco Symphony first performed “From the Diary of Anne Frank” in November 2018, in concerts commemorating the 70th anniversary of UNICEF’s Declaration of Human Rights, with Isabel Leonard as narrator. This marks the 16th Grammy award for the San Francisco Symphony. Since his tenure, Michael Tilson Thomas has received numerous awards and recording honors; his first recording with the symphony, Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet, won a 1997 Grammy. San Francisco Media is the Symphony’s in-house media production company and label, launched in 2001. Since its inception, the label has earned nine Grammy awards. All San Francisco Symphony Media recordings and videos are available online at https:// www.warnerclassics.com/artist/ Michael Tilson Thomas san-francisco-symphony/releases. “From the Diary of Anne Frank and Meditations on Rilke” is available on various platforms, including iTunes and Amazon.
articles.title: SF Symphony album wins Grammy for MTT compositions
