articles.text: Richard Sharp and Shailene Woodley in Adrift. Movie review by Chris Honoré Before you see Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story or the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is two stories. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin). Both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), having just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color, easy-does-it people. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them out and about while embracing an existence far off the grid. Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45- footer, from Tahiti to San Diego. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class plane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film, but also something I will avoid mentioning in this review. This is a compellingly entertaining film, especially well-acted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated: PG-13.
articles.title: Adrift an amazing, can’t miss film

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré The Zookeeper’s Wife, based on the 2007 best-selling work of nonfiction by Diane Ackerman, opens with an idyllic series of images. Antonina Zabinski (Jessica Chastain) is lounging on a sun-splashed bed with two sleeping lion cubs that she holds and nuzzles. We soon see her opening the gates to a zoo, which she and her husband own. Jan (Johan Heldenbergh) welcomes families to enter and enjoy what is the equivalent of a peaceful, self-contained ark, an island of enchantment. Later, she rides her bicycle through the zoo, followed by a young camel, while she happily checks on the animals. The year is 1939. The city is Warsaw. But abruptly, Antonina’s life is upended, first with an air raid when explosions rock the zoo, killing many animals and telegraphing what is coming next: the German army has rolled into Poland and will occupy not only Warsaw but the zoo as well. The animals must go, she and Jan are told by Herman Goering’s zoologist, Lutz Heck (Daniel Bruhl), a man who, as it turns out, is a Nazi first and proves to be a danger to Antonina. Soon the couple learns that all of Warsaw is occupied and the city’s Jews had been rounded up and confined to what became known as the Warsaw Ghetto. Though the Zabinskis are gentiles and allowed to live within the zoo’s gates, many of their close friends are Jews. The Zookeeper’s Wife is told from the point of view of Antonina, and it is through her eyes that we see her struggle to comprehend the unnecessary cruelty of the occupiers. There is one scene where soldiers shoot an elephant as well as the young camel, taking great pleasure in the moment. Of course, Jan is also filled with rage at what the soldiers have done to the zoo where they had housed for years their lovingly cared-for animals. But in his travels he is exposed to the remorselessness of the Germans, realizing that what he is witnessing extends far beyond the zoo. He knows evil when he confronts it. There is a scene where he is watching small, trusting children and their terrified parents herded onto railroad cars, headed for concentration camps. It’s heart-rending. And it is at that moment that the Zabinskis make a life-changing decision. Their existential choice was to smuggle Jews from the ghetto to the zoo. The journey, while short, under the guise of collecting kitchen garbage for the zoo’s pigs, is harrowing and fraught with danger. Many of the Jews who they rescue are hidden in the basement of their home. Others are quickly trucked out of Poland. What Jan and Antonina did transcends the word “courageous.” They risked their lives while hiding Jews in what was once a sanctuary for animals and is now used as a completely different kind of haven. It’s actually a wonderful metaphor, and it’s all accomplished while surrounded by German soldiers. In the film this choice occurs quietly, absent any spoken deliberations or hesitation, with a kind of fearful fearlessness. I can only assume that for them it was a crossroads of sorts; history has shown that others did not do what the Zabinskis chose to do. They were, in most respects, ordinary people who did something extraordinary. In 1965 Israel honored them for their courage as “Righteous Ones.” They were two among those few across Europe who stepped forward while so much of the world remained silent. One last point: The Zookeeper’s Wife is, of course, a story about the holocaust. But the horror that this time represented is touched upon indirectly. While there are scenes from the Warsaw Ghetto that are breathtakingly tragic and ultimately inexplicable, it was not the intent of director Niki Caro to make a film that illustrated the graphic malevolence brought to bear by the Nazis. Films such as Night and Fog, Shoah, and Schindler’s List do this superbly. What Caro does is tell a very personal story about small acts of courage that in the aggregate were beyond heroic. It is to her credit that she found the book and enlisted Jessica Chastain, who gives a remarkable performance, to help her tell the story. The Zookeeper’s Wife. Directed by Niki Caro. Starring Jessica Chastain, Johan Heldenbergh and Daniel Bruhl. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from The Zookeeper’s Wife.
articles.title: The Zookeeper’s Wife a powerful tale of courage during Nazi occupation of Poland

Starring Jessica Chastain, Johan Heldenbergh and Daniel Bruhl. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG-13. Richard Sharp and Shailene Woodley in Adrift. Movie review by Chris Honoré Before you see Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story or the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is two stories. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin). Both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), having just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color, easy-does-it people. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them out and about while embracing an existence far off the grid. Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45- footer, from Tahiti to San Diego. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class plane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film, but also something I will avoid mentioning in this review. This is a compellingly entertaining film, especially well-acted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated: PG-13. A scene from The Zookeeper’s Wife.

articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Moana. Review by Chris Honoré Moana is a family friendly animated feature by Disney. It is a Polynesian story about a strongwilled, adventurous girl named Moana (Auli’i Cravalho), 16, the daughter of her tribe’s chief, Tui (Temuera Morrison). Set on the pacific island of Motunui, an emerald paradise, the story begins with Moana, looking toward the horizon, ever curious, wondering what’s beyond, understanding that for years her tribe has been afraid to venture past the reef that surrounds the island. But a strange cloud now hangs over the island. The fish are not as plentiful and the coconuts dry and tasteless. Moana’s grandmother, Tala (Rachel House), tells her that the ocean has chosen her to return the island’s goddess, Te Fifi, an idol stolen by the demigod, Maui (Dwayne Johnson), a millennia ago. Late at night, in the pale moonlight, Moana takes a beached canoe, a camakan, and sets out beyond the reef in search of the hulking, overly confident demigod Maui. Her mission is to break the spell cast over her people. Moana is clearly Disney’s attempt to feature a young woman who does not need to be rescued by a prince, an almost iconic story line. Instead, the studio approaches the character of Moana with a light hand, the inherent feminism subtle but compelling. Moana is independent, courageous and never burdened with an oppressive patriarchy. It is her destiny to become the eventual chief of her tribe. There is also no love story, no rugged islander waiting to marry her. Moana is simply a story of an empowered teenage girl on a quest. The directors of the film, John Musker and Ron Clemens (The Little Mermaid, Aladdin) consulted with South Pacific locals, regarding their history and folklore. They also cast a wide net in search of the Hawaiian teen Auli’i Cravalho as the voice of Moana. As well, Dwayne Johnson, adding star power, has Samoan heritage. Voicing Moana’s father, chief Tui, is New Zealander Temuera Morrison of Maori background. Know as well that Moana is sprinkled with 10 songs, sung by Moana and Maui (as it turns out, Johnson has a solid voice) and written by Lin-Manuel Miranda of Hamilton fame. Plus, the animation is rich in tropical colors. Moana. Animation by Disney. Directed by John Musker and Ron Clemens. Voices of Auli’i Cravalho, Dwayne Johnson and Rachel House. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Swedish soprano Jenny Lind Life in the American Wild West of the mid-1800s was difficult. Americans were open to almost anything. But what they craved more than anything else was culture. They were starved for entertainment. The great showman PT Barnum saw this as a great opportunity, and he took advantage of the situation. He had heard of the famous Swedish soprano Jenny Lind, so he contacted her and proposed a concert tour in America. He added – none too subtly – that she would reap a fortune. A contract was signed and Barnum got to work doing what he did best. Jenny Lind’s name became instantly famous throughout the entire country. The year was 1852. She toured throughout the U.S., especially in the Wild West. Americans loved her. There is even a California town named Jenny Lind in the Gold Rush country, one of the many places where she performed concerts. In one year alone, she earned $350,000. That was a tremendous amount in those days. But Barnum, being Barnum, netted $500,000. That was OK because Barnum delivered the publicity and Lind delivered the entertainment. Everybody was happy. Remembering violinist Henri Vieuxtemps But Jenny Lind was not the first great musician to concertize in the Wild West. The first great artist of any note was the Belgian violinist Henri Vieuxtemps. Concerts were a lot different in those days. Almost all of them were variety shows or vaudeville shows with one or two instrumentalists and one or two singers. Some shows even had a poet added to the showbill. Appearing as the co-star with Vieuxtemps was the equally famous European pianist Sigmund Thalberg. As you can imagine, American audiences were not very sophisticated in their knowledge of music. So, the musical stars played some classical music, but they also performed popular music which Belgian violinist Henri Vieuxtemps American pianist Louis Moreau Gottschalk Norwegian violinist Ole Bull catered to the common man. One of Vieuxtemps’ famous pieces was his version of the Arkansas Traveler. Another was his version of Yankee Doodle Dandy. This was standard fare on the concert stage in the mid- 1800s, and the American public loved it all. Most of the well-publicized musicians came from Europe, but America did have one really great star. Louisiana-born Louis Moreau Gottschalk, a pianist. Barnum offered to promote concerts for Gottschalk, but the musician would have nothing to do with the razzle-dazzle style of promotion for which Barnum was noted. Gottschalk chose to do his own promotion, and he was a fabulous success everywhere he went. Unfortunately, his career was ruined by a trumped-up sex scandal. He was concertizing in San Francisco and took the ferry across the Bay to Oakland. He and a friend went to see some girls in Oakland, and that innocent event was blown into a scandal. Gottschalk barely evaded the vigilantes and fled to South America. His death was truly dramatic. Knowing that he was dying, he went to the piano one last time and played one of his famous compositions, titled Morte. He died mid-performance. The music of Ole Bull I have saved one of the most colorful characters for the end of this article. If Arnold

articles.text: The popular annual Piedmont Art Walk, now in its 2nd year, is benefitting from its success last year. To date, more than 40 local artists have registered to display their art outside on Sunday, May 2 between 12:00-5:00 p.m. Paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, and photography will be displayed and shown by local artists in front of their homes The community is invited to enjoy this outdoor art event and fundraiser hosted by local Piedmont artists and the Piedmont Arts Fund. Purchases support artists in town, and 20 percent of proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Arts Fund to support art in the schools. This fundraising event brings together live art, artists, and community members while following Alameda County’s COVID-19 guidelines to keep everyone safe. The event is spread out over Piedmont to avoid crowds and ensure social distancing. When the COVID quarantine took effect in last March, the Piedmont Arts Fund (formerly PAINTS and CHIME) had to cancel their spring fundraisers. The diminished school budget outlook for next school year makes this year’s fundraising critical for maintaining robust art programs in Piedmont schools. The Art Walk features a Who’s Who of Piedmont artists (see list on the website), and residents and students may not realize how many accomplished artists live in Piedmont. Plan now to take a walk on Sunday afternoon, May 2 to visit the artists during the second Annual Piedmont Art Walk. Who knows? You may find a new art piece that brightens your day and supports art in the schools. For more information and to see a gallery of artists, visit https://piedmontartsfund.org/ piedmont-art-walk-2021
articles.title: List of artists grows for Piedmont Art Walk on May 2

articles.text: Charismatic Gerard Bertrand is a leading figure in the resurgence of the wines of Southern France. The Languedoc-Roussillon area in southwest France is the largest wine producing region in the world. They make more wine there than the entire United States. Unfortunately, for many years, most of it wasn’t very good. Much of it was sold in bulk and farmers were paid by the ton. The emphasis was on quantity rather than quality. After a visit to the region this summer and the chance to taste many of the region’s wines I am happy to report that the wine scene in the Languedoc is now very different. Many producers are now bottling their own wines with their name on the label and are striving mightily to improve quality. You can see the pride on their faces as they pour their wine and watch the surprise on the face of the taster who is not expecting much from a Languedoc wine. The region now seems to rival the Rhone valley in producing great wines from Syrah, Grenache, Carignan and Mourvedre. Thankfully prices have not caught up with the surge in quality and the wines remain great values in a world filled with overpriced wines. In this column and next month’s column I will be exploring and sharing some of these interesting wines with the readers. Today I want to introduce one producer who stands head and shoulders above others in terms of quality and innovation. Gerard Bertrand was born into a wine-making family with his father owning a property in the appellation of Corbierres. His early passion was rugby and he spent some time playing professionally but eventually the call of the vines overcame sports and he began developing several wine properties in the area of Narbonne and also in Roussillon. One by one he kept expanding his holdings and adding other wineries to his portfolio. Eventually he had the opportunity to purchase Chateau L’Hospitalet, a wine estate south of Narbonne in the heart of the La Clape Massif conservation area overlooking the Mediterranean Sea. There are 1,000 hectares of pine trees and vines and the estate includes a charming hotel, art gallery and exquisite gourmet restaurant. The estate also hosts a wildly popular jazz festival each summer that brings hordes of people to the property. Bertrand’s latest project is to create a “first growth” quaity wine – the Lafite of the Languedoc. He found a plot of land while hiking the La Liviniere area of Minervois, which seemed a perfect place to build a small modern, ultra high quality winery with no expense spared – thus Clos d’Ora was born. This fall they are celebrating their fourth vintage. Like all of Gerard’s properties, the farming is done by the principles of Biodynamics – a philosophy of farming (and of life) that is growing rapidly in popularity in many wine regions around the world. pages.text: Wednesday, March 31, 2021 23 The Wine Corner Discovering Languedoc – the wines of Gerard Bertrand Charismatic Gerard Bertrand is a leading figure in the resurgence of the wines of Southern France. By Pierre DuMont The Languedoc-Roussillon area in southwest France is the largest wine producing region in the world. They make more wine there than the entire United States. Unfortunately, for many years, most of it wasn’t very good. Much of it was sold in bulk and farmers were paid by the ton. The emphasis was on quantity rather than quality. After a visit to the region this summer and the chance to taste many of the region’s wines I am happy to report that the wine scene in the Languedoc is now very different. Many producers are now bottling their own wines with their name on the label and are striving mightily to improve quality. You can see the pride on their faces as they pour their wine and watch the surprise on the face of the taster who is not expecting much from a Languedoc wine. The region now seems to rival the Rhone valley in producing great wines from Syrah, Grenache, Carignan and Mourvedre. Thankfully prices have not caught up with the surge in quality and the wines remain great values in a world filled with overpriced wines. In this column and next month’s column I will be exploring and sharing some of these interesting wines with the readers. Today I want to introduce one producer who stands head and shoulders above others in terms of quality and innovation. Gerard Bertrand was born into a wine-making family with his father owning a property in the appellation of Corbierres. His early passion was rugby and he spent some time playing professionally but eventually the call of the vines overcame sports and he began developing several wine properties in the area of Narbonne and also in Roussillon. One by one he kept expanding his holdings and adding other wineries to his portfolio. Eventually he had the opportunity to purchase Chateau L’Hospitalet, a wine estate south of Narbonne in the heart of the La Clape Massif conservation area overlooking the Mediterranean Sea. There are 1,000 hectares of pine trees and vines and the estate includes a charming hotel, art gallery and exquisite gourmet restaurant. The estate also hosts a wildly popular jazz festival each summer that brings hordes of people to the property. Bertrand’s latest project is to create a “first growth” quaity wine – the Lafite of the Languedoc. He found a plot of land while hiking the La Liviniere area of Minervois, which seemed a perfect place to build a small modern, ultra high quality winery with no expense spared – thus Clos d’Ora was born. This fall they are celebrating their fourth vintage. Like all of Gerard’s properties, the farming is done by the principles of Biodynamics – a philosophy of farming (and of life) that is growing rapidly in popularity in many wine regions around the world. The philosophy eschews The vines of Minervois from the Mount D’Ora winery. Working the vines of Mount D’Ora with mule and plow – Biodynamics at work. chemicals and pesticides and uses all natural methods to nurture the vines. At Clos d’Ora that includes using a mule instead of a tractor to till the soil. Planting and harvesting are done according to the movements of the stars and tides. Alongside the powerful presence of the biodynamic philosophy, the other aspect of Bertrand’s winemaking style that was powerfully evident is a meticulous, perfectionist’s attention to detail – especially cleanliness. I have visited a lot of wineries and bottling facilities in my time, but this was the first time everyone had to don white disposable lab coats to tour the plant. The size of the main facility is enormous and he makes a staggering number of wines. The wines described below are my favorites from his vast portfolio and are available online at Wine.com. from a blend of Syrah and Carignan, this wine is drinking perfectly now but also has the tannin and structure to last at least a decade. It reminds me of a baby Hermitage. • 2013 Chateau de Villemajou Grand Vin Corbieres Boutenac, $40 This is the estate Gerard Bertrand’s father bought in 1970 and the place where Gerard got his start in making wine. The wine is a mix of Carignan, Grenache, Syrah and Mourvedre. It has an intense, perfumed nose of violets and anise and tons of plum and cassis flavors in the mouth. It is a largescale wine but balanced, and will be best after a few years in the cellar. • 2015 Gris Blanc, $14 At first glance you could mis take this for a white wine. It is the palest rose I have ever seen. Made from the Grenache Gris grape, it has an enchanting nose of strawberries and wildflowers with soft peach fruit on the palate. It is crisp, dry and tremendously refreshing. The perfect summer quaffer. • 2014 Clos D’Ora, $220 There is no doubt about this being the first growth of the Languedoc. It is lovingly handcrafted from Grenache, Syrah, Mourvedre and Carignan grapes that are meticulously farmed and sorted so only the finest grapes • 2015 Cigalus Blanc, $45 This powerful white wine is made from an unusual mix of Chardonnay, Viognier and Sauvignon Blanc. The Vigonier gives the lovely floral nose, the Chardonnay the body, and the Sauvignon the freshness and acidity. They come together in the mouth to form a harmonious wine with great power and length. Very creative effort. • 2013 Grand Terroir Tautavel, $20 This region in Roussillon near the Spanish border is an up and coming one and Bertrand has a contract for most of the area’s grapes. The wine is medium bodied with a wild earthy nose the French call “Garrigue”, which basically means scrub brush. It has plum and cassis notes on the palate with a clean balanced finish. Very easy to drink and a great partner to grilled chicken. • 2013 Terroir Minervois, $21 (BEST VALUE) This wine stole my heart and made a lasting impact. It is bigger and richer than the Tautavel and is jam packed with blackberry and blueberry fruit with layers of spices and earth mixed in. Made Gerard Bertrand’s Minervois is an outstanding wine as well as a great value. go into the bottle. It is incredibly powerful and yet refined at the same time, with layers upon layers of flavors and a long, lingering finish. Absolutely superb. Previously published in the Piedmont Post on September 7, 2016

articles.text: Since 1996, Guy Orban, owner of Kiss That Frog, a wholesale manufacturer and distributor that stocks the shelves of stellar boutiques, has welcomed guests at the door of his biannual warehouse sale in June and November. Le Marché Pop-Up, previously called Le Marché Bay Area, is a curated treasure trove of wellpriced, ethically made products for the modern home with timeless French touches. Last year due to COVID-19, for the first time in 25 years, Guy and his team were unable to open the doors to guests. They quickly took their inventory online. “We knew we had to make our annual event happen. People look forward to our events every year. It had been such a miserable year that we wanted to bring a little ray of sunshine,” said Orban. “Our June sale was incredibly fun; we saw so many of our regular shoppers as well as newcomers. We were able to greet guests from all over the place to our sale. That’s why we chose to drop the “Bay Area” from our name and go with “Pop-Up”. The first pop-up sale will take place April 23-25, with a preview sale starting April 17, using its new website, lemarchepopup.com.
articles.title: Le Marché must go on

articles.text: When people hear the term “Great Pacific Garbage Patch,” the image that comes to mind is an endless island of plastic bottles, bags, and garbage. Actually, the Patch is primarily made up of small pieces of plastic, known as microplastics. Unfortunately, the prefix “micro” doesn’t begin to cover the macro effect these materials can have on the environment and our bodies. They are tiny, they are ubiquitous, and they are mysterious. Technically, microplastics qualify as any piece of plastic that is less than 5 mm in length. Despite their inauspicious name, microplastics are the most common source of pollution in bodies of water. Since mass production began in the 1950’s, over 8 billion tons of plastic have been created. About 8 million tons a year end up in oceans. Plastics don’t break down easily like organics do. Microplastics generally start out as larger plastics which gradually break down over time into smaller and smaller pieces. These microplastics stay in the environment unless they are consumed by an organism. Microplastics are in everything. Microplastics can be found in every living organism on the planet and in drinking water sources. Humans ingest them every day in food and water. The average person eats over 40 pounds of plastic over their lifetime, the vast majority of that being microplastics. This is largely due to how common plastics have become. The average American throws away almost a pound of plastic per day. Plastics are used to wrap and package foods, make clothing, and as a lightweight and sturdy shipping material. Plastics have become a cornerstone of worldwide trade, with the top 50 plastics companies conducting over $1 trillion in sales each year. Microplastics accumulate in larger organisms due to the nature of the food chain. Thus, consumers (people) tend to eat a lot more plastic than other organisms. The mysterious part of all this is nobody can say for certain what the health effects are of all this plastic. Plastic molecules are “endocrine disruptors,” meaning that they can mimic and disrupt human hormones. The issue of plastics is not black and white. They are beneficial in some respects and are often a cheap alternative to more expensive options. At the same time, they also are a major pollutant in water. It is unclear what the long-term effects of plastic consumption will be on the environment and on our bodies. Fixing this problem is difficult. Microplastics are an established part of our ecosystem, and they will be here for hundreds of years. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Norma Cadenasso, a longtime member of the Piedmont Seniors group, passed away peacefully on February 22, 2021 after 95 years of a life well spent. Born on November 16, 1925, Norma was the daughter of Peter and Esther Crestetto and younger sister to Ernestine Crestetto McCart. Norma graduated from Piedmont High School, UC Berkeley and the UCSF School of Nursing. As a Registered Nurse, she worked at the Alameda and Oakland Unified School Districts for many years. Her chosen career suited her well given her kind nature, positive attitude, and concern for the well-being of others. She met her loving husband Gene at a church function in Oakland and they spent over 49 wonderful years together, including traveling the world. They particularly enjoyed touring Italy and exploring their family’s origins. Another favorite vacation spot was spending summers at Lake Tahoe, where relatives and friends gathered for endless hours on the beach in conversation, laughter, and marveling at nature’s beauty. Norma also had a number of interests. She was a long-time member of the Bellevue Club in Oakland where she made numerous lasting friendships, played bridge, and shared many joyful occasions with her mother and sister Ernestine. As a member of the Oakland Lawn Bowling Club, she became a skilled player who participated in various tournaments involving other clubs. She Longtime Piedmont resident Norma Cadenasso died on February 22 at age 95. primarily enjoyed it for the camaraderie and opportunity to meet others. She was a member of the Alpha Delta Pi sorority. As a lover of animals, upon retirement she volunteered at the local SPCA where she spent many enjoyable hours exercising the dogs. She also had a strong bond with her pet cat, Peanut, who was often purring comfortably on her lap while she read one of her favorite mystery novels. Even when deer would visit the backyard of her home and make a snack of her roses, she would always greet them with an affectionate gaze. The family wishes to acknowledge with great appreciation the exceptional care Norma received from the Skilled Nursing Staff at St Paul’s Towers in Oakland during her final three years. She is predeceased by her beloved husband, Gene, who died in 2006. Norma is survived by her daughter Teresa and sonin-law Scott Garland, grandchildren Bryan and Lauren Garland, a son Eugene and daughter-in-law Dorothy Cadenasso, and son John Cadenasso. Norma will be laid to rest at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland. There will be a celebration of her life at a later date. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations in her honor be made to East Bay SPCA or Catholic Charities of the East Bay. retirement plan or in other investment accounts. articles.text: If you own a small business, you typically don’t get a lot of recognition, so you may be pleased to learn that March 29 is National Mom and Pop Business Owners Day. You might not necessarily think of your business as a “Mom and Pop” operation, but it certainly contributes to the well-being of your family now, and possibly to that of future generations, too – if you make the right moves. Depending on the nature of your business, you may have spent the past several months more concerned about today than tomorrow, given the serious economic repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still placing stress on a great many business owners across the country. If your business has been adversely affected by the pandemic, you might be eligible for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. As you may know, recent legislation provided $285 billion more for this program. To learn more, and to start the application process, visit the Small Business Administration website at www.sba.gov. You have until March 31 to apply for a PPP loan. Other relief also may be available. But regardless of whether you apply for one of these loans, you can take other steps to help maximize the benefits you get from your business – and perhaps even extend its longevity. Here are a few suggestions: • Establish a retirement plan. If you don’t already have a retirement plan, it’s never too late to set one up. As a business owner, you have several options, including an “owner-only” 401(k), a SIMPLE IRA and a SEP-IRA. All these plans are fairly easy to establish and can offer potential tax advantages, as well as providing you with a source of retirement income in the future. You may want to work with a financial professional to pick the right plan for your needs. • Coordinate your business assets with your investment portfolio. Like most business owners, you may have a great deal of your personal wealth tied up in your business. And, as the past year has certainly shown, this can be risky. Consequently, you’ll need to weigh this risk factor when deciding on investing in your
articles.title: Business owners’ issues go beyond ‘mom and pop’ label

Business owners’ issues go beyond ‘mom and pop’ label If you own a small business, you typically don’t get a lot of recognition, so you may be pleased to learn that March 29 is National Mom and Pop Business Owners Day. You might not necessarily think of your business as a “Mom and Pop” operation, but it certainly contributes to the well-being of your family now, and possibly to that of future generations, too – if you make the right moves. Depending on the nature of your business, you may have spent the past several months more concerned about today than tomorrow, given the serious economic repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still placing stress on a great many business owners across the country. If your business has been adversely affected by the pandemic, you might be eligible for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. As you may know, recent legislation provided $285 billion more for this program. To learn more, and to start the application process, visit the Small Business Administration website at www.sba.gov. You have until March 31 to apply for a PPP loan. Other relief also may be available. But regardless of whether you apply for one of these loans, you can take other steps to help maximize the benefits you get from your business – and perhaps even extend its longevity. Here are a few suggestions: • Establish a retirement plan. If you don’t already have a retirement plan, it’s never too late to set one up. As a business owner, you have several options, including an “owner-only” 401(k), a SIMPLE IRA and a SEP-IRA. All these plans are fairly easy to establish and can offer potential tax advantages, as well as providing you with a source of retirement income in the future. You may want to work with a financial professional to pick the right plan for your needs. • Coordinate your business assets with your investment portfolio. Like most business owners, you may have a great deal of your personal wealth tied up in your business. And, as the past year has certainly shown, this can be risky. Consequently, you’ll need to weigh this risk factor when deciding on investing in your retirement plan or in other investment accounts. This doesn’t mean you should try to avoid all risk only by pursuing the most conservative vehicles – which would be counterproductive to achieving enough growth to meet your retirement income goals – but you will need to pay close attention to your investment mix to ensure it provides you with an appropriate balance to what you’ve invested in your business. • Develop a transition strategy. How will you make the transition from business owner to the next phase of your life? Will you sell the business outright? Will you gradually transfer it to a family member? If so, what mechanism will you use? It’ a good idea to have these types of plans in place well before you need to enact them, so you may want to consult with your financial, legal and tax advisors soon. A “Mom and Pop” business may sound quaint and carefree – but, as you know, running a business of any size can be an all-consuming endeavor and always involves significant financial concerns. articles.text: COVID vaccination happy hour at the Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living. March 11, 2021 marked the one-year anniversary of the World Health Organization’s declaration of COVID-19 as a global pandemic. Although the seasons have changed four times since then, I feel as though we have experienced a year-long winter. Winter is often viewed as a time of waiting and the pandemic has forced us into a time of stillness and a slower pace. With vaccinations, the sharp decline in COVID-19 cases has resulted in our lives slowly returning to normal. It seems that we are experiencing a fresh new beginning. In this extralong transition from winter into spring, there are “green shoots” representing new and positive changes everywhere - if you look for them. These changes are noticeable here at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community. Our residents, now fully vaccinated, are free to walk around mask-free within our community. They are able to engage with one another with ease and I can once again see the smiles on their faces. Following current CDC guidelines, our exercise teachers, art instructor and choir director have all returned, vaccinated and wearing masks. We had our first live music performance for residents in over a year and masked-up families and friends are visiting again. It feels great! The biggest and most welcomed change is in our beautiful restaurant, The Terrace Room. No longer restricted to having only two persons per table behind a plastic barrier, residents are happy to sit together in small groups and socialize. One resident said that “along with enjoying the great food here, being able to share a meal with others completes the perfect dining experience.” “The timing for the change couldn’t be better,” said Executive Chef Michael Cook. “Our favorite produce company’s sales rep always says that asparagus is the harbinger of spring, and I couldn’t agree more. It’s always great to incorporate locally grown fruits and vegetables into the menu, so I look forward to spring.” Choosing the right produce is an important part of healthy eating for older adults, and Chef Michael knows what to look for. Of the abundance of newly grown spring greens, he said, “You can’t eat enough of them. They provide you with a seriously useful amount of vitamin C to support your immune system and vitamin K to build bone strength. And don’t forget about fresh fruit, especially strawberries,” Michael added while holding up a plump, dark red berry. “These little guys are known to protect your heart, lower your blood pressure and are filled with antioxidants.” For many, food is a source of joy – and one that can help us live life at its fullest. Judy, a resident, said, “Tuesday is my favorite day in The Terrace Room. It means a new lunch menu for the week and a special salad creation. Last week we were treated to a Chef Michael original: poached salmon on a bed of quinoa with cucumbers and asparagus with a Meyer lemon aioli dressing. It was outstanding. I can’t wait to see what he does next.” As we slowly emerge from this year-long winter, I know we will continue to see positive changes. No matter how long the winter, we can celebrate the coming of spring knowing that family, friendship and good food are sure to follow. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. For more information call 510- 903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com. articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a new MacBook Air, that is still in the box. I am trying to decide if I should transfer all of my files with Time Machine or just start fresh? I have years of stuff that I don’t use, and I started to have some trouble opening some of my files. Also, some of my applications (on my old laptop) have been shutting down unexpectedly. All I really do these days is use my email, write a few Word files, and take photos. My email is through Gmail. The salesperson at Best Buy suggested that I use Dropbox or iCloud to store and transfer my files. Can you explain how that would be different than transferring everything with Time Machine? -Lissa M., Oakland Dear Lissa: This is a great question, and it’s your second sentence that leads me to my answer. Since you are having some application crashes and also have a ton of old files you don’t need, I would recommend setting this up as a new machine. That being said, it would also be possible and even desirable to use Dropbox or iCloud to transfer the files you do want. If you only have a few files that you want to keep (less than a gigabyte or so), I would recommend moving them to a folder in Dropbox before you set up your new Mac. Dropbox is a cloud service. You can think of it as a virtual hard drive. You must have an account, and most likely if you’re going to use it to sync files you already have on your computer, you’re going to want one of their paid accounts. You download the application, sign into your account, and then you would have a folder in finder called, “Dropbox”. Anything that you move into Dropbox; folders, files, pictures, etc. can be synced with other machines that are signed into the same Dropbox account. This gives you the most control over what you want to move over to the new machine. You could create a folder on the desktop of your old machine, called something like “To Be Transferred” or “Keepers”. Then you would simply upload that folder to Dropbox, which is as simple as dragging to the Dropbox icon in Finder. There are plenty of tutorials online about using this application, and their website, www. dropbox.com has very good ones. The nice thing about this is that you can cherry pick things to move over. If you use iCloud to sync your desktop and documents, it will sync everything on your desktop and documents. Anything you don’t want to be stored in iCloud, you have to move out of your documents folder and off of your desktop. This system is great if you want everything to look the same on more than one machine, but not practical if you only want to move a few files over. In your situation, I think Dropbox makes more sense. As far as your photos go, if you haven’t already, I would enable iCloud Photos to sync on your laptop as well as your phone before you set up the new machine. This way, when you sign into iCloud on your new Air, and enable iCloud Photos, all of your photos will come into your photo library. If you have tens of thousands of photos, then make sure to do this well enough ahead of time that the complete library has a chance to upload to iCloud. Since you use Gmail, when you set your email up on the new machine, everything that’s on Gmail’s servers will come into your mail application, so that’s no problem. What won’t come over are any emails you are saving locally, that means folders stored under “On my Mac” in Apple Mail. If this is the case, re-create these folders under Gmail in the folders list in Mac mail, and copy any of the emails in the local folders to Gmail ones. Again, there are lots of tutorials online about how to do this. Here is what makes all of this different than using your Time Machine back up drive to transfer your data. When you use Time Machine, it copies everything on your current computer every hour onto an external drive. This includes everything you see, like documents, files, folders, pictures, your music and photo library, all of your applications, as well as things you don’t see, like preferences, drivers, and files that live in the user and system library. So, if one or more of those files are corrupt, Time Machine still copies it. If you migrate these files to a new computer, it is possible you will inherit any problems you had on your old machine. For this reason, in your case, I would recommend the Dropbox solution. Personally, I use a combination of iCloud and Dropbox. And of course, if you need help, you can contact me, and I can help with the new set-up. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com and themacmama.blogspot.com.

articles.text: themselves as a source of wisdom and morals, a valued elder, a storyteller, teacher, and conveyor of family history and lore. For grandparents who live geographically close enough to their grandchildren to see them often, the opportunity to thrive in their roles is great. They’re more likely to understand their adult children’s daily lives and can see where they might be needed to pitch in with the grandchildren. During caregiving, a grandparent builds intimate bonds with their grandchildren. These are also the moments when grandparents can find ways to achieve their self-concept of valued family elder. In 2002 Dr. Arthur Kornhaber wrote The Grandparent Guide – The Definitive Guide to Coping with the Challenges of Modern Grandparenting. He begins his book by asking the reader to think about the many roles that grandparents play for grandchildren, the family, and society. Grandparent roles serve different many functions. At times you may be a nurturer, mentor, or teacher. Other times you will serve as a buddy, hero, role model, spiritual guide, or historian. While one role or another may feel most comfortable for you, no doubt you’ll find yourself from time to time occupying a less familiar function. So, is there really one version of the ideal grandparent? Of course not. Families are unique. But parents and grandparents can align their visions of the ideal grandparent with the right intention. With common sense and mutual respect, families can come up with a shared concept of the role that grandparents will play in their own family. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com.
articles.title: Is there an ideal grandparent?

articles.text: The next monthly meeting of the East Bay Chapter of the Hearing Loss Assn. of America will be held o April 10. The guest speaker is Steven L. articles.text: Caregiving is about more than just one person fulfilling a list of tasks; it’s about human relationships and connection. When someone is looking for home care services for a loved one or themselves, they might be in need of help with bathing, dressing, assistance with using the toilet, medication reminders, meal preparation, or transportation. Professional caregivers receive hours of training so that they can specialize in everything from proper lifting techniques to dementia care at different stages of the disease. Caregiver training, assistance with activities of daily living, and meeting the needs of clients are top priorities, but that is not everything. When a call comes in for a caregiver, a process begins to find a suitable match. In addition to the physical and practical services needed, questions may be asked about personal preferences, unique history, and simple pleasures. This approach to care is to get to know each individual beyond their diagnosis so that they can be expertly paired with a caregiver with whom they can develop a bond, trust, and even true companionship. It’s these connections between clients and caregivers that take home care to the next level, where a spark happens, and two people can get fired up about their common backgrounds or shared interests. These connections lead to more laughter, more smiles, and a caregiver-client relationship that is more than daily tasks and changes in abilities for someone. Whether someone is receiving 24/7 care or just a couple of hours per week, how they connect with their caregiver can have an impact on their overall well-being. But don’t think that this is all about what the caregiver does. Many touching stories of a perfect match are about the client teaching the caregiver something new, such as knitting, playing the piano, or going fishing. These dynamics can reinforce the notion that everyone has something to share, and they are in a care partnership together. Homewatch CareGivers, located at 3820 Broadway in Oakland, is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www. CarePiedmont.com.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 31, 2021 29 Is there an ideal grandparent? By Cynthia Kane Part 4 in a series When young parents and grandparents are asked “What three words would you use to describe the ideal grandparent?” their responses are pretty similar: loving, supportive, patient. New parents want the support of the grandparents, and hope that grandparents will be affirming, respectful, and non-judgmental. Grandparents know this. Books, articles, and websites caution the newest grandparent to “Zip the lip!”, “Follow the parents’ instructions”, “Be a listener”, “Don’t give any unsolicited advice”. Becoming an ideal grandparent in the eyes of your children and grandchildren may well include all of these behaviors, and yet, grandparents have their own vision of their role in the family. According to a 2018 AARP survey, 81% of grandparents polled believe they play a strong role in their grandchildren’s lives. Grandparents do see themselves as caregivers, but they also see themselves as much more. While over a third of those surveyed describe having a role as caregiver/babysitter for young grandchildren, additionally, they see themselves as a source of wisdom and morals, a valued elder, a storyteller, teacher, and conveyor of family history and lore. For grandparents who live geographically close enough to their grandchildren to see them often, the opportunity to thrive in their roles is great. They’re more likely to understand their adult children’s daily lives and can see where they might be needed to pitch in with the grandchildren. During caregiving, a grandparent builds intimate bonds with their grandchildren. These are also the moments when grandparents can find ways to achieve their self-concept of valued family elder. In 2002 Dr. Arthur Kornhaber wrote The Grandparent Guide – The Definitive Guide to Coping with the Challenges of Modern Grandparenting. He begins his book by asking the reader to think about the many roles that grandparents play for grandchildren, the family, and society. Grandparent roles serve different many functions. At times you may be a nurturer, mentor, or teacher. Other times you will serve as a buddy, hero, role model, spiritual guide, or historian. While one role or another may feel most comfortable for you, no doubt you’ll find yourself from time to time occupying a less familiar function. So, is there really one version of the ideal grandparent? Of course not. Families are unique. But parents and grandparents can align their visions of the ideal grandparent with the right intention. With common sense and mutual respect, families can come up with a shared concept of the role that grandparents will play in their own family. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com. Piedmont parent Cass Caulfield called into the March 24 board meeting after sending in a petition signed by 600 parents students and community members. The petition called for: • Immediately increasing all in-person instructional hours for all grade levels for the remainder of the 2020-21 school year • Passing a formal board resolution committing to opening all Piedmont schools in the Fall. The board stated it was more powerful to have administrators and all labor partners sign the joint agreement than merely reasserting the board’s position. “We hear you guys; we are not giving up. With every year in the ground, meadow plants support more life and build healthier soil. This makes them quite efficient at parking carbon – the opposite of a resource-guzzling lawn. Lawns are among the ways we burden nature. Meadows give back to the earth much more than they take.” Regenerative agriculture This is the term that sums up a new approach to farming, landscaping and gardening. Practiced on from large farms to backyard gardens and urban streetscapes, it focuses on conserving and revitalizing topsoil, increasing biodiversity, improving water cycle, sequestering carbon, and increasing resilience to climate change. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Supervisor Erin Rivera announced her retirement yesterday, March 30. Rivera joined the Piedmont Recreation Department (PRD) in 1993 as the Wildwood Schoolmates Site Coordinator and was promoted to Recreation Supervisor three years later. She has served in that capacity for 27 years. During her tenure, Rivera supervised pre-school and elementary school-aged programming, including the Schoolmates program. The city also credits Rivera with growing the department’s preschool programs from an enrichment program into a full preschool program, offering six classes five days a week. “Erin has dedicated her entire career to the Piedmont Recreation Department,” said her boss, Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “She is responsible for building PRD’s wonderful Schoolmates, Preschool, and camp programs. Her creativity, dedication and service to the Piedmont community has been a cornerstone in the success of the Department for the past 27 years.” Rivera worked to expand the city’s offerings of summer programming as well. She lists Camp Cottontail, Camp Ishi, Camp 1973, Huckleberry, Outdoor Explorers, and Camp Everything as her favorites. She added that she is most proud of the CIT and Junior CIT programs, created in 1995, that have helped match thousands of youth with summer employment opportunities. “I have had the opportunity to work with amazing people over the last 27 years, and we were all always focused on the same goal of providing care and experiences that were good for kids,” Rivera said. “Erin’s enthusiastic dedication to providing great programs that were good for kids has been evident to me since my first day as Recreation Director,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. “She deserves tremendous credit for the programs she developed and the experiences she’s given to kids in her nearly three decades of work at the Recreation Department.”
articles.title: Erin Rivera retires from Rec. Dept.

articles.text: Schwarzenegger had played the violin, his name might have been Ole Bull. The Scandinavian violinist was a giant of a man, good-looking, blonde and blueeyed. He looked the part of a romantic matinee idol of millions of women. But make no mistake – he was a great violinist. His concerts included some of the classics, but he also catered to less sophisticated popular music of the times. In the U.S. Bull was sometimes accused of being a musical charlatan. He wasn’t, but many people like to downgrade a genius. One of the favorite stories about him was when he was on a riverboat going down the Mississippi River. He stepped outside for a breath of fresh air, when somebody came up to him and stuck a gun in his ribs – like the old Jack Benny routine, “your money or your life.“ Bull looked at the guy, picked him up like a professional wrestler would, and threw him overboard into the Mississippi. And then he enjoyed the rest of his stroll around deck of the paddle wheeler. articles.text: Piedmont High School juniors and seniors returned to the school campus for in-person instruction yesterday, March 23. It was the first time in 372 days they were in a classroom. The oldest students in the district were the last to return to class, and their arrival marks the completion of the school district’s phased reopening. A palpable sense of excitement could be felt, and the weather followed suit as well. One would be hard pressed to find a lovelier day this time of year, the fourth day of spring. “My first class was AP Literature. It was amazing, so fun. It felt so good to sit in a class and just do a group exercise with my classmates.” said Senior Class President Audrey Edel, Yesterday, students could be seen carrying goodie bags created by members of the student body government (ASB). Included in each bag was a golden cardboard crown (for seniors), snacks, stickers, a drink. and – of course – a hand sanitizer. “It was super nice to hand out these goodie bags and just to see people happy again,” Edel added. Juniors and seniors at PHS will be on campus this week Tuesday through Friday and freshmen and sophomores will return the week after. This alternating schedule allows for smaller class sizes to accommodate a six-foot distance between students. “It felt really good to be back but, definitely a little weird. I’m sure it will come more naturally eventually, but for now there’s a bit of ‘how do I do this again?” said 12th grader Jonah Bloom. The school day is divided in half into cohorts A and B. Only cohort A attends class in the morning Tuesday and WednesPHS seniors Greg Gately and Audrey Edel hold up goodie bags given to all high school students by ASB, the student body government. PHS seniors on their first day of school one year later: Bridget Bentley (left), Jackie Remick, Orly Sanborn, Paxton Grimmer, Bella Kjellen, and Charlotte Hubbel. day, all students must leave campus during lunch and then cohort B arrives for the afternoon. This schedule flip-flops on Thursdays and Fridays, with cohort B in the morning and A in the afternoon. Each high schooler at PHS that signed up for this hybrid (partial in-person) learning model has 8 hours 45 minutes of class time every other week, averaging to 4 hours and 22 minutes per week. If students have one or two free periods, as is common for seniors, they may only be on campus for six or seven hours every other week. “The first day went really well. It seemed like time flew by, and then all of a sudden it was over. Even though the schedule is the same as Distance Learning, the day just went faster,” said junior Anabel Loucks with a smile. Students, parents and teachers may not need to get too used to this schedule as the chance of longer hours in class improved last week. On March 19, Governor Newsom and the California Department of Public Health aligned with new federal guidance by reducing the required space of social distancing from six feet to three feet. spacing requirements more students can be in a class at once. This crucial step makes room for an expansion of in-person instruction time. Equally important for this goal is the vaccine rollout for teachers. However, the teachers and the school district still have to come to terms on any change in the schedule regardless of state guidance. Secondary schools can reopen as long as COVID case counts are below 7.0 per 100,000 residents in a county. Yesterday, March 23, Alameda County‘s case count went down to 3.3 cases. Alameda County will be eligible to enter the Orange Tier on March 31. 32.

articles.text: Negotiations with the teacher’s union have now lasted more than 365 days with more negotiations this week. After immense public pressure, including hundreds of lawn signs demanding a discussion about what will happen in the 2021-22 school year in the fall, the school board agreed to put that discussion on the table tonight, March 24, 2021. Plans for extending hours this spring and the 2021-22 school year just got easier thanks to health agencies revising the minimum distance between student desks from 6 feet down to 3 feet, allowing classes to fill up with students like it was 2019. But we are not done just yet. Union contracts still dictate 6 feet between desks and the administration is citing numerous logistical challenges. Many things about the entire reopening process were opaque. Schedules were created with fewer hours of in-person instruction than parents expected due to surprise blockers with little explanation. Hundreds of questions sent to the school board remain unanswered. Memoranda of understanding with unions were arrived at after negotiation and then celebrated and approved at school board meetings. Negotiations between administrators and teachers are a window into both what the administration is looking for and what unions are looking for. Keeping that entire process hidden was a key contributor to the frustration and surprises that many hundreds of parents and students felt. I was curious about why this process was so secretive, unlike much more open negotiations in other unionized industries, like healthcare. It was suggested that I learn about the Rodda Act, known formally as EERA. It is named after its sponsor, former State Senator Albert Rodda. The EERA is regulated by the California Public Employment Relations Board

A little-known provision in the Rodda Act mandates that school districts reveal the initial bargaining positions of both sides at a public school board meeting, allow public input on what the administration should be asking for, and the school board vote on their initial proposal. All of these steps have to occur prior to the start of the negotiation. Unfortunately, Piedmont Unified never followed this procedure. This sunshine clause was enacted as Government Code 3547 and was used correctly by at least one other school district, Fremont Unified. This law is very clear, helpful, and should be followed. After emailing the superintendent and school board I got a response from Randy Booker stating he prefers all parties create language collaboratively at the bargaining table. This no-paper-trail approach leaves nothing for public discussion and school board vote and thereby bypasses the spirit of the Rodda Act. To read the language of the Rodda Act, click on on Government Code 3547 (https:// leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/ codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3547). articles.text: This past week our country has witnessed a heartbreaking continuation of violence focused on people of Asian descent. Recent attacks against those of Asian descent have been traumatic. The deadly shooting in Atlanta last week understandably increases the concern, fear, and trauma especially for our Asian community. Furthermore, these disturbing attacks are targeting the most vulnerable in our communities. As your Chief of Police, I want our entire community, and particularly our community members of Asian descent, to know their police department stands with them. We have been following these events closely and have been in contact with the Oakland Police Department and our other county partners. I have also made it a priority to reach out to local community stakeholders and representatives of the Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) to offer my support following these intolerable crimes. Any race-based attacks and incidents borne of ignorance will be thoroughly investigated and will not be tolerated in Piedmont. We will coordinate any investigations with the Alameda County District Attorney’s newly formed Special Response Team, which has been assembled to assist local law enforcement and our community with the recent violent attacks. The team, made up of Deputy District Attorneys, inspectors and victim/witness advocates, is in place to support our investigative efforts. Finally, I encourage anyone in our community to speak up and speak out. If you’ve been the target of a race-based attack, please call our police department. Violence against anyone in our community affects us all. We at the Piedmont Police Department will continue to do all we can to support and protect everyone. We are mindful of the specific trauma those of Asian descent are experiencing now. We are in this together. Jeremy Bowers is Chief of Police of the City of Piedmont. articles.text: Any residential home or property that is sold or transferred in Piedmont must now provide a Home Energy Score or a Home Energy Audit to both potential buyers and the city’s Planning and Building Department, following the adoption of Ordinance 751 N.S. The passage of the new Home Energy Assessment Ordinance (Ordinance 751 N.S.) was unanimously approved by the City Council on February 1. The ordinance became effective 30 days later. The expectation is that a Home Energy Assessment will assist homeowners in their efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Over 50 percent of emissions in Piedmont come from residences. The ordinance will also ensure that the community meets standards and goals set in the city’s ambitious Climate Action Plan. Now, when listing a property for sale, a report from a Home Energy Audit, or Score, must be provided to potential buyers and the city. A Home Energy Audit is a detailed report of identified treatments for improving a home’s energy use resulting from a whole-house evaluation, including diagnostic testing using specialized equipment.The Score is based on a standard assessment of energy-related assets, to easily compare energy use across the housing market. Sellers of single-family homes in Piedmont are required to obtain and disclose an Audit or Score, which would estimate the energy-related use, associated costs, and cost-effective solutions to improve the home’s efficiency. Getting a Home Energy Score involves a few simple steps that can be accomplished while still living in the home. You can schedule a home energy assessment by contacting an authorized Home Energy Assessor before listing, or otherwise announcing your home for sale. Once you choose an assessment company, a Home Energy Assessor will visit your home to assess it. They will collect information about a home’s foundation, insulation, walls, and windows, as well as its heating, cooling, and water systems. To prepare for your assessment, make sure the assessor has clear access to your garage, basement, and attic, as well as any crawl spaces within the home. The U.S. Department of Energy recommends also providing any records on energy improvement you’ve made to your home already. This includes insulations, the installation of solar paneling, or new furnaces. Once the assessor has completed the evaluation, they will provide you with a Home Energy Score promptly, usually within a few days. The report you receive will provide a list of recommended home energy upgrades. Completing a Home Energy Audit is often a more expensive and lengthy process than the Home Energy Score, according to Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. An audit may take several hours depending on the size of the home, with the auditor employing equipment such as infrared cameras and a blower door test. Coupled with computer modeling, these tools are used to analyze a more detailed assessment of a home’s energy use. For more information, contact the Piedmont Planning Department at 420-3039. articles.text: Editor: The League of Women Voters of California condemns all xenophobic and hateful acts targeting Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) communities. articles.text: Over half of Piedmont has received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of March 20, and about one-third of the City’s population is fully vaccinated, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD). In recent days, Alameda County has joined other Californian counties in opening vaccine eligibility to people aged 16 to 64 years old “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk due to complex health conditions,” the county’s website states. While the state began permitting healthcare providers to vaccinate individuals with health conditions back on Monday, March 15, the county waited several days to expand eligibility due to supply constraints. The county reports that 4,384 Piedmonters – 52.7 percent of the City’s adult population – have received at least one dose and 2,730 Piedmonters, 32.8 percent of the City, have been fully vaccinated. Vaccines created by Moderna and Pfizer require two doses administered several weeks apart. A recently approved vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose, but just a few thousand doses of this vaccine have arrived in the county so far. Much more are expected to arrive in the coming days. Piedmont leads Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population, but rates across the county have increased in recent weeks. In all of Alameda County, about 683,000 total doses have been administered and around 19 percent of the county’s population is fully vaccinated. In Oakland, about 35 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 18 percent have been fully vaccinated. Over the past seven days, the county began vaccinating residents with health conditions that put them more at risk for COVID-19 mortality. The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found at the ACPHD website at covid-19. After people with comorbidities, the county is moving to an age-based priority framework in determining vaccine eligibility. Contra Costa and Solano counties already have expanded eligibility to people aged 50 and above. Vaccines should be available to all Californians who want one in the coming months. The state’s guidelines now say “all Californians should have access to COVID-19 vaccines by spring 2021.” President Joe Biden, bolstered by the rising supply rates of the Johnson and Johnson and other vaccines, announced this month that all American adults should be eligible for vaccination by May 1. Pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca announced this week that it has applied to the Food and Drug Administration for emergency use authorization for its COVID-19 vaccine, another vaccine that requires only one dose. Once approved, adding a fourth manufacturer to the effort would greatly increase the nation’s supply. California has administered about 15.2 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 19.3 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 285,000 people per day. About 20 million Californians are now eligible for the vaccine, a little over half of the state’s population. acgov.org/vaccines.page. Furthermore, people aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. Residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments.
articles.title: Alameda County opens eligibility to people with COVID-19 comorbidities

articles.text: California moved three Bay Area counties – Marin, San Francisco and Santa Clara – into a less restrictive tier for reopening yesterday, Tuesday, March 23, but Alameda County was not among them. These three counties join San Mateo County in the Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, for reopening their economies due to declining COVID-19 cases. While Alameda County has met the benchmarks for moving to the Orange Tier for over a week, the state waits two weeks for counties to meet thresholds before moving tiers. California moved Alameda County into the Red Tier last Tuesday, March 9 as new cases of COVID-19 decrease in the area. The Red Tier, or Substantial Tier, is the second-most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric. Before that, the county was in the Purple, or Widespread, Tier – the most restrictive tier. Indoor dining, movie theaters, museums and gyms are allowed for counties in the Red Tier. Small private gathers among no more than three households are permitted indoors, although gathering outdoors is strongly encouraged. In the Orange Tier, the capacity limits for indoor activities increase and non-essential offices can open at 25 percent capacity. In Marin, San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, these changes will go into place today, Wednesday, March 24. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County dipped to 1.2 percent as of Monday, March 23 – its lowest point since the pandemic began a year ago. The positivity rate is now below an earlier nadir in October before the worst surge of the pandemic seen so far hit in the winter. The county meets the positivity rate benchmark to move into the Orange Tier – it will need to stay below 4.9 percent for Alameda County to move tiers. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 3.9 – right now there are 3.3 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to be below 5.2 percent – it is currently 2.4 percent in Alameda County. One new case was reported in Piedmont over the past seven days, the second case recorded in the City in March. In total, there have been 170 COVID-19 cases reported in Piedmont. Across Alameda County, the total caseload for the county is 82,747, less than a 1 percent increase week-over-week. There have been 25,706 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,984 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,370 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,549,101 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 56,596 deaths due to the disease statewide.

articles.text: We all know about the impact of donating to important causes and volunteering, but have you considered that your investments are also a tool for social and environmental change? Join a panel discussion on Thursday, April 8 from 7:00 to 8:15 p.m. on Zoom to learn about making a positive difference through your investments without sacrificing financial returns. The virtual event, co-sponsored by Piedmont Connect and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, will feature a panel of three experts who will discuss the links between investments and racial, gender, environmental, and other social justice issues. The panelists are Stephen DeBerry, founder and managing partner of the Bronze Venture Fund; Piedmont resident Dr. Kristin Hull, founder and CEO of Nia Capital; and Morgan LaManna, senior manager of investor engagements at Ceres, an environmental nonprofit that makes the business case for sustainability and works with investors, businesses, and regulators. Register to attend this free Zoom event at http://bit. ly/2Q3RcNn. If questions, email piedmontracialequity@gmail. com.
