articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will perform a concert on April 10. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) is set to begin its first concert of the spring on Saturday, April 10, at 4 p.m. with the Choir’s advanced choral ensembles, Ensemble, ECCO, and Ancora groups, performing. They will sing stories of the earth in an event entitled “Making History–Singing the Earth.” The concert, in partnership with the Stanford Chamber Chorale, will also include the world premiere of Kerry Andrew’s Wake Up!, a meditation on the climate crisis as seen through the eyes of young climate activists. Expect songs of spring as the Choir also collaborates with Finnish youth choir Vox Aurea and medieval ensemble Yr Awen. The program will include rarely heard partsongs by the Black English composer Samuel Coleridge-Taylor. The concert begins at 4 p.m., and will last approximately one hour. PEBCC is able to offer the 2020-2021 virtual concert season for free through the generosity of its patrons. To donate and reserve a spot for the April 10 performance, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs. org/event-calendar.
articles.title: Piedmont Children’s Choir “Singing the Earth” virtual concert on April 10

articles.text: A year away from campus has been devastating for many students. Zoom fatigue, lack of social contact, and not enough personal interaction with teachers is driving them crazy. They are desperate to get back to school and to their friends and daily routines as soon as possible. But not all students are eager to go back. The thing that has surprised me most throughout the pandemic is the fact that some of my students are thriving at home. For them, not having to summon the energy for superficial social interactions at school is a huge benefit to remote learning, as is not feeling depleted at the end of a bustling day on campus. Being in the relative quiet of their own homes, and having time to luxuriate in their own thoughts, has been a gift this past year. And some of them don’t want to give it up. Take Alexa, for instance. Alexa transitioned to remote learning effortlessly. She was able to stay motivated with her coursework because she no longer experienced the social anxiety that used to consume her when she was on campus. At home, she doesn’t worry about saying the wrong thing, or not looking perfect--common teenage preoccupations that kept her on edge during in-person learning. Alexa has blossomed in the comfort of her own home, something her teachers and peers have noticed. Not all students want to return to school So how can parents help students like Alexa—the introverts—readjust to a return to campus? First, if your child is an introvert, and if they have liked being at home, start by acknowledging this fact. Especially for older students, those who consume a lot of media and understand the national push to return to campus, they may feel hesitant to share their feelings. Being an introvert is a challenge at school, and so let them know their feelings are normal. Second, honor their introversion. This is especially important if parent(s) are extroverts and aren’t hardwired to love peace, quiet, and solitude. As your child transitions back to school, consider creating introverted family rituals, like reading books in the same room, or having planned quiet time during family activities, such as car rides or walks. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. At the top of the essay include the following information: the title, your first and last name, city of residence (must be Piedmont), name of your school, and your current grade. Essays must be typed and double-spaced and submitted in a .pdf format. All entries are to be submitted to lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The deadline is April 17. Winners will be announced on May 1.
articles.title: Deadline to enter League of Women Voters contest is April 17

articles.text: In the dark cloud of a pandemic, it can be tough to find the silver lining. As hard as it’s been, 17-year-old pianist Liam Charron says it’s also been helpful. He’s been able to focus, practice, learn and compose like never before. “Music is a conversation between you and other people, and when there are no other people, you struggle to find meaning in it,” said the Piedmont High School senior. “But without Covid, I think I would not have been the player I am now.” Just prior to California’s shelter-in-place order one year ago, Charron wasn’t all that motivated, he said. But then he toured some colleges where he could pursue his love of music with a major in jazz studies with a focus on piano. “Seeing the end goal with my own eyes made all the difference,” he said. “That’s when I decided: I’m going to hunker down and do this. So I started practicing much longer, much smarter in some ways. I’ve had so much more improvement … than I could have imagined.” A member of the Jazz Band and Jazz Combo at PHS, Charron started with piano more than 10 years ago, and has since learned to play other instruments. He used downtime last summer to accomplish a major goal — an album on Spotify. “I played all the instruments, I sang all the vocals,” he said. “I had to judge my own content, but Piedmont senior and pianist Liam Charron. it was really good, because with every song I grew and got more confident and put new things in.” Now that the college application process is finished, Charron is working on his piano technique, transcribing the music of jazz greats like Bill Evans, and exploring the compositional aspects of playing ballads. “I’ve been learning things that I’ve been wanting to learn,” he said. “There’s no point to stop learning now.” Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for students in Piedmont schools.
articles.title: Pandemic can’t stop this Piedmont musician

articles.text: On March 17, Mills College president Elizabeth Hillman announced that the school will no longer enroll first-year students. Located in Oakland, Mills College is a nationally renowned liberal arts college for women and gender-binary students. The college was founded as the Young Ladies Seminary in 1852 and was the first women’s college west of the Rockies. It currently offers more than 45 undergraduate majors and minors, as well as 30 graduate degrees, certificates, and credentials. Beginning this year, the college will phase out its degree programs to instead become Mills Institute. It will hand out its last degrees in 2023. Hillman explained that “the economic burdens of the COVID- 19 pandemic, structural changes across higher education, and budget deficits” led to the decision. Mills has weathered years of financial instability and declining enrollment. Currently, the prestigious college enrolls just about 900 students, a roughly 30 percent decline since 2015. The college is beginning to transition its academic programs by creating options and degree pathways for all Mills students, Hillman explained. The Provost’s Office will develop plans for each degree program that the college currently offers. The Admissions Office will serve a role in supporting students who pursue transfer opportunities outside Mills College. “While Mills’ role as a degree-granting college will end, its mission will endure. Mills intends to continue to foster women’s leadership and student success, advance gender and racial equity, and cultivate innovative pedagogy, research, and critical thinking by creating a Mills Institute housed here on campus,” Hillman said. “This year, faculty, trustees, staff, students, and other community stakeholders will consider potential structures and programming for the proposed institute,” she added. U.S Rep. Barbara Lee (Oakland), a Mills graduate, said in a statement that she was “heartbroken and outraged” by the announcement. “Personally, I owe a debt of gratitude to Mills College. Five decades ago, I was able to attend college and earn a degree as a young single mother on public assistance, who often had to bring her sons to class - something that would have been impossible at many other colleges and universities,” Lee said. She added that Mills College was where she met her mentor, Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm, and where her “passion for public service and politics began.” The school has been essential in recruiting underrepresented students, Lee said. In 2014, Mills College became the first single-sex college in the United States to adopt an admission policy explicitly welcoming transgender students. Fifty-six percent of current undergraduate students self-identify as students of color.
articles.title: Mills College to discontinue granting degrees

articles.text: Governor Gavin Newsom visited Ruby Bridges Elementary School in Alameda on Tuesday, March 16, to discuss the state’s progress toward reopening campuses. Ruby Bridges Elementary and other schools in the city of Alameda welcomed students back for in-person instruction on March 15. During his visit, Gov. Newsom said that about 9,000 of California’s nearly 11,000 public schools have reopened or announced dates to reopen this spring. But, like Piedmont, Alameda Unified’s reopening is only a partial “hybrid” model. On March 1, Gov. Newsom and lawmakers forged a $6.6 billion reopening bill. He stated that, after the height of the winter surge in COVID-19 cases, the conversation shifted from “whether to reopen schools, to when.” Since the governor’s announcement, the state has collaborated with county health departments, the Biden Administration and providers such as Kaiser Permanente to accelerate vaccine access for K-12 school staff. Access to vaccination proved to be a significant hurdle in reopening some districts, particularly Los Angeles Unified. The bill allocates $2 billion to fund safety measures that support in-person instruction, such as personal protective equipment, ventilation upgrades and COVID-19 testing. A proposed $4.6 billion will fund expanded learning opportunities, such as summer school, tutoring, and mental health services. The bill also requires that, by April 1, all California public schools offer “in-person instruction to grades K-2 for all students, [or] lose one percent of eligible funds every day thereafter if they do not.” Districts that don’t open by May 15 will lose eligibility for funding. This money should provide incentives for reopening; however, no language in the bill mandates reopening. “We are seeing real progress, real momentum,” Newsom told Photo by Jeff Chiu, Associated Press reporters at Ruby Bridges Elementary School. He attributed reopening success to “plummeting COVID-19 case rates statewide.” About 80 percent of students voluntarily returned to Ruby Bridges Elementary on March 15, a number that Newsom said he expects will grow. “Parents need to have confidence [to send kids back], not just the teachers, the custodial staff, bus drivers, or the folks that make schools like this work,” he said. According to California’s Safe Schools for All Plan, Piedmont Unified has received $1,057,073 in state funding, and three months worth of PPE. The district provided a safety plan to the California Department of Health on January 31, 2021.
articles.title: Gov. Newsom visits grade school in Alameda

articles.text: It’s been 53 weeks since I last set foot on campus. Not in the shortcut-to-Mulberry’s way; I’ve done plenty of that, when my mom couldn’t handle the lockdown cooking anymore and sent me to buy lunch, but in the real, go-to-school way. Walking to school on March 19, 2021, one year and one week after Piedmont schools had closed due to Covid-19 pandemic, I was nervous that I was forgetting something, especially forgetting something of importance. I was correct: I forgot my computer and felt like an idiot. But can you blame me? I hadn’t been on campus for over a year! As I walked onto campus and saw real people again, it was as if I was a little kid and just got a puppy for my birthday. People I hadn’t seen in the flesh for so long had been only small moving figures on my computer. To be sure, like the rest of Piedmont I was shocked to learn that in the reopening plan my middle school day would be a measly two hours, and only once a week. But I guess even that was better than nothing. Why Piedmont Middle School has been singled out to have the shortest school week on the planet is anyone’s guess. On the first day of going back to in-person learning, I was all over the place. In the morning I had an online class and after that I would be going to school. My sister, who tore herself away from checking college acceptances on various portals, helped me pick out an outfit, so that I could look like a model. During quarantine, I had been trying on various entertainments for my lonely self, and modeling is the latest. I figured that I’d walk those school halls like I was at London Fashion Week. (As model Kendall Jenner said, “The world is your runway.”) On my way to school, I met up with my friend, and we walked together. As we reached Wildwood playground for our shortcut to the middle school, we discovered that that the gate had been locked. We were already late, so if we took an alternate route we would have arrived even later. So, I may or may not have climbed a fence to open the gate from inside. articles.text: After months of sheltering at home due to the Covid pandemic, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 are getting together to explore the great outdoors. Last Sunday morning, March 21, a big group of 55 members of Scouts and Scout leaders rode their bicycles along the Bay Trail from Oyster Bay Regional Shoreline (near the west end of Davis Street in San Leandro) to the San Mateo Bridge, a 12-mile round trip. Much of the trail is packed dirt, with some pavement and some gravel. The Scouts wore masks and traveled in groups of four. Many Scouts were happy to habe a change of scenery. The trail crosses marshlands where tidal flows bring Bay water hundreds of yards inland via a network of sloughs. The Troop 15 trek occurred at low tide -- revealing mud flats which were being probed by sandpipers. Great blue heron, snowy egrets and Canadian Geese were seen fishing along the sloughs. Patrol leader Nate Woodley observed that “marshlands look grey and yucky, but it is cool how twice a day the tide brings nutrients in, then goes out to expose mud where the birds find food.” Earlier in the week, Troop members met at Becker Field at Havens School for their first time together in five months. Dividing into patrol groups, they worked on first-aid skills. Troop 15 next plans a camping trip in Marin County the weekend of April 10-11. Summer Camp runs from July 11-17 this year. Currently Troop 15 Scouts meet on Becker Field on Tuesday evenings at 6:30 p.m. Girls and boys age 11-17 and parents are welcome to visit. For more information, contact Scoutmaster Glen Tripp at Glen@Galileo-Learning.com. Scouts learn about the effort to restore the marshlands. A Great Blue Heron fishes from alongside a slough. Canadian geese looking for food. Four 7th grade members of Troop 15’s Handyman Clan at a rest stop: Daniel Lou, Gabriel Barbosa Topete, Caleb Canada and Jason Shum. A snowy egret crosses the marsh. Riding near the approach to the San Mateo Bridge. ® Scouts take a rest break on The Bay Trail. Scout Caleb Canada and his dramatic custom bike helmet. Scouts starting up after a brief rest break.

articles.text: Piedmont High tennis teams went different directions last week. The boys’ team traveled to Moraga, where it edged out Campolindo 5-4 on Wednesday, March 17. Playing at home, the girls suffered a 5-2 loss to Berkeley at home the previous day, “The boys beat Campolindo in a mighty ‘fourth-quarter comeback’,” exuded PHS coach Jim Landes. “We were behind 4-2 with three matches left. They just needed one point [to win], but we got ‘em. The girls lost 5-2 but we were missing our top singles and doubles starters. Despite being without them, we put up a good The boys’ team had a big league match with Berkeley set for March 18, but rain postponed the match until tomorrow, March 25. Boys edge Campolindo 5-4 In a non-league match at Camplindo in Moraga, the teams played six singles matches and The Highlanders opened with a win at No. 3 doubles by Linus Lee and Charlie Sullivan, winning in straight sets 6-2, 6-4. Piedmont gained its second point when Charlie Olcott won at No. 5 hand for a clean winner.” Girls lose to Berkeley Playing at home, Piedmont lost to Berkeley 5-2 in a return match. The team was without No. 1 singles Makenna and No. 1 doubles starter Amanda Becker. The girls previously beat the Yellowjackets by the same score in the season-opener on March 6. Piedmont’s wins came from No. 2 doubles Rosie Siemers and Kate Dorman, 6-1, 7-5, and the No. 3 doubles team of Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro, 6-3, 6-2. Girls at Carondelet The girls’ team traveled to Concord to play Carondelet yesterday, Tuesday, March 23. They won handily, 7-2. See next week’s Post for match details. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, March 24, 2021 Sports Piedmont Tennis By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High tennis teams went different directions last week. The boys’ team traveled to Moraga, where it edged out Campolindo 5-4 on Wednesday, March 17. Playing at home, the girls suffered a 5-2 loss to Berkeley at home the previous day, Tuesday, March 16. “The boys beat Campolindo in a mighty ‘fourth-quarter comeback’,” exuded PHS coach Jim Landes. “We were behind 4-2 with three matches left. They just needed one point [to win], but we got ‘em. The girls lost 5-2 but we were missing our top singles and doubles starters. Despite being without them, we put up a good fight.” The boys’ team had a big league match with Berkeley set for March 18, but rain postponed the match until tomorrow, March 25. Boys edge Campolindo 5-4 In a non-league match at Camplindo in Moraga, the teams played six singles matches and three doubles. The Highlanders opened with a win at No. 3 doubles by Linus Lee and Charlie Sullivan, winning in straight sets 6-2, 6-4. Piedmont gained its second point when Charlie Olcott won at No. 5 Boys beat Campo 5-4; Girls lose to Berkeley 5-2 hand for a clean winner.” Girls lose to Berkeley Playing at home, Piedmont lost to Berkeley 5-2 in a return match. The team was without No. 1 singles Makenna and No. 1 doubles starter Amanda Becker. The girls previously beat the Yellowjackets by the same score in the season-opener on March 6. Piedmont’s wins came from No. 2 doubles Rosie Siemers and Kate Dorman, 6-1, 7-5, and the No. 3 doubles team of Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro, 6-3, 6-2. articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ lacrosse team split two games last week. It lost to Carondolet in Concord 16-6 on Thursday, March 18, and then defeated Berkeley 21-10 at Witter Field on Saturday, March 20. “The Carondolet game was tough. Our starting goalie Sophia Ethington suffered a thumb injury in the first half,” explained PHS coach Carlton Chan. “They also had a very good goalie who stopped a lot of tough shots. Berkeley was a different story. We came fired up and had a lot better ball movement.” It was a big pair of games for Caroline Devine, who scored four goals against Carondolet plus six goals and six assists against Berkeley. Senior captain Sadie Tschider, meanwhile, netted five goals with six assists against the Yellowjackets. Katherine Kinne scored six goals and one assist against Berkeley. “Katherine had a breakout game with six goals. Our offense was much more balanced against Berkeley. Most of the scores came off of assists, 12 assists on 20 scores showed we moved the ball much, much better. We got a lot of good contributions from our attackers,” explained Chan. PHS tops Berkeley 21-10 Despite the one-sided victory for Piedmont, the score was closer at halftime with the Highlanders holding an 11-7 lead. Devine opened scoring two minutes into the game. Piedmont led 3-0 with goals from Charlotte Theut and Tschider netting her and an assist. NEXT UP Sadie Tschider had five goals and six assists against the Yellowjackets. articles.text: The Piedmont’s track and field team traveled to Berkeley High on Wednesday, March 17 for a dual meet with the Yelllowjackets. The Highlanders won 11 events, including Ellie Black winning the 1600 and 3200, and Jack Stein and Seamus Chamberlain-Carr placed 1st and 2nd with times of 10:23 and 10:24, one second apart. The two runners have led their teams since the start of the season. Black, who was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2020, clocked a personal record time in the 1600 meters in 5:47.1, a 7-second improvement from her time one year ago. She won in a field of nine runners. Her winning time of 12:31.7 in the 3200 was in a field of seven runners. Stein set a personal record in the 3200 meters of 10:23.4, a 16-second improvement from his previous PR set on March 6’s against Castro Valley. Girls Results Alongside Black in the 1600 was senior leader Aya Troyer in second place in 5:53.8, marking a record time for her, eight seconds faster than in March of 2020 at the Sunset Invitational. Also in the 1600, freshman Jamie Schwarz has a time if 6:12 and Valerie Xiong finished in 6:19. Troyer placed second of seven runners in the 3200 in 12:54.9, and Molly McWeeny clocked in at 13:41. Schwarz, a freshman, also won the 800 meters with a time of 2:44.4. She also raced as the second leg of the 4x400 relay with teammates Adri McAuliffe, Valerie Xiong, and Kristen DiBella. They placed 2nd to Berkeley. McAuliffe also placed second of seven in the 300 hurdles in 54.7. DiBella recorded a 56.5 and freshman Jasmyn Milsum clocked a 1:01.3. McAuliffe won the long jump against four other athletes with a distance of 14 feet, 3 inches. PHS freshman Breah Bell placed 2nd with a leap of 12 feet, 4.5 inches. In an all-Piedmont event, Jasmine Ghaderi won the shot put at 22 feet, 5 inches, Cassia Gray was 2nd at 16 feet, 3.5 inches; Katie Korn had a toss of 16 feet, and Yanela Roberts was 4th at 14 feet, 3.5 inches. Ghaderi also won Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Jack Stein won the 3200 with a PR time of 10:23.4 at the WACC Tri-Meet against Berkeley and Arroyo. Ellie Black separates herself from the pack in the 1600 at Berkeley High, which she won in 5:47.1. Black also won the 3200. Jamie Schwarz won her second consecutive 800-meter event. the pole vault at 8 feet, 6 inches. She was also the only competitor in the triple jump and won with a leap of 28 feet, 5 inches. Gray also won the discus event in 44 feet, 8.5 inches. Roberts was next at 37 feet, 11 inches. Boys Results Sophomore Parker Long placed 4th in the 3200 in 10:48.3 in his first time competing in the event. In the 1600 meters, sophomore Christian Taylor finished 2nd of 35 runners with a time of 4:51.9. Senior Collin Mortimer placed 3rd in 4:56.2. Also competing was Alex Ware in 8th, 5:02 and freshman Xander Sasse-Schulte in 11th, 5:04. Taylor also tied for third of 10 runners with senior Edward Marcus in the 400, both clocking times of 1:00.5. Junior Luke Alban placed third of 27 runners in the 100 meters in 11.6 seconds. Piedmont’s 4x400 relay team of Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, Matthew Riordan, Collin Mortimer, and Luke Alban won the event with a time of 3:57, five seconds faster than Berkeley. Aaron Valva won the discus throw with a distance of 71 feet, 0.5 inches, and was second in the shot put at 24 feet, 0.5 inches. NEXT UP Piedmont toes the line today, Wednesday, March 24, in a dual meet with San Leandro at 3:30 p.m. Piedmont’s cross-country teams will compete on Saturday, March 27 for a 10:30 a.m. meet.

articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team improved its record to 2-1 after winning two consecutive games with great pitching coupled with late-hitting heroics. PHS recorded a 2-0 win against the visiting Oakland Tech Bulldogs on a sunny Saturday, March 20, and followed that with a 5-4 victory over Mt. Eden two days later. On Saturday, pitcher Cal Barna threw 12 strikeouts in six innings, while reliever Julian Scherman gained a save to close out the win in the seventh. Monday featured Ben Levinson throwing five innings with 11 strikeouts and just one hit; Scherman gained the victory. But as good as coach Eric Olson’s pitching staff is proving, the Highlanders’ bats have come through when it mattered most. Piedmont’s 2-0 victory against Tech featured sophomore Michael Aikawa hitting a game-winning RBI double in the bottom of the fifth. In the victory over Mt. Eden, senior slugger Lars Derr hit the game-winning RBI to the right field fence at Witter Field in the bottom of the seventh. 2-0 win over Oakland Tech Barna was dealing heat on the mound in Saturday’s victory against the Bulldogs. The University of Hawaii-bound player showed confidence on the mound, effectively mixing his arsenal of pitches between fastball, slider, sinker, changeup, and curveball. He made sure to praise catcher Davis Alazraqui for his performance as well. “I woke up feeling good and ready to play. My catcher [Davis Alazraqui] played great. Getting out of those first-inning jitters and Davis doing so well behind the plate made it even better. In the third, fourth, and fifth,” said Barna. The game remained scoreless through five innings, but a oneout double by Michael Aikawa broke the scoring drought in the bottom of the fifth. The inning started with PHS first baseman Garren Riley taking a fastball on his backside to reach first, then took second on a wild pitch. Aikawa, behind 1-2 in the count, found what he was looking for – a low fastball right in his wheelhouse. “I saw a low fastball, it’s what I like. I was waiting for it,” said Aikawa. With a tenuous 1-0 lead, the Highlanders added an insurance run in the bottom of the sixth with Nico Defazio singling to centerfield then advancing on a wild pitch. Evan McConathy reached base on a throwing error, advancing Defazio to third. He eventually scored on an infielder’s choice by Alazraqui for the 2-0 final. In the top of the seventh, Scherman entered the game as the closer, allowing a one-out single but swiftly got the job done with a strikeout and groundout. Final stats include: Barna’s stellar six innings and 12 strikeouts; he allowed three hits and one walk. Aikawa went 2-for-3 with one RBI, Alazraqui gained the other RBI. Lars Derr and Defazio had one hit. 5-4 win over Mt. Eden Playing at home on Monday, Piedmont won 5-4 with more stellar pitching and situational hitting. Macalester College-bound pitcher Ben Levinson had 11 strikeouts in five innings but missed getting the win when Mt. Eden mounted a comeback to tie the game 4-4 in the sixth inning. . In the bottom of the seventh. Defazio hit a fly ball to left field and advanced to second base on a fielding error. Enter Derr, Piedmont’s designated hitter. On the very first pitch, he went opposite-field to smack a fly ball off the right field fence to bring in Defazio to score the winning run. He finished Monday’s game 4-for-4 with five RBIs after the walk-off winner. “I was hitting batting practice the other day and came in feeling loose. I felt really comfortable at the plate,” said Derr. Final stats: Aikawa had one hit and a walk, Will Sprague scored two runs and drew a walk, Defazio scored twice, had one hit and a walk, Aiden Mitchell had a hit. On the mound, Scherman gained the win after entering in the top of the seventh. The Hayward Farmers then visit Humphries Diamond on Friday, March 26, 4:00 p.m. Staff Photo Pitcher Cal Barna had 12 strikeouts in six innings against Oakland Tech. Piedmont wins back to back with late heroics By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s baseball team improved its record to 2-1 after winning two consecutive games with great pitching coupled with late-hitting heroics. PHS recorded a 2-0 win against the visiting Oakland Tech Bulldogs on a sunny Saturday, March 20, and followed that with a 5-4 victory over Mt. Eden two days later. On Saturday, pitcher Cal Barna threw 12 strikeouts in six innings, while reliever Julian Scherman gained a save to close out the win in the seventh. Monday featured Ben Levinson throwing five innings with 11 strikeouts and just one hit; Scherman gained the victory. But as good as coach Eric Olson’s pitching staff is proving, the Highlanders’ bats have come through when it mattered most. Piedmont’s 2-0 victory against Tech featured sophomore Michael Aikawa hitting a game-winning RBI double in the bottom of the fifth. In the victory over Mt. Eden, senior slugger Lars Derr hit the game-winning RBI to the right field fence at Witter Field in the bottom of the seventh. 2-0 win over Oakland Tech Barna was dealing heat on the mound in Saturday’s victory against the Bulldogs. The University of Hawaii-bound player showed confidence on the mound, effectively mixing his arsenal of pitches between fastball, slider, sinker, changeup, and curveball. He made sure to praise catcher Davis Alazraqui for his performance as well. “I woke up feeling good and ready to play. My catcher [Davis Alazraqui] played great. Getting out of those first-inning jitters and Davis doing so well behind the plate made it even better. In the third, fourth, and fifth,” said Barna. The game remained scoreless through five innings, but a oneout double by Michael Aikawa broke the scoring drought in the bottom of the fifth. The inning started with PHS first baseman Garren Riley taking a fastball on his backside to reach first, then took second on a wild pitch. Aikawa, behind 1-2 in the count, found what he was looking for – a low fastball right in his wheelhouse. “I saw a low fastball, it’s what I like. I was waiting for it,” said Aikawa. With a tenuous 1-0 lead, the Highlanders added an insurance run in the bottom of the sixth with Nico Defazio singling to centerfield then advancing on a wild pitch. Evan McConathy reached base on a throwing error, advancing Defazio to third. He eventually scored on an infielder’s choice by Alazraqui for the 2-0 final. In the top of the seventh, Scherman entered the game as the closer, allowing a one-out single but swiftly got the job done with a strikeout and groundout. Final stats include: Barna’s stellar six innings and 12 strikeouts; he allowed three hits and one walk. Aikawa went 2-for-3 with one RBI, Alazraqui gained the other RBI. Lars Derr and Defazio had one hit. 5-4 win over Mt. Eden Playing at home on Monday, Piedmont won 5-4 with more stellar pitching and situational hitting. Macalester College-bound pitcher Ben Levinson had 11 strikeouts in five innings but missed getting the win when Mt. Eden mounted a comeback to tie the game 4-4 in the sixth inning. . In the bottom of the seventh. Defazio hit a fly ball to left field and advanced to second base on a fielding error. Enter Derr, Piedmont’s designated hitter. On the very first pitch, he went opposite-field to smack a fly ball off the right field fence to bring in Defazio to score the winning run. He finished Monday’s game 4-for-4 with five RBIs after the walk-off winner. “I was hitting batting practice the other day and came in feeling loose. I felt really comfortable at the plate,” said Derr. Final stats: Aikawa had one hit and a walk, Will Sprague scored two runs and drew a walk, Defazio scored twice, had one hit and a walk, Aiden Mitchell had a hit. On the mound, Scherman gained the win after entering in the top of the seventh. articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team returned for a busy opening week. They lost 7-0 to tough division foe Mt. Eden on March 17 on opening day, then torching the San Lorenzo Grizzlies in San Lorenzo 24-0 on Friday, March 19. They had their first win at home on Monday, March 22 in a 13-3 game against St. Mary’s. Both wins ended after the bottom of the fifth due to the 10-run rule. “Against San Lorenzo, we established more plate discipline and had some fun. Then today [St, Mary’s] we hit well and I was really impressed with the consistency the girls showed,” said Piedmont coach Gene Denard, a former coach at St. Mary’s. After losing to a tough Monarchs’ squad, the Highlanders’ responded mightily with 37 runs in the next two games. Junior slugger Chiarra Lundin, who lines up at catcher, cracked a home run against San Lorenzo to go along with three runs batted in and four runs scored. She also went 3-for-4 against St. Mary’s with three doubles, four RBIs, and two runs. “It was just getting past those first-game jitters,,” she said. “A lot of it comes from the energy from the team in the dugout – that really affects you. Getting your confidence back with hitting is a big deal,” said Lundin, who was The Post’s 2019 Freshman of the Year. 13-3 win over St. Mary’s St. Mary’s opened with a 1-0 lead in the top of the first, but Piedmont quickly responded with two runs in the bottom half and never relinquished the lead. Staff Photos Chiarra Lundin smacked a home run against San Lorenzo and had three doubles against St. Mary’s. Aside from the hitting junior Izzy Epstein threw a complete game with eight strikeouts and two walks allowed. Sophomore shortstop Leah Bell opened the game with a leadoff double, and Lundin had the first of three doubles to score Bell and Annabel Castronovo, who reached after getting hit by a pitch. Piedmont blew the game open 7-1 in the second inning with a five-run, two-out rally. Lundin hit to the opposite field fence to score Castronovo. With the bases loaded, sophomore Gretchen Gerhardy was hit by a pitch to bring in Hunt. Lundin then took home on a wild pitch, Epstein and Gerhardy scored on two straight throwing errors. Three more scored for Piedmont in the bottom of the third to make it 10-1. Bell led off with a single, then Epstein started a twoout rally with a single to score Morgan Hunt, shown running to third base, had a grand slam home run against San Lorenzo. Pitcher Izzy Epstein had eight strikeouts against St. Mary’s and 15 against Mt. Eden. Bell, Epstein and Hunt scored on another error. St. Mary’s added two runs in the top of the fourth, but Piedmont tacked on three in the bottom of the fifth for the final. Lundin smashed her third double to right field to score Hunt from first. Lundin stole third and scored on an Epstein groundout, finishing with Gerhardy scoring on a wild pitch. Full stats: Lundin’s three doubles and four RBIs; Bell had two hits, one double, and two runs scored, Castronovo scored two runs, Hunt scored three runs and walked twice, Gerhardy scored twice and had one RBI. Epstein had one hit, two RBIs, and one walk. PHS 24, San Lorenzo 0 Piedmont walked onto San Lorenzo’s field with a mission to respond to their 7-0 loss to Mt. Eden earlier. They scored 10 runs in the first inning and scored in each inning in the five-inning game. The Highlanders batted around the order in the first inning, with Lundin hitting the team’s first home run of the year, a three-run shot. Hunt, meanwhile, hit a grand slam homer in the top of the third on a line drive that rolled through the Grizzlies’ left field to the tree line near the freeway. Final stats: Lundin had two hits, three RBIs, and four runs scored. Hunt had two hits, two runs, and five RBIs. Denison had three RBIs and two runs scored. Banuelos scored twice and had two RBIs. Ronen had one hit, one RBI, and one run. Epstein had three hits, four runs, and two RBIs. Gerhardy had three hits as well with three RBIs and two runs scored. Castronovo pitched five shutout innings with eight strikeouts, two hits allowed, and no walks. Mt. Eden 7, PHS 0 Epstein pitched a complete seven innings with 15 strikeouts, but Lundin had the team’s only hit. Bell had a possible double snatched away from an incredible headfirst diving grab into the right-centerfield fence from Mt. Eden’s speedy centerfielder, Erin Londry. articles.text: Piedmont Softball teams came out swinging this past weekend, playing their first games of the 2021 spring season on Saturday and Sunday, March 20-21. This year the Foundation has five softball teams made up of 6 & Under, 8 & Under, and 10 & Under players, playing a single game for each division each weekend. “It’s been a long time coming, and with the loss of last season we have many relatively new players,” said Anne Hawkins, Commissioner for 6 & Under and 8 & Under teams. “We could not have been prouder of all the players. I am so impressed by their enthusiasm and willingness to try new things. I am grateful to all the parents who have come out to coach and ensure that we’ve been able to return to play safely while still having a ton of fun.” 8 & UNDER Night Wolves vs Killer Pandas The Night Wolves took on the Killer Pandas in the season opener. Between the two teams, six rookie pitchers took the mound, throwing strikes from the full wind-up, including Sophie Shartsis, Bailey Gregovich, and Evelyn MacMichael for the Night Wolves, and Mackenzie Ewen, Sarina Hill, and Alice Sorensen for the Killer Pandas. The Night Wolves came out swinging, setting the tone for the season with a single by Abby Gregovich off the first pitch of the game, and a second-inning triple to center by Eisa DeAvila. Sarina Hill on the mound for the Killer Pandas.

articles.text: Filoli House and Garden in Woodside. Filoli House and Gardens is hosting a virtual, botanical art graduate exhibit. Each artist chose a theme represented in five separate paintings. Themes range from the native buckeye, to the joy of cooking with vegetables. A total of ten botanical artists participated, all graduates of Filoli’s botanical art certificate program. The program includes over 200 hours of class and homework, then an average of 12 months on their final project. All student work is under the guidance of instructor Lee McCaffree. “I am fascinated by the subalpine plant communities of rock outcrops – and how these plants have established on such thin, skeletal soils,” said artist Elizabeth Bergstrom, whose illustrations detail plants of the Gravelly Mountain Range of southwest Montana. “I always decorate my family’s table with beautiful vases of flowers,” said artist Hyunjin Cho, whose illustrations include vivid watercolors of lilies. “I especially liked the lily and decided to use that as my theme, and have completed it in various ways, compositions, arrangements, and materials.” Visit https://filoli.org/botanical-art-exhibit/ to see the work of all 10 students. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is now streaming Hieroglyph, a play by Erika Dickerson-Despenza, through April 3. The play follows the story of 12-year-old Davis, who wrestles with the cultural landscape of living in a new city and attending a new school after Hurricane Katrina devastated her native city, New Orleans. She is reeling from the trauma of sexual assault and the divorce of her parents. The play deals with themes of environmental racism, sexual violence, and displacement, while examining the effects of a “state-sanctioned, man-made disaster on the most vulnerable members of the Katrina diaspora.” Jamella Cross plays Davis, in a cast that includes Safiya Fredericks, Khary Moye, and Anna Marie Sharpe. The play is directed by Margo Hall, and is co-produced by SF Playhouse and Jamella Cross and Khary Moye perform at SF Playhouse in Hieroglyph. Lorraine Hansberry Theatre. Play w r ig ht D icke r sonDespenza is a feminist poet and playwright, a cultural worker and educator from Chicago. Her residencies and fellowships include Tow Playwright-in-Residence at The Public Theater in New York (2019-2020), U.S. Water Alliance National Arts & Culture Delegate (2019), New York Stage and Film Fellow-in-Residence (2019), and New Harmony Project Writer-in Residence in New Harmony, Indiana (2019). To watch Hieroglyph, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/upcoming-plays/.

articles.text: Berkeley Rep productions will return to the stage this fall. Berkeley Rep has announced that live theater will return this fall, with seven productions planned for its 2021 season. The productions include Cambodian Rock Band, Goddess, Octet, The Ripple, The Wave that Carried Me Home, Sanctuary City, Swept Away, and Wintertime. Many of these will be West Coast or world premieres. The first show, Cambodian Rock Band, is an award-winning hit show across the country and off Broadway. With a live band playing contemporary Dengue Fever band classics, as well as Cambodian oldies, this play moves back and forth in time as father and daughter face the music of the past. San Francisco-born and Steinberg Award-winning playwright Lauren Yee makes her Berkeley Rep debut with Cambodian Rock Band, which is directed by Chay Yew. Berkeley Rep will follow state, county and Berkeley’s Department of Health Services guidelines when reopening. In the event that a production will be cancelled, ticket holders will be entitled to a refund. Single tickets for each individual production will go on sale to the general public 10 weeks in advance of that production’s opening date. Subscription packages are available for purchase now. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/season/ to learn more about the planned productions. articles.text: The Grammy-award winning Ying Quartet will perform on Sunday, April 11, as part of Music at Kohl Mansion’s Virtual Chamber series. The Ying Quartet came to prominence in the early 1990’s as a resident quartet of Jesup, Iowa. The Quartet, now in its third decade, has performed in the world’s most important concert halls and even at the White House. articles.text: Cristiana Pegoraro, a world-renowned pianist from Narnia, Italy, who has performed in Piedmont, has received United Nations patronage for her new music video release of “Rain.” Composed and performed by Pegoraro, “Rain” commemorates World Water Day, which has been celebrated on March 22 by the United Nations every year since 1992. Through her music, the pianist brings attention to our consumption of the valuable resource. The video features beautiful landscapes of Pegoraro’s homeland Umbria, a lush Italian region bordering Tuscany. The magnificent Marmore Waterfall and Lake Piediluco are the backdrop for “Rain.” The video was produced by Imprenditori di Sogni and directed by Yuri Napoli and Adriano Natale. This year’s theme is about what water means to people, its true value, and how we can better protect the resource. Pegoraro’s work Christiana Pegoraro in “Rain” is a tribute to Umbria, as well as a gift to “those who make themselves active and caring guardians.” “This work was a new experience, a way to express myself during the pandemic,” Pegoraro said. “When I was unable to perform and travel the world for concerts and activities, I brought my creativity to a new path and enriched my artistic vein of new stimuli.” To watch “Rain,” visit https:// www.youtube.com/watch?v=euPtUtEMqlo.
articles.title: Christiana Pegoraro’s music receives U.N. Patronage for World Water Day

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony has announced the launch of REAL Berkeley, a four-episode virtual film series that feature special guests from the Berkeley community, through curators, local videography, and chamber music performed by musicians of the orchestra. The series will begin Sunday, March 28 at 4 p.m. with writer and curator Kate Schatz. Schatz, a feminist writer, activist and educator, is the creator of the Rad Women book series, along with illustrator Miriam Klein Stahl. Her children’s book, Rad American Women A-Z, was published by the well known Bay Area-publisher City Lights in Spring 2015, and was on the New York Times bestseller list for 11 weeks. The first episode will feature three works by prominent female composers: Reena Esmail’s Meri Sakhi Ki Avaaz (My Sister’s Voice), Gabriella Smith’s Tessellations and Clara Shumann’s Piano Trio. The next episode will be released on May 16. REAL Berkeley is produced by Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel, in partnership with Symphony Music Director Joseph Young and Bay Area-based media company Reneff-Olson Productions. The series will shine a light on unique aspects of Berkeley that have had a positive and significant impact on both the orchestra, and its community members. “The importance of a strong and resilient community has been displayed throughout the past year as residents, businesses, organizations, and many others have all come together to provide support for one another during these difficult times,” Mandel said. “REAL Berkeley pays tribComposer Reena Esmail ute to a community that we are proud to represent. We look forward to celebrating these wonderful aspects of our city through adventurous music and imagery that represent the diversity and ethos of Berkeley.” Visit https://www.berkeleysymphony.org/ for more information on how to watch the upcoming series.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Perhaps every generation lives through some form of revolution that alters, sometimes profoundly, how they live. Imagine the seismic shifts caused by the Gutenberg press, electricity, the telephone, flight, or the car. We are living through a communication-techno revolution that continues to impact countless facets of our lives. The computer, in all its permutations, has changed everything, and there is no going back. The worldwide web, the online world, the hardware and the software, represent a gestalt that is reconfiguring our society and the world community in ways that we are still trying to comprehend. Just seven years ago the concept of a social network called Facebook was unimaginable. A sophomore sitting in a Harvard dorm room with some friends did imagine it. And in 2010 a movie arrived about those nascent years. We are told, some 500 million people have joined this electronic community of suggested intimacy. The Social Network is a remarkable film, written by Aaron Sorkin, creator of West Wing, a superb wordsmith whose signature style includes intelligent, snappy dialogue. The narrative is driven by conversation, in dorm rooms, sitting in front of screens, and in conference rooms where depositions are being taken, conversations that reveal the complexity and animosities and intentions of the many compelling characters. It’s simply wonderful writing, for which Sorkin received an Academy Award in 2010 for Best Screenplay. One example takes place in the opening scene between the film’s protagonist, Mark Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg), and his girlfriend, Erica (Rooney Mara), over beers in a Harvard hangout. The brief encounter is revelatory, and frames nicely Zuckerberg’s arrogant, enigmatic, computer persona. It’s a wonderful beginning to what proves to be an engaging story. At first blush, a narrative about the founding of Facebook would seem to lack intensity, peopled by nerds who can write computer code and understand algorithm apps. And yet because Andrew Garfield as Eduardo Saverin and Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg in David Fincher’s The Social Network. of David Fincher’s top drawer directing (Fight Club, Seven, Zodiac) and Sorkin’s dynamite script – based on the book, Accidental Billionaires by Ben Mezrich – the movie transcends the esoteric and captures the unsettling mood of a generation. The movie is filled with irony and is a study in contrasts. While Zuckerberg is brilliant seated in front of his computer, and shows flashes of real genius, he can’t marshal the skills to even adequately engage with others. Yet counterintuitively he constructs a network that is predicated on the desire to interact with others. His story turns out to be a riveting though often unflattering character study in which his one friend, the co-founder of Facebook, Eduardo Saverin (Andrew Garfield), is forced to sue Zuckerberg for his rightful share of the company. It’s tempting to extrapolate from the phenomenon known as Facebook (now a verb), and wonder if for all of our unrelenting contact with one another – cell phones, twitter, texting, social networking – are we not still caught in a riptide of loneliness and angst for which ultimately there is no antidote? If you have not seen the trailer to The Social Network, google “Choral version of Radio Head’s Creep.” Click on the first listing and you will view not only a preview of the film, but hear the haunting choral soundtrack performed by Scala, a Belgian choir, led by the Kolachny brothers, one directing the other on piano. It captures perfectly the tone of the film. A variation of this trailer should have been used before the final credits rolled, it’s that good. The Social Network (2010). Directed by David Fincher, with screenplay by Alan Sorkin. Starring Jason Eisenberg, Andrew Garfield, Justin Timberlake and Arnie Hammer. 2 hrs., 1 min. Rated PG-13
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Social Network – the revolution of social media

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The White Ribbon, nominated in 2009 for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film (from Germany), won the Palm d’Or at Cannes for Best Feature Film. Directed by Michael Haneke (Cache), it is artful, superbly cast, and beautifully photographed in stark black and white. The year is 1913, on the cusp of World War I. The film opens with a lovely shot of farmers and villagers harvesting the summer wheat, followed by a celebration heralding the end of one season and the beginning of another. It’s tempting to romanticize this bucolic setting – a small town surrounded by the flat expanse of rural northern Germany, filled with hardworking people whose lives follow the rhythms of the land. But then Haneke grimly pulls back a curtain and reveals that behind this seemingly benign image is a bleak and cruel reality that is astonishing in its severity. There is no overt violence in the film except for a set piece in the first minutes of act one when a doctor, riding home on his horse, is brought down by an all but invisible trip wire. At first the incident, called an accident, seems an aberration. But then other events take place of equal premeditation, testimony to the fact that a malevolent and mysterious perpetrator resides in the village. Though these chilling acts of violence are linchpins throughout the film, what is far more disturbing is the authoritarian, patriarchal cruelty leveled against the village’s children. The adults, charged with loving them, are so consistently perverse in their anger and punishments that it’s as if we’re watching and exorcism of their childhood innocence. In a particularly unsettling scene, the village Pastor, blinded by his own narrow Protestantism, ties white ribbons around the arms of his children as reminders that they have violated his trust, betrayed their purity, and disappointed their parents. He will not remove the ribbons until they have demonstrated that they are pure once again. The ribbons torment the children and are reminders of the hypocrisy and heartlessness of those adults to whom the children look for protection and, yes, love. The f ilm also answers Haneke’s own question: is the heart of man inherently dark? His answer is, in frame after frame, an unequivocal yes. He also asks the audience to extrapolate from the microcosm of this small village to the fascism that eventually grips all of Germany. To contemplate The White Ribbon is to feel simultaneously revulsion and admiration. Overly long (almost 2 ½ hours), unrelentingly dour and forbidding, it is also unfailingly honest regarding the ability of one generation to do great harm to the next, for reasons that are not limited to one people but to mankind. For some, this film will be more than they want to endure. Others will watch in fascination while being repelled. Regardless, all must acknowledge that Haneke is a superb filmmaker. The White Ribbon. Starring Christian Friedel, Leonie Benesch, Urich Tukur and Ursina Lardi. Directed by Michael Haneke. 2 hrs., 25 min. Rated R
articles.title: The White Ribbon a social view of Germany pre-WWI

articles.text: A scene from Saban’s Power Rangers. Movie review by Chris Honoré Saban’s Power Rangers is an unabashed movie for older teens with lots of CGI action and other wild, over-the-top stuff that kids will love. Personally, I’m a sucker for origin films and the first act (plus part of act two) is a good one. You have five kids who all look like they are on the Student Council but somehow end up in detention, ala The Breakfast Club. Each one feels powerless and definitely misunderstood. And there lies the real story of The Power Rangers and all other comic book movies that take wimpy kids and give them super powers. What adolescent doesn’t wish he or she had some serious mojo? You can start with Spiderman and go through the deep Marvel and DC comics bench and it’s all about power and how it’s used. Kids love this idea. It’s brilliant. In Power Rangers you have five young people who are given the gift (similar to Harry Potter). Now it’s up to them to make use of it. Acts two and three of this nostalgic reboot – based on a 1993 TV series – go nuts with Naomi Watts showing up as ultra-campy Rita Repulsa (how’s that for a name?). She is evil incarnate and wants to lay waste to all, including the bucolic town’s Krispy Kreme donut shop. Really. But here’s the deal: Rangers is all about friendship, bonding, and finally morphing. It’s also got a quirky robot named Alpha 5, portrayed by Bill Harder, as well as a very cool spaceship buried deep in a quarry. I mean, the kids could have gone back to school and hassled some bullies (one does get his mild comeuppance); but they have bigger things to do. Like save their families and their town. This is a popcorn movie. But a good one. And for kids, it’s been a dry spell. They were overdue for a kids’ movie that just goes for it with enthusiasm and has a good heart at its center. Saban’s Power Rangers. Directed by Dean Iaraelite. Starring Dacre Montgomery, Naomi Scott and RJ Cryer. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Saban’s Power Rangers is perfect for teenagers

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré If there was life left in this long-running franchise, which came perilously close to jumping the shark, it had to reside with X-Men, the early years, long before the mutant heroes were galvanized into a world-saving, shape-shifting crew. First Class, released in 2011, is based on the iconic Marvel comic books created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. It proves to be good entertainment. It’s always interesting to ask why mutants, aka Superheroes, have such generational appeal, seeming to resonate decade after decade, going back to the 30s. It was 1963 when Lee and Kirby revealed a series of contemporary mutants: Spider-Man, the Hulk, Iron Man, the Fantastic Four, and, of course, the X-Men, all following their antecedents: DC’s Superman (why is it hard to think of Superman as a mutant?) and Batman (a man with lots of suspend-your-disbelief gadgets and a great costume), to name just two. Actually, the list of those with extraordinary powers is huge, creating a comic book genre that has had countless incarnations. X-Men: First Class includes all the usual suspects – only younger. Think of this as “X-Men: Roots.” And, of course, there is the resident villain, pre-Magneto, played nicely by Kevin Bacon. The film opens in a Nazi concentration camp, the year is 1944, and stretches to the Cuban Missile Crisis when the U.S. and Russia played a serious game of chicken. The “X-Men” fans (and their numbers are considerable) should find this film solidly entertaining, a yearbook of their heroes. It has a globe-trotting plot, beginning in Germany and then Russia, Miami, Argentina, London and Las Vegas. Of course, these films increasingly take advantage of stateof-the art special effects. Filmmakers doing comic books and graphic novels must worship at the shrine of CGI. Or at least genuflect. There is nothing that the writers from DC and Marvel can put on paper that the special effects folks can’t put on the screen with stunning realism. They help create stories that teens and pre-teens will enjoy with jaw-dropping enthrallment. Tangentially, it’s hard not to think of these films as being a bit camp, bordering on kitsch. Mutants? Really? But then there is likely not an adolescent out there who can’t identify with these characters in some way. It’s not easy growing up, convinced you’re different. There likely are times when mutant superpowers would come in handy, say, walking down the middle school hall while mind reading. In fact, is it a stretch to think of Harry Potter, magician extraordinaire, and all the residents of Hogwarts, as mutants? An aside: X-Men: First Class is in 2-D. The debate still continues as to whether 3-D really enhances the movie-going experience. It likely pumps up the volume and the revenue, but does it have legs? This “X-Men” is engaging without the glasses and those hyped-up, leap-off-the-screen moments that have become de rigueur. X-Men: First Class. Starring James McAvoy, Michael Fassbinder, January Jones, Rose Byrne, Kevin Bacon and Jennifer Lawrence. Directed by Matthew Vaughn. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated PG. pages.text: Wednesday, March 24, 2021 19 MOVIES FOR KIDS Saban’s Power Rangers is perfect for teenagers A scene from Saban’s Power Rangers. Movie review by Chris Honoré Saban’s Power Rangers is an unabashed movie for older teens with lots of CGI action and other wild, over-the-top stuff that kids will love. Personally, I’m a sucker for origin films and the first act (plus part of act two) is a good one. You have five kids who all look like they are on the Student Council but somehow end up in detention, ala The Breakfast Club. Each one feels powerless and definitely misunderstood. This is a popcorn movie – but a good one. And there lies the real story of The Power Rangers and all other comic book movies that take wimpy kids and give them super powers. What adolescent doesn’t wish he or she had some serious mojo? You can start with Spiderman and go through the deep Marvel and DC comics bench and it’s all about power and how it’s used. Kids love this idea. It’s brilliant. In Power Rangers you have five young people who are given the gift (similar to Harry Potter). Now it’s up to them to make use of it. Acts two and three of this nostalgic reboot – based on a 1993 TV series – go nuts with Naomi Watts showing up as ultra-campy Rita Repulsa (how’s that for a name?). She is evil incarnate and wants to lay waste to all, including the bucolic town’s Krispy Kreme donut shop. Really. But here’s the deal: Rangers is all about friendship, bonding, and finally morphing. It’s also got a quirky robot named Alpha 5, portrayed by Bill Harder, as well as a very cool spaceship buried deep in a quarry. I mean, the kids could have gone back to school and hassled some bullies (one does get his mild comeuppance); but they have bigger things to do. Like save their families and their town. This is a popcorn movie. But a good one. And for kids, it’s been a dry spell. They were overdue for a kids’ movie that just goes for it with enthusiasm and has a good heart at its center. Saban’s Power Rangers. Directed by Dean Iaraelite. Starring Dacre Montgomery, Naomi Scott and RJ Cryer. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from X-Men:First Class. Kids love X-Men: First Class Film review by Chris Honoré If there was life left in this long-running franchise, which came perilously close to jumping the shark, it had to reside with X-Men, the early years, long before the mutant heroes were galvanized into a world-saving, shape-shifting crew. First Class, released in 2011, is based on the iconic Marvel comic books created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. It proves to be good entertainment. It’s always interesting to ask why mutants, aka Superheroes, have such generational appeal, seeming to resonate decade after decade, going back to the 30s. It was 1963 when Lee and Kirby revealed a series of contemporary mutants: Spider-Man, the Hulk, Iron Man, the Fantastic Four, and, of course, the X-Men, all following their antecedents: DC’s Superman (why is it hard to think of Superman as a mutant?) and Batman (a man with lots of suspend-your-disbelief gadgets and a great costume), to name just two. Actually, the list of those with extraordinary powers is huge, creating a comic book genre that has had countless incarnations. X-Men: First Class includes all the usual suspects – only younger. Think of this as “X-Men: Roots.” And, of course, there is the resident villain, pre-Magneto, played nicely by Kevin Bacon. The film opens in a Nazi concentration camp, the year is 1944, and stretches to the Cuban Missile Crisis when the U.S. and Russia played a serious game of chicken. The “X-Men” fans (and their numbers are considerable) should find this film solidly entertaining, a yearbook of their heroes. It has a globe-trotting plot, beginning in Germany and then Russia, Miami, Argentina, London and Las Vegas. Of course, these films increasingly take advantage of stateof-the art special effects. Filmmakers doing comic books and graphic novels must worship at the shrine of CGI. Or at least genuflect. There is nothing that the writers from DC and Marvel can put on paper that the special effects folks can’t put on the screen with stunning realism. They help create stories that teens and pre-teens will enjoy with jaw-dropping enthrallment. Tangentially, it’s hard not to think of these films as being a bit camp, bordering on kitsch. Mutants? Really? But then there is likely not an adolescent out there who can’t identify with these characters in some way. It’s not easy growing up, convinced you’re different. There likely are times when mutant superpowers would come in handy, say, walking down the middle school hall while mind reading. In fact, is it a stretch to think of Harry Potter, magician extraordinaire, and all the residents of Hogwarts, as mutants? An aside: X-Men: First Class is in 2-D. The debate still continues as to whether 3-D really enhances the movie-going experience. It likely pumps up the volume and the revenue, but does it have legs? This “X-Men” is engaging without the glasses and those hyped-up, leap-off-the-screen moments that have become de rigueur. X-Men: First Class. Starring James McAvoy, Michael Fassbinder, January Jones, Rose Byrne, Kevin Bacon and Jennifer Lawrence. Directed by Matthew Vaughn. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated PG. articles.text: Photos courtesy of Oakland Women’s Board Volunteers with the Oakland Museum Women’s Board sorting through the many donations they’ve received thus far. The highly anticipated annual White Elephant Sale, Oakland Museum of California’s largest fundraiser, will be entirely virtual this year. “We realized that we would not be able to have our traditional White Elephant Sale in the warehouse, with thousands of shoppers and all our volunteers. So we started planning and looking at alternative ways to raise money for the museum,” said Sherry Westernoff, President of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, a group of over 100 members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has generated over $23 million for the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont – some of whom are members of the Board. The board has been very fortunate in that they have been able to recruit volunteers with experience in e-commerce and online sales, explained Westernoff. An online store had to be built “from the ground up” in the transition. “We’ve been very lucky in that we have an incredible team of volunteers who are able to get [the virtual sale] up and running,” she said. “A number of our volunteers have been very excited to learn about this new way to sell our items.” The sale traditionally has a one-day Preview Sale a month in advance and two days of the actual Sale. Both events attract thousands of shoppers from the Bay Area and beyond to the white Elephant Sale Warehouse near the Estuary in Oakland’s Fruitvale District. Last year, hundreds of thousands of items were sold, but this year’s virtual sale will be scaled back a bit. “This year will be a smaller version of the traditional sale. We have hand-picked items to post onto our store [website]. We’ll have wonderful items – many very unique treasures and collectables,” Westernoff said. The team of volunteers is also smaller as many volunteers were not able to come into the warehouse due to Alameda County’s stay-at-home order. “The average age of our volunteers is over 65. One of our first priorities was to make sure that our warehouse was set up for social distancing, and that all proper equipment was in place so that our volunteers could come back to a very safe and healthy environment when they were allowed to return,” Westernoff explained. Due to the shutdown in March 2020, volunteers did not return to the warehouse until October, which is typically when volunteers begin planning for the next sale. “There’s usually a one-month break from the previous sale, and then we start all over again. It’s really a year-long operation – a real labor of love,” she said. It’s no secret that COVID-19 and subsequent closures have negatively impacted arts industries, and Oakland Museum is not immune to the fallout. This means that funds raised from this year’s White Elephant Sale are all the more crucial. The 61st sale, held on March 7 and 8 last year, raised over $2.4 million on behalf of OMCA - just one week before the county enacted its shelter-inplace order. That was able to help the museum keep afloat during the closures. “The money we earn from the online store will then go to the museum towards its coming year’s activities and exhibitions. With funding down and the museum still being closed, I think anything that we can raise will be so much appreciated by the Oakland Museum,” Westernoff said. Virtual shoppers can expect many unique treasures that you can only find at a sale like this - everything from antique items, vintage furniture, costume, jewelry, art, and more. The 2021 sale will open online Saturday, May 1, at 8 a.m. and will close on Sunday, May 23 at 6 p.m. There will be over 10,000 items for sale, all available on a first-come basis. Donations for the sale are still being accepted. For a list of items that can be accepted, visit: https:// www.whiteelephantsale.org/ donate. To schedule a pickup for your donation, call 510-839-5919. OMCA is dedicated to the art, history, and natural science of California and contains more than 1.8 million items dedicated to “telling the history of California” within its 110,000 square feet of gallery space. The Museum celebrated its 50th anniversary last year as a leading cultural institution of the Bay Area. The White Elephant Sale is touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale.

articles.text: Let me take you back in time. It is mid-March 1921. Boxing was yet to have its first million-dollar gate and Babe Ruth was just beginning to make baseball the great American pastime. Football and basketball were minor sports. The great sports personalities of the time were paid peanuts. Ty Cobb, the most famous and feared baseball player of his time, could barely make ends meet with his salary. There was little difference between classical music and pop music. Jazz was just in its early stages of development. So… what was the most popular form of entertainment? It was opera. And opera reigned supreme across every aspect of the population. There were lots of popular opera stars. They were paid thousands of dollars per performance. But nobody was as famous as Enrico Caruso. The paparazzi pestered Caruso just like they do with the stars of today. Caruso often wished he could go out without the long line of paparazzi following him. He would go to a small restaurant in Little Italy with his wife just for a quiet plate of spaghetti and a quiet game of cards with the chef. That made him very happy. There were great singers from the dawn of music. History books give us an idea of what they were able to do. Much of it is astonishing. But we really didn’t know what they sounded like until Edison invented the phonograph. The first singers to record for Edison were born in the 1820s. If you use your imagination, you have a vague idea how they sounded. And then along came Caruso. He single-handedly popularized the recording industry. Everybody started buying records - especially recordings by Caruso. He made so much money that he lived a luxurious life in New York City, where he a had a large suite atop the Knickerbocker Hotel. His summer retreat was the stupendous Bellosguardo estate in Florence, Italy. The public wanted to know everything about their favorite opera star. They knew that he was very generous. He was also one of the greatest caricaturists ever. And in addition to his singing talents, he was a composer and a poet. For all his fame, ironically he had stage fright that was almost paralyzing. Caruso’s career ended exactly 100 years ago, in mid-March 1921. Despite his disciplined work ethic, he simply didn’t take care of himself physically. He ate to excess, and despite good medical advice, he was a chain smoker of expensive Egyptian cigarettes. Those things did him in. He developed pleurisy and had Tenor Enrico Caruso surgery on his lungs. The surgeons operated on him in his suite at the Knickerbocker. The newspapers reported that he was making a good recovery. He returned to his hometown of Naples to recover. But it was too late, and he died five months later in August. My father attended a Caruso performance at the Metropolitan Opera around 1918. His description of the event was one of my greatest inspirations. The recordings give us a faint idea of how glorious his voice was. There are many stories describing what an inspiration he was, always willing to help young singers. One story is particularly funny. During a performance of La Bohème, the soprano singing the part of Mimi was having trouble with her costume. While she was singing, she went behind a large sofa and was able to pull off her slip and then returned to center stage. Caruso, seeing what happened got a mischievous look in his eye. He immediately went behind the sofa and held up the slip for the entire audience to see. The audience burst into laughter. The general director of the Metropolitan Opera disciplined both Caruso and the soprano. She said to Caruso, “Didn’t you know that we would be disciplined?” He replied: “Oh, yes, I knew. But didn’t we have fun!” Listen to some of the old 78 rpm recordings of Enrico Caruso. I think you’ll agree with me that his was a voice for all time. Try to imagine what the voice was like in person, not the fuzzy and scratchy sound that emanates from the primitive recording techniques. Not only did he have a great voice, and a great technique but he made the music come alive. You don’t even need to understand the words. The emotion is evident. As one of the great musicians of the time wrote, “It was one of those portraits that hang in the gallery of memory untarnished by the passing of time.” And now, exactly 100 years later, we can listen to the recordings of Enrico Caruso. His was a life cut short at the age of 47 and yet he lives in that gallery of memories to this very day.

articles.text: Dear Jim: We are considering doing a basement renovation but also would like to do some remodeling on the existing upstairs of our home at the same time. What is the process like for this type of project and what are first steps? How long does it take? Do we need to move out? Thanks for your help with this. –Charles S. Charles: I’ve written recent articles on the topic of basement renovations, but I wanted to take that one step further. What if you also want to work on the rest of your house at the same time? We will look at a recent job we are close to wrapping up to discuss how this went and what you might expect on a typical project. The nature of this job was to do a complete basement dig out and renovation along with a partial remodel of the upstairs including a new master bedroom and bath, new windows, and other cosmetic upgrades. What we encountered here may help you think about questions you may have if you wish to embark on similar projects in the future. Phase 1: The Dig Out For this recent multiple floor remodel, the general workflow involved starting at the bottom and working upwards. While noisy, the basement project alone did not require the clients to move out and they continued to live in the house while working remotely at home. What we call the “dig out” phase involved excavating the basement and crawlspace in its entirety to 9’ to achieve a final height of 8’, along with installing new foundations. It also involved adding exterior drainage, a new The dig out. concrete floor, and the installation of the interior structural walls required to remove the beams and other supports for the upstairs, which were temporary during construction. This part of the work took around 4 months to complete. Phase 2: The more challenging remodel Once the dig out was done, I swapped out our structural crew and brought in the remodeling team. Following the Dig Out, initial work downstairs also involved installing windows, stuccoing the outside, and installing the rest of the interior walls. Then, we completed all of the rough electrical, mechanical and plumbing work. Accommodations were made for tying in the utilities upstairs once we moved out of the basement. Our strategy changed at this point regarding the rest of the work. Because of the house lifting, there were some cracks in the plaster above. We were adding new electrical and mechanical (heating and air conditioning), and our clients wanted special heating registers that required cutting bigger holes in the walls. Given that there were also various plaster textures in different rooms that were going to be hard to duplicate, we decided it would make more sense to tear out the remaining plaster upstairs (except in the kitchen and bath which had already been remodeled). Now that the upstairs work had become more invasive, involving most of the spaces, the client agreed that they would move out for 4 months to allow us to work more effectively there. This new plan allowed us to do a number of things that would have been impossible otherwise, such as insulate the outside walls and the ceilings, add curved archways between some of the common rooms and change some of the trim details. Final Phase: The work nears completion Once the electrical, mechanical and plumbing were completed upstairs we were able to get our rough inspections and then sheetrock both the upstairs and downstairs at the same time. Our main focus continued to be the upstairs work, including trim, door installation, the bathroom remodeling, and floor repairs, refinishing and paint. Now that the upstairs is almost done, we are shifting our focus back to completing those same phases downstairs after the clients move back in a few weeks. The upstairs will be 100% complete (except for the master bath tile that is taking 4 months to arrive from Italy). What we learned With basement-only projects it is common for our customers to continue living in their homes throughout the job. We were originally hoping our clients could stay at home for the duration, as the remodel initially only involved the bedroom, bath and family room above. But we soon realized that we could accomplish more in a shorter period of time and make changes that would otherwise not be feasible if they moved out. Plus given all the social distancing and protective requirements for isolating the work area due to Covid, that was going to add another layer of complexity to the process of working in the same space as our clients. Our final plan – completing the rough basement first, having our customers move out for the minimum amount of time to complete the upstairs work, and finally finishing the downstairs – became the best approach. The upstairs with the plaster removed. How the design-build approach worked best As design-build contractors, we were able to adapt quickly to make changes. Working directly with our clients to make decisions minimized the need to involve the architect and the City of Oakland’s building department, which have been taking longer than usual to approve plan changes. (see previous articles we wrote about current challenges we’re facing with some East Bay city building departments). Fortunately, most of these decisions were non-structural alterations that didn’t affect the drawings except for a few minor changes the inspector let us defer until the end of the project. And because removing the plaster upstairs sped up our work, and we were able to give the owner a credit back for the wall repairs no longer needed, we achieved a better result in less time for a better price. Jim Gardner is a long-time Piedmont resident who has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. To schedule an estimate or for more information, please go to the website at jimgardnerconstruction.com. The living room is almost completed. New non-structural beams were added in the living room to accent the existing living room beams.
