Our main focus continued to be the upstairs work, including trim, door installation, the bathroom remodeling, and floor repairs, refinishing and paint. Now that the upstairs is almost done, we are shifting our focus back to completing those same phases downstairs after the clients move back in a few weeks. The upstairs will be 100% complete (except for the master bath tile that is taking 4 months to arrive from Italy). What we learned With basement-only projects it is common for our customers to continue living in their homes throughout the job. We were originally hoping our clients could stay at home for the duration, as the remodel initially only involved the bedroom, bath and family room above. But we soon realized that we could accomplish more in a shorter period of time and make changes that would otherwise not be feasible if they moved out. Plus given all the social distancing and protective requirements for isolating the work area due to Covid, that was going to add another layer of complexity to the process of working in the same space as our clients. Our final plan – completing the rough basement first, having our customers move out for the minimum amount of time to complete the upstairs work, and finally finishing the downstairs – became the best approach. The upstairs with the plaster removed. How the design-build approach worked best As design-build contractors, we were able to adapt quickly to make changes. Working directly with our clients to make decisions minimized the need to involve the architect and the City of Oakland’s building department, which have been taking longer than usual to approve plan changes. (see previous articles we wrote about current challenges we’re facing with some East Bay city building departments). Fortunately, most of these decisions were non-structural alterations that didn’t affect the drawings except for a few minor changes the inspector let us defer until the end of the project. And because removing the plaster upstairs sped up our work, and we were able to give the owner a credit back for the wall repairs no longer needed, we achieved a better result in less time for a better price. Jim Gardner is a long-time Piedmont resident who has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. To schedule an estimate or for more information, please go to the website at jimgardnerconstruction.com. The living room is almost completed. New non-structural beams were added in the living room to accent the existing living room beams.

articles.text: As I walk and look around Piedmont, I suspect that Craftsman homes and their closely related variations make up the most common architectural style in town, in fact, maybe even in the entire Bay Area. The Craftsman, or American Craftsman style of architecture developed to a large degree in tandem with the same style in England. Both are offshoots of the Arts and Crafts movement of the late 19th century, which idealized simplicity, harmony with nature, and honesty in construction. It developed as an alternative to the ornate and opulent style of the Victorian age and indeed resulted in simpler, cleaner and what the architects of the time thought of as a more honest design. Valued and expressed in this architecture was the hand crafting of the building components both on the exterior and interior of the buildings. Even though it may have been largely developed because of nostalgia for the handworked aesthetic of the pre-industrial era, Craftsman buildings were thoughtful and very well constructed by craftspeople who took pride in the quality of their work. Photos by Will Adams Like all good architecture, the inside of a Craftsman home is designed in sympathy with the character of the outside. Here that includes the use of natural materials, fitted exposed beams, wood paneling, and most notably, extensive built-in wood bookshelves, cabinets and window seats. Both Bernard Maybeck and his disciple Julia Morgan are among the famous architects who designed and worked closely with outstanding craftspeople to produce many buildings in this style throughout the East Bay, including a number of homes in Piedmont. Like all styles in the continually evolving field of architecture, there are variations of the American Craftsman genre. These include the Craftsman Bungalow, the Prairie style, and even the Mission Revival style (which we have discussed previously), which according to some historians falls into the Craftsman category, certainly having many of the same characteristics. The development of the Craftsman Prairie style, attributed mainly to Frank Lloyd Wright, is considered by many historians to be the first truly American architectural style! It shares many of the Craftsman characteristics but is generally distinguished and recognizable by a very strong horizontal feeling created by low slope hipped or even flat roofs with even larger overhangs than normal. Wright set an example for the Craftsman movement by completely designing these buildings inside and out, including the beautiful cabinetry, stained glass

articles.text: The Fairy Gate at Children’s Fairyland reopened for guests again on March 19, 2021, one year after first being forced to close due to the Covid pandemic. Since reopening, the park has made some changes. Puppeteer Randal Metz now walks through the park instead of putting on large performances on the puppet stage. The 10-acre space is open for business (and fun), including the slides, and nearly 60 storybook sets. Fairyland is operating under Covid red tier restrictions and anxiously awaits entering the orange tier to further unleash the magical world that has dazzled kids since 1950. When orange tier restrictions go into effect, the puppet shows, the Children’s Theater and amusement rides will all be fully open. Fairyland experienced a long delay before it reopened briefly on October 3, 2020, due to its complex status of whether it was an amusement park, historic garden, zoo, or an outdoor museum. It is all four, and eventually had to close again December 7 when the number of COVID cases increased significantly locally and across the entire country. Once Alameda County enters the orange tier, the Jolly Trolly, Alice’s Wonder Go-Round, Anansi’s Web Mini-Ferris Wheel, and the Flecto Carousel can reopen. It will then be classified as an amusement park as opposed to its current designation as an outdoor museum. “Our members really carried us through the pandemic. We received 3,500 donations in three months,” explained Executive Director Kymberly Miller. “They are extraordinary. We are just grateful for them and fully realize how much people really love it here.” Fairyland is currently operating three days a week, Friday through Sunday. Admission is split into two different shifts, morning and afternoon. Tickets may be purchased for either time slot. It is scheduled to move to a five-day schedule (Wednesday through Sunday) on March 31, with plans to return to its seven-day schedule on June 7. Miller has powered through a challenging first year as Executive Director and the place looks clean, bright and cheerful. “Willie the Whale is bright and shiny with a fresh coat of paint, as is our dragon,” said Miller. All indoor features such as the gift shop and member services are outdoors now, and the staff has been increased to meet Covid sanitation requirements. Paths are designated as one way and there is a separate exit now. All the water fountains were upgraded to modern water bottle fillers that turn on with the press of a knee. Masks are required for everyone 3 years old and up. Donations for maintenance, sanitation, and payroll are always welcome during a time of coronavirus. Children’s Fairyland is a non-profit located at Lake Merritt at 699 Bellevue Avenue in Oakland. Hours are Friday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 12 noon, and 1:00 to 4:00 p.m. Purchase tickets online at www.fairyland.org. For questions, call 510-452- 2259. Fairyland visitors enjoyed a little sunshine after the morning rain the day the park reopened. Kid’s enter the belly of Willie the Whale, a crowd favorite which received a fresh coat of paint during the latest closure. Children’s Fairyland Executive Director Kymberly Miller works her way through the iconic Alice in Wonderland maze, which is a bit easier to navigate when you are tall. Ryan Gorman (left) and Deborah Wood pose for a photo before Ryan heads down the Dragon Slide. Post reporter Jay Russell finds his way to Fairyland via the tunnel under The Woman Who Lives in a Shoe’s home. New Executive Director Kymberly Miller, does it all, even snapping this photo. Fairyland staffers Paul Jordan and Sella Davies describe renovations to the Old West Junction’s livery stable, bank, jail, and water-tower slide.

articles.text: Jay Russell Former Piedmont resident and Piedmont High alum Stephen Bechtel Jr. passed away March 15, 2021 in his Pacific Heights apartment in San Francisco. He was 95. Bechtel transformed the family Bechtel construction and engineering company into a global giant with high profile projects including BART, Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport and work on the Channel Tunnel between Britain and France. Unfettered by fortune and fame, Bechtel never forgot his roots. One of his many philanthropic endeavors, supporting the Piedmont Boy Scout Council, helped it become the top-performing council in the nation. Born Stephen Davison Bechtel Jr. on May 10, 1925 in Oakland, Steve Jr., as he was known, grew up in Piedmont and frequently accompanied his father on inspection trips to Bechtel company projects. One of those projects was the Hoover Dam, 60-stories tall, and considered one of the greatest engineering achievements in history. During Stephen Bechtel, Jr. summers Steve Jr. worked as a sweeper and surveyor’s stake puncher. At an Eagle Scout reunion at the Berkeley City Club in 2010, Bob Coleman, a past president of the Piedmont Scout Council, with tongue in cheek, told the audience that Hoover Dam was actually Mr. Bechtel’s Eagle Scout Project. As a sophomore at Piedmont High, Bechtel became an Eagle Scout. Before graduating from the Piedmont High School Class of 1943 he enlisted in the Marine Corps Reserve. After high school, he initially attended the University of Colorado to study engineering. He later transferred to Purdue University and graduated in 1946 with a Bachelor of Science degree in Civil Engineering. He married Elizabeth Mead Hogan (Betty) the same year. After briefly serving as a Lieutenant in the Marine Corps, he earned a Masters of Business Administration degree at Stanford in 1948. Also in 1948 he officially joined the Bechtel family company. He became its CEO at age 35, and ran the San Francisco-based, global company from [L to R] The Honorable George Schultz, Sam Cardoza, Gideon Cohn-Postar, Wes Motlow, Austin Kelley, Brendan Kelley, Larry Kelley, Stephen Bechtel, and [front center] scouts Will McBain and Connor Christiansen. Stephen Bechtel, Jr. (left) accepts a Giclee copy of a Norman Rockwell painting of the Boy Scouts from Bob Coleman, former President of the Piedmont Scout Council. 1960 to 1990, building major projects throughout the world, including nuclear, security, environmental, oil, gas, chemical and mining. After taking over leadership from his father, he expanded the Bechtel group’s sales 11-fold. Under his leadership as CEO, the Bechtel Group built King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia, Jubail Industrial City in Saudi Arabia, oil platforms in the North Sea, and liquefied natural gas plants in Algeria, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates. Locally, the largest Bechtel construction project was BART, the Bay Area’s first rapid transit system. He was named to presidential or national committees by U.S. Presidents Lyndon B. Johnson, Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford. He retired in 1990 at age 65 and was succeeded as CEO by his son, Riley Bechtel. Stephen Jr’s grandson Brendan Bechtel succeeded Riley in 2016. The company was started by Stephen Jr.’s grandfather, Warren A. Bechtel, in 1898. In the company’s 122- year history, more than 25,000 projects have been completed in 160 countries on all seven continents. But for all the success of the Bechtel Group, he never forgot his hometown and maintained a lifelong involvement with Scouting. In addition to his long list of accomplishments, Bechtel was also a distinguished Eagle Scout from Piedmont’s Troop 4. A lifelong Scout, Bechtel earned his rank of Eagle in 1940. Sixty-five years later, in 2005, he was recognized by the Boy Scouts of America with the Silver Buffalo award for distinguished service to the youth of America. In 2009 the S.D. Bechtel Jr. Foundation made a $50 million donation to the Boy Scouts of America allowed the acquisition of 14,000 acres of land in West Virginia. It was the largest donation in the history of the BSA. The land is now known as the The Summit Bechtel Family National Scout Reserve. “Mr. Bechtel was a champion of Scouting everywhere, but he remained close to Piedmont Scouting,” said former Piedmont Scout Executive Director Jo Hazelett. “He helped the Council in so many ways over the years and he was very kind.” “One memory that stands out is in 2010, when he learned that I had never been to a [National] Jamboree. He insisted on picking up my husband, my dog, and me as we ended a backpacking trip in the Continental Divide in Montana and taking us to the Jamboree in West Virginia on his jet,” said Hazelett. “We had a blast, but it sort of ruined commercial flying for us for a while.” Scouts from throughout the U.S. use The Summit year-round for high adventure and leadership training. It serves as the permanent home for the National Scout Jamboree, a gathering of thousands of members every four years. Stephen Bechtel’s bronze statue at the Summit Bechtel Reserve in West Virginia. Stephen Bechtel, Jr. in 1948, when he first joined his family’s company.
articles.title: Piedmont’s native son a world leader of industry, engineering, Scouting and philanthropy

articles.text: University of California, Berkeley’s Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (OLLI) is a learning community for audiences of age 50 and up. Taught by Cal faculty and other experts and scholars, OLLI provides a year-round lineup of lectures, workshops, discussion groups, clubs and activities. “This [spring] session is full of opportunities to both broaden your knowledge base, and develop new skills,” said OLLI Director Susan Hoffman. “Study the great European masters while you create your own botanical drawings, listen to Romantic string quartets while you decipher country music or Stephen Sondheim’s lyrics, and study the suburban fiction of your youth while developing your own legacy writing.” Offering this spring will showcase an eclectic and well-rounded repertoire of topics, from “Science in the Movies” to “Faith in Politics.” The speaker series will begin on Monday, March 29, and will continue through May 20. The schedule will continue in the same order each week through the end of May. Class times are between 9:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. To sign up for classes, call OLLI at (510) 642-9934, or sign up online at https://olli.berkeley.edu/.
articles.title: OLLI spring programs begin March 29

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 24, 2021 25 OLLI spring programs begin March 29 By Allyson Aleksey University of California, Berkeley’s Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (OLLI) is a learning community for audiences of age 50 and up. Taught by Cal faculty and other experts and scholars, OLLI provides a year-round lineup of lectures, workshops, discussion groups, clubs and activities. “This [spring] session is full of opportunities to both broaden your knowledge base, and develop new skills,” said OLLI Director Susan Hoffman. “Study the great European masters while you create your own botanical drawings, listen to Romantic string quartets while you decipher country music or Stephen Sondheim’s lyrics, and study the suburban fiction of your youth while developing your own legacy writing.” Offering this spring will showcase an eclectic and well-rounded repertoire of topics, from “Science in the Movies” to “Faith in Politics.” The speaker series will begin on Monday, March 29, and will continue through May 20. The schedule will continue in the same order each week through the end of May. Class times are between 9:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. To sign up for classes, call OLLI at (510) 642-9934, or sign up online at https://olli.berkeley.edu/. From at least 1931 to the late 1960s, Gustav Springman operated the successful Springman’s Pharmacy. Also, a full service store, the pharmacy delivered prescriptions and goods to their customers. Highland Sweet Shop In 1921, Joseph H. Cheatham opened the Highland Sweet Shop with a candy store, soda fountain, and tea room. His design included a deeply arched entrance with Churrigueresque relief and a decorative niche to the left. American Trust operated this branch until the 1960s when it became part of Wells Fargo Bank. A small office building behind the bank was the Alexander Allen realty office and later the Robert F. Atkinson realty company. Later, it became the local barber shop, which served generations of Piedmonters. Demolition In 1970, Wells Fargo Bank demolished the 1913 Albert Farr Commercial Center and built the new bank and commercial center. Today, the Wells Fargo Bank building houses a branch of the bank, a realty office, a barber shop, and office space upstairs. Sacks grocery on Piedmont Avenue, now the Piedmont Grocery. While residents enjoyed living in a completely residential city, they began to feel the need for a commercial center. To protect the city from what the Oakland Tribune called “an invasion of cheap and unsightly stores,” a group of residents, headed by Wallace Alexander, formed the Piedmont Commercial Association. The Association purchased 2 acres from Frank C. Havens directly across from Piedmont Park, and Alexander hired Albert Farr to design the commercial building. Farr did not design a square box for Piedmont’s stores. He designed three storefronts that gracefully followed the curve of Highland Avenue. For those who missed it, Ms. Singer took issue with the posting of socially progressive signs promoting the best interests of children and minorities, displayed on private property, as “blights” to the City of Piedmont. That someone in our community felt it necessary to scold her fellow Piedmont residents for publicly exercising their constitutionally protected freedom of expression is upsetting. Several other Piedmont community members told me that they were equally appalled by Ms. Singer’s tone-deaf, insensitive comments. I cannot think of a less controversial and less intrusive means of expressing my opinions than posting a modest sized sign in front of my own residence. Piedmonters put up signs on their lawns to show that they care about issues, people, and causes. Our BLM poster says to friends and community members that I am an ally to my black friends, and it publicly acknowledges the pain and hardships of historically marginalized peoples who have been wrongly arrested, prosecuted and convicted or victims of racial profiling or unjustified police violence. Recently Asians in local communities have been violently attacked because people have been brainwashed by racist, ignorant politicians into believing that Asian-Americans are somehow the cause of COVID. I support my fellow Asian community members and thus I have a sign out saying “In This House We Believe” to show support to women, immigrants, black lives and science. As the mother of two schoolaged children, I can attest to the fact that kids are struggling with many aspects of the pandemic. We decided to place a “Open Our Schools” sign in front of our home because the lack of full time in-person educational services in PUSD has been traumatic and challenging for our kids. Supporting the efforts to get kids safely back in school this fall feels right because I believe that in-person learning is best for all our children. Putting comfort and aesthetics above people is the kind of nonsense that gives Piedmont a bad reputation for being elitist. The world is very imperfect right now and there is much that needs to change. Putting up signs to support important causes is just a small step that gives many of us peace and hope of better things to come for the children we are raising in this community. Let’s try to be better and do more. Dr. Tanny Karunakar is an Emergency Physician and mom. A way to make Blair Park suitable for housing Editor: In my opinion, Blair Park is not suitable for housing because it is a north-facing hill with sporadic sunshine. It is a steep hill with little room for gardens in the back, and driveways to each garage would probably mean backing out into Moraga. Instead, I suggest the City consider a plan that includes a centrally located surface parking area for say 8 to 10 cars with turnaround possibility (eliminating the need to back out.) My suggestion includes a continuous sidewalk linking both sides of the parking area with a low fence that prevents small children and off-leash dogs from running onto Moraga Avenue, and a few picnic tables. In my mind, this represents the highest and best use of this lovely green area, now with yellow tulips, for the enjoyment of our citizens. –William Blackwell. articles.text: Sue Smegal has quietly and competently worked behind the scenes of Scouting in Piedmont for decades. For many years, her service on the Piedmont Council’s Executive Board, Advisory Board, and her continuing service on the Eagle Board of Review has upheld the Council’s mission to support youth and families throughout the community. She was an active volunteer supporter of Troop 15 when her son was in Scouts, serving in various unit roles. She’s never sought recognition and has consistently served youth in the community with humility and grace. Considered the consummate event organizer, she was responsible for chairing three major fundraising events for the Scouts. She co-chaired with Allan Dachs a banquet at the Claremont Hotel in 2006 honoring Bob Coleman and celebrating his receiving the Distinguished Eagle Award. In 2010 she chaired an Eagle Scout Celebration honoring 100 years of Scouting in Piedmont. The event was held at the Historic Berkeley City Club. When Bob Coleman introduced Stephen Bechtel, Bob said that Mr. Bechtel’s Eagle Project was building Hoover Dam. (Mr. Bechtel laughed harder than anyone.). In 2014 Sue chaired Roast and a Toast at Golden Gate Fields for Piedmont Post founder Gray Cathrall, a longtime member of the Piedmont Scout Advisory Board. He was presented with the Boy Scouts of America Distinguished Citizen Award. The dinner for Coleman and Cathrall raised significant funds for the Piedmont Council Boy Scouts of America Foundation. Outside of her work with Scouting, Sue served as a middle school teacher for 11 years, followed by eight years as a member of the Piedmont School Board. She recently was recognized with the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award by the Piedmont School District for over 45 years of youth-focused service. She also served with several other nonprofits, including the Ann Martin Center, Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland, and the Alameda County Child Abuse Prevention Task Force. She clearly lives the value of “Always Kids First”.

articles.text: All Piedmont school campuses have reopened for part-time in-person learning as of yesterday, March 16. However, at Piedmont Middle School, students are only in class for two and a half hours a week. This translates to only 30 hours of in-class instruction for the remaining 12 weeks of the year. a fraction of a normal 28-30 hour school week, it is 75% more time than middle schoolers receive. In contrast, elementary school students receive more than either. They are in class 9 hours weekly (2 hours, 15 minutes four times a week). This is more 360% more time than middle schoolers. “How are we supposed to explain to our older son that his little brother gets four times the amount of in person school than him and have that be fair and equitable?” asked Kevin Ma and Liana Wu parents of a 7th grader and a 4th grader. The reopening of schools aims to repair social-emotional health and learning loss, but many Piedmont students in middle school (grades 6 – 8) are being left behind. For anyone, the pre-teen years can be especially challenging and awkward. Students move to a new campus, now have multiple teachers, are introduced to new classmates and start receiving letter grades. All of this occurs while their bodies, minds and thoughts are rapidly changing. —Michelle McGilloway, parent Piedmont parents are flabbergasted by the anemic schedule and are now speaking out. articles.text: Piedmont High School freshmen and sophomores began their first week of in-person instruction yesterday March 16, as did half of the 7th graders at Piedmont Middle School. All Piedmont schools closed one year prior, on March 16, 2020, due to the COVID-19 Shelter in Place restrictions. Purple and white welcome banners and balloons fluttering in the chilly spring wind greeted students at both school campuses. Students, teachers, administrators and classified staff were all in their favorite first-day-of-school outfits with matching masks. Sixth graders have been on the PMS campus since February 23, but yesterday marked the first day for students at PHS. Half of the 8th graders will have their first day today, March 17, and high school juniors and seniors will step foot on campus in one week on March 23. It was a major day of firsts at 800 Magnolia, the high school campus. It’s $30 million, 3-story classroom building saw foot traffic by students for the first time. The campus has directional arrows all around campus to control the flow of traffic. Freshmen and new incoming students received tours of the campus last Thursday from upperclassmen to prevent lost students meandering through hallways. During the campus tours PHS junior Maya Kumar said, “Hopefully they work out the kinks the first week, so that when we go back in a week things will go smoothly.” “The freshmen and sophomores are the guinea pigs,” 11th grade tour guide Wesley Jeng, added. “I’m excited but a little nervous. A sign posted on City Hall read that it would be “closed to public access for all non-essential business, March 16 through March 29.” The limitation is still in place one year later. articles.text: I am so disappointed and frustrated to see the latest crop of obnoxious signs that have popped up around town (“Open our schools”, see March 10 Post front page article). In a town that prides itself on its beautiful parks and yards, as also featured in the March 10 Post, it is unbelievable how many signs have shown up in the last year – political signs that should have been removed months ago (per City code), BLM signs, “We believe in science”, Giving Campaign, Senior Class, Girl Scout cookies, plus the ongoing Covid warnings and usual contractor advertisements. Enough is enough. The Senior Class signs showed up in January, so they’ll be up until at least June; these “Open our schools” signs refer to fall classes, so they’ll be up until at least September. The proliferation of such blight not only detracts from the attractiveness of most yards but is also a distraction to drivers, who are constantly catching sight of them and taking their eyes off the road. Perhaps the most frustrating aspect is that the homeowners themselves who display these signs don’t have to look at them; rather, it’s the neighbors, walkers and drivers who are harassed by them. Not to mention the fact that I seriously doubt if anyone in the School District will be influenced by a street sign campaign. So, what is the point? Please respect your community and remove unnecessary signs – or, if you’re that passionate about an issue, put it on your own porch so you can look at it constantly instead of the rest of us. Thank you for your consideration of others. –Patricia Singer
articles.title: No more signs, please

articles.text: Even though Alameda County has not expanded eligibility for the COVID-19 vaccine to the extent allowed by California, almost half of Piedmont residents have received at least one dose of vaccine as of Sunday, March 14. On Monday, March 15, California permitted healthcare providers to vaccinate individuals ages 16 to 64 with certain health conditions that leaves them more at risk to COVID-19 mortality. However, as of press time, this additional group of people is not yet eligible in Alameda County. According to the Alameda County Public Health Department, the groups currently eligible for vaccination are based on age, employment and specific living situations. People aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are now eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. Alameda County residents reported signing up for vaccination due to health conditions, but access and availability has been spotty. Officially, ACPHD says that people with qualifying comorbidities will become eligible in “midMarch,” but an official timeline has not yet been revealed. The bulletin from the state directs healthcare providers to “use their clinical judgement” to vaccinate people “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk for morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 as a direct result of one or more of the severe health conditions.” The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found with the state’s guidance at the California Department of Public Health’s website at www.cdph.ca.gov. Residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. After people with comorbidities, the county is moving to an age-based priority framework in determining vaccine eligibility. In his first primetime address to the nation, President Joe Biden on Thursday, March 11 said that all adults should be eligible for vaccination by May 1. Even though supply, distribution and access issues have plagued the vaccine rollout in California, experts are hopeful that the state will hit this goal set out by the White House. A large factor in this timeline was the approval this month of a vaccine created by Johnson & Johnson. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine is the third COVID-19 vaccine available after ones produced by Moderna and Pfizer. Unlike the vaccines created by the latter two companies, though, the Johnson & Johnson vaccine requires only one dose. Moderna and Pfizer vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. As of press time, about 49 percent of Piedmont’s adult population – some 4,046 people – have received at least one COVID-19 vaccine. The county reports that 2,220 Piedmonters, or about 28 percent of the City’s adults, have been fully vaccinated. Piedmont leads all other municipalities in Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population, but other cities have begun to close the lead. In Oakland, over 30 percent of the population – more than 103,000 people – have received at least one dose and 14 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Across Alameda County, almost 590,500 total vaccine doses have been administered, and about 187,500 people have been fully vaccinated – this means that about 15 percent of the county’s population has been fully vaccinated. The state has administered over 12.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 16.7 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 200,000 people per day. About 19.5 million Californians are now eligible for the vaccine, or roughly half of the state’s population. “I have a great idea to discuss. Ask Dude to bring in the “Yes Team.”

articles.text: As Alameda County cautiously reopens, new cases of COVID-19 continue to drop according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County dipped to 1.4 percent as of Monday, March 15. The positivity rate has not been this low since mid-October, when positivity rates dipped before a rapid winter surge of the disease. California moved Alameda County into the Red Tier for reopening its economy last Tuesday, March 9 as new cases of COVID-19 decrease in the area. The Red Tier, or Substantial Tier, is the second-most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric. Before that, the county was in the Purple, or Widespread, Tier – the most restrictive tier. As of last week, indoor dining, movie theaters, museums and gyms reopened with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions on retail and grocery stores were reduced. Small private gatherings among no more than three households are permitted indoors, although gathering outdoors is strongly encouraged. Masks and distancing are required. As of yesterday, Tuesday, March 16, Alameda County meets all of the metrics to move into the Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, the second-least restrictive tier. To move into the Orange Tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 4.9 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 3.9 – right now there are 3.6 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to be below 5.2 percent – it is currently 2.4 percent in Alameda County. In the Orange Tier, more indoor business operations are permitted with modifications. San Mateo County was moved into the Orange Tier by the state this week and is the only Bay Area county currently not in the Red Tier. Neither ACPHD nor the state have remarked on Alameda County’s status this week, but the state typically waits for a county to meet metrics for at least a week before moving them to a less-restrictive tier. One new case was reported in Piedmont over the past seven days, the first case in March recorded in the City. In total, there have been 168 cases reported in Piedmont. Across Alameda County, the total caseload for the county is 82,168. There have been 25,502 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,910 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,330 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,530,055 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 55,372 deaths due to the disease statewide.
articles.title: One new case of COVID-19 in Piedmont in March

pages.text: Wednesday, March 17, 2021 3 Covid News Alameda County meets Orange Tier metrics; stays in Red Tier for now One new case of COVID-19 in Piedmont in March By Barry Eitel As Alameda County cautiously reopens, new cases of COVID-19 continue to drop according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County dipped to 1.4 percent as of Monday, March 15. The positivity rate has not been this low since mid-October, when positivity rates dipped before a rapid winter surge of the disease. California moved Alameda County into the Red Tier for reopening its economy last Tuesday, March 9 as new cases of COVID-19 decrease in the area. The Red Tier, or Substantial Tier, is the second-most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric. Before that, the county was in the Purple, or Widespread, Tier – the most restrictive tier. As of last week, indoor dining, movie theaters, museums and gyms reopened with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions on retail and grocery stores were reduced. Small private gatherings among no more than three households are permitted indoors, although gathering outdoors is strongly encouraged. Masks and distancing are required. As of yesterday, Tuesday, March 16, Alameda County meets all of the metrics to move into the Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, the second-least restrictive tier. To move into the Orange Tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 4.9 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 3.9 – right now there are 3.6 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to be below 5.2 percent – it is currently 2.4 percent in Alameda County. In the Orange Tier, more indoor business operations are permitted with modifications. San Mateo County was moved into the Orange Tier by the state this week and is the only Bay Area county currently not in the Red Tier. Neither ACPHD nor the state have remarked on Alameda County’s status this week, but the state typically waits for a county to meet metrics for at least a week before moving them to a less-restrictive tier. One new case was reported in Piedmont over the past seven days, the first case in March recorded in the City. In total, there have been 168 cases reported in Piedmont. Across Alameda County, the total caseload for the county is 82,168. There have been 25,502 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,910 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,330 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,530,055 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 55,372 deaths due to the disease statewide. Nearly half of Piedmonters have been vaccinated Demand for vaccine continues to outstrip supply in Alameda County By Barry Eitel Even though Alameda County has not expanded eligibility for the COVID-19 vaccine to the extent allowed by California, almost half of Piedmont residents have received at least one dose of vaccine as of Sunday, March 14. On Monday, March 15, California permitted healthcare providers to vaccinate individuals ages 16 to 64 with certain health conditions that leaves them more at risk to COVID-19 mortality. However, as of press time, this additional group of people is not yet eligible in Alameda County. According to the Alameda County Public Health Department, the groups currently eligible for vaccination are based on age, employment and specific living situations. People aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are now eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. Alameda County residents reported signing up for vaccination due to health conditions, but access and availability has been spotty. Officially, ACPHD says that people with qualifying comorbidities will become eligible in “midMarch,” but an official timeline has not yet been revealed. The bulletin from the state directs healthcare providers to “use their clinical judgement” to vaccinate people “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk for morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 as a direct result of one or more of the severe health conditions.” The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found with the state’s guidance at the California Department of Public Health’s website at www.cdph.ca.gov. Residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. After people with comorbidities, the county is moving to an age-based priority framework in determining vaccine eligibility. In his first primetime address to the nation, President Joe Biden on Thursday, March 11 said that all adults should be eligible for vaccination by May 1. Even though supply, distribution and access issues have plagued the vaccine rollout in California, experts are hopeful that the state will hit this goal set out by the White House. A large factor in this timeline was the approval this month of a vaccine created by Johnson & Johnson. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine is the third COVID-19 vaccine available after ones produced by Moderna and Pfizer. Unlike the vaccines created by the latter two companies, though, the Johnson & Johnson vaccine requires only one dose. Moderna and Pfizer vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. As of press time, about 49 percent of Piedmont’s adult population – some 4,046 people – have received at least one COVID-19 vaccine. The county reports that 2,220 Piedmonters, or about 28 percent of the City’s adults, have been fully vaccinated. Piedmont leads all other municipalities in Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population, but other cities have begun to close the lead. In Oakland, over 30 percent of the population – more than 103,000 people – have received at least one dose and 14 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Across Alameda County, almost 590,500 total vaccine doses have been administered, and about 187,500 people have been fully vaccinated – this means that about 15 percent of the county’s population has been fully vaccinated. The state has administered over 12.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 16.7 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 200,000 people per day. About 19.5 million Californians are now eligible for the vaccine, or roughly half of the state’s population. articles.text: The city has launched a community fair housing survey, which is accessible through its new “Piedmont is Home” website. The website will serve as a space for direct information from the city about a new housing policy in Piedmont, including project updates and public engagement opportunities. The website will focus on three main tenets of the city’s housing policy: • Senate Bill 2 Housing Programs Project • Measure A1 (Alameda County) grant • Update on the next Housing Element (2023–2031) Information and an FAQ (frequently-asked-questions) sample is available for each project. The website also includes an interactive “pinnable” map of Piedmont that asks users to place a pin in areas of the city that they believe could support more housing. Both the interactive map and the community fair housing survey were made accessible to residents on Friday March 12 and will be available until April 15. Completing the survey and “pinning” new housing sites on the map gives individuals a chance to win a $50 Mulberry’s Market gift card. The survey is one of several opportunities throughout the 18-month city-led effort to “ensure that new housing in Piedmont is feasible to develop, high in quality, affordable, and fits in the neighborhood context,” the website stated. The Piedmont is Home planning initiative will look specifically at multi-family housing, residential mixeduse development, and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) as avenues for affordable housing. The survey can be completed in 20-25 minutes. Visit https:// www.surveymonkey.com/r/piedmontishome-communitysurvey to be directed to the survey, or visit https://www.piedmontishome. org/ to view all current resources related to housing projects. Emails can be directed to piedmontishome@piedmont.ca.gov. The city has asked for volunteers to serve on its first Housing Advisory Committee, which will include five to seven Piedmont residents to be appointed by the City Council. All applications were due today, March 17. The committee’s first meeting is scheduled for April 20.

articles.text: The popular annual Piedmont Art Walk, now in its 2nd year, will take place on Sunday, May 2 between 12:00-5:00 p.m. Paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, and photography will be displayed and shown by local artists in front of their homes The community is invited to enjoy this outdoor art event and fundraiser hosted by local Piedmont artists and the Piedmont Arts Fund. Purchases support artists in town, and 20 percent of proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Arts Fund to support art in the schools. This fundraising event brings together live art, artists, and community members while following Alameda County’s COVID-19 guidelines to keep everyone safe. The event is spread out over Piedmont to avoid crowds and ensure social distancing. Organizers are working closely with City officials and Piedmont Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers to create a fun and safe event. Participating artists agreed to follow Alameda County’s COVID-19 social distancing guidelines and visitors are asked to do the same. When the COVID quarantine took effect in last March, the Piedmont Arts Fund (formerly PAINTS and CHIME) had to cancel their spring art events and fundraisers. The diminished school budget outlook for next school year makes this year’s fundraising critical for maintaining robust art programs in Piedmont schools. The Art Walk features a Who’s Who of Piedmont artists (see list below), and residents and students may not realize how many accomplished artists live in Piedmont. Plan now to take a walk on Sunday afternoon, May 2 to visit the artists during the second Annual Piedmont Art Walk. Who knows? You may find a new art piece that brightens your day and supports art in the schools. articles.text: Harry and Rosemary Wong are the foremost authorities on how to be an “effective teacher.” The Wongs are authors of many books on education, including The First Days of School: How To Be An Effective Teacher, which has been translated into seven languages and sold 3.9 million copies around the world. It is meant to walk any teacher, whether novice or veteran, through the necessary procedures on the all-important first day of school. Harry and his wife, Rosemary, are both teachers. Harry is a Bay Area native, a graduate of Lowell High School and UC Berkeley. He’s been awarded numerous accolades, including the Horace Mann Outstanding Educator Award, Upton Sinclair Award, Outstanding Secondary Teacher Award, the Science Teacher Achievement Recognition Award, the Outstanding Biology Teacher Award, and the Valley Forge Teacher’s Medal. Teachers have been using the “Wong Method” for decades because, in short, it works. Many teachers that I’ve spoken to say they followed The First Days of School religiously as novices, but then learned to tweak it and make it work for their teaching style and their students’ learning preferences. Of course, the text is often read in the summer, in preparation for the start of the academic year; but now with students returning to school in droves across the Bay Area, it never hurts to revisit a classic. Parents who have become impromptu educators in 2020 and 2021 may find these tips useful as they gear up to send their child back to school. beginning that, “what you do on the first day will determine your success or failure for the rest of the school year.” While quite “The first days are critical.” The text asserts in the very Harry and Rosemary Wong, authors of The First Days of School.

articles.text: dramatic, the Wongs believe that the tone you set on day one will determine how your students respond to you. For parents, this is just as critical, especially now. In the first days and weeks it’s important to be accessible, positive, transparent, and clear in your expectations. “If you do not have a plan, you are planning to fail.” The Wong Method calls for procedure, routine, and planning. Getting back into some semblance of a routine will be difficult and not without practice. Parents of students in hybrid learning models should replicate a typical school day to the best of their abilities so that the eventual return to normalcy will not be such a shock. “Teachers + Parents = good students.” The Wongs were steadfast in their belief that name recognition matters and improves student focus. “Drop-off” and “pick-up” is also a valuable time to chat with parents – not necessarily about their child, but simply for both parties to be “available.” In a COVID world, students are shuffled from car to classroom in haste. While there may be no way around this for now, as a parent it is imperative that your child knows that you want to have a positive relationship with their teacher. After all, you both are a team. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department is setting up another scavenger hunt scattered in Piedmont’s parks. This time the treasure is irresistible: Leprechaun Gold. A city-wide Spring Scavenger Hunt will begin this Saturday, March 20, and will continue for one week. Search through the parks in Piedmont for clues; unravel the riddles and work through the mind-boggling puzzles. The Rec. Department’s Halloween Treasure Hunt last Autumn took families on a quest to help the swashbuckling Explorer Cavendish find his buried pirate treasure. This challenge has an even grander storyline brought to life with an alluring backstory via the Actionbound app. Venture through Piedmont Park; comb through the four-leaf clovers in Dracena Park in search of the end of the rainbow. The week-long event will be a fun mystery that will have every member of the family wishing for the luck of the Irish to find the golden prize. The gold will vanish a week after the event starts, so don’t wait. Registration is $5 and signups are now available on the CommunityPass page: register.communitypass.net/reg/cat_program_list. cfm?season_id=24069. For more information, contact Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns at jstearns@piedmont.ca.gov. And remember to wear green for the Luck of the Irish. .

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. At the top of the essay include the following information: the title, your first and last name, city of residence (must be Piedmont), name of your school, and your current grade. Essays must be typed and double-spaced and submitted in a .pdf format. All entries are to be submitted to lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The deadline is April 17. Winners will be announced on May 1.
articles.title: Deadline to enter League of Women Voters contest is April 17

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Mock Trial team placed first at the Alameda County Philip A. Harley Memorial Mock Trial Competition on February 25, beating Bishop O’Dowd in the finals and advancing to the State competition. Led by history teacher and coach Dave Keller, Piedmont’s prosecution narrowly defeated O’Dowd’s defense, 772 to 761. The round was presided over by Judge Noël Wise from the Alameda County Superior Court and scored by a panel of five attorneys. Piedmont’s team was undefeated through the entire competition, which took place in January and February. In nearly two months of events, Piedmont beat Albany, Berkeley, Granada, and American high schools in the first four rounds and defeated Amador Valley in the semi-finals, 587 to 583. This marks the first time in over six years that PHS has won the Alameda County championship. The last time PHS competed in the county finals was 2018. Piedmont now advances to the state competition where it will represent Alameda County against other schools in California. Mock trial is a simulated trial competition based on the California criminal courts system. Each round requires about two hours. The Alameda County competition is named in memory of Philip Harley, a Piedmont resident and member of the Kazan Mcclain Satterley & Greenwood Law Firm.
articles.title: Piedmont wins Mock Trial County title, advances to State

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team made short work of the visitors from Alameda on Saturday. March 13, sweeping their league opponent 6-0. The tam was set to face Bishop O’Dowd two days earlier, but the match was canceled due to complications in the Dragons’ athletic department. “To be honest, I was worried before the match [with Alameda] because we were missing about a quarter of the team due to a fourday weekend. I guess I didn’t need to be. We blanked Alameda without losing a single set,” said Piedmont coach Jim Landes. Junior Charlie Lambert made his second appearance at No. 1 singles under some interesting circumstances. “Charlie took the SAT in the morning but still came back clear-headed enough to defeat Alameda’s Mason Conlin 7-6 (7-5), 6-2. Charlie hit some fabulous forehands, big serves and played some great defense too,” said Landes. Senior Sajan Srivastava won at No. 2 singles in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4, while freshman Ben Breber won at No. 3 in a 6-1, 7-5 victory. Senior Luke Hawkins was in good form at No. 4 singles winning in straight sets. “Luke is already getting in his late-season form winning decisively with strong ground strokes mixed in with his signature slices and drop shots,” said Landes. In doubles, Landes had high praise for the three doubles teams, each of whom won in straight sets, and all three doubles teams holding Alameda to three or fewer points. “All three teams overwhelmed their opponents,” commented Landes. “One of the Alameda coaches told me our doubles players seemed to always know where they needed to be. Well, Photo by Brian Mahany Sajan Srivastava won his No. 2 singles match against Alameda in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4. they should,” chuckled Landes. “They get an earful from Neil [Rothenberg], Corey [Reich] and myself,” he said. At No. 1 doubles, Charlie Olcott and Kai Baudendistel defeated the Hornets’ top pair handily, 6-2, 6-1. Oliver Maxwell and Monte Imburg won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 2 doubles, while Carson Hicks and Charlie Sullivan, in their varsity debut, easily winning No. 3 doubles, 6-1, 6-0 to complete the sweep. Halfway into the season, the boys ramp up this week with two matches in two days, today at Campolindo in Moraga, and a home match tomorrow, March 18, with Berkeley. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1) travels to Campolindo today for 3:30 p.m. matches, returning to the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, March 18 against Berkeley, also at 3:30 p.m. Staff Photo Charlie Sullivan made his varsity debut against Alameda at No. 3 doubles, helping win 6-1, 6-0 with Carson Hicks as his teammate. ®

articles.text: urday, March 13 in the Hercules Piedmont cross-country runners competed in a 4-school meet with league teams Berkeley, Castro Valley, and Alameda on Sathills. The boys’ team came away with the winning score of 35, led by junior Jack Stein who won with a time of 15:54 in a field of 30 runners. Competing in a field of 28 runners, PHS junior Ellie Black won the girls varsity race with a time of 19:45. It marked the second meet of the season for both the boys’ and girls’ teams. Stein’s 15:54 was an improvement of five seconds and a new PR for him. He was 11 seconds ahead of Alameda’s David Song, who placed 2nd. Piedmont sophomore Christian Taylor was 6th, and freshman Xavier Schulte-Sasse right behind him in 7th, 17:09. Junior Seamus Chamberlain-Car r placed 10th in 17:21, while senior Collin Mortimer was alongside in 11th, 17:22. “We have a really deep class this year. This team is really close together in time and running well,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. Big win for Black Black’s time of 19:45 demolished the field, besting Alameda’s Sophia Carpenter by 30 seconds. Although the Highlanders finished three of four, they were narrowly edged by Berkeley—both with 51 points, coming down to time difference. Piedmont junior Juliette Palacios was 8th in a field of 27 runners with a time of 21:17. Classmate Mara Lovric finished 11th in 21:48, senior Adri McAuliffe clocked a 22:27 in 14th, followed by senior Valerie Xiong in 17th, 22:47. The teams will have 10 days to learn of the location of its final meet of the league season on March 27. A prospective League Championship is tentatively scheduled to Hayward High on April 10. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team split its last two matches, both on the road, narrowly losing 4-3 to University in San Francisco on Thursday, March 11, and taking a close 4-3 win against league opponent Alameda two days later. “We played a lot of tennis this past week, we’re back at it! We lost a close one against University but got it back against Alameda,” said coach Jim Landes. The two matches featured Makenna Thiel at No. 1 singles winning both of her matches with 6-0, 6-0 victories against University’s top singles starter and Alameda’s Kyra Yee. She also completed a 6-0, 6-0 win against Berkeley. “The best bagels can be found in Piedmont,” joked Landes, referencing a recent viral New York Times article about bagels in Berkeley. “She continued her great play and produced another two bagels, bringing her total to six and counting.” No. 3 Bridgette McEfee won twice, 6-2, 6-0 over University, and 6-0, 6-1 against Alameda. It was a great way to respond after losing to Berkeley in the season opener. “Bridgette learned from her previous match against Berkeley where the consistency of her opponent was problematic. This time, Bridgette steadied her play and trounced both of her opponents,” said Landes. Photo by Brian Mahany Makenna Thiel added two more double-bagels to her record this season, defeating University and Alameda’s top singles starters by scores of 6-0, 6-0. season. “They make a good team. Kate has a lot of power and realized that she doesn’t need to overdo it to be effective,” said Landes. At No. 2 singles, Audrey Edel dropped a heated three-set match, 7-6 (7-4), 0-6, 6-4, while Jumper lost 6-3, 6-3 at No. 4. PHS loses 4-3 at University Playing at Mountain Lake Park in San Francisco’s Presidio Terrace neighborhood on March 11, Piedmont came up short in a 4-3 loss to University High. McEfee began the day with a slick 6-2, 6-0 win at No. 3 singles. University brought the contest back to 1-1 after their No. 1 doubles pair defeated Mahany and Becker, 6-4, 6-3, while the Red Devils took a 6-1, 7-6 (7-5) win at No. 4 singles against Jumper, making it 2-1 University. Dorman and LaForte won a three-set contest at No. 2 doubles, 2-6, 6-3, 10-8, to keep it deadlocked at 2-2. Thiel then won her match quickly 6-0, 6-0 at No. 1 singles, but Edel took a loss at No. 2 by scores of 6-4, 6-3. The clincher came down to Siemer and Frankel who fell in three sets, 6-1, 3-6, 10-1, at No. 3 doubles. Berkeley match The Highlanders hosted Berkeley yesterday, Tuesday, March 16 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. See next week’s Post for match details. McNeal also had a strong day, landing a perfect 30-yard high-arcing touchdown pass to Hilton in the back of the end zone and another 25-yard fade to Hilton on a corner route in one-onone coverage. The quarterback did well to buy extra seconds in the pocket against Miramonte’s pass rush. “It’s been a long time coming, it’s felt like we’ve been putting this together since last March just trying to get out and play football. Dealing with the pass rush did feel different because they were really trying to hit me, but it’s nothing we weren’t ready for. I think we did well responding to them today,” said McNeal. Receiver Ben Marshburn had one of the best plays of the evening, turning a 10-yard crossing route into a 40-yard touchdown by flattening a Miramonte defensive to the ground with a stiffarm. It ignited his Highlander teammates, coaches, and supporters into celebration. It was a good performance for Piedmont football ahead of the 2021 season after having just two weeks of full-pad practices. They are now set to face Castro Valley at Witter this Friday, March 19 at 7:00 p.m. for a league game in the newly created Mission League of the Western Alameda County Conference. It starts their brief five-game schedule. The WACC has planned to have three divisions for football since the conclusion of last season – Foothill, Shoreline, and Mission leagues – after adding some schools to its ranks: Washington High and Kennedy of Fremont will compete in the Mission Division; Moreau of Hayward and Union City’s James Logan jump to the Foothill, while Newark Memorial and Fremont’s American and Irvington High joins the Shoreline. Piedmont, now set for the Mission Division, has competed in the Foothill Division since 2016. After Castro Valley, they will face Mt. Eden in Hayward on March 27, head to Berkeley on April 2, then to Washington in Fremont on April 10, and finish against Kennedy on April 16. NEXT UP Piedmont opens the season against Castro Valley at Witter Field this Friday, March 19 at 7:00 p.m. Piedmont residents may have heard familiar sounds coming from Witter Field on Saturday, March 13. It was a football scrimmage between PHS and Miramonte; a long awaited reunion of pads cracking, helmets smacking, and student-athletes jawing back and forth. Football is back, and we sure did miss those Highlanders. Football was recently permitted by the state to begin full contact interscholastic games. “It’s been something we’ve been waiting for,” said coach Jerome Johnson. “Our kids are excited about this beginning, and I think our coaches were more excited than anyone. We executed the way we thought we would, and we weren’t as rusty as I anticipated. I’m excited for these kids. Let’s see what we can do next week against Castro Valley.” The Matadors rolled into town with a full-house, packing in both varsity and junior varsity rosters, in addition to their 40-plus member cheer squad. Parents from both schools gathered around the Witter Field concourse and chainlink fences, while other Piedmont students could be spotted peering in from Wildwood Avenue. The atmosphere was electric, and for the Piedmont High football team, it meant their very first competitive action since the 2019 fall concluded – a year and a half ago. “It’s great to be back and just to be out with all my teammates. It’s been a while to actually play against another team. Going against ourselves in practice, we don’t really hit each other or be violent with your teammates,” said senior Alex Hilton. The Matadors took the field first with both teams having four total offensive possessions. Brian Cain, who starts at both running back and linebacker, was eagerly awaiting that first hit to get the jitters out. “We had defense first, so the first-hit jitters were already gone by the time our offense got on the field. First carry, I don’t even remember how many yards I got, but it was a good welcome-back to get tackled and go to the ground,” said Cain. Despite a lack of live-action and full-contact drills, while possessing a vastly smaller roster compared to their Miramonte counterparts, Piedmont fought valiantly against the historically mighty Matadors. The Highlanders’ offense had several big plays on the day. Joe Hempeck scored on a 40-yard touchdown as a fullback, and quarterback Tommy McNeal did well to sell a misdirection run

articles.text: Piedmont Baseball and Softball is back, returning the long-standing tradition of youth sports on the hill after a year’s hiatus. All around town over the weekends of March 6 and March 13, some of the newest and youngest players joined the seasoned veterans to welcome back America’s pastime to the town on the hill. “The decision to cancel last year was necessary but heartbreaking,” said PBSF president Mike Bishop. “The return to play is almost as joyful to the same degree that last year was heartbreaking. Seeing the kids start to play again and have real games provides a sense of normalcy around town. We’re very excited that everyone is playing again.” It wasn’t the typical Opening Day fanfare with guest speakers, a singing of the National Anthem, and a ceremonial first pitch by the youngest and oldest players of the league, culminating with teams running through the balloon the PBSF’s famous balloon archway. This time, players received their jerseys one by one, and at least 17 games were played from age 5 to 14, bringing the familiar sound of that crack of the bat filling the air across the fields in Piedmont. “We usually have a big celebration on an open field. This year, we just returned to play. We distributed all the uniforms to the teams, scheduled games, and Broncos (U12) level slugger Brandon Dicke at the plate for the Bulldogs. went ahead and started playing,” added Bishop. The league has reunited some 500 Piedmont families with their favorite sport. Parents of kids have shown extreme gratitude for the PBSF return. “We started the season and had our second game this last weekend. The kids are having a blast and you can sense their excitement to be out on the field with their friends, and to make new friends. articles.text: The Piedmont High girls’ lacrosse team took a one-sided 20-6 loss to the Miramonte Matadors on the road in Orinda on Friday, March 12. It marked sweet-revenge for Miramonte, which last lost to the Highlanders 19-13 in the 2019 Division 2 North Coast Section semifinals, PHS went on to win the title—the last postseason lacrosse game to be played in the NCS. Photos by Todd Mashburn Piedmont senior Caroline Devine had two goals and three assists against Miramonte. Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! BEST of Oakland 2017 - 2019 License # 414359 RESPONSIVE • PROFESSIONAL • GUARANTEED 3333 Martin Luther King Jr. Way, Berkeley • (510) 228-4388 • AlbertNahmanPlumbing.com “It was a tough game, they had too many wheels. Their key player [Emerson Bohlig] is a Division 1 recruit to Northwestern and was really fast out there. Miramonte is a really good team,” said Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont kept it close in the first half, down 9-5 at halftime but within striking distance. Caroline Devine scored the first goal of the game for Piedmont after a minute of play, but Bohlig scored four of her nine goals for a 4-1 lead after nine minutes. The Matadors never relinquished the lead. “Contributions from the defense again,” said Chan. “Maya Galbreth and Bella Kjellen did well on defense. They were the main duo on double teams, but with Miramonte moving the ball and their speed, we didn’t have enough to keep a constant double.” Piedmont had their chances on net, but Miramonte goalie Mina Jenab stuffed several shots. Katherine Kinne managed to score have a first half hat trick and Devine added a second goal, but the Matador defenders played well. “We played really well in the first half; we double-teamed Emerson and forced her to pass the ball. We left about four or five shots on the table,” explained Chan. “Sadie [Tschider] had some beautiful feeds, but their senior goalie stuffed us.” Miramonte came out on fire in the second half, holding Piedmont scoreless until five minutes were left in the game. Despite the loss, Chan have high praise for his team’s tenacity while playing undermanned. “With just 14 players and only three true midfielders, it was just difficult to keep up the intensity for a full match. Our ‘tenacity award’ goes to Eliza Keville, she gave their offense fits by knocking down balls and playing scrappy defense. We moved her to midfield with eight minutes left and she scored on a wonderful cut,” said Chan. Final stats include: Kinne with three goals, Devine with two goals and three assists, Tschider had one assist, and Keville had one goal. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1) travels to Carondolet in Concord tomorrow, March 18 for a 7:00 p.m. match.

articles.text: The clouds broke over Piedmont on Saturday, March 13 right around 2:00 p.m., allowing the sun to shine down on Humphries Diamond. Piedmont‘s baseball team got its 2021 season started in a narrow 2-1 loss to Albany It marked the program’s first game the previous season ended after just four games. “It’s been over a year since my last organized baseball game. It’s so much fun to be out here with the guys,” said Piedmont coach Eric Olson. “It was a beautiful day and the field was fantastic. We’re just super grateful to be out here. Everyone is healthy, and it was a great ballgame, despite coming out on the short end,” The Highlanders went with three pitchers on the day, starting with senior Ben Levinson going three innings with four strikeouts and no walks. Classmate Cal Barna entered for 2.1 innings, striking out four as well, and Aidan Mitchell went 1.2 innings and didn’t allow any runs. With a shortened season of just 14 games – compared to 25 in previous years – Olson is eager to see his talented pitchers see some action. “You saw how quality our arms are. We threw three guys today and that is our plan – to get everybody into every ballgame. That’s my goal. I think the kids had a blast. We’ll ramp up to starters throwing longer, but we have quality players and I want to see all of them play,” said Olson. The Highlander pitchers did well to work out of jams. Levinson, his first full pitching session in a year, struck out Cougars’ first-baseman Ben Newton with a 3-2 count and a runner on third in the top of the 3rd inning. “It felt great,”’ he said. “I haven’t pitched in a really long time. It was exciting to get back out there and I felt really good with all my pitches. I’ve maybe thrown a max of 20-pitches in a row in the past year,” Levinson added. Levinson began the game by striking out the side in the top of the first. Albany’s starter Mateo Okimoto threw a complete game, gaining two of his eight strikeouts in the bottom half; some rust on the part of batters probably was a factor in the low-scoring affair. Staff Photo PHS shortstop Nico Defazio (8) turns a double play in the top of the sixth inning. Staff Photo Piedmont starting pitcher Ben Levinson pitched three innings and gained four strikeouts, allowing just one hit. “We had an inter-squad scrimmage, but that’s not really the same seeing other pitcher’s sliders and curveballs. It was fun to be out here again,” said senior slugger Lars Derr, who vats No. 3 in the lineup. He had the first extra-base hit of the season for Piedmont with a leadoff double in the bottom of the fourth. The Highlanders had a chance to break the game open in the bottom of the fifth inning after loading the bases with Will Sprague and Michael Aikawa drawing two-out walks, while Derr reached base on an infield single. But playing at the hot-corner was Albany third-baseman Kai Yovanovich, who snatched a hard hit ground ball by Evan McConathy with a diving grab and a throw to first, ending the inning with three Highlanders stranded on base. In the next inning, the top of the 6th, Albany scored its two runs after loading the bases with one out. Mitchell was able to force a groundball double-play to keep Piedmont alive. Piedmont‘s baseball team got its 2021 season started in a narrow 2-1 loss to Albany It marked the program’s first game the previous season ended after just four games. “It’s been over a year since my last organized baseball game.
