articles.text: Oakland Museum of California The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is offering online exhibitions that celebrate Women’s History Month on the museum’s website. You can access the Dorothea Lange: Photography as Activism archive online at any time. A world-renowned documentary photographer, Lange played an instrumental role in humanizing the impact the Great Depression had on Americans in the 1930’s. Her photography was designed to provoke social and political change, and questioned the role or class, race, and justice in a growing country. You can explore her powerful work on OMCA’s Dorothea Lange Digital Archive at https:// dorothealange.museumca.org/. Works by Mine Okubo, Helen Nestor, Favianna Rodriguez, Hung Liu, and Faith Ringgold are also available to view. You can view all featured artists, all of whom have had their work showcased at OMCA, by visiting the museum’s website at https://museumca.org/blog/celebrating-womens-history-month-omca. An upcoming, in-person exhibit at OMCA is Mothership: Voyage into Afrofuturism, which features contemporary works such as a Dora Milaje costume from the Marvel comic film Black Panther, as well as author Octavia E. Butler, avant-garde jazz musician Sun Ra, and filmmaker Kahlil Joseph. Mothership offers a “powerful reason to gather and celebrate Black imagination.”
articles.title: Dorothea Lange, Favianna Rodriquez among featured artists

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum reopened to the public on March 7 following San Francisco County’s move to the less restrictive red tier. The museum offered free admission on its first day, and is showcasing a mix of old and new exhibitions; including some that ended abruptly due to the pandemic and subsequent museum closures one year ago. One of the current exhibitions, Zheng Chongbin’s “I Look for the Sky,” is an art installation using transparency and light to explore how ephemeral changes can alter the viewer’s perception of place. Also currently on view is “After Hope: Videos of Resistance,” an exhibition that showcases an eclectic selection of more than 50 short videos that “explore the role of hope in contemporary art and activism.” Chanel Miller’s “I was, I am, I will be” inaugural work is still available to view on the façade of the building, facing Hyde Street. The art installation represents healing in a three-part process: reflecting on the past, being mindful in the present, and envisioning the future. Growing up in Palo Alto, Miller said she frequented the museum but never dreamed that one day she would be featured. “Whenever I was upset, I’d take a sharpie to the wall and sit for hours and let these ‘creatures’ come to life. I could create landscapes that don’t have narrow borders. That’s the scene that came out of this feeling,” Miller said. Even though the museum’s doors were closed due to shelterin-place orders, Miller’s exhibit was visible without even setting foot into the building. At night, Miller’s black and white figures are illuminated and visible from the street. The Asian Art Museum is open 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Thursdays and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Monday; the museum is closed on Tuesday and Wednesday. Reservations and timed ticketing is required, and tickets can be reserved at https://about. asianart.org/plan-your-visit/. The use of face masks and coverings and social distancing must be observed.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum reopens to the public

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of Modern Art Two weeks shy of a full year with its doors closed due to the COVID pandemic, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) announced on March 2, that it has reopened to the public following San Francisco County’s move to the less-restrictive Covid red tier. The museum officially opened with a Free Community Day and free parking on Sunday, March 7. The museum is reopening with a range of exhibitions, including Close to Home: Creativity in Crisis, which highlights seven local artists’ responses to a year of sheltering in place. Carolyn Drake, Rodney Ewing, Andres Gonzalez, James Gouldthorpe, Klea McKenna, Tucker Nichols, and Woody De Othello demonstrate a vast range of artistic, emotional and political responses. It will be on display until September 5. Off the Wall, also on display until September 5, shows five contemporary artists who transform one medium to another. Liz Deschenes, Oliver Chanarin, Sarah Sze, Dayanita Singh, and Lieko Shiga are the featured artists who transform photographic art into sculpture. Finally, New Work: Charles Gaines is a new installation of two major works that explore the history of racism in the United States. New Work begins with the 1857 Dred Scott Decision. “We are delighted to welcome our community back to SFMOMA after such a challenging year for so many,” said SFMOMA Director Neal Benezra. “Deep thanks to our dedicated staff, whose creativity helped keep our audiences engaged and inspired online during closure, and whose hard work enables us to safely reopen. We’re thrilled to provide safe and uplifting in-person art experiences in our spacious, airy galleries once again.” SFMOMA’s hours will be Friday through Monday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. SFMOMA is limiting the number of visitors each day to 25 percent of its regular capacity. Masks are required for all who enter the museum. For more information, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/off-the-wall/.
articles.title: SFMOMA reopens to the public

articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson San Francisco Ballet dancers perform Ratmansky’s Symphony No. 9, part of the Shostakovich Trilogy. Choreographer Alexei Ratmansky’s Symphony No. 9, part of the Shostakovich Trilogy, will stream through March 24 as part of the San Francisco Ballet’s third digital program. Created for 21 dancers and performed in May 2019 at the War Memorial Opera House, Symphony No. 9 highlights two lead couples and a solo male, all set against designer George Tsypin’s backdrop of grays and reds, recalling works of Socialist realism, set to the music of composer Dmitri Shostakovich. The performance is an archival capture. Ratmansky had Russia in mind when he created the Shostakovich Trilogy, according to American Ballet Theater Ballet Master Nancy Raffa. “This is an homage to Shostakovich, because of Alexei’s enormous admiration for his talent and for what he symbolizes for Russian people,” she said. “But it’s also an homage to [Ratmansky’s] heritage. He grew up listening to and loving Shostakovich, so this was like a gift [to the composer]. And a gift to Russia.” In creating Symphony No. 9, Raffa said that Ratmansky considered the time the piece was written, and the emotions behind what was happening in Shostakovich’s life - the regime, the Communist party, and the “Stalin mentality.” “He wanted them to be almost a caricature, expressing the sarcasm in parts of the score. But everything is abstract. He kept saying, ‘There’s no story, but there’s a lot of meaning’,” Raffa said. To watch Symphony No. 9, visit https://www.sf ballet.org/ productions/digital-program-03/.
articles.title: SF Ballet streaming Ratmansky’s Symphony No. 9 through March 24

articles.text: In this pandemic era, it’s still feasible to produce ensemble music with eloquent messages, up to a point. For the S.F. Symphony’s latest SoundBox aphoristic set “Lineage” curated by mezzo Julia Bullock, a nonet performs under a conductor on a sound stage, assisted by a far-off chorus, with some musicians entering remotely via modern technology – with most of them well-spaced and masked. Welcome to the unique era of Covid and formats which will try many fans attempting to explain to baffled grandchildren many years hence. With the technology, Bullock assembled a moving and high-quality program appropriate to our unique times, lifting spirits and consoling, while showing creativity of several black artists and of women composers. In the 45 minutes of the streamed SoundBox format we get a mosaic of pieces small and even smaller, ranging from Bach to 12th-century hymns to poet Langston Hughes’ lament on behalf of “the sick, depraved,… all the scum.” Anyone accessing this “Lineage” program should know that the vocalist/pianist Simone was a heroic American figure of a half-century ago, battling discrimination while producing deeply affective songs that stand the test of time. All this is carried out with imaginative camera work (a mite too restless in its brief, shifty images) and artistic background projections. And when Bullock isn’t “taking the stage” from distant recording studios, we have conductor Daniel Stewart (of the Santa Cruz Symphony) leading ensembles in the late George Walker’s “Lyric for Strings” and an excerpt from Elizabeth Ogoneck’s “In Silence” with Benjamin Beilman on lead violin, backed by SF Symphony players. “Lineage,” a Soundbox discovery program, created by mezzo Julia Bullock, with members of the S.F. Symphony, streaming on https://www.sfsymphonyplus.org/products/lineage-julia-bullock, or on www. sfsymphony.org. For further info, call (415) 864-6000. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, also writes reviews for www.artsSF.com. Mezzo soprano Julia Bullock It’s like digging into a bowl of mixed candies, only not as sugary. And Bullock’s bits-andpieces programming is superlative. If there is a more soulful mezzo than Bullock around these days, you have a long search ahead of you. She brings forth the depths of emotion and reflection with her keen musical sense and a voice even delving down in the contralto range for Nina Simone’s “Images” sung a cappella over a pedal-point held over from that 12th-century hymn by St. Hildegard – a brilliant juxtaposition that may have the latter composer smiling benignly from above.
articles.title: SF Symphony turns to streams in evolving format

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony has announced the launch of REAL Berkeley, a four-episode virtual film series that feature special guests from the Berkeley community, through curators, local videography, and chamber music performed by musicians of the orchestra. The series will begin Sunday, March 28 at 4 p.m. with writer and curator Kate Schatz. Schatz, originally from San Jose, is a feminist writer, activist, and educator. She is the creator of the Rad Women book series, along with illustrator Miriam Klein Stahl. Her children’s book, Rad American Women A-Z, was published by the well known Bay Area-publisher City Lights in Spring 2015, and spent a combined 11 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list. The first episode will feature three works by prominent female composers: Reena Esmail’s Meri Sakhi Ki Avaaz (My Sister’s Voice), Gabriella Smith’s Tessellations and Clara Shumann’s Piano Trio. The second episode will be released on May 16. REAL Berkeley is produced by Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel, in partnership with Symphony Music Director Joseph Young and Bay Area-based media company Reneff-Olson Productions. The series will shine a light on the unique aspects of the city that Author Kate Schatz have had a positive and significant impact on both the orchestra, and its community members. “The importance of a strong and resilient community has been displayed throughout the past year as residents, businesses, organizations, and many others have all come together to provide support for one another during these difficult times,” Mandel said. “REAL Berkeley pays tribute to a community that we are proud to represent. We look forward to celebrating these wonderful aspects of our city through adventurous music and imagery that represent the diversity and ethos of Berkeley.” Visit https://www.berkeleysymphony.org/ for more information on how to watch the upcoming series.
articles.title: REAL Berkeley virtual film series begins March 28

articles.text: Each weekend in March, San Francisco Opera will stream soldout performances from the 2018 Ring Festival production for free. The festival continues with free streaming of Richard Wagner’s four-part The Ring of the Nibelung, as well as live ticketed events online. It features additional interviews, panel discussions and lectures with artists and scholars, which has been updated, including the addition of two new free events. Each week will feature panel events with scholars, critics, and singers discussing the long and complicated history of “the Ring.” The festival officially began on March 6 with Das Rheingold, and archived performances are available on https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on/ringfestival/. The fesIréne Theorin in the role of the Valkyrie tival kicked off with an “Opening Salute”, a ticketed Zoom event with Director Francesca Zambello, conductor Donald Runnicles, and Greer Grimsley, who sang Wotan. The next event is Becoming Brunnhilde on March 19 at 1 p.m. It will feature a conversation with three acclaimed sopranos who have performed the role of the Valkyrie on the War Memorial Opera House stage: Jane Eaglen (1995 and 1999), Nina Stemme (2010 and 2011) and Iréne Theorin (2018). To watch the upcoming episode, visit https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on/ringfestival/ringevent-pdp29/. LMBInteriors.com | 510.531.8438
articles.title: San Francisco Opera’s Ring Festival continues

articles.text: Festival Opera, in collaboration with Piedmont Center for the Arts and the City of Piedmont, will open its 2021 season with a recital by Carrie Hennessey and Jennifer Reason. Hennessey and Reason, both internationally renowned artists, will perform in honor of Women’s History Month in a performance exploring the world of female composers, entitled “And Yet She Persisted: Women in Classical Music.” Listeners will hear music crafted by mezzo-soprano Pauline Viardot and composer Amy Beach, and Grammy Award-Winning Libby Larsen compose music to the text of letters written by the American frontierswoman Calamity Jane. Julia Seeholzer said that her “Portraits of Disquiet,” originally composed during the 2016 election, feels “more potent now in our present day.” Kendall A, who remains “off the grid” purposefully, offers a song that details the relationship between her and her parents. Kendall includes quotes directly from Dante’s Inferno in Italian. Barbara Strozzi’s Lagrime Mie, a baroque lament, is musically quoted in Seeholzer’s opening line. Hennessey, a soprano, and pianist Reason both bring their own unique energy to the concert. A series of piano and vocal recitals will be produced in accordance with strict COVIDCarrie Hennessey 19 testing, and safety measures as advised by the Center for Disease Control and the county. This first Artist Recital of the season will be streamed to the public on Sunday, March 28 starting at 5 p.m. Tickets for Festival Opera’s SalON Demand series are available for $40 per household for a high-definition video link, available to stream on any device. Tickets can be purchased at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ and-yet-she-persisted-women-i n- classical-music-t ickets-89304352723. Following its digital release, a live chat with the artists, as well as Festival Opera’s General Director Zachary Gordin, will be hosted by Ruchi Kapila on Facebook Live. Ticket buyers will have access to the live chat event.
articles.title: A return to Festival Opera

Symphony’s latest SoundBox aphoristic set “Lineage” curated by mezzo Julia Bullock, a nonet performs under a conductor on a sound stage, assisted by a far-off chorus, with some musicians entering remotely via modern technology – with most of them well-spaced and masked. Welcome to the unique era of Covid and formats which will try many fans attempting to explain to baffled grandchildren many years hence. With the technology, Bullock assembled a moving and high-quality program appropriate to our unique times, lifting spirits and consoling, while showing creativity of several black artists and of women composers. In the 45 minutes of the streamed SoundBox format we get a mosaic of pieces small and even smaller, ranging from Bach to 12th-century hymns to poet Langston Hughes’ lament on behalf of “the sick, depraved,… all the scum.” SF Symphony turns to streams in evolving format Anyone accessing this “Lineage” program should know that the vocalist/pianist Simone was a heroic American figure of a half-century ago, battling discrimination while producing deeply affective songs that stand the test of time. All this is carried out with imaginative camera work (a mite too restless in its brief, shifty images) and artistic background projections. And when Bullock isn’t “taking the stage” from distant recording studios, we have conductor Daniel Stewart (of the Santa Cruz Symphony) leading ensembles in the late George Walker’s “Lyric for Strings” and an excerpt from Elizabeth Ogoneck’s “In Silence” with Benjamin Beilman on lead violin, backed by SF Symphony players. “Lineage,” a Soundbox discovery program, created by mezzo Julia Bullock, with members of the S.F. Symphony, streaming on https://www.sfsymphonyplus.org/products/lineage-julia-bullock, or on www. sfsymphony.org. For further info, call (415) 864-6000. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, also writes reviews for www.artsSF.com. Mezzo soprano Julia Bullock It’s like digging into a bowl of mixed candies, only not as sugary. And Bullock’s bits-andpieces programming is superlative. If there is a more soulful mezzo than Bullock around these days, you have a long search ahead of you. She brings forth the depths of emotion and reflection with her keen musical sense and a voice even delving down in the contralto range for Nina Simone’s “Images” sung a cappella over a pedal-point held over from that 12th-century hymn by St. Hildegard – a brilliant juxtaposition that may have the latter composer smiling benignly from above. San Francisco Opera’s Ring Festival continues By Allyson Aleksey Each weekend in March, San Francisco Opera will stream soldout performances from the 2018 Ring Festival production for free. The festival continues with free streaming of Richard Wagner’s four-part The Ring of the Nibelung, as well as live ticketed events online. It features additional interviews, panel discussions and lectures with artists and scholars, which has been updated, including the addition of two new free events. Each week will feature panel events with scholars, critics, and singers discussing the long and complicated history of “the Ring.” The festival officially began on March 6 with Das Rheingold, and archived performances are available on https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on/ringfestival/. The fesIréne Theorin in the role of the Valkyrie tival kicked off with an “Opening Salute”, a ticketed Zoom event with Director Francesca Zambello, conductor Donald Runnicles, and Greer Grimsley, who sang Wotan. The next event is Becoming Brunnhilde on March 19 at 1 p.m. It will feature a conversation with three acclaimed sopranos who have performed the role of the Valkyrie on the War Memorial Opera House stage: Jane Eaglen (1995 and 1999), Nina Stemme (2010 and 2011) and Iréne Theorin (2018). To watch the upcoming episode, visit https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on/ringfestival/ringevent-pdp29/. LMBInteriors.com | 510.531.8438 Berkeley Symphony REAL Berkeley virtual film series begins March 28 By Allyson Aleksey Berkeley Symphony has announced the launch of REAL Berkeley, a four-episode virtual film series that feature special guests from the Berkeley community, through curators, local videography, and chamber music performed by musicians of the orchestra. The series will begin Sunday, March 28 at 4 p.m. with writer and curator Kate Schatz. Schatz, originally from San Jose, is a feminist writer, activist, and educator. She is the creator of the Rad Women book series, along with illustrator Miriam Klein Stahl. Her children’s book, Rad American Women A-Z, was published by the well known Bay Area-publisher City Lights in Spring 2015, and spent a combined 11 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list. The first episode will feature three works by prominent female composers: Reena Esmail’s Meri Sakhi Ki Avaaz (My Sister’s Voice), Gabriella Smith’s Tessellations and Clara Shumann’s Piano Trio. The second episode will be released on May 16. REAL Berkeley is produced by Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel, in partnership with Symphony Music Director Joseph Young and Bay Area-based media company Reneff-Olson Productions. The series will shine a light on the unique aspects of the city that Author Kate Schatz have had a positive and significant impact on both the orchestra, and its community members. “The importance of a strong and resilient community has been displayed throughout the past year as residents, businesses, organizations, and many others have all come together to provide support for one another during these difficult times,” Mandel said. “REAL Berkeley pays tribute to a community that we are proud to represent. We look forward to celebrating these wonderful aspects of our city through adventurous music and imagery that represent the diversity and ethos of Berkeley.” Visit https://www.berkeleysymphony.org/ for more information on how to watch the upcoming series. A return to Festival Opera by Carrie Hennessey By Allyson Aleksey Festival Opera, in collaboration with Piedmont Center for the Arts and the City of Piedmont, will open its 2021 season with a recital by Carrie Hennessey and Jennifer Reason. Hennessey and Reason, both internationally renowned artists, will perform in honor of Women’s History Month in a performance exploring the world of female composers, entitled “And Yet She Persisted: Women in Classical Music.” Listeners will hear music crafted by mezzo-soprano Pauline Viardot and composer Amy Beach, and Grammy Award-Winning Libby Larsen compose music to the text of letters written by the American frontierswoman Calamity Jane. Julia Seeholzer said that her “Portraits of Disquiet,” originally composed during the 2016 election, feels “more potent now in our present day.” Kendall A, who remains “off the grid” purposefully, offers a song that details the relationship between her and her parents. Kendall includes quotes directly from Dante’s Inferno in Italian. Barbara Strozzi’s Lagrime Mie, a baroque lament, is musically quoted in Seeholzer’s opening line. Hennessey, a soprano, and pianist Reason both bring their own unique energy to the concert. A series of piano and vocal recitals will be produced in accordance with strict COVIDCarrie Hennessey 19 testing, and safety measures as advised by the Center for Disease Control and the county. This first Artist Recital of the season will be streamed to the public on Sunday, March 28 starting at 5 p.m. Tickets for Festival Opera’s SalON Demand series are available for $40 per household for a high-definition video link, available to stream on any device. Tickets can be purchased at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ and-yet-she-persisted-women-i n- classical-music-t ickets-89304352723. Following its digital release, a live chat with the artists, as well as Festival Opera’s General Director Zachary Gordin, will be hosted by Ruchi Kapila on Facebook Live. Ticket buyers will have access to the live chat event.

articles.text: Baykali Ganambarr and Aisling Franciosi star in The Nightingale. Film review by Chris Honoré I encourage you to not miss The Nightingale. I feel compelled to say that as a narrative it’s a hard watch. But know that it’s powerful, provocative, and filled with moments that bleed into every scene. The performances to a person are extraordinary. The setting is Tasmania. The year is 1825. A young Irish woman, Clare (Aisling Franciosi), an ex-convict, is awaiting parole having completed a seven-year sentence for a theft committed in Ireland. Her release, which she is desperate to obtain, is dependent on a British lieutenant Hawkins (Sam Claffin). He requires Clare, considered an indentured servant, to wait on his troops in barracks and entertain them with her beautiful voice, singing songs from the homeland (hence the title). And though married with a child in arms, she is forced to yield to his constant sexual assaults while remaining mute as she awaits her freedom. She also understands that should her husband find out, his reaction would put her release in jeopardy. It is at this point that two rending violations occur, both involving Hawkins. The second, an unbearably difficult scene to watch, results in an unimaginable loss for Clare. And it is this scene that frames the rest of the story. Learning that Hawkins has left on foot with some men for the north, where he anticipates securing a promotion, Clare, on the verge of madness, sets out on a journey of jaw-clenching revenge. This deeply damaged woman, who has known only oppression, realizes that she can’t make the trek through rugged and deeply forested terrain alone, and so hires an aboriginal tracker named Billy (Baykali Ganambarr) to guide her, following Hawkins’ trail. Together they forge a fragile alliance, their harrowing, unrelenting voyage taking them into the darkest places in the human heart. They are forced to face an unforgiving barbarity and racist malevolence, all too familiar, carried out by the British colonizers toward the aboriginal people with impunity. However, despite their grudging partnership and Clare’s deep need for help – Billy is fully aware of the danger they both face. It is only gradually, after a tortuous walkabout, that they come to rely on one another and find common ground and unexpectedly come to recognize in each other a mutual humanity that transcends their individual circumstances and histories. Powerlessness and oppression have been part of Clare’s life experience; and it is all Billy has ever known. But in one powerful scene, the sky above now dark, a pervasive sense of hopelessness griping them, Clare reaches out and takes Billy’s hand in her own acknowledging that where they have been and where they are now has been for both of them transformative. The Nightingale is a remarkable piece of filmmaking, and for all of its dark vision it is ultimately hopeful. At one point Clare and Billy stand on a stretching beach and watch as a rising sun fills the horizon. They find in this moment a negation of Clare’s earlier admonishment to Billy when she says, “Welcome to the world, boy, full of misery from top to bottom.” The Nightingale. Directed by Jennifer Kent. Starring Aisling Franciosi, Sam Claflin and Baykali Ganambarr. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré In retrospect, the Soviet Union and the United States managed to navigate almost 50 years of adversarial encounters without a confrontation that would have taken us past the brink of the deterrence known as mutual assured destruction (aka MAD). Part of the kabuki dance that the two superpowers engaged in, however, was based upon elaborate and sustained spying. Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies, is a taut, well-made film based on a true story. It begins in 1957 with the arrest by the FBI of a Soviet spy, Rudolf Abel (Mark Ryance). The government, certain it has overwhelming evidence of his clandestine activity, decides to put him on trial. James Donovan (Tom Hanks), an insurance attorney, is selected to defend Abel who has stoically resisted all attempts by the CIA to extract information from him. What the government does not anticipate is that Donovan mounts a rigorous defense on Abel’s behalf, followed by an appeal of his conviction. Donovan was denigrated for carrying out what he felt was his constitutional obligation. He also suggested to the trial judge that Abel not be given the death penalty, arguing that should one of our spies be captured we just might need Abel should there be a proffered swap. So that’s the protracted set up. But Bridge of Spies, written by the award-winning writers and directors, brothers Joel and Ethan Coen, is a remarkable two-act story. Act one is the Abel capture and trial. Act two involves Donovan’s prescient statement about a possible trade at some point in the future – our guy for your guy. Our guy, as it turned out, was Francis Gary Powers, the U2 spy plane pilot, shot down in 1960 by the Russians. What could go wrong does go wrong. He is captured and put on trial. The Soviets now have their spy. This is a wonderful, spare, retro piece of moviemaking, delivered as only Spielberg can. Act two is launched. Donovan is selected to negotiate the exchange and arrives in East Germany just after the Berlin wall was built (1961) to talk to the Soviets and the East Germans about how to achieve the grudgingly agreed upon trade. It’s winter, the skies are leaden, East German buildings and streets are awash in institutional grays. Donovan, suffering from a tenacious cold, walks ever closer to a precipice, lost in a world of duplicity and obscure signals. He never knows if he is in discussion with the decision-makers or straw men. All that has occurred, from 1957 to 1962, leads to that intersection on a bridge which divides East from West. The outcome is always in doubt, the distrust between the players palpable. Tom Hanks gives a nuanced and spot-on performance. But not to forget Mark Ryance, accomplished stage actor, as Abe. His character is laconic in the extreme while laced with a humor so dry that it crackles. He is scene-stealing superb. As is this very entertaining film. The film won three Academy Awards in 2015: Best Performance by an Actor in a Supporting Role (Ryance); Best Motion Picture of the Year (Spielberg); and Best Writing, Original Screenplay (Coen brothers). Bridge of Spies. Directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Tom Hanks, Mark Rylance and Alan Alda. 2 hrs., 21 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Daisy Ridley and John Boyega star in The Force Awakens. Movie review by Chris Honoré Star Wars: The Force Awakens, released in 2015, is the seventh in what is one of the most successful franchises in film history. Over the decades – dating to the first release in May 1977 – the generic Star Wars has morphed into a cultural phenom, one that has captured the imaginations of moviegoers globally, even when the sequels and prequels didn’t quite reach the level of the initial trilogy (Star Wars IV: A New Hope, The Empire Strikes Back, and Return of the Jedi). Woven through all the Star Wars films is the question: what is there about these stories, these characters, that is so compelling and has consistently resonated with wide-ranging audiences, generating huge box office numbers? Perhaps the genius pf writer and original director George Lucas was in crafting a blend of high tech/low tech medieval lore (Princesses, Jedi Knights, mystical swords and dark Lords), combined with those mid-20th century Republic serials that kids flocked to every Saturday to watch cliff-hanging installments of action and adventure (Don Winslow of the Navy, Flash Gordon, or white hat/black hat westerns). And hands down, there’s never been a better example of a character from the dark side than Darth Vader (aka Lord Vader), his black mask menacing, covering a visage we can only imagine, every breath a wheezing sound, surrounded by armed stormtroopers. His persona – voice, stature – was inspired and breathtaking (pardon the pun). This was sci-fi fantasy unlike anything we had ever seen before. And so, began a narrative that would span three movies and would introduce a galaxy far, far away that was both myth and entertainment and proved to be irresistible. Ultimately, these films (to include The Force Awakens) are wonderfully constructed morality plays, primal fantasies that reduce our complex world, filled with ambiguity and uncertainty. They displayed good vs. evil, as exemplified by an outgunned Rebellion/Resistance struggling to defeat the forces of the Empire/The First Order. The loosely structured band of Rebels – never ominously militaristic – also represents the best impulses of men and women who yearn for Democracy. And they still possess those familiar X-Wing fighters, while remaining ready to confront Fascism’s jack-booted soldiers and their deadly armaments to include a Death Star equipped with a planet-destroying ray. Regarding this release, The Force Awakens, it is the first installment of a fresh trilogy that introduces a new generation of characters such as Rey (Daisy Ridley), a space junk scavenger; and Finn (John Boyega), a reluctant stormtrooper; as well as Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), a hotshot Resistance pilot sent in search of Luke Skywalker. And not to forget Darth Vader’s masked acolyte, Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), who kneels at the feet of the supreme leader, Snoke (Andy Serkis), one very large dude. The story manages to skirt a precipice of nostalgia while avoiding being maudlin as it builds a bridge between the original trilogy, featuring Han Solo (Harrison Ford), Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher), now a general in the Resistance, and at some point Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill). Clearly, the coming films will focus on what will be the ongoing battle, in all its permutations, between The Resistance and The Front. So, if The Force Awakens is considered in great part prologue, then some of the best is yet to come. In essence, it is the first reboot of the initial Star Wars and pays homage to those first three films that so completely solidified the brand (enough to survive Jar Jar Binks and company). For the proto fans who sat down for the first time, back in 1977, and watched the yellow block script scroll slowly into the dark distance, words that framed the battles ahead, well, even today that moment remains unforgettable, if not iconic. But that was then and this is now. Kids having that exact same experience with The Force Awakens won’t be disappointed. The force is beginning to awaken. Wait for it. Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Directed by J.J. Abrams. 2 hrs., 16 min. Starring Harrison Ford, Daisy Ridley and John Boyega. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Star Wars: The Force Awakens another gem in the series

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré Don’t let Wonder slip away without corralling the kids and taking them to see this remarkable film. It is a touching family narrative about a 10-year-old boy, Auggie (Jacob Tremblay), who since birth has suffered with a craniofacial, genetic disorder, an affliction that has distorted his face – he has endured some 27 surgeries. While at first blush it could be considered an early adolescent film, Wonder is so much more. It is life-affirming and brims with a surprising and unrelenting humanity. Auggie has always been homeschooled by his mom, Isabele (Julia Roberts). But now he finds himself confronting leaving the safety and embrace of his home and family – to include his father Nate (Owen Wilson) and his sister Via (Izabela Vidovic). He is about to begin his first year in middle school, a place where he will confront for the first time the judgment of his peers. As Isabel and Nate walk him to school, Isabel utters a quiet prayer, saying, “Please, don’t let the kids be cruel.” And yet she knows that by definition cruelty can define so many aspects of middle school. So, of course, Wonder is how Auggie strives to adjust to an environment for which he is profoundly unprepared. But to this film’s credit, it is never overly sentimental or maudlin; rather it inserts into the story other points of view. As example, Via, who for much of her life has felt on the periphery of the family, understanding intellectually that Auggie has required so much of her parents’ attention, yearns to find a closeness with her family that she has found to be elusive. Via’s perspective gives the movie a dimension that could easily have been left out. It brings to the film a conflicted complexity that adds to its sense of reality, one that is deeply humane. Wonder also doesn’t dwell on Auggie’s past medical experiences nor does a doctor appear to give sage diagnostic advice. This is a family’s story, one that is imperfect and at moments heart wrenching. But for all of its emotive power, it is also about the resilience of the human heart. For though Auggie is bright and understands the reactions of his fellow students to what they see, he also realizes that he is fearful and untrusting of anyone who approaches him with an outstretched hand. To its credit, Wonder is from the first frame understated. It is subtle and subdued. It gently presents its narrative and draws you not only into Auggie’s world but also into that of his family and thereby fashions a realm in which the audience is asked, repeatedly, to look beyond Auggie’s mask and see what is a mere shadow of who this young boy really is as he struggles with his isolation. It’s a wonderful movie going experience. There’s a line in the film that resonates from beginning to end: “When given a choice between being right and being kind, choose kind.” That alone sums up this film. Wonder. Directed by Stephen Chbosky. Starring Julia Roberts, Owen Wilson and Jacob Tremblay. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG-13. Coupon is good every Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday Not valid with other discounts. But now he finds himself confronting leaving the safety and embrace of his home and family – to include his father Nate (Owen Wilson) and his sister Via (Izabela Vidovic). He is about to begin his first year in middle school, a place where he will confront for the first time the judgment of his peers. As Isabel and Nate walk him to school, Isabel utters a quiet prayer, saying, “Please, don’t let the kids be cruel.” And yet she knows that by definition cruelty can define so many aspects of middle school. So, of course, Wonder is how Auggie strives to adjust to an environment for which he is profoundly unprepared. But to this film’s credit, it is never overly sentimental or maudlin; rather it inserts into the story other points of view. As example, Via, who for much of her life has felt on the periphery of the family, understanding intellectually that Auggie has required so much of her parents’ attention, yearns to find a closeness with her family that she has found to be elusive. Via’s perspective gives the movie a dimension that could easily have been left out. It brings to the film a conflicted complexity that adds to its sense of reality, one that is deeply humane. Wonder also doesn’t dwell on Auggie’s past medical experiences nor does a doctor appear to give sage diagnostic advice. This is a family’s story, one that is imperfect and at moments heart wrenching. But for all of its emotive power, it is also about the resilience of the human heart. For though Auggie is bright and understands the reactions of his fellow students to what they see, he also realizes that he is fearful and untrusting of anyone who approaches him with an outstretched hand. To its credit, Wonder is from the first frame understated. It is subtle and subdued. It gently presents its narrative and draws you not only into Auggie’s world but also into that of his family and thereby fashions a realm in which the audience is asked, repeatedly, to look beyond Auggie’s mask and see what is a mere shadow of who this young boy really is as he struggles with his isolation. It’s a wonderful movie going experience. There’s a line in the film that resonates from beginning to end: “When given a choice between being right and being kind, choose kind.” That alone sums up this film. Wonder. Directed by Stephen Chbosky. Starring Julia Roberts, Owen Wilson and Jacob Tremblay. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: The University of California at Berkeley Botanical Garden set a goal of raising $65,000 in a 24-hour fundraising campaign. It announced that a total of 339 donors raised $141,714, far exceeding anyone’s expectation. The money will be used to restore the Tropical House (pictured). The Big Give is UC Berkeley’s annual campus-wide 24-hour fundraiser. This year’s campaign was held on March 11. A total of 15,991 gifts raised $11.8 million for the university, a portion of which are dedicated to UC Botanical Garden’s Tropical House restoration project. The Tropical House has been a main fixture in the garden for nearly 50 years. It has been a challenge to maintain throughout its history, however. Heating and irrigation systems in the house regularly failed, resulting in plant damage. More recently, glass panes cracked and fell, and engineers advised that the building required renovation and seismic retrofitting. The Tropical House was closed to the public in early 2020. “As the Tropical House structural improvements near completion, Garden staff see a new opportunity to renovate and refresh the house’s interior. UCBG Advisory Board member and well-known landscape architect Ron Lutsko is donating his firm’s services to design a modern interior that will engage and educate visitors with an intimate tropical experience. The project includes adding a shade strucUC Botanical’s Tropical House ture to the adjacent patio where small groups gather, and refreshing exterior plantings around the building,” Garden Director Lew Feldman said. Volunteer Mara Melandry agreed that the Tropical House needed a “major overhaul.” “The first phase was to reskin the entire building with polycarbonate material to replace the glass. This material does not need whitewashing and is twin-walled for greater insulation; other project elements included earthquake retrofitting and a new heating system to replace the ancient heaters. By August of 2020 the reskinning and earthquake retrofitting were in process. The next step is the redesign of the interior to enhance the visitor experience,” she said. For more information on the UC Botanical Garden and the tropical house, visit https://botanicalgarden.berkeley.edu/collections/tropical-house.
articles.title: Fans of Botanical Garden raise $141,000 in Big Give campaign

articles.text: It has been a challenging year. You don’t need me to tell you that. But all indications are telling us that things are looking up. With this in mind I suggested a mini vacation. Bodega Bay seemed to be ideal. I called a hotel which had been recommended to me. I asked for a modestly priced room. The manager said they had a room with a queen bed and a partial view… Modestly priced. “Six fifty” she said. That’s the way people talk today. In my day 650 meant six dollars and fifty cents. The manager reassured me that one night was actually $650. After overcoming my initial shock, I thanked her very much and decided on a different plan. My son invited me to lunch with him at a crêpe restaurant on Solano Avenue. Suzette Crêpe Café is a pleasant restaurant which offers a wide range of crepe possibilities. It is owned by a young Cambodian couple who really know what they’re doing. The husband does the cooking, and though born in Cambodia, he was raised in Normandy, France. After his parents were killed by the Khmer Rouge regime, he was adopted by a French couple. And Normandy is sort of the home of the crêpe. I chose a crêpe with Gruyere cheese, spinach and avocado. It was very good and had just the right amount of “al dente” as the Italians say. For dessert I had a coffee latte and a lemon crêpe with sugar butter and lemon juice. Everything was made to order – authentic and a very pleasant atmosphere. Feel free to engage the owners in a lively conversation. It was lots of fun. On Saturday my wife and I went to Speisekammer, the wellknown German restaurant in Alameda. It resembles an informal German countryside restaurant. Its owner is from the north of Germany but raised in Berlin. Some of the recipes come from his grandmother who grew up in the German area of Poland. Because of this I chose as my main course stuffed cabbage leaves with ground beef and a tangy herb sauce. My grandmother’s specialty was stuffed cabbage leaves. But those at Speisekammer are just about as good. The large portion priced at $21 gives you two large cabbage rolls and a large portion of mashed potatoes. We began the dinner with a superb red bell pepper soup, followed by a vegetable strudel. I enjoyed speaking with the owner, and some of the background music took me back to those exciting days when the Weimar Republic lead the world in all artistic things. Unpleasant truths It is interesting to contemplate what great musicians of the past would have to say about the present state of musical affairs. The publicity machines proclaim that these are the best of times and that no musicians have ever been better. As an historian I look back at what the geniuses of the past had to say, and I would also like Socrates to lead an open discussion. I’d like to have a Helios to shine light on the situation, and a Diogenes to look for some honesty and sincerity. It doesn’t matter where you look, the artists of today are all in a form of lockstep thinking. They attempt to justify everything they do. However, a philosophy of perpetrating erroneous facts and misconceptions is fallacy. When I challenge them and ask them why they do things, the response is always the same: “That’s the way they did it.“ This response is simply not true. Among earlier musicians, there was no uniformity... anywhere. The fact is that every country had its unique way of doing things. Every individual city had its unique way of doing things. And, furthermore there were individual styles of playing based on the precepts of your teacher.
articles.title: Six fifty

articles.text: H e l g i To m a s s o n h a s announced that he will conclude his tenure as Artistic Director and Principal Choreographer of San Francisco Ballet by mid- 2022. He has led the ballet company for nearly 40 years. “The unprecedented challenges we faced as individuals and as a community during 2020 only served to reconfirm for me the power of dance as a form of artistic expression, connection, and humanity,” he said. “Over the past ten months, we had to innovate and completely reconceive how to bring dance to our audiences, since they could not come to us. “Looking to the 2022 season, my aim is to build on these achievements and to bring the Company back to the stage for live performances. Because of the year we all lived through together, the Company has never been stronger than it is today. As we look ahead the timing felt right to begin a transition to a new Artistic Director, who will build on this legacy and lead the Company into its next chapter.” Tomasson was a distinguished dancer before assuming artistic leadership of San Francisco Ballet in 1985. Under his direction, the Ballet became a company widely recognized as one of the finest in the world. He has choHelgi Tomasson reographed more than 50 works for the Company, including fulllength productions of Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, Romeo & Juliet (taped for Lincoln Center at the Movies’ Great American Dance), Giselle, and The Nutcracker (taped for PBS’s Great Performances). Tomasson has also connected San Francisco Ballet to the world, through co-commissions with American Ballet Theatre, The Royal Ballet, and Dutch National Ballet; and major tours to Paris, London, New York City, China, and his native Iceland. Last year, Tomasson was nominated to receive the San Francisco Arts Medallion, created by the Museum of Performance and Design to recognize those individuals whose leadership, action, and generosity have benefited the cultural life of the San Francisco Bay Area. The medal will be officially bestowed when in-person events can resume. “Helgi is a visionary whose creativity, brilliance, and stewardship of the Ballet is reflected both in the caliber of the Company’s work, as well as in the thoughtful transition plan that he helped conceive to support the organization’s ongoing vitality,” said Sunnie Evers, Co-Chair of the SF Ballet Board.
articles.title: Helgi Tomasson to retire after 4 decades leading SF Ballet

articles.text: The Sonoma International Film Festival (SIFF) will offer a mix of digital and live events this year. Three films will be offered as drive-in screenings. Six Minutes to Midnight (2020), directed by Andy Goddard and filmed in Wales, UK, will be shown on the opening night, Wednesday, March 24. Skywalker will be shown on Friday, March 26, and The Comeback Trail will close the festival on Saturday, March 27. All live drive-in screenings will begin at 6:15 p.m. at the Sonoma Skypark, an outdoor film venue with a 40-foot screen and FM transmission to car radios. The bulk of screenings will be available digitally. The festival’s catalog of films is available now to preview and preorder, and viewing access will begin on March 24. A “virtually everything pass” includes access to over 100 films, 20 film premieres, and cooking and wine tasting demos. To see a full catalog of films, visit: https://watch.eventive.org/ sonoma2021.
articles.title: Live drive-ins, virtual screenings, cooking demos

articles.text: Children’s Fairyland in Oakland Children’s Fair yland is reopening to the public this Friday, March 19, after a four-month closure due to COVID-19 health restrictions. The storybook theme park, located at Oakland’s Lake Merritt, has been closed since December 2020 due to Alameda County’s stay-at-home order. Now that the county has moved to the less restrictive “red tier,” Fairyland is ready to welcome guests once again. Per County guidance, the theme park will operate at reduced capacity with 1,000 attendees per day split between two sessions, mornings from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m., and afternoons from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. These shifts will serve as two timed-entry sessions to ensure social distancing between guests. Masks are required for everyone over the age of two, and must be worn at all times, including when waiting in line for entry. The only exception is when you are in a designated eating area. The café will be open with a limited menu that is expected to expand this summer. The indoor gift store is now open, and visitors will be allowed to enter one “social bubble” at a time. Fairyland encourages guests to order from the retail store online. Rides, puppet shows, and other entertainment will resume when Alameda County enters the “orange tier.” This includes the Jolly Trolly, Wonder-Go-Round, Anansi’s Magic Web, and the Flecto Carousel. On Sunday, March 21, the afternoon shift is available for Fairyland members only. The park is currently open three days a week, Friday through Sunday. Beginning March 31, the park will be open five days a week. Fairyland will be open all week beginning June 7. Tickets are available online now at https://childrensfairyland. brushfire.com/fairyland. Guests must reserve tickets in advance.
articles.title: Children’s Fairyland reopens this Friday

articles.text: If you’re a brand-new parent, or even if you’ve been one for a little while, you’re no doubt filled with the many joys your child brings you. But as caught up as you are with the feelings and experiences of today, you also need to think about the future – specifically, the financial issues that accompany a growing family. What are some of the key moves you need to make? Here’s “checklist” to consider: • Establish a budget If you’re going to meet the additional expenses of a child, plus make progress toward other objectives, such as paying down debts, you’ll need to know where your money is going. Setting a budget, and sticking to it, may seem difficult, but once you’ve gotten into the habit, it will become easier – and for many people, following a budget actually gives them more of a sense of control over their finances. Over time, expenses related to your children will change, so you’ll need to adjust your budget accordingly – for example, once a child is in school full-time, childcare expenses may drop, which could allow you to boost your savings. • Protect against the unexpected If something were to happen to you, how would your child, or children, be affected? Even a family with two working parents can face serious financial difficulties if one of the parents were to die prematurely, or even just drop out of the workforce temporarily due to illness or injury. To help ensure your family could still stay in your home and your children could still afford to pursue higher education, you’ll want to create an appropriate protection strategy involving both life and disability insurance. Your employer may offer both, but the coverage provided may not be sufficient for your needs, so you may need to purchase your own policies. And here’s another protection-related idea: Try to build an emergency fund containing three to six months’ worth of living expenses, with the money held in a low-risk, liquid account. Without such a fund, you might have to tap into your longer-term investments to pay unexpected costs, such as a major car repair. • Prepare for high cost of higher education You may already be thinking about sending your child to college. Financial checklist for new(er) parents If you’re a brand-new parent, or even if you’ve been one for a little while, you’re no doubt filled with the many joys your child brings you. But as caught up as you are with the feelings and experiences of today, you also need to think about the future – specifically, the financial issues that accompany a growing family. What are some of the key moves you need to make? Here’s “checklist” to consider: • Establish a budget If you’re going to meet the additional expenses of a child, plus make progress toward other objectives, such as paying down debts, you’ll need to know where your money is going. Setting a budget, and sticking to it, may seem difficult, but once you’ve gotten into the habit, it will become easier – and for many people, following a budget actually gives them more of a sense of control over their finances. Over time, expenses related to your children will change, so you’ll need to adjust your budget accordingly – for example, once a child is in school full-time, childcare expenses may drop, which could allow you to boost your savings. • Protect against the unexpected If something were to happen to you, how would your child, or children, be affected? Even a family with two working parents can face serious financial difficulties if one of the parents were to die prematurely, or even just drop out of the workforce temporarily due to illness or injury. To help ensure your family could still stay in your home and your children could still afford to pursue higher education, you’ll want to create an appropriate protection strategy involving both life and disability insurance. Your employer may offer both, but the coverage provided may not be sufficient for your needs, so you may need to purchase your own policies. And here’s another protection-related idea: Try to build an emergency fund containing three to six months’ worth of living expenses, with the money held in a low-risk, liquid account. Without such a fund, you might have to tap into your longer-term investments to pay unexpected costs, such as a major car repair. • Prepare for high cost of higher education You may already be thinking about sending your child to college. And it is indeed a good idea to start planning early because college is expensive, and it’s getting more so every year. However, you can prepare for these expenses through a college-savings vehicle, such as a 529 plan. A financial professional can help you pick the investment, or investment strategy, that’s appropriate for your needs. But whatever route you decide to follow, you won’t want to wait until your child is close to college age. • Keep long-term goals in mind Even while planning for the costs associated with raising a child, including saving for college, you can’t forget your other longterm goals. It isn’t selfish to build resources for your own retirement – in fact, you’ll ultimately be helping your family greatly by taking steps to maintain your financial independence throughout your life. So, during your working years, try to consistently contribute as much as you can afford to your IRA and your 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan. Having a child is obviously a life-changing event, and one with considerable financial challenges. But they can be manageable if you make the right moves at the right times. articles.text: Dr. Joel Parrott has announced that he will retire this spring after serving 37 years as President and Director of the Oakland Zoo. After three years of working as a veterinarian at the zoo from 1981- 1984, he was handed the reigns as the zoo’s new Director. Over a span of nearly four decades, Parrot has transformed the Oakland Zoo into a shining model of excellence, now world renowned. “After 37 years, my time has come,” Parrott said with a smile. “I have been working towards a goal for so long, right from high school. Really, there’s nothing like liberty and freedom.” Wearing his signature Australian bush hat, Dr. Parrott speaks at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the Karibu Village in 2000. During Dr. Joel Parrott’s 37-year tenure, Oakland Zoo expanded from 17 full-time employees to 180 and added 780 volunteers. Bruck has known Parrott for those 37 years through the Oakland Rotary Club. “He set the zoo on a course to really thrive and excel in the future. He has not only built up the zoo but has established a great legacy with the conservation and educational programs. articles.text: The Kistler family recently lost its cherished patriarch. Henry B, (Harry) Kistler died recently at the grand age of 98. He was a father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, yet so much more. Reflecting on his life, Harry often said, “I don’t know how one person can be so lucky.” Born in 1922, Harry attended the Le Rosey School in Switzerland, Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire, and had just started his freshman year at Yale when World War II broke out. During the war, he served as a submariner in the Pacific. After the war ended, Harry resumed his studies at Yale, playing hockey and earning an undergraduate degree in Chemical Engineering. He went on to earn a graduate degree in Chemical Engineering at the University of Cincinnati. In 1949, Harry joined the Bechtel Corporation where he spent his entire 37-year professional career in a variety of positions including Project Engineer and Project Manager in the Engineering, Business Development, and Project Management departments. His work took him to Kuwait and other countries around the globe. Harry inherited a true love of sports from his father, an All-American football player in college. Harry loved skiing and spending time in the mountains. As a young father, he taught all his children how to ski on the slopes around Lake Tahoe. If snow had fallen the night before, 1946 and they had six children: Stephen, Henry, David, John, Lisa, and Maria. He was always a steady, guiding force in each of their lives. Years later, Harry met and fell in love with Ardagh Marie Veitch and they married in 1971. Ardagh Marie’s three children, Blake, Roxanne, and Edward, joined the large Kistler family, and Harry welcomed them with open arms. Each year, Ardagh Marie and Harry’s Christmas parties were the highlight of the holiday season for family and countless friends over several decades. Harry’s upbeat, positive personality was infectious and won everyone over. His winning smile, hearty laugh, strong hugs, powerful handshakes, and joy for living made everyone want to be in his presence. Harry is predeceased by Ardagh-Marie, who died three years ago. His memory will endure forever in the lives of his children, his 10 grandchildren, and three great-grandchildren. It is time to say goodbye and thank you to a well-loved and well-lived man. He has left us with many stories, unique sayings, and a legacy that makes us proud as family members. When asked what advice he would give his grandchildren, Harry said, “Work hard, play hard, enjoy life – but the last one after the first two.” The family is incredibly grateful to his caregivers, Nicky and Emma, for their love, care and devotion. Henry B. (Harry) Kistler, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away at age 98. he would rally the whole family to be up before dawn to be the first on the chairlift and the chance to make fresh tracks in the new snow. It was a passion he enjoyed well into his 70s. His tradition of making the “first chair” has been passed on to his children and their families. Harry also loved to play golf and would often take his children out at sunrise so that they could be the first group on the course. At age 80, he shot an 80, a remarkable achievement. He was a familiar sight walking for miles on trails in the East Bay hills with his walking sticks, even in the rain. He walked regularly until he was in his 90s. Above all else, Harry thrived in the company and love of his family. He married Sally Ede in

articles.text: University of California, Berkeley’s Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (OLLI) is a learning community for audiences of age 50 and up. Taught by Cal faculty and other experts and scholars, OLLI provides a year-round lineup of lectures, workshops, discussion groups, clubs and activities. “This [spring] session is full of opportunities to both broaden your knowledge base, and develop new skills,” said OLLI Director Susan Hoffman. “Study the great European masters while you create your own botanical drawings, listen to Romantic string quartets while you decipher country music or Stephen Sondheim’s lyrics, and study the suburban fiction of your youth while developing your own legacy writing.” Offering this spring will showcase an eclectic and well-rounded repertoire of topics, from “Science in the Movies” to “Faith in Politics.” The speaker series will begin on Monday, March 29, and will continue through May 20. The schedule will continue in the same order each week through the end of May. Class times are between 9:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. To sign up for classes, call OLLI at (510) 642-9934, or sign up online at https://olli.berkeley.edu/.

It might be 3-year-olds or 10-year-olds and their families and the schools that support that. That is exactly the group that you want to reach, because that’s when core values are established. And if those visits to the zoo with your family are a warm memory you are going to have a bond to nature and you will step up to protect it. Q: What specific conservation efforts does the Oakland Zoo participate in? A: We try to support animals in the wild that we actually have here at the zoo. We have elephants on exhibit here, so we raise money and support for elephant conservation in Kenya and Tanzania In the case of protecting chimpanzees, for over 20 years we have been supporting the Budongo Forest Preserve in Uganda, by supporting ranger patrols in the preserve. We support [ARCAS] a rehabilitation center in Guatemala. [Which annually provides care for 250-350 animals like spider monkeys, jaguars and marine turtles that have been rescued from poachers.] We support the effort to reintroduce bison to the American West in the Black Feet Native American’s Reservation in Glacier National Park. And right here at home, we help the threatened yellow legged frog. [The Foothill yellow-legged frogs are reared at the Oakland Zoo. They are the last remaining population surrounding the area effected by the Camp Fire. Field biologists had to add water to the pools as they scooped up the tadpoles with teaspoons literally an hour or so before the isolated pools they were in dried up.] There’s also the vaccination program for the riparian brush rabbit, an effort to reintroduce wolves in Northern California. And the California condor reintroduction program is huge. Q: What are your thoughts on people that are critical or even opposed to the existence of zoos? A: The truth is that animals are adaptable. You can’t put animals, especially wildlife, in cages. The grand question is, is it even feasible to provide a quality life for them? We are constantly asking are they happy here? Our grizzly bears come from Alaska. Their mothers had to be euthanized, so we’ve got four orphans. They are cubs, so they can’t just go back to the wild. It’s an enormous educational opportunity, because how many people in the East Bay are heading for Alaska and are going to see a grizzly bear? That is incredibly important because just seeing them on film does not make you really appreciate them. We’ve got to take care of them here in the zoo and we’ve got to take care of them in the wild. If a zoo is still putting them in cages, that doesn’t work. Q: What are your proudest achievements during your tenure? A: A couple of things have been paramount: we constantly improved the quality of the life for the animals with better exhibits. We tore down the cages and got rid of that past. When I started at the zoo we had about 17 full time employees. We are now at about 180 full time employees, but with seasonal and weekend crews our staff is at about 250- 300. I’m also proud to watch the staff and our volunteer program grow to a point where they now generate their own energy, they come up their own ideas. We have around 780 docents and volunteers to help our keepers and help with horticulture. In the early 80’s we were just financially trying to stay alive. It took until 1988 to stabilize financially – a big achievement at the time. Then we hit the pandemic and the bottom fell out of the whole thing. For me, the great irony was at the other end of my career with the pandemic, we were just fighting to stay alive. It’s crazy, I was thinking, what’s this all about!? We always grew very carefully. As more attendance accrued, we added more staff. We were very careful financially with our business model. When we were in dire straits this summer, the 13,000 donations we received were extremely gratifying for me. Not only did we begin to understand fully how important the zoo was to the community, but we certainly learned how crucial the community is to us. It is really a mutual love affair I am so proud of. articles.text: Photo by Brian Mahany A large Japanese Maple can be viewed next to the Tea House in Piedmont Park. Heritage Tree nominations are due this Friday, March 19. The Heritage Tree program is an opportunity for the community to seek out and to recognize the distinctive trees in Piedmont’s urban forest. Nominated trees will be considered based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits and must grow on public property, such as parks, medians, and streets. An example of a Heritage Tree with excellent aesthetics is the stunning large Japanese Maple, Acer palmatum, next to the Tea House in Piedmont Park. It was nominated by Eileen Ruby in 2020. Japanese Maples have been cultivated in Japan for hundreds of years and around the world since the early 1800s. Some are shrub sized, while others can grow to a height of over 30 feet. They can be upright or weeping and have palmately lobed leaves that vary widely in shape and color. Most have vibrant fall colors. A Japanese Maple is a lovely focal point in any park, garden or patio. They can be grown in large containers and make excellent bonsai trees, although they otherwise do not require pruning. The 2021 Heritage Trees will be announced at the Park Commission hearing on April 7 and honored at this year’s virtual Arbor Day celebration on April 30. To nominate a tree, complete the downloadable form on the City’s website, https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city_news___notifications/heritage_tree_nominations_open, For more information, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or call 510-420-3064. Amber Brumfiel and Brian Mahany are members of the Piedmont Park Commission.

articles.text: A newly installed lawn sign advocates for guaranteeing Staff photo full-time instruction of Piedmont students. Approximately 400 lawn signs have been distributed by a group of parents who are urging the school district to open schools for full-time, in-person learning. The group, Advocates for Full-time In-person Piedmont Schools, organized the campaign in an effort to get a definitive commitment from the school district and school board that classes in all grades, beginning in August 2021 at the start of the next academic year, would be full-time and with in-person instruction. “We define reopening as fulltime and in-person - that is what students need and want after being at home in virtual learning for a year,” said Rebecca Pelle, a campaign organizer. “There has been an extreme emotional, physical, and academic toll on our students. With [COVID] cases dropping and vaccination availability rising, it’s time to follow the science and get students in classrooms – all day and every day,” she said. School Board President Cory Smegal said that the board has “been pretty clear in saying that [the district’s] intent, and commitment, is to open full-time this fall,” and added that the issue will be discussed at their next school board meeting, which will be held
articles.title: Lawn sign campaign demands commitment for full-time school in Fall

articles.text: The house at 55 Craig Avenue, once the residence of Piedmont’s first mayor Hugh Craig, was built in 1879 and designed by Charles L. Bugbee. Gail Lombardi, Chair of the Piedmont Historical Society, confirmed that Hugh Craig built the house and lived there from its construction to his death in 1920. The house was built in the center of Craig’s land on Highland Avenue (then Vernal.) “He moved the house to its present location in 1912 in order to subdivide his land. Its original location was at the crest of what is now Craig Avenue,” Lombardi said. 55 Craig Avenue is the recipient of the Excellence in Historic Restoration Award. See page 28 for all 2021 Piedmont Design Awards, as awarded by the Planning Commission.

articles.text: High school students in Piedmont will begin their longawaited phased return to in-person this week. Starting tomorrow, Thursday, March 11, the school plans to have a “soft opening” in the form of campus tours for incoming freshmen and students new to the district. Students in grades 7-10 will return to campus on Tuesday, March 16. All Piedmont schools were closed exactly one year ago. March 16, 2020, due to the COVID-19 Shelter in Place order by the Alameda County Department of Public Health. Only yesterday, March 9, Alameda County officially entered the less restricted COVID Red Tier, allowing schools in the county to reopen if they have an approved reopening plan and teacher agreements in place. March 9 marked the second week in a row that the daily new adjusted COVID case counts in the county were below 7.0 per 100,000 residents (down to 4.8). As students and teachers prepare for next week’s return to campus, they have an extra four days without school. Today and tomorrow, March 10-11, are asynchronous learning days where students work independently outside the classroom. articles.text: The Exedra, with its Blue Vase, is the most iconic place in Piedmont. Iron gates lead from Magnolia and Highland Avenues to Exedra Plaza, flanked by a group of 10 Highland Poplars. These stately oval Poplars were designated as Heritage Trees in 2018 upon the nomination of Jim Horner. They offer shade to park goers and enhance the beauty of Exedra Plaza year-round. Highland Poplars are cotton-less cottonwood trees that are fast growing and adaptable. They are drought tolerant, disease resistant, unbothered by urban pollution, and not particular to any soil type. They are shady deciduous trees with large heartshaped leaves that turn a lovely yellow in the fall. Highland Poplars can be expected to grow 50 feet tall and require only occasional maintenance. This hybrid species was propagated by a nursery in Colorado. It is just a happy coincidence that they found a home along Highland Avenue in Piedmont. Piedmont’s Park CommisPhoto by Brian Mahany A group of 10 mature Highland Poplars flank the Exedra Plaza. sion is accepting nominations for 2021 Heritage Trees now through March 19. The Heritage Tree program is an opportunity for Piedmont to recognize its distinctive trees on public land. The community is invited to nominate trees growing on property such as parks, medians, and streets. Nominated trees will be considered based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits. Chosen trees will be announced at the Park Commission hearing on April 7 and honored at this year’s virtual Arbor Day celebration on April 30. To nominate a tree, visit the City’s website, http://www. ci.piedmont.ca.us/ and complete the downloadable form. For more information contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or 510-420-3064. Amber Brumfiel is a member of the Piedmont Park Commission.

Iron gates lead from Magnolia and Highland Avenues to Exedra Plaza, flanked by a group of 10 Highland Poplars. These stately oval Poplars were designated as Heritage Trees in 2018 upon the nomination of Jim Horner. They offer shade to park goers and enhance the beauty of Exedra Plaza year-round. Highland Poplars are cotton-less cottonwood trees that are fast growing and adaptable. They are drought tolerant, disease resistant, unbothered by urban pollution, and not particular to any soil type. They are shady deciduous trees with large heartshaped leaves that turn a lovely yellow in the fall. Highland Poplars can be expected to grow 50 feet tall and require only occasional maintenance. This hybrid species was propagated by a nursery in Colorado. It is just a happy coincidence that they found a home along Highland Avenue in Piedmont. Chosen trees will be announced at the Park Commission hearing on April 7 and honored at this year’s virtual Arbor Day celebration on April 30. articles.text: The late Eugene Peterson was one of the great pastors and biblical interpreters of our time. He is best known for The Message, a very popular translation of the New Testament into contemporary English. This is the way he translates the story of the healing of Simon Peter’s mother-in law in the Gospel of Mark. Directly on leaving the meeting place, they came to Simon and Andrew’s house, accompanied by James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law was sick in bed, burning up with fever. They told Jesus. He went to her, took her by the hand, and raised her up. No sooner had the fever left than she was up fixing dinner for them. I would not challenge Peterson’s translation. He is a scholar of impeccable credentials. However, I would suggest, especially in the midst of Women’s History Month, that “she was up fixing them dinner” is not the only way to read the passage. The word all the gospel writers use for the service Peter’s motherin-law provides is an important one. It is diekonei. It can mean all kinds of service, help and ministry. It is worth noting that when the New Testament writers describe what church leaders do, they often use the root word diakonia. I don’t think it is far-fetched to say that the healed woman ministered to Jesus and his community of followers. I don’t think it is far-fetched to suggest that the ministry she provided may have looked a lot like communion, even before there was a well-established tradition of communion. articles.text: Editor: The old Piedmont pool served our community nearly sixty years. It can be hoped that the new pool will serve us just as long – until at least the year 2080. But what will the world be like in 2080? In particular, how will we be getting our energy, and how can the pool we build now anticipate this changed energy world? A pool facility that simply continues to heat and power itself with fossil fuel, as the old pool did, is out of line with the changes we must make to our energy sources to combat the most devastating effects of climate change. Both the State of California and the City of Piedmont have committed to reducing their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to 80% or more below 1990 levels by 2050, with an interim target of 40% below 1990 levels by 2030. As our community begins to reflect on how to design the new pool, we need to consider how to minimize its GHG emissions. A main decarbonization strategy in California is to electrify all appliances that currently run on natural gas, which is a fossil fuel (despite the gloss the gas industry tries to put on it). Using electric heat pumps and other green technologies instead of natural gas to warm the pool would eliminate the pool’s GHG emissions from natural gas usage; and, as California’s electricity mix moves towards California’s 2045 goal of it being 100% from renewable sources, GHG emissions associated with the facility’s electrical use would decrease over time, giving us a carbon neutral pool by 2050. We could perhaps get to carbon neutral even sooner by generating some of our own electricity from renewable sources (for example, solar). At present, there are no cookie cutter models for designing an all-electric public pool, but we know of at least one other city (Mountain View) that is currently trying. With all the can-do energy, talent, and resources of the Piedmont community, we believe we can take on this challenge of designing and building an all-electric, energy-efficient pool, serving as a role model for other cities across the state and nation. -Indira Balkissoon Amy Griffith Garrett Keating Marianne Mitosinka Margaret Ovenden Tom Webster For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: The list of people who are eligible for COVID-19 vaccine in California will expand greatly next week when the state allows healthcare providers to vaccinate people with certain health conditions starting on Monday, March 15. Starting next week, healthcare providers can vaccinate individuals ages 16 to 64 with certain health conditions that leaves them more at risk to COVID-19 mortality. The bulletin directs healthcare providers to “use their clinical judgement” to vaccinate people “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk for morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 as a direct result of one or more of the severe health conditions.” The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found with the state’s guidance at the California Department of Public Health’s website at www.cdph.ca.gov. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. This new group of eligible residents will join thousands of other people who can get vaccinated in Alameda County. The initial group that could get vaccinated back in December is called Phase 1A and includes healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. This group includes an estimated 145,000 people in the county. Last month, Phase 1B became eligible. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. Phase 1B numbers approximately 325,000 residents countywide.
