articles.text: Last year there was a lot of attention on the Black experience in America, and one topic that must be included in that discussion is the impact of Black climate activists. Research shows that climate change does not impact all populations equally, and that Black communities face the negative effects of climate change more often than others. Due to this unequal burden, there is a long and important history of Black Americans leading the way on climate crises. This disparity can be seen in obvious ways, such as the infamous Flint, Michigan water and public health crisis, which impacted tens of thousands of people. Flint has a population that is over 50 percent African American, and the crises’ impacts on the community will be felt for decades. Another example is the Hurricane Katrina disaster, which killed over 1,000 people in New Orleans, a city which is 60 percent African-American. After Katrina, Black homeowners received $8,000 less in government aid than white homeowners because of housing value disparities. Predominantly black communities are more likely to be adjacent to landfills, hazardous waste sites, and industrial facilities. Black Americans are 40 percent more likely to have asthma than White Americans. These health outcomes are a direct effect of policy decisions that perpetuate unequal outcomes for different races in America. These health outcomes can be seen close to home. Oakland, which is 64 percent non-White, has childhood asthma rates of 18.3 percent. Compare this to Piedmont, which is approximately 75 percent white, and has child asthma rates of 12 percent. While mere miles apart, the discrepancies are vast. Black Americans, and particularly Black women, have been at the forefront of movements to make the environment a more equitable place to live for all. A local example is the Black Panther movement in Oakland which has organized drives to keep predominantly Black neighborhoods free of waste, host free health clinics, and educate communities on the dangers of pollution. Now, there are numerous groups in Oakland, throughout the Bay Area, and the state, that are focused on environmental issues, often helmed by Black people. One of these groups include the Climate Action Coalition located in Oakland. The Coalition works on numerous issues such as transit, food justice, and adaptation to climate change. Their overarching mission is racial and economic justice, which is directly related to climate solutions. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, March 10, 2021 Local Items Environmental impacts on Black Americans By Nate Redinbo Last year there was a lot of attention on the Black experience in America, and one topic that must be included in that discussion is the impact of Black climate activists. Research shows that climate change does not impact all populations equally, and that Black communities face the negative effects of climate change more often than others. Due to this unequal burden, there is a long and important history of Black Americans leading the way on climate crises. This disparity can be seen in obvious ways, such as the infamous Flint, Michigan water and public health crisis, which impacted tens of thousands of people. Flint has a population that is over 50 percent African American, and the crises’ impacts on the community will be felt for decades. Another example is the Hurricane Katrina disaster, which killed over 1,000 people in New Orleans, a city which is 60 percent African-American. After Katrina, Black homeowners received $8,000 less in government aid than white homeowners because of housing value disparities. Predominantly black communities are more likely to be adjacent to landfills, hazardous waste sites, and industrial facilities. Black Americans are 40 percent more likely to have asthma than White Americans. These health outcomes are a direct effect of policy decisions that perpetuate unequal outcomes for different races in America. These health outcomes can be seen close to home. Oakland, which is 64 percent non-White, has childhood asthma rates of 18.3 percent. Compare this to Piedmont, which is approximately 75 percent white, and has child asthma rates of 12 percent. While mere miles apart, the discrepancies are vast. Black Americans, and particularly Black women, have been at the forefront of movements to make the environment a more equitable place to live for all. A local example is the Black Panther movement in Oakland which has organized drives to keep predominantly Black neighborhoods free of waste, host free health clinics, and educate communities on the dangers of pollution. Now, there are numerous groups in Oakland, throughout the Bay Area, and the state, that are focused on environmental issues, often helmed by Black people. One of these groups include the Climate Action Coalition located in Oakland. The Coalition works on numerous issues such as transit, food justice, and adaptation to climate change. Their overarching mission is racial and economic justice, which is directly related to climate solutions. Another group, Communities for a Better Environment, works in low-income Latino and African-American communities in Richmond and Oakland to address health hazards in these communities. Their overarching goal is to prevent and reduce pollution and build healthy communities and environment. The California Environmental Justice Coalition (CEJC) is led by people of color and low-income communities. CEJC follows the principles of environmental justice and is committed to environmental, social, and economic justice. articles.text: The city of Piedmont is seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA 6) Planning Period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. The City Council unanimously approved the proposal at its meeting on March 2, and a Requests for Proposal [RFP] was issued the following day. The City’s current Housing Element of the General Plan was adopted in 2011 and outlines the city’s housing goals from 2015 to 2023. The State of California requires that each jurisdiction’s housing element be updated every eight years and certified by the State. While most portions of a General Plan are updated every 20 to 25 years, State law requires that the Housing Element be updated in 8-year cycles. Piedmont will begin updating its Housing Element for the 2023- 2031 period, and a major component of this update is the 6th Cycle Regional Housing Needs Assessment (“RHNA”), in which the State estimates each region’s housing needs for all income groups. Piedmont expects an RHNA 6th cycle of approximately 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in RHNA 5th cycle, representing a 979 percent increase. The expected allocation includes 163 very low-income units, 94 low income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate income units. To ensure that the city meets its housing needs assessment, it will seek a consulting firm. Barry Miller, Principal of Barry Miller Consulting, prepared the city’s documents for the last three cycles, but is not available this year. While the firm selected will be asked to address a number of important housing issues, the most significant work effort is expected to be meeting the RHNA numbers in this upcoming cycle, according to City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Submission of the next cycle’s adopted Housing Element is due to the State by January 2023. To meet this requirement, the city is listing Summer 2021 as a tentative due date for any RHNA appeals, and the first review of the draft housing element to take place in Summer 2022. The RFP was issued on March 3, and proposals are due by April 5. The City Council consideration of the contract is expected to be May 3.
articles.title: City seeks consulting firm to assist with next Housing element cycle

articles.text: Jon Schleuning Piedmont residents have been busy making creative, colorful quilt squares based upon a theme of “Things That Matter” as part of the Community Art Quilt. articles.text: COVID has been the absolute worst for screen time and my kids. To say their screen time has increased would be the understatement of the century. My boys use gaming as their only way of connecting with friends, so I say yes because I know they are lonely and miss their friends, but if the boys are on, my daughter wants to be on...and the cycle continues. So, here are five totally wacky ideas to get kids off screen, even if it’s for just a few extra minutes. 1. Ipad Scavenger Hunt Hide the ipad. Yes, for real, hide it really well. Then create a series of clues directing your kids all over the house or backyard – or both – in order to find it. Clues can be simple, like “the place you might find a popsicle,” then they would go to the freezer and in the freezer find a note that says, “this is where you catch some ZZs,” so they go to their pillow on their bed, etc. etc. until they find their ipad. This doesn’t get them off screens for the whole day, but at least you know they spent a few minutes using their brains and moving their bodies first. 2. Make it a Game OK, I am not necessarily advocating for a bribe in a traditional sense, but what if the next time your kid is begging for more screen time, you say, “Let’s play a game. For every 15 minutes you play, you give me a ‘no-is-not-anplay Roblox or Minecraft or Fortnite. Invite your kids to teach you how to play their favorite games. This becomes interactive and also a great way to connect and communicate while validating their interests. 5. Live action video game This one’s for when you’ve got a little bit of extra energy... which as a parent I understand is the hardest thing to come by right now. For little ones, you can encourage an imagination game that mimics their favorite video game. How do they “level up?” What are the obstacles they have to battle? Get the video off the screen and into their imagination. I hope these creative tools are helpful. In the meantime, let’s all be kind to ourselves. We have been parenting in the craziest time ever. Who needs mom-guilt on top of a pandemic? Maybe, they just play video games for an extra hour? I know I watched a ton of crappy 80s sitcoms in my childhood, and I came out OK (I guess). articles.text: With happy kids coming home from school again, it feels like a new day in town. We thank every support staff member, teacher, administrator, and school board member for getting our kids back in the classroom. It’s heartwarming and a relief, but we must say—we’re already worried about school in the fall. On Monday night, Berkeley Unified School District announced their elementary schools would start full-time instruction on March 29. Other Bay Area districts now plan to open full-time this spring for all grades. Meanwhile, PUSD and the school board say the current schedule is all we can count on. For Piedmont Middle School, that’s two and a half hours at school once a week. Most of the school board say it’s their intention and hope to bring back students full-time this fall, but they can’t possibly commit due to outside circumstances. “Hope” and “intention” are not strategies that will bring PUSD students back full time. We’re told it’s difficult for Piedmont teachers and administrators to be out of step with their fellow Alameda County unions and districts. We say shouldn’t Piedmont lead by example, showing a possible safe return for all students elementary through high school? We’re told it’s difficult for PUSD to plan now when the guidelines may change. We say why not plan with the current set of guidelines? This March, we urge the school board to: • Pass a resolution to open PUSD for full-time in-person instruction to the maximum extent allowable by law for the 2021-2022 school year. • Direct PUSD to plan for full day classroom instruction and to make the shift at the earliest possible date this spring. It’s our understanding that Alameda County does not necessarily require six foot spacing. In June of 2020, almost 800 Piedmont parents, students, and community members signed a petition calling on PUSD to utilize the time, talent, and treasure of Piedmont residents to make space a non-issue. pages.text: Wednesday, March 10, 2021 7 Parents Campaign Continued from page 1 tonight. She pointed to a newsletter, entitled “Piedmont Ahead,” that shows the district is communicating their plans with parents weekly. “We both have the same desires, which is opening fulltime this fall,” Smegal said. Currently, K-6 grades are open for hybrid instruction, and grades 7-12 will have their first days between March 16 and March 23. But the group maintained that “many parents and students are not satisfied with the limited in-person hours for spring and want a commitment and a plan for a full-time schedule in the Fall.” “[School officials] said that they have every intention of opening up full-time [in the fall], but they have not shared with us concrete plans on how they plan to get there,” said campaign organizer Kate Kittredge. “This advocacy group is pushing the board and district to make a plan for fall, but also for [in-person, fulltime instruction] this spring,” she added. Numerous members of the group have independently voiced concerns and desires for a full reopening to school officials, either by email or during public comment at school board meetings. But the lawn sign campaign is the first collective effort of Piedmont parents who wish to see full-time, in-person instruction. The hashtag that appears on the signs, “FullTimeinTheFall,” is meant to advocate for a full-time program and educate Piedmonters who may not be aware that the district has not presented a formal plan for full-time instruction. The group added that “the school district also does not have an agreement with the teachers’ union for full-time instruction.” Lauren Maestrelli, founder of the group, said that parents are already looking for “backup plans” if the school does not return for in-person learning at the start of the next academic year – this includes leaving the district and enrolling kids in private schools. “There are no guarantees at this point, and most of us feel that in-person, full-time is absolutely essential next [academic] year, especially now that teachers are vaccinated,” she said. “As time wore on, my concerns were more with students’ mental health. There was a mental health survey from the district that showed really concerning results for our secondary students. The bottom line is this – distance learning does not work, long-term, to meet kids’ needs,” said Maestrelli. “We both have the same desires, which is opening full-time this fall.” – Cory Smegal, Piedmont School Board President Maestrelli agreed that the current hybrid learning model is a compromise, but the group is particularly frustrated with “the fact that middle schoolers will have only two [and a half] hours of in-person learning [per week] with the hybrid schedule,” which is the lowest amount of hybrid learning for middle school students in the Bay Area. No commitment by PUSD Smegal said that right now the school district is not able to make a commitment for a full-time schedule this fall. “No one knows what the state of the pandemic will be in August. There’s an assumption, which is why we have scenario planning, but nobody can definitively say what it will be like in August,” she said. Scenario planning was mentioned by the district in a Piedmont Ahead newsletter sent to parents on Friday, March 5. It stated, “on March 24, the Board will have a discussion about the contingencies required under each of these scenarios.” Both Maestrelli and Kittredge pointed to the fact that Berkeley Unified School District expects to reopen elementary schools for in-person learning later this month, offering a five-day a week schedule. Like Piedmont, Berkeley is in Alameda County; but Berkeley is not within the jurisdiction of the Alameda County Public Health Department. It is one of just three cities in California that has its own public health agency, separate from the county. The group believes that the successes in Berkeley could still be replicated in Piedmont, though. “To have a neighboring school district in Alameda County, which is larger than PUSD, be able to provide the leadership to offer full-time, in-person learning for its students really shows that there should be absolutely no obstacles for our school district to be able to provide the same for our student body,” Kittredge said. Students in Berkeley will attend five full days of school, and classrooms have been reconfigured for maximum social distancing, according to Berkeley Unified Supt. Brent Stephens, who said that “based on the continuing positive dialogue with our Berkeley Federation of Teachers and Berkeley Council of Classified Employees partners, and also thanks to the successful vaccination program offered to BUSD staff by the City of Berkeley, we expect to be able to offer elementary school families the option to return their students to a five-day schedule of on-campus learning.” While the red tier means a full reopening for Berkeley Unified, Smegal did confirm that the development will allow Piedmont students in grades 7 through 12 to return to classrooms next Tuesday, March 16. Tours for incoming high school freshmen and new high school students are planned for sometime this week. School reopening strategies of “hope” and “intention” are not working With happy kids coming home from school again, it feels like a new day in town. We thank every support staff member, teacher, administrator, and school board member for getting our kids back in the classroom. It’s heartwarming and a relief, but we must say—we’re already worried about school in the fall. On Monday night, Berkeley Unified School District announced their elementary schools would start full-time instruction on March 29. Other Bay Area districts now plan to open full-time this spring for all grades. Meanwhile, PUSD and the school board say the current schedule is all we can count on. For Piedmont Middle School, that’s two and a half hours at school once a week. Most of the school board say it’s their intention and hope to bring back students full-time this fall, but they can’t possibly commit due to outside circumstances. “Hope” and “intention” are not strategies that will bring PUSD students back full time. We’re told it’s difficult for Piedmont teachers and administrators to be out of step with their fellow Alameda County unions and districts. We say shouldn’t Piedmont lead by example, showing a possible safe return for all students elementary through high school? We’re told it’s difficult for PUSD to plan now when the guidelines may change. We say why not plan with the current set of guidelines? This March, we urge the school board to: • Pass a resolution to open PUSD for full-time in-person instruction to the maximum extent allowable by law for the 2021-2022 school year. • Direct PUSD to plan for full day classroom instruction and to make the shift at the earliest possible date this spring. It’s our understanding that Alameda County does not necessarily require six foot spacing. In June of 2020, almost 800 Piedmont parents, students, and community members signed a petition calling on PUSD to utilize the time, talent, and treasure of Piedmont residents to make space a non-issue. We urge PUSD to end its use of the six foot distancing rule and use all its facilities and other Piedmont public spaces so all students can attend school. We are grateful to all who have worked to get our kids back in the classroom, and to our exceptional teachers for continuing the great education they provide. We also thank the parents for helping create a Covid testing program for students, raising funds for air purifiers, and providing masks for the district. We aren’t enemies. We’re great partners. Let’s continue to work together. articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1978 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.

Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee 2 vacancies; 3-year term Reviews and provides comment on five year projections contained in the City’s annual budget proposal, the proposed funding and expenditures from several long-term funds, and the proposed mid-year budget adjustments; Provides a financial review of new programs in excess of $250,000 per year. Civic Improvement Projects (CIP) Review Committee 2 vacancies, 3-year term The committee makes recommendations to the City Council regarding the expenditure of the capital budget (construction, repair or rehabilitation of city facilities). articles.text: The American Booksellers Association helps independently owned bookstores stay alive and thrive. Each month it publishes a list of 20 inspired recommendations, the “Indie Next List,” from the booksellers. Each title below includes a recommendation by a bookstore owner. For full book reviews, more information and ways to order the books, see: www.indiebound.org/ indie-next-list We Begin at the End, by Chris Whitaker, was published by Henry Holt and Co in March of 2020. It has won multiple awards including Best Thriller of the Year by The Guardian and Express The Lost Apothecary “A wonderful melding of two timelines told by a trio of female voices. A small, blue apothecary bottle links the women and the timelines together. Penner skillfully guides us along the path each woman chooses.” –Sandi Madore, Magnolia’s Bookstore, Seattle, WA Brood “Over the course of a year, told in a collection of snapshots, Brood shows the life of a woman grieving by doing anything but. The beauty in this book lies in the narrator’s acceptance of the everyday, and of all the things—bad, good, but mostly in-between—that come therein.” –Cat Chapman, The Oxford Exchange, Tampa, FL The Rose Code Paperbacks “Kate Quinn presents a new angle on the BletchleyPark/code breaker part of WWII. Three magnificent main characters who must navigate the turbulent waters not only of the war, but of a new puzzle to solve shortly before the royal wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip.” –Sarah Danforth, Towne Book Center, Collegeville, PA The Windsor Knot “When a Russian pianist is found dead at Windsor Castle, the new head of MI5 muddles the case and makes the mistake of treating the Queen like his doddering granny. It’s up to the Queen to secretly and skillfully line up the pieces of the puzzle for MI5 to solve.” –Margo Grimm Eule, East City Bookshop, Washington, DC Vera “Experience the San Francisco earthquake of 1906 like never before, from inside the family of one of the most famous brothel madams. Edgarian combines lyrical writing and a cast of unforgettable characters.” –Gayle Shanks, Changing Hands, Tempe, AZ Infinite Country: A Novel Press/Simon & Schuster “Patricia Engel’s new book is a true gem, a family story in which each voice is equally interesting and dynamic as well as a great examination on the brutish nature of the U.S. government and citizens toward people traveling stateside to start a new life.” –James Harrod, Malaprop’s Bookstore/Café, Asheville, NC Cosmogony: Story Collection “Ives writes boldly; her stories are strong and wild, as if she left the door open to the dream world and let all that magic saturate. Her writings are grounded in the real world, but there’s a shimmering rind to them, magical realism at its toughest.” –Aimee Keeble, Main Street Books, Davidson, NC The Girls Are All So Nice Here Simon & Schuster “The Girls Are All So Nice Here is the first, but not the last, lie you will read when you devour this dark and disturbing novel about college girls and how they treat each other in order to be popular or important.” –Nancy McFarlane, Fiction Addiction, Greenville, SC Act Your Age, Eve Brown (The Brown Sisters #3) “A satisfying conclusion to an absolutely delightful series. In the final installment of the trilogy, we follow the youngest Brown sister, Eve, a lovable hot mess who is looking to prove to her parents that she can get her life together.” –Tyrinne Lewis, Cafe Con Libros, Brooklyn, NY Good Eggs Books “The Irish setting is especially welcome on this side of the pond. Of the three plotlines following different generations, the absolute best paints 83-year-old pistol of a grandma Millie as a delightfully quirky and determined soul. A charming, offbeat novel – perfect to savor as we emerge from this particular winter.” –Deb Wayman, Fair Isle Books, Washington Island, WI Band of Sisters “Willig’s Band of Sisters pulled me in and took me on a journey of complicated friendships that grew and matured in the midst of hardship and trial. Between mishaps with roosters, snowstorms, and reminders of the kindness and resilience of people, this historical fiction is a delight to read.” –Laura DeLaney, Rediscovered Books, Boise, ID The Echo Wife “Wow! I am so delighted that there are writers like Sarah Gailey producing science fiction of this caliber. Her latest novel, The Echo Wife, kept me riveted from beginning to end with elegant prose and a compelling, vulnerable protagonist who narrates the story in a wonderfully intimate first-person point of view.” –Christine Havens, BookPeople, Austin, TX Float Plan Griffin “Whenever I pick up a romance novel, it’s generally because I want a happy ending. I want rainbows and heartthrobs, and for everything to turn out perfectly. Float Plan gives us way more than that. We are introduced to a character at her lowest point and through a self-imposed challenge, she ventures through comedy, heartbreak, defeat, and more.” –Miranda Atkins, A Little Bookish, Ooltewah, TN Every Last Fear: A Novel “This is a riveting debut crime novel featuring a nonstop propulsive plot with twists and turns that will keep you up at night racing through the pages to fig-

articles.text: Q: What 30th wedding anniversary gift can a man get his wife that’ll be sure to please her? A: Two tickets to Paris – one for her and one for her closest girlfriend. Q: A: Q: A: Q: A: Q: Is there a good stretching routine for women in their 60s? Tell people you’re in your early 50s. That’d be a stretch. How do 60-year-olds keep track of the days of the week? Where are all 60-year-olds the picture of health? In their high school yearbooks. For people age 60, what’s the difference between giving information and giving too much information? A: Giving information is referring a friend to your gastroenterologist. Giving too much information is showing your friend a video of your colonoscopy. Q: A glass or two of fine wine at dinner is good for your health and may even prolong your life. True or false? A: Absolutely true! (Vintners may send samples to the author in care of the publisher.) Q: What’s a common malady of retired union workers? A: Pension headaches. Q: After giving so much to their children, what are 60-year-old parents entitled to request in return? A: Grandchildren. Q: Whom do grandparents visit to feel younger? A: Their parents. Q: What should a 60-year-old man have before starting a second family? A: Second thoughts. Q: After many years of marriage, can a 60-year-old woman change her husband’s ways? A: That’s an old wives’ tale. Reprinted from What You Don’t Know About Turning 60 by P.D. Witte, 2006, Running Press. The book is currently available through Amazon.com at $7.99. Piedmont resident Phil Witte is the creator of FLIP, a single panel cartoon appearing weekly in the Piedmont Post.

A: Two tickets to Paris – one for her and one for her closest girlfriend. Q: A: Q: A: Q: A: Q: Is there a good stretching routine for women in their 60s? Tell people you’re in your early 50s. Wednesday, March 10, 2021 11 It's Springtime in Piedmont By Allyson Aleksey Spring doesn’t officially arrive until March 20, but don’t tell that to all the daffodils, tulips and flowering trees throughout Piedmont. It’s early March, and the city is bursting with color – and spring fragrances. The city’s Public Works Department planted approximately 16,000 tulip and daffodil bulbs in November last year. Bulbs were planted around City Hall, the Community Hall, the Exedra Plaza, the Center for the Arts, Civic Center traffic medians, Piedmont Park, Crocker Park, Hampton Park, Dracena Park, the Coaches Field entry, Blair Park, Hall Fenway, Grand Avenue traffic medians, and the traffic triangles at Linda-Kingston, and Hampton-Indian. Some spots are starting to bloom already, but the most visible locations are in Crocker Park and Piedmont Park. And possibly the best is yet to come. The dazzling cherry trees in Piedmont’s Main Park will be blooming soon, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalés. Red tulips Photo by Rob Yelland Pink and white tulips are complimented by small violets in front of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. articles.text: Saturday, March 6 brought a familiar sight of parents lining the fences of the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Bonita and Vista Avenues. In a long-awaited return of sports to Piedmont, Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team easily rolled past Berkeley, the 2019 WACC champions, with a score of 5-2. “The girls had a great time and everyone played well. It was 5-2 but Berkeley played us pretty tight, there were a lot of close points,” said coach Jim Landes. Playing their first match at the Piedmont Courts felt like justice-served for a team whose fall season was wiped out due to all sports cancelled to Covid-related health restrictions. They practiced week after week during the summer, hoping that a schedule would be confirmed for September and October. But nothing occurred. And now they enter the spring season. “It’s so nice to be playing again. It was really great; I didn’t realize how much I missed cheering people on and watching my team play. It feels right to be back. I’m really happy that I get to have a senior season,” said senior leader Audrey Edel, a regular at the preseason clinics. The match materialized quickly. Piedmont was initially scheduled to face Castro Valley on March 6 only to learn that their opponent had no coach. “After Castro Valley canceled, I called Berkeley’s boys’ varsity coach, but he said they were playing De La Salle. But then, I ran into [Berkeley girls’ coach] Mary Bedford here at the courts, I see her here all the time, and she said that they could play the match,” explained Landes with a wide smile. Berkeley has problems with adequate practicing and playing Photo by Brian Mahany Senior Audrey Edel runs down a volley at No. 2 singles on her way to a 6-4, 6-1 victory against Berkeley. Photo by Brian Mahany Audrey Mahany gets ready for a powerful forehand. She paired with Mara LaForte at No. 2 doubles to get Piedmont’s first win of the day, 6-2, 6-3. Photo by Brian Mahany The No. 1 doubles pair of Amanda Becker (left) and Michaela Bini won 6-4, 6-4 over Berkeley’s top pair. locations. Their match against Piedmont marked the team’s first match of the season and was greeted by Yellowjacket parents around the courts voicing their gratitude for finally having a match. Berkeley’s varsity girls’ coach Mary Bedford explains their situation: “In the last few years, we’ve been able to use the Cal practice courts,” explained Bedford, Berkeley’s coach. “This year the University has shut down due to COVID. We’re using the [Berkeley] Middle School courts sharing with the boys at the same time, so the girls almost get no court-time. We get two days a week and two hours a day, it is almost no chance of court-time.” from all positions, backcourt, mid court and the net. It was great to see her playing so well,” said Landes. Soon after, varsity newcomers Rosie Siemers and Kate Dorman won their doubles match in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2 to put Piedmont ahead 4-2. . The last match on was the senior, Audrey Edel, who won her match at No. 2 singles 6-4, 6-1, against Andrea Morales. She notably closed out the first set 6-4 with a big forehand winner, while her second-set 6-1 victory came at the tail-end of three mighty serves. “It got a little nerve-wracking in the first set. We beat Berkeley in our first match; they are the defending league champions, it makes me really excited about how the team is looking,” added Edel. NEXT UP The Highlanders’ girls’ team travels to Golden Gate Park on Thursday, March 11for a match with University at the brand-new tennis complex in San Francisco. Both boys’ and girls’ tennis teams are scheduled to host Bishop O’Dowd at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, March 11 for 3:30 p.m. matches. Both teams also face Alameda on the road this Saturday, March 13 at 9:30 a.m. Match Details The Highlanders won their 5-2 visit from the Yellowjackets by sweeping all three doubles matches and taking two of four at singles. Piedmont and Berkeley split the first two matches of the day; No. 3 singles Bridgette McEfee lost 6-1, 6-2 while No. 2 doubles of Audrey Mahany and Mara LaForte won 6-2, 6-3 with a flurry of hard forehands to the Berkeley backcourt. “All three of our doubles’ teams played well today. Some great serving and big forehands seemed like a common theme,” said Landes. The meeting remained deadlocked at 2-2 following Anne Jumper’s 6-1, 7-6(1) loss, while the No. 1 doubles pair of Amanda Becker and Michaela Bini won in straight-sets 6-4, 6-4 against Berkeley’s top-duo Isabella Ingersall and Lydia Schrag. Becker, in her usual fashion, gained many points with angled volleys in front of the net with Bini sending well-placed shots out of the back. From there, it was all Piedmont. They never lost another match. M a ke n n a T h iel d o uble-bageled Maya Curry, Berkeley’s talented, strong No. 1 player. Her 6-0, 6-0 sweep gave Piedmont its third win. “There were some great points with Makenna striking winners Staff Photo Makenna Thiel double-bageled Maya Curry at No. 1 singles, 6-0, 6-0. Staff Photo At No. 4 doubles, Kate Dorman (left) and Rosie Siemers won their match 6-3, 6-2.

articles.text: Coach Eric Olson’s boys return this Saturday, March 12 with a 2 p.m. season-opening game against Albany High in Piedmont. It marks an exciting start of the 2021 season of Piedmont High sports, and the first action on the diamond in over a year when the 2020 squad closed its brief season with 3-1 record. “We’re excited. We’re for sure happy to be back out on the field. We’ve been practicing and conditioning since around Thanksgiving. We just dusted off the game-cobwebs on Saturday [March 6] with an inter-squad game, it was fun to see guys throwing to each other, hitting and playing defense. It was a very casual setting without umpires or uniforms,” said Olson. This year’s season will be different. articles.text: In observance of Women’s History Month, Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is offering a women’s speaker series via Zoom throughout March. The series will feature trailblazing women in the fields of horticulture, architecture, and gardens, in the series of moderated discussions. The women will discuss their stories, experiences, and provide valuable insight on breaking through the “glass ceiling.” On Tuesday, March 16, Executive Director of San Francisco Botanical Garden Stephanie Linder will join Filoli in discussing her 20 years in conservation. She has been a member of many women’s organizations, including Santa Barbara Botanic Garden, Sierra Club, the Trust for Public Land, and Planned Parenthood. Linder is an alumna and former Board Chair of Emerge California – a training program for women seeking elected office, with a majority of graduates being women of color. She has also taught U.S Women’s History at the college level. The Zoom event will begin next Tuesday, March 16 at 2 p.m., Stephanie Linder, Director of San Francisco Botanical Garden, will be featured in a speaker series sponsored by Filoli House & Gardens in Woodside. and will run approximately one hour. The series will conclude on March 23 with a forum hosted by the Women of Filoli’s horticulture team. To reserve your spot, visit https://51772.blackbaudhosting. com/51772/tickets?tab=2&txobjid=d202779d-0817-460f-9208- 1a451ba29f81. C L E A N B E A U T Y

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet began its third digital program of the season on March 4 with choreographer Alexei Ratmansky’s Symphony No.9, which will stream through March 24. With music by Dmit r i Shostakovich, Symphony No. 9 was created for two lead couples and a solo male, all set against designer George Tsypin’s backdrop of grays and reds, recalling works of Socialist realism. The performance is an archival capture. In creating the work American Ballet Theatre (ABT) Ballet Master Nancy Raffa said that Ratmansky considered “the time the piece was written and the emotions behind what was happening in Shostakovich’s life - the regime, the Communist party, the whole Stalin mentality.” “He wanted them to be almost a caricature, expressing the sarcasm in parts of the score. But everything is abstract. He kept saying, ‘There’s no story, but there’s a lot of meaning’,” Raffa said. To watch Symphony No, 9, visit https://www.sf ballet.org/ productions/digital-program-03/.
articles.title: SF Ballet streaming Ratmansky’s Symphony No.9 through March 24

articles.text: Brandon Jovanovich (Siegmund) and Karita Mattila (Sieglinde) in a scene from San Francisco Opera’s 2018 production of Wagner’s Die Walküre. Wotan, Siegfried, Brünnhilde, the Norns and the Rhine Maidens all return to San Francisco Opera, as the company begins a monthlong “Ring Festival” with selections from earlier productions of Richard Wagner’s The Ring of the Niebelung. Each weekend throughout March the Opera will stream sold-out performances from the 2018 production for free. The festival officially began last Saturday with Das Rheingold, but you can still catch the archived performance on https:// sfopera.com/opera-is-on/ringfestival/. On Friday, March 5, the Festival kicked off with the “Opening Salute” – a ticketed Zoom event with Director Francesca Zambello, conductor Donald Runnicles, and Greer Grimsley, who sang the role of Wotan. Each week will feature panel events with scholars, critics, and singers discussing the long and complicated history of “the Ring.” The next episode, panel, held at 10 a.m. on Friday, March 12, will feature Brandon Jovanovich and Karita Mattila as Siegmund and Sieglinde in San Francisco Opera’s 2018 production of Die Walküre. The pair joins San Francisco Chronicle classical music critic Joshua Kosman to discuss how they tackled these iconic roles of twins turned lovers. Kosman has covered classical music for the Chronicle since 1988, and has reviewed and reported on the wealth of orchestral, operatic, chamber, and contemporary music throughout the Bay Area. To watch the upcoming episode, visit https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on/ringfestival/ringevent-pdp29/. Free Delivery to Piedmont Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera’s Ring Festival begins

articles.text: SF Jazz will stream an archived performance by the ACS Trio (Geri Allen, Terri Lyne Carrington and Esperanza Spalding) this Friday, March 12, at 5 p.m. Allen (piano) Spalding (bass) and Carrington (drums) are among the top female musicians in jazz. The program is part of SF Jazz’s “Fridays at Five” series of weekly pre-recorded concerts that aspire to connect audience members with music during shelter-in-place restrictions. The November 2015 performance by the trio was one of the most well-attended events to occur on the Miner Auditorium stage. It was Allen’s last appearance at the SF Jazz center before her passing in 2017. Allen is regarded as one of jazz’s most influential artists, Jazz pianist and composer Geri Allen will be featured in SF Jazz’s next Fridays at Five episode. and as a visionary pianist and composer. Spalding had already earned a place as jazz’s “brightest young artists,” long before her Grammy Award as Best New Artist in 2011. Carrington has also built a longstanding career as a bandleader and composer and has been named a 2021 National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) Jazz Master. The collaboration between the three women emerged out of Carrington’s Grammy winning 2011 album The Mosaic Project. To watch this Friday’s episode, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/fridaysatfive/.

articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Simone McIntosh joins the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco for a concert premiering this Friday, March 12 at 7:30 p.m. Titled Art of the Voice, the concert will also be available on Sunday, March 14 at 6 p.m. The program takes viewers on a journey from the dark and stormy into the sunrise. Be transported by Beethoven’s passionate String Quartet Op. 18 no. 4, the haunting melodies of Respighi’s Il Tramonto, and the gentle glow of Haydn’s Sunrise Quartet. McIntosh’s powerful and soulful voice, possessing a wide range, captivates audiences. She will encore with Nadia Boulanger’s tender and serene Cantique, in a world premiere arrangement for voice and string quartet. Back by popular demand, the concert will include a trivia segment entitled “The Secret Lives of Divas and Divos – stars of the Opera.” “We are dedicated to performing chamber music in intimate and personal ways,” explained violinist Natasha Makhijani, a founding member of CMS of SF. “We carefully curate an experience that captures the imagination with exceptional music, while sharing the complexities of the musicians’ lives and their creative process.” “For years we’ve wanted to do a project with voice where the lyricism and story of the text come first. Right now is the opportunity, when our online concerts have the visual flexibility to transport you into the story itself,” added co-founder Samsun van Loon, “This story is Shelley’s poem The Sunset, the eternal story of love, loss, and perseverance, set to music by Ottorino Respighi as Il Tramonto for mezzo-soprano and string quartet. Filling for violist Clio Tilton, who is on maternity leave, will be Ivo Bokulic. The concert will stream on-demand through Sunday, March 21. For tickets, click on https:// chambermusicsocietysf.org/digital-concerts.

articles.text: Ben Affleck portrays Jack Cunningham in The Way Back. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Way Back is a remarkably good film that takes a familiar trope and course corrects, resulting in an honest, well-acted film that is far more than a formulaic sports story. Actually, it’s an intense character study, resulting in one of Ben Affleck’s finest performances in what has been a storied career. His portrayal of Jack Cunningham, a middle-aged construction worker, is a perfect fit, delivered with a personal authenticity that abandons the movie star/matinee idol persona. He fully embraces a role about a man deeply wounded by a life experience, one so profound, so wrenching that his recovery is uncertain. To the filmmakers’ credit, the arc of the story is neither the familiar tale of a faltering high school basketball team, nor is it simply a search for personal redemption. Instead, Affleck slowly opens a window into his character, Jack. In one scene, before work, he stands in the shower drinking a beer while shampooing; later, he spikes his morning coffee while on the job. He is a big man, thick through the middle, covered perpetually with a sheen of sweat as if his body is trying to expel the

articles.text: Cynthia Ervio as Harriet Tubman. Movie review by Chris Honoré Harriet attempts to capture the essence of the historical figure Harriet Tubman (also known in her early years as Araminta Ross or “Minty”). While this film is a respectful and laudatory view of Harriet it feels like there is more to this courageous woman. As we’re told, Harriet (Cynthia Ervio) escapes slavery from a plantation in Bucktown, Maryland. The year is 1849. She is hunted from almost the first moment she is discovered missing, her value measured in dollars. Chased to a bridge, with slave hunters, her master (Joe Allwyn), and hounds in pursuit she climbs over the railing and jumps into a raging river. It’s a decision that is not only life threatening but symbolic. Clearly she would rather die than return to the plantation and live as a slave. She makes what proves to be a remarkable 100-mile trek to Philadelphia where black people live free. However, not long after arriving, it is evident that she is tormented by the memories of those she left behind, including her husband John (Zackary Momoh) and so she decides to return to Maryland and lead her husband and family to freedom. Thus begins a series of missions, each high risk/high gain. She knows that if she is caught, she will be killed. Eventually she guides some 70 slaves to Philadelphia through what became known as the “Underground Railroad.” She eventually became one of its most valued “conductors.” Tubman is an iconic character and deserves her story told on the big screen. Hers is a narrative of remarkable bravery. But it is also a story of slavery, which was an institution of extraordinary cruelty and brutality. It’s from that reality that Harriet escaped, making it all the more remarkable that she chose to return to help other slaves find freedom. What Harriet fails to do is reveal the horrible price paid by people who were treated like chattel, hundreds of thousands held against their will, countless killed or worked to death. That is the missing contrast to Harriet’s courage and humanity as well as her fierce determination. We’re told this quality was later recognized when she was given the command of an armed expedition during the Civil War; something unheard of up to that point. Harriet does deliver a profile in courage. But it also suggests that there is more to this remarkable woman’s story that needs to be told. Harriet. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s The Jungle Book. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Jungle Book is a dazzling, vibrant film that will draw kids in and easily keep them in their seats. Starring Neel Sethi as Mowgli (the only human, also known as the “man cub”), the film is a marvel of CGI. A thought that comes to mind is that kids today may take for granted the seamless creation of animals, such as the bear Baloo (Bill Murray), or the panther, Bagheera (Ben Kingsley). For those of us who have watched movies over the years, the technical accomplishments of this film are nothing short of astonishing. Using the original Jungle Book story by Rudyard Kipling as the source material, Mowgli is confronted with a difficult choice. If he is to survive, he must leave his family of wolves and all that he has known and escape the lethal wrath of Shere Khan (Idris Elba), a tiger that hates men so much that he is intent on killing Mowgli. His journey takes him deep into the Indian jungle where he is confronted with one adventure after the next. It is there that he meets the lazy Baloo, who asks Mowgli to climb a steep cliff to get at the honey hives hanging from the rocks. He also falls under the spell of an enormous snake Kaa (Scarlett Johansson), and meets to his peril King Louie, a Gigantopithecus (Christopher Walken), from whom he barely escapes. Mowgli’s goal – the purpose of his adventure – is to find a place of human habitation in order to escape Shere Kahn. At his side is Bagheera, his wise and helpful mentor, who urges him on, for the panther knows that Mowgli’s life is in danger. Shere Kahn will never stop his relentless pursuit. Kids will lose themselves in this movie. It’s technologically breathtaking. But keep in mind that it can also be intense and may be a bit scary for youngsters under 8. There are moments when the animals confront each other and the outcome can be sad and final. The Jungle Book is a joy to watch; it is lush and energetic with scenes that are light-hearted and will make the kids smile. Enjoy. The Jungle Book. Directed by Jon Favreau. Starring Neel Sethi, Bill Murrray and Ben Kingsley. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: The Jungle Book ideal viewing for kids

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The idea, which comprises the essence of Pixar’s Inside Out, is inspired. Written and directed by Piedmont resident Pete Docter in 2015, the film won an Academy Award as Best Animation Feature. Of significance, the filmmakers confronted the third dimension in movies (emotion). It is, after all, a world in which animators can take a step that otherwise would be impossible in a photographed feature. Knowing that a filmed narrative cannot penetrate a character’s mind (except by using a voiceover), they tell a familiar story of an 11-year-old girl named Riley (Kaitlyn Dias). She lives happily in the embrace of her parents in Minnesota, has loads of friends and plays on a hockey team. For Riley life is better than good. That is until her father takes a new job and they must relocate to San Francisco. Up to this point, Riley’s default setting is contentment and joy – school, friends, sports all fit into a much-enjoyed spectrum of childhood on the cusp of being a teenager (Riley defines the word tween). With the move across the country, Riley’s world is rocked. She is confronted with challenges that are new to her. Her new house is a bit grim, as is her neighborhood. She tries out for hockey and it doesn’t go well. Suddenly Riley begins to slide into a funk. And though her parents ask her if everything is all right (of course, Riley grumbles that all is fine), the emotions taking place inside are a different story. The Pixar storytellers craft a kind of emotional wheelhouse (in Riley’s head, so to speak) and personify all of Riley’s emotions. It’s wonderful. There’s Joy (Amy Poehler), Fear (Bill Hader), Anger (Lewis Black), Disgust (Mindy Kaling) and Sadness (Phyllis Smith). Each emotion is a unique and funny and engaging character, and all coping with Riley’s new world and a bevy of feelings that are at first decidedly unsettling. Riley has always been encouraged to be happy. To smile. But then she has been grounded in a spiffy life. Hence Joy, vivacious and energetic, has always had her hand on the tiller, suddenly Anger and Fear and Sadness (most especially) find that their roles in Riley’s emotions are growing. Meanwhile, Joy, becomes lost in a labyrinth of Riley’s mind and must struggle to find its way back to emotion central before things get really awful for Riley. Inside Out a complete gem from Pixar Movie review by Chris Honoré The idea, which comprises the essence of Pixar’s Inside Out, is inspired. Written and directed by Piedmont resident Pete Docter in 2015, the film won an Academy Award as Best Animation Feature. Of significance, the filmmakers confronted the third dimension in movies (emotion). It is, after all, a world in which animators can take a step that otherwise would be impossible in a photographed feature. Knowing that a filmed narrative cannot penetrate a character’s mind (except by using a voiceover), they tell a familiar story of an 11-year-old girl named Riley (Kaitlyn Dias). She lives happily in the embrace of her parents in Minnesota, has loads of friends and plays on a hockey team. For Riley life is better than good. That is until her father takes a new job and they must relocate to San Francisco. Up to this point, Riley’s default setting is contentment and joy – school, friends, sports all fit into a much-enjoyed spectrum of childhood on the cusp of being a teenager (Riley defines the word tween). With the move across the country, Riley’s world is rocked. She is confronted with challenges that are new to her. Her new house is a bit grim, as is her neighborhood. She tries out for hockey and it doesn’t go well. Suddenly Riley begins to slide into a funk. And though her parents ask her if everything is all right (of course, Riley grumbles that all is fine), the emotions taking place inside are a different story. The Pixar storytellers craft a kind of emotional wheelhouse (in Riley’s head, so to speak) and personify all of Riley’s emotions. It’s wonderful. There’s Joy (Amy Poehler), Fear (Bill Hader), Anger (Lewis Black), Disgust (Mindy Kaling) and Sadness (Phyllis Smith). Each emotion is a unique and funny and engaging character, and all coping with Riley’s new world and a bevy of feelings that are at first decidedly unsettling. Riley has always been encouraged to be happy. To smile. But then she has been grounded in a spiffy life. Hence Joy, vivacious and energetic, has always had her hand on the tiller, suddenly Anger and Fear and Sadness (most especially) find that their roles in Riley’s emotions are growing. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Jungle Book is a dazzling, vibrant film that will draw kids in and easily keep them in their seats. Starring Neel Sethi as Mowgli (the only human, also known as the “man cub”), the film is a marvel of CGI. A thought that comes to mind is that kids today may take for granted the seamless creation of animals, such as the bear Baloo (Bill Murray), or the panther, Bagheera (Ben Kingsley). For those of us who have watched movies over the years, the technical accomplishments of this film are nothing short of astonishing. Using the original Jungle Book story by Rudyard Kipling as the source material, Mowgli is confronted with a difficult choice. If he is to survive, he must leave his family of wolves and all that he has known and escape the lethal wrath of Shere Khan (Idris Elba), a tiger that hates men so much that he is intent on killing Mowgli. His journey takes him deep into the Indian jungle where he is confronted with one adventure after the next. It is there that he meets the lazy Baloo, who asks Mowgli to climb a steep cliff to get at the honey hives hanging from the rocks. He also falls under the spell of an enormous snake Kaa (Scarlett Johansson), and meets to his peril King Louie, a Gigantopithecus (Christopher Walken), from whom he barely escapes. Mowgli’s goal – the purpose of his adventure – is to find a place of human habitation in order to escape Shere Kahn. At his side is Bagheera, his wise and helpful mentor, who urges him on, for the panther knows that Mowgli’s life is in danger. Shere Kahn will never stop his relentless pursuit. Kids will lose themselves in this movie. It’s technologically breathtaking. But keep in mind that it can also be intense and may be a bit scary for youngsters under 8. There are moments when the animals confront each other and the outcome can be sad and final. The Jungle Book is a joy to watch; it is lush and energetic with scenes that are light-hearted and will make the kids smile. Enjoy. The Jungle Book. Directed by Jon Favreau. Starring Neel Sethi, Bill Murrray and Ben Kingsley. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. A scene from Pixar’s Inside Out.

The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on March 1. Thirteen readers were on the call to discuss their March selection, Drive Your Plow over the Bones of the Dead, by Polish author Olga Tokarczuk. Participating were Mike Bandrowski, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Sally Arney, Albert Chen, Karin Fetherston, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead is Tokarczuk’s 2009 mystery novel. The book’s title is from a William Blake poem, “Proverbs of Hell,” which contains the line, “In seed time learn, in harvest teach, in winter enjoy. Drive your cart and your plow over the bones of the dead.” The book was originally published in Polish and later translated to English by Antonia LloydJones. The novel received a wide release in 2019 when it was published in the United States. It received strong, poitive reviews, and Tokarczuk was awarded the 2018 Nobel Prize in Literature for her writings, two months after the novel’s U.S. release. Tokarczuk’s protagonist is Janina, an aging astrologist who lives in a secluded Polish village on the Czech border. She spends her time pontificating on broad concepts, translating the poetry of Blake, and predicting people’s futures through her sophisticated astrology. The storyline takes the reader through a number of murders in the village to the ultimate solution of them, and a happy ending of sorts. Almost all the members of the group enjoyed the book. articles.text: Schools are opening…finally. This is an open letter to parents and students. Studying music offers many wonderful opportunities. Some of the things that music does approaches miracle status. Here is a case in point. Many years ago, I played a concert in a senior residence home. After the concert, one of the residents came up to me and engaged me in conversation. She told me about her honeymoon some 50 years earlier. She and her husband went to Norway. As she continued to reminisce, she described going to the Ole Bull museum outside Bergen. For those of you who do not recognize the name, Ole Bull was Norway’s greatest violinist and also contributed greatly to American culture. There’s even a song about him and the Utopian society he sought to create: “Oleana”. The woman’s description of her honeymoon was vivid in every detail. She even described seeing Ole Bull’s violin which had a man’s head sculpted at the top. I enjoyed my conversation with her very much. When she departed for dinner, the nurse came up with the most astonished look I have ever seen on a person’s face. The nurse told me that this lady had severe and profound dementia, and she hadn’t spoken a word in months. My music stirred her in a miraculous way. That is only one reason for music. But students at all ages should have the opportunity to learn and appreciate music. The easiest thing to do is to take a music appreciation class. I do not know if Piedmont Middle School or the high school offer music appreciation classes. For more than 25 years Joe Piazza, and before him Alan Harvey taught music theory and music appreciation classes at Piedmont High, classes that proved to be popular year after year. Psychological tests have proved that simply listening to music increases the intelligence and does good things for the spirit. Playing music is even better because it is a participation sport. You will learn another language. At the same time, you learn to work together as a team as well as improve personal discipline. It’s always a good idea to remember that participation in music is fun. You learn problem-solving in enjoyable ways. There is also the social aspect. That was what kept my son involved in music. He enjoyed himself so thoroughly that he decided to make music his life. Musicians lead exciting lives. We have friends everywhere in the world and have the opportunity to travel extensively and visit and perform with them. One other thing to consider is that audiences love what musicians do. It isn’t just the applause; audience members Virtuoso Norwegian violinist and composer Ole Bull. will come to the stage and want to speak to the performers. If that isn’t gratification, I don’t know what is. So many of the great musicians were also great role models. So… Let me mention two of them. One is Ezzard Charles. His nickname was the “Cincinnati Cobra”. To those who know about boxing, Ezzard Charles was one of the great boxers of all time and the Heavyweight champ of the world. A Black man, he grew up in the segregated south. But he valued education. During World War II he was stationed in Italy. He came back speaking Italian. There is a beautiful news clip in which he is speaking in Italian with his nemesis, Rocky Marciano. For two great rivals, this was a perfect example of respect and friendship. A less publicized part of his life was the fact that Ezzard Charles played the cello. Another good example is a friend from Oklahoma City. Virginia Campbell was laid to rest just a few days ago at the age of 88. Her story is extraordinary. She married at a young age and had four children. After the four children got married and left the house, Virginia got a college degree in music, with a major in piano performance. Rather than embark on a playing career, she became the most important impresario in Oklahoma City. For 35 years she presented concerts of international quality. She got a church to donate its facilities as a concert hall, with all post-concert receptions catered. All concert artists were of international quality. Virginia was chosen as Miss Senior Oklahoma and was a finalist in the Miss Senior USA “beauty-talent“ competitions. She did perform and traveled throughout the world giving concerts and teaching. Consider all of the things she did, and then know that Virginia Campbell was legally blind. Studying music is all for the good. Do it because it makes you smarter. Do it for all the reasons above but, remember that playing music is lots of fun. The opportunities are there. Remember the adage: when opportunity knocks, it’s a good idea to open the door.

articles.text: Because England had such a strong cultural influence on early America, it was inevitable that we would inherit various architectural styles as well. While walking through Piedmont it is easy to come across the prominent Tudor style and its variants, maybe one of the most lasting of our British legacy. The Tudor we see in Piedmont today is really Tudor Revival, which was an early 1900’s reinvention of the medieval prototypes from the English Tudor dynasty of the 16th century. What we end up with is a stately looking architecture that is also picturesque – the feeling of a country estate, which seems to be aesthetically suited for the large single family lots we have here. Intricate lower-level brick or stonework is also a common component as seen in these fine Piedmont homes.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 10, 2021 21 Features Tudor Style Architecture Part 15 in a biweekly series By Will Adams Because England had such a strong cultural influence on early America, it was inevitable that we would inherit various architectural styles as well. While walking through Piedmont it is easy to come across the prominent Tudor style and its variants, maybe one of the most lasting of our British legacy. The Tudor we see in Piedmont today is really Tudor Revival, which was an early 1900’s reinvention of the medieval prototypes from the English Tudor dynasty of the 16th century. What we end up with is a stately looking architecture that is also picturesque – the feeling of a country estate, which seems to be aesthetically suited for the large single family lots we have here. The popularity of this style in the early 1900’s was to a large degree an alternative to the modThe Tudor style is characterized by steeply pitched, front facing gable roofs. There are, however, frequent variations and exceptions in this “playful” style of architecture with hipped roofs sometimes used in conjunction with the gables. ernism that was being developed in Europe with machined components and lack of ornamentation. People wanted a more handcrafted feeling that ended up being expressed in Tudor homes. As a matter of fact, the Tudor style was closely associated with the Arts and Crafts movement which was being developed at the same time for many of the same reasons. I often wonder why a certain architectural style becomes popular and then remains so for so many years. I think that certainly one reason is because these styles were well developed over a long period of time. Proportions, material selections, and detailing conventions were worked out over the years on different buildings until they became….fine architecture! Certainly. this was the case on the cathedrals that took hundreds of years to build. After building a part of it, seeing it for a few years or even decades, the sponsors and architects were able to re-design and correct functional and aesthetic components, sometimes even changing the architectural style completely. In any case, the Tudor style developed into an appealing and desirable architecture all over this country. The visual giveaway of course is the half-timbered walls, consisting of a squared heavy timber frame structural system originally infilled with masonry or a stucco like mixture know as wattle between the timbers. The timber frame became unnecessary a long time ago, but the look was so favored and enduring that it continues to be imitated as a decorative motif instead of a structural necessity. articles.text: Lately, I’m obsessed with curation. Essentially, curation is about thoughtfully selecting, styling, and accessorizing. Curation can be applied to any art form, whether we are dressing ourselves, cooking a meal or designing a room. There’s an awareness and a sensitivity to making the selections and knowing how to put them all together. I find that the most soulful environments, and even my favorite outfits, come together when I source items that are made of quality materials, often by hand, and have been collected over time. Layering items – vintage and new, colors and textures – how they speak to each other is part of the magic. There is a difference in how my clients respond to the energies of things. I can see their reaction when they are picking up a double-weight alpaca boucle blanket from Rosemary Hallgarten vs. a synthetic West Elm throw that’s supposed to look luxe but is made with synthetic materials. The latter may trick your eye, but it doesn’t trick your heart. When I am designing a space with thoughtfully curated pieces, I have that feeling that I imagine a conductor of a symphony might have, waving my baton to pull in the flute at the exact moment when the music needs it. This spring, my team has brought five design projects to completion at nearly the same time; which means that we are executing on five reveals, with five accompanying photo shoots. My world has been a beehive of activity for days — shopping and curating. Honestly, getting everything together for the reveal, styling the space, this final pulling together of art and objects is so satisfying. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, March 10, 2021 Keys to Style: Quality, History, and Layers By Laura Martin Bovard Lately, I’m obsessed with curation. Essentially, curation is about thoughtfully selecting, styling, and accessorizing. Curation can be applied to any art form, whether we are dressing ourselves, cooking a meal or designing a room. There’s an awareness and a sensitivity to making the selections and knowing how to put them all together. I find that the most soulful environments, and even my favorite outfits, come together when I source items that are made of quality materials, often by hand, and have been collected over time. Layering items – vintage and new, colors and textures – how they speak to each other is part of the magic. There is a difference in how my clients respond to the energies of things. I can see their reaction when they are picking up a double-weight alpaca boucle blanket from Rosemary Hallgarten vs. a synthetic West Elm throw that’s supposed to look luxe but is made with synthetic materials. The latter may trick your eye, but it doesn’t trick your heart. When I am designing a space with thoughtfully curated pieces, I have that feeling that I imagine a conductor of a symphony might have, waving my baton to pull in the flute at the exact moment when the music needs it. This spring, my team has brought five design projects to completion at nearly the same time; which means that we are executing on five reveals, with five accompanying photo shoots. My world has been a beehive of activity for days — shopping and curating. Honestly, getting everything together for the reveal, styling the space, this final pulling together of art and objects is so satisfying. But also it’s hard work, with much angst, hunger (emotional and physical), and running around from vendor to vendor. Still, I have grown to love all of it. Which is not to say I’m only shopping in the final days before a photo shoot. For example, styling our most recent project started a month ago. My studio director (a.k.a. work A few finds from a day on the coast: birds, books, lamp. wife) Darshan and I were having a girls’ weekend, staying at a client’s vacation house on the coast. One day we headed out in search of lunch and a view of the ocean and we ended up finding this fantastic vintage store. We were there for over two hours wandering through a place so full of treasures. The owner stayed late with us and we had such fun picking through her wares, thinking about our different projects — shopping and mentally curating. We found a gorgeous mid-century lamp with a black carved-wood sculptural base. We brought it last week to its place of destiny – a client’s entry console table (see the photo). I love to decorate with antique books. At this same shop we found a pristine three-volume dictionary in a rich dark blue, and a set of the collected works of Edgar Allan Poe, several small volumes bound in red. What we look for when we are styling bookcases is not just books but also objects to display on the shelves. A set of carved birds, a small antique desk globe, a mid-century ashtray with a horse motif (that will go to our client who smokes cigars); a very large crystal cluster that will be perfect for another client’s powder room vanity. It’s not just the beauty of the objects themselves, but the stories they hold – why and how they were created, the life they may have had before they came to us, how they came into Photo by Lauren Anderson, Sen Creative Sneak peek from a recent photo shoot with lamp all fixed up and installed on a console table. Bringing it all together: layers revealed in a recent kitchen install. Photo by Mo Saito Photo by LMB Interiors our lives, the way that energy builds up in a piece so that it is richer and has more depth and feeling. And then, when we put these disparate or matching things together, how they sit in relation to each other. The colors, textures, shapes, reflective qualities, ages, stories and vibrations all come together to make a room something more than just a room. It is now an experience of beauty that is transcendent. It’s the feeling that happens when a room comes to life — that is the addictive transformation that keeps me in this business, happily, over all of these years. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. For information see laura@lmbinteriors.com.

articles.text: Stephen Edward Block, age 84, died peacefully in his sleep on January 18, 2021, with Dale, his wife of fifty years, by his side. Stephen was a life-long East Bay resident and a long time East Bay real estate developer. Born Stephen Edward Block in Oakland on March 16, 1936, he was the son of George and Gladys Block. He attended Crocker Highlands Elementary and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1954. He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Civil Engineering from the University of California, Berkeley in 1958, While at Cal Stephen joined his older brother George as a member of the Zeta Beta Tau fraternity and was also a member of the U.S. Army Reserve Officer Training Corps. After graduation, he served as an officer in the Army’s Counterintelligence Corps. Blessed with an impish sense of humor, while in the Army he was known for using the Presidio parade ground as a driving range. In 1970, Stephen married Dale Block (née Forrest), and in 1972 they welcomed their only son Adam. As his family grew, Stephen invested his energies in his real estate business as well. Over the years he developed a range of office, industrial, and residential projects, including Moraga Country Club, Kelton Court, and a variety of build-to-suit warehouses. Piedmont alums Clark Wallace and Bob Goetz, along with Block were the brains and brawn behind the Moraga Country Club project in 1971. Wallace, a well-established Moraga real estate broker and developer, served as the organization’s president; Block was a Stephen Block behind the wheel of his 1938 BMW 328 at the 2007 Monterey Historic Automobile Races. developer and contractor who handled the day-to-day operations; Goetz, an architect and land planner, designed the Club’s Master Plan; and Bob Wooldridge, a local contractor and homebuilder, managed the building of the Club facilities and homes. Stephen’s most recent project was centro1331, Berkeley’s first LEED-certified sustainable office building. Always community-minded, while growing his real estate business Stephen also served as President of the East Bay chapter of Associated Home Builders, as a member of the finance committee of the Jewish Federation, and as a community representative on the team that created the West Berkeley Plan. With his family, Stephen was a generous supporter of the Oakland Museum of California, Bay Area Tumor Institute, the Cancer League, and Head-Royce School. Stephen and Dale Block at Chez Panisse on New Year’s Eve in 2013. Stephen Block at the Paris Retromobile in 2004, presenting the Pegaso Z102 he restored over two decades. A true renaissance man with a zest for life, Stephen was well known for his enthusiastic pursuit of diverse interests, whether collecting antiques, model trains, or Japanese stamps — or playing bridge, golf, or basketball. But for a man of many hobbies, his greatest love by far was collecting, restoring, touring, and racing vintage European automobiles. Recognized in the community for his deep knowledge of 1950s and 1960s sports cars, he took particular pleasure in serving as Class Host at the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, where he also showed many of his exotic cars over the years. Stephen was instrumental in the selection of Pegaso — a rare Spanish sports car from the 1950s — as the featured marque at the 1994 Pebble Beach event. He helped bring a unique collection of 12 Pegasos from all over the world. An avid golfer and bridge player, Stephen was a member of the Concordia Club of San Francisco, Lake Merced Golf and Country Club, Claremont Country Club, and was a founder of the Moraga Country Club. Stephen gave generously of his time and experience; he took particular interest in young entrepreneurs in whom he recognized kindred dealmaking spirits and was a mentor to many. A “family first” gentleman who derived great pleasure from the achievements of his wife, son, and daughter-in-law Eve, Stephen was always excited to hear about a recent success or dive deeply into a thorny problem. He also maintained an abiding interest in his niece and nephews Audrey, Greg, and Jerald Block and their families, nephew Anthony Bernard, his wife Tara and their children Gabriel and Emilia, and nephew David Forrest (Carrie) and great nephew Ethan. The family wishes to acknowledge with deep appreciation the expressions of love, concern, and kindness shown to them in this time of bereavement. A life tribute to Stephen will be held at a later date. Donations in Stephen Block’s memory may be made to the Bay Area Tumor Institute (400 30th St., Suite 301, Oakland CA 94609) or to the Michael J. Fox Foundation (michaeljfox.org).

Arched arcades on each side led to the home economics and music classrooms on the left. The science, chemistry and biology labs were to the right, and the cafeteria was on the lower level. The main entrance to the school opened to an oak paneled foyer with a fireplace and the principal’s office beyond. Traditions Once the school was built, the student body set many of Piedmont High School’s traditions that first year. The student body chose purple and white as the school colors and “Achieve the Honorable” as the school motto. Jack Cook designed the school shield, still on the school’s website. Students chose a Scottish theme. Piedmont is a highland, just like Scotland. The Scottish have never been conquered by an invading force; hence we derive the Piedmont spirit that never gives up. The Scottish theme also extended to the athletic teams (the Highlanders and Scots), the yearbook (the Clan-O-Log), the school newspaper (the Highlander) and the annual carnival (the Highland Fling.) Since so many students came from different schools that first year, the student body felt it was important to create an inclusive A 1921 sketch shows the future Piedmont athletic field. nature throughout the school. The yearbook was named the Clan-OLog, a log of the clans or all who came to Piedmont. The yearbook was to be a record of all students. Expansion Piedmont Junior High School was built in 1924 to ease the crowding in the high school. The building had 13 classrooms, a gymnasium, print shop and auto shop. Seventh, eighth and ninth graders attended class in the junior high, relieving the crowding in the high school. Landscape architect Howard Gilkey designed the new athletic field. It was built on the site of the former hedge Maze in Piedmont Park. Gilkey’s plans included a football field, quarter mile track and a baseball field. It was completed in 1924. Piedmont’s teams finally had a home field. Piedmont’s football team on the athletic field in 1922 before Gilkey’s improvements. Note the dirt field.
