articles.text: Piedmont Park, created by Frank C. Havens, was to be sold in 1916. Havens was deeply in debt, and his creditors planned to sell the park at a foreclosure auction in 1917. With news of the eminent sale of the park, the Piedmont School District approved a bond measure to purchase 13 acres for a new high school and athletic field. (The city also passed a measure to reimburse Wallace Alexander for the purchase of the remaining park land. The School District immediately began plans to build a new high school. Officials conferred with architect William H. Weeks and ultimately approved his plans in November, 1920. Although construction did not begin until 1921, school officials started the new school curriculum in August, 1920. For the first year, only a junior high school curriculum was offered. Forty students who completed the 8th grade at Havens and Lake (now Beach) schools formed the new 9th grade. The 7th and 8th graders from the elementary schools joined this first junior high school population. Their classes were held in the old Piedmont Park buildings, in classrooms in the remodeled Piedmont Springs Clubhouse, the Art Gallery and in temporary shacks for two years. Wildwood School was not built until 1923. High School dedicated in 1922 Piedmont High School was dedicated on June 1, 1922. Originally constructed as a junior-senior high school, the school offered classes for 7th through 12th grades. When the school opened in September 1922, school officials expected 260 students, but 325 students enrolled. Many of these students formerly attended high school in Oakland, and paid a fee. Enrollment grew to 400 students by the end of the first semester and to 600 by the end of the year. Architect William H. Weeks planned to make the Piedmont High School design his masterpiece. It was considered the finest high school in the state, with two floors of classrooms, an auditorium, study halls, science laboratories, a cafeteria and a radio room. It was among the first schools to have a public address system in all the classrooms. Weeks designed an elegant Mediterranean style school with a symmetrical façade. The central auditorium had five tall, arched windows trimmed with glazed terra cotta. Two stories of classrooms overlooked the ravine The oak paneled foyer in Piedmont High School had a fireplace with the school’s shield. articles.text: More then a half year ago, a 76-year-old Piedmont woman was robbed at gunpoint in front of her home. On the evening of July 10, 2020 she stopped at the In-n-Out Burger on Hegenberger Road in Oakland. Unaware, she had been followed to her home in Piedmont by 23-year-old Christopher Ware. At approximately 7 p.m. he forced open the driver door of her car and stole her purse at gunpoint. Her purse contained a credit card, a driver’s license, and two iPhone 8s. (One phone has since been recovered.) Ware was seen running on foot on Arbor Drive and getting in the passenger side of a white Lexus RX300. Ware and the accomplice fled the city, but an automated license plate reader captured the license plate number. A detailed description of the individual and the gun was given to the police by the robbery victim. This information was shared with other local law enforcement agencies. Two weeks later, at 1:00pm on July 25, 2020, Ware robbed another victim, a 43-year-old woman in the parking lot of a grocery store in San Lorenzo. He ran up behind the woman as she was attempting to get in her car, knocked her to the ground, and ripped her purse from her arm. In a coordinated effort by Piedmont and Oakland police officers, Ware was arrested for both crimes six days later on July 31, 2020. On February 18, 2021 a jury convicted Ware of second-degree robbery with personal use of a firearm, an additional second degree robbery, identity theft, possession of a firearm as a convicted felon, and several other firearms and ammunition offenses. Background to an investigation On July 31, 2020, the day of his arrest, Oakland Police officers noticed Ware on Douglas Avenue in Oakland. They observed him get into the driver’s seat of his white Lexus RX300 and detained him before he could drive away. Officers found an unregistered and loaded black Smith & Wesson .45 caliber handgun next to the driver’s seat. The handgun had multiple distinctive markings on it consistent with the detailed description provided by the Piedmont victim. “What really cracked [the case] was that her credit card was used at [the] Target [store] in San Leandro. We were able to get video surveillance and it matched up with surveillance we had in Piedmont,” explained Piedmont Detective Jeff Spranza. Investigative efforts by Spranza and Piedmont Det. John Lagios confirmed Ware as the suspect. “At the time [of the crime] the car was not registered in his name. Through investigation we learned that he purchased that vehicle in February 2020. We confirmed the sale of the vehicle with the previous owner who sold it to him,” said Spranza. Ware’s girlfriend, Dashantay Walker, was identified as the accomplice and was arrested. Her case is pending. Ware remains in Santa Rita Jail on a no-bail hold and has a sentencing date of March 18. He could be given a term of 18 or more years in prison. “With this investigation we were able to identify two suspects and brought closure to the victim and the residents of Piedmont. This is reassurance that Mr. Ware will not be offending anytime soon,” said Spranza. Anyone with additional information or inquiries related to this case is asked to contact Piedmont Detectives Jeff Spranza or John Lagios at (510) 420-3013. have been hit the hardest by COVID-19, data often shows that the richest zip codes across the country have the highest vaccination rates. articles.text: Editor: As many of you know, my family has been deeply involved with Children’s Hospital Oakland for nearly 40 years. Children’s was a free-standing non-profit children’s hospital and affiliated with UCSF Children’s Hospital, now collectively called UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospitals. One of the major goals of the affiliation was to preserve and expand the excellent array of critical care services to the families in the SF East Bay, especially to the most vulnerable families. Since the affiliation, there has actually been a reduction of services in Oakland. Moms from East and West Oakland are now required to take their sick children to Mission Bay, SF instead of being seen by great doctors in Oakland. I have attached the link to an Oaklandside article that was recently published on the role UCSF has played in diminishing the access families have in the East Bay to obtain care for their sick kids in Oakland. The California Nursing Association has been active in trying to retain critical care services in Oakland. Along with a group of interested community parties and Oakland doctors, we have been working hard for four years to draw attention to this. We have a petition for people to sign (Online Action | National Nurses United at: https://www. n a t io n a l n u r s e s u n it e d .o r g / online-action#/73) which we will deliver to the UC Board of Regents and post on our website (https://www.keepkidscareinoakland.com/) with more details. I know you care tremendously for kids in our community. Please take time to read the article and if you support our efforts, please sign the petition and forward on the information to others. There will be a Town Hall Zoom meeting on Wednesday, March 10th at 5:30 pm. The link to the article is: https://oaklandside.org/2021/02/25/childrenshospital-oakland-joined-ucsf-7- years-ago-was-it-a-good-move/ -Jeff Cheung (cheungjeff88@ gmail.com) There have been 1,293 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,507,266 total cases of COVID- 19 in the state and 54,224 deaths.

A large factor in this timeline was the approval this month of a vaccine created by Johnson & Johnson. Only about 5,500 doses of this vaccine have arrived in Alameda County so far, but that number is expected to balloon in time. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine is the third COVID-19 vaccine available after ones produced by Pfizer and Moderna. Unlike the vaccines created by the latter two companies, the Johnson & Johnson vaccine only requires one dose. Moderna and Pfizer vaccines, require two doses administered several weeks apart. Over 20 percent of Piedmont’s adult population has been fully vaccinated against COVID-19 as of Sunday, March 8, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. pages.text: 30 Wednesday, March 10, 2021 CRIME REPORT By Jay Russell Arrest made in armed robbery of elderly woman in July Piedmont, Oakland PD combine for 2 arrests, 1 conviction More then a half year ago, a 76-year-old Piedmont woman was robbed at gunpoint in front of her home. On the evening of July 10, 2020 she stopped at the In-n-Out Burger on Hegenberger Road in Oakland. Unaware, she had been followed to her home in Piedmont by 23-year-old Christopher Ware. At approximately 7 p.m. he forced open the driver door of her car and stole her purse at gunpoint. Her purse contained a credit card, a driver’s license, and two iPhone 8s. (One phone has since been recovered.) Ware was seen running on foot on Arbor Drive and getting in the passenger side of a white Lexus RX300. Ware and the accomplice fled the city, but an automated license plate reader captured the license plate number. A detailed description of the individual and the gun was given to the police by the robbery victim. This information was shared with other local law enforcement agencies. Two weeks later, at 1:00pm on July 25, 2020, Ware robbed another victim, a 43-year-old woman in the parking lot of a grocery store in San Lorenzo. He ran up behind the woman as she was attempting to get in her car, knocked her to the ground, and ripped her purse from her arm. In a coordinated effort by Piedmont and Oakland police officers, Ware was arrested for both crimes six days later on July 31, 2020. On February 18, 2021 a jury convicted Ware of second-degree robbery with personal use of a firearm, an additional second degree robbery, identity theft, possession of a firearm as a convicted felon, and several other firearms and ammunition offenses. Background to an investigation On July 31, 2020, the day of his arrest, Oakland Police officers noticed Ware on Douglas Avenue in Oakland. They observed him get into the driver’s seat of his white Lexus RX300 and detained him before he could drive away. Officers found an unregistered and loaded black Smith & Wesson .45 caliber handgun next to the driver’s seat. The handgun had multiple distinctive markings on it consistent with the detailed description provided by the Piedmont victim. “What really cracked [the case] was that her credit card was used at [the] Target [store] in San Leandro. We were able to get video surveillance and it matched up with surveillance we had in Piedmont,” explained Piedmont Detective Jeff Spranza. Investigative efforts by Spranza and Piedmont Det. John Lagios confirmed Ware as the suspect. “At the time [of the crime] the car was not registered in his name. Through investigation we learned that he purchased that vehicle in February 2020. We confirmed the sale of the vehicle with the previous owner who sold it to him,” said Spranza. Ware’s girlfriend, Dashantay Walker, was identified as the accomplice and was arrested. Her case is pending. Ware remains in Santa Rita Jail on a no-bail hold and has a sentencing date of March 18. He could be given a term of 18 or more years in prison. “With this investigation we were able to identify two suspects and brought closure to the victim and the residents of Piedmont. This is reassurance that Mr. Ware will not be offending anytime soon,” said Spranza. Anyone with additional information or inquiries related to this case is asked to contact Piedmont Detectives Jeff Spranza or John Lagios at (510) 420-3013. Covid Vaccination Continued from page 3 based on state rules, and California hopes that vaccines are available to everyone by the summer. A large factor in this timeline was the approval this month of a vaccine created by Johnson & Johnson. Only about 5,500 doses of this vaccine have arrived in Alameda County so far, but that number is expected to balloon in time. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine is the third COVID-19 vaccine available after ones produced by Pfizer and Moderna. Unlike the vaccines created by the latter two companies, the Johnson & Johnson vaccine only requires one dose. Moderna and Pfizer vaccines, require two doses administered several weeks apart. Over 20 percent of Piedmont’s adult population has been fully vaccinated against COVID-19 as of Sunday, March 8, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. Almost 43 percent of Piedmonters, some 3,550 people, have received at least their first dose of vaccine. Piedmont leads every other city in Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population by a wide margin. However, Census estimates claim that only 21.5 percent of Piedmonters are 65 years and older. Across Alameda County, almost 462,000 total vaccine doses have been administered, and about 128,000 people have been fully vaccinated – this means that about 10 percent of the county’s population have been fully vaccinated. Piedmont’s high rates of vaccination compared to the rest of the county has been linked to wider nationwide questions about vaccine access. Only 9 percent of Oakland’s population has been fully vaccinated. While many low-income areas have been hit the hardest by COVID-19, data often shows that the richest zip codes across the country have the highest vaccination rates. In terms of per capita income, Piedmont ranks among the top 20 cities in California. To improve equity in vaccination, the state and county are working to target thousands of vaccine doses to some of the zip codes hardest hit by COVID-19. These include several Oakland neighborhoods as well as parts of Hayward, Ashland and Cherryland. “Alameda County supports every effort to ensure our communities that have been disproportionally impacted by COVID-19, where we observe higher case and mortality rates, are first in line for vaccine,” Dr. Kathleen Clanon, the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency Medical Director, said in a statement. The state has administered over 10.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 14.5 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. LETTERS - CONTINUED Continued from page 3 UCSF reduces Critical Care services for families Editor: As many of you know, my family has been deeply involved with Children’s Hospital Oakland for nearly 40 years. Children’s was a free-standing non-profit children’s hospital and affiliated with UCSF Children’s Hospital, now collectively called UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospitals. One of the major goals of the affiliation was to preserve and expand the excellent array of critical care services to the families in the SF East Bay, especially to the most vulnerable families. Since the affiliation, there has actually been a reduction of services in Oakland. Moms from East and West Oakland are now required to take their sick children to Mission Bay, SF instead of being seen by great doctors in Oakland. I have attached the link to an Oaklandside article that was recently published on the role UCSF has played in diminishing the access families have in the East Bay to obtain care for their sick kids in Oakland. The California Nursing Association has been active in trying to retain critical care services in Oakland. Along with a group of interested community parties and Oakland doctors, we have been working hard for four years to draw attention to this. We have a petition for people to sign (Online Action | National Nurses United at: https://www. n a t io n a l n u r s e s u n it e d .o r g / online-action#/73) which we will deliver to the UC Board of Regents and post on our website (https://www.keepkidscareinoakland.com/) with more details. I know you care tremendously for kids in our community. Please take time to read the article and if you support our efforts, please sign the petition and forward on the information to others. There will be a Town Hall Zoom meeting on Wednesday, March 10th at 5:30 pm. The link to the article is: https://oaklandside.org/2021/02/25/childrenshospital-oakland-joined-ucsf-7- years-ago-was-it-a-good-move/ -Jeff Cheung (cheungjeff88@ gmail.com) Covid Update Continued from page 3 each other safe.” No new cases have been reported in Piedmont over the past three weeks. There have been 1,293 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide. articles.text: The Piedmont Rec. Dept. has planned a scavenger hunt for the last week of March, and the treasure is irresistible: Leprechaun Gold. A city-wide Spring Scavenger Hunt will begin on Saturday, March 20 and continue for one week. Search through the parks in Piedmont for clues; unravel the riddles and work through the mind-boggling puzzles. The Rec. Department’s Halloween Treasure Hunt last Autumn took families on a quest to help the swashbuckling Explorer Cavendish find his buried pirate treasure. This challenge has an even grander storyline brought to life with an alluring backstory via the Actionbound app. Venture through Piedmont Park; comb through the four-leaf clovers in Dracena Park in search of the end of the rainbow. The week-long event will be a fun mystery that will have every member of the family wishing for the luck of the Irish to find the golden prize. The gold will vanish a week after the event starts so don’t wait. Signups begin this Friday, March 12 on the Rec. Department’s CommunityPass page: register.communitypass.net/reg/ cat_program_list.cfm?season_ id=24069 For more information, contact Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns at jstearns@piedmont. ca.gov. Advice to all explorers: remember to wear green.

articles.text: Creativity and community spirit came together in a Virtual Quilting Bee last Saturday, March 6, to help create pieces for the “Things That Matter” Community Art Quilt. “It was great connecting with other members of the community, sharing ideas and talking about different expressions of creativity,” said textile artist Amanda Ward, who helped manage the event. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Virtual Quilting Bee was an opportunity to find inspiration and instruction on making quilt squares that will eventually come together into a community quilt. A limited number of quilt squares and quilt kits are still available from the Piedmont Arts Fund. All money raised is earmarked for visual and performing arts programs in Piedmont schools. articles.text: On Monday morning, March 8, a water main break occurred on Oakland Avenue. The failure occurred on a 20 inch, 100-yearold iron pipe near the northeast corner of El Cerrito Avenue. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) isolated the break within an hour after it occurred. “When I visited the site about 30 minutes after the break occurred, EBMUD was onsite, and the break was isolated when the surrounding water valves were shut off. Fortunately, EBMUD was able to isolate the break and keep water service on for residents in the surrounding area, so we didn’t have any reports of water service being interrupted,” Gonzales said. Oakland Avenue – a main thoroughfare and a bus route – was closed off on Monday between San Carlos Ave. and Carmel Ave. while repairs were made. Gonzales added that repairs took the better part of the day. A portion of the sidewalk and curb will need to be replaced following the break. “Public Works crews performed clean up and verified that our sewer pipeline wasn’t damaged by debris or by the force of the water,” Gonzales said.
articles.title: Portion of sidewalk to be replaced

articles.text: A rise in violent attacks against Asian individuals across the country has sparked federal, state, and local response. Some of the most brazen attacks have occurred locally, specifically in Oakland’s Chinatown district. Oakland Chamber of Commerce President Carl Chan explained that community underreporting, coupled with recent Oakland Police Department budget cuts, may be contributing to the surge in violent crimes. “These kinds of attacks did not just happen yesterday,” said Chan. “They’ve been going on for years. The severity of the attacks began at the start of the pandemic, beginning in January of last year.” Most of the assaults then were verbal, he said, but have progressed to violent assaults in recent weeks. Learning about mercy through gentleness By Rev. Jim Hopkins Kate Bowler’s book Everything Happens For a Reason: And Other Lies I Have Loved is so worth reading that in April I decided to preach a three-sermon series based on it. Kate, a professor at Duke Divinity School and a respected researcher into the Prosperity Gospel, wrote the book after being diagnosed with stage four colon cancer. The sermons in my series were: April 8: “The Lie of Control” (Romans 8:26-28); April 15: “The Gift of Uncertainty” (Job 23: 1-17); April 22: “The Blessing of Gentle Words” (Matthew 5:7) In my first sermon I reflected on her words. “We love to tell ourselves that the world is ultimately fair. We try to convince ourselves that we can curate our lives, minimize our losses and stand on our own successes. We need to quit lying to ourselves.” The emphasis in the sermon fell on our understanding of Romans 8:28, the verse that many take to mean “everything happens for a reason.” I argued that the best way to read the verse is “in all things God works for those who love God” as opposed to “all thing work together for good for those who love God.” In the latter reading it seems is that everything that happens is ultimately caused by God. In the former reading God is at work with us, in the face of everything that happens, to bring about good. The former reading leads to a “Blueprint Theology” while the latter leads to a “Being-There Theology.” In my second sermon I noted that one of the pleas Kate makes to her well-meaning friends as she faced the possibility that she might not live to see her two year old son turn three was “Do not pour your certainty on my suffering.” In the biblical book of Job this is one of the central tensions. The suffering Job has lost everything and the only message his well-intentioned friends can deliver is “We know that suffering is the result of sin. You are clearly suffering so clearly you have sinned. Just repent and God will make you well.” They poured their certainty on his suffering with the result being that while they felt better, their suffering friend felt much worse. In the final sermon of the series the words of Jesus from his Sermon on the Mount were central: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy.” My theme was that when someone we love is suffering, a gentle word, a gentle touch or even a gentle silence can be a great mercy. articles.text: At the request of Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, Interim Fire Chief Despain and Recreation Director Putzer provided updates on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on their respective departments. The city has just completed a full year of restrictions. Updates were provided during a Monday night, March 1 City Council meeting. Fire Department Interim Fire Chief Micheal Despain offered an overview of vaccine availability in the county, and how residents can gain access to it. He also noted that if COVID-19 cases continue to drop, Alameda County can be moved to the less restrictive “Red Tier” as early as next week. “The [COVID-19] caseload is coming down considerably each and every week, and we could be changing into the Red Tier soon, which opens up a lot of options,” Despain said. Alameda County health officials should have enough data to make a determination as to whether or not the county will move into the Red Tier. If this happens, restrictions would be similar to “early November,” making indoor dining and gym access possible. Despain added that there is evidence of an expanded rollout of vaccine availability in Alameda County, though the actual number of vaccines administrated in the county hasn’t changed much. It is averaging about 15,000 doses per week. “As weeks go by, we’re seeing improvement. But what changed [in terms of availability] is that FEMA opened two mega-PODs [points of distribution] in California, and we’ve got one at the Oakland Coliseum,” he noted. There are expectations that the ease of access should increase actual distribution. The fastest way to get a vaccine, Despain said, is through your healthcare provider; then through the county health signup, and then myturn.ca.gov signup. You can be on all three of these “lists” at once. “Think of it as multiple routes – if your healthcare provider calls you and says ‘you’re up,’ you can go through that process, or through the county,” he added. “We caution people that it’s ok to sign up three times, but whatever ‘lane’ you get into, you get your shot, and stay in that
articles.title: Fire Chief, Rec. Director provide updates at council meeting

articles.text: As the number of new coronavirus cases drop, Alameda County has hit all the metrics to enter a less-restrictive phase of reopening, but no change in status has been announced as of yesterday, Tuesday, March 2. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County has dipped to 2 percent as of Monday, March 1, its lowest point since early November last year. Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Several neighboring counties have moved out of the Purple Tier, including Marin, San Francisco, San Mateo Santa Clara, and Napa counties. They were moved into the Red Tier, which is the second-most restrictive tier in the state system. The adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people dropped to 6.3 in Alameda County, now below the 7 per 100,000 needed to move into the Red Tier. The case rate, positivity rate and positivity rate in the least advantaged census tracts all are meeting state guidelines to move into the Red Tier as of yesterday afternoon. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. After acknowledging that COVID-19 cases have plummeted compared to December and January, Gov. Gavin Newsom said Monday that “we are seeing a little bit of a plateau, and one needs to be mindful of that.” No new cases of COVID have been reported in Piedmont in two weeks. The city has had 167 cases reported so far. Across Alameda County, 1,182 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, an uptick week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 80,780. There have been 25,075 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,705 cases in Hayward. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,481,611 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 52,497 deaths due to the disease statewide. Health experts remain concerned that more contagious strains of COVID-19 could spread in Alameda County. Variants first identified in South Africa, the United Kingdom and Denmark have all been discovered in the county, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention believe these variants spread more easily. This week, Alameda County officials reported a second case of a South African variant of COVID-19 known to be more resistant to certain vaccines. The cases are unconnected, and both were reported in individuals who had recently returned from international travel. The CDC believes both individuals were infected while overseas. “How is your corporate malaise coming along?”

Director provide updates at council meeting By Allyson Aleksey At the request of Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, Interim Fire Chief Despain and Recreation Director Putzer provided updates on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on their respective departments. The city has just completed a full year of restrictions. Updates were provided during a Monday night, March 1 City Council meeting. Fire Department Interim Fire Chief Micheal Despain offered an overview of vaccine availability in the county, and how residents can gain access to it. He also noted that if COVID-19 cases continue to drop, Alameda County can be moved to the less restrictive “Red Tier” as early as next week. “The [COVID-19] caseload is coming down considerably each and every week, and we could be changing into the Red Tier soon, which opens up a lot of options,” Despain said. By next Tuesday, March 9, Alameda County health officials should have enough data to make a determination as to whether or not the county will move into the Red Tier. If this happens, restrictions would be similar to “early November,” making indoor dining and gym access possible. Despain added that there is evidence of an expanded rollout of vaccine availability in Alameda County, though the actual number of vaccines administrated in the county hasn’t changed much. It is averaging about 15,000 doses per week. “As weeks go by, we’re seeing improvement. But what changed [in terms of availability] is that FEMA opened two mega-PODs [points of distribution] in California, and we’ve got one at the Oakland Coliseum,” he noted. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County has dipped to 2 percent as of Monday, March 1, its lowest point since early November last year. Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Several neighboring counties have moved out of the Purple Tier, including Marin, San Francisco, San Mateo Santa Clara, and Napa counties. They were moved into the Red Tier, which is the second-most restrictive tier in the state system. The adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people dropped to 6.3 in Alameda County, now below the 7 per 100,000 needed to move into the Red Tier. The case rate, positivity rate and positivity rate in the least advantaged census tracts all are meeting state guidelines to move into the Red Tier as of yesterday afternoon. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. After acknowledging that COVID-19 cases have plummeted compared to December and January, Gov. Gavin Newsom said Monday that “we are seeing a little bit of a plateau, and one needs to be mindful of that.” No new cases of COVID have been reported in Piedmont in two weeks. The city has had 167 cases reported so far. Across Alameda County, 1,182 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, an uptick week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 80,780. There have been 25,075 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,705 cases in Hayward. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,481,611 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 52,497 deaths due to the disease statewide. Health experts remain concerned that more contagious strains of COVID-19 could spread in Alameda County. Variants first identified in South Africa, the United Kingdom and Denmark have all been discovered in the county, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention believe these variants spread more easily. This week, Alameda County officials reported a second case of a South African variant of COVID-19 known to be more resistant to certain vaccines. The cases are unconnected, and both were reported in individuals who had recently returned from international travel. The CDC believes both individuals were infected while overseas. articles.text: As reported in “City Asks County for 1 More Year to Create Affordable Housing Plan,” (February 3, 2021), the City of Piedmont is currently exploring ways to use its $2.2 million in Measure A1 funds from Alameda County to build affordable rental housing. Given the enormous crisis of housing affordability in the Bay Area, and in light of the history of discriminatory housing policies--from racial covenants to redlining--that restricted who could live in Piedmont for over half a century, we have an urgent responsibility as a community to create more inclusive, diverse, and affordable housing. We should look to build dwellings that will enable teachers, city staff, seniors, and families of diverse income levels to reside within our community. We are Piedmont residents who believe the city should strive to take full advantage of the Measure A1 funds. Our group includes affordable housing professionals, urban planners, architects, land use attorneys, and experts in urban history and policy. We bring more than 150 years of combined experience in these fields. At the February 1, 2021, City Council meeting, over a dozen Piedmont residents spoke in support of new housing in our community. Carol Galante, a Piedmont resident, Director of UC Berkeley’s Terner Center for Housing Innovation, and a former assistant director of HUD, urged the city to explore all available options. In addition to accessory dwelling units, Piedmont should explore the potential to create attractive apartments or townhomes along Grand Avenue, in the Civic Center, and at Blair Park, which would enable more family housing. The city should also look to update our zoning code to enable the creation of duplexes and incrementally denser and more affordable housing, as many cities throughout the country have already done. Rather than view new housing as having a negative impact on Piedmont, these changes can make our community even better. Given that the state is asking Piedmont to plan for nearly 600 new housing units as part of its next 10-year housing plan, an “all of the above” solution will likely be needed. Let’s take full advantage of the funds provided by Measure A1 and tackle the challenge by doing what Piedmonters do best: coming together and leveraging the extraordinary talent, expertise, and commitment to equity among our residents, leaders, and city staff. Let’s be a model for other small cities around the Bay Area in charting a progressive, innovative path towards meeting the housing challenge. We invite anyone interested in learning more about affordable housing to email us at piedmontracialequity@gmail.com. Sofia Barandiaran Chris and Meghan Bennett Jessica Berg Irene Cheng Elise Marie Collins Frances and Jeremy Fisher Susan Fizzell Leslie Gray Amy Griffith Brett Hondorp Sarah Karlinsky Diana Lee Deborah Leland Nick Levinson Jane Lin Jill Lindenbaum Andy Madeira Louis Mirante Claire Parisa Rebecca Posamentier Rick Raushenbush Andrea Ruiz-Esquide Hope Salzer Brett Snyder Alice Talcott Randolph Wu

articles.text: Last year, there was a lot of attention on the Black experience in America, and one topic that must be included in that discussion is the impact of Black climate activists. Research shows that climate change does not impact all populations equally, and that Black communities face the negative effects of climate change more often than others. Due to this unequal burden, there is a long and important history of Black Americans leading the way on climate crises. This disparity can be seen in obvious ways, such as the infamous Flint, Michigan water and public health crisis, which impacted tens of thousands of people. Flint has a population that is over 50 percent African American, and the impact of the crisis on the community will be felt for decades. Another example is the Hurricane Katrina disaster, which killed over 1,000 people in New Orleans, a city which is 60 percent African-American. After Katrina, Black homeowners received $8,000 less in government aid than white homeowners because of housing value disparities. Predominantly black communities are more likely to be adjacent to landfills, hazardous waste sites, and industrial facilities. Black Americans are 40 percent more likely to have asthma than White Americans. These health outcomes are a direct effect of policy decisions that perpetuate unequal outcomes for different races in America. These health outcomes can be seen close to home. Oakland, which is 64 percent non-White, has childhood asthma rates of 18.3 percent. Compare this to Piedmont, which is approximately 75 percent white, and has child asthma rates of 12 percent. While mere miles apart, the discrepancies are vast. Black Americans, and particularly Black women, have been at the forefront of movements to make our environments a more equitable place to live for all. A local example is the Black Panther movement based in Oakland. Members organized drives to keep predominantly Black neighborhoods free of waste, hosting free health clinics and educating communities on the dangers of pollution. There now are groups in Oakland, throughout the Bay Area, and the state, that are focused on environmental issues, often helmed by Black people. One of these groups is the Climate Action Coalition in Oakland. The Coalition works on numerous issues, such as transit, food justice, and adaptation to climate change. Their overarching mission is racial and economic justice, which is directly related to climate solutions. Another group, Communities for a Better Environment, works in low-income Latino and African-American communities in Richmond and Oakland to address health hazards. Their goal is to prevent and reduce pollution and build healthy communities and environments. The California Environmental Justice Coalition (CEJC) is led by people of color and low-income communities. CEJC follows the principles of environmental justice and is committed to environmental, social, and economic justice. Thanks to these groups and many others, things can change for the better. Coupled with these organizations, municipal, regional, and statewide efforts can make a real difference to impacted communities. Keeping pressure on local policy makers can help make transportation, waste, and water systems more equitable for all people. Blackled movements in the community have historically made a difference and will continue to do so in the future. Nate Redinbo is the City of Piedmont’s Civic Spark Fellow in 2020-21. Call 420-3060 for more information (nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov).
articles.title: Environmental impacts on Black Americans

articles.text: Representative Eric Swalwell of Dublin introduced four anti-corruption bills on Tuesday, February 23, in response to the second failed impeachment of former president Donald Trump. The reintroduction is aimed to ensure that future presidents cannot “perpetrate some of the same corrupt acts,” Swalwell said. The bills would require that candidates, campaigns, and companies report any foreign interference in U.S. elections; enhance protections for ‘whistleblowers’ who come forward to expose official wrongdoing; and make it a criminal offense for the President, Vice President, or their families to enrich themselves from foreign sources. Swalwell, a member of the House Judiciary, Intelligence, and Homeland Security committees, previously introduced the bills between 2018 and 2020. “Donald Trump showed disdain for the moral and ethical norms we have always expected from an American president, so Congress must make sure these expectations are spelled out explicitly in law and are punished when violated.” “America needs these reforms to move ahead. We must make sure that these abuses can never happen again,” he said. The Duty to Report Act, which Swalwell introduced in June 2018 and April 2019, would closed sue for injunctive relief or monetary damages. Swalwell began drafting the bill after former President Trump and others attacked a whistleblower who raised concerns with the Director of National Intelligence’s Office of Inspector General about Trump’s actions in relation to Ukraine, which led to his first impeachment. “Republicans and Democrats alike for decades have agreed that threatening and trying to expose whistleblowers is wrong and undercuts long-established policy to encourage people to come forward with allegations of wrongdoing,” Swalwell said. “Trump’s actions showed our existing laws aren’t strong enough to protect whistleblowers’ right to anonymity.” The U.S. Constitution and current laws civilly prohibit government employees, including elected officials, but not their relatives, from receiving “emoluments” or gifts from foreign states, except as allowed by Congress. The Prevent Corrupting Foreign Influence Act, introduced by Swalwell in 2018, would expand the prohibition’s scope from merely gifts to include “anything of value.” “Unlike past Presidents, Donald Trump refused to adequately distance himself from his private business interests,” Swalwell said. “Americans deserve to know that their President is working for them and only them.” Photo by Getty Images East Bay Congressman Eric Swalwell impose a legal duty on federal campaigns, candidates, and political action committees (PACs) to report offers of assistance from foreign entities or nationals. The Corporate Duty to Report Act, introduced by Swalwell in May 2019, would require companies to disclose to the U.S. government when a foreign person, country, or organization attempts to subvert elections with political advertisements. The Enhancing Protections for Whistleblower Anonymity Act, introduced in June last year, would impose criminal penalties on any federal official who communicates the identity of a whistleblower, or information which would reveal such a person’s identity, except to other government officials when permitted by existing law. Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Environmental impacts on Black Americans By Nate Redinbo Last year, there was a lot of attention on the Black experience in America, and one topic that must be included in that discussion is the impact of Black climate activists. Research shows that climate change does not impact all populations equally, and that Black communities face the negative effects of climate change more often than others. Due to this unequal burden, there is a long and important history of Black Americans leading the way on climate crises. This disparity can be seen in obvious ways, such as the infamous Flint, Michigan water and public health crisis, which impacted tens of thousands of people. Flint has a population that is over 50 percent African American, and the impact of the crisis on the community will be felt for decades. Another example is the Hurricane Katrina disaster, which killed over 1,000 people in New Orleans, a city which is 60 percent African-American. After Katrina, Black homeowners received $8,000 less in government aid than white homeowners because of housing value disparities. Predominantly black communities are more likely to be adjacent to landfills, hazardous waste sites, and industrial facilities. Black Americans are 40 percent more likely to have asthma than White Americans. These health outcomes are a direct effect of policy decisions that perpetuate unequal outcomes for different races in America. These health outcomes can be seen close to home. Oakland, which is 64 percent non-White, has childhood asthma rates of 18.3 percent. Compare this to Piedmont, which is approximately 75 percent white, and has child asthma rates of 12 percent. While mere miles apart, the discrepancies are vast. Black Americans, and particularly Black women, have been at the forefront of movements to make our environments a more equitable place to live for all. A local example is the Black Panther movement based in Oakland. Members organized drives to keep predominantly Black neighborhoods free of waste, hosting free health clinics and educating communities on the dangers of pollution. There now are groups in Oakland, throughout the Bay Area, and the state, that are focused on environmental issues, often helmed by Black people. One of these groups is the Climate Action Coalition in Oakland. The Coalition works on numerous issues, such as transit, food justice, and adaptation to climate change. Their overarching mission is racial and economic justice, which is directly related to climate solutions. Another group, Communities for a Better Environment, works in low-income Latino and African-American communities in Richmond and Oakland to address health hazards. Their goal is to prevent and reduce pollution and build healthy communities and environments. The California Environmental Justice Coalition (CEJC) is led by people of color and low-income communities. CEJC follows the principles of environmental justice and is committed to environmental, social, and economic justice. Thanks to these groups and many others, things can change for the better. Coupled with these organizations, municipal, regional, and statewide efforts can make a real difference to impacted communities. Keeping pressure on local policy makers can help make transportation, waste, and water systems more equitable for all people. Blackled movements in the community have historically made a difference and will continue to do so in the future. Nate Redinbo is the City of Piedmont’s Civic Spark Fellow in 2020-21. Eric Swalwell reintroduces four bills in response to failed impeachment By Allyson Aleksey Representative Eric Swalwell of Dublin introduced four anti-corruption bills on Tuesday, February 23, in response to the second failed impeachment of former president Donald Trump. The reintroduction is aimed to ensure that future presidents cannot “perpetrate some of the same corrupt acts,” Swalwell said. The bills would require that candidates, campaigns, and companies report any foreign interference in U.S. elections; enhance protections for ‘whistleblowers’ who come forward to expose official wrongdoing; and make it a criminal offense for the President, Vice President, or their families to enrich themselves from foreign sources. Swalwell, a member of the House Judiciary, Intelligence, and Homeland Security committees, previously introduced the bills between 2018 and 2020. “Donald Trump showed disdain for the moral and ethical norms we have always expected from an American president, so Congress must make sure these expectations are spelled out explicitly in law and are punished when violated.” “America needs these reforms to move ahead. We must make sure that these abuses can never happen again,” he said. The Duty to Report Act, which Swalwell introduced in June 2018 and April 2019, would closed sue for injunctive relief or monetary damages. Swalwell began drafting the bill after former President Trump and others attacked a whistleblower who raised concerns with the Director of National Intelligence’s Office of Inspector General about Trump’s actions in relation to Ukraine, which led to his first impeachment. “Republicans and Democrats alike for decades have agreed that threatening and trying to expose whistleblowers is wrong and undercuts long-established policy to encourage people to come forward with allegations of wrongdoing,” Swalwell said. “Trump’s actions showed our existing laws aren’t strong enough to protect whistleblowers’ right to anonymity.” The U.S. Constitution and current laws civilly prohibit government employees, including elected officials, but not their relatives, from receiving “emoluments” or gifts from foreign states, except as allowed by Congress. The Prevent Corrupting Foreign Influence Act, introduced by Swalwell in 2018, would expand the prohibition’s scope from merely gifts to include “anything of value.” “Unlike past Presidents, Donald Trump refused to adequately distance himself from his private business interests,” Swalwell said. “Americans deserve to know that their President is working for them and only them.” Photo by Getty Images East Bay Congressman Eric Swalwell impose a legal duty on federal campaigns, candidates, and political action committees (PACs) to report offers of assistance from foreign entities or nationals. The Corporate Duty to Report Act, introduced by Swalwell in May 2019, would require companies to disclose to the U.S. government when a foreign person, country, or organization attempts to subvert elections with political advertisements. The Enhancing Protections for Whistleblower Anonymity Act, introduced in June last year, would impose criminal penalties on any federal official who communicates the identity of a whistleblower, or information which would reveal such a person’s identity, except to other government officials when permitted by existing law. articles.text: More and more high school graduates are taking time off before heading to college. An increasing number of students are choosing to take a gap year – a year off before beginning the college studies. A gap year may consist of educational and developmental activities while exploring the world, or looking into interests locally. Piedmont Parents Network hosted a conference on February 2 demystifying the concept of gap years and provided accounts of two 2020 Piedmont graduates, Ryan Tripp and Eliana Bloomfield. In some European countries as many as 30-35 percent of high school graduates take a gap year. Approximately 25 percent of students in Australia took a gap year even before the pandemic. Gap years became more common in Piedmont starting four years ago as families began embracing the benefits of a student taking a year off prior to college. The spiraling tuition costs of colleges contributed directly to some of the decisions to choose a gap year. As colleges went to online instruction last year due to the coronavirus epidemic, the gap year became an attractive option. Katherine Stievater, the founder of Gapyearsolutions. com, spoke at length during the Feb. 2 Zoom meeting on gap year possibilities. According to her research two to three percent of students in the U.S. took a gap year before the pandemic. But in the past year that number has tripled, with a total of 7-8 percent of incoming freshmen taking a gap year in the U.S. Eliana Bloomfield graduated from PHS last May and was accepted to Wesleyan University in Middletown, Connecticut. But in mid-July she switched gears and decided to take a gap year. In a span of three days, she applied Ryan Tripp, taking a gap year before attending Dartmouth, is pictured near Spider Lakes in Bridger Lakes Wilderness, Wyoming in the Wind River Range. At the time, last September, he was on a 26-day backpacking trip. for the gap year and created a plan. In the first part of her gap year in 2020, she signed up for a program with Outward Bound in the Boundary Waters of Northern Minnesota. Her group backpacked for a week and canoed through 200 miles of the frigid and rugged territory for three weeks, with breaks to carry 100 pounds of gear individually. “It was the hardest thing I have ever done, somewhere between army boot camp and a nature camp. I am so thankful for the experience,” she said. She next volunteered to work on an organic farm for a month Eliana Bloomfield collecting river water for her Outward Bound group on the Superior Hiking Trail in the Boundary Water in October 2020. in Maine through Worldwide Opportunities on Organic Farms. The experience opened her eyes to a new way of life, one that is sustainable, rural and communal. Bloomfield’s plan has allowed her to explore her different interests in one- or two-month stints. She soon will complete an accelerated five-week Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) training course in Santa Cruz, where she is renting an apartment. “I was partly inspired by COVID to be an EMT. I am hoping to help out in the local world in any way I can,” she said. “I am so thankful for this year,’ she added. “I definitely do feel different now. I’m better at adapting and being spontaneous and I feel more independent.” To learn more, contact her at elianabloomfield@gmail.com. Ryan Tripp, a 2020 classmate, decided to take a gap year three days before the deadline for requesting a deferent at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. In the fall he enrolled in a three-month program with National Outdoor Leadership School (NOLS), a leadership and global wilderness school. An Eagle Scout with extensive outdoor experience, it was a natural fit. His journey began with a month of backpacking in Wyoming, and then three weeks of rock climbing in the Colorado Rockies. After a month of backpacking in the canyons of Utah, he spent 10 days backcountry skiing. He is now living in Washington, D.C. working as an intern and tutoring students. “It is a new realm of independence,” he said. “I am pretty much living on my own and doing many of these very much adult things.” A four-year member of Oakland Strokes, Tripp plans to row competitively when he starts school at Dartmouth.
articles.title: Major growth of Gap Year during time of COVID

articles.text: Unpredictable and sudden changes of policy over the course of the past year by the county and state have caused numerous scheduling problems and considerable confusion for parents, students, teachers and school administrators. Data of COVID testing positivity rates have been low enough for a number of weeks, so the key requirement for Red Tier county classification is to have adjusted new case rates beneath 7 daily cases per 100,000 residents. The numbers are delayed seven days, so they are an average of cases 8-14 days prior. The “adjusted” rate rewards counties with high testing rates (like Alameda County) by decreasing unadjusted numbers . “I am looking forward to being back. It has been almost a year since we’ve been in class. It has been hard on the students and the teachers. It will be a return to a sense of normalcy,” said PHS science teacher John Savage. “It doesn’t feel real, honestly,” said Senior Class President Audrey Edel. “I am so, so excited, especially because this is our last year in school. We want to be with our classmates one last time,” she added. Lower COVID case rates, and increased vaccinations suggest the school reopening could actually happen. PUSD has completed parent surveys on in-class vs. distance learning preference, memoranda of understanding have been agreed to by staff and teachers, and grades K-6 were reopened in February.

Piedmont High School’s advanced acting class will present an online production of Clue. the classic board game that became a hit movie. Tickets are $15 for a link watch on Broadway on Demand from 7:00 p.m. Friday, March 5 through 6:59 p.m. Monday, March 8. Click on www.broadwayondemand.com for a “ticket” at Broadway on Demand and watch Clue at your leisure throughout the weekend. Scroll down to “Want to watch a specific school?” Type in Piedmont High School and you’ll get to the link. The cast of Clue includes juniors and seniors Emily Adams, Jonah Bloom, Liam Gordon, Molly McWeeny, Fernanda Meagher, Elsie Pines, Corrin Richards, Izzy Rosselli, Joyce Stern, Katherine Stormer, Laney Tellegen, Jackson Temple and Sadie Tschider. Ella Meil is the stage manager/audio engineer. “We were looking for a wellknown and fun play to lift everyone’s spirits, and it was perfect that the writers of Clue recently created an online version of it,” drama teacher and director Kimberly Taylor said. “Because it’s a goofy mystery, fun for the whole family, and it works well online, it’s currently one of the most produced high school plays in the country.” Clue is the well-known farcemeets-murder mystery that’s fun for the whole family. Gathered at a remote mansion, six mysterious guests -- Mrs. Peacock, Miss Scarlett, Mrs. White, Colonel Mustard, Professor Plum, and Mr. Green assemble for an unusual dinner where murder and blackmail are on the menu. The host turns up dead and everyone is a suspect. But who did it, and how? Emily Adams, who plays Wadsworth the butler, said, “Performing a play in an online space isn’t ideal, [but] we still have the fun and cool tech skills. Blackmail, murder and Sharkfin soup? Clue has it all.” Clue: Stay at Home High School Version is based on the screenplay by Jonathan Lynn, written by Sandy Rustin with additional material by Hunter Foster and Eric Price. Clue is based on the Paramount Pictures motion picture based on the Hasbro board game Clue.

articles.text: Roses and Rivets is an all-girls high school robotics team competing in the First Tech Challenge League. The team was founded to create a more accepting and inclusive environment for girls to participate. It provides a solid foundation for beginners to gain more experience in various software and mechanical areas of robotics. Roses and Rivets hope to inspire more young girls to pursue a STEM career and overcome some gender bias that exists. Due to the pandemic, the robotics season last year and this has been difficult. It has significantly impacted kids’ learning. The team has gathered different STEM engineering activities for kids and compiled them in a pamphlet available in the link shown below. Team members have grouped the activities together with different levels of difficulty. Most of the materials needed for these activities are available around the house. Click on tinyurl.com/rosesandrivetsrobotics to see the activities and details of how to participate. For more information contact Roses & Rivets co-founder Julia Banuelos at jbb3047@gmail.com.

articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1978 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.
articles.title: Art Hecht Award nominations due March 15

Team members have grouped the activities together with different levels of difficulty. Most of the materials needed for these activities are available around the house. Click on tinyurl.com/rosesandrivetsrobotics to see the activities and details of how to participate. For more information contact Roses & Rivets co-founder Julia Banuelos at jbb3047@gmail.com. Wildlife within the park includes rare species such as the golden eagle and Alameda striped racer. The park is a lovely place for all, big or small, to walk amongst giants. The park is great for picnicking, jogging, hiking, and even horseback riding along the 40 miles of park trails. Take the kids to visit an outdoor and interpretive museum featuring educational exhibits, a working observation beehive, freshwater viewing ponds, five habitat islands, and a geodesic dome for injured birds. Right next door is the Bonsai Garden, which houses some of the coolest (and cutest) tiny trees. National Marine Sanctuary System sanctuaries.noaa.gov/vr/ Virtual Dive Tours The National Marine Sanctuary System oversees a network of underwater parks covering more than 600,000 square miles of oceans and lakes. Kids will be amazed at the 360° videos of dives visiting wild sea lions near the Channel Islands. Also check out the turtles, volcanoes and whales in Hawaii, a treasure hunt through Lake Heron’s Shipwreck Alley and the coral restorations in the Florida Keys. Dive in without getting wet, videos are available on a computer screen or can be integrated into a virtual reality headset. Glowfari will entertain every member of the family young and old with the hundreds of brilliantly lit and life size animal lanterns along with realistic animatronic dinosaurs. Advanced ticketing is required. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). articles.text: OTR/L What is the best tool in my Occupational Therapy toolbox? If you were to ask my past and present students, the pink swing or Hedgie would likely be the top contenders. Having a suspended swing system is certainly a coveted sensory integration tool for occupational therapists, but it is not the best tool in my toolbox. Hedgie? He’s pretty darn cute and offers a soft option for a quiet space to calm and regroup. But he is not my best tool. The best tool in my toolbox is not an object or piece of equipment. Drum roll… The best tool in my toolbox, by far, is breathing. Conscious, mindful breathing. Truthfully, I had never pondered the question of which of my OT tools was the best. The question (and answer) occurred to me during a distance learning session with a kindergarten student. The recent transition to hybrid learning had been an exciting but dysregulating experience for this first-time student. Therefore, we began with a breathing exercise from the book Alphabreaths: The ABC’s of Mindful Breathing by Chris Willard and Daniel Rechtschaffen. S is for Superhero Breath Breathe in and imagine you are a superhero. Breathe out and imagine how you will help someone. How will you help someone? This has been a constant and troubling question for me over the past year, as I have had to navigate a new way to deliver services without many of the tools that I had come to rely on. At that moment, I realized that the answer was right in front of me, a kindergarten student practicing “S is for Superhero Breath.” I didn’t need the pink swing or Hedgie to support self-regulation. I had all that I needed even with the constraints of distance learning. Conscious breathing as an exercise has the power to reduce stress, calm, improve focus, in other words, self-regulate. Breathing exercises are a step toward managing emotions and behaviors and developing students’ self-awareness. Breathing is a superpower! The best part? Breathing exercises can be done anytime and anywhere. There is no age limit; however, the younger you start with your child the better. Begin teaching, modeling and practicing breathing exercises as early as preschool. Practice during periods of calm so that when needed, your child is ready to use the breath. Encourage, notice and name how they (and you) feel before and after. By teaching and modeling conscious breathing for your child, you will be providing them with a life-long tool for healthy self-regulation and ultimately success. How should you begin with the younger child? A great place to start is to read books together in order to build your child’s (and yours) toolbox. My recommendations include: • Calm with the Very Hungry Caterpillar by Eric Carle. A great book for preschool/TK students. • Breathe with Me: Using Breath to Feel Strong, Calm and Happy by Mariam Gates. Five simple breathing techniques for ordinary but challenging moments during the day. Watch and breathe with the author as she reads her book to elementary students on YouTube. It’s absolutely delightful. • Alphabreaths: The ABC’s of Mindful Breathing by Chris Willard and Daniel Rechtschaffen. Practice a fun and novel breath for each letter of the alphabet. I’d be remiss if I did not mention middle and high school students. You might be surprised to learn that your student has likely participated in some form of conscious breathing with their classroom teachers, especially over the last year. Start the conversation and ask them about it. What did they notice? When I include conscious breathing with tweens and teens, they report feeling calm, less stressed or simply “that was nice.” You know that you are onto something when a tween or teen answers a direct question with more than one word! Though I try to avoid recommending activities that require a screen, there are many popular guided breathAlphabreaths by Chris Willard and Daniel Rechtschaffen teaches children helpful breathing techniques. Calm with the Very Hungry Caterpillar by Eric Carle is a great book for preschool/TK students. ing lessons on YouTube as well as phone applications such as Headspace or MyLife. And for your taking the time to read this article to the end, here is my thanks to you. H is for Hugging Breath Close your eyes, Give yourself a hug, And gently breathe in and out. (Repeat 3 times) Feels nice doesn’t it? Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, March 3, 2021 BOOK REVIEWBETWEEN THE PAGES Stephen King’s The Gunslinger the start of 7 epic tales By Jay Russell Stephen King’s novel The Gunslinger initiates the unforgettable, must-read seven book epic series The Dark Tower. The Gunslinger introduces Roland of Gilead, a hero of classic westerns brimming with gruff stoicism and armed with cold steel. The hardened anti-hero of a stiff moral chivalrous code gets tossed into vivid and dynamic realms of science fiction. “The man in Black fled across the Desert, and the Gunslinger followed,” starts the saga. Roland Deschain, of King Arthur’s Knights lineage, chases the enigmatic but definitely maleficent Man in Black through a post-apocalyptic old west desert on a kamikaze mission. The Gunslinger’s odyssey intercepts the tale of Jake, a boy recently departed from “our” universe, as King’s dynamic multiverse begins to unfold. After crossing the desert, the hunt for the Man in Black takes Jake and Roland blindly through a tunnel called the Dark Chambers where The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger by Stephen King was originally published by Donald M. Grant, Inc. in 1982. they discover that “one could grow as hungry for light as for food.” Eventually, King unveils an impossible decision to be made between the life of an innocent and the pursuit of many lifetimes. The lingering aroma of macabre increases the suspense in all of King’s works, and readers do not have the comfort of knowing everything’s going to be okay. The fact that the “good guy” doesn’t have a free pass to survive in King’s stories injects them with realism, even when the tale lies firmly in fantasy (at time bordering on the insane). Aside from the potential impending doom, the series isn’t specifically in the horror genre. Librarians may choose to put the series under Western – or possibly Science-Fiction. More than anything The Dark Tower series enthralls readers. The stories are compelling, breathtaking, and a sterling example of originality. The 300-page length allows readers to test the waters of the entire 4,250-page series. Characters and universes from King’s other books interconnect with The Dark Tower, so reading it also serves as a portal to King’s entire collection. King labeled The Dark Tower saga as his Magnus Opus, his greatest achievement. He began The Gunslinger at the age of 22 in 1970 and it took him 12 years to circle back and finish the novel. The last installment of The Dark Tower was published in 2004, allin-all a 34-year enterprise. In contrast, you may want to avoid the 2018 movie called The Dark Tower, the horrendous botching of an entire legendary series of novels into a 90-minute advertisement for ineptness. No need to move your cursor onto the title on your streaming service. Just scroll past it, turn the TV off and enjoy your dark quarantine nights with The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger novel. articles.text: Troop 4 Scouts from Piedmont hike as the sun sets at Sibley. Scouts work on rope skills in Dracena Park. Despite difficult pandemic conditions, Troop 4 continues to provide a welcome social outlet for Scouts to engage with each other in outdoor community service projects, hikes and bicycle trips, and advancement activities, in addition to regular troop meetings via Zoom. Their outdoor activities are carefully calibrated to comply with the current County public health orders. In a range of other activities, Scout meetings in the future will feature discussions with a former Navy SEAL, an FBI agent and an Air Force pilot. Troop 4 has two new leadership roles, a Hikemaster and a Bikemaster, who regularly organize safe and socially distanced hikes and bike rides for Scouts. A hike led by Scout Mollie King was a unique sunset journey in Sibley Regional Park in Oakland. On a bike ride led by Scout Justin Katter across the Bay Bridge to Yerba Buena Island, Troop 4 Scouts were joined by former Beach Dads Club President Darrell Smolko and his two sons, for a beautiful afternoon of riding and camaraderie. “Kids are spending so much time on their screens with distance learning, we need to find a way to get them outside and physically active,” said Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. “One of the aims of Scouting is physical fitness, and the program is designed to be outdoors. articles.text: Saturday, February 27 was a big day for Piedmont High and a few other schools in Northern California. Piedmont was among a handful of cross-country teams invited to compete in a meet at Dublin High. The event marked the official return to high school sports after an absence of nearly 12 months of competition. Schools participating included Bellarmine Prep of San Jose, St. Francis of Mountain View, Foothill of Pleasanton, Livermore, and Piedmont. “I think the students were very nervous because we usually have one or two meets ahead of something like this. Going right into a three-mile event against some really large and strong teams did some really good stuff for our teams, though,” said PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund. Dublin created the three-mile event on a course on its school grounds, wrapping around sports fields, dirt paths, and passing by classrooms. They had separate start times for boys’ and girls’ varsity, junior varsity, and frosh/ soph events. “Everyone had plenty of room,’ said Holmlund. “You have to give it to Chris Williams [Dublin cross-country coach]. He did a really great job of putting everything together.” “There were some really talented schools and Div. 1 runners there. When you’re just practicing with your own team, it does feel limited by how much you can push yourself. Having those other schools there really helped Aya Troyer (left) and Juliette Palacios. Piedmont junior Ellie Black finished 14th in 19:33. freshman Jamie Schwarz placed third in 22:10.9. Junior Kristen DiBella placed 11th of 24 in 24:32.7, while freshman Jasmyn Milsum timed at 25:08. Freshmen Xander Schulte-Sasse and Julien Lee placed 5th and 6th overall in the boys’ JV race with times of 17:19 and 17:19.1. NEXT UP On Saturday, March 6, the cross-country team will take part in a track meet at Witter Field with Castro Valley, starting at 9:30 a.m. Sprinters will include Jack Zirkelbach, Jasmine Ghaderi, Conner Kim, Spencer SorensenWald, and Katie Korn. Piedmont junior Molly McWeeny won the Junior Varsity race with a time of 21:52. Jezebel Droga clocked 21:49 in Saturday’s meet.

articles.text: Photo by Shirley Lee Kai Baudendistel serves in a match yesterday with Miramonte in Orinda. His doubles partner is freshman Monte Imburg. In a return to live sports more than halfway through the school year, Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team opened its season on March 2 with a non-league match against Miramonte. The 6-3 loss was view was considerably less significant than the official resumption of high school sports after a full year of silence due to COVID. “It was a good match; some of the matches we lost were very close. But it’s great to be back, “said coach Jim Landes. “You can tell some of the boys were nervous. Miramonte has been playing matches for a couple of weeks now, so they didn’t have any jitters. Miramonte is always a strong team and Corey [assistant coach Corey Reich] and I were proud of our boys’ play and their competitiveness,” Landes added. The match came together quickly for the team, which originally was set to have a season opener against Castro Valley on Saturday, March 6. But regardless of nerves and playing a stout Division 1 school, the Highlander tennis is back. In the six singles matches, junior Charlie Lambert, playing No. 1, lost in straight sets, 6-4, 7-5. At No. 2, senior Sajan Srivastava took his match to a third-set, but lost 6-7 (7-3), 6-4, 10-5. After splitting the first two sets, the two teams prior agreed to play 10-point tiebreakers as the third. “Charlie Lambert lost a pretty close match against a good player. Sajan lost in a 10-point breaker, winning the first set but losing the second,” said Landes about his top two singles starters. There was some real excitement about the addition to the team of freshman Ben Breber, younger brother of Carson, who played No. 1 singles in 2018 and 2019. “No. 3 was a bright spot,’ said Landes. “Ben, our freshPhoto by Shirley Lee Senior Sajan Srivastava at No. 2 singles lost a 3-set barn-burner at Miramonte, 6-7 (7-3), 6-4, 10-5. Linus Lee serves at No. 2 doubles with Jake Cota. man, won in straight sets, 6-3, 6-1. He’s played very well in our tennis clinics. He played very aggressively, hitting a lot of big forehands and serves that overwhelmed his opponent,” said Landes. At No. 4, senior Akash Kothari lost 7-6 (7-2), 6-3, and No. 5 Charlie Olcott lost 6-4, 7-5. Senior Luke Hawkins won in straight sets at No. 6 singles, 6-3, 6-2. “Luke normally plays higher up in the lineup, but he was dealing with blisters. He won easily at No. 6. He usually comes on strong late in the season,” explained Landes. Returning varsity starter Kai Baudendistel and freshman Monte Imburg led the doubles matches, winning in three sets, 6-3, 3-6, 10-6. “Our other freshman, Monte, teamed up with Kai to win a close match in the third-set 10- point tie break. Monte and Kai complement each other well. with Kai hitting a lot of big forehands that allow Monte to finish points with deft volleys,” said Landes. Piedmont dropped the other two doubles matches. No. 2 Jake Cota and Linus Lee lost 6-3, 6-0, while Ethan Pham and Oliver Maxwell lost 6-2, 7-6 (7-3) at No. 3. Staff Photo Looking ahead The girls’ tennis team opens its season on Tuesday, March 9 against University in San Francisco. Both the boys’ and girls’ teams face Bishop O’Dowd in Piedmont on Thursday, March 11 at 3:30 p.m. Landes recently announced that he has scheduled a match with on Wednesday, March 17, with details to follow. articles.text: Mackie McDonald backed up his impressive fourth-round run in the Australian Open with a championship victory at ATP Challenger Tour’s Forte Challenger 100 in Nur-Sultan, Kazakhstan from February 22-28. He picked up five very nice victories over host-nation’s Mikhail Kukushkin, Uzbekistan’s Denis Istomin, Frederico Silva of Portugal, Switzerland’s Henri Laaksonen, and Jurij Rodionov of Austria. McDonald walked into the ATP Challenger as the world’s No. 139 ranked player after picking up 53 spots from the Aussie Open, now vaulting another 21 positions to No. 118 following his title run in Kazakhstan. Mackie, 25, had his highest word-ranking of No. 57 at the time of his injury in April of 2019 when he sustained his torn hamstring tendon, to which he dipped to No. 132 around the time of his return in January 2020 and fell out of the Top 250 to No. 272 due to a length recovery. McDonald entered as one of two unranked Americans in the Kazakhstan Challenger, knocking off No. 1 seeded Kukushkin in straight sets 7-5, 7-5. Kukushkin was the hometown favorite and tournament’s only top-100 player at No. 96. Mackie dominated Kukushkin on the serve with seven aces and winning 72 percent of his first serves. His defensive prowess that shined in Australian Open wins against Borna Coric and Lloyd Harris carried over the Forte Challenger, scoring 39 receiving points and four break points. McDonald marched through No. 195 Istomin in the Round of 16 with scores of 6-2, 6-3, again with dominant defense with 27 receiving points and five of six break points gained. His toughest test came in the quarterfinals in a three-set contest against No. 179 Silva of Portugal, winning 6-4, 3-6, 7-6 (7-3). Both players had 11 aces and three break points, but it all came down to a heated seven point tiebreaker, where Mackie opened up 3-0, which included a beautiful crosscourt forehand for the third point. Silva battled back to 5-3, but a backhand volley approach shot and a Silva unforced error into the net was enough to seal it for the Pride of Piedmont. In the semifinals, McDonald faced the only other competitor who entered with a higher ranking than him, Laaksonen at No. 134, who was also the Challenger’s No. 5 seed. Mackie won handily in straight sets, 6-2, 6-1, recording six aces. Similarly, McDonald made quick work of No. 152 Rodionov 6-1, 6-2 on the way to the championship. He recorded seven aces, four break points, and 23 receiving points. Mackie was back at it this week in Nur-Sultan at the Forte Challenger 125. He defeated Canada’s Brayden Schnur in three-sets, 6-3, 4-6, 6-4 in the Round of 32 in the early hours of Tuesday, March 2.

articles.text: Piedmont MTB zwift avatar. It’s race day during the global pandemic. The peloton began to wind its way up the side of an active volcano, starting in mass at the same time, stretching out as the steepness of the road increased. Lava scaled down the mountain and rain started to fall in the cyclists’ virtual wonderland, Watopia, which is the oldest course on Zwift – a massive multiplayer online game and training program for cyclers and runners.
