articles.text: Piedmont High School’s mountain bike team will host its first annual Piedmont MTB Classic race from March 7-21 and registrations are now open to the public. All proceeds will support the team, which receives no support from the high school or Piedmont Boosters because of its club status. The event will take place over a two-week period so that every racer can independently participate on their own time, thus making it a socially distanced, safe event. Each participant will record their times on designated trail segments using the Strava app, and prizes will be awarded for the fastest entrants in a number of categories: Middle School, High School, Adult and Overall. There will be two options for the race, the Short Course and the Long Course. The short course covers just over 9 miles of trail, and an elevation gain of approximately 900 feet. The Long Course covers 15 miles and 2,500 feet of elevation gain. The cost to participate is $40 per rider. Race proceeds will be used to purchase a team trailer to help transport equipment to season races It will be dedicated to Lynden McLaughlan, a team coach who passed away unexpectedly in 2019. To learn more about the race and the team, go to www.Piedmontmtb.com.

articles.text: The Post has a hidden treasure for you this week in Stanislaus National Forest. Let’s say you couldn’t land a camping spot inside Yosemite National Park and were aching to see thriving rivers and powerful waterfalls. Outside Groveland on the way to Yosemite on Highway 120 is a short 1.4 mile out-and-back (2.8 mile roundtrip) hike along the South Fork of the Tuolumne River that has four magnificent waterfalls. Opposite Rainbow Pools, a popular summer swimming hole, is a descending trail that currently is almost completely free of other hikers during these cool winter months. You’ll be hard-pressed finding a better hike of less than three miles. The unnamed trail starts at 2,884 feet in elevation, dropping to 581 feet while walking alongside the river. We passed just six people on a Saturday. It you’re accustomed to hiking inclined trails, like the ones found in the Oakland and Berkeley hills, this trail is comparable. Your eyes will be glued to the river. The view gets better and better on your hike. The waterfall furthest upstream is 25 feet tall. The Middle Fork’s cascade is estimated at 182 feet and forms a confluence with the South Fork.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 3, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON Cascades of the South Fork of Tuolumne River Outside Groveland are Rainbow Pools, 1.4-mile hike By Jonathan Comeaux The Post has a hidden treasure for you this week in Stanislaus National Forest. Let’s say you couldn’t land a camping spot inside Yosemite National Park and were aching to see thriving rivers and powerful waterfalls. Outside Groveland on the way to Yosemite on Highway 120 is a short 1.4 mile out-and-back (2.8 mile roundtrip) hike along the South Fork of the Tuolumne River that has four magnificent waterfalls. Opposite Rainbow Pools, a popular summer swimming hole, is a descending trail that currently is almost completely free of other hikers during these cool winter months. You’ll be hard-pressed finding a better hike of less than three miles. The unnamed trail starts at 2,884 feet in elevation, dropping to 581 feet while walking alongside the river. We passed just six people on a Saturday. It you’re accustomed to hiking inclined trails, like the ones found in the Oakland and Berkeley hills, this trail is comparable. Your eyes will be glued to the river. The view gets better and better on your hike. The waterfall furthest upstream is 25 feet tall. The Middle Fork’s cascade is estimated at 182 feet and forms a confluence with the South Fork. Staff Photos Continuing down the path leads to the third waterfall, a powerful 45-foot cascade that drops into a large pool. A trail along the South Fork of the Tuolumne River provides a short walk with four magnificent waterfalls. Pictured here are a pair of falls where the Middle Fork (left) and South Fork (right) meet. Your eyes will stay locked on the rushing waters to your left, with views that improve with every step, it seems. After a mile, a pair of impressive falls are seen a mere hundred feet from each other. The first is around 25 feet tall that drops into a large pool, a place where swimmers would be in the summer. Continuing on the path toward the bridge is the Middle and South Fork Confluence, where the Middle Fork of the Tuolumne River ends with an estimated 182-foot-tall cascade that merges with the South Fork. Hikers can take in the sheer size and force of the falls by standing next to the small pool at the base, while the bridge provides a clear glance at both falls to your left and right. After another short walk around the bend is another glorious 45-foot waterfall. It’s worth noting that you’ll be passing through an area with warning signs of potential rockslides. The trail continues to a concrete viewing area and a stairwell that leads closer to the river. Pack a lunch and enjoy it here before traveling back to your car. While resting at the base of the stairs we noticed what looks to be a fenced-off former mining shaft, which has thick-metal wiring lining over the river to an opposite shaft entrance. Traveling down to the river gives a clear look of the South Fork. You can see the former base of a bridge that connected the two shafts. To reach this location, there is an off-road parking area shortly after passing the bridge which spans the South Fork of the Tuolumne. Follow the paved path, which reads Forest Rte 1N07 on GPS devices, taking the gravel trail that emerges on your right after 0.4 mile. Be wary of an area of rockslides near the third waterfall. The path leads down to the river, where you can spot the last waterfall, also around 25 feet tall. A view of the South Fork of the Tuolumne River with a platform of a former bridge in the face of a rocky cliff.

articles.text: For 25 years I’ve walked all around the San Francisco Tribal & Textile Art Show – eyes dazzled, spirit awakened, brain and heart stimulated, aesthetic sense challenged – until my feet ached. The Fort Mason Pier felt like my homey museum, my eyes were so happy, but the damn concrete floor made my feet ache. I loved seeing and studying – and sometimes buying – audacious artworks from ancient and fascinatingly cultures different from mine. As an art lover, collector at heart and art dealer, every February the Tribal Show and the Indian Show were the winter’s highlights. I always showed a double booth full of African and Oceanic art in the Tribal Show, and a medium booth of Pre-Columbian art in the Indian Show. I’d sell a lot, buy a lot, talk a lot, even listen to the old collectors who are my old friends. As I see it, this is Our Year of Adaptation. This year’s Tribal Show which I love, just opened and runs through Wednesday midnight. This year it is online – a virtual show. May I suggest that if you love art, take a virtual trip to exotic foreign cultures from your armchair and see stunning examples of art from Africa, Oceania, The Americas, and Tribal Asia. Before it closes tomorrow night at midnight, click on: https://www. virtualtribalandtextileartshows. com /cms/product- categor y/ dave-deroche-art-of-africa-oceania-the-americas/ Ceremonial Dance Mask. Lwalwa tribe. D.R. Congo. A striking, dramatic example of innovative artistic abstraction in African art, which modern artists like Picasso, Braque, and Vlaminck ‘borrowed’ from heavily in ‘inventing’ Cubism. Offered by Dave DeRoche in the Virtual/Online SF Tribal Art Show for $6000. Leave your passport behind. No traffic. No parking problem. No ticket line. And no cost. What could be better? Stay in your bathrobe if you wish. Travel with your eyes. Imagination, personality, and wisdom. Traditions and soul are built right into the object that catches your eye. Ask questions of the exhibitors. They’re lonely this year, too. Learn from them. They love their art objects and they would love to tell you about them. They might even sell them to you so they can acquire something new for themselves. For more information, see: https://www.virtualtribalandtextileartshows.com/
articles.title: Art in a year of Adaptation

articles.text: The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco have announced the reopening of the de Young Museum this week. It is scheduled for members on March 4 and 5, and to the general public this Saturday, March 6. Visitors will be excited to not only return to the museum, but to see the U.S. debut of an exhibit with works of Alexander Calder and Pablo Picasso. The exhibit includes more than 100 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and photographs that explore the relationship between Calder and Picasso, largely regarded as two of the most influential artists of the twentieth century. The exhibition Frida Kahlo: Appearances Can Be Deceiving has been extended through May 2, and is available for ticket reservations. Uncanny Valley: Being Human in the Age of AI has also been extended through June 27 and is available with a general-admission ticket. The de Young Museum and the Legion of Honor are maintaining rigorous health and safety measures based on county guideDigital programming In addition to reopening the de Young in Golden Gate Park on Saturday, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco have announced a series of virtual programming through summer 2021, to include community partnerships with renowned artists, historians, musicians and activists. All museum programming will be offered in digital form through June 2021. A new partnership between Alexander Calder (left) and Pablo Picasso, two of the best-known names in 20th-century art, share a number of striking similarities in artwork - all on display in the Calder-Picasso exhibition. [photo courtesy of Musee National Picasso-Paris] San Francisco’s deYoung Museum in Golden Gate Park. lines. Visitor capacity is reduced to 25 percent, and timed tickets are required. To obtain tickets, visit https://deyoung.famsf.org/ exhibitions. the Fine Arts Museums and the SeeBlackWomxn collective will launch a five-part series focused on the contemporary Black Arts scene. The collective was founded by artists and activists Tahirah Rasheed, Angela Hennessy, Dana King, and Jamani Montague, and celebrates the lineage and legacy of Black women in contemporary arts. SeeBlackWomxn will serve as a collective narrative of artists and writers who contribute to Black feminist theory. The platform emphasizes self-representation and aims to stray from the stereotypical tropes assigned to Black women and identifying women. The series is programmed through the museums’ “Virtual Wednesdays” and Local Voices podcast, which aims to explore the impact of public art on the Bay Area community. This year, notable artists contributing to the podcast include Lava Thomas, Catherine Wagner, and Alison Saar, musical duo Mercury Soul, Fredrika Newton of the Huey P. Newton Foundation, the #SayHerName Movement, Susan Cervantes of the Precita Eyes Muralists, artist duo Rue Bainbridge, artist and composer Gryphon Rue, and artist Peter Simensky. Visit https://deyoung.famsf. org/virtual-wednesdays to view upcoming and past Virtual Wednesdays programs. 510-525-5656 Monday-Friday 8:30-5:30 Saturday 9:00-5:00 Sunday Closed CARPET | VINYL | WOOD | LINOLEUM BETWEEN GILMAN & BUCHANAN ST. CL#788850 www.floordimensions.com 1081 Eastshore Hwy. Berkeley
articles.title: Museum to reopen with U.S. debut of Calder-Picasso Exhibit

articles.text: Cal Shakes will host a virtual fundraiser on Friday, March 26, entitled “Lights Up!” It will feature Artistic Director Eric Ting, Managing Director Sarah Williams, and Bay Area artists for an evening devoted to raising funds to get artists back to the stage once again. The virtual celebration will serve as “a love letter to classic stories and the extraordinary people that make them come to life.” The event will be a night of fun and celebration, joy and laughter, and a moment to come together in support of the resiliency of the arts. Cal Shakes started as an artistic collective in 1973, and became an official company – Berkeley Shakespeare Festival – at John Hinkel Park in 1974. Over the past 40 years, Cal Shakes has become a cornerstone and mainstay of Bay Area Theater, producing works from the Shakespeare canon and beyond. In 1991, the company built the Bruns Amphitheater in the hills of Orinda. Visit https://calshakes.org/ lightsup/ to register for the fundraiser.
articles.title: “Lights Up” fundraiser for Cal Shakes on March 26

articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Simone McIntosh joins the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco for a concert premiering Friday, March 12 at 7:30 p.m. Titled Art of the Voice, the concert will also be available on Sunday, March 14 at 6 p.m. The program takes viewers on a journey from the dark and stormy into the sunrise. Be transported by Beethoven’s passionate String Quartet Op. 18 no. 4, the haunting melodies of Respighi’s Il Tramonto, and the gentle glow of Haydn’s Sunrise Quartet. McIntosh’s powerful and soulful voice, possessing a wide range, captivates audiences. She will encore with Nadia Boulanger’s tender and serene Cantique, in a world premiere arrangement for voice and string quartet. Back by popular demand, the concert will include a trivia segment entitled “The Secret Lives of Divas and Divos – stars of the Opera.” “We are dedicated to performing chamber music in intimate and personal ways,” explained violinist Natasha Makhijani, a founding member of CMS of SF. “We carefully curate an experience that captures the imagination with exceptional music, while sharing the complexities of the musicians’ lives and their creative process.” “For years we’ve wanted to do a project with voice where the lyricism and story of the text come first. Right now is the opportunity, when our online concerts have the visual flexibility to transport you into the story itself,” added co-founder Samsun van Loon, “This story is Shelley’s poem The Sunset, the eternal story of love, loss, and perseverance, set to music by Ottorino Respighi as Il Tramonto for mezzo-soprano and string quartet. The concert will stream on-demand through Sunday, March 21. For tickets, click on https:// chambermusicsocietysf.org/digital-concerts.
articles.title: Chamber Music Society of SF, mezzo Simone McIntosh in Art of the Voice concert

articles.text: Kate Winslet and Idris Elba star in the thrilling survival story, The Mountain Between Us Movie review by Chris Honoré The Mountain Between Us is a title offering a nifty summary of what this film is about from it’s opening set-up to the last frame. Of course, it uses a familiar template but is still solidly entertaining with two superb actors. Briefly, and trying to avoid touching on acts two and three, Dr. Ben Blass (Idris Elba) and Alex Martin (Kate Winslet) meet by chance at the Boise, Idaho airport. Their flight, they are told separately, has been cancelled. He is desperate to get to Denver and then Baltimore where he will, as a neurosurgeon, perform a lifesaving operation. Alex, a photojournalist, is looking for a way to get to Denver in time to complete the final preparations for her wedding that is scheduled for the following day. They agree to charter a plane for the trip to Denver. The pilot is an old timer (Beau Bridges) who brings his golden lab along and who rides in the second seat. All goes according to plan (speaking of plan, guess who forgot to file one?) until there is a riveting, breathtaking crash that occurs on a harrowing stretch of a snow-covered mountain range. It’s January and the weather is unforgiving. In effect The Mountain Between Us is two stories. The first is one of survival that is reminiscent of The Revenant. The cold is penetrating. The odds are against them. The decision to be made is, should they stay with the crash site and hope that the homing beacon in the tail section of the twin-engine plane is working, or take as much gear as possible and try and hike out. One impediment to that plan is that Alex has suffered a severe leg injury. The second story embedded in this tale of survival against all odds is the relationship between Alex and Ben. Almost from the outset the audience knows that despite the stress of their situation there is a palpable attraction. Of course, their consuming priority is to do all that is physically possible to prevail against their overwhelming circumstances. But still… Movies of this type never fail to resonate with me. Once the film has begun, I’m in it for the full hour plus change. And though the story may seem somewhat incredible, Winslet and Elba do a masterful job of keeping the narrative moving forward on both levels. One small spoiler: the dog survives the crash. The Mountain Between Us. Starring Idris Elba, Kate Winslet and Beau Bridges. Directed by Hany Abu-Assad. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: The Mountain Between Us – a survival story

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré “Raped while dying.” “And Still No Arrests” “How come, Chief Willoughby?” On a side road outside of Ebbing, Missouri, Mildred Hayes (Francis McDormand) has rented three billboards, and each possesses one of the lines above, painted in black on an attention-getting red backdrop, asking the seminal question regarding solving the rape and murder of her daughter: “How come?” It’s been seven months since her daughter was murdered and Mildred has decided that the Chief of Police, William Willoughby (Woody Harrelson) has had more than enough time to find the killer. The signs are her protest. And so begins what was one of the best films of 2017. It is a dark and tragic comedy that is not in any way a murder mystery. Rather, it is a character study of how three individuals react to the demand, posed by Mildred, for an investigation, and more importantly, an arrest. Though Mildred has made her statement, she is nowhere close to being finished. For her, the billboards are just act one. This narrative is not a police procedural. Three Billboards is something else entirely and takes the expectations of the audience in a totally different direction. Think of it as a cultural autopsy of a small, fictional heartland town. At the center of this film, at its essential core, is Mildred, trapped between grief and rage. She crosses line after line with her anger until the town, which was once sympathetic because of her loss, turns against her. The Chief is much cared for and he makes every effort to convince Mildred that he has done all that is possible to find the killer of her daughter. Mildred of course is not satisfied. To make the film even edgier is the Chief’s second in command, a surprisingly dim deputy, Jason Dixon (Sam Rockwell), known for his racism and abuse of authority. He lives with his mother and regards his badge as a license to do just about anything he pleases. In some strange way his anger mirrors that of Mildred but for very different reasons. That he wears a uniform defies understanding, especially considering the compassionate persona of Willoughby, a family man (two daughters) and a lovely wife. Three Billboards is a study of personal demons and regret and courage. It is irreverent, a tsunami of revenge, yet a web of moments of kindness that surprises. All the minor characters that satellite the Chief, Mildred and Dixon are outstanding in their verisimilitude. Most, especially Mildred, are consistently scatological, dark and ragged at the edges, unforgiving – and yet forgiving. It should be no surprise that this film won two Academy Awards – for McMormand as Best Female Actress, and Rockwell as Best Supporting Actor. A note: I have done my best to say as little as possible about the plot, while avoiding describing any scenes in detail. Three Billboards should be seen fresh, allowing the twists and turns to catch the audience by surprise, and to enjoy its creative quirkiness. But realize that it is steeped in moments of violence that appear and then vanish like so much mist. Once again: this film is stunningly well acted; it’s raw and ambiguous; and, finally, redemptive. Well, sort of redemptive. But in the end the audience is asked to decide. Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. Directed by Martin McDonagh. Starring Francis McDormand, Woody Harrelson and Sam Rockwell. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated R. Frances McDormand stars in Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.
articles.title: Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri

articles.text: Hailee Steinfeld stars as Charlie in Bumbleebee. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Transformers film franchise made its debut in 2007, followed by four sequels, each directed by Michael Bay and each, incrementally, shredding the original charm and solid story telling. Bay seemed content to indulge his predilection for CGI chaos, over-the-top histrionics, explosions, and bot slams. In every way the recently released Bumblebee (a prequel) is not only redemptive, but resurrects that sweet spot mined by Shia LaBeof, as Sam Witwicky, in the first Transformers when he negotiates with his dad for a car. He finds a hard-used, yellow Camaro on a lot and convinces his dad that this rusty ride works for him. And so his adventure begins. Ditto Charlie Watson (Hailee Steinfeld), who is on the cusp of turning 18 and declares that, like Sam, all she wants is a car. Any car. After a brief lead-in segment where the Autobots/Optimus Prime and the Decepticons/Megatron are locked in a destructive battle on Cybertron, their home planet, the narrative shifts to 1987. The place is the San Francisco Bay Area. Charlie is grieving for her father who died two years before of a heart attack while they were restoring a vintage Corvette that still sits in the garage. As it turns out, she’s an appealing but rebellious gear head who works on old cars at a local garage when she’s not going to school. She also feels unheard and alienated at home. Her mom (Pamela Adion) has remarried, her stepdad is okay, and her younger brother is doing just fine. It’s Charlie who feels adrift. Nosing around the junk-laden garage where she hangs out daily, Charlie discovers a vintage yellow VW Beetle hidden under a tarp. She is immediately smitten and pleadingly negotiates with the owner of the garage for this clearly abandoned ride. As it turns out, the key is in the ignition, the engine works and, with the owners blessing (Happy Birthday, he tells her), she’s soon driving off toward home and that empty spot next to her dad’s Corvette. With the Beetle safely in the garage, she walks around its exterior and decides to check its undercarriage. It’s at his moment that there is a classic and wondrous reveal. As she is shinning a light under the rusty chassis, she sees two large aqua blue eyes looking back at her. Abruptly, unexpectedly, the benign-looking VW transforms and there standing before her is a huge banana yellow bot. It’s a meet cute scene that ends with a startled, at-first-disbelieving Charlie naming the Transformer Bumblebee. As she learns, he proves to be a gentle, even timid, giant. And after catching her breath, she and B.B. tentatively bond. Actually, as it turns out, both, in a way, are hiding out – though for B.B. the stakes are much higher. They begin what proves to be a touching friendship. It’s at this point in the story that Charlie’s adventure begins. This is a relationship story. Even when the Decepticons locate Bumblebee (who we learn from the initial set up that he is on a mission for Optimus Prime), the film doesn’t drop off a cliff into vacuous violence that became the brand for the five sequels. Bumblebee is a genuinely good movie that engages and entertains. It’s perfect for those tweens and newbie teens who likely don’t have a clue what life was like in 1987, but understand what it feels like to discover a bot in their home garage. The film comes along at Christmas time, and beckons to parents and kids alike to spend two hours with this Hasbro endorsed tale that has the iconic E.T. embedded in scene after scene. It is distinctly a user-friendly family film. Bumblebee. Directed by Travis Knight. Starring Hailee Steinfeld, John Cena and Pamela Adion. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG-13. Originally published on January 2, 2019 and reprinted on May 5, 2020. A scene from Bumbleebee.
articles.title: Bumblebee a sweet family film

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Before discussing the most recent Star Trek incarnation, consider the following: Star Trek Beyond is the 13th movie in a 50-year-old franchise which also includes six TV series and some 100 million books and comics sold during the last half century. Star Trek is now a cinematic senior citizen and this fact begs the question: why? What is there about these films – about these characters who spend most of time encapsulated in a large Frisbee with enormous thrusters – that sets them apart from other franchise films? Is it because they dare to go where no travelers have gone before, into the final frontier – space? It’s a remarkable pop culture phenom (now rebooted), supported by countless Trekies, some covert others nostalgically closeted, but all fans of the premise. Beyond perhaps offers up an answer as to why. This film, like most of its predecessors, is a solid, straightforward adventure story, packaged in 23rd century technology (much of it dreamy and ersatz but still cool, like, say, a phaser on stun). There is a heterogeneous crew, always a merciless villain. In the case of Beyond he’s a biped E.T. with a very bad complexion named Krall (Idris Elba), intent on putting the Federation astronauts in sustained jeopardy. In the initial set up, the Enterprise receives a distress call from a stranded ship and is lured by Krall into an ambush that turns out to be a swarm of metal “bees,” meaning tiny weapons that look like a hundred thousand starlings rising, turning and then attacking. Why the attack is initiated has something to do with an Abronath, which holds the key to ultimate power, and is coveted by Krall, who, by the way, is one very bad dude. When the Enterprise crashes on said planet, that’s when the games begin. It’s one set piece after another of hyper-action, with Captain Kirk (Chris Pine) and Spock (Zachary Quinto), along with their crew fighting for their lives. A new character, Jaylah (Sofia Boutella), is introduced as one of the lone rebels fighting Krall. She’s fresh and resilient and interesting with kind of a goth, white-face, zebra-stripes look. The nuts and bolts, carried out with spectacular ingenuity, consist of old machinery (an ancient starship) made serviceable; new machinery that breaks down and is repaired; Spock, injured, is healed plenty pronto by Bones (Karl Urban); and all this is buttressed by a still functional oldtimey transporter. The fan base will be satisfied. The newbies don’t need to get caught up because Beyond stands on its own. If you’re inside the tent with the franchise and ready to suspend your disbelief, then go happily where countless fans have gone before. Star Trek Beyond. Starring Chris Pine, Zachary Quinto and Zoe Saldana. Directed by Justin Lin. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated PG-13. Zachary Quinto as Commander Spock, Sofia Boutella as Jaylah and Karl Urban as Doctor ‘Bones’ McCoy in Star Trek Beyond.

The place is the San Francisco Bay Area. Charlie is grieving for her father who died two years before of a heart attack while they were restoring a vintage Corvette that still sits in the garage. As it turns out, she’s an appealing but rebellious gear head who works on old cars at a local garage when she’s not going to school. She also feels unheard and alienated at home. Her mom (Pamela Adion) has remarried, her stepdad is okay, and her younger brother is doing just fine. It’s Charlie who feels adrift. Nosing around the junk-laden garage where she hangs out daily, Charlie discovers a vintage yellow VW Beetle hidden under a tarp. She is immediately smitten and pleadingly negotiates with the owner of the garage for this clearly abandoned ride. As it turns out, the key is in the ignition, the engine works and, with the owners blessing (Happy Birthday, he tells her), she’s soon driving off toward home and that empty spot next to her dad’s Corvette. With the Beetle safely in the garage, she walks around its exterior and decides to check its undercarriage. It’s at his moment that there is a classic and wondrous reveal. As she is shinning a light under the rusty chassis, she sees two large aqua blue eyes looking back at her. Abruptly, unexpectedly, the benign-looking VW transforms and there standing before her is a huge banana yellow bot. It’s a meet cute scene that ends with a startled, at-first-disbelieving Charlie naming the Transformer Bumblebee. As she learns, he proves to be a gentle, even timid, giant. And after catching her breath, she and B.B. tentatively bond. Actually, as it turns out, both, in a way, are hiding out – though for B.B. the stakes are much higher. They begin what proves to be a touching friendship. It’s at this point in the story that Charlie’s adventure begins. This is a relationship story. Even when the Decepticons locate Bumblebee (who we learn from the initial set up that he is on a mission for Optimus Prime), the film doesn’t drop off a cliff into vacuous violence that became the brand for the five sequels. Bumblebee is a genuinely good movie that engages and entertains. It’s perfect for those tweens and newbie teens who likely don’t have a clue what life was like in 1987, but understand what it feels like to discover a bot in their home garage. The film comes along at Christmas time, and beckons to parents and kids alike to spend two hours with this Hasbro endorsed tale that has the iconic E.T. embedded in scene after scene. It is distinctly a user-friendly family film. Bumblebee. Directed by Travis Knight. Starring Hailee Steinfeld, John Cena and Pamela Adion. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG-13. Star Trek Beyond – Episode #13 in a 50-year-old franchise Movie review by Chris Honoré Before discussing the most recent Star Trek incarnation, consider the following: Star Trek Beyond is the 13th movie in a 50-year-old franchise which also includes six TV series and some 100 million books and comics sold during the last half century. Star Trek is now a cinematic senior citizen and this fact begs the question: why? What is there about these films – about these characters who spend most of time encapsulated in a large Frisbee with enormous thrusters – that sets them apart from other franchise films? Is it because they dare to go where no travelers have gone before, into the final frontier – space? It’s a remarkable pop culture phenom (now rebooted), supported by countless Trekies, some covert others nostalgically closeted, but all fans of the premise. Beyond perhaps offers up an answer as to why. This film, like most of its predecessors, is a solid, straightforward adventure story, packaged in 23rd century technology (much of it dreamy and ersatz but still cool, like, say, a phaser on stun). There is a heterogeneous crew, always a merciless villain. In the case of Beyond he’s a biped E.T. with a very bad complexion named Krall (Idris Elba), intent on putting the Federation astronauts in sustained jeopardy. In the initial set up, the Enterprise receives a distress call from a stranded ship and is lured by Krall into an ambush that turns out to be a swarm of metal “bees,” meaning tiny weapons that look like a hundred thousand starlings rising, turning and then attacking. Why the attack is initiated has something to do with an Abronath, which holds the key to ultimate power, and is coveted by Krall, who, by the way, is one very bad dude. When the Enterprise crashes on said planet, that’s when the games begin. It’s one set piece after another of hyper-action, with Captain Kirk (Chris Pine) and Spock (Zachary Quinto), along with their crew fighting for their lives. A new character, Jaylah (Sofia Boutella), is introduced as one of the lone rebels fighting Krall. She’s fresh and resilient and interesting with kind of a goth, white-face, zebra-stripes look. The nuts and bolts, carried out with spectacular ingenuity, consist of old machinery (an ancient starship) made serviceable; new machinery that breaks down and is repaired; Spock, injured, is healed plenty pronto by Bones (Karl Urban); and all this is buttressed by a still functional oldtimey transporter. The fan base will be satisfied. The newbies don’t need to get caught up because Beyond stands on its own. If you’re inside the tent with the franchise and ready to suspend your disbelief, then go happily where countless fans have gone before. Star Trek Beyond. Starring Chris Pine, Zachary Quinto and Zoe Saldana. Directed by Justin Lin. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: He was famous; but he wanted to be a composer. His name was Lionel. Lionel Blythe. He was really famous. So were his younger siblings. His younger brother, John, was so famous that all you had to say was “the profile“ and everybody knew who you were talking about. His sister was famous, too. Of course, you don’t know them by Lionel Blythe, John Blythe and Ethel Blythe. Somewhere along the line the entire family changed its name. When I tell you that the name they chose was Barrymore, you probably think you know where I’m going with this story. But you are wrong. You see, Lionel Barrymore never wanted to be an actor. He was coerced into acting by the rest of the family. Lionel Barrymore’s talents lay in other areas of the arts. I guess he became an actor simply because it was the easiest way to make a living. But he really wanted to be a composer. He came to music rather late in life. I think his first piano lessons were at the age of 17. But he went to Paris to study art. He was a very good artist, and you can buy some of his artwork on e-Bay. I became interested in the music of Lionel Barrymore because I first heard him as the host on a famous “Concert Hall“ program. He introduced the great violinist Jascha Heifetz. Soon after that I found out that Lionel Barrymore was a very enthusiastic composer. His music impressed me. But he was a modest guy and didn’t push his music nor did he pull rank in any way. The first piece of his that I heard was a musical memorial to his brother, John Barrymore, in 1942. The performance was by the Philadelphia Orchestra conducted by Eugene Ormandy. It was a tone poem of scope and profound musical sensitivity. Some music critics took cheap shots at Lionel Barrymore’s music. They accused him of being too conservative. Perhaps they confused his music with his support of Thomas Dewey over FDR. His art was also conservative. In this he shares a kinship with Velasquez. It all depends on how you view the artist and his work. But if we analyze Lionel Barrymore‘s music, we must conclude that he continued a wonderful American tradition of composers. He was very friendly with Edward MacDowell – and no one denigrates MacDowell. So, music lovers, go onto the Internet and listen to some of the music of Lionel Barrymore. Just imagine: he could have written the musical scores for his own movies and be respected like two Lionel Barrymore famous composers, Max Steiner and Erik Wolfgang Korngold. A look at Center for the Arts The sphere of music makes many connections. This was driven home to me last week with the news about a classic Victorian home in San Francisco being moved to a new location a few blocks away. Maybe you saw it. The Englander House was justifiably famous, but not only because it was a classic Victorian. Its interior boasted those mysterious gaslights which were in the famous Hollywood movie of the same name, Gaslight. I played many concerts in the Englander Mansion when I was concertmaster of the San Francisco Concerto Orchestra. This orchestra was a noble venture. It showcased the talents of the finest musicians from every orchestra in the area. The repertoire consisted entirely of concertos. The gaslights were extinguished, and the orchestra died a slow death. Why? The musicians supported the venture wholeheartedly, but the press ignored the venture completely. So did the politicians in San Francisco. I see some similarities to our beautiful city of Piedmont, where the Piedmont Center for the Arts has been the cultural gem of our city for some 10 years. We hear people asking about diversity, but the incontrovertible fact is that the arts are colorblind. No one can tell the religion, the race, or the gender of any performer by listening. Likewise, it is not possible to identify the political stance of a performer. All you have to do is look at all orchestras, choruses, opera companies and dance companies. All you see wherever you are is diversity. But artists and musicians rarely talk about it. Art, after all, is based upon talent regardless of a person’s origins or race or gender. The Piedmont Center for the Arts, which enjoys a sterling reputation throughout the Bay Area, is the city’s cultural gem. Without it, Piedmont is just another bedroom community.
articles.title: Life and death in the arts

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s 2021 digital programming continues with a 10-episode podcast series. The podcast was launched on January 12 with “The Fundamental Kiss, With Overtones” by Eisa Davis. The story follows a young oboist and pianist during a chance meeting in Berkeley. After the premiere, a new episode was released weekly, to conclude with “For the Record” by Sean San Jose. Ten writers, inspired by events in their own personal histories, take audiences on an auditory journey to specific locations around Berkeley. Subscribers will receive via e-mail a map of the locations illustrated by a New Yorker cartoonist. Other featured writers include Philip Kan Gotanda, Daniel Handler, Aya de Leon, Adam Mansbach, Richard Montoya, Itamar Moses, Kamala Parks, and Sarah Ruhl. Anecdotes range from comedic, to dramatic, to avant-garde. Each audio episode is approximately 10 minutes in length. To purchase podcast episodes, visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/season/2021/15861.asp. Photo by Pete Rosos Author Aya de Leon is featured in Berkeley Rep’s newest podcast.

articles.text: If you own a small business, you typically don’t get a lot of recognition. You may be pleased to learn that March 29 is National Mom and Pop Business Owners Day. You might not necessarily think of your business as a “Mom and Pop” operation, but it certainly contributes to the well-being of your family now, and possibly to that of future generations, too – if you make the right moves. Depending on the nature of your business, you may have spent the past several months more concerned about today than tomorrow, given the serious economic repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still placing stress on a great many business owners across the country. If your business has been adversely affected by the pandemic, you might be eligible for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. As you may know, recent legislation provided $285 billion more for this program. To learn more, and to start the application process, visit the Small Business Administration website at www.sba.gov. You have until March 31 to apply for a PPP loan. Other relief also may be available. But regardless of whether you apply for one of these loans, you can take other steps to help maximize the benefits you get from your business – and perhaps even extend its longevity.
articles.title: Business owners’ issues go beyond ‘mom and pop’ label

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok A ham and sweet potato strata is a lovely brunch during springtime. Spring brunch time is nigh, and this “strata” features the classic pairing of ham and sweet potatoes. Technically the method here doesn’t layer the ingredients (a strata), but over the years I’ve found the layering process doesn’t make a big difference in the end result. So, I opt for an easier preparation. If you feel inclined, you can layer the ham-sweet potato-onion mixture with slices of bread and cheese, then pour the milkegg mixture over all of it. Or go with the simpler version here and mix everything together in a big bowl and transfer it to the baking dish. This is an excellent vessel for leftover meats and vegetables. As with many of my recipes, pandemic or not, this one is flexible on ingredients and flavorings. Eggs, half-half, and bread are the basis upon which you build, with additional ingredients that influence the resulting dish. I happened to have a package of ham steak and leftover roasted sweet potatoes, which are the basis here. Kale is a staple at our house. If you enjoy this recipe, check out my blog for Piedmont Brunch, using sausage, zucchini and bell peppers. Ham and Sweet Potato Strata INGREDIENTS • 4 ounces bread, cut into 3/4” cubes, about 3 - 4 cups • 1 - 2 teaspoons olive oil • 12 ounces fully cooked ham, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 - 2 cups cooked sweet potato, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 medium bunch kale, sliced crosswise in 1/2” wide strips, about 2 - 3 cups • 1 cup yellow onion, diced • 5 extra-large eggs • 2 cups half and half • 1 teaspoon dry mustard powder • • • • Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste Pinch of cayenne pepper, to taste 5 ounces jalapeno jack cheese, shredded, about 1 cup 1/4 cup green onions, thinly sliced for garnish PREPARATION Preheat the oven to 350˚. Place bread cubes on baking sheet. Bake for 10 - 15 minutes, until dry and firm. Remove from oven and let cool. Heat olive oil in a large skillet on medium heat, add onions and cook stirring frequently, until they become soft and translucent. Add sliced kale and continue cooking until the kale has just barely wilted. Remove from the skillet and transfer to a large mixing bowl, at least 3-quart size. In a medium mixing bowl, combine the eggs, whole milk, grated cheeses, dry mustard, salt and pepper. Make sure the eggs are fully scrambled within this custard mixture. Add the ham and sweet potations, kale and onions; then stir until evenly mixed into the custard. Fold in the toasted bread. Pour everything into a well buttered, 2-quart baking dish. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate at least four hours, up to 24 hours. When ready to bake, preheat the oven to 350˚. Remove the plastic wrap from the dish, place it on oven rack in the middle position in the oven. Bake for one hour or until fully set. Test by inserting a clean knife into the center of the dish. If it comes out clean, the custard is set. It should be nicely browned and puffy; and pulling slightly away from the sides of the dish. It will settle as it cools, so know that the gorgeous puff is fleeting. For more information or to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok at PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: Ham and Sweet Potato Strata a springtime treat

articles.text: It has been almost a year since the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group has been able to walk together. The pandemic put their walks on hold in March 2020, and many members of the group miss seeing one another. At the good suggestion of member Priscilla Wanerus, and with the technical support of John Wilk at the Recreation Department, 16 members of the group had a Zoom call on February 17. Calendar conflicts kept many walkers from participating in the call, but it was a happy conversation and time that the walkers – now talkers – had together. Participating in the call were: Barry Gant, Harriette Louie, Noemi Alvarado, Sarah Johnson, Carol Long, Priscilla Wanerus, Pauline Marx, Alan Goldhammer, Brenda Ferrero, Jeri Lockhart, Nancy Lenahan, John Lenahan, Claudia Lopez, Alicia Rivera, Jim Kao, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The 45-minute call gave the group an enjoyable opportunity to see one another again, and a chance to catch up and share what everyone has been doing since last year. Noemi Alvarado – on her treadmill when the conversation began – got the call off to a “running start.” She told the group that she and husband Mark Davis are expecting their first grandchild. Dick Carter announced that his daughter had gotten engaged last fall. Jeri Lockhart shared that she is in the process of moving to Seattle. The walkers and talkers are sorry to be losing Jeri, and also Nancy and Cliff Pender who have moved to Lafayette. The conversation included progress people have made getting vaccinated for the virus. The good news is that most of the 16 members of the group held a Zoom call on February 17.
articles.title: Walking on Wednesdays – one year later

pages.text: Wednesday, March 3, 2021 21 Features Business owners’ issues go beyond ‘mom and pop’ label If you own a small business, you typically don’t get a lot of recognition. You may be pleased to learn that March 29 is National Mom and Pop Business Owners Day. You might not necessarily think of your business as a “Mom and Pop” operation, but it certainly contributes to the well-being of your family now, and possibly to that of future generations, too – if you make the right moves. Depending on the nature of your business, you may have spent the past several months more concerned about today than tomorrow, given the serious economic repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still placing stress on a great many business owners across the country. If your business has been adversely affected by the pandemic, you might be eligible for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. As you may know, recent legislation provided $285 billion more for this program. To learn more, and to start the application process, visit the Small Business Administration website at www.sba.gov. You have until March 31 to apply for a PPP loan. Other relief also may be available. But regardless of whether you apply for one of these loans, you can take other steps to help maximize the benefits you get from your business – and perhaps even extend its longevity. Here are a few suggestions: • Establish a retirement plan. If you don’t already have a retirement plan, it’s never too late to set one up. As a business owner, you have several options, including an “owner-only” 401(k), a SIMPLE IRA and a SEP-IRA. All these plans are fairly easy to establish and can offer potential tax advantages, as well as providing you with a source of retirement income in the future. You may want to work with a financial professional to pick the right plan for your needs. • Coordinate your business assets with your investment portfolio. Like most business owners, you may have a great deal of your personal wealth tied up in your business. And, as the past year has certainly shown, this can be risky. Consequently, you’ll need to weigh this risk factor when deciding on investing in your retirement plan or in other investment accounts. This doesn’t mean you should try to avoid all risk only by pursuing the most conservative vehicles – which would be counterproductive to achieving enough growth to meet your retirement income goals – but you will need to pay close attention to your investment mix to ensure it provides you with an appropriate balance to what you’ve invested in your business. • Develop a transition strategy. How will you make the transition from business owner to the next phase of your life? Will you sell the business outright? Will you gradually transfer it to a family member? If so, what mechanism will you use? It’ a good idea to have these types of plans in place well before you need to enact them, so you may want to consult with your financial, legal and tax advisors soon. A “Mom and Pop” business may sound quaint and carefree – but, as you know, running a business of any size can be an all-consuming endeavor and always involves significant financial concerns. Get the help you need to meet these challenges. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. T.J. The 45-minute call gave the group an enjoyable opportunity to see one another again, and a chance to catch up and share what everyone has been doing since last year. Noemi Alvarado – on her treadmill when the conversation began – got the call off to a “running start.” She told the group that she and husband Mark Davis are expecting their first grandchild. Dick Carter announced that his daughter had gotten engaged last fall. Jeri Lockhart shared that she is in the process of moving to Seattle. The walkers and talkers are sorry to be losing Jeri, and also Nancy and Cliff Pender who have moved to Lafayette. The conversation included progress people have made getting vaccinated for the virus. The good news is that most of the 16 members of the group held a Zoom call on February 17. group have been able to get their first shots. Members of the group also shared how they have been keeping active during the pandemic by walking and occasionally seeing one another when they are outside. Alan Goldhammer said he has taken up bird watching at Lake Temescal, and noted that the water doesn’t seem very clean, but the birds don’t seem to mind. Priscilla Wanerus has been going to the Montclair Driving Range and the UC Botanical Gardens for exercise, and Sherry Jacobs has found biking around Lake Merritt to be enjoyable. Claudia Lopez recommended kayaking on Lake Chabot. Others have been having get-togethers with friends on their driveways and enjoying takeout meals from restaurants. The group looks forward to being able to resume their weekly walks on Wednesday mornings in the not-too-distant future. For information on joining the Wednesday Walkers (and Talkers), contact Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net. Photo by Deborah Quok A ham and sweet potato strata is a lovely brunch during springtime. By Deborah Quok Spring brunch time is nigh, and this “strata” features the classic pairing of ham and sweet potatoes. Technically the method here doesn’t layer the ingredients (a strata), but over the years I’ve found the layering process doesn’t make a big difference in the end result. So, I opt for an easier preparation. If you feel inclined, you can layer the ham-sweet potato-onion mixture with slices of bread and cheese, then pour the milkegg mixture over all of it. Or go with the simpler version here and mix everything together in a big bowl and transfer it to the baking dish. This is an excellent vessel for leftover meats and vegetables. As with many of my recipes, pandemic or not, this one is flexible on ingredients and flavorings. Eggs, half-half, and bread are the basis upon which you build, with additional ingredients that influence the resulting dish. I happened to have a package of ham steak and leftover roasted sweet potatoes, which are the basis here. Kale is a staple at our house. If you enjoy this recipe, check out my blog for Piedmont Brunch, using sausage, zucchini and bell peppers. Ham and Sweet Potato Strata INGREDIENTS • 4 ounces bread, cut into 3/4” cubes, about 3 - 4 cups • 1 - 2 teaspoons olive oil • 12 ounces fully cooked ham, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 - 2 cups cooked sweet potato, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 medium bunch kale, sliced crosswise in 1/2” wide strips, about 2 - 3 cups • 1 cup yellow onion, diced • 5 extra-large eggs • 2 cups half and half • 1 teaspoon dry mustard powder • • • • Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste Pinch of cayenne pepper, to taste 5 ounces jalapeno jack cheese, shredded, about 1 cup 1/4 cup green onions, thinly sliced for garnish PREPARATION Preheat the oven to 350˚. Place bread cubes on baking sheet. Bake for 10 - 15 minutes, until dry and firm. Remove from oven and let cool. Heat olive oil in a large skillet on medium heat, add onions and cook stirring frequently, until they become soft and translucent. Add sliced kale and continue cooking until the kale has just barely wilted. Remove from the skillet and transfer to a large mixing bowl, at least 3-quart size. In a medium mixing bowl, combine the eggs, whole milk, grated cheeses, dry mustard, salt and pepper. Make sure the eggs are fully scrambled within this custard mixture. Add the ham and sweet potations, kale and onions; then stir until evenly mixed into the custard. Fold in the toasted bread. Pour everything into a well buttered, 2-quart baking dish. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate at least four hours, up to 24 hours. When ready to bake, preheat the oven to 350˚. Remove the plastic wrap from the dish, place it on oven rack in the middle position in the oven. Bake for one hour or until fully set. Test by inserting a clean knife into the center of the dish. If it comes out clean, the custard is set. It should be nicely browned and puffy; and pulling slightly away from the sides of the dish. It will settle as it cools, so know that the gorgeous puff is fleeting. articles.text: Oftentimes, a simple refresh on a fixed budget can give your bathroom a whole new look and feel. Recently, HDR Remodeling completed a bathroom refresh in a guest bathroom in Oakland and we’re sharing how we made it happen. Our clients came to us with a request for a makeover of their guest bathroom with a contemporary design. They loved the charm of their 1920s-era house but wanted to liven up this space. In the original bathroom, the toilet sat in the center of the room and was the first thing guests saw as they approached. The fixtures and finishes were also of the original 1920s era. The driving factor of our design was to maintain the existing architectural details of the house, while infusing our client’s personal style – a blend of modern and vintage – with an appreciation for unique natural handmade materials. We collaborated closely with our clients who wanted to incorporate an organic and natural form of wood into the bathroom. That became the source of our inspiration and a focal point for the bathroom. Open shelving and natural elements also create a sense of openness in tight spaces. Bathroom before refresh. Bathroom refresh with natural countertops and bold backsplash. Because our goal was to remain within the footprint of the existing bathroom, we had to be creative with the space we had. We shifted the layout of the bathroom, repositioning the original bathtub and relocating the toilet using a wall-mounted tank behind the door. This gave us additional valuable square footage and made space for the statement piece of the bathroom - a custom wood countertop and shelves sourced from our client’s family member, Revival Woods of Kapa’au, Hawaii. To add dimension, we built a deep tub ledge for seating and to hold bathing necessities. A bold patterned tile adds interest to what would otherwise be a simple, tiled wall. By not changing the square footage, we were able to keep costs down and allowed for some major changes to upgrade this bathroom. Incorporating intentional fixtures and key finishes is pivotal in transforming a small space and giving it new life. articles.text: Photo by Amber Brumfiel Dark pink buds are starting to appear on the bare branches of Piedmont’s Eastern Redbud trees. The groundhog may have seen its shadow this year, but spring is in the air as you look at the flowering trees in Piedmont’s urban forest. There are beautiful examples all around town, including the cluster of Eastern Redbuds (Cercis canadensis) that greet you at the entrance to Witter Field and Piedmont Park at the intersection of Wildwood and Prospect Avenues. Nominated by former resident Lisa Kieraldo, these cheerful trees were designated as Heritage Trees in 2019. Dark pink buds are just starting to appear on the bare branches of these trees. Considered long lasting, the showy blossoms will last for a few weeks once they fully bloom. Green leaves will then start to appear. The Eastern Redbud is the state tree of Oklahoma. This deciduous tree has heart shaped leaves and some varieties around town have stunning fall colors that add to their enjoyment as small garden trees. The Eastern Redbud is sometimes referred to as the Spicewood Tree because its bark and green twigs are sometimes used as seasoning for wild game. The Piedmont Park Commission is accepting nominations for 2021 Heritage Trees through March 19. The Heritage Tree program is an opportunity for Piedmont to recognize its distinctive trees. The community is invited to nominate trees growing on public property, such as parks, medians, and streets. Nominated trees will be considered based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits. The chosen trees will be announced at the Park Commission hearing on April 7 and honored at this year’s virtual Arbor Day celebration on April 30. To nominate a tree visit the City’s website, http://www. ci.piedmont.ca.us/ and complete the downloadable form. For more information, contact Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov (510- 420-3064). Amber Brumfiel is a member of the Piedmont Park Commission.

articles.text: Dear Abby: Have you found out anything new about COVID-19 and our pets? Can we spread it to them? Too young to be vaccinated yet, –Jordan and Fat Cat Dear Jordan and Fat Cat: Here’s what I found on the CDC’s website on February 10, 2021: • We do not know the exact source of the current outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), but we know that it originally came from an animal, likely a bat. • At this time, there is no evidence that animals play a significant role in spreading SARSCoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, to people. • Based on the limited information available to date, the risk of animals spreading COVID-19 to people is considered to be low. • More studies are needed to understand if and how different animals could be affected by COVID-19. • We are still learning about this virus, but it appears that it can spread from people to animals in some situations. • People with suspected or confirmed COVID-19 should avoid contact with animals, including pets, livestock, and wildlife. Hope this helps calm Fat Cat’s concerns, –Abby Dear Abby: With all these pet adoptions, we are having trouble finding a trainer to help us with our new adopted boy, Elvis, the cutest dog ever. Any ideas? Perplexed and pooped, –Eve, Jacob & Elvis Dear Eve, Jacob and Elvis: This is the tricky side of pet adoptions. Trainers are booked up teaching dogs how to live with their humans. Give Heidi Kistler a call of Pawsitively Pampered Pets in Oakland, 510-336-9861. I’m not sure what she and her husband Ryan have available but at the very least, she may be able to add Elvis to a dog walking group which helps any dog with socializing and adhering to basic commands. Heidi also walks and takes care of a lot of Piedmont dogs and can help if you start to travel to allocation where Elvis can’t join you. Can’t wait to meet Elvis. Can he sing? –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.
articles.title: Can we spread COVID to our pets?

articles.text: 2019 Bokisch Albarino Terra Alta Vineyard • 2017 Bokisch Tempranillo Liberty Oaks Vineyard This begins with intimations of blackberries and cherries that inform a ripe, lush and expansive palate. Tobacco and earth lend interest and incisive energy to a lingering and satisfying finish with soft, subdued tannins. While drinking beautifully now, this wine should improve for a decade. • 2017 Bokisch Graciano Las Cerezas Vineyard This lovely varietal is seldom seen bottled on its own, so this is a nice treat. It has an intense blueberry and dark plum-tinged bouquet. The palate is medium-bodied with a rounded, sensual entry. It is very supple and caressing in the mouth, with a slight touch of oak on the finish. Drink over the next five years. This has been a tough year for wineries, and that is an understatement. Without the ability to sell directly to the public – their most profitable sales – many wineries have struggled to sell wine and to keep up ties with loyal customers. Thank God for wine clubs where many people have signed up with their favorite wineries to have wine shipped directly to them on a regular basis. I have also noticed that many wineries have gotten creative in finding ways to not only sell wine but interact creatively with their customers. I recently received an email invitation from Bokisch Vineyards in Lodi to be a part of a “Virtual Taste of Spain” Educational Series and I jumped at the opportunity. Here’s how it worked. Participants paid $125 for a ticket which could be shared by more than one person. The winery shipped four different bottles of wine and sent the Zoom code for the seminar. For one hour on two succeeding Wednesday nights owners Markus and Liz Bokisch and their winemaker Elyse Perry led a seminar on a wide range of subjects – the history of winemaking in Spain, a summary of the major growing regions, a tutorial on major Spanish grape varietals, and finally a discussion of two of the wines they had sent. The evening I attended the wines were Grenache Blanc and Tempranillo. It was fun to be drinking the wine while listing to the winemaker talk about how it was produced and the decisions that went into making it. It wasn’t interactive (which was probably a good thing) but you could submit questions in the chat forum. All and all, it was fun and informative. Bokisch Vineyard was founded in 1995. Markus’s heritage is Catalan and their emphasis is on grape varieties from the Iberian Peninsula. That is wonderful news, as the last thing the world needs is another Cabernet Sauvignon or Chardonnay. It is refreshing to be able to try Albarino, Graciano, and Tempranillo. For information on availability check their website at bokischvineyards.com. articles.text: Diane (Di) Paulhamus Anderson, a lifelong resident of Piedmont, passed away at her St. Helena home on February 24 after a short illness. She was 88. Above all, Di was a loving wife, devoted mother and grandmother and an exceptionally generous friend. Invariably, she was the first to reach out to a family member or to one of her countless friends if they were in any sort of need. It is remarkable how many of Di’s friendships extended through two, three and more generations of families. Di was also a forceful presence, getting what she felt was best for those close to her. She was always in charge in the most positive of ways; very little got past her. Di was born June 3, 1932 in Seattle to Dwight Randolph Paulhamus and Eleanor Jackson Paulhamus. They were a pioneering Puyallup Valley family and among the founders of the Washington State Fair. Her paternal grandfather, W.H. Paulhamus was a Washington state senator. As a child, Di and her family moved to Piedmont where she would reside for the rest of her life. It was at Piedmont High School, class of 1950, where she started dating her future husband, Jack Blair Anderson. Di attended the University of Arizona and was a member of the Delta Gamma sorority. Returning to the Bay Area, she started working in the personnel department for Kaiser Corporation, and resumed her romance with Jack. Di and Jack were married February 11, 1956 and enjoyed a love affair for the following 62 years. Their three children, Ellin, John and Michael were raised in Piedmont and attended public schools there. Jack passed away in 2018. For nearly 40 years, Di and Jack divided their time between Piedmont and St. Helena. In addiDiane P. Anderson, a lifelong resident of Piedmont and a consummate hostess, died on February 24 at her home in St. Helena. She was 88. tion to allowing Di an additional home to decorate, St. Helena gave her the opportunity to extend her circle of friends to the wine country. A consummate entertainer, Di was known for countless parties, most notably her blacktie Christmas Eve celebration in Piedmont and New Year’s Eve luncheon in St. Helena. articles.text: John Cottell, a resident of Piedmont in the late 1980s, died in Eugene, Oregon on January 13, 2021. He was 96. Born on December 4, 1924 in Lincolnshire, England, John Edward Cottell was a Colonel in the British Army who earned the titles of MVO (Member of the Royal Victorian Order, a British order of knighthood), and MBE (Most Excellent Order of the British Empire). He was also awarded the Croix de Guerre with Palmes and the Military Cross. He was a descendant of settlers arriving with William the Conquerer in the 11th Century He served with the British forces in World War II, and worked undercover as a member of the Special Operations Executive (SOE), conducting espionage, sabotage and reconnaissance for England. He was wounded and captured in the battle of Arnhem and rescued by the Sixth Armored Division of the U.S. Third Army under the command of Gen. George Patton. Following the war Cottell went to work with M16, Britain’s secret service equivalent of the CIA in the U.S. He was captured again, this time by the Russians and spent time in the Lubyanka Prison before being released in a prisoner exchange. His story is recounted in a book called No Cloak No Dagger. In 1989 while on the lecture circuit, he spoke at the Bellevue Club through the work of his future wife, Candance Cottell. They were married in Piedmont Community Church in 1989 and lived in Piedmont until 1991 when they moved to Eugene, Oregon. John is survived by his wife Candace, his daughter Leonie Rique of Rio de Janeiro, and the extended McNie family. John is predeceased by two sons, Peter and Simon Cottell. A family gathering will be held in the future to celebrate his life.

articles.text: Dear Jim: We are planning a basement renovation project but have been struggling to find the right person for the job. It seems most contractors, architects and engineers we’ve been referred to are booked months in advance. Also, preliminary prices are higher than we expected. Is this also your experience, and how would you suggest we move forward with our remodel? As I’ve mentioned in previous articles, residential remodeling and repair are being highly affected by current world events and economics in a way that is significantly impacting contractors and their clients. Since the changes may have a major effect on your timelines and budget, it is important that you understand their potential impact on projects you are now considering. Huge demand for home live/ work spaces Most of the clients we are currently working for have moved their “headquarters” home and concepts relating to “remote” work have contractors adapting to this move toward home-based work/living spaces. In addition to keeping staff safe, it is becoming evident that decentralizing the office is also a cost-effective model for the modern work world. As a result, a need for new living and recreation space, storage, home offices, and basement units has increased substantially, thus directly affecting all lead times for home remodeling businesses, including designers, subcontractors, architects, and engineers. With backlogs currently the norm, and people becoming more aware of the defects in their homes or simply wanting to eke out more space, supply and demand is putting pressure on the home renovation industry. Prices have increased dramatically. Additionally, Coronavirus-induced mill shutdowns along with a booming housing market have led to huge increases in lumber costs. For example, plywood sheathing costs (one of our biggest purchases) have doubled in the last year – from $20 a sheet to around $40. As a consequence, wood-based manufactured products affected by shutdowns, such as windows and doors, have also seen spikes in cost. Concrete and steel are also seeing price jumps, but not as dramatic as the lumber industry. Labor costs have increased as well, with skilled employees and laborers demanding higher wages and jumping ship to other companies due to labor shortages and high demand for their services. One striking example of these inflations are when potential customers I gave estimates to 2-3 years ago return ready to begin a project, requiring me to reprice the project with increases averaging around 30%. Building Departments struggle to keep up. Another pressure of getting a project started but with long delays is the process of permit approvals, which is different city by city. Even before Covid, permitting, particularly with remodeling projects, involved planning, zoning and extensive plan checking. It is not uncommon for contractors to have to wait 4-6 months for permits on more extensive jobs in certain cities (not Piedmont, of course). Simple repair jobs which I used to be able to have permits issued the same day or in a few days and over the counter, are now subject to a lengthier process, creating challenges in getting projects off the ground. In Berkeley, for example it can take me 3-4 days to get the cashier to respond to an e-mail request to pay for a permit that is ready to issue, something which in the past could have been resolved with a 5-minute phone call. For a while I thought that the lack of distractions for home-based workers might actually improve efficiency, but I now believe the lack of personal face-to face interaction can make things more complex. Some cities are still relying on video inspections, which can be slow and challenging with poor internet connections. Supply-chain issues significantly impacted Other reasons for delay are ongoing problems with the manufacturer, shipping and delivery of products. We are currently working on a large home remodel and many items are often out of stock, with lead times on the building of doors, windows, cabinets etc. often doubled or tripled. Even basic, mass produced items, like IKEA cabinets, are constantly out of stock. We’ve been waiting months, along with other contractors, to gather a few at a time as they become available. Certain production facilities and specialty shops have closed down completely. They are working with reduced staffing and report difficulty procuring raw materials. Shipping is slowed, and even paying more to expedite delivery is often impossible. Items are regularly arriving weeks behind scheduled delivery dates, shoving dates for starting, completing, or continuing projects all over the calendar. Final word The bottom line is that your construction project may not only be more expensive than expected, but also due to the numerous pressures outlined above, it may be difficult to find a contractor right away. My best advice is to anticipate this as a new reality, even as Covid potentially wanes. More efficient systems may be slow to return, and contractors will continue to be very busy, especially if the economy improves and working at home becomes more of a staple. Be sure that you plan your project well in advance, and have proper expectations about costs and a time frame for completion to avoid the pitfalls associated with construction in 2021. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Mention of honey bees provokes a variety of responses. The buzz of a bee and the contrasting yellow and black colors inspire thoughts of golden honey. They incite fear of the sting. And they symbolize our dependency on pollinating insects. Whatever thoughts come to mind, keeping bees can be a fascinating connection with the wildness we find around us. Although bees live in painted rectangular boxes, they are still wild insects. They forage for their food and propagate on their own. Opening a hive of honey bees is like opening a window to the wildness we can find even in the city. This time of year, a hive is small but growing. Most of the nectar and pollen collected is used to raise more bees. The nectar provides the carbohydrates; pollen is the protein source. Honey bees literally work themselves to death and live only six weeks during the busy season. The queen bee is no slouch either. She can lay more than her body weight in eggs in a single day. Despite the independence of bees, a beekeeper must still tend them. Those stacks of white boxes grow taller through the spring to give the colony more room to store honey and more room for bees. If a colony senses that its home is full of bees and honey, it will swarm. The name sounds scary and the sound of a swarm of honey bees is scary. I have heard sevThe white powder on the head and thorax of the bee is pollen from a Rosemary blossom. Beekeeper Nils Kaufman next to one of his hives. eral in recent years pass over my house. They are loud. But in reality, the honey bee is most docile during a swarm. She has no home to defend and is looking for one. She does not want to sting. In fact, honey bees are bred for gentle behavior. If you see a swarm of bees cluster on a branch or under the eaves, call a beekeeper. If possible the beekeeper will collect the bees and give them a new home. I have done this wearing a T-shirt and shorts; the bees are very calm. Compared to other backyard agricultural pursuits such as gardening or raising chickens, beekeeping does require some specialized knowledge but much less time. Beekeepers check on their bees every two weeks during the spring and summer, and less frequently in the fall. The population of bees decreases in the fall. They do not want more mouths to feed than necessary, but they do need enough bees to cluster and stay warm. The biology of these fall bees changes as well to allow them to survive several months of winter. The biggest threat to honey bees is the varroa mite, in Latin, varroa destructor. There are organic treatments that kill these mites, and with care, varroa are little more than a nuisance. Piedmont is an almost ideal place to raise bees. A hive or two in the backyard is not a bother as long as there is sufficient space and adequate care. The reward? The honey harvested will be as prized as any home-grown tomato. In addition to supporting novice beekeepers, Nils Kauffman has played bagpipes for the high school and Piedmont Scout events. For more information, contact him at: nils.j.kauffman@ gmail.com.

It is just really a wonderful community effort,” said Littlefield. ”It is an incredible building and this is just going to be awesome.” The funds will be used for computer-aided fabrication equipment such as a CNC router, laser cutter, 3D printers and more in the lab. It will also employ a dedicated lab staff member to help teachers create course offerings. When the engineering lab is fully outfitted, the lab will function as the home base for the Piedmont Highlanders FRC (FIRST Robotics Competition) Team. The engineering lab will be a workshop for design and prototyping, equipped with both manual and computer-controlled tools. It is a modern version of a wood or metal workshop and will allow PHS students to make almost anything, big or small, technical or artistic, serious or whimsical. Piedmont Makers have been busy of late, recently acquiring a 100 Watt laser cutter and engraver. PHS Physics teacher Marna Chamberlain recently came by the Makers’ temporary Engineering Lab with a guitar she built at a guitar engineering course. It is a course she already has proposed to teach next year as part of the curriculum at the high school. Henry Lambert, a senior at PHS, found some files of one of Sammy Hagar’s favorite guitars, the Gibson Explorer, and cut out the pattern on the laser cutter and a plywood body on the CNC router. The check presented this week marks the largest capital campaign in the history of Piedmont Makers. The organization was launched in 2014 to support and inspire S.T.E.A.M. education in Piedmont at all grade levels. Programs include events like the annual School Maker Faire and robotics competitions. In the last four years, the Piedmont Makers robotics programs have grown from one team of 10 high school students to 34 teams and 220 students from kindergarten through 12th grade.

Recent videos of attacks in Oakland and San Francisco – caught on residential and commercial security cameras – have circulated online and on social media. Even with this blatant evidence, however, a victim’s refusal to report an assault or burglary can hinder investigations. “These [victims] will tell me about an attack or robbery, but they are unwilling to share that with the authorities. They tell me they’re afraid of retaliation, and they also feel that since it has already happened, what’s the use in reporting,” Chan explained. Chan noted that he has worked closely with both Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley, and the Oakland Police Department (OPD), to address underreporting concerns. Chan acknowledged that both offices are aware that underreporting is an issue. In a press conference in February, newly-appointed Oakland Police Chief LeRonne Armstrong said that the reported data on Asian-targeted hate crime incidents do not reflect the actual number of incidents because many altercations go unreported. In addition, the City of Oakland has slashed $15 million from the department’s overtime spending, which Chief Armstrong said is hampering the department’s ability to “keep the peace.” It is also hampering the department’s ability to respond to victims who do report. Some victims have waited hours for police to arrive after reporting a burglary or assault, mentioned Chan. “When the incident happens, and the perpetrator has left, it no longer becomes a priority,” he said. Officers will encourage victims to file a report online, but that can present language barrier issues. Chan said he understands that the Oakland Police Department is stretched thin with its budget cuts. Community members across the Bay Area have recognized this, too, and have offered to help protect vulnerable communities. Volunteers have offered to patrol the streets of Chinatown in an effort to deter physical violence, robberies, and vandalism, with offers of help coming from as far away as Stockton and San Jose. A fundraiser, with a goal of $80,000, was initiated by Oakland resident Joanna Au on gofundme.com to hire armed patrol security guards for Chinatown merchants. It surpassed its goal within 24 hours. “When we are seeing so many bad things happening, we’re also seeing good deeds from the community, and residents coming to support us,” Chan acknowledged. “We understand that this is a sensitive issue, and we understand the calls to defund the police [departments]. But we want to make sure the departments have sufficient resources.”
