articles.text: Many families reluctantly pulled children from Piedmont schools this past year to enroll them in schools that are safely and successfully offering in-person instruction. Looking ahead to the 2021/22 school year, our family desperately wants to return to PUSD; however, we – and all families – need assurances that the district’s top priority is to reopen its schools for full-time in-person instruction for all grades in August. As more and more data show that schools can reopen safely with proper precautions, as all teachers in Piedmont will likely be offered COVID vaccines by this summer, and most importantly, as growing evidence has shown that long-term distance learning is doing real harm to our children, full-time in-person instruction is absolutely essential for the 21/22 school year. Without it, many families, like mine who left the district this year, will likely stay away, and many more will leave in the coming months. While I have been thrilled to see grades K-6 begin some in-person instruction over the last few weeks, the current hybrid schedules (ranging from 2-4 hours of weekly in-person instruction for secondary students to 9 hours for elementary) are simply not enough to make up for the social, emotional, and academic losses caused by one year of distance learning. Knowing that families soon need to make school decisions for next year (most private school deposits, for example, are due in March), I asked Piedmont School District to survey families about their intentions to stay in the district next year. Superintendent Booker declined the request. As a result, a group of parents conducted their own survey. It ran from February 2–14, with over 400 PUSD families participating. The results are telling: • Nearly 50% of the respondents (198 families) said they are very or somewhat likely to leave the district if the school year begins with hybrid instruction. These numbers are vastly different from the enrollment projections the school district released this week. It predicted that district enrollment will decline by only 54 students next year. • An additional 51 families said they are not in a position to leave the district if 2021/22 begins with hybrid instruction, but they would if they could. • More than 270 families who had previously donated to the Piedmont Education Foundation, representing 66% of all survey respondents, said they would reduce their annual donation or give nothing next year if Piedmont schools do not open for full-time in-person instruction. With this important data in hand, we call on Superintendent Booker and PUSD’s school board to demonstrate a firm commitment to reopening PUSD’s schools for full-time in-person instruction in August this year so that families are not forced to leave a school district that they want so much to be a part of. articles.text: What does the Bible say? One answer is: absolutely nothing. Maybe it’s the politics in the air and perhaps even in our drinking water, but whatever the source, it seems like there is a renewed desire to be on God’s side. The introductory phrase “the Bible says…” is back with a vengeance. But I can assure you that any sentence that begins with those words makes no sense whatsoever. That babbling Bible has told women to sit down and shut up, called science a tool of the devil and fueled anti-Semitism and racism. This theological ventriloquism has led people through valleys of guilt, shame and fear, no doubt to support the status quo and keep the powerful in power. This arrogant preface is defended with the argument that a true believer takes the word of God literally. But which word are we talking about? If we are talking about the actual words composed by the original authors of the books of the Bible then shouldn’t those who feel so strongly about the literal word only quote from the original language? Obviously the first thing to note is that the Bible is a translation in progress. For example, the Greek word for “sin” is the same word used in archery to describe an arrow that has simply missed its mark. In the original language the sense is that one might be just a little off from center and yet in many circles “sin” has come to be understood as a dark and gruesome plague that compels us to feel guilt, shame and self-loathing. The Bible says nothing without our help, and to suggest that dozens of books and even more authors spread out over two millennia all agree and speak with

articles.text: Americans have been paying attention to the Biden-Harris Administration’s climate actions as the unrelenting pace of climate change marches on. Former President Trump never took interest in pursuing extensive climate action, instead opting to reverse former executive actions and open up formerly inaccessible federal lands for fossil fuel extraction. The Trump Administration’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was helmed by a fossil fuel magnate, and Trump consistently rolled back environmental progress, perhaps most famously when he withdrew the United States from the 2015 Paris Climate Accord. With the Biden-Harris administration in its early days, let’s take a look at what the president has done so far, what his plans are, and how he hopes to shape environmental policy. A few weeks into his term, most of President Biden’s significant policies have been overturning the executive actions that Trump enacted in office. President Biden has recommitted the U.S. to the Paris Climate Accord, cancelled the Keystone Pipeline, undone Trump’s rollback of automobile mileage requirements, and frozen a series of Trump’s executive actions related to air quality. While admirable, some of these executive actions could potentially get mired in court, leading to lost time on critical issues. Additionally, executive actions are fickle. They need to be reinforced by legislation, otherwise they can easily be negated by the following president. With full control of both congressional chambers until 2022, Democrats have a chance to pass environmental legislation that can impact decades of emissions. The new administration has signaled that climate actions will be tied to both infrastructure spending and jobs. Two-thirds of the buildings that exist today will still be here in 2050, showing how infrastructure actions we take now are incredibly important. Biden’s congressional representatives run the range of ideologies, with some asking for more progressive actions like the “Green New Deal,” while others call for caution and restraint moving forward. It will take bold action to guide party members and attain the votes necessary to actually pass bills. President Biden has called for numerous plans and goals related to climate action. This includes calling for 100 percent clean energy by 2035, a promise certain to raise eyebrows. Progressive California has only set a goal of 2045 for this metric, and achieving this on a national scale would require that no coal or gas-powered plants could exist in 14 years. Unlikely? Perhaps. But this kind of aggressive action is what is necessary to limit emissions. President Biden’s website says he will upgrade 4 million buildings before 2025, as well as provide direct cash rebates and financing to upgrade and electrify home appliances. Electrification is a priority here in Piedmont due to the direct impact it has on natural gas emissions. Biden wants to “spur the construction of 1.5 million sustainable homes”, although this sounds more open ended than the cash rebates promise. The overarching promise of the administration is to “build modern infrastructure.” We will have to wait to see what that means in practice, but it is an important next step towards increasing the nation’s sustainability efforts. Finally, the administration claims it will set new federal netzero standards for new commercial buildings by 2030. A good goal, but an earlier deadline could have an even greater impact. Perhaps most importantly, many of these goals suggest that the federal government will be focusing attention on climate and energy issues in a way that local and state governments have been shouldering over the last few years. In addition to Biden’s admirable promises, numerous areas of concern still remain. pages.text: Wednesday, February 24, 2021 3 News What a new administration means for federal climate action By Nate Redinbo Americans have been paying attention to the Biden-Harris Administration’s climate actions as the unrelenting pace of climate change marches on. Former President Trump never took interest in pursuing extensive climate action, instead opting to reverse former executive actions and open up formerly inaccessible federal lands for fossil fuel extraction. The Trump Administration’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was helmed by a fossil fuel magnate, and Trump consistently rolled back environmental progress, perhaps most famously when he withdrew the United States from the 2015 Paris Climate Accord. With the Biden-Harris administration in its early days, let’s take a look at what the president has done so far, what his plans are, and how he hopes to shape environmental policy. A few weeks into his term, most of President Biden’s significant policies have been overturning the executive actions that Trump enacted in office. President Biden has recommitted the U.S. to the Paris Climate Accord, cancelled the Keystone Pipeline, undone Trump’s rollback of automobile mileage requirements, and frozen a series of Trump’s executive actions related to air quality. While admirable, some of these executive actions could potentially get mired in court, leading to lost time on critical issues. Additionally, executive actions are fickle. They need to be reinforced by legislation, otherwise they can easily be negated by the following president. With full control of both congressional chambers until 2022, Democrats have a chance to pass environmental legislation that can impact decades of emissions. The new administration has signaled that climate actions will be tied to both infrastructure spending and jobs. Two-thirds of the buildings that exist today will still be here in 2050, showing how infrastructure actions we take now are incredibly important. Biden’s congressional representatives run the range of ideologies, with some asking for more progressive actions like the “Green New Deal,” while others call for caution and restraint moving forward. It will take bold action to guide party members and attain the votes necessary to actually pass bills. President Biden has called for numerous plans and goals related to climate action. This includes calling for 100 percent clean energy by 2035, a promise certain to raise eyebrows. Progressive California has only set a goal of 2045 for this metric, and achieving this on a national scale would require that no coal or gas-powered plants could exist in 14 years. Unlikely? Perhaps. But this kind of aggressive action is what is necessary to limit emissions. President Biden’s website says he will upgrade 4 million buildings before 2025, as well as provide direct cash rebates and financing to upgrade and electrify home appliances. Electrification is a priority here in Piedmont due to the direct impact it has on natural gas emissions. Biden wants to “spur the construction of 1.5 million sustainable homes”, although this sounds more open ended than the cash rebates promise. The overarching promise of the administration is to “build modern infrastructure.” We will have to wait to see what that means in practice, but it is an important next step towards increasing the nation’s sustainability efforts. Finally, the administration claims it will set new federal netzero standards for new commercial buildings by 2030. A good goal, but an earlier deadline could have an even greater impact. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will hold a public forum on homelessness on March 2 Margot Kushel, MD, the Director of the UCSF Center of Vulnerable Populations and the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital, will present her latest research on solutions to “Housing the Homeless in the Time of COVID-19”. Her research aims to prevent and end homelessness and mitigate the effects of housing instability on healthcare outcomes. Dr. Kushel works with diverse stakeholders to implement programmatic and policy changes based on her research. She is the primary investigator of several multi-year studies on homeless populations in the Bay Area from 2012 to the present. The discussion will take place on Tuesday, March 2 from 4:00 to 5:00 p.m. and will be available on YouTube at: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg/featured. To register, click on lwvpiedmont. org and get the Zoom information on the League’s website. The program is free and open to the public. Dr. Kushel is a practicing general internist at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital. Margot’s research examines the causes and consequences of homelessness and housing instability, with the goal of preventing and ending homelessness and ameliorating the effects of homelessness on health. She has appeared at the local, state and national level about homelessness, and provides testimony to legislative bodies. She received her AB from Harvard College, her MD from Yale and completed residency, chief residency and fellowship in internal medicine at UCSF.

articles.text: At its meeting on February 11, the Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) discussed the results of its community engagement safer streets survey. The survey was open for approximately six weeks, from November 20, 2020 to January 3, 2021, and contained 19 questions. The city received 338 responses. According to the survey, residents noticed that walking and biking has increased throughout Piedmont throughout shelter-inplace orders – since March 2020. Survey respondents reported noticing that drivers “seem to be speeding more on main streets, such as Highland Avenue, Moraga Avenue, Grand Avenue, Oakland Avenue and Mountain Avenue.” Grand Avenue draws mixed feelings from survey respondents. Some felt that conditions for cyclists and pedestrians had improved but pointed to increased congestion and more traffic and speeding on adjacent streets. Almost all respondents reported noticing more people walking in the roadway due to social distancing requirements, and concern over lack of sidewalks in some areas. In response to the question of how the city could improve traffic and pedestrian safety, 162 offered suggestions. Ideas included reducing posted speed limits, having educational camResidents have expressed interest in a slow streets program in Piedmont. paigns to address speeding, and adding more pedestrian and bicycling infrastructure, such as speed bumps, wider sidewalks, lighted crosswalks, signage, and bike lanes. Respondents also suggested piloting a “slow streets” program, similar to programs Oakland and San Francisco have launched in response to shelter-in-place restrictions. Residents said that this would “calm traffic while encouraging more walking and biking.” The slow streets program in other Bay Area cities are designed to limit through traffic on certain residential streets, and allow them to be used as a shared space for people traveling by foot and bicycle – more common in Europe than the U.S. Residents also said that educating cyclists and pedestrians of all ages about safe use of streets, including encouraging people to walk on sidewalks, would improve traffic safety in Piedmont. The report found that there “is an appreciation for the increased number of stop signs” in Piedmont, especially on Magnolia Avenue and Hampton Road, as speeding continues to be a top concern. About 49 percent surveyed “strongly support” speed humps for certain residential streets. Only 9 percent of those surveyed said they strongly opposed speed humps. To read the full survey findings, see: https://e36eb74c- 2d11-4079-bf83-e415caf952f1. filesusr.com/ugd/06d7f0_a3b2af0027414911a5ee553bf8b3cf0d. pdf The next PBAC meeting will be held on Zoom on April 8, 2021, at 5:30 p.m.
articles.title: Residents voice interest in piloting “slow streets” program

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s Schoolmates afterschool program is currently operating as Camp Smart Start and Play Pods. Both camps have served as the city’s distancelearning programs while schools in the district remain closed due to the ongoing health crisis. “Now that students are beginning to return to schools, these programs will be adjusted,” Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns said at a February 17 Recreation Commission meeting. Smart Start acted as the distance learning camp during traditional school hours, and Play Pods served as an afternoon camp from 2:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. Camp Smart Start originally followed the school district’s bell schedule for distance learning. Previously, groups were formed around age group or grade level, while still on a.m. and p.m. distance learning scheduling based on PUSD’s schedule. “It was challenging trying to coordinate two different schedules across 12 kids [a pod]. Going forward, in our new session, everyone is either on a morning schedule or an afternoon schedule,” he said. “This also means that we had to move around staff [schedules], to ensure that we had coverage at all sites. The good news is that with schools reopening, we’ve seen more parents who are interested in registering for the [afterschool] programs.” In the first session in January, 64 students were enrolled in Camp Smart Start and Play Pod programs. For the upcoming session, the Recreation Department is at maximum capacity of 72 students. “The fact that we are at capacity is a really good sign,” Stearns said. Stearns added that sign-up restrictions will likely be set in place for the foreseeable future. “We’re not going to go back to what Schoolmates looked like, pre-pandemic. In all likelihood, I don’t feel confident that we will go back to hourly registration, kids signing up the night before, or drop-ins. We’re not going to be able to be as flexible [in scheduling] as we used to be, but I’m hopeful that we will be able to offer more spots based on vaccinations and county guideline changes,” he said. The Piedmont Recreation Department is also hiring Recreation Leaders for its after-school program. Interested applicants may call the Department at 420- 3070, or contact Stearns at jstearns@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The COVID experience has been hard for all of us, but especially hard for students. Every morning at exactly 8:30 a.m. we would log onto our computers and talk into the screen for over two hours. Even though we “see” all of our classmates regularly on the screen, it’s strange to think that we have not assembled as an in-person class this entire school year. I am excited to go back to school and see my classmates and teacher in 3D. Before the pandemic, I probably would have been excited to be behind a screen all day, but now that I’m actually doing that, I realize that in-person school is so much better. There were definitely times during the year when I thought going back to the actual classroom was a goal that was out of reach. Now that we have worked extra hard, stayed socially distant, worn our face masks even though we probably didn’t want to, we accomplished our goal. Thank you to everyone who helped make this happen, and especially to our teachers who have been there every step of the way! Sofia Meyer is a 5th grade student at Wildwood Elementary School.
articles.title: As we return to school, thanks to our teachers

articles.text: I recently received an email from a parent saying that it was time I “demand” teachers return to the classroom. This parent was livid that school isn’t open, and his anger was directed squarely at teachers. Apparently, he sees teachers as the only thing standing between him and a return to But this father isn’t alone in David Brooks, in his recent New York Times op-ed, entitled Children Need to Be Back in School Tomorrow (January 28, 2021), takes aim at teachers and suggests that teachers and their unions are willfully adding suffering to a year of national misery. Framing the issue of reopening schools in such simplistic terms – that it’s just about what teachers want – lends credence to a growing effort to blame teachHere’s what Brooks doesn’t understand – and what all parents need to know. The situation of reopening schools is complicated, and here’s what teachers would Kids and teachers gather together while exchanging ideas. tell you, if they could: Teachers would tell you that most school buildings are old, cramped, and poorly ventilated. No business or restaurant on the planet would be allowed to operate at full capacity in a setting as poorly designed as the average public school. Teachers would tell you that there isn’t enough room in the average school hallway to have students come and go at the same time safely without military-style precision. Teachers would tell you that the last people in the world who are capable of military-style precision are children, and that for the most part they simply can’t behave in advance of their developmental stage. This means children can’t not get squirrely, they can’t not be impulsive, they can’t not touch each other just for the fun of it. I supervised teenagers just last week and several of them inadvertently touched each other because they wanted to share something on their phones. Teachers spend every day with groups of children in schools, and as a result they know the limitations of school settings and childhood behavior better than anyone. Period. I encourage all parents to spend a moment thinking about one of your child’s favorite teachers, maybe the one who taught them to read, or to spell their name, or to do a geometry proof; the teacher who encouraged your child to stretch beyond what they thought was possible, and who praised them when they did. Imagine the teacher who wiped your child’s nose, hugged them when they fell in the playground, and taught them the beauty of poetry. Teachers want to return to schools. They want to be with your children. They want to return to the work that they love. They just want to be safe. That’s all. So, parents, please don’t be angry at teachers. They are not the enemy – they are your greatest ally. Teachers are the people who will be there for you and your children on the other side of this tragedy, to help pick up the pieces and heal. I know for a fact that teachers can’t wait to safely return to schools and do what they do best: help raise your children. This parent was livid that school isn’t open, and his anger was directed squarely at teachers. Apparently, he sees teachers as the only thing standing between him and a return to normal life. They are not. But this father isn’t alone in seeing teachers as the enemy. David Brooks, in his recent New York Times op-ed, entitled Children Need to Be Back in School Tomorrow (January 28, 2021), takes aim at teachers and suggests that teachers and their unions are willfully adding suffering to a year of national misery. Framing the issue of reopening schools in such simplistic terms – that it’s just about what teachers want – lends credence to a growing effort to blame teachers for our current situation. Here’s what Brooks doesn’t understand – and what all parents need to know. The situation of reopening schools is complicated, and here’s what teachers would As we return to school, thanks to our teachers By Sofia Meyer The COVID experience has been hard for all of us, but especially hard for students. Every morning at exactly 8:30 a.m. we would log onto our computers and talk into the screen for over two hours. Even though we “see” all of our classmates regularly on the screen, it’s strange to think that we have not assembled as an in-person class this entire school year. I am excited to go back to school and see my classmates and teacher in 3D. Before the pandemic, I probably would have been excited to be behind a screen all day, but now that I’m actually doing that, I realize that in-person school is so much better. There were definitely times during the year when I thought going back to the actual classroom was a goal that was out of reach. Now that we have worked extra hard, stayed socially distant, worn our face masks even though we probably didn’t want to, we accomplished our goal. Thank you to everyone who helped make this happen, and especially to our teachers who have been there every step of the way! Sofia Meyer is a 5th grade student at Wildwood Elementary School. articles.text: Now that we’ve put another Valentine Day behind us, let’s reflect upon this curious holiday. February 14th usually rings bells in most people’s minds because the whole world turns into Cupid’s playground. But it doesn’t work the same way for everyone. Imagine a person with a pollen allergy – it must be their worst nightmare. Everywhere I went on February 14th I saw, smelled and felt the presence of flowers. We’re talking vibrant, love-declaring, fragrant flowers everywhere – in vases, cups, mugs, bowls. To all of you who suffer from pollen allergies, may your eyes and nose rest in peace. I feel for you. By now your eyes have secreted more liquid than when you’re cutting onions, and you probably scared dozens of germaphobes by sneezing. Not only does Valentine’s day come with flowers, it also comes with chocolates. Fewer people have chocolate allergies – but that’s dangerous in a different way. The whole day is a chocoholic’s dream come true. It doesn’t matter if you are single or not, you can always go to CVS or Safeway and get enough chocolate to make your own chocolate geyser if you melt it down. articles.text: Troop 4 held a Zoom-based, socially distanced Eagle Court of Honor ceremony on January 9 to celebrate Diego Jerez and Tom Robinson having achieved the rank of Eagle, the highest rank in uniformed Scouting. It requires significant Troop involvement and leadership, earning at least 21 merit badges, 13 Eagle-required badges, and the completion of a service project. Scouts are eligible to complete the Eagle requirements prior to their 18th birthday. Jerez and Robinson have been friends for most of their lives and joined scouting together, making this a significant achievement for both. They both distinguished themselves in Troop 4 by serving as a Senior Patrol Leader (Diego), and Troop Guide (Tom). Both scouts completed an impressive number of camping nights (Diego clocked an amazing 85 nights, a Troop 4 Robinson’s project involved beautifying the playground at Maya Angelou Academy in Oakland, a school for preschool through 5th grade. The playground is dominated by a large shipping container, which looked very industrial. Robinson, with help from other Troop 4 Scouts, primed and painted the shipping container, adding color and design to make a cheerful addition to the school yard. Jerez and Robinson were the most recent Scouts from Toop 4 to attain the rank of Eagle during the past year. Other Eagles included Roman Rodriguez, Brian Cain, Jack Blodgett, Jonathan Wu, Kevin Blodgett and Gavin Horne. Jerez is a freshman at UC Santa Barbara, and Robinson is in his first year at the Univeristy of Wisconsin in Madison. If your son or daughter is interested in being involved with a scouting troop that is safely active in the time of COVID with a long record of scouts achieving the rank of Eagle, please contact Sarah King (sarahdmertz@ yahoo.com) to learn more about Troop 4. Eagle Scouts Diego Jerez (left) and Tom Robinson at the Eagle Court of Honor. record) and hiking many miles. They both participated in Troop 4’s rigorous annual 50-mile backpacking trips. Jerez’s Eagle project involved building two storage benches and a wetsuit rack for Alameda Community Sailing Center. The storage benches hold backpacks for students while they sail and do double duty as seating. The wetsuit rack has wheels so the wetsuits can be moved from location to location Diego Jerez’s mobile rack for surfing wetsuits. Storage boxes were built as part of Diego Jerez’s Eagle Project. Members of Troop 4 add a festive, colorful design to a shipping container at Maya Angelou Academy.

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Council BSA tuned in this past Sunday to watch the national Be The Change event, where the inaugural class of female Eagle Scouts was showcased. Girls were welcomed into the Scouts BSA program, formerly Boy Scouts of America, in Spring 2019. The prestigious rank of Eagle Scout is the ultimate milestone of this program and girls have begun earning the rank of Eagle Scout. One of the members of the class, Kendall Jackson of Illinois, noted “My mom is a Scoutmaster, so I was just always around. Now that I am officially an Eagle Scout, I am ecstatic to be a part of something so historic and be a part of the first class. It’s never something I thought I would ever be able to do.” Though Piedmont did not have Eagle Scouts represented, Piedmont Scouts on Sunday watched the ceremony in awe. Mollie King of Piedmont’s Troop 4, said she was inspired by Kendall Jackson’s Eagle project, which involved conducting a workshop for high school seniors on financial responsibility and time management. “I thought this was really cool because I think a lot of people forget that Boy Scouts of America is about more than outdoor skills - it challenges youth to be bration made me feel like we are a part of something bigger and a part of something important. Their successes impact everyone in the Scouting community.” The Piedmont Scout Council is excited to know that one day it will welcome Piedmont’s first female Eagle Scout. She will join over 1200 youth who have earned the rank of Eagle since the Council was founded in 1921. This year marks the Piedmont Council’s 100-year anniversary. Yearlong festivities will be kicked off with a virtual auction starting on March 17. The Council’s 100th annual Recognition Dinner will follow one week later, on March 25. For event details, see: www. piedmontbsa.org/. Eagle Scouts Facts • In 1912, the first Eagle Scout class in the U.S. included 23 Eagle Scouts. In 1982, the 1 millionth Scout earned the Eagle Scout award. In 2020, more than 46,044 Scouts attained the rank of Eagle. There are nearly 1,000 female Eagle Scouts in the inaugural class. In 2020, more than 5 million service hours were provided by Scouts to local communities. An Eagle Scout celebrates being part of the inaugural class of female Eagle Scouts in the national Scouts BSA organization. innovators, humanitarians and leaders,” said King. CBS Evening News Anchor Norah O’Donnell congratulated the class, noting, “As the very first female Eagle Scouts, you’ve set a high bar. You’ve learned that you can create something new, that you can bring communities together, and make them better. Be prepared is great advice that will help you make a difference in this world. In the end, you change the world. That’s pretty remarkable. Our country needs people like you to lead us into a bright future”. Capt. Amy Bauernshmidt, the first female to command a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, remarked, “Be the change you want to be. Robinson, with help from other Troop 4 Scouts, primed and painted the shipping container, adding color and design to make a cheerful addition to the school yard. Girls were welcomed into the Scouts BSA program, formerly Boy Scouts of America, in Spring 2019. The prestigious rank of Eagle Scout is the ultimate milestone of this program and girls have begun earning the rank of Eagle Scout. One of the members of the class, Kendall Jackson of Illinois, noted “My mom is a Scoutmaster, so I was just always around. Now that I am officially an Eagle Scout, I am ecstatic to be a part of something so historic and be a part of the first class. It’s never something I thought I would ever be able to do.” Though Piedmont did not have Eagle Scouts represented, Piedmont Scouts on Sunday watched the ceremony in awe. Mollie King of Piedmont’s Troop 4, said she was inspired by Kendall Jackson’s Eagle project, which involved conducting a workshop for high school seniors on financial responsibility and time management. “I thought this was really cool because I think a lot of people forget that Boy Scouts of America is about more than outdoor skills - it challenges youth to be bration made me feel like we are a part of something bigger and a part of something important. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

Worse, Paris may be experiencing a third wave of Covid-19 with the spreading United Kingdom mutant dubbed the UK-variant. France continues to enforce curfews and ban international travel with no end in sight, though England is predicting some normalcy by mid-May. For now, Paris parks are open, and as the days gently warm, there are greenbelt options to get some fresh air while practicing social distancing. Paris, though not ranked in the world as a green city, has more than 400 parks. Jardin des Serres d’Auteil is a secret garden of greenhouse exotics at the southern tip of Bois de Boulogne. The Jardin des Plantes, the city’s vast botanical garden whose roots took hold for apothecary herbs to treat the Renaissance royals, is a top choice. On its grounds are the National Natural History Museum and academies for botany, mineralogy, and geology, while the gardens and natural history museum are a magnet for energetic children on school tours. La Coulée Verte, from the Bastille to Bois de Vincennes A high line park was built atop an obsolete railway spur from the Place de la Bastille to Bois de Vincennes, and since its opening in 1993 is a popular greenway. If the idea of converting an elevated Aligre market between Bastille and Nation plazas is a good place to pick up fresh produce, meat, fish, deli, and charcuterie before trail walking or afterwards to carry home for dinner. train line into a parkway seems familiar, the New York City High Line was inspired by the Paris trail and opened in 2007, running from the meatpacking district to 34th Street. The stairway entrance to this Paris elevated parkway is at the back of the Opéra Bastille along Rue de Lyon. The park, called the “green river”, is not an exact translation of La Coulée Verte. And earlier moniker was Promenade Plantée (the planted promenade). The walkway is a mile and a half of easy strolling through an assorted green trail of paths laden with roses, plantings, and flower gardens, wild greenery, a short canal. At varying locations, it branches into wider spaces with bench seating. Further along, the pathway narrows over the Jardin de Reuilly and snakes downhill to street level for bicyclists and walkers who will arrive at the entry to Bois de Vincennes in another mile and a half. Trail walkers may wish to bring food and drinks on sunny days and choose a scenic spot to picnic at Reuilly park. A favorite Bastille location, Marché d’Aligre with open stalls and covered counters stacked with produce and fresh foods, is open six days a week. A lot of the trail fun is the sheer elevation – walking on a raised platform places you eye to eye with the third or fourth level of buildings. One is peering over the railings at street intersections and gazing at apartments with glimpses of balconies and people walking below: it’s an urban adventure. The Opéra Bastille that opened to grand fanfare in 1989 was built on the spot that Gare de la Bastille occupied from 1859 to 1969. This second opera house designed for the Paris general populace is immense in size, holding: 2,745 seats; a 500-seat amphitheatre; a 230-seat studio theatre; set and costumes workshops; rehearsal rooms; and offices. Controversy has dogged the project including criticism about “disappointing” acoustics. Once you reach Reuilly, it’s decision-time with a half dozen options. From here you can take the stairs to street level to the Viaduc des Artes and stroll by workshops, cottage businesses, cafés, and retailers along Avenue Daumesnil, where the walk returns strollers to the Bastille. More options open when you decide to walk the entire Coulée Verte and reach the Bois de Vincennes. One may alternately catch the 46 bus on Avenue Daumesnil headed south and ride the mile and a half to the park. Vincennes is the largest park in Paris with crisscrossing foot trails clocking some 50 miles in length. Bicycle trails are also abundant. At the entry to Vincennes, Palais-Porte Dorée is an intriguing museum full of curiosities from the time of the French Colonial Gare de la Bastille, about 1900. The railroad spur to Bois de Vincennes ended in 1969.

articles.text: Makenna Thiel, a state ranked player, will return to the Piedmont tennis team for her senior year. The season, historically played in the fall, will take place this spring over the next two months due to COVID-related scheduling complications. “I’m looking forward to being on the team again. It’s definitely much different than the other seasons but I’m looking forward to the fun experience,” said Thiel, who travels extensively to tournaments often out of state. She has committed to play for UC Berkeley next year. “Makenna’s going to play. We talked her into it!” said veterans PHS tennis coach Jim Landes with a laugh. The team will have its two most ardent fans as coaches this spring, with both Landes and his predecessor, Hall of Fam coach Neil Rotenberg. “Having both coach Jim and coach Neil will be awesome,” exclaimed Thiel. Coach Neil hasn’t been able to coach me yet, so I know it’s going to be a great experience. When deciding to play on the team, he was a big factor. He helped me out a lot when I was first getting into tennis. He’d hit with me every Wednesday when I got out early from elementary school,” she added. Rothenberg notably was the will be over by April 17. “I wasn’t aware of what the season was going to look like, but I was going to play regardless. It’s my senior year and I’ve already committed to a college, so I don’t need to travel as often.” “I’m excited to be back on the Piedmont team,” said Thiel. For the 2021 season, the Western Alameda County Conference has said that coaches will be allowed to create their own format prior to match day. There’s even a possibility of having co-ed mixed doubles this season. articles.text: Members of the PHS mountain bike team practice riding the Long Course of the Piedmont MTB Classic. Piedmont High School’s mountain bike team will host its first Piedmont MTB Classic race in March. Registration is now open. All proceeds will support the team, which is a club sport with no financial support from the high school. The event will take place over two weeks, March 7-21, so that riders can independently participate in the equivalent of time trials. Each participant will record his or her time on designated trail segments using the Strava app, and prizes will be awarded for the fastest riders in four categories: • Middle School • High School • Adult • Overall There are two options for each race, Short Course and the Long Course. The short course covers roughly 9 miles of trail with an elevation gain of approximately 900 feet. The Long Course is 15 miles with 2,500 feet of elevation gain. The cost to participate is $40. Race proceeds will be used to purchase a team trailer to help transport equipment to races. It will be dedicated to Lynden McLaughlan, a team coach who passed away unexpectedly in 2019. To sign up for the Classic and learn more about the race and the team, go to www.Piedmontmtb.com.
articles.title: Piedmont Mountain Bike Classic to take place in March

In Piedmont, this pushes sports like lacrosse, baseball, softball, and football into midMarch, while soccer and water polo aren’t likely to start until after April 19. For football, this comes after the sport was considered an Orange Tier athletics event, clearing the way for North Coast Section schools to complete their seasons by April 17. They will have a five-game season from March 19 to April 16, meaning there will be no post-season. “They’ve been hard-pressed to have a five-game season. We’re excited about that and anything else is just gravy. We’d just appreciate a heads up to get prepared for the appropriate plan,” said PHS football coach Jerome Johnson. Football is set to get its season underway the week of Friday, March 19 with a home game against Castro Valley. They will need to accomplish at least 14 days of practice before competing in a game. Athletes must have 10 individual days of practice in order to play – a far cry from the usual summer-long offseason festivities. The issue, however, comes with COVID-19 testing. Football and water polo will require weekly virus screenings. This means that football programs throughout the state, with extensive groups of volunteer coaches, must find a way to get tested and remain safe. “There are a lot of volunteers that need to be considered in the process… Outside the scope of the district, I’d like everyone to know that we have volunteers coming in who are extremely dedicated with a non-salary position to coach. We’d like to have more input and have our state officials be more considerate of our time,” added Johnson. Smet affirms that testing will be provided by the state, but the school is waiting for a solid commitment in writing from the California Department of Public Health. “The kids and coaches will have to be tested weekly for football and water polo. Testing will be paid for by the California Department of Public Health. However, we haven’t gotten an official confirmation from the state yet on how we are facilitating testing. Are we paying for it and getting reimbursed? We’re still waiting to find out,” he added. Another issue is the schedule of practices. Lacrosse, for instance, has yet to begin full-speed, game-simulation style practices. “It’s my understanding that March 1 is the magic date for full-on contact practices. Up to this point we’ve done very non-contact and very non-defense drills. We want to make sure this feels right. We’ve really only had four days where we’ve been allowed to pass,” said Piedmont girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan. The team initially planned to have its season start on March 3 against Washington HS of Fremont and March 10 against Oakland Tech, but neither school is fielding a team. “Another issue is playing against some of these schools with first-year lacrosse teams. We’re scheduling some team meetings just to talk about how the season is going to go,” said Chan. There is also a question of how games will be officiated and scored. “We don’t know how the reffing will look and if parent volunteers on the field can be there. We know about no huddles and no high-fives, but are there other types of masks we have to wear? We want to make sure we cover everything,” said Chan. It is possible that both lacrosse teams (boys and girls) could fill empty spots on their schedule with non-league matches. “I know Bradley [Smet] is doing the best he can to find field space in order for us to have nonleague games at home,” said Chan. “Miramonte even reached out to us about playing on March 1.” Baseball and softball appear to be planning on 10-game seasons starting Wednesday, March 17 and going until April 16. Soccer teams now have the green-light to return after April 19 following the tennis, baseball, softball, football, and running seasons. Gavin Newsom there won’t be any costly overlap between popular sports that prevents some kids from competing in multiple sports. “We start later in April and that helps a few kids who want to play multiple sports. For example, the boys’ side has a lot of football players who would have had to choose,” explained girls’ soccer coach Dan Chubbock. However, the back and forth between the California Interscholastic Federation representing high schools and club sports not affiliated with schools has been an ongoing problem, claiming that athletes should not or cannot compete on a club team and high school team at the same time. Ironically, club soccer is the very backbone of the best high school soccer programs in the U.S. The CIF initially rescinded its rule against kids playing club and school sports simultaneously last May, then rescinded its ruling – twice. Did someone say Recal? “The CIF changed their policy again on club and high school sports but the county only allows one cohort. By the time games actually start for soccer, I’m hopeful that the kids will be able to do both. I’m still hopeful that there will be some coordination between club and high school soccer in order to fit season. It’s all about giving kids the most opportunities possible in a safe manner,” mentioned Chubbock. Soccer would host an eightgame season after April 19 with a potential for a league championship game. The girls’ soccer program would play the four schools within the Foothill Division: Bishop O’Dowd, Castro Valley, Berkeley, and Alameda. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross-country teams return to competition this week with a meet on Saturday, February 27 at Dublin High. Other top-level schools entered in the race include Bellarmine Prep and St. Francis of Mountain View from the Peninsula, Livermore, Foothill (Pleasanton) and host Dublin. The meet came quite suddenly for Piedmont after initially being slated for a virtual format. That was scrapped when East Bay MUD announced on Monday this week that it cannot host a cross country event at San Pablo Reservoir. But Piedmont coach Jeanine Holmlund had the presence of mind to respond upon seeing an e-mail invitation from Dublin High School. “I had been working on a permit for a trail at San Pablo Dam and was making headway, but they decided that it wasn’t consistent with they were telling their recreation advisors for their boat launch and other facilities, so East Bay MUD said no on Monday. On the same day, this invitation fell into our laps,” she said. “I got an email from Chris Williams from Dublin asking if we’d like to be in this meet. I said, ‘Yes! We’d love to be in it!’ as quickly as possible. It’s super cool,” added Holmlund. The meet will host 227 runners. The school said its course can safely allow 100 runners at the same time, beginning with socially-distanced teams at the starting line. The meet will have separate races for Varsity, Junior Varsity, and Frosh-soph teams. Holmlund and the PHS Athletic Department have another two weeks to finalize locations for the next two meets, on March 13 and March 27. But both East Bay Regional Parks and East Bay MUD have said that using parks for cross-country events is unfeasible due to the increased foot traffic in local parks during COVID-19. Piedmont runners are anxious to begin running again, and Holmlund has a solid group of experienced varsity girls and a squad of boys with a lot of depth and competition amongst the team. “We’ve got a pack of girls who are all closely running together, but I won’t know who my front-runner is for sure until I see a race. The kids never like to race each other and always do well in competitive settings,” she said. Ellie Black returns as a junior after being named the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2020, helping the squad qualify for its eighth consecutive State Meet/ She will be joined by seniors Aya Troyer, Adri McAuliffe, and juniors Molly McWeeny, and Mara Lovric. The boys’ team has perhaps the most depth of teams in recent years. Collin Mortimer, Seamus Chamberlain-Carr, and Parker Long are back. Jack Stein has moved up quite a bit from last year and is looking good. Rowen Connelly is running well; Christian Taylor is a sophomore who worked super-hard last season and is improving steadily,” said Holmlund. “We have 11 runners who are running really tight times together, I don’t know if I’ve ever had this amount of depth,” she said. Photo by Gary Zalewski Junior Seamus Chamberlain-Carr (right) returns for his third year as a varsity runner.
articles.title: Preview of school’s first sport to return to competition

articles.text: The Warriors sit in 8th place after defeating the New York Knicks yesterday 114-106. They cling to a 17-15 record with five games left before the All-Star Break. Still looking for a three-game win streak, Golden State fell to lesser ranked Eastern Conference foes, the Orlando Magic 124-120, and Hornets 102-100 without Stephen Curry. But both Curry and rookie center James Wiseman – and forward Kevon Looney – played in last night’s win against New York. Looking ahead, they play the East’s No. 4 Pacers today at 4:30 p.m. They have a return game with the Hornets on Feb. 26, before challenging playoff Western Conference foes ahead of the break: the Lakers (Feb. 28), Blazers (Mar. 3), and Suns (Mar. 4). With Steph in the lineup, the Warriors could put together their first three-game win streak of the season.
articles.title: Warriors still hovering at 8th

articles.text: Saying Tottenham and manager Jose Mourinho are in hot water may be a bit of an understatement. The water is boiling, and the reported dysfunction within the Spurs’ organization has fans looking at Tottenham chairman Daniel Levy as the bad guy. 24 games into the Premier League’s 38-match season, the Hotspur sit in 9th with a 10-6-8 record after holding first place in early December. Reports from The Athletic and NBC Sports emerged that Mourinho could have until the end of the season before getting the boot, with Germany’s RB Leipzig manager Julian Nagelsmann seen as the leading candidate for the job. However, reputable Football.London reporter Alisdair Gold retorted that Mourinho is viewed as a “long term project” and will stick around. An early sacking of Mourinho would cost Tottenham $30 million in order to honor his contract. The organization is a reported billion-euros in the hole after building its new stadium and COVID-19 rendering teams without attendance, so can a team with revenue issues afford another coach only two years into his contract? For Mourinho, winning the Europa League could be the last drawing point for the manager. That will be a tough task with Manchester United, Leicester City, Ajax, AC Milan, and Napoli in competition. Premier League to watch this week: Manchester City vs. West Ham (Sat, Feb. 27, 4:30 a.m.), Leicester City vs. Arsenal (Sun, Feb 28, 4:00 a.m.), Chelsea vs. Man. United (Sun, Feb 28, 8:30 a.m.), Everton vs. Southampton (Mon, Mar 1, 12 p.m.) Photo courtesy of the Evening Standard Tottenham manager Jose Mourinho is in hot water with his team in 9th place.
articles.title: Tottenham manager in hot water?

articles.text: International violinist Dmitry Sitkovetsky. Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players will present a concert this Sunday, February 28, featuring legendary violinist Dmitry Sitkovetsky and his work with the Sphinx Orchestra. The virtual concert will feature a rare personal exploration of his career, including his work as a soloist and as founder of the New European Strings Orchestra. Sitkovetsky has worked closely with Sphinx Orchestra founder Aaron Dworkin to mentor emerging musicians. The Sphinx Orchestra is a Detroit-based national organization dedicated to transforming lives through the power of diversity in the arts. Stikovetsky has selected two of the musicians to perform for Gold Coast Chamber audiences. This weekend’s performance includes Xavier Foley (double bass) and Sterling Elliot (cello). The program includes music by Ceasar Franck, Luigi Dallapiccola, Bach, Foley, and Rouhollah Khaleghi. Sitkovetsky, a resident of New York City and London, appeared in a solo concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on September 15, 2019. The concert will be streamed live via YouTube live at 4 p.m. on Sunday, February 28. The concert link will remain active for one week following the performance date. A Zoom after-party will take place, and Elliott and Foley will join patrons to answer questions and socialize. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s digital program of “Let’s Begin at the End” is available for viewing through March 3. The ballet, by Dwight Rhoden, returns digitally following its success at the 2018 Unbound Festival. It features the music of J.S. Bach, Philip Glass, and Michael Nyman. The program continues with San Francisco Ballet Soloist Myles Thatcher, known for his signature blend of movement and social consciousness, who will showcase a new work in a world premiere. The program concludes with an archival capture of Sandpaper Ballet, a clever tongue-in-cheek piece from San Francisco Ballet choreographer Mark Morris. Behind-the-scenes resources can be found on San Francisco Ballet’s website. To obtain tickets, visit: https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/digital-program-02/.
articles.title: SF Ballet to show Let’s Begin at the End on live stream

articles.text: San Francisco Opera House San Francisco Opera is slowly but surely signaling a return to live performances. It recently announced plans for 11 “drive-in” performances this spring season. Tickets will go on sale starting March 23. Live performances will begin with a new adaption of Rossini’s The Barber of Seville, starting April 23. It will be performed without intermission, and sung in English, with performances at the Marin Center in San Rafael. The opera also will have three performances of “The Adlers: Live at the Drive-In,” a recital by the Adler Fellow resident artists, which will be held in the open-air. In addition to its spring season, San Francisco Opera has announced it will be offering more digital content, including its “Opera is On” archive streaming series. SF Opera also is launching a series called “In Song” – 10-minute video profiles of six singers well-known to San Francisco audiences. Another series, “Atrium Sessions,” will have art songs and arias recorded in performance at the Atrium Theater. A new behind-thescenes podcast will complement the opera’s digital offerings. To purchase tickets to drive-in operas, or browse San Francisco Opera’s digital resources, visit https://sfopera.com/on-stage/.
articles.title: Tickets go on sale starting March 23

articles.text: This Sunday, February 28, the Telegraph Quartet will be featured in a performance filmed at the Noe Valley Ministry and presented by Noe Music’s Online MainStage Series. The Telegraph Quartet, Eric Chin and Joseph Maile (violins), Pei-Ling Lin (viola), and Jeremiah Shaw (cello), will perform Korngold’s String Quartet No. 3 and Brahms’ String Quartet in A minor, Op. 51 No. 2. It will be followed by a live question and answer and discussion with the musicians and Noe Music Artistic Directors Meena Bhasin and Owen Dalby. The performance video will be sent to registered ticket holders and available to watch until March 7. The Quartet was founded in 2013 with a passion for standard chamber music repertoire and contemporary, non-standard works alike. Recent and Telegraph Quartet to perform recorded concert on Sunday upcoming highlights include the group’s debut on the Lincoln Center Great Performers series, a concert with acclaimed composer-vocalist Theo Bleckmann at San Francisco Performances, and performances at Gretna Music, Friends of Chamber Music, Morris Museum, Mill Valley Chamber Music Society, Chamber Music Houston, and Chamber Music Society of Utica. Sunday’s performance will begin at 7 p.m. For tickets, visit www.noemusic.org/winter2021/ telegraph-quartet.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The Old Man & the Gun is billed as Robert Redford’s farewell role. And what a wonderful tip of the hat it is. It’s an easygoing, amiable crime comedy, of sorts – not laugh-out-loud comedy but filled with moments that create a long-lasting smile because of its sheer enjoyment. Redford portrays Forrest Tucker, a fedora-wearing oldster who happens to be a bank robber (and a prison escape artist). Every frame of the film, set in the early 1980s, has an old-timey feel to it, most shot in soft sepia tones. The look of it is a perfect fit for Redford and cast. Robert Redford and Sissy Spacek star in The Old Man & The Gun. The film opens in a small town inside a small bank. Forest walks up to the manager and with a smile explains that he’s not there for a loan or to make a deposit. He’s there to rob the bank. Flashing his gun in his waistband, he asks politely, still smiling, for the cash on hand. He is so pleasant, so gentlemanly that those he robs describe him in endearing terms. Getting what must be his second or third wind, Forrest cuts a crime-spree bank-heist swath across the Southwest. Clearly, he feels more alive than anything else and more himself when strolling into and then out of a bank with an old, worn briefcase full of teller cash. On his way home from one such “job” he stops to help a woman, Jewel (Sissy Spacek), who is having car trouble. Offering her a ride home, they make a stop for a cup of coffee. And, like everyone else that Forrest meets, she takes a liking to him. Ditto detective John Hunt (Casey Affleck), who is determined to catch up with not only Forrest but with his two partners in crime (Danny Glover and Tom Waits). What makes this film exceptional is how it allows the audience to be completely on Forrest’s side. As well, the small ember of a romance between Jewel and Forrest rings true – from their first coffee shop chat and then, later, when he tells her he’s a bank robber. She laughs and says something to the effect, “Yeah, right.” Perhaps she believes him; however, he is genuinely likable and good company. Redford is now age 82. In this role he aces Forrest Tucker like he’s slipping into a much-washed flannel shirt. It’s not a stretch for Redford to inhabit this sly old guy whose face is deeply lined but filled with good intentions. As Forrest, he exudes style and integrity. Clearly, it’s not about the money. As well, the movie is filled with small moments. One scene I found so very charming was when there was a quick cut from Forest being chased by the police to three kids with an old paint Robert Redford protrays bank robber Forrest Tucker in The Old Man & The Gun. can, painting a fence, just around the corner from the bank. Then it was back to the cops and Forrest. Just great stuff and confident filmmaking. Bottom line, it’s Redford and Spacek who create the unadorned delight of this film. They react to one another with warmth and caring, leavened by years of life experience, conveying their characters’ hidden loss, absent even a hint of the maudlin. If this is truly Redford’s adios, then he has chosen a small gem of a film to frame his exit. So nice. But I do hope he reconsiders. The Old Man & the Gun. Directed by David Lowry. Starring Robert Redford, Sissy Spacek, Casey Affleck and Danny Glover. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: A scene from An American Tail. Movie review by Chris Honoré An American Tail, directed by Don Bluth, was the second feature by the Bluth studio, following The Secret of Nimh. Like NIMH, it’s a wonderfully animated adventure film, layered with award-wining songs and focused on a 7-year-old mouse named Fievel Mousekewitz. The year is 1885, and Fievel’s journey begins in Russia where his family – Papa Mouskevitz (Nehemiah Persoff), Mama Mousekevitz (Patricia Vohn), and Tanya Mousekevitz (Amy Green) – is attacked by Cossacks and cats and their home burned down. Fleeing Russia, they managed to board a tramp steamer on its way to America, where they believe there are no cats. During a thunderstorm, Fievel is separated from his family and washed overboard. His family is distraught, believing that Fievel is lost forever. Actually, remarkably, he is safely ensconced in a bottle, and washes up in the harbor of New York City where his quest to find his parents begins. Little Fievel is a stranger in a strange land, feeling very alone in a teeming city of tenements, yet determined to find his mother and father and sister. Safely on the dock, he firsts meets a French pigeon, Henri (Christopher Plummer), who takes him under his wing, so to speak. But he is only the first in what will be a rich cast of characters from a variety of countries. What he quickly learns is that there are indeed cats in America and one is named Tiger (Dom DeLuise) who befriends him. But there are also conniving rats, one called Warren T. (John Finnegan) who actually taking Fievel to a sweat shop where he is forced to work until he manages to escape with the help of an Italian mouse, Tony Toponi (Pat Musik). And so the quest continues. Fievel runs into the Mott Street Maulers, a take no prisoners gang of cats. In conflict with them is Gussie Mouseheimer (Madeline Kahn),a rich and domineering mouse. Meanwhile, Fievel’s parents grieve for their small son, convinced he couldn’t possibly have survived; however, it is only Tanya who insists that her brother is alive, telling her parents that she can feel it. The plot is a bit convoluted (perhaps busy is a better word) as Fievel makes his way from one close call to the next, with cat chases galore, always pushing forward, ever convinced that he will soon be reunited with his family. An American Tail is a compelling, at times a softly harrowing adventure, one that will capture the attention of a young audience who will be captured by the escapades of a small Russian mouse. An American Tail (1986). Animation. Directed by Don Bluth. With the voices of Philip Glasser, Dom DeLuise and Amy Green. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated G.
articles.title: The story of a Russian Mouse lost in the U.S.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The Red Turtle is a breathtaking fable, written and animated by Oscar-winning Dutch filmmaker Michael Dudok de Wit in 2016, working in collaboration with Studio Ghibli, the renowned Japanese house of animation perhaps best known for creating the feature Ponyo. Note that though The Red Turtle has a PG rating and is only 80 minutes long, it is not simply kid friendly. What gives this film its emotional power is that not a single word is spoken, nor is a single word needed. In fact, the silence of the film falls away as the filmgoer is transported into a captivating story that is completely unexpected, one that gives the illusion of being slight but is instead deeply complex and almost Zen-like in its composition. The film opens with a raging, storm-tossed sea and abruptly the head of a man appears floating just above the surface, struggling to survive. He spots a capsized lifeboat and clings to it as the wind howls and the water churns. When the sun rises, the sky now clear, the man is lying on a wide sandy beach. He doesn’t stir until a small sand crab crawls up the leg of his pants and bites him. It’s then that he wakes, slowly stands, and looks around. He is alone. All he sees is ocean and a necklace of sand, finally noticing that just beyond the beach is a forest of lush green bamboo that covers the island. He searches the interior of the island and finds a fresh water lagoon in the interior. There is also fruit within reach. Following in his footsteps near the ocean’s edge is a small chorus of curious sand crabs. Days pass. The night sky is awash with stars and a soft crescent moon. Gradually the reality of his circumstances is revealed. His isolation is total. One day he imagines there is a string quartet playing on the beach. Determined to escape, using the bamboo from the forest, he builds a raft. But he barely gets beyond the breakwater sandbar when something hits his raft from below and shatters it. He is mystified, but he tries again. After more days of hard work using the plentiful bamboo, he launches into the ocean. Again, the raft is wrecked just beyond the shore. It is then that an enormous turtle with a bright red shell emerges from the deep. This time when he swims back the turtle follows, crawling awkwardly up onto the sandy beach. Angry and wracked by loneliness, his plan to escape once again ruined, he turns the massive turtle upside down and leaves it in the hot sun. What happens next is magical and I am reluctant to explain more. But suffice it to say that it is then that the narrative arc of the film is revealed. It invites the audience to step into a reverie that is so quietly offered up it can only be called a meditation on life. With a palette of vibrant and muted colors by the animators, it is all but impossible not to be drawn in, pulled, like a gentle out-going tide swirling around your ankles, the sand slipping from under your feet. The Red Turtle is a parable, in parts allegorical and archetypal, filled with moments that are profoundly moving. What is real and what is surreal is left courageously unanswered. And all that takes place as the film unfolds will linger, nudging the filmgoer to ponder its minimalist poignancy and its utter beauty. This film is the antidote to the cacophony of so many movies made for a younger demographic. But its depth, its silence, may be a bridge too far for some young viewers; it may require a patience beyond their reach. In contrast, adults will likely find The Red Turtle to be a universal story, its artistry incomparable, its humanity evocative and deeply moving. The Red Turtle (La Tortue Rouge, 2016). Animation. Directed by Michael Dudok de Wit. Produced by Studio Ghibli. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated PG. Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! articles.text: Russia is in the news a lot these days. Depending on your socio-political outlook, the slant could be favorable or unfavorable. When I was in Russia a few years ago I noticed that the people maintained a negative outlook on just about everything. They were very quick to say “nyet” despite ample evidence to the contrary. The restaurants served a wide variety of Russian food. Everything was prepared to order, and portions were large. Your food arrived at the table when it was prepared. This meant that everything arrived at different times. Dining could be a very lengthy affair; sometimes lasting about two hours. There are not many Russian restaurants in the United States. So, when I saw the Kolobok Russian food truck in Rocky’s Market parking lot on Leimert Blvd. two weeks ago, I said to myself: “let me try some of the things.“ I engaged the owner in conversation and found out she was from Piedmont. Who could have known? I selected some dessert crepes. I enjoyed my conversation with the owner and was delighted with the crepes. Kolobok later announced a special dinner for Valentine’s Day. That was all I needed. They offered a set menu and it was sumptuous, to put it mildly. My wife and I ordered two dinners. One was a salmon fillet enveloped by a flaky pastry. The English would be tempted to claim it in the name of Wellington because it is a fish version of Beef Wellington. Not since the days of the old Stagecoach restaurant in downtown San Francisco have I had anything this good. Preparing a Wellington is a very tricky thing and this one was done to perfection. The flaky pastry was perfectly browned. Other ingredients were included which only increased the delectability. The other main course was a large lamb shank braised in Georgian wine and fragrant root vegetables. The meat was delectable and ever so tender. To accompany these main courses were salads which included some smoked salmon. Even though it was a dinner for two, there was enough food to feed at least six. In considering how many people the meal could feed, the price was unbelievably low. Only one thing was missing: It was a take-out meal rather than dining in an elegant imperial dining room. It wasn’t a problem, however. We brought the food home, set the table with some nice China and poured a glass of red wine. Memories of my childhood returned when I saw that Kolobok offers stuffed cabbage. Their version was similar to what my grandmother made. My grandmother’s stuffing was entirely beef and Kolobok’s is a mixture of different meats. For quality, quantity, convenience, and price, Kolobok is a very good bet. Oh, I forgot to tell you… Kolobok is named for Russia’s national fairytale. The character is similar to the gingerbread man. I created my own version. In my version Kolobok is a cute little gourmet who ventures into the forest gathering rare and expensive mushrooms and forest berries. Instead of being eaten by the sly fox, Kolobok prepares a sumptuous dinner for his friends. What could be better? For a future treat, contact Ellen Doren, owner of Kolobok, at kolobokfood@gmail.com. Ellen Doren and Bular with their Kolobok russian food truck.
articles.title: Kolobok: Russia at its best

articles.text: This Sunday, February 28, SF Jazz will host an online panel discussion that examines the intersection of jazz and race, as well as its historical context. The discussion will be hosted by educator, author, and SF Jazz Board Trustee Claude Steele. Panelists for this discussion include four nationally acclaimed artists and writers, all with unique perspectives: • Drummer and composer Terri Lyne Carrington • Author Nate Chinen • Author and educator Angela Davis • Multi-instrumentalist and vocalist Rhiannon Giddens A question and answer forum will follow the discussion, allowing viewers to submit questions to panelists. The event will begin at 11 a.m. Jazz drummer Terri Lyne Carrington SF Jazz is a recognized international leader in jazz creation, presentation, and education, located in San Francisco’s downtown. The company explores the full spectrum of the genre, from the music’s origins in the African American community, to its diverse modern expressions around the world. This live panel discussion is a free event. articles.text: Drive-in movies continue to be shown at Fort Mason in San Francisco with an eclectic line-up of classic films and the latest 21st-century cinematic releases. Screenings are presented by and housed on Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture’s historic waterfront campus. Fort Mason Flix is a pop-up drive-in theater showing hit movies six days a week, from family favorites and cult classics to blockbusters and art house cinema. Tonight, at 8 p.m., Fort Mason will feature The Farewell, a 2019 drama directed by Lulu Wang. It is an intergenerational drama, loosely based on her own famFort Mason Drive-In theater at Fort Mason in San Francisco. ily, and follows protagonist Billi (Awkwafina) as she grapples with a fellowship rejection and the news that her grandmother Nai Nai (Zhao Shu-zhen) has terminal cancer. She also learns that her family plans to keep the diagnosis a secret from the elderly Nai Nai. As they reroute a cousin’s wedding to Nai Nai’s hometown in China, planning the celebration as a secret good-bye, Billi’s parents encourage her to maintain her own silence by staying in New York. Billi crashes the party in Changchun and struggles to keep the family’s peace. Run time of the film is 100 minutes. Social distancing guidelines must be observed, and patrons are asked to wear masks at all times when not in their car. Tickets may be purchased online at: https://fortmason.org/event/flix/.

Kolobok: Russia at its best By Joseph Gold Russia is in the news a lot these days. Depending on your socio-political outlook, the slant could be favorable or unfavorable. When I was in Russia a few years ago I noticed that the people maintained a negative outlook on just about everything. They were very quick to say “nyet” despite ample evidence to the contrary. The restaurants served a wide variety of Russian food. Everything was prepared to order, and portions were large. Your food arrived at the table when it was prepared. This meant that everything arrived at different times. Dining could be a very lengthy affair; sometimes lasting about two hours. There are not many Russian restaurants in the United States. So, when I saw the Kolobok Russian food truck in Rocky’s Market parking lot on Leimert Blvd. two weeks ago, I said to myself: “let me try some of the things.“ I engaged the owner in conversation and found out she was from Piedmont. Who could have known? I selected some dessert crepes. I enjoyed my conversation with the owner and was delighted with the crepes. Kolobok later announced a special dinner for Valentine’s Day. That was all I needed. They offered a set menu and it was sumptuous, to put it mildly. My wife and I ordered two dinners. One was a salmon fillet enveloped by a flaky pastry. The English would be tempted to claim it in the name of Wellington because it is a fish version of Beef Wellington. Not since the days of the old Stagecoach restaurant in downtown San Francisco have I had anything this good. Preparing a Wellington is a very tricky thing and this one was done to perfection. The flaky pastry was perfectly browned. Other ingredients were included which only increased the delectability. The other main course was a large lamb shank braised in Georgian wine and fragrant root vegetables. The meat was delectable and ever so tender. To accompany these main courses were salads which included some smoked salmon. Even though it was a dinner for two, there was enough food to feed at least six. In considering how many people the meal could feed, the price was unbelievably low. Only one thing was missing: It was a take-out meal rather than dining in an elegant imperial dining room. It wasn’t a problem, however. We brought the food home, set the table with some nice China and poured a glass of red wine. Memories of my childhood returned when I saw that Kolobok offers stuffed cabbage. Their version was similar to what my grandmother made. My grandmother’s stuffing was entirely beef and Kolobok’s is a mixture of different meats. For quality, quantity, convenience, and price, Kolobok is a very good bet. Oh, I forgot to tell you… Kolobok is named for Russia’s national fairytale. The character is similar to the gingerbread man. I created my own version. In my version Kolobok is a cute little gourmet who ventures into the forest gathering rare and expensive mushrooms and forest berries. Instead of being eaten by the sly fox, Kolobok prepares a sumptuous dinner for his friends. What could be better? For a future treat, contact Ellen Doren, owner of Kolobok, at kolobokfood@gmail.com. Textile artist Amanda Ward Amanda Ward has created plenty of quilts over the last eight years, but she’s excited about the big challenge ahead – the “Things That Matter” Piedmont Community Art Quilt Project that will raise support for PUSD visual and performing arts. “I’m hoping it’s going to be a ridiculous job because that means we’ll get a lot of support,” said the 39-year-old textile artist. “This will be a true community quilt.” Long intrigued by quilting, Ward didn’t get started until 2013, when she made one for her daughter’s birthday. Since then, she’s finished close to 40 quilts, with several more in progress, using her collection of vintage sheets, fabric scraps, and other textile discards. “I collect things and then pull them out and that’s the beginning of the inspiration,” she said of her designs. “Just working with what I have, working with things that might not go together. articles.text: The Community Art Quilt Project provides a creative outlet for an inclusive community conversation about “The Things that Matter” for everyone during these unique times. That can mean social justice, climate change, family, friendship, health, hope, and community. Whatever the pandemic has made you realize what matters to you, can be the theme of your piece of the quilt. Sponsored by the Piedmont Arts Fund (www.piedmontartsfund.org), the project encourages residents to create a square that will be included in the community quilt that will later be displayed in the new Alan Harvey Theatre. Make -it-yourself qui lt square packets are available for purchase through February 27. Donations help fund performing and visual arts programs in the schools. Quilt kits are available free (pay what you can with a suggested donation to PUSD). More information about the quilt kits can be found at: https://piedmontstore.org/products/thingsthat-matter-piedmont-art-community-quilt-project. “We intentionally called it an art quilt,’” said Piedmont Arts Fund co-chair Christiana Reining. “We want to invite members of the community to express themselves not just sewing, but with paints, dyes, lettering, stencils, whatever medium they prefer.” Quilt kits Quilt by Chambers family IRT-1848F-A
