articles.text: When walking through Piedmont it is interesting and fun to recognize, and try to name, the various architectural styles employed in the homes and municipal buildings in town. As we have noted previously, this is in fact a big part of the aesthetic appeal of the place – the opposite of a large tract development all of the same architectural type. There are various reasons why certain styles were (and are) chosen for a building, including response to local climate, geography, material availability, as well as simply preference or architectural fashion. To begin with, because Piedmont lies on latitude 38, the same as the Mediterranean Sea, and because many early California settlers were from that area, it is only natural that the imported culture would include architectural inspiration from the surrounding countries, primarily Spain. Like a culture’s language and art, architecture is constantly evolving, constantly changing. It must, since “new” things like automobiles, appliances and superior construction materials and methods didn’t even exist when the styles we are still emulating first came into use. Although Mission Revival, Spanish Colonial, Spanish Colonial Revival are some of the names given to sub-categories of the Mediterranean Style family, it is well to remember that even the baseline style (“Spanish”) is only a snapshot of an architecture at one point in time, itself derived from previous iterations. Confusing? It can be. Architectural scholars can spot a certain type of detail on a building and know exactly how it fits into the historical timeline, but they often disagree on a number of things, including the various labels. But back to the Mediterranean style. Although the variations share many recognizable characteristics (see photos), they all were, and continue to be, eclectic, meaning they are derived from a range of different sources. The basic Spanish architecture from which Mediterranean style Photos and Sketches by Will Adams The most common way to identify architectural styles is from the exterior. Any good work of architecture has a strong consistency between the exterior and interior design. In the Mediterranean styles, this is often reflected in high ceilings, exposed rough- hewn beams, textured plaster walls, and of course the continuation of the employment of arched openings. The floor plans are often L shaped, to form “enclosed” exterior courtyards, patios and terraces.

articles.text: Walter Schey of Piedmont passed away peacefully at home on February 18, 2021, following his beloved wife Monika in death nearly three years to the day. He was 87. Born Walter Martin Schey in Berlin, Germany on April 30, 1933, he was the son of Jewish parents Sigmund and Jenny Schey during the rise of the Third Reich. His father succeeded in getting the family to Russia before emigrating them to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 1939. Walt grew up in the Squirrel Hill community of Pittsburgh and attended the Carnegie Institute of Technology (now Carnegie Mellon) where he earned a B.S. in Chemical Engineering in 1955. He served his country as a pilot in the U.S. Air Force and received an honorable discharge in 1963. Upon graduating from the UC Berkeley School of Law in 1961, Walt took a fellowship in Munich where he met his beautiful bride, Monika, and they began a sweet courtship. Monika eventually followed him back to San Francisco, where they were married in 1963 and subsequently moved to Oakland. They relocated to Piedmont in 1975, where they raised two children: Martin (PHS Class of 1988) and Juliet (PHS Class of 1993). Walt had a long and well-rewine, especially in the cherished company of family and friends. He was a life-long reader of spy novels and religiously pored over the weekly Barron’s magazine for investment news as part of his diligent study of the stock market. Weekends often found Walt outside, as he loved to sit in the sun to read. He was a great story-teller, who relished in reciting a mischievous joke and particularly mastered the art of making eloquent toasts. Both children followed in his footsteps into the legal profession. His son Martin joined him in his law practice, forming the Schey & Schey partnership that lasted over 20 years. As Walt and Monika’s children married and started their own families, Walt took great pride in his wonderful children-in-law and five gorgeous grandchildren. Walter is survived by his son Martin and daughter-in-law Shonnon of Piedmont, and their children, Samantha and Connor. He is also survived by daughter Juliet and her husband Michael Meinert of Alamo, along with three children, Robbie, Schey and Molly. Walter is predeceased by his wife, Monika, and his parents. A private memorial will be held, and a public celebration of life will be planned at a later date when conditions allow. Walter Schey sipping a glass of fine wine. articles.text: A large, drive-through COVID- 19 vaccination clinic was opened at the Alameda County Fairgrounds in Pleasanton on Wednesday, February 17. The county hopes to offer as many as 1,000 vaccination appointments per day in the coming weeks at this location. The Alameda County Fairgrounds clinic is a joint operation between the county, Stanford Health Care-ValleyCare and Sutter Health. Sutter is opening appointments for patients 65 years and older, while Stanford Health Care– Valleycare has appointments for both senior citizens and healthcare workers. Alameda County is only scheduling appointments at the Fairgrounds for seniors and healthcare workers by invitation. Appointments will be open to other essential workers when “vaccine supply permits,” the county’s website says. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. The county says as many as 5,000 vaccine doses could be administered every day at the Fairgrounds soon. However, issues caused by disastrous winter weather around the nation has limited vaccine supply in California and many other states. “Our goal is to provide broad access to vaccine across the county, and this site is a cornerstone of our planning for the future,” said Kathleen Clanon, the Medical Director for the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency. “We are putting in place an infrastructure that provides immediate access to seniors and essential workers and allows us to scale up quickly if vaccine supply increases.” The Fairgrounds is the second large-scale vaccination operation in Alameda County. On Tuesday, February 16, the Oakland Coliseum opened as a “mega vaccination site,” the first federally funded “supersite” in the United States. On February 8, the county began vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1, as defined by the state’s eligibility framework. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. Several teachers and other staff members for the Piedmont Unified School District reported receiving vaccine doses in recent days. This entire phase of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents countywide. People in Tier 1, Phase 1A continue to be vaccinated. This phase, comprised of healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities, was the first group eligible when the first doses arrived in December. In Alameda County, Phase 1A includes an estimated 145,000 people. Both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccine being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. As of Sunday, February 21, the Alameda County Public Health Department reported that 2,736 Piedmonters have received their first dose of the vaccine. Furthermore, 924 Piedmonters have received their second dose and are now fully vaccinated. A total of 319,814 vaccine doses have been administered in Alameda County. Its Public Health Department reported that 79,893 county residents have been fully vaccinated, roughly 5 percent of Alameda County’s population. On Monday, March 15 new state guidance goes into effect that allows healthcare providers to decide whether to vaccinate individuals ages 16 to 64 with certain health conditions that leaves them more at risk to COVID-19 mortality. After Phase 1A, Phase 1B Tier 1 and people with underlying health conditions, the state has said it is moving toward “age-based prioritization” but has not provided many details about who will be eligible after these three groups. Earlier frameworks suggested that vaccination eligibility would widen significantly in the spring, but the state has not released an updated timeline. The state has administered over 7.4 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 8.8 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. Statewide, Phase 1A includes about 3 million people while Phase 1B Tier 1 includes another 12 million.
articles.title: Healthcare providers can vaccinate people with comorbidities on March 15

articles.text: The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County has dipped to 2.6 percent as of Monday, February 22, its lowest point since November 15, 2020. While positivity rates and daily new cases drop after a spike through December and January, doctors remain concerned about new coronavirus variants appearing in the Bay Area. The COVID-19 death toll in Alameda County increased to 1,200 after 78 more people died in the past week. The United States just surpassed a grim milestone – over 500,000 Americans have died of COVID-19 since the pandemic began in March of last year. Piedmont In Piedmont, only one new case was reported during the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. In total, there have been 168 cases reported in the City. Across Alameda County, 715 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, a significant slowdown week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 79,598. There have been 24,751 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,456 cases in Hayward. Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Only 11 counties in California are not in the Purple Tier, including San Mateo and Marin counties. Yesterday, Tuesday, February 23, these two counties were moved into the Red Tier, or Substantial Tier, the second-most restrictive tier according to the state system. While the positivity rate is low enough that Alameda County could move into a less restrictive tier for reopening businesses and activities, cases per day per 100,000 people in the county is 9.5. While this figure has dropped steeply over the past week, it needs to dip below 7 for the county to reopen further according to California’s current system. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,450,058 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 49,563 deaths due to the disease statewide. Health experts remain concerned that more contagious strains of COVID-19 could spread in Alameda County. Variants first identified in South Africa and Denmark have all been discovered in the county. While the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said that there is no evidence that these variants cause severer symptoms, data suggests they might spread more easily. Another variant first identified in the United Kingdom has been connected to several COVID-19 cases in Alameda County. The CDC says there is some evidence that this strain could be more deadly, but the findings are unconfirmed. However, the U.K. variant seems to spread easier and quicker.

articles.text: University of California Health (UCH) and the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) are launching an innovative data modeling consortium to ensure public health policy makers have timely, relevant analysis to support pandemic-related decision making. Berkeley Public Health’s Dr. Maya Petersen is co-chair of the new group. Petersen is an associate professor of Biostatistics and Epidemiology and Head of the Division of Biostatistics at Cal. She focuses on the development and application of novel causal inference methods to problems in health and community-based interventions. “Through this collaboration, UC researchers will be able to respond quickly to the needs of public health officials. We’ve not experienced a public health emergency of this intensity in our lifetimes, and this real-time partnership is a very tangible way in which UC is supporting its mission to the people of California,” Petersen said. The modeling consortium is a regular forum in which 150 faculty members across the University of California system, primarily in epidemiology, infectious diseases, economics, statistics, computer science, ecology, and data modeling and statistics, work with CDPH modelers and public health experts to develop information to inform the pandemic response in California. Researchers will use the platform to share results of their ongoing analyses with public health leaders to provide real-time evidence to inform decision-making. Dr. Erica Pan, the State Epidemiologist said “[CDPH’s] ability to leverage the brain-trust of the UC system in addressing critical public health challenges will have far reaching implications beyond COVID-19. This type of partnership will provide the infrastructure and model we need to not only enhance public health action for this pandemic, but for other public health priorities as well.” The group is tasked with accomplishing major legwork in the state’s fight against the current health crisis. UC investigators contributing to the consortium include: • Short-term forecasts of COVID- 19 metrics such as case rates, hospitalizations and intensive care unit occupancy; • Scenario models that quantify the likely impact of various potential public health decisions, as well as vaccine distribution strategies, therapeutic use and adherence to non-pharmaceutical interventions; • Cross-cutting health equity analytics to deepen understanding of COVID-19 disparities throughout the state; and • Economic modeling to answer questions about cost, and overall economic effects of COVID-19, such as the effect of changes to social services and benefits on hospitalizations or deaths. “The UC consortium exemplifies our State’s commitment to using science and evidence to drive our public health decision making. We are very proud to launch this academic and public health consortium. Expanding the engagement with our academic partners will improve the timeliness and relevance of evidence being generated for decision-making and proves that we can meet the challenges of this pandemic, together,” said Dr. Tomas Aragon, Director of the California Department of Public Health and adjunct professor at Berkeley Public Health.
articles.title: UC Health partners with State Dept. of Public Health to accelerate COVID data modeling

Another variant first identified in the United Kingdom has been connected to several COVID-19 cases in Alameda County. The CDC says there is some evidence that this strain could be more deadly, but the findings are unconfirmed. However, the U.K. variant seems to spread easier and quicker. ers said. On Febr uar y 18, Oakland Police Chief Armstrong announced that Officer Mae Phu would act as a Community Liaison with the Oakland Chinatown community in response to the violent attacks in the neighborhood. “It’s a good feeling that they want me to represent the community,” Phu said. “I’m here now and hopefully we can address [these] issues.” The rise in attacks has also prompted a federal response. President Joe Biden, in his first week on the job, signed an executive memorandum acknowledging that “inflammatory and xenophobic rhetoric has put Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) persons, families, communities, and businesses at risk.” Chief Bowers said that, if members of the public witness a hate crime, they should immediately call the Piedmont Police Department at 420-3000. The Alameda County District Attorney’s Office also maintains a hotline: (510) 208-4824.

articles.text: Spanish Revival architecture has many of the same basic elements (and appeal) as the Mission style except with more architectural detailing and embellishment. Seen here is the artistic ironwork common to the genre, and the more extensive ornamentation around the fenestration (door and window openings in the walls). ture is the informality. This is reflected in the relaxed asymmetry of the design, in both the plans and elevations (generally the more symmetry, the more formal the style). Another clue is the extensive use of inside/outside spaces. The “outdoor rooms” we discussed a few months ago are very common, formed by building walls and arcades, resulting in small patios, and/or large courtyards. These all have a strong connection via large doors with many lites (windows) to the interior rooms. Arched openings of windows, doors, and arcades are pervasive and normally in irregular compositions of various types and shapes, further contributing to the informality of the design. Regardless of the often subtle differences of the various subgroups, this style of architecture is generally a very casual one with warm character, well suited to the climate and attitudes of California and Piedmont. Next: Tudor Style Architecture Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com This finely proportioned Piedmont home is less rustic still, with “cleaner” (more finished) lines, additional detailing and ornamentation (classically inspired). However, it retains all of the characteristics of the Mediterranean Style buildings. I would also call this Spanish Revival. It is a beautiful work of architecture.

articles.text: Surely you have seen the magnificent stands of Coast Redwoods around Piedmont, but have you noticed the row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing along the back of the former quarry in Dracena Park? Nominated by Lyle Gordon, these beauties were designated as Heritage Trees in 2018. The Dawn Redwood, or Metasequoia glyptostroboides, is a prehistoric tree that was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in 1941 in China. Unlike Coast Redwoods, which are evergreen, Dawn Redwoods are deciduous, and shed leaves annually. They are fast growing and have delicate, feathery leaves, and distinctive, rounded cones. These trees are a wonderful part of Piedmont’s urban forest and worth seeking out on a walk or Dawn Redwoods are known for their distinctive, rounded cones. Dawn Redwoods have fastgrowing, delicate, feathery leaves. visit to the park. You can read the fascinating story of the rediscovery of the Dawn Redwood at https:// landscapearchitecturemagazine.org/2016/01/19/the-metasequoia-mystery/. The Piedmont Park Commission is now accepting nominations for 2021 Heritage Trees through March 19. To nominate a tree, visit the City’s website, http://www.ci.piedmont.ca.us/ and complete the downloadable form. The trees selected this year will be recognized at the annual Arbor Day virtual celebration on April 30. For more information, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont. ca.gov, or 510-420-3064. Amber Brumfiel is a member of the Piedmont Park Commission.

This is reflected in the relaxed asymmetry of the design, in both the plans and elevations (generally the more symmetry, the more formal the style). Another clue is the extensive use of inside/outside spaces. The “outdoor rooms” we discussed a few months ago are very common, formed by building walls and arcades, resulting in small patios, and/or large courtyards. These all have a strong connection via large doors with many lites (windows) to the interior rooms. Arched openings of windows, doors, and arcades are pervasive and normally in irregular compositions of various types and shapes, further contributing to the informality of the design. Regardless of the often subtle differences of the various subgroups, this style of architecture is generally a very casual one with warm character, well suited to the climate and attitudes of California and Piedmont. Next: Tudor Style Architecture Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com This finely proportioned Piedmont home is less rustic still, with “cleaner” (more finished) lines, additional detailing and ornamentation (classically inspired). However, it retains all of the characteristics of the Mediterranean Style buildings. I would also call this Spanish Revival. Piedmont’s Heritage Trees: Dracena Park’s Dawn Redwoods By Amber Brumfiel Surely you have seen the magnificent stands of Coast Redwoods around Piedmont, but have you noticed the row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing along the back of the former quarry in Dracena Park? Nominated by Lyle Gordon, these beauties were designated as Heritage Trees in 2018. The Dawn Redwood, or Metasequoia glyptostroboides, is a prehistoric tree that was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in 1941 in China. Unlike Coast Redwoods, which are evergreen, Dawn Redwoods are deciduous, and shed leaves annually. They are fast growing and have delicate, feathery leaves, and distinctive, rounded cones. These trees are a wonderful part of Piedmont’s urban forest and worth seeking out on a walk or Dawn Redwoods are known for their distinctive, rounded cones. Dawn Redwoods have fastgrowing, delicate, feathery leaves. visit to the park. You can read the fascinating story of the rediscovery of the Dawn Redwood at https:// landscapearchitecturemagazine.org/2016/01/19/the-metasequoia-mystery/. articles.text: Today the City of Piedmont is issuing a Request for Proposals (RFP) as the first step in the search for a Project Manager for the design and construction of a new Piedmont Community Pool. The RFP was authorized by the City Council at its meeting on February 16. A bond for $19 million, Measure UU, was approved by voters in November 2020 as the basis of funding for a new municipal pool and aquatics complex on the location of the existing pool. Since November, the city staff began structuring an internal team to ensure that the project is successful and meets community expectations, explained City Administrator Sara Lillevand. articles.text: I recently asked my congregation to give up something for the season of Epiphany. Perhaps it’s something to consider for Lent as well. I suggested that when someone asks them how they were doing, instead of responding “I’m fine”, consider a response that might be more honest. I sometimes respond, “I think I am going to make it”. This response is hopeful, maybe even a little humorous and it doesn’t scare off the person asking about your well-being. It also might present an opportunity for deeper conversation that both of you just might benefit from. You are not alone in those struggles you hide from others. I really do think I am going to make it, but recently I had to admit how much this time of isolation was impacting me. As someone trying to lead a congregation through a pandemic, I found myself coming face to face with my own tiredness. It happened in the vegetable aisle in Safeway. I dropped my grocery list on the floor and as I bent over to pick it up, discovered I was still wearing my slippers. I have never been so grateful for my mask. articles.text: Photo by Brian Mahany Do you have a favorite tree in Piedmont? One that you especially admire or that catches your eye every time you go by? For some, it is the beloved reclining Coast Live Oak in Piedmont Park pictured. This gem was designated as a Heritage Tree in 2019. The tree was nominated by brothers Will, Finn, and Max Brumfiel, who call it “The Climbing Tree.” The bark on the accessible branches is smooth from the hands of decades of children at play. The tree is visually interesting, and families take photos What else makes this tree special? The Coast Live Oak, quercus agrifolia, is a workhorse and hero of our urban forest. This California native has something for everyone. It is both fire resistant and deer resistant and has a life span exceeding 200 years. The Coast Live Oak offers a tremendous canopy of shade and its branches create an unbeatable climbing structure for It grows west of the Sierra Nevada mountain range from Mendocino County to Baja California. It typically has a manybranched trunk and reaches a mature height of between 35 and 80 feet, with a trunk diameter up In this time of climate change, the real value of this tree is its hospitality. Native oaks offer homes to hundreds of insects; in particular, pollinators like moths and butterflies. In fact, more insects call the Coast Live Oak “home” than any other tree or shrub. Now, when our pollinator population is in decline, this stalwart, faithful species is much more than pretty; it is crucial to the survival of countless insects on which we depend. Over the next few weeks, the Piedmont Post will feature brief articles and photos of Heritage Trees. Other trees include: • the grove of Eastern Redbuds at the west end of Piedmont Park off Wildwood, nominated by Lisa Kieraldo • the massive Coast Redwood in front of 71 Hazel Lane, nominated by Cindy Rafton • the four evergreen Himalayan Dogwoods that frame the entrance of City Hall, nominated by Bobbe Stehr and Mark Enea • the dense grove of 18 Coast Redwoods in the triangle at Wildwood, Nova and Magnolia Avenues, nominated by Gail Lombardi and Claire Faughnan • the Coast Redwood outside Community Hall (used as the annual holiday tree), nominated by Sue Herrick and Cameron Wolfe • a group of 10 Highland Poplars framing the backdrop of the Exedra, nominated by Jim Horner • a row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing in the former quarry at Dracena Park, nominated by Lyle Gordon • the Southern Magnolia in the median roundabout at Lexford and Hampton Road, nominated by Betsy Goodman The public is encouraged to seek out these trees to appreciate their beauty, history, and significance. By learning more about the trees that comprise Piedmont’s urban forest, the Park Commission hopes to inspire everyone to seek out special trees in the community and encourage nominations for Heritage Trees this year. Nominations will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical metrics. Nominations are welcome from everyone in the community. Trees must be on public property, such as parks, streets, and medians. After vetting by Public Works Department arborists, qualifying trees will be forwarded to the Park Commission for review and selection. Nominations are due by March 19 to City Hall. The winning trees will be announced on April 30 at this year’s Arbor Day celebration, to be held virtually. Nomination forms for Heritage Trees are available on the City’s website: www.ci.piedmont.ca.us. For more information, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont. ca.gov or 510-420-3064. articles.text: In its continuing movement to live by its own words, the City of Piedmont hired Alyssa Dykman on November 30 as its first Sustainability Program Manager. She is already reeling from a major achievement – the city’s approval of reach codes on February 1, a goal she helped achieve with extensive community outreach. As the community continues to make strides toward its ambitious Climate Action Plan, she will be tasked with leading the citywide programs and activities that advance its efforts. The Climate Action Plan is meant to be a roadmap for residents that outlines collective and individual actions to combat the climate crisis. Piedmont’s goals are especially ambitious: to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions 40 percent by 2030 and 80 percent by 2050. The creation of Dykman’s new title comes from the city’s long-standing support for sustainability issues, including Piedmont Connect, an organization that supports citizen initiatives and city efforts to build a more sustainable future. “One of the top priorities from the city’s Climate Action Plan was to invest more in staff’s capacity to pursue sustainability, and the creation of this position reflects just that,” Dykman said. Many responsibilities fit under this new title. Dykman will oversee programs and activities that pertain to environmental management and sustainability, including Alyssa Dykman the areas of climate action, clean water and solid waste collection and diversion, recycling, and more. She also serves as a liaison for external, technical, and advisory groups in these areas at the local and regional level. In Piedmont she works with all city departments to establish procedures and ensure compliance with sustainable practices. The position requires wearing a number of hats, Dykman admitted, including having a comfortable command of public engagement and education initiatives. Immediately after being hired, Dykman had to hit the ground running. She joined the city staff after the first reading of reach codes. pages.text: Wednesday, February 17, 2021 3 News Heritage Tree nominations being accepted at City Hall A city serious about sustainability Alyssa Dykman hits the ground running as Piedmont’s first Sustainability Program Manager Photo by Brian Mahany By Amber Brumfiel Do you have a favorite tree in Piedmont? One that you especially admire or that catches your eye every time you go by? For some, it is the beloved reclining Coast Live Oak in Piedmont Park pictured. This gem was designated as a Heritage Tree in 2019. The tree was nominated by brothers Will, Finn, and Max Brumfiel, who call it “The Climbing Tree.” The bark on the accessible branches is smooth from the hands of decades of children at play. The tree is visually interesting, and families take photos there all year round. What else makes this tree special? The Coast Live Oak, quercus agrifolia, is a workhorse and hero of our urban forest. This California native has something for everyone. It is both fire resistant and deer resistant and has a life span exceeding 200 years. The Coast Live Oak offers a tremendous canopy of shade and its branches create an unbeatable climbing structure for kids of all ages. It grows west of the Sierra Nevada mountain range from Mendocino County to Baja California. It typically has a manybranched trunk and reaches a mature height of between 35 and 80 feet, with a trunk diameter up to 10 feet. In this time of climate change, the real value of this tree is its hospitality. Native oaks offer homes to hundreds of insects; in particular, pollinators like moths and butterflies. In fact, more insects call the Coast Live Oak “home” than any other tree or shrub. Now, when our pollinator population is in decline, this stalwart, faithful species is much more than pretty; it is crucial to the survival of countless insects on which we depend. Over the next few weeks, the Piedmont Post will feature brief articles and photos of Heritage Trees. Other trees include: • the grove of Eastern Redbuds at the west end of Piedmont Park off Wildwood, nominated by Lisa Kieraldo • the massive Coast Redwood in front of 71 Hazel Lane, nominated by Cindy Rafton • the four evergreen Himalayan Dogwoods that frame the entrance of City Hall, nominated by Bobbe Stehr and Mark Enea • the dense grove of 18 Coast Redwoods in the triangle at Wildwood, Nova and Magnolia Avenues, nominated by Gail Lombardi and Claire Faughnan • the Coast Redwood outside Community Hall (used as the annual holiday tree), nominated by Sue Herrick and Cameron Wolfe • a group of 10 Highland Poplars framing the backdrop of the Exedra, nominated by Jim Horner • a row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing in the former quarry at Dracena Park, nominated by Lyle Gordon • the Southern Magnolia in the median roundabout at Lexford and Hampton Road, nominated by Betsy Goodman The public is encouraged to seek out these trees to appreciate their beauty, history, and significance. By learning more about the trees that comprise Piedmont’s urban forest, the Park Commission hopes to inspire everyone to seek out special trees in the community and encourage nominations for Heritage Trees this year. Nominations will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical metrics. Nominations are welcome from everyone in the community. Trees must be on public property, such as parks, streets, and medians. After vetting by Public Works Department arborists, qualifying trees will be forwarded to the Park Commission for review and selection. Nominations are due by March 19 to City Hall. The winning trees will be announced on April 30 at this year’s Arbor Day celebration, to be held virtually. Nomination forms for Heritage Trees are available on the City’s website: www.ci.piedmont.ca.us. For more information, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont. ca.gov or 510-420-3064. By Allyson Aleksey In its continuing movement to live by its own words, the City of Piedmont hired Alyssa Dykman on November 30 as its first Sustainability Program Manager. She is already reeling from a major achievement – the city’s approval of reach codes on February 1, a goal she helped achieve with extensive community outreach. As the community continues to make strides toward its ambitious Climate Action Plan, she will be tasked with leading the citywide programs and activities that advance its efforts. The Climate Action Plan is meant to be a roadmap for residents that outlines collective and individual actions to combat the climate crisis. Piedmont’s goals are especially ambitious: to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions 40 percent by 2030 and 80 percent by 2050. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will hold a public forum on homelessness on March 2. Margot Kushel, MD, the Director of the UCSF Center of Vulnerable Populations and the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital, will present her latest research on solutions to “Housing the Homeless in the Time of COVID-19”. Her research aims to prevent and end homelessness and mitigate the effects of housing instability on healthcare outcomes. Dr. Kushel works with diverse stakeholders to implement programmatic and policy changes based on her research. She is the primary investigator of several multi-year studies on homeless populations in the Bay Area from 2012 to the present. The discussion will take place on Tuesday, March 2 from 4:00 to 5:00 p.m. and will be available on YouTube at: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg/featured. To register, click on lwvpiedmont. org and get the Zoom information on the League’s website. The program is free and open to the public. Dr. Kushel is a practicing general internist at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital. Margot’s research examines the causes and consequences of homelessness and housing instability, with the goal of preventing and ending homelessness and ameliorating the effects of homelessness on health. She has appeared at the local, state and national level about homelessness, and provides testimony to legislative bodies. She received her AB from Harvard College, her MD from Yale and completed residency, chief residency and fellowship in internal medicine at UCSF.
articles.title: LWV to host meeting on homelessness

articles.text: Kay Chesterfield, Inc. is a furniture reupholstery business with deep Piedmont roots. Like so many businesses, they are fighting to survive the coronavirus pandemic. The market for reupholstering furniture has swayed dramatically. Businesses no longer prioritize the furnishing of indoor spaces since there are limited indoor customers. To stay in business, owner Kriss Kokoefer had to adapt their work to focus on residential clients. Kokoefer bought the company in 2013 from long-time owners and Piedmont residents John and Jo Anne Jones. Kay Chesterfield, Inc. is celebrating its 100th birthday this year. Some reupholstery businesses have seen a boom in business during the pandemic, leading to long wait times of multiple months. Kay Chesterfield differs from other reupholstery business as their primary income has been from commercial clients. Without that business their lead time is down to three or four weeks once the furniture and fabrics come in. “Our commercial business is down, which makes sense because people are not in the office right now. Another big part of our business comes from hospitality and hotels, and they are pretty much hurting now, too,” Kokoefer said. Kay Chesterfield’s biggest customer has been San Francisco airport, but with travel drastically reduced, so goes Kay Chesterfield. With a smile, Kokoefer continued. “The flipside is residential sales are going crazy. People are home, and they have time to actually do home projects. Many people are sitting at home and just staring at their furniture,” she explained. Kokoefer’s business is a big operation, with 16 employees. Most upholsters work out of their garage or a small storefront and maybe have one or two employees. The Chesterfield firm is unique in that it is large enough to have project managers. Customers receive a lot of hand-holding to ensure they get exactly what they want. “Residential is not sustaining our business, however. The PPP loan helped, but we need to Kriss Kokoefer, owner of Kay Chesterfield Upholstering, stands under the iconic Kay Chesterfield sign across from the Oakland Coliseum. crawl out of the hole,” Kokoefer explained. Kokoefer started off in the industry by selling furniture but then got interested in the impact upon human health when furniture is thrown away. Furniture disposal and cleaning furniture involves toxic materials. Revamping existing chairs, couches and tables has a big impact on the health of the environment. Kay Chesterfield launched a website in January (www. kaychesterfield.com) with a shiny new slogan that sounds more like the Army: “Re-Up.” But it hits the mark on reminding businesses and individuals to focus on why reupholstering furniture is sustainable, while explaining the environmental impacts of disposing of the old pieces. Furniture waste is substantial, 9.8 million tons of furniture goes to landfills per year in the U.S. alone. Each year around two tons of old furniture pieces end up getting burned at U.S. waste sites. Two large sectional sofas produce 1.5 tons of CO2 when burned, which is equivalent to a car driving 4,000 miles. Kokoefer pointed out popular trends taking place in the world of redoing home furnishing. “People are taking something that looks like a wing chair or an antique chair and putting on modern fabric. The juxtaposition of old and new highlights that you were able to create something unique that nobody else has,” Kokoefer explained. Wools have become the en vogue fabric according to Kokoefer. Wools are inherently antimicrobial, stain resistant, and easily cleaned. Also, they have no added toxins and are biodegradable. Kay Chesterfield is located at 6365 Coliseum Way in Oakland. To contact them, call Kriss Kokoefer at 510-533-5565. A Kay Chesterfield chair manufactured in 1940 with the original label was brought in for repair and reupholstery. The renovated chair, circa 2020.
articles.title: Reupholstering firm is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year

articles.text: Did you know Mars has earthquakes? Or rather… Marsquakes? Scientists theorize that these quakes are similar to what we experience on Earth; however, it is unclear exactly what goes on beneath the surface of Mars to cause them. Volcanic activity, meteor impacts, and planetary shifting are believed to be the source, yet there is still much to learn. In order to search for an answer, scientists are using data collected from the InSight lander to reveal information about the inner-workings of the Red Planet. InSight will not only help us determine the source of the quakes but how often and severe they are as well. This information may be helpful to know since NASA is planning to send humans to live on Mars. If the planet experiences extreme quakes, it must be taken into consideration. Habitats must be built and tested against conditions like quakes in order to safely achieve long-term human survival on Mars. How do we know Marsquakes are happening? Mars is a rocky planet like Earth, so scientists can expect similar geographic phenomena to occur. By comparing satellite imagery of Mars to Earth, scientists have been searching for signs that indicate a seismic history. One such example is the magnetic striping on Mars’ southern region, which reveal that there may have been slow movement of the planet’s crust at one time. Another example is Valles Marineris, the “Grand Canyon of Mars”, which may have grown wider and deeper as quakes shook through its walls. These small but convincing indicators have led scientists to believe that Marsquakes are happening. At what rate and severity, however, is still to be determined. What could be the cause of Marsquakes? The exact cause of Marsquakes still remains a mystery. Current theory points to meteor impacts, planetary shrinkage, sub-surface shifting, or volcanic activity. Volcanic activity is likely, considering Mars is home to the largest known volcanoes in our solar system. One volcanic plateau alone contains several massive shield volcanoes, including Olympus Mons. These volcanoes could create events powerful enough to send rumblings across NASA’s InSight Mars Lander the planet when active. The current status of the volcanoes is unknown, but signs show of an active past. How are we studying Marsquakes? NASA is currently relying on their robotic lander, named InSight, to help collect data that will reveal more about the nature of Marsquakes. InSight stands for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport. This lander, which arrived on Mars in 2018, is equipped with advanced tools designed for drilling, measuring quakes, and scanning deep below the surface of Mars to study its inner core. Its mission is to help scientists learn more about the rocky planets, how they may have formed, and how they may change over time. InSight is also tracking Marsquakes. Each time the surface shakes, InSight’s seismometer (a tool that measures the shaking of a quake) collects data to send back to Earth. Scientists will use that to determine how often and how intense Mars’ quakes are. It will also determine what the source of the quakes may be, depending on the movement’s behavior, direction, and intensity. What has InSight told us so far? In December of 2020, NASA released an update, summarizing what InSight’s data has told us so far. Faint rumblings appear to be normal, with most quakes detected at a magnitude of 3.7 or below. This was surprising to scientists, who had predicted to see more. This could mean that Mars is less seismically active than predicted, or that it is simply experiencing less quakes at this time. InSight’s mission has recently been extended through December of 2022. Collecting more, long-term data will lead to a better understanding of Mars’ seismic status and interior struc-

articles.text: Editor: The past week was an exciting and uplifting one, as our youngest learners returned to beautifully decorated campuses and were welcomed back into their classrooms by smiling teachers. As chair of the Board of the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF), I want to thank our district administrators and staff, our school board members, our teachers, nurses and our dedicated and incredible parents for working through distance learning and now getting K-6 students back to the classroom safely. We should also be so proud that through our community’s generosity, PEF was able to clear out its reserves last year and make a one-time grant to the school district for $360,000 for COVID-related school safety improvements. To our donors, this means your contributions helped upgrade air ventilation systems, purchase PPE and sanitation stations, and fund additional health care staff. Additionally, our breathtaking result of $3 million raised during this year’s Giving Campaign ensures PUSD has the resources it counts on for the 2021-22 school year to ensure our students receive a stellar education. Almost 1,200 families donated; they are super stars. For more than 45 years PEF has had a single focus: to provide sustained financial support to Piedmont schools through fundraising and community engagement. No matter the issues of the day, or how lacking state and local funding for public schools may be, PEF is here to generate financial support and ensure that students receive the best education possible. We are grateful to everyone in the community who makes this possible. In a few weeks, we will launch Spring Fling. Our theme this year is Piedmont Unity: Piedmont Community. Our goal remains the same – to work together to meet the shortfall in what PUSD receives from state and local funding. We hope to fund COVID-specific district needs this year and we will certainly make Spring Fling relevant, fun, and rewarding. I’m excited to note that the middle and high schools will be included in Spring Fling this year. Please reach out to PEF at info@piedmontedfoundation. org if you’d like to get involved. This spring is a perfect time to step up, get involved with PEF, and make a difference for our schools and our community. –Nicki Gilbert, Chair, PEF Board of Directors
articles.title: Ed. Foundation steps in to help with COVID funding

articles.text: The Mars Perseverance rover will land on the red planet on Thursday, February 18 at 12:30 p.m. after a seven-month, 300-million-mile journey. Chabot Space & Science Center will celebrate the landing of NASA’s Mars Perseverance rover with a virtual watch party tomorrow, Thursday, February 18 from 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. During this historic, virtual event, guests are invited to witness the landing with Chabot astronomers and NASA experts who worked on the mission. Tune in to see the landing live on Facebook and YouTube with Chabot’s watch party at chabotspace.org/calendar/nasamars-perseverance-rover-landing-watch-party/. The Perseverance rover will make history when it touches down on the red planet at 12:30 p.m. PST. Before landing, the rover must face the “seven minutes of terror,” a complex and critical landing phase with a series of specific maneuvers. Chabot astronomers will answer questions throughout the landing and make live observations. After the landing, learn more about the mission at a virtual Q&A session with NASA scientists at 1 p.m. NASA’s Ames Research Center engineers Shanna Withrow-Maser and Winnie Kuang will discuss their roles in Mars exploration and answer questions from the public. To celebrate the rover landing, Chabot Space & Science Center is providing a variety of free Mars-themed activities, virtual events and teacher resources.
articles.title: Chabot Space & Science Center hosts watch party for Mars rover landing

articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1998 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.
articles.title: Nomination period opens for Art Hecht Award

articles.text: A panel discussion titled “Embracing Clean Energy” will be held on February 25 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. as the first of three panel discussions as part of Readmont, the annual community read in Piedmont. This year’s selection is Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate. The panelists include: • Jessica Tovar of the Local Clean Energy Alliance in Oakland, an NGO working in advocacy for clean energy. (http:// localcleanenergy.org/) • Angel Fierro, husband of Millennium HS principal Shannon Fierro and co-partner of Plexus Solutions, which joins large scale clean energy projects with capital. http://www.plexussolutions.services/leadership • Dr. Max Auffhammer, George Pardee Jr. Professor of Sustainable Development and Associate Dean in the Division of Social Sciences at UC Berkeley. He is also an Assistant Professor of Agricultural and Resource Economics and International and Area Studies at UC Berkeley and Chair at the Political Economy, UC Berkeley. (https://onpointanalytics.com/ experts/maximilian-auffhammer/) This year, Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at Piedmont High School. To register, visit piedmontconnect.org/readmont-2021. The hope is that this common reading experience will forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members. The next event will be “Youth Summit on Environmental Justice” on April 24, an event open to high school students across the Bay Area, ready to take action to preserve the planet. All Piedmonters are encouraged to read This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate by Naomi Klein. The author argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied, but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. Copies are available for checkout at the PHS library. Interested readers can contact PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us to borrow a copy. A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair Village is offering a 20% discount on this title.

articles.text: Distance learning presents impediments to all students, and for some, learning exclusively on a computer can seem all but impossible. For decades, educators at all levels have attempted to diversify how lessons are taught to account for the different ways in which students learn best. Unfortunately, with every lesson on a screen, education has become one dimensional (or 2-D at best). There’s really no substitute for on-campus, in-class learning. But until then, try getting the leftbrain involved. For students considered solitary, auditory, mathematic or visual learners, screen-based learning may be okay. Roughly 25 percent pf Piedmont families with elementary school age students have chosen to continue with distance learning. While many factors went into those decisions, it is fair to say that distance learning is tolerable for some students. Students who learn most efficiently from social, verbal and physical teaching may be struggling the most with distance learning. Using color, making artistic representations, utilizing alternative school supplies and employing music can awaken the left brain often forgotten in education. Piedmont kindergarteners went back to in-person learning last week on February 10. Much insight can actually be gleaned from the youngest learners to help older students. The joy of learning has vanished for many. An overarching goal for a tutor, beyond re-explaining course material, is to inspire passion and make education fun. Something as simple as using different color pens, or pencils can make note-taking easier and more enjoyable. In college I adopted the habit of going over my notes right after a lecture or discussion and adding comments in a different color. When looking at the notes later, Give your computer a rest and use a typewriter, like this 1920’s Corona machine. It’s fun, auditory and a tactile way to hammer out schoolwork. I would use another color. This keeps a record of how thoughts develop. Drawing picture representations in the margin of notes can really solidify material too. Having a fancy set of color pencils can make all the difference. It can be tricky to get the left brain involved in a subject like math, but it’s not impossible. Again, investing in school supplies can make all the difference. While often shunned and forgotten as archaic, writing with quill and ink, or using a vintage typewriter can bring excitement to the most droll of subjects. While cursive handwriting has been phased out of grade school education, for some, the graceful font can be just enough artistic activity to keep sentences flowing. Enliven the left brain When pre-schoolers, students, or professionals, are totally swept up in a project and just going for it, productivity is at a maximum. Often that occurs when both sides of the brain are engaged. It doesn’t take a CT scan to notice that people are the most entrenched in their tasks when creativity and the whole brain are unleashed. Music in the background can help set the right mood for studying. Classical music and jazz have a mellow cadence and the songs are long, which encourage long periods of unbroken attention without too much change. For more contemporary music fans, instrumental beats, or electronic music can accomplish the same thing. Try lowering the volume or listening to music without lyrics if tunes with vocals are distracting. Students who are musicians may want to try turning course material into songs or simply reading out loud while adding a cadence to it. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, February 17, 2021 “Embracing Clean Energy” panel discussion Feb. 25 Part of Readmont 2021, the annual community read A panel discussion titled “Embracing Clean Energy” will be held on February 25 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. as the first of three panel discussions as part of Readmont, the annual community read in Piedmont. This year’s selection is Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate. The panelists include: • Jessica Tovar of the Local Clean Energy Alliance in Oakland, an NGO working in advocacy for clean energy. (http:// localcleanenergy.org/) • Angel Fierro, husband of Millennium HS principal Shannon Fierro and co-partner of Plexus Solutions, which joins large scale clean energy projects with capital. http://www.plexussolutions.services/leadership • Dr. Max Auffhammer, George Pardee Jr. Professor of Sustainable Development and Associate Dean in the Division of Social Sciences at UC Berkeley. He is also an Assistant Professor of Agricultural and Resource Economics and International and Area Studies at UC Berkeley and Chair at the Political Economy, UC Berkeley. (https://onpointanalytics.com/ experts/maximilian-auffhammer/) This year, Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at Piedmont High School. To register, visit piedmontconnect.org/readmont-2021. The hope is that this common reading experience will forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members. The next event will be “Youth Summit on Environmental Justice” on April 24, an event open to high school students across the Bay Area, ready to take action to preserve the planet. All Piedmonters are encouraged to read This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate by Naomi Klein. The author argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied, but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. Copies are available for checkout at the PHS library. Interested readers can contact PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us to borrow a copy. A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair Village is offering a 20% discount on this title. ADVICE FROM A TUTOR: Use the left brain By Jay Russell Distance learning presents impediments to all students, and for some, learning exclusively on a computer can seem all but impossible. For decades, educators at all levels have attempted to diversify how lessons are taught to account for the different ways in which students learn best. Unfortunately, with every lesson on a screen, education has become one dimensional (or 2-D at best). There’s really no substitute for on-campus, in-class learning. But until then, try getting the leftbrain involved. For students considered solitary, auditory, mathematic or visual learners, screen-based learning may be okay. Roughly 25 percent pf Piedmont families with elementary school age students have chosen to continue with distance learning. While many factors went into those decisions, it is fair to say that distance learning is tolerable for some students. Students who learn most efficiently from social, verbal and physical teaching may be struggling the most with distance learning. Using color, making artistic representations, utilizing alternative school supplies and employing music can awaken the left brain often forgotten in education. Piedmont kindergarteners went back to in-person learning last week on February 10. Much insight can actually be gleaned from the youngest learners to help older students. The joy of learning has vanished for many. An overarching goal for a tutor, beyond re-explaining course material, is to inspire passion and make education fun. Something as simple as using different color pens, or pencils can make note-taking easier and more enjoyable. In college I adopted the habit of going over my notes right after a lecture or discussion and adding comments in a different color. When looking at the notes later, Give your computer a rest and use a typewriter, like this 1920’s Corona machine. It’s fun, auditory and a tactile way to hammer out schoolwork. I would use another color. This keeps a record of how thoughts develop. Drawing picture representations in the margin of notes can really solidify material too. Having a fancy set of color pencils can make all the difference. It can be tricky to get the left brain involved in a subject like math, but it’s not impossible. Again, investing in school supplies can make all the difference. While often shunned and forgotten as archaic, writing with quill and ink, or using a vintage typewriter can bring excitement to the most droll of subjects. While cursive handwriting has been phased out of grade school education, for some, the graceful font can be just enough artistic activity to keep sentences flowing. Enliven the left brain When pre-schoolers, students, or professionals, are totally swept up in a project and just going for it, productivity is at a maximum. Often that occurs when both sides of the brain are engaged. It doesn’t take a CT scan to notice that people are the most entrenched in their tasks when creativity and the whole brain are unleashed. Music in the background can help set the right mood for studying. Classical music and jazz have a mellow cadence and the songs are long, which encourage long periods of unbroken attention without too much change. For more contemporary music fans, instrumental beats, or electronic music can accomplish the same thing. Try lowering the volume or listening to music without lyrics if tunes with vocals are distracting. Students who are musicians may want to try turning course material into songs or simply reading out loud while adding a cadence to it. Student isolation lends itself to singing out loud, even during class (just make sure the microphone is muted). Taking this principle to the next level, a student could employ a younger sibling to translate course material into a play or into a stand-up routine. Type up a script and get theatrical. It can be fun and memorable. Whether studying, doing homework or merely trying to stay awake during class, using unique study methods can give students a little edge – and a boost of confidence. Jay Russel has over 10 years of experience as a tutor; he specializes in essay writing and algebra. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Appointments are now available for eligible Alameda County residents for COVID-19 vaccinations at the Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum. This is the first federally operated vaccination “supersite” in the country. The vaccination site opened yesterday, February 16, and is jointly operated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the State of California through the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES). In addition, a mass vaccination site was established at California State University, Los Angeles, as part of Gov. Newsom’s pilot project as part of the wider effort to establish 100 vaccination sites nationwide in the federal administration’s first 100 days. “In the fight against COVID- 19, partnership is key, especially when it comes to reaching Californians in underserved areas,” said Newsom. “These new sites will help us get available supply to some of the California communities most in need. I thank the Biden Administration for standing with us as we continue our efforts to safely, swiftly and equitably vaccinate all Californians.” FEMA is providing resources and federal staffing support to establish these new community vaccination centers, as well as operational support. The Oakland Coliseum mass vaccination site will eventually have the capacity Health professionals at the Oakland Coliseum are now prepared to administer COVID-19 vaccinations to eligible Alameda County residents, beginning February 16. to administer up to 6,000 vaccine doses per day. The two locations chosen for these efforts, Los Angeles and Alameda County, are communities that have been disproportionately impacted by COVID-19 and are home to essential workers who have “borne the brunt of keeping the economy open over the past year,” Newsom said. “This additional resource and infusion of vaccine is much needed in our community and will help us to reach more people more quickly,” Colleen Chawla, Director of the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency (HCSA), said. “We look forward to working with the site team to support outreach, education and access for our highest risk communities.” Alameda County Health Director Nicolas Moss advised that precautionary measures should still be taken, even after receiving the vaccine. “While we work to vaccinate County residents, we urge everyone to continue the other measures proven to slow the spread of COVID-19, including wearing masks and practicing physical distancing,” Moss said. “These simple strategies are the best way for people to remain safe and to protect their loved ones and co-workers until more people are vaccinated.” You can sign up for an appointment by visiting https://myturn. ca.gov/. Everyone in California will have an opportunity to get vaccinated to prevent COVID-19 at no cost. At this time, the state is beginning to vaccinate those at highest risk, such as individuals with a high risk of exposure and people ages 65 and older. To find out if you are eligible at this time, click on https:// myturn.ca.gov/.
articles.title: Appointments now available at Oakland Coliseum mass vaccination site

articles.text: Congresswoman Barbara Lee of Oakland announced on February 10 that $2 billion in Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) funds would be used to allow families to afford proper funerals for loved ones who have died as a result of COVID-19. The program will allow families to be reimbursed up to $7,000 for funeral expenses and will be retroactive through the beginning of the pandemic (January 2020) to December 31, 2020. It replicates the funding used for funeral assistance in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and was inspired by legislation introduced by Congresswoman Lee and Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14) in May 2020. “This must be a top priority in our response to this crisis. I’m proud to have partnered with Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Schumer on this crucial relief measure for families in California and across the country already beset by unimaginable grief,” Lee said. Ocasio-Cortez’s bill directs FEMA to provide financial assistance to individuals and funeral homes for the funeral expenses of an individual who died of COVID-19 without sufficient insurance to pay for such Rep. Barbara Lee expenses. The bill also limits assistance for funeral expenses to $10,000 for each deceased individual and prohibits FEMA from requiring residence in a presidentially declared disaster area as a condition for receiving assistance. “No one should struggle to afford a proper funeral for a loved one. During this time of unprecedented pain and economic hardship, it’s a moral imperative that the federal government step in and provide relief,” Lee said. “FEMA is authorized for $2 billion as of right now and it is retroactive, reimbursing back to January 2020. Those interested in participating in the program will need expense documentation, a death certificate, and other personal information documents.”
articles.title: Rep. Barbara Lee announces federal funding for COVID-19 funeral expenses

articles.text: One case of a more contagious strain of a COVID-19 variant was discovered in Alameda County, according to a report from the Alameda County Public Health Department on Wednesday, February 10. The variant, known to scientists as the B.1.351 variant of SARS-CoV-2, was first identified in South Africa last October. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said that there is no evidence that this variant causes more severe symptoms, but data suggests it might spread more easily. The single case in Alameda County and another reported in Santa Clara County were the first cases of the South African variant reported in California. Details of the Alameda County case have not been released. “The case in Alameda County remains under investigation,” the County said. In the Santa Clara County case, however, the individual had recently returned from traveling internationally in mid-January. The individual and other members of the household followed the county’s 10-day mandatory travel quarantine and remained in their apartment. The cases were detected by genomic sequencing done through Stanford University. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, February 17, 2021 Covid News Appointments now available at Oakland Coliseum mass vaccination site By Allyson Aleksey Appointments are now available for eligible Alameda County residents for COVID-19 vaccinations at the Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum. This is the first federally operated vaccination “supersite” in the country. The vaccination site opened yesterday, February 16, and is jointly operated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the State of California through the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES). In addition, a mass vaccination site was established at California State University, Los Angeles, as part of Gov. Newsom’s pilot project as part of the wider effort to establish 100 vaccination sites nationwide in the federal administration’s first 100 days. “In the fight against COVID- 19, partnership is key, especially when it comes to reaching Californians in underserved areas,” said Newsom. “These new sites will help us get available supply to some of the California communities most in need. I thank the Biden Administration for standing with us as we continue our efforts to safely, swiftly and equitably vaccinate all Californians.” FEMA is providing resources and federal staffing support to establish these new community vaccination centers, as well as operational support. The Oakland Coliseum mass vaccination site will eventually have the capacity Health professionals at the Oakland Coliseum are now prepared to administer COVID-19 vaccinations to eligible Alameda County residents, beginning February 16. to administer up to 6,000 vaccine doses per day. The two locations chosen for these efforts, Los Angeles and Alameda County, are communities that have been disproportionately impacted by COVID-19 and are home to essential workers who have “borne the brunt of keeping the economy open over the past year,” Newsom said. “This additional resource and infusion of vaccine is much needed in our community and will help us to reach more people more quickly,” Colleen Chawla, Director of the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency (HCSA), said. “We look forward to working with the site team to support outreach, education and access for our highest risk communities.” Alameda County Health Director Nicolas Moss advised that precautionary measures should still be taken, even after receiving the vaccine. “While we work to vaccinate County residents, we urge everyone to continue the other measures proven to slow the spread of COVID-19, including wearing masks and practicing physical distancing,” Moss said. “These simple strategies are the best way for people to remain safe and to protect their loved ones and co-workers until more people are vaccinated.” You can sign up for an appointment by visiting https://myturn. ca.gov/. articles.text: Grayson Fishman, a kindergarten student, has figured out two pretty fast ways to get to school – by scooter or bicycle. His mom, Arielle Harris, shared his joy. “On his first day of kindergarten, Grayson was so excited he got up early, got dressed right away, and came into our room around 7 a.m. asking if it was time to go yet,” she said, smiling. On the second day Grayson couldn’t contain his excitement to go back, so they ended up biking around the neighborhood for 30 minutes before school and ended up sitting outside of the school waiting for it to open. Gabe Kesler president of the APT, the Association of Piedmont Teachers, spoke at the School Board meeting February 9 to give a pat on the back to his teaching colleagues. “Kindergarten teachers’ professionalism and dedication got us through this, and they gave a fabulous welcome for returning kids.” Meanwhile 6th graders eyed their return to school by taking tours of their new campus on February 11 and 12 led by middle school staff members and principal Ryan Fletcher, who explained what to do and where to go when they return February 23 from the current weeklong Presidents’ Day break. All students in all grades will have online instruction exclusively on Mondays this year. On Tuesday, February 23, 3rd graders and 6th graders return. Fourth graders return to class on Wednesday, February 24, and the phased reopening will be complete on Thursday, February 25, with the return of all fifth grade students. Second grader Kian Spina brought purple violets for his teacher, Sally Samuth, at Beach School. Beach School 1st graders line up on campus on February 10 for their first day of school in 11 months.

articles.text: He’s back! Neil Rothenberg, Piedmont High’s Hall of Fame tennis coach who was inducted in 2018, has come out of retirement for the 2021 season. “Don’t put much attention on me,” said Rothenberg with a laugh, diving quickly into the circumstances surrounding the upcoming 2021 season. “It’s about the team, but it’s going to be fun… I truly miss coaching; I just really enjoy high school and college tennis. For tennis at PHS, the unique challenge of operating during a pandemic has required both girls’ and boys’ tennis teams to play their seasons concurrently. That will require all hands on deck for a program that will continue to support JV teams for both boys and girls. “I’m glad to have his help,” said current coach Jim Landes, who was Rothenberg’s JV coach and stepped into the varsity role when Rothenberg retired on 2015. “We may have to do boys’ and girls’ simultaneously at different sites. It’s great to have Neil here.” Neil Rothenberg in an earlier photo. “He’s a great coach with a lot of experience. It’s really good news,” Landes added. The Highlanders are scheduled to face its four Foothill Division opponents: Alameda, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, and Castro Valley. However, issues come with transportation to-and-from games, notably for away matches. There are questions that haven’t been answered yet, such as whether seniors can drive to the matches, because there is no carpooling allowed. That means that Tennis coaches Jim Landes [right] and Neil Rothenberg talk strategy at a recent practice. parents will have to drive their own kids. “There are a lot of things that have to be worked out,” he added. “We’re requesting the Park Courts in order to have a JV team.” Rothenberg, who strings racquets for the UC Berkeley tennis program, mentioned that Berkeley High may not even have a place to call home. “There are a lot of questions for other schools, too. Castro Valley and Berkeley have always had a difficult time with carpooling. And Berkeley High has an issue with courts. They are practicing at different times at Edwards Stadium (at UC Berkeley) and they are being very cautious. I don’t think the Berkeley Tennis Club will give up any courts for the matches. The members keep the courts pretty full most of the time,” said Rothenberg. Landes previously mentioned that the WACC (league) will allow teams to structure their own matches – meaning instead of splitting sites home and away, boys and girls could potentially have mixed doubles. “That is a possibility. As far as the league is concerned, anything is allowed as long as both coaches agree. I’m thinking we could even do a team-tennis format, where instead of five matches, it’s 10 matches. That would allow two mens’ and womens’ singles and doubles, two mixed doubles, or even more to the mix. Even speed tennis could be played,” mentioned Rothenberg. Rothenberg pointed out the hard work that Landes has put into keeping tennis alive in Piedmont. With all the questions surrounding classes, forming cohorts, and protocols for interscholastic sports, tennis has been the one constant for PHS athletes. Staff Photos Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame tennis coach Neil Rothenberg at his induction ceremony in 2018. Neil Rothenberg with assistant coach Corey Reich at his Hall of Fame induction. “That’s a big part of why we talked about coming back. This is a very unique season. The idea is to get these kids on the courts who have been pouring their heart and soul into the sport. What Jim has done to keep his programs going is just amazing,” said Rothenberg. Rothenberg retired after the 2015 season after taking the program after Ted Scherman and helping build it into a powerhouse tennis program known throughout Northern California. The Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team has won the league title for 19 consecutive years, a state record. When he retired in 2015, Rothenberg’s teams amassed a record of 501-103 and won three consecutive NCS Team titles. Although Rothenberg has been away from coaching, it may not seem that way for many of the players. The former coach always stayed close to the game; peering over matches and practice at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, often spotted on the corner of Bonita and Vista using the recycling can for VIP seating. Rothenberg, a natural baseball historian and fanatic, made sure to reference some specific comparisons to his return in Piedmont. “I feel like Tony La Russa and Jim Palmer,” said Rothenberg laughing, citing La Russa’s return to managing with the White Sox, while Palmer returned to pitching for the Orioles in 1991. “That’s where the comparisons stop, though.” In a time where nothing seems normal, some Piedmont High tennis greatness sounds like a refreshing course for the small town on the hill. Neil Rothenberg received a Gatorade bath in 2015 after Piedmont won the North Coast Section Team Tennis Championship.
articles.title: Hall of Fame coach Neil Rothenberg returns for 2021

articles.text: A small group of members of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is reaching out to the community for support to raise $3000 to purchase a trailer to transport their pit equipment to races. The coed team is a club sport at Piedmont High School and must independently raise money for operating expenses. “In a year that has been marked by limitations on almost every typical activity for our students, biking has been one of the few exceptions,” said Sally Aldridge. “Our team has grown over the past few years from five riders to over 50, and our racers have earned podium spots as well as qualification in the state championship. “With your help, we will continue to help give more local boys and girls the chance to experience the thrill of mountain biking and the joys of racing as a team.” To view the GoFundMe page visit: https://gf.me/v/c/nwt/help-piedmont-mtb-team-fund-a-trailer.
