articles.text: Photo courtesy of the Toronto Star Mackie McDonald reached the Round of 16 of the prestigious Grand Slam tournament, the Australian Open, defeating three Top-100 players in the process. The Pride of Piedmont, Mackenzie “Mackie” McDonald, reached the Round of 16 of the prestigious Australian Open for the second time in his career, upsetting three players before falling to the world’s No. 4 player, Daniil Medvedev in straight sets on Sunday, February 14. His journey in the Grand Slam tournament made his hometown – and fans everywhere – proud. It matched his longest appearance in a Grand Slam tournament, the Wimbledon’s Round of 16 in 2018. He was the only American player left in Australia Open last week. Mackie upset No. 22 Borna Coric of Croatia on Wednesday, February 10 in four sets, 6-4, 6-2, 4-6, 6-4, and followed up with a straight-set victory over South Africa’s Lloyd Harris, 7-6 (9-7), 6-1, 6-4, who entered as the world’s No. 91 ranked player. Reaching the rarified air of the Round of 16 was justification for the 25-year old professional. Making his fourth Australian Open appearance and the first Grand Slam of 2021 carried vindication after his long recovery from a severe hamstring injury that caused him to miss nearly all of 2019. “I’m proud of making the Round of 16 at the Australian Open to kick off the year! This result means a lot to me knowing how hard I’ve worked to get back to the highest level of tennis after an injury. I’m looking forward to continuing to improve and setting the bar higher,” said McDonald on his official social media. His injury was bad enough to end many careers, a torn hamstring tendon off the bone. articles.text: East Bay Regional Parks District is hosting its annual trail challenge, where entrants can earn a free commemorative pin by completing five of its 20 listed trails – or walk at least 26.2 miles of trails within East Bay Regional parks. More than 10,000 people participate in this free self-guided hiking and bicycling program to explore the East Bay regional parks and to keep fit outdoors. Each year the Trails Challenge highlights 20 trails for all abilities. Trails include easy, moderate, and challenging routes; many with scenic destinations in a variety of parklands and shorelines, according to the District’s website. The 20 available loops for hikers to use are listed in the Photo courtesy of East Bay Regional East Bay Regional Parks District is hosting the 2021 trail challenge. Earn a commemorative pin by accomplishing five of its listed trails or 26.2 miles of walking within their parks. 2021 Trail Challenge Guidebook (https://www.ebparks.org/civicax/filebank/blobdload.aspx?blobid=33795). East Bay Regional’s 20 listed parks range from Easy, Moderate, and Challenging. Their Staff Photo A view of the French Trail in Redwood Regional Park. guidebook provides useful information on each destination like total mileage, elevation gain, and whether dogs are permitted, while also mentioning features and highlights of each trail. The Park District is featuring two trails near Piedmont, Redwood Regional’s Stream to French trails—listed as moderate, and a 7.9-mile loop through Tilden Park, rated as challenging. The full list of the 20 trails can be found at: https://www.ebparks. org/TC This intrepid writer decided to tackle the closest trail to home. Rated moderate, the Redwood Regional path is a 6.2-mile loop with an elevation gain of 967 feet. The hike starts at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road, going two miles along the Stream Trail until intersecting with the Tres Sendas Trail, which jolts up 332 feet in elevation to the French Trail. Along the Stream Trail is ladybug season, about 1.5 miles in are bushels of ladybugs that gather during the winter months. Scientists note that this behavior is a way for the species to reproduce and to cope with a limited winter food supply. On every branch, post, and rock are swarms of ladybugs piling on one another, laying eggs on the underside of leaves. “Here in Redwood, they wait out the winter, often along the creeks,” wrote East Bay Regional Parks on their informative panel. “They are likely attracted to the area by chemicals in the air, or from pheromones, or scent markers, left behind in their footprints.” The walk along the French Trail goes 2.5 miles until intersecting with the Orchard Trail to take hikers back to their car at Canyon Meadows.

articles.text: A bit of the steep uphill section toward Murietta Falls. How about discovering a waterfall barely one hour from Piedmont? Murietta Falls, located in Del Valle Regional Park in Livermore, awaits you. It is considered the highest waterfall in the Bay Area at an elevation of 3,000 feet in the Ohlone Wilderness. A small stream cascades over a 199- foot cliff to create the waterfall. This destination requires lots of legwork; a trip of slightly over six miles outand-back, or six miles overall with about 4,100 feet in elevation gain. The prize of Murietta Falls is well worth the grind. Hikers would be wise to come early given this trail will require 6-7 hours of hiking. Showing up at 11:30 a.m. meant that this reporter was nearly the last hiker to leave the park. We passed 53 people, all but two on the trek toward the waterfall. The Ohlone Wilderness Trail stretches for 28 miles and is known as a popular backpacking area for overnight hikers. The trail to Murietta Falls starts across the bridge on Del Valle Road, heading down the blocked off road to the Sailor Camp Trail, which eventually becomes the Ohlone Wilderness Trail. Follow the red Ohlone Wilderness Trail markers on each trail post. The hike begins with a bang, with 1,150 feet in the first half mile, then a level area in the next half-mile so you can catch your breath. But then another jolt of nearly 1,200 feet in elevation gain takes place in the next 1.3 miles. That means over 2,300 feet in elevation gain over the first 2.3 miles of the trail with some gradients above 20 percent. Picking up 1,000 feet per mile is an arduous task that will prepare hikers for the toughest of challenges. For instance, the SF Chronicle’s most difficult trail in the Bay Area, Mt. Diablo’s Burma Road Trail, has an equally difficult two-mile elevation trial. But you’re not done. The 3-mile mark means trail goers will embark on the final climb to the falls after descending over a small creek. After passing the creek, you begin another ascent of 1,530 feet over the next 1.5 miles. After the final climb, the trail opens up to a valley, turning right past Johnny’s Pond. This means you have less than a mile to Murietta Falls, finally! The creek wraps through a rocky gulch and over the near 100-foot cliff face. The hike back to the car has much less ascent and is quicker. Hikers will face a climb of around 350 feet walking back, with one more uphill challenge of around 500 feet—but aside from those two sections, it is mostly downhill. Follow the red trail markers to stay on the Ohlone Wilderness Trail. Once past the creek, moss covers nearly everything in sight. Johnny’s Pond on the right means you’re on the homestretch to Murietta Falls.
articles.title: Murietta Falls in Del Valle Regional Park in Livermore

articles.text: A scene from San Francisco Ballet’s Midsummer Night’s Dream. Dance review by Paul Hertelendy Shakespeare and ballet usually means Romeo and Juliet. But there’s more. For a rare in-depth look at George Balanchine going back to his Russian roots, check out his lavish Midsummer Night’s Dream on a stream at San Francisco Ballet. It’s a stunning phalanx of 50 or more perfectly attuned dancers, a spectacle of palatial elegance and dance perfection. If only it had similar sparkle or propulsion. We regard Balanchine as a great, one of the fathers of modern ballet. In this 1962 “Dream” however he reverted to the spirit of 19th-century Petipa days back in St. Petersburg, executed beautifully, as if you were coming upon a room full of rare china and crystal chandeliers. At first glance it’s a show to take the kids to, as much as Nutcracker. But the humor and whimsey are in short supply, even with that cutup Puck cavorting about the stage doing his boyish magical mischief. The convoluted madness of the Shakespearean plot is crammed in the first half, where a large cast plays out the fantasy of mismatched lovers, the result of a magical flower radically reorienting every one’s love interest in zany ways. Only a true Shakespearean can tell apart the soloistic ladies – Hermia, Helena, Hyppolyta, Titania – or tell which truly belongs paired off with Lysander, Theseus, Oberon or Demetrius. The philandering Puck can scramble the lineup of lovers with glee until finally the bumpkin Bottom is turned into a donkey, sought after as the ludicrous ardent love object of the spellbound, queenly Titania. Both Balanchine and Sir Frederick Ashton did ballet versions of Shakespeare’s Dream in the 1960s to grace each side of the Atlantic. Both use as foundation stone Mendelssohn’s score embodying some of the most deft tone-painting of any German-romantic music. The biggest difference lay in the role of the donkey – in Ashton, farcically pawing a hoof on the ground to accompany the asinine “bray” in the priceless score, while in Balanchine playing a dignified, gentleman-like role with halting steps – at least, as dignified as that giant donkey’s head would permit. In addition, Ashton created a one-act performance, while Balanchine made it evening-length, adding snippets of other Mendelssohn as needed, particularly for the grand but soulless ballet spectacle in breathtaking glittering costumes that makes up the old-line act-two divertissements. Curiously enough, for the balletomane the high point comes in the lengthy and highly demanding act two pas de deux, done here by Frances Chung with Ulrik Birkkjaer. Each time you think they will wilt in this nonstop seven-minute duo, they come back with yet more arabesques and lifts with an Olympian energy. It is a breathtaking tour de force that, in streaming, you might want to view over and over. The take-away here is the near-infinite depth of SF Ballet, even in a casting devoid of some of the top company stars. It’s as if the troupe defies you to find any weakness in the endless lead parts, whether Sasha De Sola (Titania), Elizabeth Powell (Hermia) or Sarah Van Patten (Helena), or alternatively Luke Ingham (Demetrius), Esteban Hernandez (Oberon), Myles Thatcher (Lysander), Tiit Helimets (Theseus) or that endearing man-donkey Bottom, played by Lucas Erni. The spell-caster Puck was Cavan Conley, more mischief than merriment. The national backgrounds of these were most diverse: Mexico, Argentina, Estonia, Canada, Denmark, Australia, USA. Of note in a tour-de-force role leading the hunters was the athletic Sasha Mukhamedov playing Hyppolyta – part Amazon, part archer. Uniquely, at the end, she could take her bow while carting her bow. Martin West led the pit orchestra, to which my meager laptop speakers cannot do justice. San Francisco Ballet in Balanchine’s 1962 Midsummer Night’s Dream, filmed at the S.F. Opera House in March 2020. Now available on streaming. This and other streams are available by subscription online. To view, visit www.sfballet.org, or call (415) 865-2000.

articles.text: The California Shakespeare Theatre, commonly known as Cal Shakes, has announced that its 2021 Season will be called a Season of Shared Light, and will include community groups, artists, and arts and culture organizations from across the Bay Area. The decision was made in response to the ongoing pandemic and movement for racial equity in the arts and beyond. “At Cal Shakes, many of our performances take place—not in the relative anonymity of a dark theater—but under the sun,” noted Artistic Director Eric Ting. “It’s a thing I’ve come to love, and now miss dearly – the actors and audience alike in full view of one another, relinquishing the control we normally associate with the theater and instead navigating the complexity of each other’s very real presence across the arc of a performance, cohabiting the shared light of our space.” Cal Shakes will produce only one play in its 47th season, The Winter’s Tale by William Shakespeare, to be directed by Ting. In addition, the theatre company will continue to develop digital and in-person programming, safety permitting, throughout 2021, including Shakespeare In-Depth with Philippa Kelly, its Direct Address series, and other performance and educational opportunities. “Over the next few months we’ll be sharing the fruits of that labor - a developing vision of mutual aid rooted in creative expression and collective action,” Ting added. This summer, Cal Shakes plans to share its open-air venue with Bay Area arts organizations, to include West Edge Opera, Destiny Arts, and Bandaloop. “We know that outdoor space will continue to be a premium in 2021, so sharing our grounds with our fellow arts and cultural organizations feels like exactly the thing we should be doing this year,“ Managing Director Sarah Williams said. “We are eagerly looking forward to the summer, and operating under the assumption that by May we will be able to responsibly return in some capacity. Above all, we will continue to be flexible and monitor the mandates around reopening to ensure the safety of our artists, staff, and community.” Due to the ongoing pandemic and uncertainties surrounding it, Cal Shakes is holding off on announcing specific dates and ticket sales for The Winter’s Tale until there is more clarity around re-opening, gathering, and social distancing guidelines. All events are subject to change. Further artistic and community initiatives as part of the Season of Shared Light will be announced over the coming months. For information visit www. calshakes.org.
articles.title: California Shakespeare Theatre to produce The Winter’s Tale this summer

articles.text: The first episode of the new season of “Aurora Connects” is “The Vietnamese-American Experience,” featuring guests Oanh Nguyen, Linda Nguyen, and Trieu Tran. The forum, which premiered on February 4, is now available to watch online. “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s bi-weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every other Thursday at 5 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. Each episode is hosted by theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello and AssociateArtistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Costello was appointed artistic director in 2019 following a national search. At Aurora, he has directed, among others, Exit Strategy, The Importance of Being Earnest, Detroit, and the award-winning world premiere of Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day. Williams has been Aurora’s Associate Artistic Director since August 2019. An Oakland-native, she was Artistic Associate and a resident artist at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival for six ing for vulnerable populations in the fields of utility, public health, social services, and environmental stewardship. She currently works in the field of diversity, equity and inclusion at a utility agency. Trieu Tran is a stage, screen and television actor. Born in Vietnam, he immigrated to Canada and grew up in Boston. He has appeared in numerous theatrical productions over the years. You can watch the discussion by visiting https://www. auroratheatre.org/auroraconnects. Oanh Nguyen seasons. Oanh Nguyen was the founding Artistic Director of Chance Theater’s in 1999. He is a recipient of TCG’s New Generations Grant and the TCG Nathan Cummings Young Leaders of Color Fellowship and was awarded the Outstanding Artist Award by Arts Orange County, profiled in Orange County Register’s “Most Influential People” series. Linda Nguyen was born and raised in the Bay Area and is the daughter of Vietnamese refugees. She has worked in local government for years advocatTrieu Tran

pages.text: 16 Wednesday, February 17, 2021 Arts & Entertainment The Ballet turns to Shakespeare A scene from San Francisco Ballet’s Midsummer Night’s Dream. Dance review by Paul Hertelendy Shakespeare and ballet usually means Romeo and Juliet. But there’s more. For a rare in-depth look at George Balanchine going back to his Russian roots, check out his lavish Midsummer Night’s Dream on a stream at San Francisco Ballet. It’s a stunning phalanx of 50 or more perfectly attuned dancers, a spectacle of palatial elegance and dance perfection. If only it had similar sparkle or propulsion. We regard Balanchine as a great, one of the fathers of modern ballet. In this 1962 “Dream” however he reverted to the spirit of 19th-century Petipa days back in St. Petersburg, executed beautifully, as if you were coming upon a room full of rare china and crystal chandeliers. At first glance it’s a show to take the kids to, as much as Nutcracker. But the humor and whimsey are in short supply, even with that cutup Puck cavorting about the stage doing his boyish magical mischief. The convoluted madness of the Shakespearean plot is crammed in the first half, where a large cast plays out the fantasy of mismatched lovers, the result of a magical flower radically reorienting every one’s love interest in zany ways. Only a true Shakespearean can tell apart the soloistic ladies – Hermia, Helena, Hyppolyta, Titania – or tell which truly belongs paired off with Lysander, Theseus, Oberon or Demetrius. The philandering Puck can scramble the lineup of lovers with glee until finally the bumpkin Bottom is turned into a donkey, sought after as the ludicrous ardent love object of the spellbound, queenly Titania. Both Balanchine and Sir Frederick Ashton did ballet versions of Shakespeare’s Dream in the 1960s to grace each side of the Atlantic. Both use as foundation stone Mendelssohn’s score embodying some of the most deft tone-painting of any German-romantic music. The biggest difference lay in the role of the donkey – in Ashton, farcically pawing a hoof on the ground to accompany the asinine “bray” in the priceless score, while in Balanchine playing a dignified, gentleman-like role with halting steps – at least, as dignified as that giant donkey’s head would permit. In addition, Ashton created a one-act performance, while Balanchine made it evening-length, adding snippets of other Mendelssohn as needed, particularly for the grand but soulless ballet spectacle in breathtaking glittering costumes that makes up the old-line act-two divertissements. Curiously enough, for the balletomane the high point comes in the lengthy and highly demanding act two pas de deux, done here by Frances Chung with Ulrik Birkkjaer. Each time you think they will wilt in this nonstop seven-minute duo, they come back with yet more arabesques and lifts with an Olympian energy. It is a breathtaking tour de force that, in streaming, you might want to view over and over. The take-away here is the near-infinite depth of SF Ballet, even in a casting devoid of some of the top company stars. It’s as if the troupe defies you to find any weakness in the endless lead parts, whether Sasha De Sola (Titania), Elizabeth Powell (Hermia) or Sarah Van Patten (Helena), or alternatively Luke Ingham (Demetrius), Esteban Hernandez (Oberon), Myles Thatcher (Lysander), Tiit Helimets (Theseus) or that endearing man-donkey Bottom, played by Lucas Erni. The spell-caster Puck was Cavan Conley, more mischief than merriment. The national backgrounds of these were most diverse: Mexico, Argentina, Estonia, Canada, Denmark, Australia, USA. Of note in a tour-de-force role leading the hunters was the athletic Sasha Mukhamedov playing Hyppolyta – part Amazon, part archer. Uniquely, at the end, she could take her bow while carting her bow. Martin West led the pit orchestra, to which my meager laptop speakers cannot do justice. San Francisco Ballet in Balanchine’s 1962 Midsummer Night’s Dream, filmed at the S.F. Opera House in March 2020. Now available on streaming. This and other streams are available by subscription online. To view, visit www.sfballet.org, or call (415) 865-2000. articles.text: On February 19, SF Jazz will host a side-by-side concert that pairs students with members of the SF Jazz Collective on Thursday, February 19. The program, titled Roots, Jazz, and American Music, will showcase original compositions and arrangements by music freshmen and veteran faculty members. Past side-by-side performances have included jazz luminaries such as Carmen Bradford, Matt Wilson, Julian Lage, Chad-Lefkowitz-Brown, as well as SF Jazz Collective members David Sanchez, Warren Wolf, and Edward Simon. The February 19 performance is the culmination of a multiple-day residency, with students working alongside faculty members in workshops to rehearse their original material and arrangements. The individual pieces will be announced from stage. Performers will include pianist Pianist Edward Simon Edward Simon, Lola Miller-Henline (vocalist, composer), Reece Cogswell (drums), and Julian Esparza (drums). The concert will begin at 7:30 p.m. A sneak peak of a similar concert held a year ago in March will also be revealed. articles.text: The San Francisco Maritime National Historic Park and the Maritime Museum will host a virtual concert of maritime songs and sea chanties from Black traditions of the United States and West Indies. The online event will be held on Saturday, February 27, and will feature four performers: Ron and Natalie Daise, Richard Adrianowicz, and Peter Kasin. The Daises, originally from South Carolina, are writers, actors, educators, and internationally renowned television performers. From 1994 to 1998, the husband-and-wife team starred in Nick Jr. TV’s award-winning “Gullah Gullah Island,” for which they also served as cultural consultants. The show was cited by TV Guide as one of the “10 best children’s shows” in 1996. They were nominees for two NAACP Image Awards and a Daytime Emmy Award. Adrianowicz’s interest in traditional music began in the early 70s when he moved from Chicago to California. He was part of several groups in the San Francisco Bay Area, including “Out of the Rain.” Adrianowicz is one of the regular shanty singers at Hyde Street Pier’s monthly shanty sings in San Francisco, held Natalie and Ron Daise aboard one of the historic sailing ships moored there. In 2002, he released Time Ashore is Over, a recording of sea shanties and sea songs featuring a chorus of singers from Hyde Street Pier. Peter Kasin, raised in Berkeley, took a strong interest in sea music after having first attended one of the monthly chanty sings in late 1989. He organizes sea music concerts and festivals in San Francisco. The event will begin at 11 a.m. and will run about 90 minutes. The virtual concert is free, but donations are welcome. Visit https://maritime.org/eventshome/afroseamusicconcert/ to reserve your spot.
articles.title: SF Maritime Museum to host event on February 27

articles.text: Piedmont blues guitarist Jules Leyhe brings his band to Piedmont Piano in February 25 for a 5 p.m. concert. Jules Leyhe and the Family Jules Band makes its first appearance at Piedmont Piano on Thursday, February 25 at 5 p.m. The concert is virtual, and can be viewed on YouTube or Facebook. Leyhe’s band is a high-energy blues quartet of some of Oakland’s greatest blues and jazz musicians. The ensemble’s blend of funky, blues and soul inspired improvisation makes for a highly entertaining performance you won’t want to miss. Leyhe, a native of Piedmont, is a blues guitarist specializing in slide guitar. The band includes Nancy Wright on saxophone, Ian McArdle on keyboards and bass, and Isaac Schwartz on drums. Improvisation is at the core of this band’s soul, always taking advantage of each bandmate’s playful ears and pushing each other’s abilities to the edge seeking a new sound over traditional styles of music like blues and soul. The band has just finished recording its latest CD, Your First Rodeo, due for release in late spring. Leyhe is well known in Piedmont for his annual appearance in the 4th of July Parade with his renditions of the iconic Jimi Hendrix recording of the Star Spangled Banner. For access to the February 24 concert, call Piedmont Piano Co. at 547-8188 or e-mail music@piedmontpiano.com. Piedmont Piano Co. is located at 1728 San Pablo Avenue in downtown Oakland. 510-525-5656 Monday-Friday 8:30-5:30 Saturday 9:00-5:00 Sunday Closed CARPET | VINYL | WOOD | LINOLEUM CL#788850 www.floordimensions.com
articles.title: Piedmont native makes debut at Piedmont Piano Feb. 25

articles.text: In a special one-night performance on Saturday, February 27, the San Francisco Conservatory of Music orchestra will be led by Michael Morgan, the acclaimed conductor and music director of the Oakland Symphony. This event features an eclectic range of music, from Revueltas, Ibert, and Hailstork to Mozart. Dimitri Murrath, the Conservatory’s Chair of String and Piano Chamber Music, will perform. The concert will be recorded in the Caroline Hume Concert Hall. In addition to directing Oakland Symphony, Maestro Morgan serves as artistic director of the Oakland Youth Orchestra and was the music director of the Sacramento Philharmonic Orchestra and Opera from 1999 to 2015 and artistic director of Festival Opera in Walnut Creek for more than 10 seasons. Morgan also teaches a graduate conducting course at the Conservatory of Music and is Music Director at the Bear ValMichael Morgan ley Music Festival in California each summer. In 2002 and 2003 he taught conducting at the Tanglewood Music Center and has led conducting workshops around the country. As Stage Director he has led productions of the Bernstein Mass at the Oakland East Bay Symphony and a modern staging of Mozart’s Don Giovanni at Festival Opera, where he has also staged Britten’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Gounod’s Faust. This performance will be available to stream online on Saturday, February 27, at 7:30 p.m. For streaming information, visit: https://sfcm.edu/ performance-calendar/event/ s f c m - o r c h e s t r a - c o n d u c t - ed- earl-lee?ut m _ sou rce=SFC V& ut m _ me d iu m=Ext e rnal&utm_campaign=SFArtsMonthly%22%3E BETWEEN GILMAN & BUCHANAN ST. 1081 Eastshore Hwy. articles.text: Katherine Heigl and Josh Duhamel star in Life As We Know It. Movie review by Chris Honoré Life as We Know It is so solidly formulaic that it should be taught to budding screenwriters as the quintessential contemporary romantic comedy (rom-com). It is a slick and predictable film, absent any real depth. Here’s how a rom-com is set up: couple meets cute or not so cute. In this film, it’s not so cute. Holly Berenson (Katherine Heigl) and Eric Messer (Josh Duhamel), are set up on a blind date by their best friends, Peter and Alison (Hayes MacArthur and Christina Hendricks). Instantly they discover they are oil and water. He is a jock with arrested development, irresponsible, a womanizer, and – what else? – rides a motorcycle. Holly is responsible, runs a bakery shop, and has had precious few dates for reasons that are never clearly explained. Because Peter and Alison include them in family events, especially the first birthday party for their daughter, Sophie, Messer (as he’s called) and Holly have multiple opportunities to reinforce their disdain for one another. And then the dark hammer falls (this is all in the trailer). Peter and Alison are killed in a car accident. Messer and Holly are told by the family attorney that according to the will they are Sophie’s designated co-guardians and, if they agree, must live in the family home and raise her together. Let the games begin. According to the formula, their mutual distaste for one another runs headlong into their commitment to Sophie. Naturally, since this is a rom-com, there are lots of issues, some slightly comedic. There’s even a crisis that results in a separation. But this film long ago telegraphed the ending. It’s just a matter of waiting and watching as two attractive people solve and resolve their differences while discovering that all that anger just might be reframed into something far more positive. As formula rom-coms go, Life as We Know It is good enough and follows nicely in the tradition of Baby Boom and Three Men and a Baby. It’s easy to watch with good-looking people who were looking for love in all the wrong places. Until now. Life as We Know It. Directed by Greg Berlanti. Starring Katherine Heigl, Josh Lucas, and Josh Duhamel. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Life as We Know It a pleasant romantic comedy

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Churchill is an intimate character study of a man who stood, however imperfectly, at the crossroads of history. A man (wonderfully portrayed by Brian Cox) who had defiantly held the people of England together through its darkest hours – a time of the London Blitz in the early part of World War II. The toll it took on that island nation’s people remains indescribable. Germany was relentless and indiscriminate, delivered nightly bombing raids that killed thousands. However, as D-Day began to take shape (referred to as Operation Overlord), according to this docudrama, Churchill’s emotions began to fray. He gradually concluded that his generals’ plans would result in untold carnage and result in the Allies losing the war. And so, he began to do battle with the generals. He confronted Gen. Dwight Eisenhower of the U.S. (John Slatterly), and England’s Gen. Bernard Montgomery (Julian Wadham) with his doubts, often haranguing them, questioning their tactics. He argued for diversionary battles to the north and south of Normandy. He was drinking too much, and treated those close to him shabbily, to include his wife Clementine (played by the always wonderful Miranda Richardson). While Eisenhower and Montgomery were unyielding in their commitment to carry through with plans for the invasion of Normandy Beach in June 1944, they waited, the weather being their only consideration. Churchill agonized and even prayed for a massive storm. Suddenly, after being central to England’s survival he was now required to sit on the sideline, powerless to influence events. It was not a role he could abide. He was also haunted by his very personal memories of the battle of Gallipoli in world War I where more than 200,000 English troops perished, a campaign he had supported and led and one which he regretted all of his life. He was convinced that D-Day would be a repetition and it felt unendurable. What he did not realize was that while he was still fighting WWI, the generals were embarking on a historic invasion unlike anything the world had ever seen. Finally, of course, Churchill yields and gives a memorable, historic speech to the people of England on the day of the invasion. Whether Anglophiles may take exception to the portrayal of Churchill in this film, it is still engaging. It demonstrates that while Churchill remains a legend, he was to the good fortune of England the right man at the right moment in history. He was fundamentally a tower of strength and intelligence, though flawed. Churchill. Directed by Jonathan Teplitzky. Starring Brian Cox, Miranda Richardson and John Slatterly. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG. John Slatterly as Dwight Eisenhower, Danny Web as Alan Brooke, and Brian Cox as Winston Churchill in Churchill.
articles.title: Churchill – the story leading up to D-Day in WWII

Naturally, since this is a rom-com, there are lots of issues, some slightly comedic. There’s even a crisis that results in a separation. But this film long ago telegraphed the ending. It’s just a matter of waiting and watching as two attractive people solve and resolve their differences while discovering that all that anger just might be reframed into something far more positive. As formula rom-coms go, Life as We Know It is good enough and follows nicely in the tradition of Baby Boom and Three Men and a Baby. It’s easy to watch with good-looking people who were looking for love in all the wrong places. Until now. Life as We Know It. Directed by Greg Berlanti. Starring Katherine Heigl, Josh Lucas, and Josh Duhamel. Rated PG-13. Brian Cox as Winston Churchill in Jonathan Teplitzky’s Churchill. Churchill – the story leading up to D-Day in WWII Movie review by Chris Honoré Churchill is an intimate character study of a man who stood, however imperfectly, at the crossroads of history. A man (wonderfully portrayed by Brian Cox) who had defiantly held the people of England together through its darkest hours – a time of the London Blitz in the early part of World War II. The toll it took on that island nation’s people remains indescribable. Germany was relentless and indiscriminate, delivered nightly bombing raids that killed thousands. However, as D-Day began to take shape (referred to as Operation Overlord), according to this docudrama, Churchill’s emotions began to fray. He gradually concluded that his generals’ plans would result in untold carnage and result in the Allies losing the war. And so, he began to do battle with the generals. He confronted Gen. Dwight Eisenhower of the U.S. (John Slatterly), and England’s Gen. Bernard Montgomery (Julian Wadham) with his doubts, often haranguing them, questioning their tactics. He argued for diversionary battles to the north and south of Normandy. He was drinking too much, and treated those close to him shabbily, to include his wife Clementine (played by the always wonderful Miranda Richardson). While Eisenhower and Montgomery were unyielding in their commitment to carry through with plans for the invasion of Normandy Beach in June 1944, they waited, the weather being their only consideration. Churchill agonized and even prayed for a massive storm. Suddenly, after being central to England’s survival he was now required to sit on the sideline, powerless to influence events. It was not a role he could abide. He was also haunted by his very personal memories of the battle of Gallipoli in world War I where more than 200,000 English troops perished, a campaign he had supported and led and one which he regretted all of his life. He was convinced that D-Day would be a repetition and it felt unendurable. What he did not realize was that while he was still fighting WWI, the generals were embarking on a historic invasion unlike anything the world had ever seen. Finally, of course, Churchill yields and gives a memorable, historic speech to the people of England on the day of the invasion. Whether Anglophiles may take exception to the portrayal of Churchill in this film, it is still engaging. It demonstrates that while Churchill remains a legend, he was to the good fortune of England the right man at the right moment in history. He was fundamentally a tower of strength and intelligence, though flawed. Churchill. Directed by Jonathan Teplitzky. Starring Brian Cox, Miranda Richardson and John Slatterly. 1 hr., 50 min. articles.text: A scene from Tim Burton’s Dumbo. Movie review by Chris Honoré Let’s assume that if the live-action reboot of Dumbo was going to soar at the box office, as did the original 1941 animated feature, then the Disney producers and writers paused and said something akin to, “The kids loved Dumbo in 1941; but that was then, and this is now.” A small toddler of an elephant with big blue eyes and enormous ears, soaring through the big top and buzzing the audience might not work. The kids in the audience are weaned on Marvel and DC superheroes, veterans of films replete with state-of-the-art CGI that is only limited by the writers’ imaginations. These kids have been there, done that. So how can the screenwriters take a small, adorable, semi-orphaned pachyderm and create a sequel that will engage kids, each hoping to be not only wowed, but touched by the story to the point of caring about Dumbo. So, the writers open with two children, Milly and Joe (Nico Parker, Finley Hobbins) who have just lost their mother to the flu pandemic of 1919. Happily, their father, Holt (Colin Farrell), though missing an arm from an injury in World War I, .has recently returned to the circus, and to them. And then begins Dumbo in earnest. The year is 1919. The place is Sarasota, Florida, and the circus is in town. It’s owned by a hyperbolic Max Medici (Danny DeVito). It’s a small, shoestring operation, a collection of society’s flotsam and jetsam all working for a slightly frayed Big Top. The wagons are paint-peeling tired, the elephants mistreated. Even Jumbo’s mom, pregnant, is about to be returned to a previous owner, since Max is unhappy with the price he paid. That is until Dumbo is born and spreads his ears while holding a feather, cheered on by Milly and Joe while Max sees his circus’ salvation. Director Tim Burton, for all of the steampunk color and 19th century texture, soon folds the small Medici Circus featuring Dumbo, into a much larger Coney Island/Disneyesque operation. It’s now called Dreamland, much of it decidedly not kid-friendly, headed by the villainous V.A. Vandervere (Michael Keaton), who is accompanied by his aerialist companion, Collette (Eva Green). The plan is to exploit Dumbo no matter the cost or outcome. When Vandervere discovers that Dumbo’s mother is locked up on the amusement park’s grounds and is an unnecessary distraction for little Dumbo, his solution is to put Jumbo down. Meanwhile, Milly and Joe and their dad, Holt, all seem helpless, as if pushed to the background, until finally they and the Medici crew set about executing a plan to rescue both Jumbo and Dumbo. This proves to be a precarious operation, one that stirs some real excitement. Regrettably, the final scenes of Dumbo seem almost an afterthought, with a quick nod to the environment when Jumbo and Dumbo are put onto a steamship and returned to their natural habitat somewhere in India. A nice thought needing a bit more explanation. Dumbo. Starring Colin Farrell, Eva Green, Michael Keaton and Danny DeVito. Directed by Tim Burton. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG. A scene from Tim Burton’s Dumbo.
articles.title: Dumbo remake an entertaining sequel

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Secretariat is a Disney film about a magnificent chestnut racehorse nicknamed Big Red, but more formally known as Secretariat, considered by many as the greatest racehorse of all time. In 1973 Red won the Triple Crown of racing – the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness and the Belmont Stakes. It was then, and remains still, the Holy Grail of horse racing, a trifecta that is rarely attained. No one does movies about animals better than Disney and Secretariat is filled with excitement: tight shots of jockeys clutching the reins as horses weighing some 1,200 pounds charge around an oval track more than a mile long. It’s intense, even thrilling. Of course, it’s irresistible for Disney not to give Secretariat a sentient intelligence. In one scene, Penny Chenery (Diane Lane), owner of Secretariat, stands holding the horse’s bridle, looking the horse in the eyes, while he looks and conveys to Penny that he’s ready to race. Disney loves to anthropomorphize animals (Bambi, et al); however, thankfully, director Randall Wallace shows restraint. A horse by any other name is still a horse. While the hub of the film is Secretariat and his ability to run, the focus throughout is on Penny, a Denver suburban housewife who tenaciously, with grit, takes a huge gamble on Secretariat when others in the old boys’ network suggest that she is a fool. It’s only because of her determination that she not only manages to keep control of her father’s Meadow Farms, in Doswell, Va., but enters Secretariat in races that will eventually lead to the Triple Crown. Disney has always been enamored with Jiminy Cricket characters like Penny (animated or otherwise) who wish upon a star, insisting it makes no difference who you are, while believing that dreams can come true. That theme is woven through countless Disney films, animated and not. It’s a nice thought and has resonated with audiences for more half a century. The real treat in this film is watching Diane Lane make the character of Penny Chenery her own. Lane is a hugely gifted actress, nominated for an Oscar for her performance in Unfaithful (a tour de force film for her). In this case, she carries Secretariat from the first frame. Lane is helped by the enormously talented actor John Malkovich portraying Lucien Laurin, the colorful French-Canadian trainer, and Margo Martindale as the longtime family secretary. Both are exceptional character actors. Malkovich’s breakthrough film was Places in the Heart. Secretariat is top-drawer family entertainment, especially for kids, say, eight and older. Adults will also be engaged by the sometimes sentimental yet compelling story of this remarkable horse and its equally remarkable owner. Secretariat. Directed by Randall Wallace, Starring Diane Lane, John Malkovich, Scott Glenn, and Margo Martindale. Rated PG. Diane Lane, John Malkovich and Margo Martindale in Disney’s Secretariat.
articles.title: Disney’s Secretariat a treat from start to finish

articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts has announced the addition of Aparna Rao to its Board of Directors, made effective on February 16. Most recently Rao served as the Interim Executive Director for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir and is a choir parent. She holds a diverse range of experience in law, marketing, media, design and corporate charitable giving. She worked as a production intern for Michael Krasny at KQED, and as a Marketing Assistant at Pioneer Investments and Fleet Bank, both in Boston. She has served as a lecturer at UC Berkeley since 2000. She has a Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy from Brandeis University and a Masters of Arts equivalent in Philosophy from Cal. “I wholeheartedly believe in the importance of the arts and respect PCA’s mission to offer artists an affordable space to share their work with Piedmont and, more broadly, Bay Area residents. There is something truly beautiful in having a center for community to coalesce around the arts,” Rao said. “I am particularly moved by the board’s current commitment of reaching out to a larger group of artists that reflect the diversity of the greater Bay Area. I hope that the connections I have made to arts organization directors, diverse artists, arts educators and arts journalists through my experience as Interim Executive Director of the Piedmont ChilAparna Rao dren’s Choir, and as an Oakland artisan will prove to be an asset.” PCA President Sue Malick said that Rao will extend the center’s reach for contacts in the greater Bay Area arts community. “We are so delighted to have Aparna as a member of the board. I got to know her when she served as the Interim Executive Director for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Her enthusiasm, leadership, devotion to the arts and her connections throughout the Bay Area will be a strong addition to the board,” Malick said. “When I interviewed Aparna Rao and reviewed her background, I was impressed by her commitment to a wide range of artistic endeavors. Her leadership of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, her work as an artisan, and her training in the management of non-profit arts organizations made her an ideal person to add to the Board of Directors of the Piedmont Center for the Arts,” said PCA board member Tom Reicher.
articles.title: Aparna Rao joins PCA board

articles.text: Jazz pianist Chick Corea Jazz great Chick Corea died last week. You don’t need to be a jazz aficionado to appreciate his art. You see, he represented and lived the best of humanity. Lofty dedication like this is often the sphere of a religious person. I do not know if Corea was a religious person, but with his devotion he easily could have been a Sunday school teacher. One of my friends is a very insightful music critic. He is also a fine jazz pianist. Naturally, I asked my friend Richard Ginell if he had any contact with Chick Corea. Yes he did, and his observations were insightful to say the least. The first thing that impressed me was that Chick Corea was also an excellent classical pianist. He recorded Mozart piano concertos and was very adept at Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. Just that by itself is impressive enough. All I need to do is quote him a little bit and his words speak directly to the heart and to the intellect. His music does not need an intermediary – music never does. His words of farewell were San Francisco Symphony musicians will perform during the orchestra’s virtual Chinese New Year program.
articles.title: Chick Corea: A jazz great who led by example

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony’s annual Chinese New Year celebration will be hosted this year by Bay Area actress Joan Chen, and features conductor Ming Luke and soloists Tao Shi (erhu), Wenying Wu (yanqin) and Samantha Cho (piano). The musicians will perform works by Yuan-Kai Bao, YaoXing Chen, Julian Yu, Zhao Long and Chen Yi, as well as Wu’s arrangement of “Tajiks Festival,” a traditional celebratory song. San Francisco Symphony will also broadcast the premiere of its first virtual celebration, with both pre-concert and post-concert receptions at 3 p.m. and 4:30 p.m. this Saturday, February 20, with exclusive musical offerings and special guests. The performance can be viewed on NBC Bay Area at 4 p.m. on February 20 and February 27; and on KTSF 26 on Sunday, February 21, and Saturday, February 27, at 3:30 p.m. It is also available to stream for SFSymphony Plus subscribers starting February 20 at sfsymphony.org/CNY.
articles.title: SF Symphony’s Chinese New Year virtual celebration

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, February 17, 2021 The Musical Gourmet glowingly empathetic. “I want to The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet thank all of those along my journey who have helped keep the music fires burning bright. It is my hope that those who have an inkling to play, write, perform or otherwise, do so. If not for yourself then for the rest of us. It’s not only that the world Chick Corea: A jazz great who led by example needs more artists, it’s also just a lot of fun. “Like a runner loves to run just because it feels good, I like to play the piano just because it feels good.” He was able to switch gears and change direction like the greatest of football players. His music spoke of the innocence of children. He was also a lofty idealist and a philosopher. His music told us all of these things. Music was fun. It was a game. And as he explained it, “It starts as a game...to try to capture something I envision in music. While I play, I look at things like a painter would. I try to see, while I’m playing, if my listeners agree with what I’m playing. Do they think that this is really a portrait of them? They usually do.” It is very interesting to note that the immortal classical violinist Jascha Heifetz expressed the exact same thing as Corea. They knew, more than others, that music radiates from within and from without. The performer can be the source of inspiration and at the very same time draw inspiration from the listeners. Chick Corea told everyone that he had a beautiful journey through life. It was his most fervent wish that everyone should enjoy it as he did. The vehicle was a simple one… music on wings of a thought. Music is a beautiful catalyst for all humanity. The table at the musical buffet is set. Enjoy. articles.text: Haiku contest finalists drew inspiration from Filoli’s winter blooms. Filoli House and Garden, located in Woodside, conducted a haiku contest that asked for submissions inspired by Filoli’s winter blooms. Winners were announced via Zoom and social media platforms on Valentine’s Day. A special guest judge, San Mateo County Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto, read the winning poem. Here is a sample of the finalists: Down the garden path wild turkey’s feathers shimmer in the winter sun –Alliana Lili Yang The soft hum of wings darting among the flowers seeking winter blooms –Lydia Becker In the white petals, crinkled cups holding yellow centers, a bee dines –LiAnn Yim The sky wept softly over hedges rust, poppies white such grace in fallow times –Heather Bourbeau To read all haiku finalists and winners, visit https://filoli.org/ haiku/.
articles.title: Filoli House & Garden announces winners of haiku contest

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is offering a new online series, “Takeout Tuesdays,” where museum docents and staff will offer interactive lunchtime discussion of selected artworks. The series will focus on a different topic each week and will look closely at important works using high-resolution images. Docents and staff will discuss the history of each artwork or object, as well as provide some fun facts about the collection. To re-create an in-person experience through a digital, Zoom platform, the museum invites viewers to join the discussion with observations and questions. A new program will be presented every Tuesday at 12 p.m. and will be approximately 30 minutes. Upcoming topics are listed below, and more will be announced throughout the duration of the series. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is celebrating the Year of the Ox at home with a virtual 20th Annual Lunar New Year. Patrons can view a series of short videos highlighting local and Taiwanese culture, a virtual story time with children’s author Oliver Chin, and art activities for all ages. To kick off the Lunar New Year celebration on February 12, Chin reads about the animals of the Chinese zodiac, and what makes each one unique. Author of the popular annual series, Tales from the Chinese Zodiac, he also wrote Julie Black Belt, and Welcome to Monster Isle. To watch his reading, visit https://museumca.org/LNY2021. Throughout February, the museum is offering fun at-home art projects for your family. On February 27, you can tune in for Oakland Museum of California will mark its 20th Lunar New Year celebration. a special video featuring OMCA Family Programmer Snowy Tung as she interviews family and friends in Taiwan to share their perspectives on celebrating Lunar New Year during a global pandemic. Tung has overseen OMCA Family Programs since 2003. Ox is the second in the 12-year cycle of the Chinese zodiac signs. In the Chinese culture those born under the sign of the ox are stable, honest, and hard-working. Visit Oakland Museum of California’s website to learn more about the ox, its origin story, and characteristics.

articles.text: Michael Tilson Thomas and the San Francisco Symphony will release a CD with its performances of three Alban Berg compositions. It will be made available by SFS Media on February 26. SFS Media is the symphony’s award-winning, in-house media production company and label, launched in 2001. Tilson Thomas, who recently retired after 25 years as San Francisco Symphony’s conductor and music director, is also co-founder and Artistic Director of the New World Symphony. The performances were recorded live at Davies Symphony Hall between January 2015 and November 2018. This is the newest release from the Grammy Award-winning SFS Media label, with Gil Shaham performing Berg’s Violin Concerto, and soprano Susanna Conductor Michael Tilson Thomas Phillips as soloist in Berg’s Seven Early Songs. The album will be available this spring and is available for pre-order now by clicking on: https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Discover-the-Music/SFS-Media/ Berg.
articles.title: SF Symphony to release CD of 3 Alban Berg concerts

By Allyson Aleksey Filoli House and Garden, located in Woodside, conducted a haiku contest that asked for submissions inspired by Filoli’s winter blooms. Winners were announced via Zoom and social media platforms on Valentine’s Day. A special guest judge, San Mateo County Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto, read the winning poem. Here is a sample of the finalists: Down the garden path wild turkey’s feathers shimmer in the winter sun –Alliana Lili Yang The soft hum of wings darting among the flowers seeking winter blooms –Lydia Becker In the white petals, crinkled cups holding yellow centers, a bee dines –LiAnn Yim The sky wept softly over hedges rust, poppies white such grace in fallow times –Heather Bourbeau To read all haiku finalists and winners, visit https://filoli.org/ haiku/. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, February 17, 2021 An early photo of Camp Wallace Alexander History of Piedmont Scout Council The Piedmont Scout Council’s early history is intertwined with that of the Piedmont Community Church and Wallace M. Alexander of Piedmont and Honolulu. Mr. and Mrs. Alexander moved to Piedmont in 1906, and the church was founded on March 27, 1910. Three years later Mr. and Mrs. Alexander donated one and one‑half acres, along with $50,000 to the building fund. The main church building was dedicated in 1918. The Rev. articles.text: Sometimes people ask me, a bit incredulously, how can a librarian work from home? These days I help with sidewalk service at the Asian Branch Library three days a week, and the other days I work from home. I can tell you how a librarian works from home. Besides purchasing children’s books for you to pick up at sidewalk service and online tasks like training and responding to e-mail, I meet children where they are – on Zoom. In pre-COVID days, teachers at Piedmont Avenue Elementary School would bring their classes to the Piedmont Ave. library for a fun hour of chaos: I would read them a story, kids would scramble about finding books to borrow, and then they would rush back to school. Class visits on Zoom are similarly hilarious but without the tangible satisfaction of putting books into students’ hands. In a typical visit with a class, I’ll log into the teacher’s Zoom room, read the kids a book, show them my online virtual reading room, talk about sidewalk service or another library resource, and take questions and have discussions. I try to choose funny books that are on the short side with clear illustrations and no details that might get lost on a webcam. The discussions are the most interesting. When we read Two of Everything, I asked second graders what they would like two of. Answers included “my mom,” “Zeke” (the teacher’s toddler), “PS5” (a really expensive video game console), and “999 Lions.” After some talk of odd and even numbers, the lions were revised slightly down to 998. I learned that one student used to be scared of chickens because their grandma’s chicken pecked them “and nobody saved me because my auntie was filming.” And everyone wants to be able to talk to dogs. When I show them my online virtual reading room, I highlight new books that have arrived at the library during the pandemic. They get to vote on a book to look up in the library catalog. Dog Man won in a recent week. I’ve checked with colleagues and learned this is a citywide phenomenon: the winner is invariably Dog Man. After we talk about how to request Dog Man for sidewalk pickup, it’s time for questions. These are usually, but not always, about the library. My favorite was when the discussion veered off into personal questions and ended up with my guinea pigs meeting a student’s guinea pigs. All the guinea pigs sniffed the screen, no doubt wondering if it was edible. Seeing the students’ faces is truly the highlight of my week, and I can’t wait to see all of you in person again. HOURS & LOCATION Piedmont Avenue Branch Library is located at 80 Echo Avenue in back of Piedmont Avenue Elementary School. For more information, call 510-597-5011 or see the website: https://oaklandlibrary.org/locations/piedmont-avenue-branch. Hours of operation are 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Closed Sunday and Monday. Margaret Rodriguez was the Piedmont Ave. Branch children’s librarian for many years and is now the Children’s Librarian at the Asian Branch. Content courtesy of the HOOT, the newsletter of Piedmont Avenue Library
articles.title: How does a librarian work from home?

articles.text: Stressed about current world or personal events? It’s possible to turn away from fear by gaining a clearer view of God as Love itself, which can have a tangible, healing effect in your life and in the world. At 5 p.m. on Thursday, February 18, tune in to a free, live Zoom lecture entitled, “Spiritual Discovery in a Time of Upheaval” by Tom McElroy, a Christian Science practitioner and teacher. The discussion is sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist in Oakland. “Prayer is about spiritual discovery. It’s about understanding more of what God is and learning to see our lives and the world through the lens of God’s allgood nature. It’s about stripping away surface-level appearances in order to discern what actually is,” explained McElroy. “Spiritual discovery reveals what is substantial, lasting, and powerful, and this leads to healing. What’s the outcome? Progress. Transformation. Wholeness – for anyone.” The link to attend the online talk is on the Church’s website, www.ChristianScienceOakland. org.
articles.title: Christian Science Church offers free talk tomorrow

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. Sesnon, first hosted similar salons that melded music, theatre, art, and the spoken word at their summer home, “Pino Alto” in Santa Cruz. In 2018, Molly created an exhibition of her artwork, as well as an endowment at the Mary Porter Sesnon Gallery at UC Santa Cruz’s Porter College in California. Artist Molly Cliff Hilts, who graduated from Piedmont High school in 1976, passed away on January 21. She was 62. Her gallery exhibiting her paintings stands at the edge of their garden. Her work can be viewed online at https://www.mollycliffhilts.com/#1, or through March 7 at the Brumfield Gallery in Astoria, Oregon (https://www.brumfieldgallery.com/molly-cliff-hilts. html). Her story, art, and a video interview can be seen at The Art of Connection: Interview with Portland Artist Molly Cliff Hilts | Rental Sales Gallery. Her paintings have been exhibited in solo shows in New York City, Oregon, California, Washington, and Mexico. She is represented by galleries in New York City, Philadelphia, North Carolina, and Oregon. Never complacent, she always had lots to do, artwork to create, friends to connect, young artists to mentor. Molly is survived by Dave her husband of 30 years, and two sons, Wade, 27, and Dane, 25. Additionally, she is survived by her aunt, Sue Sesnon Salt; her siblings, Daniel (and Martha), Sue aka Shanti, and Peter (and Sheila); her nephews and nieces, Will (and Ali), Janie (and Renan), Liam, Noah, Ellyn (and Nathan), Drew, and a large extended family of cousins. The family suggests that any memorial donations be made to the Molly Cliff Hilts Memorial Fund (https://connect.ucsc.edu/ hiltsfund) which provides enrichment for students in the Arts Division at UC Santa Cruz. The fund is administered by the Mary Porter Sesnon Art Gallery and will be used to benefit undergraduates pursuing a degree in art.

articles.text: As the Executive Director of The Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living, I realized that I wanted to be very proactive about securing Covid-19 vaccinations for our community members. With a limited supply in California, it seemed like a daunting task, but if you’re like me, I got in touch with my determination. Beginning in December of last year I began working the phones. Even though we are an independent living community, many of our members are vulnerable to illness due to aging, and some, if not all people, are at risk for serious illness resulting from the pandemic. For those of us in the Bay Area and beyond, who have wanted the vaccine from the beginning, the distribution efforts have been painfully slow. When I learned that a limited supply was going to be available in Alameda County, I reached out and began an effort to stay in touch with two tireless local government officials: Dustin and Andrew, who co-lead the Alameda County Health Department’s Covid Task Force. These two heroic and overwhelmed individuals were helpful and fully supportive of my mission to vaccinate the members at The Lake Merritt who wished to get the injections. Because of everyone’s efforts, diligence and can-do attitude, I am happy to announce that we held our first vaccination clinic here at The Lake Merritt in mid-January and every single one of our residents chose to be vaccinated. We will be receiving our second dose in just a few days. This is also due, in part, to another local hero of mine: pharmacist Sudhir of Clayworth Pharmacy. This community pharmacy in Castro Valley is dedicated to serving the health needs of The Lake Merritt resident Gloria receives her first vaccine shot from a Clayworth Pharmacy staffer. our area, Clayworth partnered wholeheartedly with our county administrators and are currently on a mission to vaccinate as many people as they can. As one of two small community-based pharmacies, they jumped in right away to help in this emergency. Clayworth brought their staff on-site to The Lake Merritt and vaccinated our residents here. Their daily schedule while here was three vaccinations every five minutes. Our residents gave careful consideration before getting vaccinated. Husband and wife residents Robert and Gloria said they felt ambivalent about the vaccine in the beginning since there seemed to be so many unknowns. Yet, they agreed to The Lake Merritt Executive Director Tim Johnson oversees vaccine paperwork. take it, because it seems to offer long-term protection. Resident Cleo reminded me that vaccine hesitancy in her community can be traced directly to a history of improper medical testing in addition to negative experiences with healthcare systems. “As an African American and a retired R.N., I feel it’s my responsibility to my neighbors at The Lake Merritt, and to my surrounding community, that I receive the vaccine,” Cleo said. As our residents were leaving the on-site clinic after their first injections, I asked some of them what it meant to them to get vaccinated. Pat said, “To me, it means freedom.” Cynthia agreed saying, “It means I can travel again.” Gloria added that taking the vaccine means “getting to see my grandchildren and spending time with my family again.” My advice to everyone is: don’t get frustrated with your search for the vaccine. Persistence works. First, reach out to your medical provider. Another option is the California Department of Public Health at www.myturn.ca.gov for up-todate registration and information. City agencies or county health departments may also know about new avenues and can recommend the best way for you to sign up for the vaccine. If you are not certain if taking the vaccine is right for you, consider a visit to the CDC website and read their current information: https://www. cdc.gov/vaccines/covid-19/index. html. These are very trying times, yet I’m confident that we will get through them by taking care of ourselves and each other. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living. For further information about The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street in Oakland, please call 510-903-3600 or visit www. thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: My MacBook Pro is 8 years old and running very slowly. I can’t open many web pages on Safari, it seems to take forever to start up. So, I am thinking about having the innards refreshed. I like the fact that I can play a CD or DVD from my large music collection in this laptop, and I know the newer ones don’t have that option. I called a local repair place and they can put in a Solid State Drive and more RAM for around $550. The laptop was originally a bit more than $1800, and I looked at the new version, and it would be about $2300 to get the specs that I want. The repairman told me that the new hard drive would last me several more years. Is it worth it or should I just get a new one? –Henri C., Montclair Dear Henri: Many times I get calls from customers asking me to help “clean up” or “speed up” an older Mac. Sometimes we can clean up and speed up a sluggish machine, but in many cases the computer is just too old. Let’s look at the possibilities. I have heard many stories of repair pros recommending upgrading older machines for a similar price tag; around $500. If you have the hard drive and RAM upgraded you will indeed have these new components that will likely last for years. But you will still have an 8-year-old screen, logic board and processor. And these will give out sooner than the new parts you have installed. So, it is likely that you will have partially robust insides, but the important components, like the logic board and processor will give out within a year or so. You should also note, you will still not be able to run the latest operating system (Big Sur). According to Apple, if certain conditions are met (your Mac has to be running Mojave to upgrade), Catalina (OS 10.15) is compatible. Since Catalina breaks the compatibility of older 32 bit software, many folks with older Macs find that the applications they depend on won’t run. And the success of running Catalina on an 8-year-old computer is spotty at best. And I feel your pain regarding the ability to play your CDs. I know many of us are still grumbling (including my husband) about Apple’s decision get rid of the internal optical drive. Apple did this to reduce weight and to promote the ever-expanding market of digital music. Since many music lovers are now moving to the mp3 download marketplace, CDs and vinyl recordings are becoming a thing of the past. But musicians (like me) still make CDs and some even are still recording to vinyl, since analog recordings are warmer than digital tracks. Newer models (as of 2013) do not have optical drives but you can purchase an external DVD/CD player that can attach to a new Mac. Apple’s USB Super Drive is around $80, and attaches via USB A, which means you will need a USB to USB-C adapter to use it on a new Mac. You can also share the CD/DVD drive of an older Mac across your network, but most of us want to be mobile with our laptops, so this is not always an option. So even though you can install these new components in your older laptop, in my opinion, it’s just wasted money. If you look at the life of your machine, you spend $1800 on your laptop and got 8 years of good service. That’s $225 a year. So. the idea of spending $500 to extend the life for maybe 1 more year does not make financial sense. And with the new M1 chip in the MacBook Air, now is a great time to buy a new laptop! Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com and themacmama.blogspot.com

articles.text: As our lives were transformed in the spring of 2020 as a result of the global pandemic, people turned to…baking bread. Yes, and this wasn’t the only pastime to surge in popularity as more time was being spent at home. Let’s take a look at the hobbies and activities that people have discovered or returned to as they adjusted to a new normal. While the hoarding and resulting shortage of toilet paper made headlines, another staple was disappearing from grocery store shelves: flour. In May, The Atlantic reported that one company saw baking flour sales increase 2,000%. On social media, people were sharing photos of their fresh baked goods and sourdough starters, while manufacturers and wheat producers had difficulties meeting demand. Presumably no one set out to grow their own wheat just to bake a few loaves of bread, but people did decide this was an ideal time to grow some of their own food; either out of fear about the stability of our food supply or finally having time to tend a vegetable garden. The Burpee Seed Company reported that they sold more seed in March 2020 than any time in its 144-year history. The interest was worldwide, not just in the United States, as would-be gardeners needed to learn how to start seedlings and manage their tracts of land. Some seed companies had to stop taking orders during this influx just to meet demand. Perhaps a few of the new gardeners will be practicing songs, as another surprise trend was a significant increase in orders of musical instruments, including grand pianos, according to an article in The New York Times. The demand seemed to come from families with children who needed something to do or could no longer go to their lessons in person, but also from throngs of people seeking out a form of relief in playing instruments. Other changes in behavior reported in the news over the last year have included a dramatic increase in hiking and camping, reading more books, and more person-to-person letter writing. What hobbies and activities have you adopted or renewed in your life since the global pandemic began? Which of these will you maintain as daily life begins to return to a more familiar state? articles.text: Ah, good old Piedmont. If they can make a poor decision, they will do it every time. I have lived in our house most of my life – since I was nine years old. My father had the house built. The amount of drama that has unfolded during all those years is amazing. I have heard in recent years that the school population has gone down because young families were not eagerly signing up for a house that cost millions. And so, the choice was made to allow children who had grandparents living in Piedmont to attend Piedmont schools, because the overall school population was getting smaller. As example, our class, PHS ‘64, was large, with 205 kids. I think that the decision to let grandchildren attend Piedmont schools is a good one. There have been children of City employees attending Piedmont schools as long as I can remember, and that diversity never upset the carefully crafted Piedmont applecart. One of the reasons that the school population has diminished is because not all the children who live in our city choose to go to Piedmont schools. Perhaps, the School Board and teachers should be asking themselves that question. Many parents and children choose a different route. Why? Piedmont schools are not a one-size-fits-all model. Let the grandchildren into the schools. The system will be better for that decision. They will bring a more diverse group, and a sense of Piedmont history with them (especially if the grandparents have lived here as long as we have). This is not rocket science; it is being inclusive and welcoming to children rather than exclusive. Children should not be made to feel unwelcome. It is our job as caring adults to give them a wonderful childhood. Welcome them now. Terry Sarver is a Piedmont High graduate, Class of 1964, and a resident for 65 years.
articles.title: The Piedmont Grandparents’ Rule

They have learned that even those seemingly insignificant encounters with folks in the grocery line or a passerby you might normally greet or even strike up a conversation with, are important to our well-being. Psychologists also attribute the rise of conspiracy thinking to this lack of holding each other in check through daily interaction. It made me wonder if my personal conspiracy was to pretend I was fine. Normal social interactions are like a bubbler in an aquarium, oxygenating the water. If the bubbler is cut off, the fish keep swimming but they are slowly being depleted of what they need to thrive. As our social oxygen is depleted, we become faint. We are not fine. The airlines teach us [in the event an emergency] to put our own oxygen mask on first. But what I realized that day in the vegetable aisle was that I needed to see myself on the other side of that equation. I spend most of my life trying to help others get some spiritual oxygen but this time I was the one discovering my need to have someone help me with my mask. It took a walk in my slippers through the vegetable aisle to hear God inviting me to accept some divine help. My strength was renewed by the invitation to be among those who needed oxygen, and I was given some hope that I was, indeed, going to make it – but this time I remembered that I will make it with God’s help. The bulletin directs healthcare providers to “use their clinical judgement” to vaccinate people “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk for morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 as a direct result of one or more of the severe health conditions.” The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found with the state’s guidance at the California Department of Public Health’s website at www.cdph.ca.gov. After Phase 1A, Phase 1B Tier 1 and people with underlying health conditions, the next group of people prioritized to receive the vaccine according to the state plan is Phase 1B Tier 2. This group includes workers in transportation, logistics, industrial, commercial, residential, sheltering facilities and critical manufacturing. It also includes people who live in congregate settings, like the incarcerated and the homeless. Likely, Phase 1B Tier Two will be eligible sometime in the spring. By the summer and fall of this year, anyone who wants to receive a COVID-19 vaccine should be able to receive it, the state believes. California is encouraging residents to utilize a new digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov. On the website, Californians can find out their eligibility and, if eligible, they can schedule a vaccination appointment. Those who are not eligible for vaccination can sign up for notifications when their turn is up. The state has administered over 6.2 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 8.1 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. Statewide, Phase 1A includes about 3 million people while Phase 1B Tier 1 includes another 8.5 million. LETTERS CONTINUED Continued from page 2 The Piedmont Grandparents’ Rule By Terry Sarver Ah, good old Piedmont. If they can make a poor decision, they will do it every time. I have lived in our house most of my life – since I was nine years old. My father had the house built. The amount of drama that has unfolded during all those years is amazing. I have heard in recent years that the school population has gone down because young families were not eagerly signing up for a house that cost millions. And so, the choice was made to allow children who had grandparents living in Piedmont to attend Piedmont schools, because the overall school population was getting smaller. As example, our class, PHS ‘64, was large, with 205 kids. I think that the decision to let grandchildren attend Piedmont schools is a good one. There have been children of City employees attending Piedmont schools as long as I can remember, and that diversity never upset the carefully crafted Piedmont applecart. One of the reasons that the school population has diminished is because not all the children who live in our city choose to go to Piedmont schools. Perhaps, the School Board and teachers should be asking themselves that question. Many parents and children choose a different route. Why? Piedmont schools are not a one-size-fits-all model. Let the grandchildren into the schools. The system will be better for that decision. They will bring a more diverse group, and a sense of Piedmont history with them (especially if the grandparents have lived here as long as we have). This is not rocket science; it is being inclusive and welcoming to children rather than exclusive. Children should not be made to feel unwelcome. It is our job as caring adults to give them a wonderful childhood. Welcome them now. Terry Sarver is a Piedmont High graduate, Class of 1964, and a resident for 65 years. In 1934 it cost $58.50 to send a boy to Camp Wallace Alexander for six weeks – including bus transportation. Mr. Alexander made only two charitable donations in his will; they were to the Piedmont Council ($5000) and the Piedmont Community Church ($2500). His estate was the largest the State of California had ever probated at that time. Evelyn Pattiani Craig stated in her book Queen of the Hills, “[The Alexanders’] prominence and generosity extended over a generation, becoming a constructive and dominating influence in the city’s progress.” Mrs. Alexander continued to donate to the Piedmont Council even after her husband’s death. As recorded in Board minutes, she gave at least $22,000 as well as $5000 earmarked to the church for the Scout Council’s building fund. The Church sponsored many of the original troops and provided a meeting place for them. Originally, all the troops met in the basement of the church. The Council Executive’s office was also located there. articles.text: In a speech to the Piedmont School Board on February 8, Superintendent Randy Booker offered the following comments. “I am feeling a tremendous amount of hope tonight. We are on the verge of returning more students to our campuses as COVID rates are on the decline. I am grateful for our partnerships with our teachers, staff, and administrators. And I am grateful for all of the support from our families. And I am especially grateful for the perseverance of our students. While I’m hopeful, it’s clear that the pandemic has taken a toll on our community in many ways, including diminishing the strong sense of mutual trust and respect between parents, teachers and school leaders that has been a hallmark of our community. I’ve had many painful conversations, especially during the last few weeks. Along with the Board, I am trying to listen carefully to the perspective of each and every person who reaches out or shares at a board meeting. Parents are frustrated that we were not able to open more grades last fall and that most students are still learning from home. Teachers are fearful about their own health and putting loved ones at risk as vaccinations remain difficult to obtain and new, more virulent strains of Covid-19 are reported. articles.text: I am often asked, as we enter February, if I have any suggestions for African American History month reading. This year I am suggesting: • A Promised Land by Barack Obama • His Truth is Marching On: John Lewis and the Power of Hope by John Meacham • Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents by Isabel Wilkerson • Jesus and the Disinherited by Howard Thurman As a pastor I have a particular interest in these books. They contain the stories of people who take their faith very seriously. They reflect the outlook of people who are truly committed to the well-being of others. They are accounts that touch, in the words of Amanda Gorman (National Youth Poet Laureate) the “unfinished” history of our nation and invite us to “lay down our arms so we can reach out our arms to one another.” They are works of enduring significance which include the stories of pastors and the issues we face.
