articles.text: Earlier this month Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a second reading of local energy efficiency ordinances, also called reach codes (Ordinances 750 and 751 N.S.). Reach codes are local building energy codes that reach beyond statewide requirements for energy use in building design and construction. Piedmont is one of the first cities nationwide to tie reach codes to renovations of existing residential buildings. This is a landmark achievement for local climate action. It also reflects steps toward meeting the community standards outlined in Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0. Reach codes address objectives set forth by the CAP 2.0, including increasing the use of solar energy systems and reducing natural gas use in residential buildings. Building energy is a primary cause of emissions in the City, comprising roughly half of Piedmont’s community emissions in 2018. Building energy in 2018 resulted in approximately 16,892 metric tons of CO2e, with most emissions coming from natural gas furnaces and water heaters. Measures such as the reach codes position the City to meet CAP 2.0 emissions reduction goals: reduce emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030 and 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. The ordinances are intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and achieve energy savings. They will also improve indoor air quality and health. Momentum continues to build towards enacting electrification reach codes. In addition to Piedmont, more than 40 cities and counties in California are considering or adopting local reach codes, with various approaches and requirements. This includes the nearby cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Albany, Alameda, Hayward, Fremont, Richmond, and San Francisco. Individually, these municipalities are designing pathways to reduce natural gas use and taking into account local sociocultural, political, and economic needs. Collectively, these efforts work towards achieving local and statewide climate action and energy goals. As Piedmont moves forward with the reach code approval process, including submission to the California Energy Commission and California Building Standards Commission, the City staff is preparing frameworks and resources geared at homeowners, contractors, and planners alike. These materials are forthcoming and will be posted on the City’s website. The City staff will also look to share best practices and lessons learned from the reach codes process. In turn, it is hoped that Piedmont’s reach codes will serve as a model for other municipalities that are considering the adoption of energy efficiency requirements. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be contacted at (510)420-3058 or adykman@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Reach Codes landmark: Local Climate Action initiatives approved

articles.text: No new cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont in the past seven days, representing a significant slowdown in new cases after a terrible winter surge rocked Piedmont, Alameda County and California. As of Monday, February 8, there have been 162 reported cases in the City in the past 11 months. Coronavirus continues to spread through the county, though. The number of daily new cases and the positivity rate are both significantly higher than in September and October of last year. Across Alameda County, 2,448 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, which represents about a 27 percent decrease in new cases week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 77,109. There have been 23,940 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,129 cases in Hayward. Tragically, 60 more people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County across the past seven days, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,051. Even though stricter stay-athome orders were lifted a few weeks ago, Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Only five counties in California – none of which are in the Bay Area – are not in the Purple Tier. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 4 percent, more than a full percentage point lower than one week ago. While the positivity rate is low enough that Alameda County could move into a less restrictive tier for reopening businesses and activities, the adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people in the county is 18.1. This figure needs to be below 7 for the county to reopen further, according to California’s current system. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,354,591 total cases of COVID- 19 in California, making it the hardest hit state by the virus by far. There have been 44,477 deaths due to the disease statewide.
articles.title: No new cases reported in Piedmont in a week

articles.text: People age 65 years and older, in addition to emergency services workers and essential education workers are among a new group of people that began receiving COVID-19 vaccines in Alameda County this week on Monday, February 8. The county first announced the change on Wednesday, February 3, saying that it would begin vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1 as defined by the state’s vaccination framework. Phase 1B Tier 1 includes people age 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This entire group of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Concurrently, people in Phase 1A continue to be vaccinated. This group includes healthcare workers and residents and staff of long-term care facilities. They were the first to be eligible when the first doses of vaccine arrived in December. In Alameda County, Phase 1A includes an estimated 145,000 people. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider or employer to receive a vaccination appointment. “We’ve made great progress on vaccinating health care workers in Phase 1A and are happy to be moving forward with Phase 1B,” wrote Dr. Kathleen Clanon, the county’s lead on vaccine planning. “Our strategy is to reach people who are at highest risk for severe illness and people who are at high risk for transmission because of where they live or work.” Alameda County waited a few weeks and continued to focus on Phase 1A before opening up eligibility to Phase 1B Tier 1. The state allowed counties to begin vaccinating the latter phase on January 26. Next week on Tuesday, February 16, the Oakland Coliseum is expected to open as a large vaccination site. Announced last week, the project is a partnership between the state and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). “This additional resource and infusion of vaccine is much needed in our community and will help us to reach more people more quickly,” said Colleen Chawla, director of the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency (HCSA). “We look forward to working with the site team to support outreach, education and access for our highest risk communities.” Gov. Gavin Newsom praised Alameda County’s vaccination efforts last week. “One county stands out in terms of their speed to administration, taking vaccines and getting people vaccinated, and that’s Alameda County,” Newsom said, adding, “I want to just recognize their partnership, their stewardship to the cause.” Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Only five counties in California – none of which are in the Bay Area – are not in the Purple Tier. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 4 percent, more than a full percentage point lower than one week ago. While the positivity rate is low enough that Alameda County could move into a less restrictive tier for reopening businesses and activities, the adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people in the county is 18.1. This figure needs to be below 7 for the county to reopen further, according to California’s current system. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,354,591 total cases of COVID- 19 in California, making it the hardest hit state by the virus by far. There have been 44,477 deaths due to the disease statewide. Vaccination for seniors begins in Alameda County Oakland Coliseum vaccination site to open next week By Barry Eitel People age 65 years and older, in addition to emergency services workers and essential education workers are among a new group of people that began receiving COVID-19 vaccines in Alameda County this week on Monday, February 8. The county first announced the change on Wednesday, February 3, saying that it would begin vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1 as defined by the state’s vaccination framework. Phase 1B Tier 1 includes people age 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This entire group of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Concurrently, people in Phase 1A continue to be vaccinated. This group includes healthcare workers and residents and staff of long-term care facilities. They were the first to be eligible when the first doses of vaccine arrived in December. In Alameda County, Phase 1A includes an estimated 145,000 people. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider or employer to receive a vaccination appointment. “We’ve made great progress on vaccinating health care workers in Phase 1A and are happy to be moving forward with Phase 1B,” wrote Dr. Kathleen Clanon, the county’s lead on vaccine planning. “Our strategy is to reach people who are at highest risk for severe illness and people who are at high risk for transmission because of where they live or work.” Alameda County waited a few weeks and continued to focus on Phase 1A before opening up eligibility to Phase 1B Tier 1. The state allowed counties to begin vaccinating the latter phase on January 26. Next week on Tuesday, February 16, the Oakland Coliseum is expected to open as a large vaccination site. Announced last week, the project is a partnership between the state and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). “This additional resource and infusion of vaccine is much needed in our community and will help us to reach more people more quickly,” said Colleen Chawla, director of the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency (HCSA). “We look forward to working with the site team to support outreach, education and access for our highest risk communities.” Gov. Gavin Newsom praised Alameda County’s vaccination efforts last week. “One county stands out in terms of their speed to administration, taking vaccines and getting people vaccinated, and that’s Alameda County,” Newsom said, adding, “I want to just recognize their partnership, their stewardship to the cause.” See Vaccination on page 30 Reach Codes landmark: Local Climate Action initiatives approved By Alyssa Dykman Earlier this month Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a second reading of local energy efficiency ordinances, also called reach codes (Ordinances 750 and 751 N.S.). Reach codes are local building energy codes that reach beyond statewide requirements for energy use in building design and construction. Piedmont is one of the first cities nationwide to tie reach codes to renovations of existing residential buildings. This is a landmark achievement for local climate action. It also reflects steps toward meeting the community standards outlined in Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0. Reach codes address objectives set forth by the CAP 2.0, including increasing the use of solar energy systems and reducing natural gas use in residential buildings. Building energy is a primary cause of emissions in the City, comprising roughly half of Piedmont’s community emissions in 2018. Building energy in 2018 resulted in approximately 16,892 metric tons of CO2e, with most emissions coming from natural gas furnaces and water heaters. Measures such as the reach codes position the City to meet CAP 2.0 emissions reduction goals: reduce emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030 and 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. The ordinances are intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and achieve energy savings. They will also improve indoor air quality and health. Momentum continues to build towards enacting electrification reach codes. In addition to Piedmont, more than 40 cities and counties in California are considering or adopting local reach codes, with various approaches and requirements. This includes the nearby cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Albany, Alameda, Hayward, Fremont, Richmond, and San Francisco. Individually, these municipalities are designing pathways to reduce natural gas use and taking into account local sociocultural, political, and economic needs. Collectively, these efforts work towards achieving local and statewide climate action and energy goals. As Piedmont moves forward with the reach code approval process, including submission to the California Energy Commission and California Building Standards Commission, the City staff is preparing frameworks and resources geared at homeowners, contractors, and planners alike. These materials are forthcoming and will be posted on the City’s website. The City staff will also look to share best practices and lessons learned from the reach codes process. In turn, it is hoped that Piedmont’s reach codes will serve as a model for other municipalities that are considering the adoption of energy efficiency requirements. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be contacted at (510)420-3058 or adykman@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Fireworks and family feasts At Chinese New Year celebrations people wear red clothes, decorate with poems on red paper, and give children and single people “crisp lucky money” in red envelopes or “hong bao.” Red symbolizes fire and good luck, which according to legend can drive away bad luck. The fireworks that shower the festivities also drive away evil spirits. Tangerines and oranges represent prosperity. On New Year, families clean their houses, wear new clothes, visit each other, get together for dinner and exchange food gifts. Due to COVID-19, there will be no Chinese New Year parade this year, but the Chinese Chamber of Commerce of San Francisco has commissioned several parade float artists to celebrate the Year of the Ox with 11 lifesized ox statues that now stand tall and proud at various locations across the city. One is even at the Oakland airport, and another at the San Francisco airport. There is one in Chinatown at Portsmouth Square and another at the Chinese Hospital. Photos by Mary Geong More oxen can be spotted downA large red ox, suitable for a Chinese New Year parade, on display. town in Union Square, Civic February 13, 2019 Center, Embarcadero 4, and History of Chinese Zodiac Salesforce Plaza. There’s also Legend has it that in ancient one at Pier 39. Gung Hay Fat Choy (Gong Xi Fa Cai) – “May you be happy and prosperous.” Lunar New Year is the longest and most important celebration in Asia, with over 1.5 billion people across the globe celebrating the new year in China, Vietnam, Korea, and Singapore for two weeks. Even during the Vietnam war, the Lunar New Year, a holiday called Tet, North and South Vietnamese forces would traditionally call a truce to allow soldiers to return to their families to celebrate. The Chinese year 4719, Year of the Ox, begins on Feb. 12, 2021. The Chinese use the lunar calendar, which has 13 months which explains why Lunar New Year changes every year. times, Buddha asked all the animals to meet him on Chinese New Happy Ox hunting! Year. But only 12 animals came. In order to decide their order in the Chinese Zodiac cycle, the animals held a very exciting race. The first one to cross the river to the finish line would be granted the first year, the second to come in would be the second animal in the cycle, and so on. The strong, hardworking Ox was in the lead with the Rat close by. Suddenly, the clever Rat asked the good-natured Ox for a ride on its back, but then at the last second before reaching shore, the ungrateful Rat jumped off on land to cross the finish line first to win the race. The Ox came in second, the Tiger third, and so on. The happy-go-lucky Pig took his time and came in last, and the Chinese Zodiac and its twelve signs were born... Buddha named a year after each animal and the cycle would repeat every 12 years. He announced that the people born in each animal’s year would have some of that animal’s personality. People under the Year of the Ox are usually hard working, honest, creative, ambitious, cautious, patient and handle things steadily. On the negative side, Ox people might be stubborn, narrow-minded, indifferent, prejudiced, slow and not good at communication. The Ox is a highly esteemed animal in Chinese culture because of the important role it plays in agriculture. Positive traits, such as hardworking and honest, are also attributed to the Ox. Their dedication and diligence make them ideal for professional and stressful positions such as doctors, lawyers, businessmen, politicians and teachers. Oxen are also renowned by society for their technical skills and effort in computer and engineering. Famous people like Barack Obama, Walt Disney, Princess Diana and George Clooney were born under the year of the ox. If you are an ox, this year you will be either age 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, or older. Oranges and tangerines are symbols of prosperity. Red envelopes and lucky money (hong bao).

articles.text: Marin County has had nearly all its public schools open since early last fall. They began opening up elementary and middle schools as early as September 8. With 18 school districts, almost 40,000 students and 7,000 staff, the county has had only 10 suspected in-school COVID-19 transmissions. They owe their success to a healthy relationship with a cooperative Marin County Public Health Department and lower COVID case counts than Alameda County. mont and other local school districts were still talking about possibly reopening classes, the Marin County district had logged a cumulative 800,000 student days. As of February 8, they had only 15 individual schools doing remote only learning. In the meantime, 101 schools (87 percent) were open with at least 10 percent of students in-person. Within the entire county there have been a total of 164 COVID- 19 positive cases for students, and 42 among staff. But only 10 transmissions are suspected to have occurred in school in the five months since last fall. To view their transmission and school data go to coronavirus. marinhhs.org/schools#status. “The true heroes in this are the teachers, classified staff and administration who have worked tirelessly with Public Health to bring our students back in-person,” said Marin County’s Superintendent Mary Jane Burke. While they don’t currently have high schools open, they have created in-person “Learning Hubs” for high schoolers. Hub sites are on campuses or at community centers like the YMCA, where students can do all their distance learning. The learning hubs provide a safe space, supportive adult supervision, social interaction with peers, and broadband internet access. Marin’s first Learning Hub opened at the same time as its elementary and middle schools, September 8. By December 29, 55 hubs were open in Marin County, serving 1,750 students. The Deputy Superintendent of the Marin County Office of Education, Terena Mares, described the advantage Marin County has over Alameda County: a healthy, pre-existing relationship with their Public Health Department. “We worked really closely and extensively with our County Public Health Department, and they were hugely instrumental in assisting us to create the safe kind of environments that they could put their seal on,” Mares said. “We have worked closely in the past with them on issues related to air quality and measles vaccination.” “Our public health officers have just been very approachable to work to ensure that when we open, we open safely in a way that recognizes that students are actually safer in person than they are while at home. The data is proving that,” Mares added. Those following the efforts to reopen schools in Alameda County have seen a far different story. In June, Alameda County’s Public Health Officer, Erica Pan, was promoted to the state level, thrusting Interim Officer Nicolas Moss into leadership during the greatest public health crisis in decades. Communication has not been clear between Alameda County’s public health office and schools. UCSF Professor of Epidemiology and Piedmont resident Dr. George Rutherford commented on another difference between the conditions in Marin County and Alameda County. “Marin has done a better job than others at keeping their most vulnerable [blue collar, multi-generation household] populations
articles.title: Marin: a county that knows how to keep schools open

But only 10 transmissions are suspected to have occurred in school in the five months since last fall. To view their transmission and school data go to coronavirus. marinhhs.org/schools#status. “The true heroes in this are the teachers, classified staff and administration who have worked tirelessly with Public Health to bring our students back in-person,” said Marin County’s Superintendent Mary Jane Burke. While they don’t currently have high schools open, they have created in-person “Learning Hubs” for high schoolers. Hub sites are on campuses or at community centers like the YMCA, where students can do all their distance learning. The learning hubs provide a safe space, supportive adult supervision, social interaction with peers, and broadband internet access. Marin’s first Learning Hub opened at the same time as its elementary and middle schools, September 8. By December 29, 55 hubs were open in Marin County, serving 1,750 students. The Deputy Superintendent of the Marin County Office of Education, Terena Mares, described the advantage Marin County has over Alameda County: a healthy, pre-existing relationship with their Public Health Department. “We worked really closely and extensively with our County Public Health Department, and they were hugely instrumental in assisting us to create the safe kind of environments that they could put their seal on,” Mares said. “We have worked closely in the past with them on issues related to air quality and measles vaccination.” “Our public health officers have just been very approachable to work to ensure that when we open, we open safely in a way that recognizes that students are actually safer in person than they are while at home. articles.text: We tend to think of attention as something simple. We are paying attention, or we are not. Actually, attention is a complex cognitive function which, like other multifaceted cognitive functions, matures throughout childhood. Inattention is undesirable, as is too much attention. But is distractibility a feature of attention, or a glitch? The goal is: efficient, flexible and voluntary control of our attentional resources. Nuanced attention is the basis for planning, organization, self-control and perseverance. Neuroscientists have identified the part of the brain that is important in being able to attend to one stimulus and ignore others (known as selective attention) as the prefrontal cortex. Maturation of the nervous system allows for changing from global to selective attention. Infants as young as 4 months of age attend to differences in their environment. At around 10 months of age infants can show signs of resistance to distractions. play focused attention, and by age 3, around the time many children enter preschool, their attention to task is increasing. Studies show that attention is somewhat malleable. For example, children in preschool and elementary school show decreased attention to distractors when given frequent instructions to do so. Parents and teachers can scaffold their instructions accordingly to increase the student’s attention and decrease attention to a distracting event. Children show decreased attention when experiencing distress or negative emotionality. Parents and teachers can focus on praise and warm, positive emotional environments which may correlate with improved attention. Why is selective attention critical for classroom success? Estimates are as much as 80% of classroom education is with a teacher talking and students attending, so selective attention is key. The classroom requires selective and sustained attention to a specific target (the teacher, or written materials) with the simultaneous ability to ignore distractions. One of the most common teacher/parent concerns is that their student is having trouble paying attention. The student may be “tuning out”, easily distracted, impulsive and looking around to see what everyone else is doing because he/she cannot sustain attention to the teacher. On the other hand, school activities such as art, P.E and team sports require less selective attention. In these classes more global attention is required, to pay attention to many details, sights and sounds simultaneously. When kids enter the formal school system, they are moving from the global attention of multi-sensory experiences such as play, sports and media to the selective attention of sitting still and selectively listening to a teacher. In the case of school-aged kids who are struggling with attention in the classroom, physiological issues to consider may be poor sleep, blood sugar imbalances, or vision or hearing issues. Psychological issues to consider may be anxiety, decreased confidence or perfectionism. Learning issues to consider may be sensory or auditory processing difficulties. Depending on the etiology of the observed attentional difficulties, treatment can include medication, parent training in behavior management, classroom interventions, as well as therapy. Katie Pengilly, MA,CCC,SLP, is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

A useful grandparenting skill you can develop is the ability to find ways to minimize your own needs to be right or in charge. Think about how to resolve the issue in a way that focuses on your grandchild’s needs and best interests. What would actually make things better for the grandchild? 3) Share your strengths Everyone is good at something! You have a unique set of strengths and weaknesses. You might be a wonderful chef but a tone-deaf musician. Perhaps you have been an amateur birdwatcher, yet you can’t name a single plant in your garden. You love to tell stories but forget every punchline of a good joke. Share your strengths! It takes no time at all for a grandchild to identify what Grandma and Grandpa are good at doing. Once they know, these are the activities they’ll ask you to do again and again. Your grandchildren will spend their lifetime having fun and learning with you, while you’re just going about doing the things you know you can do well. 4) Be a role model Your grandchildren are watching you. Notice how sensitive your grandchild is to your every mood. They see the occasional grumpy face and they know if you said something sharply to someone else. Your grandchildren might even expect you to be magically perfect all the time, and of course that is not possible. But when you can, find a way to be a role model for them. They will remember your words and actions much more than you can imagine. When you are kind, brave, strong, forgiving, it helps children find those same traits in themselves. Before you know it, you just might find them copying you without even realizing that they’re doing so. 5) Stay positive In the wise words of Max Ehrmann, author of Desiderata in 1927: “…With all its sham, drudgery and broken dreams, it is still a beautiful world. Be cheerful. Strive to be happy.” Positivity is contagious. Life can be tough, and sometimes is pretty disappointing. But when the respected adults in a child’s life have a positive approach to adversity, change, or the unknown, children automatically feel safe and optimistic. They begin to adopt the same approach to life, and are ready to meet the future head on. They learn to be confident and upbeat, and they develop an attitude that sets them up for positive interactions with other people and situations. At this point in history, nothing could be more important than imparting this positive approach to life to your grandchildren. Piedmont resident Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, she has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and now works exclusively with grandparents and their families. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents.

articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 198and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.

articles.text: A panel discussion titled “Embracing Clean Energy” will be held on February 25 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. as the first of three panel discussions as part of Readmont, the annual community read in Piedmont. This year’s selection is Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate. The panelists include: • Jessica Tovar of the Local Clean Energy Alliance in Oakland, an NGO working in advocacy for clean energy. (http:// localcleanenergy.org/) • Angel Fierro, husband of Millennium HS principal Shannon Fierro and co-partner of Plexus Solutions, which joins large scale clean energy projects with capital. http://www.plexussolutions.services/leadership • Dr. Max Auffhammer, George Pardee Jr. Professor of Sustainable Development and Associate Dean in the Division of Social Sciences at UC Berkeley. He is also an Assistant Professor of Agricultural and Resource Economics and International and Area Studies at UC Berkeley and Chair at the Political Economy, UC Berkeley. (https://onpointanalytics.com/ experts/maximilian-auffhammer/) This year, Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at Piedmont High School. To register, visit piedmontconnect.org/readmont-2021. The hope is that this common reading experience will forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members. The next event will be “Youth Summit on Environmental Justice” on April 24, an event open to high school students across the Bay Area, ready to take action to preserve the planet. All Piedmonters are encouraged to read This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate by Naomi Klein. The author argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied, but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. Copies are available for checkout at the PHS library. Interested readers can contact PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@ piedmont.k12.ca.us to borrow a copy. A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair Village is offering a 20% discount on this title.
articles.title: Part of Readmont 2021, the annual community read

It provides a solid foundation for beginners to gain more experience in various software and mechanical areas of robotics. Roses and Rivets hope to inspire more young girls to pursue a STEM career and overcome some gender bias that exists. Due to the pandemic, the robotics season last year and this has been difficult. It has significantly impacted kids’ learning. The team has gathered different STEM engineering activities for kids and compiled them in a pamphlet available in the link shown below. Team members have grouped the activities together with different levels of difficulty. Most of the materials needed for these activities are available around the house. articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council, BSA has announced a year-long celebration with a virtual auction, an opportunity to honor someone special, and the annual recognition dinner the week of March 17-25. The campaign will celebrate the centennial year of the Piedmont Scout Council as a chartered organization with the Boy Scouts of America. Titled “You Raise Me Up”, the campaign aims to raise awareness of Piedmont Scouts and their contributions to the community over 100 years. Chartered on March 21, 1921, the Piedmont Scout Council is one of the largest youth development organizations in the city. Its focus is character-building and teaching important life skills in leadership, citizenship, scholarship, sportsmanship and outdoorsmanship. Piedmont Scouts have evolved through the years and support the pursuits of over 1,000 boys and girls, ages 5-17 across a variety of programs, including Cub Scouts, Scouts, Explorers, Venturers and Piedmont Language School. The “Raise Me Up” campaign launches on March 17 with a virtual auction and will culminate on March 25 with a virtual version of the annual recognition dinner for community volunteers. The entire community is invited to participate in the auction and to honor their favorite Scout, Scout leader or someone important with an engraved anniversary brick. Each brick will be $100 and enshrined in a manner to be announced. Registration is free and open to the community. The auction will offer a variety of items, including vacations at beautiful vacation homes, food and wine, and themed gift baskets. Access to the auction, anniversary commemorative bricks, and recognition dinner is available at www.piedmontbsa.org. To learn more contact Kate Benson at the Scout Council office, tel. 547-4493 or by e-mail at Katherine.benson@scouting.org. Visit the Scout Council also on www.piedmontbsa.org, Facebook (www. facebook.com/PiedmontBSA) and Instagram (PiedmontBSA). History of Piedmont Scouting Piedmont Scouts have proudly served the community since 1910 when the first troop overnight event was held in Redwood Canyon in Oakland. The council was chartered eleven years later, in 1921, by the National Boy Scouts of America. Although it is one of the oldest and smallest councils in the nation, it is widely recognized for its excellence and traditions of service and quality programs. Year after year more than 50% of the eligible youth in Piedmont participate in the council’s many programs, with more than 1000 boys and girls. In support of these youth are 300 adult volunteers and three full-time staff members.

articles.text: Students for Solar, a team of 12 PHS and MHS students, are working to raise $400,000 to pay for solar panels on the new STEAM building. So far they have secured a $20,000 pledge from the school board in addition to other donations from the Piedmont community. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, February 10, 2021 “Embracing Clean Energy” panel discussion Feb. 25 Part of Readmont 2021, the annual community read A panel discussion titled “Embracing Clean Energy” will be held on February 25 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. as the first of three panel discussions as part of Readmont, the annual community read in Piedmont. This year’s selection is Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate. The panelists include: • Jessica Tovar of the Local Clean Energy Alliance in Oakland, an NGO working in advocacy for clean energy. (http:// localcleanenergy.org/) • Angel Fierro, husband of Millennium HS principal Shannon Fierro and co-partner of Plexus Solutions, which joins large scale clean energy projects with capital. http://www.plexussolutions.services/leadership • Dr. Max Auffhammer, George Pardee Jr. Professor of Sustainable Development and Associate Dean in the Division of Social Sciences at UC Berkeley. He is also an Assistant Professor of Agricultural and Resource Economics and International and Area Studies at UC Berkeley and Chair at the Political Economy, UC Berkeley. (https://onpointanalytics.com/ experts/maximilian-auffhammer/) This year, Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at Piedmont High School. To register, visit piedmontconnect.org/readmont-2021. The hope is that this common reading experience will forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members. The next event will be “Youth Summit on Environmental Justice” on April 24, an event open to high school students across the Bay Area, ready to take action to preserve the planet. All Piedmonters are encouraged to read This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate by Naomi Klein. The author argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied, but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. Copies are available for checkout at the PHS library. Interested readers can contact PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@ piedmont.k12.ca.us to borrow a copy. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Tourists from outside the continent are missing in action on the Paris scene and have been since early last March. If only the City we know had not gone missing with them. Anyone can have a look at the Eiffel Tower, but the thrill of riding to the top isn’t an option. Parks are open, though the winter weather isn’t terribly cooperative and stingy with brief spots of sun. Sacré-Coeur, the Basilica of the Sacred Heart is open daily in Montmartre; but Notre Dame Cathedral remains closed since the fire almost two years ago, and construction work is stalled. The Champs-Elysées is open for strolling the shops, but no cafés, bars or eateries. The grands magasins, department stores Galleries Lafayette and B.H.V., a stone’s throw from our apartment, just closed again due to viral resurgence. On the Left Bank, Boulevard Saint-Germain offers an almost two-mile stretch of fascinating stores, most of them open, but here, too, the museums – d’Orsay, Rodin (except its sculpture garden), Musée of the Moyen Âge (Cluny) remain closed. Pompidou Center, Carnavalet Musée, National Picasso, and all Right Bank museums are temporarily closed. Saint-Chapelle, the most soulful chapel in Paris, is temporarily closed. Père Lachaise Cemetery is open daily, though its windy hillside is a freezing climb in winter. Boutique windows change outfits on mannequins frequently, and we gawk in passing, but who’s dressing alluringly nowadays? We’re home in sweats. But this is Paris, and it’s a shame to stay away. It’s just, as masked-up browsers we feel a tad awkward that the shops are overheated. An outside queue isn’t that unusual, and even the post office locks the door and counts patrons. We tend to do just the necessary, decide fast, and leave. People do not stroll. Browse and pandemic don’t go together. Most any evening we’re scrambling to finish errands ahead of the 6 p.m. curfew. In a case of nutty planning, retired people are free to shop at 10 a.m., right? Near curfew, a shopkeeper stands sentry to ease late shoppers out the door and tell late arrivals to come back the next day. Michael compares life to an occupied Paris we’ve only read about. Winter paints the days grayer, but it’s a color that Paris wears well. When a pleasant walk in a mist or fine drizzle suddenly turns to pelting rain, we curse our forgotten gloves as cold hands stiffen while digging out the house keys. One doesn’t dream of sunny California, but gimme shelter. There just isn’t any. Hammurabi Code of laws weighs four tons and is chiseled the full 360º perimeter. The original stele resides at the Louvre. Replicas exist in many locales, including: The National Museum of Tehran, Iran; the United Nations, and at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City; Northwestern University’s Pritzker Law School, Chicago; UNESCO Museum, Berlin; Russia’s Museum of European Fine Arts; and in Istanbul, the Netherlands, and Jerusalem. When café seating is permitted again, the Galerie Véro-Dodat makes a charming stop under a covered passageway. Located between Rue JeanJacques Rousseau Rue du Bouloi in the 1e arrondissement, we traverse this walking home from the Louvre. Practically no pedestrian is at the Tuileries during a recent chilly winter day. This lovely 17th C. garden stretches from the Louvre’s Pont du Carrousel west to the Place de la Concorde. Pompidou Center, Carnavalet Musée, National Picasso, and all Right Bank museums are temporarily closed. Saint-Chapelle, the most soulful chapel in Paris, is temporarily closed. Continued from page 10 shaped symbols developed by the brilliant Sumerian civilization of Mesopotamia, now modern-day Iraq. Counting and bookkeeping likely kickstarted the need for written language, starting with numbers to keep track of grain sales. Hammurabi was the most famous Babylonian king, and the laws established procedural rules; rules to govern commerce; and family matters such as divorce and inheritance. The laws set out fines and punishments. By modern standards, many were harsh. If someone accuses an elder of a crime who’s found not guilty, the accuser could be put to death. Thieves were also put to death. The penalty was scaled to a person’s social stratum, and there were three groupings: the propertied class, freedmen, and slaves. Within each social stratum, the penalties were applied justly; so, it was deemed fair justice. The penalty for assaulting a person from a lower class was lighter than the act against a person of equal or higher class. Bias was rampant: a married woman received harsh punishment for adultery. The lovers were tied together and thrown into the water, while a man was permitted his dalliances with the servants. The code is one of the earliest judicial laws to establish the presumption of innocence. On the other hand, a doctor whose wealthy patient dies could have his hands cut off. The Hammurabi stele was discovered in 1901 during a French archeological dig of Susa, later a part of Persia. The stele, when found in Southern Iran 250 miles from the center of Hammurabi’s kingdom, was broken into three pieces. It was pillaged by the Elamites and moved to their Susa capital as spoils of mid-12th century B.C. warring. The French packed and The twin of the Lion of Mari is displayed at National Museum of Aleppo, Syria. The matched pair adorned a temple entry. The gargoyle design on bronze plate metal is of the upper body and head of a lion. shipped the stele to the Louvre, and within a year the stele was translated and publicized as the world’s first written legal code. According to Yale University archives in 1903, many laws bear striking parallels to the Hebrew Old Testament written possibly in 600 B.C. Lion of Mari I was drawn to a curious oxidized-green, bronze figure in a glass display case in the main gallery at the Louvre. Attracted by his huge, terrifying eyes, I initially took it for an angry frog, but as I drew closer to the truncated upper torso and fierce head, I realized it was instead a highly stylized lion. A pair of bronze lions was found during French excavations at Mari, a wealthy Euphrates-side city that flourished in the 22nd century B.C. France ruled Syria under a League of Nations mandate following World War I, and when local Bedouins discovered the buried city in 1933, they turned it over to the French archeologists digging all over Syria. Mari’s history as a city and regional super-power began in 2950 B.C., and the civilization thrived until wiped out by tribal wars. From the unearthed treasures, Mari was pieced together. Its rise began on an inhospitable Euphrates riverbend and eventually cornered the market in metal goods production in Northern Mesopotamia. The pair of bronze lions was dedicated to a god known as King of the Land and graced the interior of a temple in the city’s sacred precinct. Only the lion gargoyles’ forequarters are represented ,with wild eyes inlaid with limestone and shale. These are not castings; bronze sheet metal tacked with copper rivets and attached to wood frames shaped the animals. No wood survives centuries of burial. The pair was separated with one sent to the Louvre and the other retained in Syria on display at the National Museum of Aleppo. articles.text: Adri McAuliffe (left), Aya Troyer, and Ellie Black were part of last year’s varsity team. Cross-country and girls tennis are fall sports. But this year they will be competing in the spring, combining their seasons with track & field and boys’ tennis. Due to massive rescheduling caused by the coronavirus pandemic and the high school having been closed for 11 months, everyone wants to make the new gerrymandered schedule work. “We’re just happy to have tennis back,” said tennis coach Jim Landes. Out of necessity, he will be coaching the girls’ team and boys’ team concurrently, squeezing in enough matches for each team to have a relatively full season. “It’s not a season for the record books this year. We’re there to have fun. It will look different, but we’re happy to have competition again. It’s a season we’ll be playing by ear,’ he added. Later this month, the coed cross-country and track & field teams will toe the line for the school’s first official athletic competition since boys’ lacrosse closed out March 2020. On February 27, the Western Alameda County Conference will hold a virtually timed twomile event, officially the first cross-country meet of the season. The event is the first of just four for cross-country, which will likely occur at the Witter Field track. However, the league is still scrambling to finalize official locations for each of the four cross-country events. “We have meet dates, but we aren’t sure how the meets are going to transpire yet,” said PHS cross-country and track coach Jeanine Holmlund. “Some events for cross-country are up in the air because the issue is where can we run?” Piedmont’s running programs will both compete in the Foothill Division against Bishop O’Dowd, Alameda, Berkeley, San Leandro, Castro Valley, and possibly Hayward. But instead of the usual meets with three or four schools, the league will focus strictly on dual meets between two schools. Cross-country dates are on Saturdays, Feb. 27, March 13, March 27, a possible league championship on April 10, and possible makeup dates from April 12-17. Track, meanwhile, has seven possible meets, including a league championship. Piedmont will compete as follows: at Bishop O’Dowd on Saturday, March 6, hosting Castro Valley on Wednesday, March 10, at Photo by Dennis Mockel Cross-country at Piedmont High starts on Saturday, February 27 with a virtual meet (see below). It will be the first of four meets. Ellie Black at last year’s NCS Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Boys varsity runner Collin Mortimer at last year’s WACC Finals at Hayward High. Berkeley Wednesday, March 17, at Hayward Saturday, March 20, hosting San Leandro Wednesday, March 24, hosting Alameda Sat, April 3. The WACC championship is listed for Saturday, April 17. The annual league championship for running sports occurs at Hayward High, but the status of sports at Hayward is not decided. “A big question is whether or not we’d be allowed to run at Hayward High School because they are not as organized with their sports. We’re not sure if they’ve started anything at all, even conditioning. If Hayward High is not meeting yet, would they allow events at their school?” Homlund asked. Along with track and field’s meet on Saturday, March 6, it also marks the return to official competition for the boys’ and girls’ tennis programs at Piedmont High. PHS tennis will have both programs run concurrently, playing eight total matches – two each against the four other schools in the Foothill Division of WACC: Alameda, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, and Castro Valley. Tennis Similar to running sports, tennis’ official format is also considered “up in the air” a mere weeks ahead of the first match on March 6 against Castro Valley.

articles.text: The sports journalism world is an important fraternity. Like much of the world, the last 12 months have been difficult, but most particularly the last two weeks, when three sports journalists died. Terez A. Paylor, Yahoo Sports & Kansas City Star Paylor, an award-winning sports journalist while with the Kansas City Star, passed away unexpectedly on Tuesday, February 9. He was only 37 years old. Pedro Gomez, ESPN Gomez worked as a reporter for ESPN from 2003 until his passing, primarily covering baseball. He passed away on Sunday, February 7 at age 58. Chris Wesseling, Around the NFL Wesseling was a longtime member of NFL.com. He passed away on Friday, February 5 after battling cancer. Sekou Smith, NBA reporter Smith passed away at age 48 due to complications from COVID-19 on Jan. 26. He covered Atlanta basketball with Turner Sports since 2009. Vaughn McClure, ESPN McClure covered the Atlanta Falcons with ESPN since 2013. He died in October 2020, also at age 48.
articles.title: Remembering sports journalists lost in 2020-21

articles.text: The tennis Pride of Piedmont, Mackie McDonald, made the fourth Australian Open appearance of his career on Monday, February 9, upsetting No. 82 Marco Cecchinato of Italy in four sets of the Grand Slam in Melbourne, 3-6, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2. He will play a second-round match today, Wednesday, February 10, at 4:00 p.m. on ESPN’s streaming service. His opponent is Borna Coric of Croatia, ranked No. 22 in the tournament. McDonald, ranked 192 on the ATP ladder, dispatched Cecchinato in Monday’s meeting, logging 14 aces, a career high in Grand Slams for the former UCLA Bruin and Piedmont Highlander. He had a sparkling ace percentage of 14.7, marking a record for him in Major matches with a best-of-five format. After dropping his first set due to a few unforced errors, Mackie found his stroke to dominate throughout the remaining match, committing just 24 unforced Photo courtesy of Australian Open McDonald recorded 14 aces against Cecchinato with a percentage of 14.7, both career highs in Grand Slam best-of-five matches. Photo courtesy of McDonald’s official Instagram Mackenzie “Mackie” McDonald won his first-round match at the Australian Open on Monday, defeating Italy’s Marco Cecchinato in four sets; 3-6, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2. errors for the duration of the ners compared to the Italian’s match. He won the second set in nine games, 6-3, with a powerful ace – his seventh at the time, while closing the third set with his 11th and 12th aces to win 6-2. The fourth went just as smoothly, winning in eight games 6-2. Cecchintano didn’t do himself many favors by committing two double faults and 10 forced errors. McDonald is characterized by his speed on the court; able to move along the baseline and to the front of the net. He scored 15 points at the net in 26 approaches. He is also a strong return specialist. Against Cecchitano, McDonald had 40 points as the receiver, notching six return winzero. Coric is coming off a 23-ace performance against Argentina’s Guido Pella, winning in three sets: 6-3, 7-6 (7-5), 7-5. This week marks the start of the optical phenomenon as with the sight progressively becoming stronger until the end of the month on February 27. The best anticipated day is on Sunday, February 21 from 5:28 p.m. to 5:40 p.m. the best viewing times. It provided a unique starting point for a long day of hiking on Montara Mountain. El Granada’s Quarry Park was the initial site of the town’s “Burnham Plan” in 1906, a concentric-circular street layout designed by Daniel Burnham, an influential city planner in the late 1890s, The idea was for El Granada’s structure to resemble that of other seaside resort towns as a means of attracting tourists on their way to San Francisco on the Ocean Shore Railroad. (Hikers alert: the bones are fake.) automobile, resulting in the plan being abandoned. In 1995, San Mateo County purchased the land as a community park. The large 40-foot labyrinth was constructed in 2012 by artist Lars Howell on “World Labyrinth Day,” the first Saturday of May. Along with granite around the old quarry that dates back to the mesozoic-era, large non-native eucalyptus trees tower above and provide an unmistakable fresh fragrance. After 1.5 miles of hiking on the Middle Ridge Trail which merges with the Bus Trail, hikers will gain 900 feet in elevation to ascend above the tree line to Montara Mountain. The dirt road becomes paved as hikers continue up the path for another 1.2 miles, adding 400 feet in elevation to your climb. On the way and slightly off the beaten path is an unusual trailmarker called “God’s Trailhead,” where the trail merges with the Clipper Ridge Trail to continue up the mountain. Hikers will come to another junction after one mile. Turning right takes you to Mount Montara’s Southern Peak, an easier 1.5-mile climb of only 400 feet Staff Photos El Granada on the San Mateo coast has a stone labyrinth at its Quarry County Park. The circular maze, created in 2012, is 40 feet in diameter. A view of El Granada, the Pillar Point Air Force Station, and Pillar Point Harbor. in elevation. Turning left onto Scarpers Trail, however, leads you toward Mount Montara’s Northern Peak, four miles away, and another 900 feet of elevation gain. Visitors will enjoy the sweeping view of the Pacific Ocean and town of El Granada far below. From the top, you can see the Pillar Point Air Force Station tower, the Eddie Andreini Sr. Airfield, and Pillar Point harbor. Our 9.5-mile day to the Southern Peak provided an invigorating trek of over 2,100 feet gain in elevation. If solitude is what you’re seeking, this is the place. In addition to getting some great lower-leg work, we passed only eight other people during the hike. Quarry Park also includes some downhill portions with berms made for mountain biking. Without a mountain biker in sight, this would be an ideal location for a technical and arduous course. Another friendly reminder: It is now Crab Season, so it would behoove morning hikers to visit the Pillar Point Harbor to take advantage of local fishermen’s freshest catches of the day. Punch in “Quarry Park, El Granada” or “Quarry Park loop trail parking” into your GPS device to access these trails. The view toward Montara Mountain’s Northern peak. Montara Mountain’s Southern Peak has more views of the rolling hills above El Granada and Half Moon Bay.

articles.text: Bill and Mary Geong pose for a photo during a cruise while celebrating their 42nd wedding anniversary. Bill and Mary Geong plan on having a casual Valentine’s Day at home this year, with one caveat: Mary will not be cooking dinner. Instead, they will be ordering in from her favorite restaurant, Commis, and reflect on their 45 years together. The couple’s history goes back farther than 1976, though; they actually first met in high school in San Francisco. They were in the same homeroom, but didn’t really get to know each other until after graduation. At the time, Mary worked a part-time job in the Tenderloin district. Bill, she said, would routinely offer to walk her to work whenever they found each other riding the same city bus. “He was always offering to walk me to work, and he called me a lot… I thought, this guy must really like me!” Mary said with a smile. They dated for about a year in college, and then decided to “part ways,” and Mary took a one-year teaching job in New Jersey. The calls from Bill didn’t stop, though; one day he called her when she was on the East Coast and she told him that she was ready to return to California, noting that the change of seasons on the East Coast was not for her. “I experienced it for one year, but I wanted to come home after my one-year contract was up. I was homesick, I guess I just wasn’t accustomed to the cold. He asked me when I would be arriving, and that he would pick me up from the airport,” she recalled. “I thought, why not? Someone can help me with my luggage.” Years later, the couple got engaged and then married in 1976. They moved from San Francisco to Oakland, and then eventually moved to Piedmont in search of a competent school district for their growing family. Their daughters, Jennifer and Danielle, both attended Piedmont schools. Jennifer and her husband live in Belarus, and Danielle and husband live in Washington D.C. Bill and Mary are able to keep in touch thanks to our now omni-digital landscape. Asked if Valentine’s Day is significant for the couple, Mary said that she and Bill are very traditional in their celebrations. Dinner reservations at a nice restaurant in town are the norm. The pandemic will weather those plans just a bit, but they still plan on ordering from Commis, a two-star Michelin restaurant on Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. “And every Valentine’s Day, I remind my husband to get me some flowers,” Mary said with a chuckle. Valentine’s Day is actually secondary to the couple this year. A holiday with much more significance is Lunar New Year, which is roughly a week after Valentine’s Day. Mary was born during the Year of the Ox, the animal within the Chinese Zodiac that is observed this New Year. Lunar New Year begins on February 12, just two days before Valentine’s Day, and culminates with festivities on February 20. Mary confessed that she will be busy preparing celebratory activities for her colleagues at Oakland Rotary Club. The Geongs’ relationship with the holiday, like their marriage, goes back many years: Mary is a member of the Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC), a group that was founded in the late 1980s. She has served on its board for more than 20 years and was its former president. During her time on the board, PAAC expanded its membership to include a more diverse group of Asians, to include students from Burmese, Indian, Filipino and Korean cultures. It is one of the longest-standing organizations in the city. In addition to organizing upcoming virtual events, as a Certified Public Accountant, Mary will be especially busy this tax season. That makes a night in with Bill and a Michelin-approved meal an especially welcome respite, she admitted. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman and his wife Lisa will be celebrating their 25th anniversary in the summer this year. For this story, the Schermans made time to discuss their relationship, even though it was on Lisa’s birthday and Super Bowl Sunday, a big event for the couple and their three sons. This Valentine’s Day they will be remembering how they met, a tale that had both of them laughing and glowing visibly even through the phone. The sparks literally flew when Ted and Lisa first met. It was at a bonfire at The Lair of the Bear Campground outside the town of Strawberry in 1990. Both Ted and Lisa were on the UC Berkeley tennis team at the time and the bonfire was for all the staff and counselors at a summer tennis camp. Strawberry is in Tuolumne County off State Route 108.. Ted had already graduated but was at the camp because his coach was there and so were his former teammates. As luck would have it, he would meet the teammate of his life there as well. Asked what she remembered about meeting Ted, Lisa laughed heartily and said, “It was really funny, I saw him and this thought came into my head ‘I’m going to marry that person.’ I was all of 19.” After the bonfire Ted invited Lisa to play pool at the Berry, a bar in the town with a population of possibly 10 people. They had a nice time, Lisa recalled. The new tandem won their pool matches, a power couple from the start. The next day Lisa was dismayed that she could not find Ted. “I was asking around, where did that cute guy go?” she said. He was gone. In the middle of the night Ted had to leave the camp, and head back to Berkeley due to a painful attack of shingles which prevented him from sleeping. Three months later, Lisa got separated from her friends walking to Memorial Stadium for The Big Game, Cal vs. Stanford. “I kept looking for my friends, wondering where they were, thinking they were probably scattered. Before I could really look for them, I heard someone saying, ‘Lisa!’ I looked across and it was Ted. We ended up watching the Big Game together.” After the game, Lisa’s “hippie-friend Barb” whom Lisa had met once, invited Ted, Lisa and Ted’s friends to a party at the Lothlorien, the vegetarian co-op in the hills. The caveat is that it was a bit of a risqué and unusual event, a food party where you can’t feed yourself and there are no utensils. Ted’s friends all said no, and Lisa said she had a split-second thought that “If Ted says no, he might be too conservative for me.” Ted jumped at the opportunity, saying “I’ll go!” So off they went to Lothlorien, a beautiful 100-year-old building known for its arts and activism since the 70s. Inside, there was a giant chocolate fountain, and lots of fruit for fondue. Lisa recalled the events fondly. ”It was so fun, and this song by Spandau Ballet that goes “I Know This Much is True” was playing and we danced to that. We had our first kiss there, and the rest is history.” Valentine’s Day is more like Valentine’s Week in the Scherman BETWEEN GILMAN & BUCHANAN ST. 1081 Eastshore Hwy. Berkeley
articles.title: Ted and Lisa Scherman’s secret to relationship success: laughter

Asked what she remembered about meeting Ted, Lisa laughed heartily and said, “It was really funny, I saw him and this thought came into my head ‘I’m going to marry that person.’ I was all of 19.” After the bonfire Ted invited Lisa to play pool at the Berry, a bar in the town with a population of possibly 10 people. They had a nice time, Lisa recalled. The new tandem won their pool matches, a power couple from the start. The next day Lisa was dismayed that she could not find Ted. “I was asking around, where did that cute guy go?” she said. He was gone. In the middle of the night Ted had to leave the camp, and head back to Berkeley due to a painful attack of shingles which prevented him from sleeping. Three months later, Lisa got separated from her friends walking to Memorial Stadium for The Big Game, Cal vs. Stanford. “I kept looking for my friends, wondering where they were, thinking they were probably scattered. Before I could really look for them, I heard someone saying, ‘Lisa!’ I looked across and it was Ted. We ended up watching the Big Game together.” After the game, Lisa’s “hippie-friend Barb” whom Lisa had met once, invited Ted, Lisa and Ted’s friends to a party at the Lothlorien, the vegetarian co-op in the hills. The caveat is that it was a bit of a risqué and unusual event, a food party where you can’t feed yourself and there are no utensils. Ted’s friends all said no, and Lisa said she had a split-second thought that “If Ted says no, he might be too conservative for me.” Ted jumped at the opportunity, saying “I’ll go!” So off they went to Lothlorien, a beautiful 100-year-old building known for its arts and activism since the 70s. Inside, there was a giant chocolate fountain, and lots of fruit for fondue. Lisa recalled the events fondly. ”It was so fun, and this song by Spandau Ballet that goes “I Know This Much is True” was playing and we danced to that. We had our first kiss there, and the rest is history.” Valentine’s Day is more like Valentine’s Week in the Scherman See Scherman on page 30 I am a poet I am a storyteller I am a guardian of animals I am a lover of life Maré Simonet-Champlin, Resident at The Point in Rockridge Independent, Assisted Living, Memory Care Our community is full of great people like Maré. articles.text: Russ Griffith and Amy Whalen grew up three blocks apart from each other in Piedmont and one grade apart but never really knew each other growing up. Ten years after graduating from PHS they met and never looked back. Now, as Mr. and Mrs. Griffith they have started the next generation of Piedmonters with their two kids Jamie, 6, and Poppy, 3. This Valentine’s Day, the couple hopes to take time to reflect on their past and to see the beauty in their present. “For us, Valentine’s day is an excuse to just have a really nice meal. Sometimes with kids it can be hard to just sit down and have a conversation for 10 minutes. I hope to stay present and realize how lucky we are to live in Piedmont, and to be healthy. This year that takes on a whole new meaning,” Amy said. “On Valentine’s Day I think of how funny it is that we grew up three blocks away from each other and barely said anything to each other. But then, we met when we were in our late 20s when we were living almost on opposite sides of the planet from each other and it was kind of love at first sight.” “On Valentine’s Day it is nice to think of how we fell in love and got married,” Russ said. I was kind of confused because I was in this long-term relationship. I was thinking that you can’t really like someone you just met,” Amy recounted. Amy cut ties with her previous boyfriend a week after meeting Russ and booked a flight to visit Russ in London a week after that. They had a Friday to Sunday action-packed weekend getaway. They saw a play, the musical Avenue Q, went to an art show and a football match. They even had their first kiss in Westminster’s Trafalgar Square. Amy and Russ stuck with the long-distance relationship and made it work. “We wrote love letters, well, they were love e-mails,” Amy explained. “Also, we had a communication schedule, because he was eight hours ahead. We would talk for one hour every day. We normalized long distance dating by showing each other our outfits every day. In doing so you show each other your lives as they really are.” “It shows each other your humanity and personality in a really intimate way,” she added. Eight months into their relationship Russ moved back to the Bay Area and two months later they were engaged. A year later, August 13, 2011, they were husband and wife. Their wedding was on the beach of the Kona Coast of Hawaii, with 30 family members and 10 friends. Russ described it as feeling like a weeklong vacation with a wedding in the middle. This Valentine’s Day the Griffiths hope to get a fancy meal, a little free time to reflect, and as Amy requested, “lots of chocolate for me.” Their story of how they met and the distances they overcame to be with one another makes for a perfect tale to be told and remembered on Valentine’s Day. articles.text: Piedmont couple Hari Titan and his wife Roopal Desai are looking forward to spending their Valentine’s Day rather constructively this year – with a home improvement project. As a gift to his wife of 18 years, Hari said he plans on replacing the windows in their home after receiving the green light from the city to begin the project. Roopal said she is looking forward to the improvement, since both she and Hari have been observing strict stay-at-home orders since March one year ago. The couple does not plan on having a traditional Valentine’s Day dinner out at a restaurant due to the current health crisis. “We do the usual every year – dinner out or a movie,” Roopal said. “This year is definitely different – a more practical Valentine’s Day.” Hari added that the gift of manual labor trumps the traditional chocolates and flowers. “What says ‘I love you’ more than diamonds?” Hari said with a chuckle. Hari, a Ph.D Data Scientist, has been working remotely throughout the pandemic, but Desai, a physician with a specialty in Internal Medicine, will be working an overnight shift at Kaiser Permanente Medical Center. She added that she was immersed in her work when she first met Hari in Alameda 20 years ago in 2001. “I was completing my residency [at Alameda County Medical Center] and was working such long shifts,” she recalled. “My friends and family would ask me, how will you meet someone when you’re always so busy working?” The couple met through mutual friends, which was convenient for Roopal, who quipped, “I didn’t have to go out and look for someone.” Roopal and Hari were married in 2003 and moved with their son and daughter to Piedmont in 2008. Since then, the couple has been active throughout the community and the schools. Now, the couple has focused on a very pertinent goal – getting kids back for in-class instruction safely. They hope their decision to spend this special holiday at home will set an example for others to do the same. articles.text: Ashara Ekundayo San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora will host a forum on Tuesday, February 16 with guest curator Ashara Ekundayo in conversation with Yoruba Richen and Maori Holmes. The Zoom event will begin at 4 p.m. The forum, entitled “Blatant,” is a “live zine” series authored by Ekundayo that focuses on experiences of Black female artists. It is presented in conjunction with Ekundayo’s “Artist As First Responder” platform, a monthly discussion that highlights artists whose creative practices help heal communities. Richen is an award-winning documentary filmmaker. Her film, How it Feels To Be Free, premiered on PBS’s American Masters in January last month. Recent films include, The New York Times Presents: The Killing of Breonna Taylor, which premiered on FX and Hulu, and The Sit In: Harry Belafonte Hosts the Tonight Show, which was broadcast on MSNBC and is streaming on Peacock. Holmes is a curator, filmmaker and writer. She founded BlackStar in 2012 and serves as its Artistic Director and CEO. She has organized programs in film at a myriad of organizations including Anthology Film Archives, Los Angeles’ Museum of Contemporary Art, The Underground Museum, and the Whitney Museum of American Art. To reserve a place on Zoom, click on: https://www.moadsf.org/ event/blatant-a-forum-on-art-joyand-rage-8/?instance_id=15913.
articles.title: Museum of African Diaspora to host forum with Ashara Ekundayo on Feb. 16

articles.text: San Francisco Opera is making archived performances available for free through its “Opera is On” streaming series. Next up is Mozart’s romantic comedy, Cosi Fan Tuttee, which will stream on February 13 and 14 in time for Valentine’s Day. The short title, Così fan tutte, in Italian literally means, “so do they all,” and is usually translated into English as “women are like that.” It is considered Mozart’s most divisive and controversial work. In fact, Così fan tutte wasn’t popular with Mozart’s contemporaries who dismissed it as clumsy and miserable; as such, it was largely ignored. Despite being premiered in 1790, Così fan tutte didn’t become popular until the middle of the 20th century, though still dogged with accusations of misogyny. The opera follows best friends, Guglielmo and Ferrando, who are engaged to two sisters who are utterly faithful. Their relationships are put to the test in a tale of adultery and deception, wrapped in Mozart’s comedic style. Former San Francisco Opera Music Director Nicola Luisotti conducted the star-studded ensemble, which includes Ellie Dehn, Susannah Biller, and Marco Vinco. As the two men at the heart of the ruse, Francesco Demuro sings with “ardency and tonal brilliance,” while Philippe Sly delivers a Company debut “at once robust and lyrical,” the San Francisco Chronicle hailed. Visit https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on /streaming/ for streaming instructions. The opera will be available only on February 13 and 14.
articles.title: SF Opera’s free “Opera is On” presents Mozart’s Cosi fan tutte on Valentine’s Day

articles.text: Filoli House and Garden in Woodside has conducted a haiku contest to complement its “Winters at Filoli” calendar of events. The finalists will be announced via Zoom on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14. Special guest judge and San Mateo County Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto will read the winning poem online on Sunday. In addition to her laureate status, Cassinetto is the publisher of Paloma Press, an independent press that publishes poetry and prose. Widely anthologized, she is also the author of the poetry collections, Traje de Boda and The Pink House of Purple Yam Preserves & Other Poems, as well as three chapbooks through Moria Books’ acclaimed Locofo series. Her work has appeared in the Asahi Shimbun, The Banyan Review, Moss Trill, The Nonconformist Magazine, the San Francisco Chronicle, and Vox Populi. Winter at Filoli is a time of Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto quiet and reflection in the garden, and individuals in the haiku competition were asked to submit a poem inspired by Filoli’s winter garden. The winner will receive a Household Plus Membership at Filoli, in addition to a gift basket of Filoli goodies. To see poems of the finalists, see https://filoli.org/haiku/ on February 10, The winner will be shown online on February 14 at 12 p.m. when Cassinetto will read the winning poem.
articles.title: Filoli haiku contest winner to be announced on Valentine’s Day

To re-create an in-person experience through a digital, Zoom platform, the museum invites viewers to join the discussion with San Francisco Asian Art Museum observations and questions.
