articles.text: Olga and Sergey Rakitchekov will perform a concert on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14, as part of the Main Stage concerts of Gold Coast Chamber Player of Lafayette. Lafayette’s Gold Coast Chamber Players continues its virtual concerts with a series of six new programs. The next performance in their Main Stage Concerts is “Russian Valentine,” a love story of two musicians with a program for viola and harp. The concert features Olga and Sergey Rakitchekov, and will begin on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14 at 4 p.m. Audience members will get a glimpse of the couple’s home life and their history beginning in 1968 at the Moscow Conservatory of Music. Their concert features the music of Debussy, Smirinov, Reger, and Bridge. After the concert, ticket holders are invited to join the Rakitchekov couple for a Zoom “After Party” gathering, where they will answer questions from patrons. Gold Coast’s main stage concerts continue on February 28 with Russian violinist Dmitry Sitkovetsky. Virtual links to concerts remain active for one week following the performance date. All performances are live-streamed via YouTube Live, and links are provided upon ticket purchase. Tickets are available at www. gccpmusic.com, or by calling 925-283-3728.
articles.title: Gold Coast presents Russian Valentine concert Feb. 14

articles.text: Cal Performances is featuring an audience favorite, the Takacs Quartet, in concert at 7 p.m. on Thursday, February 25. In recent years the quartet has immersed Berkeley fans in single-composer cycles by Beethoven and Bartók, and numerous well-received mixed-repertoire programs. In this special program, the quartet will introduce audience members to its newest member, violist Richard O’Neill. The concert was filmed at the Lone Tree Arts Center near the group’s home base at the University of Colorado in Boulder. The quartet is comprised of Edward Dusinberre and Harumi Rhodes on violin, O’Neill on viola, and András Fejér on cello. They perform 80 concerts a year worldwide. The original group was formed in 1975 at the Franz Liszt Academy in Budapest with Gabor Takács-Nagy, Károly Schranz, Gabor Ormai and Fejér when all four were students. It received international attention in 1977 when the quartet won First Prize and the Critics’ Prize at the International String Quartet Competition in Evian, France. The concert’s diverse program will spotlight works from the Classical and Romantic era, as well at the 20th century. Viewers will hear Haydn’s Op. 77, No. 1, a work infused with the rhythmic vitality of traditional Hungarian folk music, and Britten’s moving Third String Quartet, which the group has recorded to great acclaim. A premiere watch party will begin at 7 p.m. on Thursday, February 25 and will be available on-demand through April 28. The pricing for individual Cal Performances-at-Home performances is on the honor system and is based on the number of people watching the performance. To view the concert, click on: https://calperformances.org/ events/2020-21/at-home-spring/ takacs-quartet/.
articles.title: Takacs Quartet concert to be shown February 25

articles.text: Piedmont blues guitarist Jules Leyhe brings his band to Piedmont Piano in February 25 for a 5 p.m. concert. Jules Leyhe and the Family Jules Band makes its first appearance at Piedmont Piano on Thursday, February 25 at 5 p.m. Leyhe’s band is a high-energy blues quartet of some of Oakland’s greatest blues and jazz musicians. The ensemble’s blend of funky, blues and soul inspired improvisation makes for a highly entertaining performance you won’t want to miss. Leyhe, a native of Piedmont, is a blues guitarist specializing in slide guitar. The band includes Nancy Wright on saxophone, Ian McArdle on keyboards and bass, and Isaac Schwartz on drums. Improvisation is at the core of this band’s soul, always taking advantage of each bandmate’s playful ears and pushing each other’s abilities to the edge seeking a new sound over traditional styles of music like blues and soul. The band has just finished recording its latest CD, Your First Rodeo, due for release in late spring. Leyhe is well known in Piedmont for his annual appearance in the 4th of July Parade with his renditions of the iconic Jimi Hendrix recording of the Star Spangled Banner. For access to the February 24 concert, call Piedmont Piano Co. at 547-8188 or e-mail music@piedmontpiano.com. Piedmont Piano Co. is located at 1728 San Pablo Avenue in downtown Oakland.
articles.title: Piedmont native makes debut appearance on Feb. 25

articles.text: Michael Tilson Thomas and the San Francisco Symphony will release a CD with its performances of three Alban Berg compositions. It will be made available by SFS Media on February 26. SFS Media is the symphony’s award-winning, in-house media production company and label, launched in 2001. Tilson Thomas, who recently retired after 25 years as San Francisco Symphony’s conductor and music director, is also co-founder and Artistic Director of the New World Symphony. The performances were recorded live at Davies Symphony Hall between January 2015 and November 2018. This is the newest release from the Grammy Award-winning SFS Media label, with Gil Shaham performing Berg’s Violin Concerto, and soprano Susanna Phillips as soloist in Berg’s Seven Early Songs. The album will be available this spring and is available for pre-order now by clicking on: https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Discover-the-Music/SFS-Media/ Berg. Conductor Michael Tilson Thomas
articles.title: SF Symphony to release CD of 3 Alban Berg concerts

pages.text: Wednesday, February 10, 2021 19 Gold Coast presents Russian Valentine concert Feb. 14 Olga and Sergey Rakitchekov will perform a concert on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14, as part of the Main Stage concerts of Gold Coast Chamber Player of Lafayette. By Allyson Aleksey Lafayette’s Gold Coast Chamber Players continues its virtual concerts with a series of six new programs. The next performance in their Main Stage Concerts is “Russian Valentine,” a love story of two musicians with a program for viola and harp. The concert features Olga and Sergey Rakitchekov, and will begin on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14 at 4 p.m. Audience members will get a glimpse of the couple’s home life and their history beginning in 1968 at the Moscow Conservatory of Music. Their concert features the music of Debussy, Smirinov, Reger, and Bridge. After the concert, ticket holders are invited to join the Rakitchekov couple for a Zoom “After Party” gathering, where they will answer questions from patrons. Gold Coast’s main stage concerts continue on February 28 with Russian violinist Dmitry Sitkovetsky. Virtual links to concerts remain active for one week following the performance date. All performances are live-streamed via YouTube Live, and links are provided upon ticket purchase. Tickets are available at www. gccpmusic.com, or by calling 925-283-3728. Cal Performances Takacs Quartet concert to be shown February 25 By Allyson Aleksey Cal Performances is featuring an audience favorite, the Takacs Quartet, in concert at 7 p.m. on Thursday, February 25. In recent years the quartet has immersed Berkeley fans in single-composer cycles by Beethoven and Bartók, and numerous well-received mixed-repertoire programs. In this special program, the quartet will introduce audience members to its newest member, violist Richard O’Neill. The concert was filmed at the Lone Tree Arts Center near the group’s home base at the University of Colorado in Boulder. The quartet is comprised of Edward Dusinberre and Harumi Rhodes on violin, O’Neill on viola, and András Fejér on cello. They perform 80 concerts a year worldwide. The original group was formed in 1975 at the Franz Liszt Academy in Budapest with Gabor Takács-Nagy, Károly Schranz, Gabor Ormai and Fejér when all four were students. It received international attention in 1977 when the quartet won First Prize and the Critics’ Prize at the International String Quartet Competition in Evian, France. The concert’s diverse program will spotlight works from the Classical and Romantic era, as well at the 20th century. Viewers will hear Haydn’s Op. 77, No. 1, a work infused with the rhythmic vitality of traditional Hungarian folk music, and Britten’s moving Third String Quartet, which the group has recorded to great acclaim. A premiere watch party will begin at 7 p.m. on Thursday, February 25 and will be available on-demand through April 28. The pricing for individual Cal Performances-at-Home performances is on the honor system and is based on the number of people watching the performance. To view the concert, click on: https://calperformances.org/ events/2020-21/at-home-spring/ takacs-quartet/. articles.text: The Alameda County Arts Commission has announced the 2021 Arts Fund Grant Program for Alameda County-based nonprofit arts organizations. Standard grant awards are $1,000 to $2,500 each. The application deadline is March 31. The Grant Program supports all types of arts programs, including music, theater, visual arts, dance, literature, media arts, and other forms presented by nonprofit organizations within the county. Last year’s Arts Fund Grant Program awarded grants to 45 nonprofit organizations. The Alameda County Arts Commission, a division of the County of Alameda, aims to improve the quality of life of county residents by nurturing a thriving environment for the arts, promoting economic opportunities for Alameda County’s artists and arts organizations, and encouraging public participation in the arts. “The arts are an essential component to Alameda County’s leadership in promoting communities that are vibrant, prosperous, safe, healthy and inclusive in support of Alameda County’s Vision 2026 goals,” Commission Director Rachel Osajima said. Commission staff will present two webinars to assist organizations in preparing their grant application. The first online workshop will be held tomorrow, Thursday, February 11 at 6:30 p.m., and the next one is Friday, March 5 at 10:00 am. The workshops are free, open to the public, and reservations are not required. For details on joining the webinars, see the Alameda County Arts Commission website at www.acgov.org/arts; click on Programs. The Arts Commission staff can also be reached by email at artscommission@acgov.org or phone at (510) 208-9646. Funding for the Arts Fund Grant Program is provided by the County of Alameda, and donations to the Foundation for the Arts in Alameda County.
articles.title: Application deadline is March 31; online workshop takes place tomorrow

articles.text: Ever dream of being a composer? Like so many things these days, everything is a formula. Since I am the musical gourmet, I offer you recipes for musical compositions. Choose your musical style and follow the recipe. The “One Chord” style. The easiest composition style is to master one chord on the piano. That’s it. One chord. When I was a kid there was a comedic song entitled “Johnny one note”. That was funny. But today, that is being a real composer. One chord on the piano. Who would have dreamt that the preposterous of the past would become today’s reality? I was in Rocky‘s Market on Leimert Blvd. about a week ago and they were playing some background music. While I was shopping I noticed that the pianist played the same chord over and over again...and no other cord. My internal metronome told me that the tempo was about 200 beats per minute. I figured the song lasted about 5 min. Simple arithmetic tells us that equals 1000 times playing the same note. Some of the people in the store seemed to enjoy this “music.” One chord played at least 1000 times! Sic gloria mundi. Country music I have always been a fan of classic country music and consider Hank Williams to be a treasure. His music spoke to the heart and soul of the human condition. I think this type of universality speaks to every human being. Some of Hank’s songs send chills up and down my spine. His poetry was pretty good, also. But that was the past. Today’s country music is all formula. Poetry? Forget about it. For lyrics, read from the newspaper and make sure your voice cracks on the first note of every sentence. The musical formula reads as follows: A guitar plays a four-chord introduction followed by heartbreak. Then dirt roads followed by something about Jesus. Remember to include something about America and finally some brief twangy chords to conclude. Be sure to have the recording engineer turn down the volume at the end. Cash imitating Elvis Presley. That’s a lesson in succinct and hilarious musical criticism. Blues, Pop, Rock Next is a recipe for success in blues composing: play a few chords on the guitar as an introduction then devote the bulk of the song to complaining and lamenting, and finish off with a few guitar chords. Keep repeating the same chords but have the recording engineer turn the volume down at the end. Maybe pop is your thing. This is a little bit more complicated. Pop music is often in five parts. Start out with a brief guitar introduction, and follow that with a simple “original” tune. Be sure to include a strange key change in the middle and then have the guy who’s twiddling the knobs create a fade out to nothing. Classic rock is also in about five sections. Be sure to include a brief verbal introduction telling everybody your resin Detra. (Sic!) while playing some chords on the guitar. Now turn up the volume on your electric guitar and twang away for a while and then either have some girls dancing or talk about girls, and then your drummer plays a solo and conclude with telling everybody how great the experience was. Have the recording engineer turn the volume down at the end. Despite what you hear on the news, there are some pretty funny things out there. And a lot of that passes for music. So… get your music manuscript paper ready. You have the recipe to be a (successful) composer. Laughing songs There are other inspirations. Among them are a great variety of laughing songs where somebody starts to play a song. Someone in the band plays a wrong note and that starts a cascade of laughing. “Spike Jones laughing record” comes to mind first. Then there were a number of “party records.” Some of the greatest Classical artists would record themselves doing absolutely ridiculous things. One of the best is available on YouTube. Look up “Jascha Heifetz Audition” and also the Johnny Cash imitation of Elvis Presley. Both are classics. Another is by Jo Stafford, who with her conductor/arranger husband Paul Weston, made a recording under the name Jonathan and Darlene Edwards. They lampooned popular music by singing familiar songs deliberately off-key and out of rhythm. You will be very happy that you explored this aspect of music. It is a complete delight, filled with insight, originality and plenty of side-splitting humor. In memoriam On a personal note, I note the passing of George Shultz at the ripe old age of 100. I got to know George through his sonin-law. What an honor. He had the insight of genius, because he knew what would happen even before it happened. He also had the wisdom to know what to do in every event. This is a gift given to very few. All of us hope that some of that insight will be passed on to future generations.
articles.title: Reality is hilarious

articles.text: Acronyms – helpful time saving devices? Or the tools of cult members to empower and keep secret their shorthand wisdom? Acronyms, the shortening of phrases of words into a series of first letters, can unnecessarily throw veils of confusion between a lay person and the adept. They started off as items of convenience, but soon acronyms have been wielded to cordon off wisdom from the seeker. Oh, how I hate acronyms. There are so many. Somehow, they throw off my pneumatic devices of memory. Should it be so difficult to receive full names, titles and explanations? Too many acronyms can easily bore and convolute. With sorrow I lament the fact that the use of acronyms in many industries is not only commonplace put a prerequisite for rudimentary discussion. Take the automotive industry, few wizards of wordcraft dwell in that realm. More commonly in the grease monkey world the virtues of the literate are shunned and laughed at. Car mechanics are ballerinas amongst machines, but butchers of the tongue. Nearly every automotive term has an associated acronym. RPMs, MPGs, SUVs, AWD, and PSI are common ones that have weaseled their way into the colloquial speech of all. Dig into an automotive textbook however, and the acronyms outnumber all adjectives, proper nouns, and adverbs combined. Acronyms are made for no reason at all, but the obvious observation that each word happens to begin with a letter. Are acronyms like WOT (wide open throttle), DTR (daytime running lights), and CVT (continuously variable transmission) really necessary? Using the actual words usually explains things correctly thoroughly. Daytime running lights? Hmm, those must be the little yellow lights that are on all the time. The complicated Continuously Variable Transmission is actually just like it sounds. Instead of having five gears of a fixed size, the continuously variable transmission uses a type of adjustable pulley mechanism always changing the tension of a transmission belt. The worst set of acronyms are three sets of letters that invite confusion and misunderstanding: KOER-Key On Engine Running KOEC-Key On Engine Cranking KOEO-Key On Engine Off Notice the shortening of three-letter words into one letter. A two-letter word shortened to one letter, “ON” to “O.” Really? Laziness or expedience? The worst part is that sometimes an O stands for On and sometimes for Off. And make sure not to confuse KOEO with Key Off Engine Off (that’s not a thing). But there is no Key On Engine On, that is covered with KOER (Key on Engine Running). This set of letters is supposed to be shorthand for the position your key is in while in the ignition. When you look at your car, those positions are labeled something else: LOCK, ACCESSORIES, START and RUN. My mustard-stained mustache boss eventually fired me from my lube tech position at the ole shop, but in a way I am glad. It’s like being banished from the cult before they start handing out the Kool-Aid. There are a few exceptions that prove the rule, however. For example, “SCUBA” sounds so cool that people don’t even realize it’s an acronym for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus. That’s a mouthful, so using an acronym makes sense. A personal favorite, which I suppose is the rare homophone acronym, is JEEP. It resulted from military men being fed up with the lazily named GP (general purpose) vehicles, so they sounded out the G and the P together. It must be acknowledged that acronyms can be used unjustly. Sometimes they are convenient, but they also can be used to privatize knowledge, or merely as an excuse to feign creativity. I will leave this discussion by quoting epic fantasy author Patrick Rothfuss from his first novel The Name of the Wind (2007): “What color is that boy’s shirt?” “Blue.” “What do you mean by blue? Describe it.” I struggled for a moment and failed. “So blue is a name?” “It is a word. Words are pale shadows of forgotten names. As names have power, words have power. Words can light fires in the minds of men. Words can produce tears from the hardest hearts. There are seven words that will make a person love you. There are ten words that will break a strong man’s will. But a word is nothing but a painting of a fire. A name is the fire itself.” My head was swimming by this point. “I still don’t understand.” He laid a hand on my shoulder. “Using words to talk of words is like using a pencil to draw a picture of itself, on itself. Impossible. Confusing. Frustrating.”
articles.title: HUMOR O.H.I.H.A. (Oh How I Hate Acronyms)

articles.text: Ralston Peregrine Louie, age 28, passed away on January 31, 2021, after a tragic swimming accident. Born on July 22, 1992 in San Francisco, he was the son of Robin Wu and Reagan Louie, and the younger brother of sister Ryan Louie, age 32. He was a 6th generation Californian. Ralston was smart, creative, athletic and incredibly driven in all aspects of his life. He attended Piedmont High School, where he was awarded Scholar Athlete during his senior year. He played on the varsity soccer and golf teams all four years, and ran track. He also played on Bay Oaks club soccer teams. During his senior year, he organized Piedmont High School’s first film festival, with Pixar’s Peter Docter as the special guest judge. He went on to graduate cum laude from Williams College in 2014, majoring in Asian Studies. He then attended the University of Southern California School of Cinematic Arts graduate program in Interactive Media & Games. At USC, he was a recipient of the Asian Pacific Alumni Association Scholarship Award. He was to graduate in Spring of 2021. During the past two years, he focused on his thesis project, entitled Wing Wor, an immersive and interactive virtual reality experience that takes the user into his ancestral home in China. (left), sister Ryan and father Reagan. Ralston Louie enjoyed playing soccer while in school.
articles.title: Obituary

articles.text: Ralston Louie, a Piedmont High School graduate in 2010, died on January 31 after a swimming accident. He was 28. In the Winter of 2019-20, Ralston and his father travelled together back to the village in China to take photos and film video for Ralston’s master’s thesis. Since his return, he had been working hard to finish what promised to be a breakthrough project. From his family, Ralston always had a love for China. He studied in Beijing during college, and a fellowship allowed him to continue studying Chinese and live in Taiwan after graduating from Williams. He traveled throughout different cities and provinces of China as a young adult, eager to learn more about the history of his cultural heritage and gain a greater understanding of himself. Much of his studies, creative work and projects revolved around his roots and what it meant to be Asian American. Ralston always aspired to learn more. He carried a camera with him wherever he went, as a way to capture every moment he could. He was a true storyteller, someone who engaged with the world and found every opportunity to create work to share with others. As an avid athlete, Ralston continued to find new forms of physical activity throughout his life. Growing up he played soccer, basketball, golf, football, ran track, and was an expert skier. He continued to play soccer at the collegiate level. After college, Ralston discovered a love for surfing, swimming, trail running, and biking. He enjoyed days where he could simply be outside, swim in the ocean and catch waves for hours. He was a true water man. During his time at USC he joined the Triathlon Team, learning to train for future races. Ralston is survived by his parents, Robin Wu and Reagan Louie, and his sister, Ryan Louie. Donations in Ralston’s memory may be made to the “Vivian and Stanley Wu and Ralston Louie Fund” of the Asian Pacific Fund at 465 California Street, Suite 809, San Francisco, CA 94104 or secure.qgiv.com/for/apfund. Ralston Louie (5) and sister Ryan (8) in 1997. Being outdoors was at the heart and soul of Ralston Louie. Ralston Louie at his college graduation from Williams College in 2014. He is pictured with his mother Robin Ralston Louie photographing and filming in China in his father’s ancestral village outside Guangzhou, to gather content for Ralston’s graduate thesis.

articles.text: The important quality of life characteristic of a place that planners call “walkability” now seems to be recognized and highly valued everywhere. It is considered an amenity to any neighborhood, and property values are positively affected by a good walkability rating. Simply stated, walkability is how userfriendly an area is for pedestrians; how easy, convenient and safe it is to walk from one place to the next. I am fond of this relatively recent term because as readers of this column know, I value and enjoy walking for many reasons. While in much of today’s world we have designed and built our communities to accommodate the car at the expense of pedestrians, travel on foot will always be the most basic and socially valuable form of getting around. Walking is a community enhancer. When people are on foot, the pace is slow enough to really observe immediate surroundings and the opportunity to meet and talk to other people exists, something that is pretty much impossible when we are isolated from one another in our cars. Like many planning concepts, walkability is strongly linked to other issues and considerations, and chief among them is density. If things are too spread out (low density), walking any distance doesn’t make sense much of the time. But if destinations are close enough (higher density), walking to school, church, stores or the park are feasible – and they’re healthy and fun. The walkability rating of Piedmont, like any city, varies based on the conditions in any local area. Unfortunately, published walkability scores have become inflated due to the economic value of high ratings. The only way to truly know is to judge for yourself. This map of the city shows an approximation of some walking times to the center. Variables include the steepness of the walk in addition to distance. It suggests that while we certainly can’t conveniently walk everywhere we need to go, many of us can easily walk to some of our destinations. Camino de Santiago sketches: The most remarkable example of a place with true walkability this writer has seen is in northern Spain, along the famous Camino de Santiago. People make treks of hundreds of miles solely on foot along routes that support and cater in every way to….walking! I think that much of the rest of the world can learn from this place.
articles.title: Walkability – what it really means

pages.text: Wednesday, February 10, 2021 23 Features Part 13 in a biweekly series: Walkability – what it really means By Will Adams The important quality of life characteristic of a place that planners call “walkability” now seems to be recognized and highly valued everywhere. It is considered an amenity to any neighborhood, and property values are positively affected by a good walkability rating. Simply stated, walkability is how userfriendly an area is for pedestrians; how easy, convenient and safe it is to walk from one place to the next. I am fond of this relatively recent term because as readers of this column know, I value and enjoy walking for many reasons. While in much of today’s world we have designed and built our communities to accommodate the car at the expense of pedestrians, travel on foot will always be the most basic and socially valuable form of getting around. Walking is a community enhancer. When people are on foot, the pace is slow enough to really observe immediate surroundings and the opportunity to meet and talk to other people exists, something that is pretty much impossible when we are isolated from one another in our cars. Like many planning concepts, walkability is strongly linked to other issues and considerations, and chief among them is density. If things are too spread out (low density), walking any distance doesn’t make sense much of the time. But if destinations are close enough (higher density), walking to school, church, stores or the park are feasible – and they’re healthy and fun. The walkability rating of Piedmont, like any city, varies based on the conditions in any local area. Unfortunately, published walkability scores have become inflated due to the economic value of high ratings. The only way to truly know is to judge for yourself. This map of the city shows an approximation of some walking times to the center. Variables include the steepness of the walk in addition to distance. It suggests that while we certainly can’t conveniently walk everywhere we need to go, many of us can easily walk to some of our destinations. There are many different reasons to walk and many of the benefits overlap. It’s possible to cover all the examples shown above in a single walk. But maybe the most important requirement for true walkability is a positive response to the question, “Is this a nice place to walk?” Piedmont certainly is. Some may be surprised to learn that Piedmont is a relatively dense city: twice that of Walnut Creek or Hayward, and five times greater than Orinda. Here, the higher density makes the city automatically more walkable. Terrain however, is also a factor. The steeper hilly areas in town have the opposite effect, making walking more strenuous and less convenient. Proximity of destinations is also important in determining how convenient it is to walk. Piedmont’s central core area is full of parks and civic uses but has very limited commercial and business uses. If for example you want something from a pharmacy, it is necessary to go out of town. But like “open space” that we discussed in the last column, because of proximity, we are the beneficiaries of various walkable retail districts in Oakland just outside Piedmont. If we are able to walk more, we mitigate many obvious problems endemic to our culture, including traffic jams and auto pollution. Just a small reduction in auto trips replaced by walking can make a significant difference. But perhaps most important of all, is the health benefit of walking. Researchers tell us that everything from cardiovascular strength, to healthy blood pressure, to energy boosts are improved by even a minimum amount of walking on a regular basis. I have excerpted some of her tips for you, below. Dear Future Design Client: Recently, with the help of LMB Interiors I tackled a complete floor-to-ceiling remodel, plus all new furnishings, to truly make my new home feel like my own. Now that the work is complete, I want to impart some wisdom that I gained throughout the process that may benefit others who are considering exploring their own remodel journey. Here are a few of my reflections. Lean into the adventure Whether you realize it or not, you have an opportunity to shift from an old version of yourself into a new one. Yes, you may have preferences for certain colors and design aesthetics when you start; but there is a reason you have hired an interior design expert. Not only can they see where you are today, they see where you are going into the future. Lucky for us, it is their zone of genius that illuminates this incredible transformative path. Be Courageous Know that decisions that might feel most comfortable to you now may be coming from a past version of yourself. New suggestions might feel risky, uncertain, and you might meet them with resistance. Summon up your inner courage for change and embrace the excitement of moving into the next chapter of your life which is unfolding by grand design. Literally. Be openminded to exploring new and different ideas. Where you start on the journey is not where you will end. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on February 1, with 15 readers on the call to discuss their two February selections. Led by Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long, the group had a lively discussion about Olive Kitteridge, the first Olive novel by writer Elizabeth Strout, and Olive, Again, the second book. Participating in the discussion were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Bella Almanzan, Sally Arney, Albert Chen, Pat McSwain, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter. Olive Kitteridge was published in 2008 and received critical acclaim. It was awarded the Pulitzer Prize and was made into an HBO four-part miniseries. The title character, Olive Kitteridge, is a retired schoolteacher, who lives in the fictional town of Crosby, Maine. The novel is structured into 13 chapters that are much like a set of short stories. In Crosby everyone knows everyone else’s business, and that can include murder, pedophilia, suicide, armed robbery, arson, and also true love and deep sadness. As the townspeople struggle with their problems, Olive develops a deeper understanding of herself and her life, sometimes painfully, but always honestly. This is the journey of a complex, blunt, opinionated, cantankerous woman as she grows older and interacts with her family and the members of her small town. Olive says exactly what she is thinking, and often seems to act with little regard for others’ feelings. Her targets can include her two husbands and her son, who can’t tolerate her, yet still seem to love her. Olive’s husbands accept Olive as she is with her off-putting behavior and personality, but they also love her. Strout followed up in 2019 on the success of Olive Kitteridge with a sequel, Olive, Again. Similar to the first novel, Olive, Again takes the form of 13 short story chapters that are interrelated and follow Olive from age 70 into her eighties. At the end of the book and her life, readers see Olive showing greater empathy and having a realization that, while she often tried to help others, she knows that she could have done better. The books were well received by most members of the group. Readers appreciated Strout’s detailed, descriptive, and beautiful writing; and enjoyed the stories of the different people within the novels. Strout is a masterful writer. She presents the feelings of the books’ different characters, and especially Olive, in ways that the readers found very real. Olive’s aging process and growth also provided opportunities for introspection, with some readers saying that they hope they don’t turn out like Olive. However, not all the readers were lovers of the books. While appreciating Strout’s writing, some readers simply did not like the character of Olive. articles.text: Seniors who want to maintain their health and stay out of the emergency room will want to participate in a presentation scheduled for Monday, February 22 at 3 p.m. on Zoom. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, a discussion by Emmy Fearn will describe the causes of dehydration, its danger and symptoms, how very quickly dehydration can occur, and most importantly, how to prevent it. All Piedmont seniors are invited. To receive the Zoom link to join the meeting, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. Fearn, a resident in nearby Crocker Highlands, became interested in the impact of dehydration when her otherwise healthy mother collapsed and was hospitalized, after becoming dehydrated in less than a day. Fearn has provided talks on dehydration to seniors at Piedmont Gardens, at Kaiser Hospital, and to the Piedmont Seniors. Fearn has a doctorate in Special Education and has taught at San Francisco State and CSU East Bay. She currently supervises new Special Education teachers at Mills College. Emmy Fearn will be the guest speaker at a meeting of the Piedmont Seniors on February 22.
articles.title: Emmy Fearn is guest speaker for zoom meeting on Feb, 22

articles.text: Stressed about current world or personal events? It’s possible to turn away from fear by gaining a clearer view of God as Love itself, which can have a tangible, healing effect in your life and in the world. At 5 p.m. on Thursday, February 18, tune in to a free, live Zoom lecture entitled, “Spiritual Discovery in a Time of Upheaval” by Tom McElroy, a Christian Science practitioner and teacher. The discussion is sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist in Oakland. “Prayer is about spiritual discovery. It’s about understanding more of what God is and learning to see our lives and the world through the lens of God’s all-good nature. It’s about stripping away surface-level appearances in order to discern what actually is,” explained McElroy. “Spiritual discovery reveals what is substantial, lasting, and powerful, and this leads to healing. What’s the outcome? Progress. Transformation. Wholeness – for anyone.” The link to attend the online talk is on the Church’s website, www.ChristianScienceOakland.org.
articles.title: Christian Science Church offers free talk on “Spiritual Discovery in a Time of Upheaval”

articles.text: When Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898, only the Clubhouse, the rustic teahouse, the mineral springs and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and wandering paths were there to attract visitors to the park. Havens continued to add more attractions to draw visitors to Piedmont Park and to the city itself. Many visitors enjoyed the weather and views and decided to build their homes here. Frank Havens and his Realty Syndicate was there to sell them a home site. In 1904 he built “The Maze.” Gardeners planted a large circular hedge maze in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. This privet maze challenged all who entered to reach the bright red pagoda at the center. Ladders strategically placed throughout the Maze allowed those feeling hopelessly lost to climb a ladder to the top of the hedge and get their bearings. And true to the nature and design of mazes, the Maze in Piedmont was a double challenge; the return trip out of the Maze was just as challenging as that to the center. lower entrance to Piedmont Park. Havens developed a lane from Grand Avenue to the Maze and on to the park paths. He lined it with palm trees, some of which still survive on what is now Palm Drive. The Maze from 1904 is now the location of the high school’s Witter Field. One year after the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, Havens added more attractions to Piedmont Park. Many refugees from San Francisco fled to the East Bay, and Havens wanted to draw them to Piedmont and sell them property for building homes. In keeping with the Victorian interest in the exotic, Havens added a Japanese Tea House. Built as a replica of the late-fifteenth century Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, Japan, the teahouse opened in 1907 where today’s Japanese Tea House stands. (The current tea house was moved to Piedmont Park in 1976 from an estate where Piedmont Middle School now stands.) A Japanese gate led to a Japanese-style garden with ponds and a moon bridge. Stickwork fences, pillars and benches complemented these Japanese grounds. Also in 1907, Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery on the site of today’s tennis courts in the park. The spacious art gallery had a large skylight and was built to display Havens’ collection of 375 pieces of art by English, French, Russian, American and other painters. Two additional gallery wings extended beyond the main gallery. Eleven countries in all were represented by this collection. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian masterpieces that were exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the exposition, the paintings were stored in Canada. In order to avoid paying customs This rustic teahouse was built near today’s bus shelter. fees on the paintings, they were unscrupulously appraised far below their value. Havens and his agent then snatched them up at a fraction of their worth. Havens was particularly fond of California impressionists, and his collection also included work by William Keith, Charles Rollo Peters, Gordon Couts, Thomas Hill, Xavier Martinez and others. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Couts lived and painted in Piedmont at this time. Havens’ art collection was said to be one of the finest collections in the country. Havens charged admission to the Art Gallery, and artist Richard Partington, Havens’ sister-in-law Carrie Sterling and son Seyd Havens served successively as curators of the gallery. In 1916, Havens had plans to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his paintings to San Francisco where they were auctioned off. Some paintings went to private collectors, some to the new Oakland Art Museum, and many went to the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to express my appreciation and support for the Piedmont Center for the Arts. SonoMusette has performed at PCA four times from 2016-2020 and we hope to perform there again, as soon as the local health officials deem it safe.· PCA is an important and unique performance space and it has been instrumental in the success of our music group, which specializes in the music of Paris of the 1950s. The Center has given us the opportunity to perform for a welcoming audience in a beautiful and intimate space. The staff at PCA is exceptional and should be a model for how a Performing Arts Center operates. The staff is knowledgeable, accommodating, courteous, helpful, and works hard to help promote events and make them an enjoyable experience for both performers and the audience. When we performed at PCA, it was nice to see how many audience members were from the surrounding neighborhood, and how many were able to walk to the venue. The room is very enjoyable to perform in as the fine acoustics make it easy and comfortable to perform. The intimate seating also gives the musicians a connection to the audience. It is very important for venues such as PCA to continue to operate as they fill a rare and needed place in the world of performing arts. The current pandemic is taking a costly toll on such venues and it is imperative that we all do what we can to continue the operation of venues such as Piedmont Center for the Arts. –Robert Lunceford SonoMusette
articles.title: The music of France is alive and well in Piedmont

articles.text: Editor: My name is Michael Stehr and I am one of a long list of artists that have benefitted from a relationship with the Piedmont Center for the Arts. I have exhibited many collections of paintings at the center. This is my eighth year showing at the PCA, and each year I approach the exhibit with the same goal-creating a museum type experience for the visitors in a space designed to celebrate fine art. We have enjoyed a steady stream of visitors to the center, with guests being residents and non-residents of Piedmont. My involvement with the PCA is not limited to fine art. Last April, while we were recognizing the one-year anniversary of the fire at Notre Dame de Paris, I delivered a lecture on The Cathedral, the fire, and the power of architecture. The focus of the evening was to consider why people worldwide were sobbing at the sight of flames mauling that very special building. My conclusion was that sometimes buildings are more than buildings... that there is something spiritual that happens when devoted individuals commit themselves to beauty, when beauty is the highest of priorities. The lecture drew about 70 people, from various backgrounds, representing a number of cities. The loud applause at the end of the program served as a true celebration of Notre Dame, the human spirit, and, in my opinion, the arts in general. As the Artistic Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC), I can testify firsthand to the Piedmont Center for the Arts’ extraordinary impact on the arts scene in our East Bay commw1ity. Our organization was founded in Piedmont in 1982, and since then has grown to an internationally renowned choral arts program that offers a high caliber choral education to hundreds of students each year. That trajectory would not have been possible without the presence of the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) to serve as an advocate and supporter of the arts in the Piedmont community. Piedmont Center for the Arts offers a rehearsal space uniquely well-suited to our programs. During a normal year, PEBCC offers two two-hour rehearsals ach week in the space, not to mention numerous other oneoff events such as additional rehearsals, parent meetings, and recording sessions. PCA offers us a truly exceptional rehearsal space, with beautiful acoustics; a concert-quality Steinway grand piano; ample storage space for teaching supplies; an elevated stage space; and a beautiful outdoor area for breaks. It is undoubtedly the most musically rewarding of PEBCC’s many rehearsal venues, and a joy to teach and perform in. The center’s convenient and central location, directly across from the middle and high schools, allows for easy walking access for many of our students and families. Our singers, faculty, staff, and families are grateful for the acoustic quality, ease of use, and convenient location of PCA. Piedmont Center for the Arts has also been an invaluable artistic partner to the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. When COVID-19 struck, for example, PEBCC quickly decided to record the final rehearsals of our top four performing groups to produce a digital recording of our “Music of the Pacific Rim” concert. PCA immediately offered us the use of their space for several hours, free and on a 24-hour notice. What a tremendous gift it was to be able to record in the center’s stunning acoustic and beautiful setting on such short notice, and to be able to produce a moving concert for our community despite the pandemic. Given how challenging it often is to book and work with rehearsal and. concert venues, we feel incredibly fortunate to have PCA available as a resource in our own backyard. PCA has been extremely generous with us, often allowing us to hold additional rehearsals or parent meetings on short notice. It has been integral in helping us build our own artistic community. In turn, the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir has been able to bring diverse new audiences to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Our students hail from cities across the East Bay. The center brings families from throughout the region into the heart of Piedmont, often encouraging them to spend time in the park or at Mulberry’s while their singers are in rehearsal. The sense of community built as families linger on the steps or lawn on a sunny afternoon is palpable. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is grateful, indeed, to have the Piedmont Center for the Arts as a partner and resource in supporting the arts in Piedmont and beyond. pages.text: 30 Wednesday, February 10, 2021 Supt. Booker Continued from page 1 if we could go back in time, we might handle some things differently. That being said, I hope you do not doubt that every decision was made with the goal of providing the best education possible for our students, while keeping our entire community safe and healthy by following the guidance and protocols issued by the Alameda County Public Health Department. Safety is our top priority Safety has been our top priority from the very beginning of the pandemic. Keeping students, teachers, staff and families healthy requires careful, complex planning that involved many hours of considering various scenarios. We are sorry that our communication has not been as frequent or as clear as it could be in communicating the process by which we are making decisions, and the rationale for decisions made. We are taking active steps to improve the frequency, transparency and clarity of our communication moving forward, including bringing on additional short-term staff to help me draft regular updates so that I can focus on the planning and transition as we bring students and teachers and staff back to campuses safely. How we got here We know how frustrating the last 10 months have been, especially as guidance from the County and State has changed in the past just when we thought we were ready to re-open, including just last week when the guidance on vaccinating teachers changed unexpectedly. There have been so many twists and turns over the last 10 months that it is easy, even for me, to forget everything that has happened, the decisions that were made and why actions were taken. Thank you to my hard-working leadership team. We are proud to be one of the first public school districts in Alameda County poised to re-open, and I am grateful to my hard-working team for the detailed and complex planning behind the scenes. I want to thank all of you for your patience during this difficult time of waiting and planning. We all look forward to welcoming additional students onto our campuses, and I’m hopeful that tonight’s presentation and recommendations move us closer to that goal.” Heritage Tree Continued from page 1 announced when everyone got caught up in the new COVID-related health restrictions imposed by Alameda County. The Heritage Tree awards, now in the fourth year, celebrate noteworthy and distinctive trees in the community and promotes understanding of their benefits to Piedmont’s “urban forest.” A tree must be in good health to be nominated and should not pose a hazard to pedestrians, automobiles, buildings or utilities. The designation may include a group of trees of the same species where one individual tree may not hold such status but a collective import of a group or association is greater than the individual. There are three qualifiers for tree nominations: 1. The tree should be an integral part of an architectural theme or plays an important role in framing a building or other civic feature. 2. The tree should also have historical value or be recognized as part of a memorial of early civic plantings. 3. The tree should have educational value or represent an outstanding example of its species in age, size and form. Only trees on public properties may be nominated. Any resident or staff member may nominate a tree. Those who have nominated in past years may do so this year, and there is no age limit to participate. Students in elementary, middle and high school are welcome to nominate a favorite public tree. Heritage tree applications will be posted on the city website in the near future. articles.text: Nate Redinbo On Monday, February 1, Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a second reading of the proposed reach codes. Ordinance 750 N.S. amends City Code regarding requirements for energy efficiency measures, photovoltaic systems, and all-electric construction in new or existing low-rise residential buildings. Ordinance 751 N.S. amends City Code to include requirements for the preparation of a Home Energy Audit or Home Energy Score for low-rise residential buildings. City staff initiated the process for adopting the reach codes in 2019. Along the way, there have been two public opinion surveys, several workshops, virtual town halls, two City Council meetings, and lots of feedback from community members. Now that the reach codes have been adopted, what does that mean for residents? The proposed changes can lead to additional requirements during building projects, but not immediately. Ordinance 750 N.S. will be sent to the California Energy Commission (CEC), where it will verify that the codes are at least as stringent as the California Energy Code. The reach codes are then posted for public comment for 60 days. At the end of the public comment period, CEC will approve or return the codes for edits. Additionally, the reach codes must be sent to the California Building Standards Commission for approval. If both of these commissions approve the reach codes, they will become part of the City’s building code. This means that projects will have to start abiding by them upon this approval date. We set an effective date so that the public will have ample notice of a definitive date that Ordinance 750 N.S. will go into effect on June 1, 2021. This is four months from today. Each project that requires a permit will work with a member of the City’s Planning Department, who will be able to explain the reach code requirements to applicants. Ordinance 751 N.S. will go into effect on March 3, which is 30 days after City Council approved the code.
articles.title: City Council approves Reach Codes in second reading

articles.text: Larceny theft, motor vehicle theft, and burglary has increased in Piedmont, according to an end-of-year crime report given by Police Chief Jeremy Bowers at Monday night’s City Council meeting. More arrests related to Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) were made last year than in 2019. Piedmont police officers made 17 arrests and recovered 34 stolen vehicles in events directly related to ALPR cameras. But Piedmont experienced more than a 50 percent increase in reportable offenses in 2020 as compared to 2019, from 244 offenses in 2019 to 370 offenses in 2020. The large increase was most notably due to increases in theft, auto theft and residential burglary, which has steadily increased in recent years. For example, the total number of reported larcenies in 2018 was 123, which increased to 162 in 2019, and doubled last year to 236 reported offenses of larceny theft. Motor vehicle theft tripled from 19 reported offenses in 2019, to 60 auto thefts last year. Recovered vehicle values have lowered from 2018 to 2020, however. In 2019, $257,800 worth of valuables were recovered total, in 2020, only $167,300 worth of valuables were recovered. “While the Police Department continuously conducts proactive patrols to mitigate thefts and other crimes, we cannot overemphasize the importance of residents and visitors employing basic crime prevention actions such as not leaving valuables in vehicles,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand stated in a staff report. articles.text: Editor: I am an Oakland resident and am writing in support of extending the lease and operation of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. My first time there was for the showing of a movie about a horrible situation on the 57 bus in Oakland. (The 57 Bus: A True Story of Two Teenagers and the Crime That Changed Their Lives) Then I went to the center when they were presenting a “Jazz in the neighborhood” program which introduced me to an intimate setting with great musicians. The volunteers had done a good job with a nice setting and a very welcoming atmosphere. Today, I received a video in commemoration of the liberation of Auschwitz gas chamber camp and was blown away with emotions yet I don’t have a Jewish background. So, for me, the Piedmont Center for the Arts is a place where I can safely see, hear, feel, a different, not commercial, art experience. It’s invaluable. –Elisabeth Heidorn
articles.title: Why I respect the work of the Center for the Arts

articles.text: Editor: May I add my voice to the chorus of community members who are writing in support of the Piedmont Community Arts Center and the renewal of their lease. The Arts Center is one of the most valuable of Piedmont’s many assets. It has become, as currently organized and managed, a wonderful place to hear music, view art and listen to lectures. The entire surrounding community benefits from this jewel of a site and its variety of offerings. Its popularity and ability to attract wonderful performers speaks to the incredible job being done by the current staff of devoted volunteers. As a former Art teacher at Piedmont High School, I only wish it had been available when I was there, as it is providing all students, not just those in a class, a place to pursue and display their art. articles.text: Editor: How is it that we elect all those low-life bad actors as president? No, not him. I mean Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, both Roosevelts, Hoover, and two shot and killed in office, Presidents Garfield and McKinley? The wise souls on the San Francisco School Board are forcing taking all those names off SF schools right away because of their transgressions. This is fact, not fiction. No, I didn’t call it a knee-jerk reaction, nor call the school board members jerks. Also scrubbed are schools named for Padre Junipero Serra who founded most of the early California missions, John Muir, Robert Loius Stevenson and Francis Scott Key of National Anthem fame. Maybe the anthem from F.S. Key could be replaced by some lively number by Michael Jackson? Or can we rename those schools after some of those superstar baseball players who thrived on taking power-enhancing steroids, dismissed as a much lesser sin? Or, after crazy forerunners of the past like SF’s self-styled Emperor Norton? Rest assured, California is not a loony bin, though all that sunshine we get here might alter brains and rational thinking. Because so far, apparently SF is the one school board to have taken such measures to scrub their reputations clean. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

pages.text: 2 Wednesday, February 3, 2021 Opinion LETTERS MAIN Why I respect the work of the Center for the Arts Editor: I am an Oakland resident and am writing in support of extending the lease and operation of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. My first time there was for the showing of a movie about a horrible situation on the 57 bus in Oakland. (The 57 Bus: A True Story of Two Teenagers and the Crime That Changed Their Lives) Then I went to the center when they were presenting a “Jazz in the neighborhood” program which introduced me to an intimate setting with great musicians. The volunteers had done a good job with a nice setting and a very welcoming atmosphere. Today, I received a video in commemoration of the liberation of Auschwitz gas chamber camp and was blown away with emotions yet I don’t have a Jewish background. So, for me, the Piedmont Center for the Arts is a place where I can safely see, hear, feel, a different, not commercial, art experience. It’s invaluable. –Elisabeth Heidorn As you know, PCA sponsors and founders have contributed over $200,000 in physical improvements to the building. Moreover, they have contributed uncountable benefits to our local arts and culture by hosting world-class artists and musicians, many of whom are Piedmont residents. In addition to enriching our cultural life in Piedmont, the PCA’s activities make Piedmont a preferable place to live and thereby enrich our property values as well. Thank you for supporting the PCA. –Bruce and Karen Joffe Retired head of PHS Art Dept. gives thumbs up to Center for the Arts Editor: May I add my voice to the chorus of community members who are writing in support of the Piedmont Community Arts Center and the renewal of their lease. The Arts Center is one of the most valuable of Piedmont’s many assets. It has become, as currently organized and managed, a wonderful place to hear music, view art and listen to lectures. The entire surrounding community benefits from this jewel of a site and its variety of offerings. Its popularity and ability to attract wonderful performers speaks to the incredible job being done by the current staff of devoted volunteers. As a former Art teacher at Piedmont High School, I only wish it had been available when I was there, as it is providing all students, not just those in a class, a place to pursue and display their art. I “second” Valerie Corvin’s fine letter, printed in the Post on Jan 20, and I implore you to please renew the current lease See more Letters on page 30 A tsunami of support for Center for the Arts This letter was sent to Piedmont City Council. Editor: Karen and Bruce Joffe want to add our names to the tsunami of support for the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Please act to have PCA continue in its location at the essentially free rent that it has operated under for the last decade. Or can we rename those schools after some of those superstar baseball players who thrived on taking power-enhancing steroids, dismissed as a much lesser sin? articles.text: Piedmont residents have been fully vaccinated against COVID- 19, while 1,143 Piedmonters have received the first of two doses needed for vaccination. Alameda County has administered over 145,000 COVID-19 vaccine doses as of Monday, February 1, according to the California Department of Public Health. The county is now the seventh in the state in terms of total doses administered and has administered more doses than every Bay Area county besides Santa Clara County. However, demand for the vaccine is far outstripping supply – eligible residents have reported waiting on hold for long stretches of time and general confusion about how to sign up for appointments. Last week, the state changed its vaccine distribution plan, but administration varies from county to county due to logistical delays. People 65 years of age and older are eligible for the vaccine, according to the state. Additionally, workers in education, childcare, food, grocery and agriculture sectors are eligible. This group, known as Phase 1B Tier One by the state, includes about 8.5 million Californians. As of press time the Alameda County Public Health Department has not announced that vaccine providers are open for appointments to people in Phase 1B. Instead, the county is still focused on Phase 1A, which includes healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. Phase 1A was the first group eligible for the vaccine when the first doses arrived in December. Phase 1A includes an estimated 3 million people statewide and over 145,000 in Alameda County. The county plans to start vaccinating those in Phase 1B Tier One in the “coming weeks,” according to the ACPHD. Importantly, both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccines that are being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. The county has been administering both Pfizer and Moderna vaccines on pretty equal footing, with about 7 percent more Moderna vaccines being administered than Pfizer. After Phase 1A and Phase 1B Tier One, the next group of people prioritized to receive the vaccine according to the state plan is Phase 1B Tier Two. This group includes workers in transportation, logistics, industrial, commercial, residential, sheltering facilities and critical manufacturing. It also includes people who live in congregate settings, like the incarcerated and the homeless. California’s Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said at a press conference yesterday, Tuesday, February 2 that the state hopes to outline when these groups of people are eligible by next week. Likely, Phase 1B Tier Two will be eligible sometime in the spring. this year, anyone who wants to receive a COVID-19 vaccine should be able to receive it, the state believes. With vaccine supply and the state’s distribution plans in flux, the timetable is subject to change. The state has rapidly ramped up its vaccine distribution. By the end of January, around 180,000 people per day were being vaccinated. The state is encouraging residents to utilize a new digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov. On that website, Californians can find out their eligibility and, if eligible, they can schedule a vaccination appointment. Those who are not eligible for vaccination can sign up for notifications when their turn is up. The state has administered over 3.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 5.8 million doses, according to the California Department of Public Health. As of press time, 1.5 percent of the state’s population has been fully vaccinated, according to Bloomberg news, while 7.2 percent of Californians have received at least one shot. California is still amongst the worst states in terms of vaccine distribution so far, even though it holds more total doses than any other state. Along with using the My Tool website, the county encourages people 65 years and older to contact their healthcare provider to see if vaccine doses are available to them.

articles.text: In Piedmont, four more cases of COVID-19 have been reported over the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. As of Monday, February 1, there have been 162 reported cases in the City overall. It appears that the rate of new cases in the county has slowed in recent days following a large surge during the Christmas holidays. Across Alameda County, 3,363 new cases have been reported across the past seven days. The total caseload for the county is 74,661. There have been 23,216 cases recorded in Oakland and 11,772 cases in Hayward. On Sunday, January 31, there were 383 new cases countywide, far fewer than the county’s historic high of 1,315 cases reported on January 3. Of course, the data has shown that surges can strike suddenly, so experts continue to remind residents to remain vigilant. California suddenly lifted stay-at-home health orders statewide last week after projections showed intensive care unit (ICU) capacity was trending favorably. State projections released yesterday, Tuesday, February 2 suggest ICU capacity for the Bay Area region will settle around 33 percent by March 1. However, even though the state’s stay-at-home orders have ended, Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Outdoor dining can resume under Purple Tier, or Widespread Tier, rules, but not indoor dining. Outdoor campgrounds, gyms, museums, places of worship and wineries are permitted. Indoor hair salons, barbershops, personal care services and hotels can open with restrictions. Capacity restrictions for indoor grocery stores is increased to 50 percent while for other indoor retail locations the capacity is set at 25 percent. Small, time-limited outdoor private gatherings are permitted for groups comprised of no more than three separate households, according to state guidance. Masks and physical distancing are still required for these gatherings. Only a handful of counties in California are not in the Purple Tier, none of which are in the Bay Area. Tragically, 85 more people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County across the past seven days, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 991. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 5.1 percent, slightly lower than last week. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,270,770 total cases of COVID- 19 in California, making it the hardest hit state by far. There have been 41,330 deaths due to the disease statewide. “Isn’t this the sixth year of your five-year plan?

articles.text: Congresswoman Barbara Lee of Oakland recently was named the new Chair of the House Appropriations subcommittee on State and Foreign Operations (SFOPS) on January 25. She will be the first African American member of Congress to serve as Chair of the subcommittee. The subcommittee, SFOPS, funds the state department and other foreign operations accounts, and is one of the 12 annual appropriations acts that fund the federal government each fiscal year. “I’m honored to serve as Chair of the Appropriations State and Foreign Operations Subcommittee,” Lee said. “This is a critical time for global investment and cooperation as we fight back a global pandemic, and we have much work to do.” She said that her top priorities on this committee will be investing in diplomacy, foreign assistance, and development programs. “[These] must be at the forefront of our approach, leaving behind the military first approach of the last 4 years. It’s also critical that we reinvest in the State Department and work to ensure our diplomatic corps and all aspects of our international affairs reflect the diversity of the country,” she said. Lee added that the subcommittee must take bold action in tackling the “existential threat of climate change.” She plans on using United Nations sustainable development goals as a guide to address pivotal issues such as global hunger, poverty, education, gender equality, reproductive justice, and economic equality. Lee served on the Foreign Affairs Committee for 10 years and has served on the Appropriations Committee for 14 years. She is also the Co-Chair of the Steering & Policy Committee, a senior member of the Appropriations Committee, former Chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. She also serves as Chair of the Majority Leader’s Task Force on Poverty and Opportunity. “I will lead and legislate as I always have on this committee and my entire career in Congress: through a lens of racial equity, which is needed now more than ever. I’m honored to serve in this critical moment to confront this global pandemic, put America’s priorities at the center of our funding initiatives, while respecting sovereignty of other nations, and help renew our global leadership in the world,” Lee said. In this position, Lee will be following in the footsteps of former officeholder and colleague, Ron Dellums, who was reelected 11 times from the Oakland-based district. Lee began her career in politics by serving as an intern in Dellums’ office – a place she would spend the next decade in service to her East Bay community. Upon Dellums’ retirement in February 1998, Lee was elected to succeed him.
articles.title: Barbara Lee to chair House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee

articles.text: Some Piedmont residents have questioned their neighbors’ lack of compliance to city sign ordinances to remove lawn signs following an election. The city has indicated it sent a reminder of sign ordinances on November 30, 2020. Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed that this followed an extremely high level of participation in recent elections, local and general. “We were looking for people who had put up signs to do their due diligence to remove the signs after the campaigns [had ended]. We added that on the city’s homepage to put the word out that these are the city’s rules,” he said. Current city code requires that all political signs be removed from yards within 10 days following an election. The ordinance does not regulate signs on the basis of content. The effort is mainly concerned with signs posted in yards, in windows, and on walls of residential properties. City Code Division 17.36 requires that only a maximum of 2 signs be allowed, with a maximum height of four feet per sign, including frame. Campaign signs placed on residences shall also comply with size restrictions, and any person who posts a camPiedmont City Code requires that election signs be removed 10 days following an election. paign sign on their property must remove the sign within ten days after the day of the election to which it pertains. A number of signs in Piedmont remain following the General Election on November 3, 2020, primarily signs supporting Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, now the President and Vice President of the U.S. According to Mayor Teddy Gray King, the city is sending out a letter to all residents that reiterate the specifications of lawn signs. “There are many signs throughout the town that may not meet the exact regulations. The city of Piedmont will make sure that every resident knows what the rules are,” King said, and added that Piedmont “takes seriously peoples’ right to free speech and is committed to ensuring everyone’s constitutional rights are respected, while clarifying sign regulations.”
articles.title: Residents question city’s oversight of signs

articles.text: Piedmont is continuing to explore affordable housing possibilities as a looming December 31 deadline to produce a proposal puts pressure on the city. In an effort to use available funds, Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell told city council members at their meeting on Monday night, February 1, that the city is seeking to extend the deadline by one year. Measure A1 was approved by voters in Alameda County in 2016 to create and preserve more affordable housing throughout the county. Piedmont was advised that year that it would be receiving slightly more than $2 million as an incentive to create and implement a plan. “Currently, we would need a proposal [to create affordable housing] by the end of this year. We’re asked for that deadline to be delayed for one year. That gives us time to put together the right package for Piedmont,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed. A housing element is one of seven elements, or chapters, that the state of California mandates a city or county include in its General Plan. A city’s goals for affordable housing and the measures it intends to take to reach those goals are included in a housing element. The city received $2,431,300 from Measure A-1, and is allowed to follow its own procurement processes to preliminarily select projects for funding. That funding was subsequently reduced to $2.2 million when Alameda County determined that housing developments in Oakland were at risk of failing after changes to the federal corporate tax rate, and money was reallocated from other Alameda County jurisdictions, including Piedmont, to Oakland. Given its existing development with single-family residences, Piedmont has largely relied on the construction of accessory dwelling units (granny flats) to supply new housing units, including those that are rent-restricted or otherwise affordable. The “built-out” characteristic of the city means there is less vacant or otherwise available land to utilize for new housing development than its East Bay neighbors may have. Since 2017, City staff has worked with County staff and Habitat for Humanity East Bay/ Silicon Valley to develop Measure A1 programs for affordable ADUs in Piedmont. To use the Measure A-1 funds, cities must adhere to supportive guidelines; for example, projects must be affordable for 55 years. This makes sense for a multi-family housing development, but less so for ADUs on single-family properties, which tend to change ownership more frequently. The City has asked Alameda County Supervisor Keith Carson to help facilitate a waiver from the Board of Supervisors’ Measure A-1 guidelines that requires Measure A-1 projects to have a 55-year deed restriction for affordability. This effort is still underway, according to Macdonald-Powell. According to Alameda County Housing and Community Development, the 55-year restriction was put in place to encourage long-term affordability. Piedmont’s reason for replacing the five-decade long restriction with a 10-year restriction is because a “shorter affordability term appropriate for single-family dwellings would make the program more marketable and improve its chances of success.” The possibility of “building-up” affordable units in Piedmont was brought up during the public comment portion of Monday’s meeting, and discussed amongst councilmembers. One resident pointed to Albany’s success thus far with affordable housing projects. Piedmont received the least amount of money in Alameda County, with Albany, having received $2,588,918, being the second least. Albany entered into an agreement with Satellite Affordable Housing Associates for the development of a 62-unit project located at 755 Cleveland Avenue, with an estimated completion of August 2022. The cost for the development is $43.8 million. According to Albany Community Development Director Jeff Bond, Albany is, like Piedmont, a built-out city. Piedmont, however, is unique that it is almost entirely builtout with single family homes and has virtually no commerce corridor. “Albany has a sizeable portion [of the city] that is zoned for mixed-use or multi-family units. There are a lot of parcels [in Albany], of significant size, that are zoned for this type of development, whereas Piedmont is overwhelmingly single-family residential with smaller lots,” Jackson said. “The size and availability of sites in Piedmont for the development of mid- to large-sized multi-family apartment buildings are different than in Albany, where the availability of this type of site means they can more quickly find a site as well as a development partner to [execute] that.” On August 17, 2020, Piedmont made the first step toward considering using the Measure A1 projects by entering into a contract with Lisa Wise Consulting to research incentives for the construction of ADUs. Some members of the public at Monday’s meeting questioned whether ADUs are an appropriate size for families. Resident Randy Wu stated that a 400-square-foot ADU he rented out to a Piedmont teacher “was perfect for a single individual” but not a small family, and he urged councilmembers to consider alternatives. Even if Piedmont does not use the allocated funds, they will still go toward affordable housing in Alameda County. Piedmont is not alone in asking for an extension and is not the only city in the county that has yet to use its funds. In addition, city council recommended that the Planning Commission set up an ad hoc subcommittee with the sole purpose of assisting staff and council in developing Measure A1 projects.
