articles.text: Michelle Baack shows off the Mulberry’s Market gift basket that she won in the city’s Climate Challenge Raffle. Join the challenge and do your part on climate challenge at www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org. Last month Michelle Baack got a little help ushering in the new year in the form of “the best raffle prize basket ever” as a reward for taking action on climate change. As the winner of the Piedmont Climate Challenge Raffle organized by the city, Michelle opened her front door to find a basket sitting on her doorstep – a basket filled with wine, cookies, truffles, cocktails and more, all courtesy of Mulberry’s Market. “What a way to ring in 2021,” she wrote in a thank you note. Michelle was recruited to participate in the Piedmont Climate Challenge by her neighbor and friend Claudia Harrison, one of Piedmont Connect’s Climate Challenge ambassadors. “When we joined the Climate Challenge in 2019 we had already done a lot of stuff to address climate change,” Michelle said. The Baacks had bought an older home on Trestle Glen Road, complete with avocado-colored refrigerator, so they had replaced old windows with new double-paned, more energy-efficient models and switched to LED lighting with motion sensors. Michelle and her husband, Jim, already walked to the corner to take the bus or casual carpool to work in San Francisco. Thanks to their close network of neighbors who carpooled for kids’ activities, the Baacks remained a two-car family when their children got their driver’s licenses. Now when her kids come home in the summer, Michelle rents a Zipcar when they are in a pinch. “When we travel to other cities, we use Zipcar too, so we don’t tie up a rental car for the whole time, hoping that means fewer cars overall,” Michelle said. But since COVID hit, the Baacks have been doing even more to reduce their environmental footprints. “We buy a lot more locally,” she said. When she does order from Amazon, she consolidates the order to be delivered on a certain day to reduce transportation emissions. They also have cut down on their waste. Michelle is buying food from Zero Grocery in Berkeley, the first plastic-free grocery delivery service. “My husband and I have a tiny bag of garbage after one week,” she quipped. She said she has been struck by how different attitudes and practices are in the Midwest, where her kids now live. “There is less focus on recycling in the Midwest, and what you can put in recycling bins is more limited,” she said. “There are no options for recycling plastic bags and wrappers, which our kids learned about at Havens with ‘baggy blue’ recycling.” She also observed that most apartment buildings in the Midwest don’t have compost service, either. “To-go food is mostly packaged in plastic or Styrofoam, not in compostable options that we see in the Bay Area,” Michelle said. “Here in Piedmont, we take it for granted that we can recycle so much and compost and have almost no real ‘garbage’ in our bin every week.” If you haven’t joined the Piedmont Climate Challenge yet, check it out at www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org.

articles.text: For the creative soul, inspiration can come from anywhere. When Athena Chang needed an idea for a high school art project, she found it in her pocket — and a way to highlight racial prejudice. “I really didn’t know what I was going to do,” said the 17-yearold senior. “But I was wearing this jacket with a mask in the pocket. I was playing with the mask, and I was thinking, ‘This is the most pertinent thing right now.’ And it all sort of came to me.” A face mask, so commonplace during the COVID-19 pandemic, was also a symbol of suppression, Chang said, and she turned that idea into a multi-media project for her Advanced Placement Art class at Piedmont High School. “When you’re wearing a mask, your voice is kind of muffled, and I think that’s what is happening to the Asian-American community a little bit,” said Chang. “The project is about restoring voice to the people who have sort of lost it.” Chang asked local AsianAmerican students for photos of themselves wearing masks. She also interviewed them about their own experiences during the pandemic. “Everybody was pretty open about their feelings,” she said. “I think people want to be open PHS Senior Athena Chang about it. They see the value of putting minority voices out there.” Now Chang is combining the visual and audio elements to create an immersive experience that she plans to launch online, and pandemic-permitting in a physical installation this spring. A lifelong artist, she hopes her project will help to change how people think about race and prejudice in America. “When you grow up as a person of color in this country, you know that you’ll be treated as lesser than,” Chang said. “This could be the time for that change to come.” Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for students in Piedmont schools.
articles.title: Student artist takes on challenge of racism

articles.text: The high school student group Piedmont for Consent will lead a workshop for all 2nd period classes at Piedmont and Millennium High on Wednesday and Friday, February 10 and 12. Second period classes will begin at 9:00 a.m. Students will either watch the Consent Workshop with their classmates or attend office hours. The Consent Workshop includes information about consent, boundaries, communication, physiological defense responses to stressful situations, unhealthy behaviors, alcohol and other drugs, reporting, and resources for everyone to continue the discussion and to get help. A parent workshop will be held two days prior on Monday, February 8 at 7:00 p.m. on Zoom to preview the content that the students will be discussing in the workshop that week. Piedmont For Consent is a group that formed in response to the Piedmont Protectors Instagram Account last summer. Co-Presidents Kaeli Huh and Anna Gotto, along with faculty mentor Kimberly Taylor, have led the group in conversations and education about consent throughout the fall and winter. They created the Consent Workshop when it was determined that the annual Consent Assembly was not adaptable to an online setting. It is hoped that this workshop will be a yearly addition to the Consent Assembly when it returns in person, as well as the start of this year’s Consent Education for the Piedmont community. In addition, the Piedmont for Consent group will host a discussion and debriefing of the workshop for all interested students in their weekly meeting on Thursday, February 25 from 3:15-4:30 p.m. For more information, contact Kimberly Taylor, PHS/PMS Acting and Drama Teacher and Mentor to Piedmont for Consent, at (ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us), or co-Presidents Kaeli Huh (22kaelihu@piedmont.k12.ca.us) and Anna Gotto (23annago@ piedmont.k12.ca.us).

articles.text: With Valentine’s Day around the corner, I have fond memories of time spent at my childhood elementary school decorating a white valentine bag and placing it on my desk for hand deliveries from my classmates. At home, I made individual valentine cards, folded them and then carefully inserted the finished card into an envelope. I addressed the envelope in my best handwriting while being certain to correctly copy the spelling from the class list. It was a much- loved tradition and one that has been carried over to this day at elementary schools everywhere. Occupational therapists love Valentine’s Day! For those who know me well, they may think that it’s the candy conversation of hearts and chocolates. Though the candies are a plus, OT’s love Valentine’s Day for Do It Yourself (DIY) valentine cards. One DIY valentine card encompasses drawing, coloring, folding, cutting with scissors, gluing and handwriting. It’s an OT’s dream come true. It’s a simple arts and crafts activity that includes the many necessary functional fine motor skills that a student needs in order to participate and be successful at school. More specifically, these fine motor activities require fine motor precision, a variety of grasp patterns, bilateral coordination and eye-hand coordination. But wait, there’s even more... A Valentine is more than a nice thought. One DIY valentine card also supports: • Visual Perception. For example, placement/centering written messages or designs. • Visual Motor Integration to draw heart designs. • Visual Skills for near point copying an address to an envelope. • Executive function for task initiation, sustained attention, planning and organization for a finished product. • Life skills (addressing an envelope.) • Creativity • Self esteem Whew! That’s a lot of skills for one Valentine’s Day card. You can certainly see why occupational therapists love Valentine’s Day! So, this year join occupational therapists everywhere and their love of Valentine’s Day by opting out of store-bought cards in favor of DIY. Since traditional in-class deliveries are not possible, take the opportunity for a movement break and walk to the nearby mailbox, or even hand-deliver cards to your friends’ doorsteps. Kimberly Bonacum, MS, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional information, contact mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Thinking Outside The Classroom Homemade Valentine cards much more than expression of love

articles.text: Let me start off by saying that it’s a miracle that I have made it this far in quarantine. For all the older siblings and parents reading, you will never feel our pain, but please continue reading. For the past 10 months I have been living with a sister who is graduating from high school, so all I ever hear about is college applications, and whether the college has released its decision. So, when life goes back to normal and I am out and about and trying to make small talk, all I talk about is how to apply to colleges and why a 12-point font is necessary when writing to Big 10 schools. Every day when I sit down for dinner, I am praying that maybe something – anything – would have happened so I won’t have to listen to what I now call “College Talk With The Vackers.” We talk about the acceptance rates, who is getting into which college and who isn’t, and when the next deadline will be. On top all of that, when I suggest that we might want to change the topic, everyone says, “Well then, what do you want to talk about?” It’s at that point that my mind just goes blank. It’s as if I suddenly have forgotten every talkable topic on Earth. In defeat I go back to eating my food and listening to the debate about whatever essay my sister has to finish. The next part of being a younger sibling is having to deal with the general older sibling stuff. Obviously, we last-borns had to deal with our older sisters or brothers in the pre-COVID-19 world, but now that we are in close quarters, there’s no escape. So, we have to resort to drastic measures, like saying, “Hello! Your lesser counterpart is talking. Can you please pay attention to us every once in a while? Like, Yoo-hoo. Will you take a break and maybe even talk to me. After all, I am not simply white noise.” Yes, I know you have a boyfriend, but why not also pay attention to the miracle of a sibling your parents gave you? “And another thing, please stop acting like a parent when the real parents aren’t around: it drives us crazy.” One time I was minding my own business and my sister seemed to just materialize out of nowhere, scaring the living daylights out of me. The next thing I know I’m being ordered to brush my hair, eat lunch, wear a mask, put on a jacket instead of a vest… and so on. Each time I say I am going to take a shower, my sister turns into Usain Bolt and sprints by me and inside the bathroom. Would an adult really do that? But I have to say that being younger has some perks. We actually get away with everything. I once got an “F” three times in a row on a math test and nobody batted an eyelash. My sister, on the other hand, once got a “C” and almost went into orbit. Younger siblings can get something as minor as a paper cut but get to be exempt from school for the rest of the year. Older siblings have to soldier on and go to school with a 100-degree fever. If we wanted to get takeout or watch a movie, mountains would be moved to make it happen. Let’s talk about curfew. It goes like this: eldest, 10 p.m. sharp or they’re grounded. Middle child, midnight or 1 a.m. Last but certainly not least, the youngest gets a curfew of 5 to 7 business days. We get the most love and attention, even though the parents claim they don’t have a favorite. And so, although most of the time we are overlooked by our siblings, we still know we hold the supreme position in the family. And despite what we have to endure from our older siblings, we do love them. One day in the near future when my sister goes off to start a new chapter at whatever college she attends, I will shed some tears, because I lost my partner in crime. Things won’t be the same without my second mom…oops, I mean my sister. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.

Piedmont Post For more information on placing an ad call... 626-2468 or email: nancy@cmc-ads.com Thinking Outside The Classroom Homemade Valentine cards much more than expression of love By Kimberly Bonacum With Valentine’s Day around the corner, I have fond memories of time spent at my childhood elementary school decorating a white valentine bag and placing it on my desk for hand deliveries from my classmates. At home, I made individual valentine cards, folded them and then carefully inserted the finished card into an envelope. I addressed the envelope in my best handwriting while being certain to correctly copy the spelling from the class list. It was a much- loved tradition and one that has been carried over to this day at elementary schools everywhere. Occupational therapists love Valentine’s Day! For those who know me well, they may think that it’s the candy conversation of hearts and chocolates. Though the candies are a plus, OT’s love Valentine’s Day for Do It Yourself (DIY) valentine cards. One DIY valentine card encompasses drawing, coloring, folding, cutting with scissors, gluing and handwriting. It’s an OT’s dream come true. It’s a simple arts and crafts activity that includes the many necessary functional fine motor skills that a student needs in order to participate and be successful at school. More specifically, these fine motor activities require fine motor precision, a variety of grasp patterns, bilateral coordination and eye-hand coordination. But wait, there’s even more... A Valentine is more than a nice thought. One DIY valentine card also supports: • Visual Perception. For example, placement/centering written messages or designs. • Visual Motor Integration to draw heart designs. • Visual Skills for near point copying an address to an envelope. • Executive function for task initiation, sustained attention, planning and organization for a finished product. • Life skills (addressing an envelope.) • Creativity • Self esteem Whew! That’s a lot of skills for one Valentine’s Day card. You can certainly see why occupational therapists love Valentine’s Day! So, this year join occupational therapists everywhere and their love of Valentine’s Day by opting out of store-bought cards in favor of DIY. Since traditional in-class deliveries are not possible, take the opportunity for a movement break and walk to the nearby mailbox, or even hand-deliver cards to your friends’ doorsteps. Kimberly Bonacum, MS, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional information, contact mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com. articles.text: This year’s Cub Scout Pinewood Derby was changed to a Derby Design Contest due to limitations imposed by COVID- 19. The design contest was completed last Thursday, January 28 after Cub Scouts spent the past few weeks designing, cutting, painting, and adding final touches on their cars in this iconic annual event. The entrants and winners are showcased in a video available for all to see: https://youtu.be/0XgwYP_xH4A. In lieu of a race day, Cub Scouts built their cars and entered them into a design contest instead. This event each year helps youth build their skills in project execution, design, creativity, and helps them practice motor skills while sanding and painting their cars. The design contest was the best alternative to a race and ensured the soul of the event remained intact during this difficult season. The Piedmont Council congratulates all entrants for their efforts in building their cars, with congratulations to the winners in each category. Special thanks to the Kobal family for spearheading the judging and the Wolff family for support with woodworking skills. Thanks also to Jack Gros and John Cumbelich of Troop 6 for video editing. The Piedmont Scouting Community continues the long tradition of service, leadership development, and outdoor education during the pandemic. Virtual, family, and cohort options are available for youth K-12th grade. To see upcoming events, ideas for hikes and for more information, go to https://www.piedmontbsa.org/. articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1978 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.

articles.text: The Columbus Zoo and Aquarium, now the permanent home of three orphaned mountain cubs rescued by Cal Fire firefighters last year and brought to the Oakland Zoo, has introduced their resident cougar Jessie to the brood. The three mountain lions were rescued from the devastating Zogg and August Complex fires that burned near Redding in September 2020. The severely burned orphaned male mountain lion cub, named Captain Cal after the firefighters that rescued him, fully recovered 47 days after he was first rushed to Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital by the California Department of Fish & Wildlife. With surgery, antibiotics, supportive fluids, pain medication, hand feedings, daily bandage changes, and round-the-clock care, Captain Cal survived and was ready to make the journey last November to his new home at the zoo in Columbus, Ohio. While still at the Oakland Zoo, Captain Cal was joined by two unrelated female cubs, also orphaned by the California wildfires and rehabilitated by Oakland Zoo’s veterinary team. Oakland Zoo documented Cal’s recovery and his bond with his new sisters. The litter of three quickly became “internet famous,” and a tiny but powerful reminder of the consequences of climate change. Columbus Zoo staff were given the honor of naming the two orphaned females – which they named Goldie and Poppy, as an homage to their California origin – home of the Golden poppies. Columbus Zoo kept its promise of introducing an older cougar to the young cubs. Because the three were orphaned at such a young age, they lack the skills most adult mountain lions develop; in their native range, mountain lion cubs stay with their mother until they are about two years old. After exploring their new habitat in the Columbus Zoo’s North America region, Goldie, Captain Cal and Poppy were introduced to the Zoo’s resident adult female cougar, Jessie, who is mostly blind. Zookeepers provided an opportunity for both Jessie and the cubs to explore each other’s spaces, giving them the chance to get familiar with each other. Columbus Zoo staff have observed that Goldie has proven to be the boldest, and saw her approach Jessie several times to paw at her playfully. Her sister Poppy was never far behind. Captain Cal could often be seen shyly peering out at Jessie from behind a Spruce tree while she napped in her den. “Jessie has never been a surrogate mother, but she is doing an amazing job so far,” a Columbus Zoo Facebook post stated. Staff Two female mountain lion cubs, fire survivors initially cared for at the Oakland Zoo, are now at the Columbus Zoo in Ohio and renamed Goldie and Poppy, because Golden poppies often bloom after a fire. Captain Cal has now fully recovered and is enjoying his permanent home in Columbus, Ohio. Jessie follows Goldie through their habitat. Captain Cal is a small, but powerful reminder of the consequences of climate change. The Columbus Zoo staff named the orphaned females Goldie and Poppy, as an homage to their original home, Jessie, now the cubs’ surrogate mother, is almost completely blind. California. added in the post that she has even “chuffed” back at the kittens in play, a noise her care team has never heard her make before. “Even with the cubs’ tragic beginning, their story is actually one of survival and hope. We are proud to work with our friends at Oakland Zoo, whose expertise has given these cubs another chance. We remain committed to the cubs’ care, and we will continue to share their important story with others as we work together to protect the future of wildlife and wild places,” Columbus Zoo and Aquarium President and CEO Tom Stalf said. In addition to providing a new home to the three cubs, in just the last five years alone, the Columbus Zoo has provided more than $96,000 in support of projects benefiting mountain lions and other species through People and Carnivores, which works primarily in Western Montana. You can watch the cubs’ first meeting with Jessie, and follow along with their new journey, on Columbus Zoo’s Facebook page at: https://www.facebook.com/ watch/?v=860302754753973.

articles.text: Scouts in Piedmont Troop 11 hiked from Stinson Beach to Muir Woods and back on a sunny Saturday in late January. Altogether it was a hike of 12 miles and over 3,000 feet in elevation. “My favorite part was walking through the Steep Ravine Trail and walking along the creek,” said Scout Gus Leonard. “It was really steep, and you could see a lot of stuff.” “I liked finding and looking at the fungi along the trail,” said Pierce Tindle. “My favorite part was the hiking!” said Shayna Chau. The hike started out on the Dipsea Trail, well known for the annual Dipsea Race. After enjoying a break for food and water at Muir Woods National Park, the troop started towards Stinson on the Ben Johnson Trail. This connected with the Stapleveldt Trail, which dropped into the Steep Ravine Trail before reconnecting with the Dipsea. “The views along the Dipsea are beautiful and the second half of the hike is stunning,” said Scoutmaster Tom Smegal. All the Scouts were glad they completed the strenuous hike. Scouts Will Myers and Kajsa Benson said, “Our favorite part was when we were done!” The troop took many measures to remain in line with social distancing requirements. Scouts, parents, and volunteers traveled and ate in family groups. The troop split into two hiking parties of less than 14 people each at the trailhead and staggered the time of their start. Everyone remained masked up throughout the hike, and they spaced out even further when they ate and took water breaks. “It’s been hard to keep the program going during COVID,” confirmed Smegal. “We haven’t been able to do many campouts, and we’re mostly limited to virtual meetings and day trips like this. It’s nice to have an adventure that gives us a chance to see each other in 3D and help the Scouts work on their advancement.” Troop 11 is one of five troops in the Piedmont Council Scouts BSA program. Piedmont’s Scouting program is designed for boys and girls ages 11-17, and focuses on character, fitness, life skills and leadership skills. Families interested in learning more about Piedmont Scouts are encouraged to call Kate Benson, Scout Executive, at 547-4493, or e-mail: contact@piedmontbsa.org. Scouts in the younger group paused for a group photo by the Muir Woods sign: Shayna Chau (left), Kajsa Benson, Pierce Tindle, Gus Leonard, Eric Venner, and Will Myers.

The Western Alameda County Conference recently produced its first sports schedules of the 2020- 21 school year. Instead of aiding the league in planning a sports calendar for this year and the next school year, the North Coast Section shifted responsibility for scheduling to each league. The WACC, which has 12 schools, should easily be able to schedule sports, in part because it is the largest Alameda County league. articles.text: This is the week leading to Super Bowl Sunday, where the Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers square off for the 55th edition of the America’s biggest sports attraction. Last year’s MVP, QB Patrick Mahomes, and KC could become back-to-back champions, but Tom Brady, a living legend, and the Buccaneers look to spoil the favorites. Here’s a look at this week’s game, and why The Post is selecting the Chiefs to win, despite the Buccaneers being the team to host and play in the Super Bowl. It starts on offense for Kansas City, with quarterback Patrick Mahomes, receiver Tyreek Hill and tight end Travis Kelce. Add to the mix head coach Andy Reid and coordinator Eric Bieniemy’s stellar play-calling, and an ability to grind out close yards with running backs Clyde Edwards-Helaire and Le’Veon Bell, we would have to say that Buccaneers’ defensive coordinator Todd Bowles is going to have his hands full. Lining up the Buc’s potential defense against KC’s superstars leave some predictable holes. Tampa Bay’s top cornerback, Jamel Dean, will likely square up on Hill, while TB may be required to double up on Kelce with a safety and linebacker Lavonte David, who is among the best coverage linebackers in the league. This could leave Tampa susceptible to veteran WR Sammy Watkins, rookie speedster Mecole Hardman, or plays out of the backfield to Edwards-Helaire and Bell. For the Buccaneers and Brady to pull off the upset, they will need major contributions from the receiving core of Mike Evans, Chris Godwin, Antonio Brown, while Brady enacts his Super Bowl magic. Head coach Bruce Arians and Brady could deploy a spread offense with its wideouts to thin out KC’s defensive backfield and lessen the blow of the Chiefs’ already weak pass rush. Tampa struggled mightily in the NFC Championship game against the pass rush with the Packers and likely wants to avoid that again. Furthermore, the Bucs could reap the benefit of LT Eric Fisher being hobbled with an Achilles injury. He’s currently ruled out from the Super Bowl and did not participate in any practice last week. We’ll go with the Chiefs and a one-possession ballgame: 31-27. Warriors fighting for playoff spot It’s past midway through the NBA season with the Warriors clinging to a No. 7 seed in the Western Conference standings. The Dubs faced a difficult game with the Boston Celtics last night but look ahead to four winnable games over the next week. Some unfortunate news arose on Monday with rookie center James Wiseman sustaining a wrist injury that will force him to miss at least 10 days. The Warriors play back-toback games in Texas against the No. 13 Dallas Mavericks tomorrow and February 6, followed by the No. 10 San Antonio Spurs on Monday and Tuesday, February 8-9. Golden State has not won more than two-games in a row this season in 21 games, so now would be the time to get its first winning streak of 2021 started with the hopes of earning a playoff spot. Weston McKennie making noise in Italy Typically, we reserve the final section of our Pro Sports write-up for England’s Premier League. But this week we want our sports readers to know about U,S, star midfielder Weston McKennie. He is quickly becoming one of the most influential players in the ultra-talented Serie A of Italy. McKennie, 22, signed with Italian superclub Juventus to play alongside Cristiano Ronaldo. Currently on loan from Germany’s Schalke, he made 75 appearances for the German club and scored four goals. His one-year loan contract will likely become a permanent deal due to performance incentives. In just 15 appearances with Juve, he’s already scored three goals, including a beautiful scissor kick goal in a 3-0 win over Barcelona in Champions League on December 8. Following McKennie’s most recent header goal against Bologna on Jan. 24, the youngster is quickly earning the nickname “Wizard Weston” and “Magic McKennie” after his celebration mimicked a wizard casting a spell. articles.text: Yosemite National Park re-opened on Monday, February 1 after the recent snow and windstorm pushed through the area, but with some noteworthy adjustments. Lodging and camping is permitted at select locations, but day trips will require advance reservation before visiting. Most of the park is open, but the recent windstorm toppled at least 15 giant Sequoia trees and has caused the park entrance on Highway 41 to be closed, including the Wawona, Badger Pass, Tunnel View and Mariposa Grove areas. Visitors can book reservations online at Recreation.gov between February 8-28, and reservations are already filling up fast. Dayuse reservations are valid from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. “Day use visitors who arrive by private vehicle or motorcycle must have a day use reservation. Day-use reservations are valid for seven consecutive days and must be validated on the first day that your reservation is scheduled to begin. Visitors arriving on foot or bicycle do not require a day use Photo courtesy of the LA Times Yosemite National Park reopened on February 1 with some lodging available. Starting February 8, the park will require day-use reservations. reservation,” the park advises. Reservations are valid for a full week and must be validated on the scheduled first day of your reservation, otherwise it will be canceled. But dates are already filling up, especially in the middle of the month. Yosemite’s plan coincides with the annual Firefall that is seen at Horsetail Falls between February 11-27. It is a natural phenomenon created when the setting sun reflects off Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. Photo courtesy of Aaronmphotography.com Here is a handy list of the best viewing times for the Firefall at Horsetail Falls in Yosemite Park. Lodging inside the park automatically registers your weeklong reservation. Reservations are currently available at the Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee Hotel. Private lodging is also listed at Wawona, Yosemite West, and Foresta. Camping is only available at the Upper Pines Campground. The annual Firefall of Horsetail Falls is expected to occur between February 11-27.

articles.text: Bay Area sports fans were saddened last week to learn of the passing of legendary public address announcer Dick Callahan. He died on January 29 at age 80. He was the former announcer and voice of the Oakland A’s baseball team, Golden State Warriors basketball team, and the University of California football team. He passed on Friday, January 29. “The Oakland A’s are heartbroken to learn that Dick Callahan passed away this morning. He lent his warm and welcoming voice to the Oakland faithful as our public address announcer for 15 seasons and more than 1,000 games at the Oakland Coliseum. We have lost a beloved member of our family who was a great friend to all who knew him. His passion and love for the A’s was like no other and his impact will never be forgotten. We extend our condolences to Dick’s family and friends during this time,” wrote the A’s in an official statement. Callahan took over PA duties in 2005 after his predecessor, Roy Steele, developed a rare illness. They were big shoes to fill, as A’s fans recalled Steele as the “Voice of God.” Since 2005, Callahan filled in perfectly for Steele, providing visitors to the Oakland Coliseum his enthusiastic voice in pre-game and mid-game announcements and player introductions as they stepped into the batters’ box. “He had a great voice,” said Ken Korach, A’s play-by-play broadcaster since 1980. “It was deep and it was resonant and he spoke with authority. He had a tough assignment to come in after Roy Steele and yet he did it in his own way. He didn’t try to be Roy. He just did a great job and he did it with enthusiasm.” In July Callahan chose to sit out the 2020 season due to health concerns. He had worked at least 1,000 A’s home games over his career. Callahan hit the millennium mark of 1,000 games in the game on May 7, 2019 when A’s pitcher Mike Fiers threw a no-hitter. He also called Dallas Braden’s perfect game in 2010 and Sean Manaea’s no-hitter the most memorable games of his career. “I’m still a little kid from the coal region of Pennsylvania who got lucky,” Callahan said of his 1,000th appearance to call A’s home games. Callahan was hired by the Golden State Warriors way back in 1981 and was their announcer for 19 years. For an additional 12 years, from 2000 until 2012, he became the voice of the Cal Golden Bears football team. He also worked various St. Mary’s College basketball games where he began his announcing career in 1975.
articles.title: Dick Callahan, former announcer for A’s, Warriors, & Cal, dies

articles.text: The annual Firefall routinely attracts hundreds of professional photographers to Horsetail Falls in Yosemite. Expected viewing this year falls between Feb. 11-27 with the best anticipated day to be on Feb. 21 from 5:28 p.m. to 5:40 p.m. Mother nature always calls the shots with this event, which requires a clear sky. “This unique lighting effect happens only on evenings with a clear sky when the waterfall is flowing. Even some haze or minor cloudiness can greatly diminish or eliminate the effect,” wrote park officials. Park officials are directing visitors to park at the Yosemite Falls and Yosemite Lodge Parking lot, and walk 1.5 miles to near the El Capitan Picnic Area for the best view of the Firefall. Visitors would be wise to arrive hours early to camp out for a prime viewing location, preparing for cold weather and a headlamp for the return walk in the dark. Northside Drive will have one lane closed to vehicles so pedestrians can walk on the road between the viewing area and Yosemite Falls parking. Photo courtesy of Travel & Leisure

articles.text: Our weekend adventure moved us out of the Bay Area to Morgan Hill, the location of a 1,147-acre park known for its series of waterfalls. Located on the eastern side of the Santa Cruz Mountains is Uvas Canyon County Park, found at the very end of the private Sveadal community on Croy Road. The recent rains that drenched the Bay Area helped awaken waterfalls along Swanson and Alec Creek. Hikers are greeted by the sound of babbling brooks immediately when entering the park on the Waterfall Loop trail along Swanson Creek. The first and smallest cascade, Granuja Falls, provides a fitting welcome to visitors after the first bridge. After another half mile, hikers will find the base of the Black Rock Falls on the right. Follow the water up the narrow path to a roughly 20-foot waterfall that passes over a black rock face, hence its name. Returning back to the Waterfall Loop Trail for just 0.2 of a Black Rock Falls is around 20 feet tall and feeds into Swanson Creek. Upper Falls is about 15 feet tall and is situated close to Basin Falls. Triple Falls is the final of five thriving waterfalls in the park. It’s the tallest at around 50 feet.

Upper Falls is about 15 feet tall and is situated close to Basin Falls. Triple Falls is the final of five thriving waterfalls in the park. It’s the tallest at around 50 feet. Staff Photos Uvas Canyon County Park in Morgan Hill has a collection of waterfalls that are easily accessible for hikers. Pictured here is Basin Falls. The first of the falls is the smallest, Garunja Falls. mile brings walkers to an intersection with the base of Upper Falls on the left, and a walkway to Basin Falls, which seemed to be the most thriving in the park after the rain. Basin Falls is about 15 feet in height, flowing down stones as it feeds into Swanson Creek. A fallen tree sits in its center to provide a clear perspective of its size. Returning to the Waterfall loop reunites you with Upper Falls, a two-tiered cascade that is also around 15 feet tall. Passing the falls means you are nearing the halfway point of your hike as you venture onto the Contour Trail. The Contour Trail goes for about 1.1 miles and provides some uphill climb, meaning it’s not just a scenic nature hike, but a fitting lower body workout. The trail is enveloped with the aroma of California Bay Laurels, the sprawling red bark of Manzanita, and some towering second-growth redwoods. After intersecting with the Alec Canyon Trail, turn right and hike less than a mile to Triple Falls – the final landmark of the day. It is the tallest of the falls, roughly 50 feet tall, but is really a small trickle compared to the other four. To see every waterfall on the Uvas Canyon loop is a hike of approximately 5.2 miles. It tops out at 1,273 feet in elevation gain. We passed 44 hikers on the day, but 36 were on the initial walk, the popular Waterfall Loop trail. Uvas Canyon is one of the few dog-friendly parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains, so it is safe to bring your pooch. Advance reservations are needed for parking – 24 hours in advance - otherwise you’ll be parking on the road leading in. Punch in “Uvas Canyon County Park” to your GPS device to access this South Bay park. A view of the active Swanson Creek. Hikers cross over the creek to continue on the Contour Trail. The Contour Trail is narrow and envelops hikers in the lush greenery of the Santa Cruz Mountains.

articles.text: “Entwined” by Charles Gadeken. The public art installation is located adjacent to the Conservatory of Flowers in Golden Gate Park. Visitors are now flocking to Peacock Meadow in Golden Gate Park to see its transformation into an enchanted forest of otherworldly shapes and ever-changing light. “Entwined,” a public art installation by San Francisco artist Charles Gadeken, creates a whimsical wonderland where visitors can explore paths and sit under a grove of three entwined sculptural trees while practicing social distancing. San Francisco is under a stayat-home order, but the parks are still open to the public. “Entwined” is available to view from dusk until 8:30 p.m., but the lawn portion of the meadow remains closed due to muddy conditions. Everyone must wear a mask at all times and practice social distancing. City and County of San Francisco’s current health order suggests that guests visit with household members only. Viewing is free and tickets are not required.
articles.title: Public Art now on display in Golden Gate Park

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will present its second digital program of the season on February 11. Dwight Rhoden’s “Let’s Begin at the End” returns digitally, following its success at the 2018 Unbound Festival. Composers include Bach, Philip Glass, and Michael Nyman. The program continues with San Francisco Ballet soloist Myles Thatcher, known for his signature blend of movement and social consciousness, who will showcase a new work in a world premiere. The program concludes with an archival capture of “Sandpaper Ballet,” a clever tongue-incheek piece from choreographer Mark Morris. Streaming access is available beginning 6 p.m. on February 11, and single stream access is available. Behind-the-scenes resources can be found on San Francisco Ballet’s website. Visit https://www.sf ballet.org/productions/digital-program-02/ to obtain tickets to these digital events.
articles.title: SF Ballet to present “Let’s Begin at the End” on February 11

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s Department of Diversity will present “For the Love of Opera,” a series of conversations during February about experiences of love on the lyric stage. It will follow with a Women’s History Month celebration throughout March. The first panel will explore LGBTQ+ storylines in 21st century opera. The speaker series begins with countertenor Albert Montanez, who has performed internationally and was chosen for the title role in the world premiere of the Alan Turing Opera Project in Sweden. He obtained an Artist Diploma at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London and received a full scholarship from the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. The artist discussion will begin on Sunday, February 7 at 7 p.m. Each 75-minute Zoom discussion is part of Opera Aficionado, a weekly interactive lecture series that offers music lovers around the world a front-row seat to scholarly talks, panels and conversations and an opportunity to dialogue with fellow opera enthusiasts, composers and special guests. Each virtual lecture is $20 and holds a maximum capacity of 20 attendees. A limited number of discounted tickets are available upon request for individuals in Albert Montanez need. Tickets are available until noon on the day of each event. articles.text: Freya Waley-Cohen The San Francisco Symphony has announced its new season of digital concerts, which will be available on a new video streaming service called “SFSymphony Plus.” The first event begins tomorrow, February 4, with a concert curated and conducted by Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen. “Soundbox” is a popular digital program that San Francisco Symphony has created in response to the current health crisis and subsequent venue closures. The programs offer a “backstage pass” to music curated, conducted, and produced by Symphony members. Tomorrow’s Soundbox is titled “Nostalgia,” and includes chamber works by Freya Waley-Cohen, Missy Mazzoli, and Caroline Shaw. In “Nostalgia,” the three composers look to a past that “may or may not exist, while opening new portals to the future.” Salonen’s inaugural San Francisco Symphony Soundbox is underwritten by Priscilla and Keith Geeslin. articles.text: Cristiana Pegoraro, a world-renowned pianist who has performed in Piedmont, released a new music video on January 27 to commemorate International Holocaust Day. Pegoraro, from Narni, Italy, is Artistic Director of the celebrated Narnia Festival. She is considered one of the most gifted pianists and composers of her generation. In 2006 and 2007, she toured the Gulf countries, becoming the first Italian female pianist to perform classical concerts in Bahrain, Yemen, and Oman. She is also the first female pianist to perform the 32 Sonatas for piano by Ludwig van Beethoven. In 2018 Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) welcomed her for an inspired concert, fresh from her popular appearance at Carnegie Hall in New York. Her performance at the Center was through her personal and professional friendship with PCA board member Debbie Dare and her husband Joseph Gold. Her newest composition, “Lost Love,” is available on her Youtube channel: https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=rP3EuNs2k2U&feature=youtu.be.
articles.title: Cristiana Pegoraro video commemorates International Holocaust Remembrance Day

articles.text: The Piedmont-based band, The Whiskey Talking, has been performing throughout the Bay Area for the last 15 years. But it wasn’t until last week, January 22, that the band finally released its debut album, “Grounded,” which is now available on all streaming services, CD and vinyl. The album contains 10 original songs written and sung by Piedmont resident Scott Lawson. It features Piedmont resident Paul Kasrovi on bass, as well as Terry Wit on drums. The music is a blend of rock, country, and folk, an amalgam typically referred to as “Americana.” The album comes out of the chute with a bang with a driving, punkish number called “Staggers and Jags.” “’Staggers and Jags’ is a British expression referring to delirium tremens,” explained Lawson. “The song is loosely about a couple I knew in L.A. who, like so many people down there, were constantly torn between their desire for spiritual awakening and their inherent decadence – the kind of people who would pause a meditation session to do a line.” The ballad “Red River” is a true story about the girlfriend of a former band member. “The two of them were living in New Mexico at the time. Apparently, they had a fight and she drove off into the Sangre de Cristo mountains above Taos,” said Lawson. “She was found the following day in her car, near the town of Red River, frozen to death. The car still had a half tank of gas and was working fine. Why she died is a complete mystery.” Jacket cover of CD issued by The Whiskey Talking, Scott Lawson’s Piedmont-based band. The song’s chorus asks: “Did you leave on your own terms? And were all of your lessons learned? Did you think it was better to freeze than to burn?” Over its 42 minutes, the album covers a lot of musical and lyrical ground, from the Southern-rock inflected road song, “Angel of Mercy,” to a country ballad, “Everybody Seems to Wanna Know,” to the anti-war rock of “Food Chain,” and the pastoral float of “Flying Dream.” Kasrovi said that the band members each come from different musical perspectives and those are reflected in the diversity of the genres they explore. In “previous lives,” all three band members played in modestly successful bands in Los Angeles and New York. “Scott and I both regularly played places like The Roxy and The Troubadour and The House of Blues back in the 80s and 90s, and Terry used to play at CBGB’s in New York,” Kasrovi said. “But what we have with this band is different – and better.” The album, released on Hardscrabble Records, can be heard by visiting http://thewhiskeytalking.hearnow.com or simply by searching for The Whiskey Talking on Spotify or other streaming services.
articles.title: CD 15 years in the making by Scott Lawson’s band, The Whiskey Talking

articles.text: The Fong Costanza Trio joins Ben Simon for a special extended episode of “Simon Says Show.” While the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra ensemble shelters in place, Music Director Ben Simon has put his time in quarantine to good use by launching the “Simon Says Show.” Simon has added new episodes and his series continues with a performance by the Fong Costanza Trio. The San Francisco Chamber Orchestra’s principal second violinist, Debra Fong, is joined by spouse Chris Costanza and daughter Isabella Costanza for a special family project. The trio came together via Zoom to perform on Simon’s series recently. The performance is featured in a special “extended episode” with a runtime of 52 minutes. Watch and listen to the trio at https://www.thesfco.org/simonsaysshow.
articles.title: ‘Simon Says’ show continues with Fong Costanza Trio

articles.text: The ensembla cast of Rian Johnson’s Knives Out. Movie review by Chris Honoré Mysteries represent a massive literary genre so compelling that it has found a solid niche on television and in film. A captivating example is the just released Knives Out, written and directed by Rian Johnson in which he pays homage to those writers and filmmakers who came before, unabashedly using their familiar templates. The story is set in New England, primarily in a century-old Gothic mansion. A large extended family (Jamie Lee Curtis, Michael Shannon, Don Johnson, Toni Colette and Chris Evans) has gathered to celebrate the 85th birthday of Harlan Thrombey (Christopher Plummer), a wildly successful and prolific mystery writer who has amassed a fortune from the sale of his books. Harlan sits at the titular head of the table as the unchallenged patriarch of a cohort of grown children and grandchildren, plus a young nurse, Marta (Ana de Armas). To a person (with the exception of Marta) they seem ever mindful of the inheritance dangling before them like a modifier, consuming the subtext of their interactions. Later in the evening, Harlan is discovered in his third-floor attic study by Marta, who was bringing him a meal. His throat has been cut. Terrified, she runs downstairs to the family who are gathered in a sitting room. And thus, the narrative abruptly shifts to a what/why/whodunit, giving structure to all that follows. Arriving with the police is a private detective, Benoit Blanc (Daniel Craig), who is initially content to sit in the shadows, listening. Finally, when asked, he acknowledges that he was hired by an anonymous individual and will be assisting, without police objection, in the investigation. He asks that each family member be interviewed, suggesting that they should remain at the house. They agree, anticipating a funeral service for Harlan, followed by a reading of the will. Soon Blanc morphs into the puzzle master, questioning each of them in his Col. Sanders drawl, collecting vagrant bits of information, all while assuming they are reflexively dissembling. Slowly, tenaciously, the onion is peeled in the search of motive and opportunity. Loose ends are ubiquitous and in need of being tied up. Some are quickly discarded for more likely outcomes. Suspects are everywhere (of course it could have been a suicide… or not). Detective Blanc grows increasingly more animated as he assembles the puzzle, beginning with the borders and working toward the center, waiting for an image, however obscured, to emerge. Screenwriter Johnson clearly takes genuine pleasure in the genre, the plot replete with twists and head fakes and delicious reveals. Those in the audience have to pay attention or miss what is offered up as a clue: a broken trellis, a silent dowager, footprints on a muddy path, an overheard argument, a missing medicine bag, a volatile grandson. And then there’s young, devoted Marta, the full-time nurse – an immigrant of sorts (sneeringly accused of being an anchor baby) – who is slowly pulled into the center of the Thrombey clan’s many residual issues. These are people who have more baggage than a hotel lobby and are ever prepared to pull out the knives honed by familial history and have a go at one another. I’m reluctant to say more about the plot; the pleasure derived from watching Knives Out is seeing it fresh, in effect, clueless. Thankfully, the trailer was sufficiently ambiguous, giving only a hint of what the film promised. Even Harlan speaks from the grave as the mystery inextricably unfolds. And so it does – in the attic study, with a knife, and not a candlestick anywhere to be found. Knives Out (2019). Directed by Rian Johnson. With Jamie Lee Curtis, Michael Shannon, Don Johnson, Christopher Plummer, Toni Colette and Chris Evans. 2 hrs., 10 min. PG-13. Movie review by Chris Honoré were being challenged. prejudices. their employers’ children. Daniel Craig as Detective Benoit Blanc in Knives Out.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Knives Out a splendid mystery reminiscent of Clue

articles.text: Octavia Spencer and Viola Davis stars in The Help. There is so much to like in The Help, so many reasons to recommend. And yet there is also a sense that there is something missing. Perhaps that’s because it is set in the South, during the nascent days of the Civil Rights movement, when Jim Crow laws and attitudes The film, written and directed by Tate Taylor, adapted from Kathryn Stockett’s bestseller, is from the point of view of countless black women who, in the early 1960s still worked as maids in the homes of the wealthy white families of Jackson, Mississippi. The narrative voice is Skeeter’s (Emma Stone), newly returned to Jackson from Ole Miss. She lands a job working for the local newspaper and is inspired to interview the maids of those Junior League women who lead privileged, insulated lives and are trapped by their own These daughters of the South are incapable of seeing their maids as three-dimensional people; rather, they view them as accessories, and thus avoid real engagement with their children or with the hard labor that is required to run their homes. It is the maids who cook the meals, buy their groceries, clean their houses and raise Skeeter begins by interviewing two maids – Abileen (Viola Davis) and Minny (Octavia Spencer) – probing their lives and drawing out their stories and their feelings about the white children they have nurtured. Abileen has cared for 17 children during her decades of service. Each morning, dressed in uniforms, these women leave their shotgun bungalows and take the bus to the homes of the white families. It is there that the morality play, which is at the heart of The Help, is played out. And it is there that Abileen and Minny suffer in silence, ever fearful of a misstep, as the bigoted young women display, without reflection, a racism laced with a condescending, brittle intolerance. What the film doesn’t accomplish – and perhaps it’s unfair to expect that it could – is to graphically explore the depth of the injustice and anger hidden just beneath the patina of civility. The Help is wonderfully acted, led by Viola Davis and Octavia Spencer, whose astonishing performances – which never slip into caricature – are nicely supported by Emma Stone, Allison Janney, and Bryce Dallas Howard in a tour de force of villainy. The film is predicated on the archetype of African American women – maternal, non-threatening, ever-smiling, middle aged – who, from the early days of slavery, were central to the plantation manor. The Help. Directed by Tate Taylor. Starring Emma Stone, Viola Davis and Octavia Spencer. 2 hrs., 17 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: The Help a look at Jackson, Miss. in the sixties

Screenwriter Johnson clearly takes genuine pleasure in the genre, the plot replete with twists and head fakes and delicious reveals. Those in the audience have to pay attention or miss what is offered up as a clue: a broken trellis, a silent dowager, footprints on a muddy path, an overheard argument, a missing medicine bag, a volatile grandson. And then there’s young, devoted Marta, the full-time nurse – an immigrant of sorts (sneeringly accused of being an anchor baby) – who is slowly pulled into the center of the Thrombey clan’s many residual issues. These are people who have more baggage than a hotel lobby and are ever prepared to pull out the knives honed by familial history and have a go at one another. I’m reluctant to say more about the plot; the pleasure derived from watching Knives Out is seeing it fresh, in effect, clueless. Thankfully, the trailer was sufficiently ambiguous, giving only a hint of what the film promised. Even Harlan speaks from the grave as the mystery inextricably unfolds. And so it does – in the attic study, with a knife, and not a candlestick anywhere to be found. Knives Out (2019). Directed by Rian Johnson. With Jamie Lee Curtis, Michael Shannon, Don Johnson, Christopher Plummer, Toni Colette and Chris Evans. 2 hrs., 10 min. PG-13. Octavia Spencer and Viola Davis stars in The Help. Movie review by Chris Honoré There is so much to like in The Help, so many reasons to recommend. And yet there is also a sense that there is something missing. Perhaps that’s because it is set in the South, during the nascent days of the Civil Rights movement, when Jim Crow laws and attitudes were being challenged. The film, written and directed by Tate Taylor, adapted from Kathryn Stockett’s bestseller, is from the point of view of countless black women who, in the early 1960s still worked as maids in the homes of the wealthy white families of Jackson, Mississippi. The narrative voice is Skeeter’s (Emma Stone), newly returned to Jackson from Ole Miss. She lands a job working for the local newspaper and is inspired to interview the maids of those Junior League women who lead privileged, insulated lives and are trapped by their own prejudices. These daughters of the South are incapable of seeing their maids as three-dimensional people; rather, they view them as accessories, and thus avoid real engagement with their children or with the hard labor that is required to run their homes. It is the maids who cook the meals, buy their groceries, clean their houses and raise their employers’ children. Skeeter begins by interviewing two maids – Abileen (Viola Davis) and Minny (Octavia Spencer) – probing their lives and drawing out their stories and their feelings about the white children they have nurtured. Abileen has cared for 17 children during her decades of service. Each morning, dressed in uniforms, these women leave their shotgun bungalows and take the bus to the homes of the white families. It is there that the morality play, which is at the heart of The Help, is played out. And it is there that Abileen and Minny suffer in silence, ever fearful of a misstep, as the bigoted young women display, without reflection, a racism laced with a condescending, brittle intolerance. What the film doesn’t accomplish – and perhaps it’s unfair to expect that it could – is to graphically explore the depth of the injustice and anger hidden just beneath the patina of civility. The Help is wonderfully acted, led by Viola Davis and Octavia Spencer, whose astonishing performances – which never slip into caricature – are nicely supported by Emma Stone, Allison Janney, and Bryce Dallas Howard in a tour de force of villainy. The film is predicated on the archetype of African American women – maternal, non-threatening, ever-smiling, middle aged – who, from the early days of slavery, were central to the plantation manor. The Help. Directed by Tate Taylor. Starring Emma Stone, Viola Davis and Octavia Spencer. 2 hrs., 17 min. Rated PG-13. Democracy is not a spectator sport! articles.text: Ivan Vanko, portrayed by Mickey Rourke, is Tony Stark’s nemesis in Iron Man 2. Movie review by Chris Honoré The first Iron Man movie was released in 2008. It had a high “wow factor” to be sure. It was fresh and interesting, a shiny adaptation of the Marvel Comics’ character, Iron Man, brought to life by the talented actor Robert Downey. Iron Man 1 delivered the necessary backstory regarding how Iron Man came to be, along with the astonishing technology that turned Tony Stark, industrialist, into a high-flying weapons system. The Iron Man suit defines cool. Plus, it’s always a thrill watching a superhero’s history unfold, watching as he or she begins to take control of newly discovered and unexpected abilities. Recall Superman, arriving on earth in the center of a meteor; or Spider Man, bitten by a spider, grappling with his metamorphosis. It’s a rush. Hence, that first Iron Man movie, now in franchise mode, was superb entertainment. The challenge then was how to craft a sequel that would be equally gripping. Comic book adaptations have become an entertainment staple using familiar characters: Batman, Hulk, X-Men, Superman, Spider Man, and Hellboy, to name a few. Which brings us to Iron Man 2. For writer Justin Theroux and director Don Favreau the trick was to find a story that presented a now established Tony Stark aka Iron Man in a new and interesting way. A new antagonist had to be introduced, an opponent worthy of Stark’s incomparable strength, wealth and intelligence. If not done well the filmmakers risked “jumping the shark,” meaning that the Iron Man 1 narrative had peaked with the first film and anything thereafter would be anti-climactic. The term “jump the shark” is most often used to describe the moment when a TV series or movie franchise begins its downturn and things spin off into absurdity. If “jump the shark” doesn’t do justice to the phenomenon, there’s always “Nuke the fridge,” derived from the moment in Indiana Jones and the Crystal Skull, the second in the trilogy, when Indy jumps into a lead-lined fridge and survives a nuclear explosion unscathed. The scene was so far from the inimitable first film, Indiana Jones and the Raiders of the Lost Ark, that it acquired its own moniker, “Nuke the fridge.” So, does Iron Man 2 “nuke the fridge”? Pretty much. In an effort to make Stark extraordinary and more complex, the writers make him decidedly un-heroic. He’s arrogant, hubristic, and seemingly consumed with his newfound fame and power. Basically, he’s not very appealing. In one scene he arrives before a government oversight committee with studied insouciance, flashing the peace sign, declaring world peace has been privatized, while displaying an ego that is in need of deflating. Watching Robert Downey portray even a phone book is always a treat. But this second incarnation of Stark is simply strange. Downey is, of course, a consummate actor as is Gwyneth Paltrow as Pepper Potts, his unacknowledged love interest and solidly competent girl Friday. As for Mickey Rourke, in all his grungy splendor, well, he’s passable as a Russian named Ivan Vanko, wingnut scientist, and Stark’s bad dude nemesis. Samuel L. Jackson makes an appearance, briefly, as Nick Fury as does Scarlett Johansson in the role of Natalie, aka Black Widow. The burden that any sequel carries is one of story. Once Iron Man’s history has been revealed, and his superhero talents established, it all comes down to imagination. Does Iron Man 2 have the right stuff? Sadly, the answer is no. The hardware is wonderful. The suit is still a treat to watch: wax on, wax off. But the rest, the loud climactic battle, the flights at supersonic speeds – all of it is familiar. The fallback position should be craft a great screenplay. Otherwise, the thrill is gone. Iron Man 2. Starring Robert Downey, Don Cheadle, Gwyneth Paltrow, Scarlett Johansson and Mickey Rourke. Directed by Jon Favreau. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Iron Man 2 lacks excitement of first

articles.text: A scene from The Secret of NIMH. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Secret of NIMH is a wonderful, compelling story, both whimsical and thrilling. Its handdrawn animation is extraordinary, rich in detail and color, and follows in that familiar tradition in which animals talk and reason. It was adapted from the 1971 children’s classic, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, written by Robert C. O’Brien. From the opening scene, the narrative is flooded with a sense of urgency that fully engages the audience. Mrs. Frisby (Elizabeth Harman), a widowed mouse, lives with her two children in a cinder block located in an open field on the Fitzgibbon farm. She learns that the field is soon to be plowed and she must move her family as quickly as possible to a safe place. But she is confronted with what seems an insurmountable problem: she discovers that her child Timothy is ill. She asks Mr. Ages (Arthur Mallet), a friend of her late husband, Jonathan, to come see her young son. He tells Mrs. Frisby that Timothy is very sick with pneumonia, gives her some medicine, and adds that Timothy cannot be moved for at least three weeks. The following day she learns that Farmer Fitzgibbons is going to start plowing early. Suddenly, time is of the essence, and she realizes that she needs help. With her friend Jeremy (Dom DeLuise), a clumsy but comical crow, she goes to consult the Great Owl (John Carradine) for advice. He wisely tells her to seek out the rats who live under a large rose bush near the Fitzgibbon farmhouse. It’s at this point that act two of The Secret of NIMH begins. Mrs. Frisby is increasingly frantic to find a way to move her home without risking the life of Timothy. She discovers, on her visit to the rose bush, that the rats possess a superior intelligence and have created a community that is beyond anything she has ever seen: it’s a warren of sophisticated technology and they even have electricity, which they steal from the Fitzgibbon house. It’s there that she meets the leader of the rats, Nicodemus (Derek Jacobi). He agrees to help her and gives her an amulet that will help her when she needs it most. Thus begins the adventure of Mrs. Frisby in earnest and the secret of NIMH (the National Institute of Mental Health) is revealed. NIMH is simply great storytelling by a group of ex-pats from Disney who launched a new studio headed by Don Bluth, committed to sustaining animation as an art form and not one ruled by CGI. This feature film was their first effort, and it proved to be warm and filled with thrills. One caveat, however: Though the film has a G rating it can also be darkly intense. The Secret of NIMH (1982). Animated fantasy adventure. Directed by Don Bluth. With the voices of Elizabeth Harman, Derek Jacobi, and Dom DeLuise. Rated G. 1 hr., 22 min.

articles.text: Evelyn and her Magic Violin. Evelyn Kaye, a Julliard-trained violinist, was a beautiful violinist in addition to having movie star looks. She was well-known as a featured performer with Phil Spitalny’s Hour of Charm Orchestra. Everyone needs a wake-up call once in a while. I got mine at the beginning of the year. I wanted to interview my favorite opera singer, so I went through the usual channels and contacted his manager. There was no response after three attempts. I tried once more and the manager responded. I would get no interview. The manager said that: “Larry is busy and has too many things to do.“ Some guys have all the luck. Wake-up calls like this are quite useful. They cause us to think about some pretty serious stuff… like rejection. This caused me to think about why some performers have it all and others who are equally talented languish. The history of music is illustrated by a struggle for supremacy. In politics, success is usually on the side of the biggest army. Music is not so far removed. As a case in point, King David must have had a good publicity department. So did Nero, who embraced the ageold adage that bad publicity is the same as good publicity – as long as they spell your name correctly. Politics has lobbyists; music has payola. But putting politics aside, how can we, the music loving public, discover our heroes? Are today’s icons really the best, or are the power brokers lurking in the shadows? Don King, the famed boxing promoter, is not unique in history. Long before social media took over, to be successful and be recognized, an aspiring artist had to petition the local nobleman. Only then was permission granted. The church played a similar role. Then, as now, many would sell their souls to the devil for fame and fortune. Enter Niccolò Paganini; perhaps the greatest violinist of all time. Perhaps. But there is no doubt that he was the greatest exploiter of publicity ever. Every successful performer has studied how Paganini did it – even Sinatra and Elvis and the Beatles. Everyone. Competitions are one way to stardom. Almost every first-prize winner at the Paris Conservatory enjoyed a successful career. Some notable names are Wieniawski, Sarasate, and Fritz Kreisler. In composition it was Berlioz and Bizet. They were great and unique talents. Today competitions are commonplace. Contestants go from one to the other, and in doing so stunt their growth artistically. Some performers are pure media creations. Mario Lanza is the best example. His public concerts were so rare that you can count them on your fingers. But he was a great singer, Hollywood and television not withstanding. Frank Sinatra was ever so popular. His mafia connections delivered – big time. Corporations sometimes help. I know, for a fact, that a big Japanese firm paid $4.5 million for a violin and gifted it to a notable player. In the world of race car driving, if you want to win the Grand Prix, it helps to have a Ferrari. It is always fun to be a Monday morning quarterback. Initiate the debate and then stand back. Watch from the bleachers, but never go onto the field. Sometimes the scene is funny. Remember the “merchandising“ scene from Spaceballs? George Foreman took it to heart and mastered it. But so did famed operetta composer Franz Lehar. He was pictured in a magazine ad. He had shaving cream on his face and a razor in his hand. The caption: “I get my greatest musical inspirations using brand X shaving cream.“ To prove my point, look at the visuals. Even Jascha Heifetz did it. Another example is a Maybelline ad with Evelyn and her magic violin. Some artists have all the luck. They are all things to all people – talented, savvy, well connected… and good looking. The common business model for all of them was they didn’t turn down interviews.

Wake-up calls like this are quite useful. They cause us to think about some pretty serious stuff… like rejection. This caused me to think about why some performers have it all and others who are equally talented languish. The history of music is illustrated by a struggle for supremacy. In politics, success is usually on the side of the biggest army. Music is not so far removed. As a case in point, King David must have had a good publicity department. So did Nero, who embraced the ageold adage that bad publicity is the same as good publicity – as long as they spell your name correctly. Politics has lobbyists; music has payola. But putting politics aside, how can we, the music loving public, discover our heroes? Are today’s icons really the best, or are the power brokers lurking in the shadows? Don King, the famed boxing promoter, is not unique in history. Long before social media took over, to be successful and be recognized, an aspiring artist had to petition the local nobleman. Only then was permission granted. The church played a similar role. Then, as now, many would sell their souls to the devil for fame and fortune. Enter Niccolò Paganini; perhaps the greatest violinist of all time. Perhaps. But there is no doubt that he was the greatest exploiter of publicity ever. Every successful performer has studied how Paganini did it – even Sinatra and Elvis and the Beatles. Everyone. Competitions are one way to stardom. Almost every first-prize winner at the Paris Conservatory enjoyed a successful career. Some notable names are Wieniawski, Sarasate, and Fritz Kreisler. In composition it was Berlioz and Bizet. They were great and unique talents. Today competitions are commonplace. Contestants go from one to the other, and in doing so stunt their growth artistically. Some performers are pure media creations. Mario Lanza is the best example. His public concerts were so rare that you can count them on your fingers. But he was a great singer, Hollywood and television not withstanding. Frank Sinatra was ever so popular. His mafia connections delivered – big time. Corporations sometimes help. I know, for a fact, that a big Japanese firm paid $4.5 million for a violin and gifted it to a notable player. In the world of race car driving, if you want to win the Grand Prix, it helps to have a Ferrari. It is always fun to be a Monday morning quarterback. Initiate the debate and then stand back. Watch from the bleachers, but never go onto the field. Sometimes the scene is funny. Remember the “merchandising“ scene from Spaceballs? George Foreman took it to heart and mastered it. But so did famed operetta composer Franz Lehar. He was pictured in a magazine ad. He had shaving cream on his face and a razor in his hand. The caption: “I get my greatest musical inspirations using brand X shaving cream.“ To prove my point, look at the visuals. Even Jascha Heifetz did it. Another example is a Maybelline ad with Evelyn and her magic violin. Some artists have all the luck. They are all things to all people – talented, savvy, well connected… and good looking. The common business model for all of them was they didn’t turn down interviews. articles.text: A group of artistic and entrepreneurial Piedmont and Oakland residents will gather this Saturday, February 6 on the sidewalk surrounding a Crocker Highlands home to sell their arts, crafts, homemade food products and more. With Valentine’s Day just around the corner, many of the items will be specifically designed as gifts for the February 14 holiday. The sale begins at 11 a.m. and goes until 3 p.m. The location of the sale is 855 Longridge Road at the corner of Verrada. It is approximately two blocks up from Lakeshore. Artist and former Piedmonter Lisa Scimens will be selling her original Valentine cards, coffee mugs and pillows. Also for sale will be samples from her Dancing Artist Designs online store (www.dancingartistdesigns.com) and other greeting cards featuring artwork from her paintings. All sales will benefit Family Sanity, her non-profit organization that helps parents with young adults and teens challenged by mental illness (www.familysanity.org). Former Piedmonter Megan Burke will be offering her handcrafted salves (brownandburke. com) made from toasted organic herbs from the Sierra foothills. The salves promote healing of the skin and are good for the face and the entire body. Back by popular demand, Piedmonter Adam Betta is providing his irresistible Bolognese Valentine’s Day collection by Lisa Scimens. sauce for sale. The recipe for Adam’s Spicy Bolognese was inspired by his father and motherin-law whose families come from different parts of Southern Italy. Liz Fitzgerald of Piedmont will be displaying her lovely Shibori products. Her company, shiboriazule, makes handcrafted indigo dyed items using the ancient Japanese dying process. She will have face masks, scarves, table runners and clothing items for sale. Devon and Nancy Fox will offer homemade desserts and treats for your valentine as well as your furry friends. Also available for purchase are uniquely designed seasonal wine cork decorations and lighted wine bottles. Nicole Garcia is the creator of El Nautico Creations and ASUKAR Palestinian Cuban Fusion Food. Her food is like no other and she will be selling all sorts of savory items you’ll want to take home and try. All vendors will wear masks and take Covid-safe precautions. articles.text: The University of California Botanical Garden in Berkeley. The University of California Botanical Garden in Berkeley is open to the public during COVID-19 restrictions, but reservations are required to visit. The gardens are open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Members-only hours are from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. The gardens are closed on the first Tuesday of the month. The glasshouses, water fountains and garden shop are temporarily closed due to COVID, and will reopen when Alameda County enters a less-restrictive tier of COVID-19 regulations. Guests should note that there will be path disruptions throughout the garden as staff works to manage visitation flow and allow for important horticultural projects. Restrooms, benches, and water bottle filling stations are available. Online advanced admission tickets are required for all visitors, including members. Reservations must be made online via a timed-ticketing reservation system before you arrive at the garden. To reserve tickets, click on https://botanicalgarden.berkeley. edu/covid-reopen. To experience the gardens from home, take advantage of the online exhibits. Throughout February, UC Botanical Garden will present its annual exhibition and celebration of botanical art on a digital platform. Visit the Garden’s website throughout the month of February to view a stunning array of art featuring plants from around the world. You can also join garden staff for an opening “reception” on Zoom on Saturday February 6 from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. There are also associated Zoom programs, such as a lecture on the history of botanical art on February 12, an introduction to botanical art on February 20, and a 3-part series titled “Inside the Artists’ Studio”, which will take you on a visit to the studios of six artists demonstrating techniques in botanical art. To view more online resources, see https://events.berkeley.edu/ index.php/calendar/sn/bot.html?eve nt _ I D =136805&d at e = 2021-02-06&filter=Event%20 Type&filtersel=.
articles.title: Online exhibitions continue throughout the month of February

articles.text: Celebrate the Year of the Ox with Asian Art Museum. San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum will offer an array of digital events to celebrate Lunar New Year, the Year of the Ox. Lunar New Year is the beginning of a calendar year whose months are cycles of the moon. It is widely celebrated in East Asia and Southeast Asia, as well as other parts of the world. You can learn more about how Lunar New Year is observed around the world with the museum’s cultural celebration packet. Visit https:// asianart.org/cultural-celebrations/celebrate-lunar-new-year/ to view on-line resources. Included in the celebration packets are art activities, coloring pages, and a Lunar New Year Red Envelope instructional project. A storyteller series features Fred Sheng, Miriam Mills, and Leta Bushyhead reading classic celebratory tales. A New Year poetry and calligraphy workshop will take place tomorrow, February 4, at 7 p.m. Poets Michael Warr and Chun Yu will read works in English and Mandarin that reflect the essence of the New Year – vanquishing the past, embracing new beginnings, and venerating ancestors – while Aiqin Zhou demonstrates her skillful calligraphy by illustrating some of the poems. The Ox is the second of the 12-year periodic sequence of animals, which appear in the Chinese zodiac. The Year of the Ox follows after the Year of the Rat (2020), and is followed by the Year of the Tiger (2022). To learn more about the symbolic significance of the Ox, visit https://asianart.org/.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum celebrates Lunar New Year with virtual events
