articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Mmmm, good. Chocolate Cherry Scones will put a smile on everyone’s face in time for Valentine’s Day. Scones in winter are an easy, one-bowl creation with basic ingredients many of us have on hand – flour, butter, cream, and sugar. In winter I prefer to make them by hand, using my fingers to massage the cold bits of butter into the flour mixture. It’s fast and somehow satisfying, and it’s an easier clean-up than bringing in a food processor or even a pastry cutter. I figure I’m going to need to get in there with my fingers to pat, shape and cut the scones anyway, so why not go fully manual? This version is fancy, but still using common pantry ingredients, chocolate and dried cherries. Feel free to substitute dried cranberries, snipped dried apricots, even candied citrus or ginger bits. Chocolate Cherry Cream Scones Adapted from Clair Ptak’s Cream Scones and David Burtka’s Chocolate & Cherry Scones. Makes 12 scones, about 3” diameter INGREDIENTS • • • • • • • • • • • • • 2-1/2 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for shaping 1/4 cup granulated sugar 1 tablespoon baking powder 1/2 teaspoon baking soda 1/8 teaspoon salt 1/2 cup unsalted butter, chilled and cut into 1/4-inch cubes 1/2 cup dried cherries, soft and pliable 1/2 cup dark chocolate pieces, either chopped from a bar or chocolate chips 3/4 cups heavy cream, chilled 1/2 cup buttermilk, chilled 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 1 egg, beaten Turbinado sugar, or other coarse sugar to top DIRECTIONS 0 Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. 1 Combine together the flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt; then stir in the sugar in a large mixing bowl, at least 3-quart size. Make sure all the dry ingredients are thoroughly mixed. Set aside. 2 Cut the butter into 1/ 2” cubes and rub through the dry ingredients with your fingers, a pastry cutter, or use a food processor—anyway that results in a coarse, crumbly texture. 3 Add the vanilla extract into the heavy cream, then pour the cream and buttermilk over the top of the flour mixture; gently stir with a wooden spoon until just combined. Add the chopped chocolate and dried cherries and stir to just distribute evenly throughout. 4 Turn the mixture onto a lightly floured surface and press together into a block. 5 Fold the dough in half, lifting and turning the dough over itself just once. Press together and let it rest for 5 minutes. 6 Pat the dough into about a 1” thick round. Use a 2-1/ 2” round cutter to stamp out the scones, pressing straight down through the dough and straight back out. Do not twist the cutter, as it hinders the scones’ rise. Gently reshape the dough back to a 1” thickness as needed to total 12 scones. Take care to not handle the dough too much. 7 Transfer the scones onto the lined baking sheet. Cover with plastic wrap and place in the fridge or freezer for 10 to 20 minutes to rest. This helps the scones keep their shape while baking. 8 Meanwhile, adjust a rack to the lower third position in the oven and preheat the oven to 400° F. 9 When ready, remove the scones from their chilly rest and brush each with the egg wash and sprinkle lightly with the turbinado sugar. Bake for about 20-25 minutes until golden. 10 Remove from the oven and transfer to a wire rack to cool. HAPPY VALENTINE’S DAY! pages.text: 22 Wednesday, February 3, 2021 Features your Oakland Zoo welcomes everyone back By Jay Russell Oakland Zoo reopened to the public today, February 3, after being closed for 58 days since the Shelter-in-Place went into effect December 7. And in some equally good news, Glowfari, the Zoo’s nighttime glowing lantern extravaganza, will reopen on Friday, February 5. “We’re excited to be able to reopen the Zoo and welcome back our guests,” said Joel Parrott, President & CEO of the Oakland Zoo. “During this second closure, our focus has been to go above and beyond to protect the health and safety of every guest, staff member and animal,” he added. Dr. Parrott recently announced that after 37 years with the Zoo he While the Oakland Zoo was closed, some new friends took up residence. Nonami, a Schmidt’s red-tailed monkey native to the forests of Africa’s Congo, is now available for visitors to see. Here to Help with Temporary Respite Care will be retiring later this Spring. The Zoo was more prepared to close this time, after the first closure of 132 days at the start of the pandemic. “We received a tremendous amount of support financially through donations during our first closure that was useful during our second (shorter) closure. That being said, guest admission is our primary source of revenue, and we are grateful this closure is ending sooner than the last,” said Isabella Linares, the Zoo’s Marketing Associate. Daily Zoo hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The zoo still is using a timed ticketing reservation system that requires advance online purchase for specific dates and arrival time. Big crowds are no more. The maximum capacity has been reduced to 2,900, down from a maximum of 7,000 visitors during peak normal times. Glowfari, the exciting, illuminated lantern festival, will resume as well, with tickets going on sale starting this Friday at 10 a.m. The nighttime event that took the place of Zoo Lights features something for everyone, with larger-than-life-size animal lanterns and realistic animatronic dinosaurs. Due to popular demand, Glowfari has been extended until March 13, running seven days a week from 5:30 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. The zoo has kept busy during this most recent closure. Zoo staff were able to undertake major landscaping projects to update the horticulture for guests and animals. Look who’s new at the zoo Some new friends have moved in recently, including M’Zuzi, a male Hamadryas baboon born in the zoo on December 29. More primate pals joined in the party during the closure with the addition of Schmidt’s red-tailed monkeys who now inhabit the African Savanna exhibit at the Zoo. Zoo guests will enjoy seeing their animal friends. The macaws, chimpanzees, giraffes and squirrel monkeys love interacting with guests and have needed extra attention from staff while visitors have been absent. To reserve tickets, go to oaklandzoo.org or call (510) 632-9525. Oakland Zoo is located at 9777 Golf Links Road in Oakland. articles.text: Jill Biden with the presidential dogs, Major and Champ. Dear Abby: Can you tell us anything about the First Dogs that now reside in the White House? articles.text: Joan (Jody) Earle, a beloved mother, grandmother, sister, and aunt, passed away on January 7, 2021 in Oakland, California. She was 89. Born Joan Christine Zuber on December 29, 1931 in Washington, DC, she was the daughter of Adolph and Alice Rita Zuber. She was known to all by her nickname Jody, which started when she was the editor of her high school newspaper and wrote a weekly column titled “Jody’s Jottings”. Her father was a Lt. Colonel in the Marine Corps, and she lived in many locations, including Pearl Harbor, Hawaii in 1941. She graduated from Hoover High School in San Diego California in 1949 and earned a bachelor’s degree in History in 1953 from the University of California in Berkeley. She also received a master’s degree in History at UC Berkeley in 1955. While in college she was a member of the Phi Mu sorority and the Prytanean Honor Society, which sought to promote the high ideas of scholarship, leadership, and service to the university and community. She went on to get teaching credentials in Elementary, Secondary, Community College and Special Education. She spent most of her adult life teaching children, including working with children with learning disabilities and tutoring. She was a substitute teacher in Piedmont and especially enjoyed teaching children who were classmates of her own six children. From 1989 to 2012 she taught multiple subjects at Fred French Youth Center in Oakland, a facility providing support for youth healing from trauma. She was well respected by family, friends, and students for her loving dedication to the learning and wellbeing of her students. Known for her kind gentle spirit, great sense of humor and smile she enchanted those who heard her retelling of the story of her family living in Pearl Harbor when it was attacked on Dec. 7, 1941. Quarters T, the house her family lived in on Ford Island, now with a plaque that reads “Zuber House” named after her family. A permanent sign in the Joan Earle, a survivor of the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, died of natural causes on January 7 at age 89. front yard has her family name and is close to the historic Battleship Arizona memorial, which sits solemnly on Battleship Row. Jody loved to read and write, leading her to write the book, The Children of Battleship Row, which gives generations of readers a glimpse of a 9-year old’s perspective of the attack on Pearl Harbor. She visited her home on Ford Island with her family many times making strong loving friendships with those she met. She loved and was loved by friends in the community, including Piedmont Community Church. She lived at Grand Lake Gardens in Oakland for the past eight years, She is survived by three sons, John Earle III (Jenny), David Earle (Jennifer), and Robert Earle, and three daughters, Alicia Utley (Jony), Meg Dengler (Mike), and Alison Earle. Jody is also survived by five grandchildren, Kristina and Kayla Utley, Katie Nolasco, Benjamin and Sarah Dengler. She is additionally survived by a sister, Margaret (Peggy) Unger, and three nephews a niece and numerous great nephews and nieces. Jody requested that a Celebration of Life be held and that she be cremated, and her ashes laid to rest in Hawaii. Because of the closures of restaurants and facilities at this time, this Celebration of Life will be held at a later date and an announcement will be made. articles.text: Jeanie Christopoulos, a longtime Piedmont resident and member of the Ascension Greek Orthodox Cathedral of Oakland, died peacefully in her sleep on December 19, 2020. She was 89. Born Jeanie Batestas on March 13, 1931 in Ogden, Utah, she was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Gus Batestas. Jeanie was a bright child, successful in school and driven to achieve. At an early age she enjoyed studying the piano and voice. She relocated to California in the 1950’s where she would become exceptionally active in cultural, community and political affairs in the San Francisco Bay Area. In 1961, she married Bay Area real estate developer Dan Christopoulos in one of the first wedding ceremonies performed in the newly built Greek Orthodox Church of the Ascension, now the Cathedral of the Ascension. Jeanie and Dan, along with Rev. Tom Paris and other Ascension members served on the Building and Design Committee for the Community Center built adjacent to the Cathedral in the late 1970’s. It continues to be an integral part of the community today, hosting weddings, high school proms, as well as traditional Greek Orthodox celebrations throughout the year. Jeanie was generous and giving with her time, and an excellent, self-taught cook. She was honored to teach The Art of Baklava at Ascension’s annual Oakland Greek Festival and loved promoting the Festival by teaching baklava-making on a TV news show. Jeanie was an active volunteer in her community, beginning in her children’s schools. In 1970, she campaigned for Dr. Marcus Foster to be appointed as Superintendent of Schools for the Oakland Unified School District. In 1977, Jeanie joined The Cancer League, a nonprofit that funds groundbreaking, early-stage cancer research. Jeanie was extremely proud to have been the only two-term President from 1991 to 1993. The Oakland Museum Women’s Board White Elephant Sale would eventually become Jeantrips to Manhattan visits to galleries, dealers, and museums, where she fed her keen interest in Japanese Imari. Jeanie and Dan traveled the world together, adventuring to China and Africa. Especially dear to her were their annual summer and winter trips to Lake Tahoe for skiing, boating and quality time with family and friends. At home, Jeanie and Dan loved entertaining; their home was regularly buzzing with their nearest and dearest, sharing big dinners, and spirited socializing. She was a wily Bridge partner enjoying the friendship of the same group for decades. Jeanie loved the company of the Sewing Club, where most of the time more tales were spun than anything involving needle and thread. Jeanie was a devoted follower of professional sports, ready to go toe-to-toe with the men on any topic, especially the Warriors and her favorite player, Steph Curry. Never one to fall behind on current events, nothing gave Jeanie more joy than to sit and read the NY Times cover to cover, except maybe clipping articles of interest for her family. Jeanie is survived by her son Basil and his wife Shirley of Oakland; daughter Eleni Gianopulos and husband Randall of New York, and grandchildren Rebecca, Peter, William, and Sophia. She is also survived by sister-in-law Elaine Platias and brother-in-law Tasso Voulgares, and her godchildren, Pam and Dave Fullerton, and their children John, Anastasia and George. She is predeceased by her mother Elaine Batestas, and two sisters, Maria Batestas and Becky Voulgares. Due to Covid restrictions, private Trisagion and Funeral Services were held, with Interment following services at Mt. View Cemetery in Oakland. A celebration of Jeanie’s life will be held as soon as Covid restrictions allow. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that contributions in Jeanie’s memory be made to the Ascension Greek Orthodox Cathedral of Oakland, The Oakland Museum of California, or The Cancer League, Inc. Joining the Board in 1990, Jeanie served on many committees, including Grants Committee, Hospitality Committee, White Elephant Sale Advisory Committee, and Acquisitions & Special Projects Committee. Jeanie was the Chair and Co-Chair of the Jewelry Department from 2010- 2020. What she lacked in formal Gemology study, she made up for with her tireless enthusiasm. Jeanie worked hard to educate herself and her volunteer colleagues on everything about jewelry, augmenting knowledge with strategic sales training for her colleagues – “the Jewels” as they called themselves. Jeanie and Dan lived in Piedmont for 43 years, until moving to Oakland near the Claremont Country Club, with a panoramic view of the Bay. It was her dream home, where she and her soulmate, Dan, spent their lives together utterly in love. Their marriage thrived for 56 years until Dan’s passing in 2017. Jeanie loved big cities and felt fortunate to spend a lot of time in New York City, where their daughter lived. She and Dan were avid Broadway theatergoers and were known to get off a long flight across country, hustle over to TKTS and be promptly in their seats for a show that evening. Additionally, Jeanie was particularly passionate about Asian art and always included in her by seven grandchildren, Mercedes, Ines, Sophian and Rainer Lovato of San Francisco, Amy Williams of Wellington, New Zealand, Macarena Zorraquin of Buenos Aires, and Victoria Zorraquin of Nantes, France. She is predeceased by her husband, Dr. Footer, and by her eldest daughter, Shannon Williams. In Pat’s memory, the family suggests that memorial contributions be sent to her alma mater, Holy Names High School. The school provides 70% of its students with financial aid, something she personally had benefited from enormously. Donations can be sent to the school at 4660 Harbord Drive, Oakland, CA 94618. Pat also loved the nonprofit George Mark Children’s House, 2121 George Mark Lane, San Leandro, CA 94578.

articles.text: Being told I would be expected to talk here, I inquired what sort of talk I ought to make. They said it should be something suitable to youth – something didactic, instructive, or something in the nature of good advice. Very well. I have a few things in my mind which I have often longed to say for the instruction of the young; for it is in one’s tender early years that such things will best take root and be most enduring and most valuable. incomplete training. Some authorities hold that the young out not to lie at all. That of course is putting it rather stronger than necessary. While I cannot go quite so far as that, I do maintain, and I believe I am right, that the young ought to be temperate in the use of this great art until practice and experience shall give them that confidence, elegance, and precision which alone can make the accomplishment graceful and profitable. 1 First, then, I will say to you, my young friends – and I say it beseechingly, urgently – always obey your parents when they are present. This is the best policy in the long run, because if you don’t, they will make you. Most parents think they know better than you do, and you can generally make more by humoring that superstition than you can by acting on your own better judgment. 2 Be respectful to your superiors if you have any; also, to strangers, and sometimes to others. If a person offends you and you are in doubt as to whether it was intentional or not, do not resort to extreme measures. Simply watch your chance and hit him with a brick. That will be sufficient. If you shall find that he had not intended any offense, come out frankly and confess yourself in the wrong when you struck him. Acknowledge it like a man and say you didn’t mean to. Yes, always avoid violence; in this age of charity and kindliness, the time has gone by for such things. Leave dynamite to the low and unrefined. 3 Go to bed early, get up early – this is wise. Some authorities say get up with the sun; some say get up with one thing, others with another. But a lark is really the best thing to get up with. It gives you a splendid reputation with everybody to know that you get up with the lark; and if you get the right kind of lark, and work at him right, you can easily train him to get up at half past nine, every time – it’s no trick at all. 4 Now, as to the matter of lying, you want to be very careful about lying, otherwise you are nearly sure to get caught. Once caught, you can never again be in the eyes to the good and the pure what you were before. Many a young person has injured himself permanently through a single clumsy and ill-finished lie, the result of carelessness born of days ago, right in the next farm house to the one where I am spending the summer, a grandmother, old and gray and sweet, one of the loveliest spirits in the land, was sitting at her work, when her young grandson crept in and got down an old, battered, rusty gun which had not been touched for many years and was supposed not to be loaded, and pointed it at her, laughing and threatening to shoot. In her fright she ran screaming and pleading toward the door on the other side of the room; but as she passed him he placed the gun almost against her very breast and pulled the trigger! He had supposed it was not loaded. And he was right – it wasn’t. So, there wasn’t any harm done. It is the only case of that kind I ever heard of. Therefore, just the same, don’t you meddle with old, unloaded firearms; they are the most deadly and unerring things that have ever been created by man. You don’t have to take any pains at all with them; you don’t have to have a rest, you don’t have to have any sights on the gun, you don’t have to take aim, even. No, you just pick out a relative and bang away, and you are sure to get him. A youth who can’t hit a cathedral at thirty yards with a Gatling gun in three quarters of an hour, can take up an old empty musket and bag his grandmother every time, at a hundred. Think what Waterloo would have been if one of the armies had been boys armed with old muskets supposed not to be loaded, and the other army had been composed of their female relations. The very thought of it make one shudder. 6 There are many sorts of books; but good ones are the sort for the young to read – remember that. They are a great, an inestimable, and unspeakable means of improvement. Therefore, be careful in your selection, my young friends; be very careful; confine yourselves exclusively to Robertson’s Sermons, Baxter’s Saints’ Rest, The Innocents Abroad, and works of that kind. But I have said enough. I hope you will treasure up the instructions which I have given you, and make them a guide to your feet and a light to your understanding. Build your character thoughtfully and painstakingly upon these precepts, and by and by, when you have got it built, you will be surprised and gratified to see how nicely and sharply it resembles everybody else’s. The foregoing is from a speech of the same title given by Mark Twain in 1882. Patience, diligence, painstaking attention to detail – these are requirements. These in time will make the student perfect; upon these only, may he rely as the sure foundation for future eminence. Think what tedious years of study, thought, practice, experience, went to the equipment of that peerless old master who was able to impose upon the whole world the lofty and sounding maxim that “Truth is mighty and will prevail.” It is the most majestic compound fracture of fact which any of woman born has yet achieved. For the history of our race, and each individual’s experience, are sewn thick with evidence that a truth is not hard to kill, and that a lie well told is immortal. There is in Boston a monument of the man who discovered anesthesia; many people are aware, in these latter days, that that man didn’t discover it at all, but stole the discovery from another man. Is this truth mighty, and will it prevail? Ah no, my hearers; the monument is made of hardy material, but the lie it tells will outlast it a million years. An awkward, feeble, leaky lie is a thing which you ought to make it your unceasing study to avoid; such a lie as that has no more real permanence than an average truth. Why, you might as well tell the truth at once and be done with it. A feeble, stupid, preposterous lie will not live two years – except it be a slander upon somebody. It is indestructible, then of course, but that is no merit of yours. A final word: begin your practice of this gracious and beautiful art early – begin now. If I had begun earlier, I could have learned how. 5 Never handle firearms carelessly. [Oh,] the sorrow and suffering that have been caused through the innocent but heedless handling of firearms by the young. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: This letter was sent to Piedmont City Council. Editor: I heard from a neighbor about the potential 7-year lease of a city-owned building to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. From what I understand, I am opposed. For what appears to be an unusually favorable deal that is wholly inconsistent with the treatment of other organizations right here in Piedmont, there would need to be a phenomenally compelling case to enter into this lease ... but I have not heard anything like that. When I was treasurer for a boy scout troop here, I wrote checks to the city of Piedmont for the use of city facilities. I know that other organizations do the same. As a board member for a nonprofit organization serving kids in the Oakland schools, I have never seen something like this and would find it unusual. In the name of consistency, transparency, and fiduciary responsibility, I ask you to find another approach. –Jonathan Becker

articles.text: Editor: In the Post’s Letters to the Editor, Bernard Pech effectively outlined why Reach Codes should not encourage electric ranges. But there is so much more to back up his findings. He states, “an electric range, whether heating through resistive elements or by induction, generates three times more greenhouse gases than a natural gas range if the electricity feeding the home is produced by a natural gas power plant.” “The CA energy mix in 2019 was 43% natural gas, 8% nuclear and 17% hydroelectric. These plants, due to Carnot, resistive and electrostatic transmission loss and other factors, have an energy efficiency in converting gas to electricity of about 33% (PUC report 2017), and 79-95% of plants run at 29% efficiency. Therefore, an electric range can use as much as three (3) times more gas in cooking a meal than a natural gas range.” As a 40-year resident of Piedmont owning a 1915 home, I cannot afford to ADA upgrade my kitchen and bath if I have to convert to electricity. Just because Piedmont is a Charter City and is allowed to go beyond what is required by the State, does not mean that it is rational. You are restricting the upgrading (ADA or otherwise) of Piedmont older homes, especially those of older residents on fixed incomes and the disabled. –Pat Markovich Due to volume, there was not space for all letters. More letters will be printed next week. A key component to this plan is that even if COVID cases increase, schools in progress are allowed to stay open, as confirmed by Alameda County Public Health Director Dr. Nicholas Moss. As long as Kindergarten starts on February 9, the rest of the phased reopening can continue. “I am feeling more hopeful right now than I have felt in a long time,” said School Board president Cory Smegal at the board’s meeting on January 27. “Cases are decreasing, and Dr. Moss thinks the Red Tier may be possible in the next few weeks.” School Schedules Continued from page 1 A PHS Parent Club Meeting will be held on Thursday, February 4, at 7:00 p.m. PHS Principal Adam Littlefield, the PHS administration team and School Board President Cory Smegal will answer questions on PHS reopening. Principal Shannon Fierro’s five-minute video can be seen at: www.youtube.com/ watch?v=GrONsCoPm0g&feature=youtu.be. Piedmont Middle School Piedmont Middle School’s proposed in-person schedule uses a “Two Period Rotating Trimester Model.” Only one grade level at a time would be on campus during “2 period blocks.” This amounts to each student having half a day of in-person learning (two periods) once per week. The other five periods would continue with distance learning. Depending upon how much time is left in the school year when allowed to start, the schedule would be divided into three equal parts or trimesters. If there are 15 weeks left when class starts each trimester would be five weeks. For example, in the first trimester 6th graders would be on campus for periods 1 and 3 in the morning on Tuesdays or Thursday. Then in the 2nd trimester 6th grades would have periods 5 and 7 in the afternoons Tuesday or Thursday. Finally, in the last trimester they would have periods 4 and 6 in-person Wednesday or Friday. There would be two different groups of each grade, on campus different days. No 2nd period classes would be offered this year in this plan at the middle school. Principal Ryan Fletcher’s reopening plan video is available for viewing at: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rPXug-t20_WASiogWUhipd0iLS1SdPKn/view. 6th graders may not have to wait so long however as they have been included in Newsom’s K-6 Safe Schools for All Plan and are slated to return on February 23. All grades from TK to 12th will have distance learning exclusively every Monday. articles.text: Piedmont Police interrupted an attempted auto theft on Hazel Lane at 4:03 a.m. on Friday January 29. Upon seeing the patrol car, a woman jumped into a nearby stolen car with a male accomplice. Hazel Lane is a full loop, so when the car came back, the officer was waiting for it. The male suspect got out of the car and started running away. The woman got into the driver’s seat and raced off in the car. Further down the street, the woman ditched the vehicle and ran away. The police requested backup assistance from Oakland PD, including a K9 unit. The female suspect was located and arrested. A search of the stolen vehicle produced stolen mail, a shaved key, suspected methamphetamine, and paraphernalia. It was determined that the woman was on probation and was transported to Santa Rita jail. The stolen vehicle was recovered and returned to the owner.

More details can be found on the City’s website, or talk to a member of the Planning and Building Department when you apply for a permit. • Newly constructed low-rise residential buildings and new detached ADU’s must use all electric building appliances. No gas lines can be hooked up to these buildings. • Projects that include an entirely new level or expand the total roof area by 30% or more, must install solar panels on the roof. • A renovation project that costs $25,000 or more must include an energy efficient insulation or heating system electrification improvement to include in the renovation. • A renovation project that costs $100,000 or more must include two energy efficient insulation or heating system electrification improvements to include in the renovation. • • • • • The energy efficient insulation or heating system requirement can be modified with a Home Energy Score of at least a 7 completed in the last five years. This modification is included so homes that have been pursuing energy efficiency measures can be recognized for their efforts. An application for an electrical panel upgrade must include capacity in the panel to accommodate future electrification of all appliances in the residence. An application for a kitchen or laundry area renovation must include electrical outlets for future appliance installations. At point of listing for sale of a property, a report from a Home Energy Audit or Home Energy Score must be provided to potential buyers and submitted to the City. Notably, many of these requirements will not affect most projects in Piedmont. Approximately 20 to 25 percent of renovation projects cost over $25,000. As stated before, the reach codes were put in place in order to reduce Piedmont’s natural gas emissions. Over 90 percent of emissions come from Piedmont residential living units. The reach codes are intended to slow natural gas usage, while still meeting the community standards that were published in the City’s Climate Action Plan. Piedmont is not alone in this initiative. Dozens of municipalities have passed reach codes in California. The California Energy Commission’s next update of statewide building codes (Title 24) will be implemented in 2023. Until then, these reach codes will help Piedmont homes become more energy efficient while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. For questions, please contact the planner working on your home renovation, or the City’s Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont School District and Piedmont School Board. Last March, our school board, the Superintendent, and Alameda County acted on the best available information at the time and closed our schools to help stop the spread of the COVID-19 virus. With limited data about the virus, this decision seemed wise and one that we, as medical professionals, supported at the time. In the intervening 10 months, we have learned a lot about the biology and epidemiology of the virus, both how it is transmitted and how to treat it. Early on, we assumed that children would be primary drivers of the virus. This assumption was later disproved. During these months, we have also watched as schools elsewhere found ways to reopen safely. Our initial reaction was one of caution and concern, wondering if this was the right decision. Then, data from school reopenings began to surface and it became apparent that with the appropriate safety measures in place, schools could in fact safely provide in-person instruction. It also became very apparent that the longer we kept our students out of the classroom, and the longer they were subject to distance-learning, the more harm we were doing to them. Without a doubt distance-learning is causing tremendous learning loss and profound mental health crises in children across all age spectrums. Data shows a significant increase in the number of children disclosing suicidal ideation, and dealing with acute mental health crises and eating disorders stemming from depression, anxiety, and social isolation. It is now clear that ongoing school closures are not based on evidence. Yet, despite all of this information, and despite the very serious calls from parents, students, scientists, and medical experts to reopen our schools, children in Piedmont remain in full-time distance-learning. It is abundantly clear that the decisions made by the Alameda County Public Health Department, by PUSD’s administration, and the school board have not served the best interest of our children. There should be no more delay. There should be no more excuses. It’s time to open our schools. It’s time to honor the science we teach our students. As medical and mental health professionals, we implore PUSD to return to in-person education for all students. With millions of school children around the world safely back in the classroom with their peers and teachers, we know that it can be done. articles.text: An optimistic plan has been set for Piedmont elementary schools to start a phased reopening on Tuesday, February 9. All students in grades TK-5 should be back in classrooms by February 25, according to School Superintendent Randy Booker. An e-mail message sent January 25 to parents of Piedmont provided details of a plan he will be presenting to the Piedmont School Board at its meeting tonight, January 27. “This phased-in plan assumes that beginning on Feb. 1st case rates [in Alameda County] have dropped below 25 per 100,000. If it hasn’t, we will have to push back our timeline accordingly,” his message read. Governor Newsom’s Safe Schools for All Plan (at schools. covid19.ca.gov) permits elementary students to return to campus when county-level Covid infection rates drop below an adjusted value of 25 new cases per day per 100,000 for five consecutive days. Case numbers include a seven-day lag and are a seven-day average, meaning the rate is determined by data from 7-14 days prior. Newsom’s plan marks an easing of the previous restriction which required case numbers to be under seven per day, per 100,000. Editor: Since its opening in 2011, the Piedmont Center for the Arts has provided an exceptional venue for the performing and visual arts – not just for the Piedmont community but throughout the Bay Area. I have attended a number of high-quality concerts and plays here, and have been impressed with the level of musicians, singers and actors the Center attracted – and at fair ticket prices. This, coupled with the opportunity for visual artists to show their paintings, furthering their skills and reputations, has earned the Center an outstanding place in Piedmont and beyond. I am a long-time professional performer, and gave my first Bay Area vocal recital at the Center in 2012. After visiting five facilities in San Francisco and Berkeley, which lacked the technical and instrumental needs for this performance, my vocal coach – also a Piedmont resident – recommend the Center. articles.text: As you know, Wiley has had his share of issues with Big Banks in the past. Back in June of 2016, he even conned the Editor of the Post to publish one of his horror stories, which still gives him bad dreams at night. (For background, see http://wholehoag.blogspot.com/) Well, it must run in the family, because Mrs. Wiley, aka The LW, had her own surreal experience with another Big Bank this week. And it was even worse than Wiley’s, because it involved Real People, and because we don’t even bank with them. Before we go any further, you have to understand that The LW is smarter than Wiley (not too hard, she would say), and that she had been a senior executive with a Big Bank Predecessor in a prior life. In fact, had she not decided to work part time for a few years to spend more time raising the kids, she probably would have risen to the top of their Good Old Boy Team. And, unlike Wiley, she knows how to deal with people, so when she has a people problem, you know it’s a bona fide People Problem. At any rate, The LW got a letter the other day from said Bank. When she opened it, she saw that it was addressed to her AND four other people. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, January 27, 2021 Opinion LETTERS MAIN Center for the Arts a perfect venue for recitals, concerts This letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: Since its opening in 2011, the Piedmont Center for the Arts has provided an exceptional venue for the performing and visual arts – not just for the Piedmont community but throughout the Bay Area. I have attended a number of high-quality concerts and plays here, and have been impressed with the level of musicians, singers and actors the Center attracted – and at fair ticket prices. This, coupled with the opportunity for visual artists to show their paintings, furthering their skills and reputations, has earned the Center an outstanding place in Piedmont and beyond. I am a long-time professional performer, and gave my first Bay Area vocal recital at the Center in 2012. After visiting five facilities in San Francisco and Berkeley, which lacked the technical and instrumental needs for this performance, my vocal coach – also a Piedmont resident – recommend the Center. It was perfect for us. The acoustics, the piano, the layout for a concert and reception, the intimate character of the room, and convenience for the attendees, made all of our experiences one to remember. I am in the planning stages for a second recital at your venue mid-year—COVID willing. With the Center’s new Board at the helm, I can already sense the cordiality and dedication they bring, and I look forward to working with them. I hope your decision is a positive one for Piedmont Center’s future, –Jay Krohnengold Center for the Arts: Keep its flag flying This letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: Please renew the lease for Piedmont Center for the Arts. The Center has been one of the most successful public/private projects that have happened in the city where I have resided for the last 26 years, and over the 40 years our firm has worked in it. articles.text: California announced changes to its complex COVID-19 vaccine distribution plan yesterday, Tuesday, January 26. Now, people 65 years of age and older, as well as workers in education, childcare, food, grocery and agriculture sectors, are eligible to receive the vaccine statewide. This group amounts to about 8.5 million Californians. This group is in addition to the initial group that began receiving the vaccine in December, which is comprised of healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. This group of people, numbering an estimated 3 million statewide, are still receiving vaccines. Beyond these groups, California will prioritize vaccine administration based on age, a significant change from earlier plans. The details of who will receive the vaccine next is still being hammered out by the state, but this next phase is expected to begin sometime in the spring. this year, anyone who wants to receive a COVID-19 vaccine should be able to receive it, the state believes. With vaccine supply and the state’s distribution plans in flux, the timetable is subject to change. California’s Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said at a press conference yesterday, January 26, that the state is now vaccinating 125,000 people every weekday, a huge increase in distribution since last month. The state is encouraging residents to utilize a new digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov. On the website, Californians can find out their eligibility and, if eligible, they can schedule a vaccination appointment. Those who are not eligible for vaccination can sign up for notifications when it is their turn. While some hospitals and counties were vaccinating senior citizens earlier this month, everyone age 65 and older are now eligible statewide. The state has administered almost 2.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 4.6 million doses, according to the California Department of Public Health. Importantly, both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccine that are being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. As of press time, over 371,000 people have received their second dose in California. California is still amongst the worst states in terms of vaccine distribution so far, even though it holds more total doses than any other state. As of Monday, January 25, Alameda County possesses 102,750 doses of the vaccine. Roughly half of these doses were manufactured by Pfizer and the other half were created by Moderna. Almost 64,000 of these doses have been passed onto healthcare facilities, while about 39,000 are being administered by the Alameda County Public Health Department. Of the latter, the ACPHD has already administered 54 percent of these doses as of last week. Demand continues to outstrip vaccine supply. Phase 1A, the group of healthcare workers and residents of long-term care facilities that were first eligible for vaccination, is estimated to number more than 145,000 people in Alameda County. Along with using the My Tool website, the county encourages people 65 years and older to contact their healthcare provider to see if vaccine doses are available now.
articles.title: State announces plan to prioritize age in vaccine rollout

articles.text: A midyear fiscal report for fiscal year 2020–2021 was presented by Piedmont Finance Director Michael Szczech to the city council at its January 19 meeting. The report found that the city’s general fund remains in a sound position, with revenues exceeding expenses. Szczech contributed this to “conservative budgeting, a strong real estate market [even with Covid], and prudent management of day-today operations.” The city’s finance department projects general fund revenues to exceed budget by approximately $2.4 million, and expenses to be lower than budget by approximately $400,000. Increase in revenue is largely from “higher than expected real property transfer tax receipts,” as well as mutual aid revenue for wildfire assistance, increased building permits, property tax receipts, and other taxes. The decrease in expenditures is primarily due to lower recreation-related expenses. Due to the permanent closure of the community pool and the lack of employees, the city’s finance department projects that the budgeted loss will decline by approximately 50 percent. The annual subsidy of $250,000 will not be needed, the report stated. Reve nue f rom Re c re - ation Department programs is expected to fall short of budget by $238,000. Since the bulk of recreation department expenses are variable in nature, Szczech said he expects that the decline in expenses will more than offset the revenue loss. “We are very fortunate to be in this position considering the adverse effect COVID-19 has had on many municipalities. This is due to the fact that the majority of our revenue base is property related and relatively stable, and that we are able to adjust expenditures in the areas where revenue has been affected,” Szczech stated in the staff report. Many neighboring cities have announced budget cuts amid the coronavirus pandemic. Last month, Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf said that budget cuts were unavoidable and that growing budget shortfalls needed to be addressed. The City of Oakland implemented various cost-cutting measures, including a hiring freeze, reduction of overtime spending, and curtailing the use of temporary employees. The City of Clayton, which is comparable in size and demographics to Piedmont, experienced significant revenue loss due to decreased sales and gas taxes. Clayton Mayor Julie Pierce told the Clayton Pioneer that the city is not utilizing temporary maintenance workers due to budget concerns. If the trends of the first half of the fiscal year continue, Piedmont may have the ability to add to the funding of its backlog in facilities maintenance. However, the report added that there can be “no assurance these trends will continue as the intensity of the COVID-19 pandemic is worse than it has ever been, and it is unclear when operations will go back to normal.” “Dude is leaving his brain to science. They want time to think it over.”

articles.text: Editor: Last week, the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), formerly the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, hosted the 24th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Day Celebration in partnership with the City of Piedmont. The theme was “Let Us Be Dissatisfied: Using Our Power to Bend the Arc,” recognizing that the power to fix the problems Dr. King called out over 50 years ago is in our hands. Speakers included Stanford University Professor Clayborne Carson, Congresswoman Barbara Lee, Senator Nancy Skinner and Piedmont Councilmember Tim Rood. Here in Piedmont, the willingness to address racial reckoning gave rise to racial justice resolutions passed by City Council and the School Board; a month-long flag display in support of Black Lives Matter; PUSD’s new equity policies; and a website created by resident Meghan Bennett detailing the shameful treatment and ouster of Piedmont’s first black homeowner. While working with city and school district officials on racial equity resolutions and policies, PADC took a moment to reflect on our own decades of work and envision what was next. We changed our name from “Appreciating Diversity” to “Anti-Racism and Diversity.” Our renewed mission is dedicated to rooting out racism and embracing diversity and inclusion. Our values are inclusive community, racial equity, learning culture, collective action, and transparency. We award grants to educators and community members working to advance inclusion and racial equity. Amid a global pandemic, we moved this year’s MLK event to a virtual platform. We invited partners to develop workshops. One of those, co-created by PADC and PREC, is the Jan. 28 panel discussion “Reimagining Public Safety: Can Surveillance be a Fair and Effective Tool?” PADC designed this year’s King program to provide us with tools to confront our own blind spots and move towards greater understanding and connection. We are committed to creating a more inclusive Piedmont. The MLK celebration is not just a call to honor a memory. It is a continuation of King’s work to raise our consciousness and lift up our community into the light of a new day. To do so means we must all step out of our comfort zones and build a new and better world. –Sheila Leunig and Jennifer Long PADC Co-presidents Request a Virtual or On-Site Quote
articles.title: PADC honors MLK legacy

articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) will host a virtual panel at 7 p.m. tomorrow, January 28, entitled “Reimagining Public Safety: Can Surveillance Be a Fair and Effective Tool?” The panel is also co-sponsored by the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. The panel discussion will include key individuals in the public safety sector and is a follow-up to a similar panel that the League of Woman Voters held in 2017. Piedmont’s Police Chief Jeremy Bowers will participate, along with Brian Hofer (Chair of the Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission), Jennifer Jones (Technology and Civil Liberties Fellow, ACLU Northern California) and Mathew Guariglia (Policy Analyst for Electronic Frontier Foundation). The virtual discussion, available via teleconference application Zoom, focuses on how surveillance impacts racial justice and public safety in Piedmont and the broader community. New surveillance technologies monitor, track, and predict the actions of citizens, and are becoming increasingly popular in public safety. The discussion explores whether these new technologies can usher in a new era of unbiased, inexpensive public safety and justice or if they are inherently problematic. Featured speakers will delve in to whether or not they can be used fairly and effectively within the context of our flawed public safety and justice system. The Zoom panel discussion will begin at 7 p.m., and is expected to end at 8:30 p.m. To register for the event, visit: https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1363151
articles.title: PADC, PREC and LWV to sponsor panel discussion tomorrow

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council will have a second reading of the proposed energy reach codes at its February 1 meeting. Potential energy reach codes were considered by city council during a first reading in July 2020. The first reading was approved, but councilmembers directed staff to complete additional public outreach and education before the second reading. On September 3, 2020, the city hosted a virtual town hall meeting via Zoom to provide an opportunity for residents to ask questions and learn more about the proposal. In November and December last year the research firm FM3 conducted an additional survey to complement a survey that was completed earlier in the year. Dave Metz, President of FM3, presented the results of that survey to city council on January 19. The January 19 meeting provided an informational update on public engagement related to reach codes, and adoption of reach codes was not considered at the meeting. The key takeaways from that survey found that residents’ view of reach codes as proposed is positive. The results stated that 64 percent of respondents supported requiring these improvements in order to reduce natural gas. The survey was administrated to a random representative sample of Piedmont’s registered voters, so results suggest that a majority of residents support both the overall idea of revising building codes and the specific code amendments included in the ordinances. Staff will bring forward the second reading at the next city council meeting. The report at that meeting will address lingering concerns and will include additional clarification about requirements and exemptions, according to Planning Department staff.
articles.title: City Council to hold 2nd reading of Reach Codes on Feb. 1

articles.text: A parent called me recently, convinced that her son needed to go to a different school, maybe one that does one-on-one tutoring, or perhaps a wilderness program. While there’s nothing wrong with either choice, changing schools in the middle of a school year is a dramatic move. I generally advise parents to make sure the solution matches the problem. What’s going on? I asked, hoping to help her make sense of the situation. I’m convinced my son isn’t learning anything, she explained. I think he plays video games all day long, and I don’t think he’s very engaged in what’s happening in his Zoom classes. Given that I currently teach a class on Zoom, and observe firsthand how hard it is for many students to stay dialed in, I said she had a point. You’re right, I responded. He’s probably not as engaged as usual. Then she explained that she had recently helped her son with a Spanish assignment. I could see that he wasn’t doing anything, so ..., she hesitated. I did it for him. I didn’t respond; I let her confession linger in the air. She continued. And when the teacher gave him back the assignment, she explained, he said he couldn’t use Google Translate. More silence. I know I shouldn’t do his work for him, she admitted guiltily, but I am losing my mind watching all of this! It’s really hard, I finally said. A few days later I spoke with another parent who confessed to revising all of his son’s English papers. I have to catch the run-on sentences! He exclaimed, almost in a panic. He writes too many run-on sentences!! I mean, how can you get through 10th grade and still be writing so many run-on sentences?? I spoke with each parent for almost an hour, helping them take a step back to see the bigger picture. By the end of the conversations, we had arrived at the real issues, which had little to do with how their children were doing in school. The first parent shared that her aunt had just died of Covid, and that her uncle was in the hospital, barely hanging on. The second parent revealed that his marriage was at the breaking point, and that he doesn’t know if it’s going to survive the pandemic. I feel like if I get a handle on the run-on sentences, he said, between sobs, then maybe everything will be okay. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.
articles.title: It’s a tough time for parents.

articles.text: Challenges with online learning cannot be eliminated, but by sharing tips and tricks in the community these challenges can be mitigated. As a math tutor for the last 10 years, this reporter found that healthy study habits can be just as important as the course material itself. Young people have a lowrisk of developing serious cases of COVID-19 and are shown to transmit the virus less rapidly. However, they have been mandated in many regions to stay out of school and have had to abandon their social lives for the good of the community. This is no small sacrifice, and young people should be thanked and appreciated for their selfless sacrifices even when the virus posses a minimal or reduced risk to their own health. Avoiding COVID-19 for physical health has been on everyone’s mind, but the health of the mind and the eyes must be not be sacrificed. For decades, parents have been limiting and criticizing their children’s screentime. Zenni Blokz offers stylish frames and lens for protection from excessive screen time. View www.zennioptical.com/gaming-glasses Now, students are forced into unhealthy durations of gazing into the screen. This hypocrisy has undoubtedly been noticed and announced by teens everywhere. Dangers of continuous screentime include eye pain, headaches, poor sleep and rapid vision deterioration. We all need to be creative in thinking of ways to help students (and adults) save our eyes – the windows to our soul and brain. Buying a good printer is crucial. Print out anything and everything you can. There’s no reason to do all homework on a screen. To help save the environment, buy recycled paper and print on both sides. Don’t forget that turning off the computer will save electricity. Also try to buy the textbook itself, or if not available, even owning a different book on the same subject can help. Try not to spend any screen time when not required. Remember: books rule. Blue light given off by screens has shown to disrupt sleep cycles. Take a tip from professional computer gamers and buy some gamer glasses. They are proven to reduce digital eye strain, block blue light, minimize glare, prevent dry eyes and promote better sleep. Many stylish options now exist in this booming market. The online World of Warcraft was built 12 hours a day by gamers with these glasses. It is time to get serious about eyecare and eyewear. Taking breaks from screentime will prevent lasting damage and expensive visits to the optometrist. WebMD recommends an easy eye schedule, “Follow the 20-20-20 rule. Look away from the screen every 20 minutes and look at something around 20 feet away for about 20 seconds.” Changing the eye’s focus distance is crucial for eye health, in addition to the 20-20-20 rule, go outside every hour and look at far away objects to keep your farsighted vision exercised. getting cool bifocals and taking screen breaks, students can make the online schooling experience bearable.

articles.text: Members of “Teens4Biden,” a student-led political activism club founded by Piedmont High School Senior Class president Audrey Edel, had more than a passing interest in events in the nation’s capitol on January 6 and January 20, Inauguration Day. The Post caught up with Edel and other club leaders Toshi Troyer and Laney Tellegen to get their reactions on the inauguration of Joseph Biden as America’s new President, and Oakland native Kamala Harris as it new Vice President. Teens4Biden got off to a fast start last fall by hosting a meeting one week before the student body government (ASB) set the dates of September 10-11 for the introduction of all high school clubs and student organizations. That fast action turned into the highest enrollment on Club Day this year, with about 30 students joining the club. Although most would not be age 18 by election day, thus ineligible to vote, Teens4Biden did their part by writing postcards, creating lawn signs and making calls to battleground states such as Ohio, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Nine days before election day, they hosted an online event, Bay Area for Biden, featuring impressive and significant speakers, including former U.S Ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich, Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, and recent PHS graduates Josh On January 20, Joseph R. Biden Jr. was sworn in as the 46th president

articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1978 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. The deadline for nominations is March 16, 2020. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12, School Board meeting. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, January 27, 2021 Piedmont Garden Club co-hosts symposium on protecting SF Bay Webinar draws over 700 participants By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont Garden Club, in conjunction with five other Bay Area garden clubs, sponsored a webinar that discussed the unique ecological system of the San Francisco Bay. Over 700 people joined the online event. Other Garden Clubs participating included Orinda, Marin, Hillsborough, Woodside-Atherton, and Carmel-by-the-Sea. The symposium was introduced by Julia Burke, a member of the Piedmont Garden Club and Bay Visions Committee. The Bay Visions Committee is formed by the six chapters of The Garden Club of America (GCA) with a mission to protect and restore the region’s defining bays and estuaries. The Committee works to educate its members and their communities on the bay’s critical importance to the environment. The latest virtual event, “Bay Visions 2021: The Power of Plants will Protect the Bay,” was a two-hour look at adaption, regeneration, and the role plants play in mitigating the challenges facing the San Francisco Bay. “Our goal [with the symposium] is to inspire others to be as excited as we are about the successful work being done to protect and restore the Bay utilizing plants underwater, in wetlands, along the shoreline, and upland,” explained Lori Adams, President of the Piedmont Garden Club. The program began with a slide show that featured CGA Northern California Partners for Plants (P4P) restoration projects. Each club’s efforts for Bay restoration are supported and encouraged by the Bay Visions Committee. Featured restoration projects included Carmel-by-theSea Garden Club’s North Dunes restoration, Hillsborough Garden Club’s Heron’s Head Park project, and Piedmont and Orinda Garden Clubs’ combined MLK Shoreline project. Their shoreline volunteer restoration project was at Oakport Park at Martin Luther King, Jr. Shoreline across the freeway from the Oakland Coliseum, an area that was originally wetlands. The two garden clubs worked to remove invasive plants and grasses and spread organic soil for fill. Keynote speakers following the slide show included Dr. Karina Nielsen, Dr. Katharyn Boyer, Josie Iselin, Diana Benner, and Laura Hanson. The speaker series began with Dr. Nielson, who gave an introduction on why policy matters in environmental restoration. Dr. Nielson, the director of San Francisco State University’s Estuary and Ocean Science Center, offered an overview on the complex issues facing San Francisco Bay. “If you care about the environment, then policy matters,” Dr. Nielson explained. “In California, we have been able to establish the world’s premiere network of marine protected areas – a major conservation success story. It was because of the passage of laws and political leadership, a public-private partnership, and civic engagement.” Nielson closed with positive news – the fact that federal funding for wetland restoration has increased by $4 million per year. “That is going to be incredibly powerful,” she said. “This was work that U.S. Representative Jackie Speier was advocating for a long time.” Dr. Boyer, a professor of Biology-Wetlands and Restoration Ecology at San Francisco State University, highlighted mitigation and restoration efforts by using plants as buffers and filters. She discussed the dangers of rising sea levels, which scientists anticipate will increase by three feet by 2050. “We can already visualize this when we see king tides by [China Camp State Park], especially after a storm,” Dr. Boyer said. “This is Piedmont Garden Club President Lori Adams Piedmont Garden Club members Julia Burke (left) and Linda Thompson, former chair of the Orinda Garden Club, were among the volunteers in the MLK Shoreline project. comparable to what we’d see with one foot [of increase] by 2030.” Josie Iselin, author of The Curious World of Seaweed, discussed the vital role seaweed plays in maintaining the Bay Area’s ecosystem. Her book features 16 visual narratives of iconic West Coast seaweeds and kelps, and illustrates marine algae with brilliant photographs to explain the science of seaweed. The speaker series concluded with Brenner and Hanson, co-owners of the Watershed Nursery in Richmond, whose mission is to “provide exceptional native plants and services for habitat enhancement projects throughout the San Francisco Bay and Delta Watershed,” Brenner explained. The pair provided a close look at the native plants they grow. The entire symposium is available for viewing at: https:// www.lastlink.us/content/bayvisions2021symposium. The participating garden clubs have also included a list of resources to reference, including native plant nurseries, wetlands to visit, and information on other organizations working to protect the Bay. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: European leaders are seriously eager to get to work solving the world’s catastrophes with the help of newly elected U.S. President Joseph Biden. But Biden’s attention was first focused on averting U.S. domestic disasters as he hit the ground running last Wednesday on Inaugural Day, January 20. Addressing his most urgent priorities, Biden halted the nation’s withdrawal from the World Health Organization; rejoined the Paris Climate Accord; canceled the Keystone XL pipeline; ordered mask-wearing on federal property for 100 days; ordered FEMA to open vaccination centers and OSHA to enforce worker safety; straightened out coronavirus data collection; set in motion new preventive measures against pandemic threats; ordered new guidelines for schools to open; reset international travel restrictions; lifted the ban on travel by people from Muslim countries; strengthened Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals or DACA rules; halted the construction of the wall between the U.S. and Mexico; and paused the repayment of student loans until at least September 30. Altogether, he signed about 30 executive orders in his first three days on the job. Biden spoke to North American leaders, Canada’s Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Mexico’s President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, and then spoke to the United Kingdom’s PM Boris Johnson, who is eager to drive a virtual G7 summit in a matter of weeks. He is ambitiously targeting climate threats, Covid-19, future pandemic preparedness, and relations with China. The U.K. leader is this year’s G7 summit president, a rotating title, and as the country’s host for the coming face-to-face June event, he is plowing ahead changing the G7 into a D-10. Such is his prerogative to set the agenda. According to The Guardian, “U.S. thinktanks have pushed” for the Group of 7 nations (France, U.K., Italy, Canada, Germany, Japan, and U.S.) to expand into a democracies of the world group to include India, South Korea, and Australia.” The change is not without consternation from European nations, and in particular, France and Italy are concerned about diluting their G7 power and the appearance of an anti-China maneuver. The Russian Federation joined in 1998, though Russia never ranked as a major advanced economy by International Monetary Fund indices; but when Russia forcibly annexed Crimea (from Ukraine) in March 2014, the body politic suspended Russia, and the G8 reverted to G7 again. Former president Donald Trump was G7 president for the 2020 summit that was canceled due to Covid-19. At the time he Britain’s Prime Minister Boris Johnson spoke to President Biden about deepening the long-standing alliance between the two countries; support for NATO; and the potential for a free-trade deal. President Joe Biden warns of surpassing 600,000 U.S. deaths and the need to move fast on passing his $1.9 trillion Rescue plan against Covid-19. Post WWII England was one of the “Inner Six” organized for economic prosperity by the Treaty of Paris, which bloomed into the European Economic Community, and then the European Union in the 1960s. England joined in 1973, but the first referendum was three year later when 67 percent voted to stay. England’s 2016 referendum capped years of interior conflicts -- contentious issues that were amplified by geo-political, economic, cultural, and demographic divisions. While London elites enjoyed economic prosperity and voted to Remain, North county laborers struggled in dying industries and voted to roll the dice and Leave. “Eurosceptics,” generally older conservatives who steadfastly criticized E.U. governance and lamented U.K.’s loss of sovereignty, they voted to Leave and rid themselves of the heavy taxpayer burden, forced immigrant quotas, and regulations imposing on their freedoms. One commonplace notion is that England was always an “awkward” E.U. partner; and different than the continent, because she’s an island nation and recognized as a global power. Brits use the The temperature sank to 27º with a dusting of snow in Paris that rarely lasts more than a day: a courtyard view (left) from my window and (right) from a friend’s window facing Château de Vincennes. lobbied publicly for Russia to rejoin, an unpopular premise lacking merit. He did however voice support for South Korea, Australia, and India. PM Boris Johnson is anxious to establish trade deals with allies, now that Britain’s trade with the European Union is much curtailed by new agreements finalized just days prior to the January 1st launch of U.K.’s new sovereignty. Brexit is shorthand for “British exit,” and the exit is complete, but the result is that England is besieged by traffic jams at the ports and a wild confusion of processes not yet set in place. The origin of Brexit began in 2013 when Conservative Party leader David Cameron pledged a national referendum on E.U. membership to finally settle the question once and for all. Voters were presented in 2016 with the broad question of whether the U.K. should leave or remain in the European Union. Cameron was certain the vote would be to remain, but by a slim margin of 51.8% the Brits chose to leave. U.K.’s vast array of trade, security, and migration agreements entwined with the continent had matured greatly during 47 years of association, and the ties have proved extraordinarily complex to disentangle. Brexit traffic jam of 17 miles due to new required paperwork for custom duties due to the U.K. no longer being in the European Union bloc. Blame it on Brexit: Lorries idle in both directions due to new required custom invoices now that U.K. is no longer an E.U. member.

pages.text: 12 Wednesday, January 27, 2021 HIKING WITH JON Donner Pass – a mystifying, stimulating winter adventure By Jonathan Comeaux This treasure of California is among the best wintertime hikes in the Sierra Nevada. Donner Pass, an abandoned railway that was originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. The trek takes you through hollowed out mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass above Donner Lake. Staff Photos The starting point for the trail from McGlashan Point, up a popular sledding hill to China Wall and the first tunnel. China Wall is a platform created by Chinese workers to create the Central Pacific Railroad in 1868. Snow piles into some sections of the Donner Pass trail. Free Delivery to Piedmont Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. A view of Donner Lake and the Donner Pass snow sheds appropriately covered in snow. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the Donner Party tragically met their fate in the fierce winter of 1846—becoming the namesake of the lake and surrounding state park. The walk through the train tunnels is brief at just 2.1 miles to the final snow shed, but it gives you the magic of the Tahoe winter without being knee deep in snow. It’s a great place for children, families, or beginning snowshoers. During the warmer weather, you can walk past the last snow shed and continue to Donner Peak. From our starting point, we took the same route as our 2018 summer visit from McGlashan Point over a Native American petroglyph site that can be seen in warmer months. For now, it’s a popular sledding site with fresh snow. The Central Pacific Railroad created its route through Donner Pass in the spring of 1868 after a near three-year construction effort, accomplished through the efforts of Chinese railroad workers. The Donner Pass trail’s starting point, the China Wall, is a handmade construction that was the platform for the railroad leading into the starting tunnel. Inside the 1,659 foot Tunnel #6, hikers can spot a second Chinese Wall with boulders piled neatly up to the roof. Through the hollowed out mountains, some large icicles glisten through the tiny peaks of light along the roof and walls. Even some large frozen sections of water created massive blocks of ice that are clear as a piece of glass. You’ll find few sites that combine history and artwork with graffiti covering each wall of the sheds — some pieces magnificent in detail. Peeking around unsuspecting corners and behind walls, walkers with keen eyes can find some of California’s most prominent urban artists and large murals. Proper hiking gear is required in some ice-covered areas to prevent slipping and falls. With limited parking at the entrance lot to the tunnels, some may have to park n the sside of Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook. In our five miles of hiking, we passed just 27 hikers. Another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the A frozen wall of ice creates a surreal sigh inside a snowshed. The tunnel opens and begins a walk through some fresh powder. Above is a view of Donner Peak. China Wall. To access this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook on their GPS devices for common starting areas. Remember to return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and fr a hike to Donner Peak. A long tunnel through the mountains is part of a second China Wall above Lake Donner. The entire walk has graffiti-covered walls inside the snow sheds. Some are distinctly graffiti art, such as the one on the right.

articles.text: Passing by the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Vista and Bonita avenues around 3:30 p.m. on a weekday, you’ll find some 20 or more high school tennis players getting eady for a hoped-for season this spring. And for those kids looking to sharpen their skills, coach Jim Landes’ clinics are more meaningful than just practice. To quote basketball legend Allen Iverson, “we’re not just talking about practice, man.” Since July, Landes’ weekly varsity-level clinics have provided a sense of normalcy for student-athletes, who have seen classes shuttered and moved entirely to online, and the entire spring and fall sports seasons canceled. “We’ve been doing this since July,” said the affable Landes at a recent clinic. “You see how much fun the kids are having; they’re being a team and growing together. We’re in pods of 14, Everyone is ecstatic to come out every day. [Asst. Coach] Corey [Reich] and [former coach] Neil [Rothenberg] are here.” Piedmont High’s upperclassmen have had it particularly rough, adjusting to new standards and expectations since last March. “As a senior, this is going to be my last season and be a team captain, it’s hard to not do things regularly but this has been the only social interaction I have. It’s honestly nice to have the promise of some sort of a season. Its truly nice to have Corey and Jim out here coaching us, otherwise I’d just be in my room,” said senior Audrey Edel with a laugh. Varsity player Anne Jumper reiterated how grateful she is to be with friends, and talks about feeling safe doing so. “It’s really great to be around Piedmont High senior Audrey Edel discusses how COVID-19 has impacted the high school experience. Assistant coach Corey Reich gives some pointers to Audrey Frankel. my teammates and be able to communicate again. This really is the only social thing I get to do,” said Jumper. “I’m glad to not just be in my room doing homework. It’s nice to get outside; I feel really safe with everyone in masks and staying in our pods,” added Jumper. The boys’ tennis team, traditionally a spring sport, had many of its matches cancelled last spring, 2020, after the coronavirus restrictions began in midPHS senior Sajan Srivastava is hopeful that his tennis team can have a full season. Varsity tennis players Anne Jumper (left) and Amanda Becker (right) masked up for practice. Senior Luke Hawkins plays with expressive eyes reminiscent of Cliff Richey. PHS varsity member Jake Cota ready for a backhand. Piedmont High coach Jim Landes (left) and former coach and Piedmont Hall of Fame member Neil Rothenberg talking things over at Monday’s clinic. March 2020. Sadly it occurred early in the team’s strongest start in years. It held a 9-1 record at the time of stoppage including winning its first ever California Tennis Classic in Fresno on March 6. “Being out of school, you can’t see friends, so the clinics have been an outlet to communicate with people. Of course I hope a season happens. We’re going to have to work hard to keep our skills sharp,” said senior Sajan Srivastava, who had begun a breakout junior year before the season’s abrupt end. With California dropping the Stay at Home order and Tennis being deemed a low-risk sport by the Alameda County Department of Public Health, there is some reason for optimism that the season can get started in March, as expected. But there will be some big changes. Due to the convoluted year and a compressed sports program, both boys’ and girls’ seasons will occur simultaneously, meaning the PHS programs will rotate home-and-away matches on the same days. Piedmont will schedule matches only with upper division Foothill Division teams. In accordance with the California Interscholastic Federation’s ruling, tennis will not have any post-season tournaments, meaning no North Coast Section playoffs – a sad ending to a long, successful Piedmont legacy.
