articles.text: The Golden State Warriors recently submitted an extensive plan to state and local officials to host 9,000 fans each game, representing 50 percent of the stadium’s capacity. The proposal, which relies on rapid PCR testing of everyone entering the building, was rejected by San Francisco health officials before the season last November. On November 18, a date prior to large spikes in the number of COVID cases reported and prior to the announcement of a vaccine becoming available, San Francisco health officer Tomás Aragón said the city may be willing to work with the team on a plan for a 25 percent capacity crowd, once San Francisco reaches the state’s yellow tier of reopening. Seven NBA teams currently allow limited fan capacity in their arenas. Tomorrow, January 28, the Miami Heat will start allowing 10 percent capacity in their arena with the help of coronavirus sniffing dogs. Before you say “only in Miami,” coronavirus-sniffing dogs have been put to work in airports of Dubai and Helsinki in recent months. The Warriors consulted with Dr. George Rutherford, a Professor of Epidemiology at UCSF. All fans, players, staff, and everyone entering Chase Center would have to pass a PCR-polymerase chain reaction rapid test on game day or with 48 hours prior to the game. PCR testing looks for the RNA of the virus itself and has a sensitivity rating of at least 97 percent efficient. In an interview with the Post, Dr. Rutherford called PCR testing “State of the art. It is way sophisticated – and also way expensive, too.” In comparison, antigen tests look for proteins shed from the surface of the virus. The virus’ RNA has to already be incorporated and making viruses in order to show up on an antigen test, making the accuracy much lower. Warriors owner Joe Lacob said he was willing to spend upward of $30 million dollars for testing this year. Lacob has a master’s degree in public health from UCLA and is a venture capitalist in biotechnology. Temperature and symptoms screening would weed out a portion of false negatives from the PCR tests. articles.text: The English Premier League is at its midway point of its 38-game soccer season. Seven teams are within nine points of the top spot, Manchester City (12-5-2, 41 points). But the major news coming out of England has been the firing of Chelsea manager Frank Lampard on January 25. His team is sitting far down the table in 10th at 8-5-6 with just 29 points. The team hired Thomas Tuchel, the former Paris St. Germain manager, to take over for the remainder of the season. The pressure to succeed at Chelsea is quite impossible. Lampard’s 14-year playing career with the Blues wasn’t enough to convince patience from ownership after just one full season at the helm. But the news coming out of London about Lampard was condemning. The Athletic reported that veteran center back Antonio Rudiger and midfielder Mateo Kovačić went to the front office claiming that Lampard was “quiet” and “played favoritism” with several players. Chelsea is among the most high-profile teams in the Premier League and spent £248 million over the offseason on a group of five players: center mid Kai Haverts (£71m), midfielder Hakim Ziyech (£55m), striker Timo Werner (£53m), wingback Ben Chilwell (£45m) and goal keeper Edouard Mendy (£24), meaning their descent appeared evidence as the basis for a change. articles.text: As they say nowadays, “Steph gonna Steph.” Warriors superstar Stephen Curry dropped 36 points on the Minnesota Timberwolves on Monday, January 26 in a convincing 130-108 win. After clinging to a dwindling 103-95 lead with 6:45 left in the game, the Warriors rallied for a big victory. That’s when Curry let it rain. A dunk and subsequent taunt by Wolves’ guard Malik Beasley was enough to wake up the Dubs, resulting in Steph scoring 11 points and some ridiculously long 3-pointers, as if that should be any surprise. The Warriors now look ahead to three games they could win, which would set them up nicely prior to a difficult schedule in February. They play their second game against the Timberwolves tonight, the Western Conference’s last-place team. They’ll face seventh place Phoenix Suns tomorrow, and then a game on January 30 against the Detroit Pistons, in last place in the Eastern Conference. But then it gets difficult. On February 2, they’ll play the Celtics, the East’s No. 2 tesm, then the 10th place Mavericks twice (Feb. 4 and 6), followed by backto-back games with the No. 9 Spurs (Feb. 8-9). It is way sophisticated – and also way expensive, too.” In comparison, antigen tests look for proteins shed from the surface of the virus. The virus’ RNA has to already be incorporated and making viruses in order to show up on an antigen test, making the accuracy much lower. articles.text: The sports world is mourning the loss of one of the country’s most notable – and most dignified – athletes with the passing of Major League Baseball’s all-time homerun king, Hammerin’ Hank Aaron He died on January 22 at age 86, and died peacefully in his sleep Aaron played 21 seasons with the Milwaukee/Atlanta Braves and his final two with the Milwaukee Brewers. He was the game’s career homerun leader with 755 until Barry Bonds broke his record in 2007. An asterisk accompanies Bonds’ feat. Aaron’s list of accomplishments is long and impressive: 3,771 hits, 2,297 runs batted in, a stellar career average of .305, a total of 25 All-Star selections, one MVP, one World Series, four time NL home run leader. His jersey No. 44 was retired by both the the Braves and Brewers. Aaron is No. 1 in total bases at 6,856, No. 2 in total at-bats with 12,364, No. 1 in RBIS, and No. 3 in hits. But one cannot mention Aaron’s life and history without also acknowledging the racial tension that followed him in 1974, the year he was closing in on Babe Ruth’s all-time record of 714 home runs. The days leading up to April 8, 1974, when he broke Babe Ruth’s record with a 715th home run, he received hate mail and death threats. Aaron had to dodge his way out of ballparks for the simple fact that he was a black man on the verge of supplanting baseball’s icon, Ruth, a white man. Photo courtesy of Emory University Two college students broke onto the field to congratulate Hank Aaron on his historic home run on April 8, 1974 in Atlanta. MLB’s commissioner at the time, Bowie Kuhn, did not attend Aaron’s record setting night, adding to the tension. In the 1990s, Aaron told the New York Times that his pursuit of Ruth’s record “carved a piece of my heart away” due to the hate he and his family endured, acknowledging that even his kids had to stay hidden. “It really made me see for the first time a clear picture of what this country is about,” Aaron said, in an interview with the New York Times.”My kids had to live like they were in prison because of kidnap threats, and I had to live like a pig in a slaughter camp. I had to duck. I had to go out the back door of the ballparks. I had to have a police escort with me all the time. I was getting threatening letters every single day. All of these things have put a bad taste in my mouth, and it won’t go away. They carved a piece of my heart away.” D o d g e r s ’ l e g e n d a r y announcer, Vin Scully, addressed what Aaron’s home run meant to the United States on that April 1974 night. “What a marvelous moment for baseball; what a marvelous moment for Atlanta and the state of Georgia; what a marvelous moment for the country and the world. A black man is getting a standing ovation in the Deep South [Atlanta] for breaking a record of an all-time baseball idol. And it is a great moment for all of us, and particularly for Henry Aaron. For the first time in a long time, that poker face in Aaron shows the tremendous strain and relief of what it must have been like for the past several months,” said Scully. Photo courtesy of AL.com A vintage photo of Hank Aaron early in his baseball career. Photo courtesy of Associated Press Hank Aaron passed away at the age of 86 on January 22.
articles.title: Legendary baseball player, Hank Aaron, dies at 86

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Yosemite National Park Service Yosemite National Park will be closed until Saturday, January 30 due to an upcoming storm this week. Yosemite National Park announced on Monday, January 25 that it is closing the entire park until at least Saturday, January 30 due to last week’s Mono windstorm. “Howling winds topple trees, causing power outages and closing Yosemite,” screamed the headlines from Fresno. Winds estimated at 100 mph caused extensive damage in the park, as Yosemite officials anticipated a snowstorm this week. “Park staff continue to clear roads and trails, mitigate hazard trees, and work toward restoring safe conditions for employees and visitors due to last week’s Mono wind event. A significant winter storm is forecast to begin Tuesday night. Hazardous conditions, including substantial snow accumulation, falling trees, and dangerous road conditions, are anticipated through the week,” wrote the park in a statement. Last week’s Mono wind event “clobbered” the park with high winds that knocked over two giant sequoia trees, put thousands of people without power, and caused millions in damages. “They got clobbered this morning,” said National Weather Service representative Andy Bollenbacher yesterday, January 26, “That wasn’t just in Yosemite Valley, but it got down to Wawona as well. We don’t have a lot of observations from that area, but we did record some high winds over 80 mph.” With Yosemite’s re-opening expected to occur on Saturday, weather permitting, patrons will be allowed to have overnight stays in the park after it was limited to day-use visitors in recent months. The park plans to re-open the Upper Pines Campground on February 8, while the historic Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee Hotel will open its doors on February 8. “When the park reopens, it will be open 24 hours per day. Upper Pines Campground will open on February 8. Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee will open on February 5,” wrote the park. With the closure until Saturday, oft used entrances to Bay Area residents like Highway 140’s El Portal Road and Highway 120’s Big Oak Flat Road are currently closed, but will be re-opened after the winter storm. “Visitors will be able to enter the park using El Portal Road (Highway 140), Big Oak Flat Road (Highway 120 from the west), and Hetch Hetchy Road. Areas south of Yosemite Valley (including Badger Pass, Wawona, Mariposa Grove, South Entrance, and Wawona Road) will remain closed until further notice,” wrote park officials. To check current Yosemite Road conditions, visit https:// www.nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/ conditions.htm, while more lodging information and booking can be found on https://www.nps.gov/ yose/planyourvisit/lodging.htm Here is a direct link to the Upper Pines Campground set to re-open on Feb. 8: https://www. recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/232447 Photo courtesy of Yosemite National Park Service Several cabins, power lines, and bridges were destroyed in last week’s Mono wind event.
articles.title: Park to re-open with overnight use, limited lodging

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s popular podcast series “Aurora Connects” is returning next week, February 4, with new guests. The series is Aurora Theatre Company’s bi-weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every other Thursday at 5 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. Each episode is hosted by theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Director Dawn Monique Williams. Costello was appointed artistic director in 2019 following a national search. At Aurora, he has directed, among others, Exit Strategy, The Importance of Being Earnest, Detroit, and the award-winning world premiere of Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day. Williams has been Aurora’s Associate Artistic Director since August 2019. An Oakland-native, Artistic Director Josh Costello she was Artistic Associate and a resident artist at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival for six seasons. The first episode of the new year is entitled “The Vietnamese-American Experience,” and features Oanh Nguyen and Linda Nguyen. The next episode will stream live on Thursday, February 18, at 5 p.m. Guests are to-be-announced. To view the upcoming episode via YouTube, visit https://www. auroratheatre.org/auroraconnects. You can listen to Aurora Connects on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Google Podcasts by visiting http:// auroraconnects.buzzsprout.com/.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre artistic profiles continue Feb. 4

articles.text: SF Jazz is celebrating the music of Horace Silver with a special on-demand archival performance of Dee Dee Bridgewater, available to stream now through February 28. The concert was originally performed on September 8, 2017, the opening week of SF Jazz’s season. In this fond remembrance of one of jazz’s greatest composers, Bridgewater pays tribute to Silver with a personal take on his classics. Bridgewater has had a lengthy connection to the composer and pianist beginning in the early 1970s, when her then-husband, trumpeter Cecil Bridgewater, began playing in Silver’s band. She has also featured many of Silver’s classics on her 2005 Grammy-nominated release Love and Peace: A Tribute to Horace Silver. In this performance Bridgewater is joined by trumpeter Theo Croker, saxophonist Irwin Hall, pianist Michael King, bassist SF Jazz presents Dee Dee Bridgewater Eric Wheeler, and drummer Kush Abadey. A special members-only price is offered, but others can rent the performance online as a non-member. For access, click on: https://www.sfjazz. org/sfjazz-digital/rent-dee-deebridgewater/.
articles.title: SF Jazz presents Dee Dee Bridgewater

articles.text: Celebrate Lunar New Year, the Year of the Ox, by attending a poetry and calligraphy workshop offered by San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. Poets Michael Warr and Chun Yu read works in English and Mandarin that reflect the essence of the New Year — vanquishing the past, embracing new beginnings, and venerating ancestors. Concurrently Aiqin Zhou demonstrates her skillful calligraphy by illustrating some of the poems. San Francisco-native Warr is the 2020 Berkeley Lifetime Achievement Awardee and Poetry Editor of the anthology Of Poetry & Protest: From Emmett Till to Trayvon Martin. His books of poetry include The Armageddon of Funk Power Lines: A Decade of Poetry From Chicago’s Guild Complex, as a co-eddoctoral fellow at Harvard-MIT Health Science and Technology, where she began writing poetry and stories. Her first book, Little Green: Growing Up During the Chinese Cultural Revolution, has won multiple national awards. Zhou is an internationally renowned Chinese artist, calligrapher, and poet. articles.text: San Francisco’s Independent Film Festival, which operates under the year-round, non-profit organization SF IndieFest, will begin virtually on Thursday, February 4. Now in its 23rd year, IndieFest will feature 80 new independent films from around the world, including the Bay Area. In 2019, over 20,000 people attended SF IndieFest events. This year, IndieFest will open with Book of Vision, a film produced by Terrence Malick and directed by Carlos Hintermann. The centerpiece film, Summertime, features 25 high school poets in a film by Carlos Lopez Estrada. The festival closes with Puppy Love, a semi-biographical film from director Michael Maxxis, starring Hopper Penn and Paz de la Huerta. There are many ways to enjoy screenings presented during the festival. You can watch a single screening or buy a pass for the entire festival. Visit https://sfindiefest2021.eventive.org/welcome for more information on how to attend SF IndieFest 2021.

articles.text: Fort Mason Drive-In Movie Fort Mason will be hosting Sundance Film Festival satellite screenings, presented by San Francisco’s Roxie Theater. The special screenings will begin tomorrow and will be shown through Tuesday, February 2. The Festival opens tomorrow, January 28, with two films, Coda, at 5 p.m., and Sons of Monarchs at 8:15 p.m. Coda Coda is directed by Sian Heder and produced by Philippe Rousselet, Fabrice Gianfermi and Patrick Wachsberger. The film follows the life of Ruby, a child of deaf adults who is the only hearing person in her family. When the family’s fishing business is threatened, Ruby finds herself torn between pursuing her love of music and her fear of abandoning her parents. The cast includes Emilia Jones, Eugenio Derbez, Troy Kotsur, and Daniel Durant. These screenings are part of Fort Mason Flix, Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture’s drive-through film series. It provides a socially distanced movie experience, with online ticket sales, contactless check-in, a limited capacity, safe physical distance between vehicles, expanded cleaning, and sanitation in restrooms, and PPE for all theater and security staff. Concessions are not available until San Francisco’s shelterIn-place rules are relaxed when COVID-19 pandemic conditions improve. To obtain tickets, visit https:// fortmason.org/event/flix/2021- sundance-film-festival-coda/.

articles.text: Bradley Cooper stars in Limitless. Movie review by Chris Honore’ Likely you’ve seen the commercial: An egg is shown, with voiceover saying, “This is your brain.” The egg is broken and the yoke and white are dropped into a hot frying pan. The voice over then says, “And this is your brain on drugs.” The egg sizzles, the edges grow crispy, even black. It’s a brief, cautionary tale. And so is the intense, very entertaining thriller, Limitless. The film does have a riveting premise. But first, back to the egg. “This is your brain.” And then, “This is your brain on NZT.” No frying pan, just one small, clear tab, placed on the tongue. Within minutes everything glows, bathed in an intense light. All things become possible. If you were cruising through life in first or second gear, using some 20 percent of your brain cells (which, we’re told, is par), with NZT you are suddenly in fourth gear and revving the engine to full capacity. Which is what happens to Eddie Morra (Bradley Cooper) in the story. We first see Eddie – scruffy, depressed, suffering from serious writer’s block – walking down a busy New York City street, wondering where he will find the juice to even write the first sentence of a book for which he has received a generous advance. His long-suffering girlfriend, Lindy (Abbie Cornish), has just broken up with him and he is significantly bummed. That’s when he bumps into his ex-brother-in-law, Vern (Johnny Whitworth), a long-time street hustler and dealer. Vern slips Eddie a small, plastic baggy with a gel-like pill inside and tells him it is FDA approved, no worries. Eddie, at first skeptical, takes it on his way back to his grungy apartment. And that’s when things profoundly change. This pill is not experiential. In other words, it’s not a self-induced hallucination buttressed by a lava lamp. This is extreme fuel injected, pedal to the metal, hyper-cognitive stuff. Eddie writes most of his book in one sitting and looks around and realizes that there are other dragons to slay, like the stock market. It’s at this juncture that things get very tense. Hooked, Eddie returns to Vern’s apartment and tells him that whatever that was, the NZT, well, he’ll need a steady supply. Vern agrees and suggests that first Eddie might go and pick up some breakfast and his dry cleaning. When Eddie returns, things go dark and dicey and Eddie’s path to a brave new world is suddenly replete with predators. Meanwhile, jacked up on NZT, he is transformed: designer clothes, new haircut, and an arbitrage office with computers and graphs, showcasing his newest talents. He’s a rock star of high finance. Limitless is hot. A ride. Flawed to be sure – the ending is a bit weak – but who cares, really? It is simply a good B-movie entertainment. . Limitless. Directed by Neil Burger. Starring Bradley Cooper, Robert DeNiro, Abbie Cornish and Johnny Whitworth. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré It’s important to understand going in that the Harry Potter films – six thus far – are the equivalent of chapters in a book. Each entertains, some more than others, and there is a great deal of backstory already detailed, with more to come. It’s fair to view Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince as a protracted set up for the two-film conclusion (2010 and 2011) of the seven-book saga which has so captured the imaginations of Harry Potterheads worldwide. The books have sold more than 400 million copies and have been translated into 67 languages. Keep in mind that the final Harry Potter novel, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, is a 784 page beast weighing 2.4 pounds, a book that small children hauled out of bookstores in their wagons after waiting in long lines, many wearing round peepers. Each of the movies has been solidly entertaining as well as an artful blending of characters, plotting and computer graphics. It must be a thrill for the legions of fans to read and reread the books and then sit in a darkened theater and give themselves over to the sheer wonder of seeing those images they have constructed from the words of J.K. Rowling now on the screen. Half-Blood Prince, coming some eight years since the first film, when Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) was about to turn 11, now shows Harry and Hermione (Emma Watson) and Ron (Rupert Grint) in full-bloom adolescence – hence much of the plot has to do with bumper-car romance and its many inherent misunderstandings. Of course, since Hogwarts is a school of magic, there are love potions being concocted with humorous effects. Lord Voldermot has returned as have the Death Eaters, and there’s a mystery to be solved involving young Voldermot, aka Tom Riddle, Professor Horace Slughorn (Jim Broadbent), Harry, and the head of Hogwarts, Professor Albus Dumbledore (Michael Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince is the sixth installment in the Harry Potter film franchise. Gambon). Without question, the Harry Potter films are filled with some of England’s finest actors, and Half-Blood Prince is no exception. It’s a veritable smorgasbord of fine performances by Gambon (Dumbledore), Broadbent (Slughorn), Robbie Coltrane (Rubeus Hagrid), Maggie Smith (Minerva McGonagall), and, of course, the wonderful Alan Rickman, back again as Severus Snape, a dark, word-clipping character who steals every scene. Can Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince stand alone? No. But it’s not meant to. It is, however, a wonderfully entertaining film that will more than satisfy the millions of Harry Potter fans. In fact, so satisfied are audiences with the series that the first five movies have grossed some $4.8 billion worldwide and counting. As to the question, do you believe in magic?, well, it seems the answer for the countless Potterheads is a loud, unequivocal “Yes!” Harry Potter and the HalfBlood Prince. Directed by David Yates. Starring Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, Emma Watson. 2 hrs., 33 min. Rated PG. Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! articles.text: Amanda Gorman, a 23-yearold Los Angeles-born writer and performer, currently America's Youth Poet Laureate, recited her poem The Hill We Climb at President Joe Biden and VP Kamala Harris’ inauguration on Wednesday, January 20. She became the youngest poet to perform at a presidential inauguration. Only three previous presidents have chosen to have a poem read at their inauguration: John F. Kennedy (1961, Robert Frost), Bill Clinton (1993, Maya Angelou; 1997, Miller Williams), and Barack Obama (2009, Elizabeth Alexander; 2013, Richard Blanco). Watch the video to get the full impact of her delivery, presence and performance, which were as poignant and captivating as her words. https://www.theguardian. com/global/video/2021/jan/20/ youth-poet-laureate-amanda-gorman-recital-at-biden-inauguration-video. The National Youth Poet LauNational Youth Poet Laureate Amanda Gorman recites her poem at the inauguration of Joe Biden as President of the U.S. on January 20, 2021. reate is awarded to a young person who demonstrates skill in the arts, particularly poetry and/or spoken word, is a strong leader, is committed to social justice, and is active in civic discourse and advocacy. articles.text: When day comes we ask ourselves, where can we find light in this never-ending shade? The loss we carry, a sea we must wade. We've braved the belly of the beast, We've learned that quiet isn't always peace, and the norms and notions of what just is isn't always just-ice. And yet the dawn is ours before we knew it. Somehow we do it. Somehow we've weathered and witnessed a nation that isn't broken, but simply unfinished. We the successors of a country and a time where a skinny Black girl descended from slaves and raised by a single mother can dream of becoming president only to find herself reciting for one. And yes we are far from polished. Far from pristine. But that doesn't mean we are striving to form a union that is perfect. We are striving to forge a union with purpose, to compose a country committed to all cultures, colors, characters and conditions of man. And so we lift our gazes not to what stands between us, but what stands before us. We close the divide because we know, to put our future first, we must first put our differences aside. We lay down our arms so we can reach out our arms to one another. We seek harm to none and harmony for all. Let the globe, if nothing else, say this is true, that even as we grieved, we grew, that even as we hurt, we hoped, that even as we tired, we tried, that we'll forever be tied together, victorious. Not because we will never again know defeat, but because we will never again sow division. Scripture tells us to envision that everyone shall sit under their own vine and fig tree and no one shall make them afraid. If we're to live up to our own time, then victory won't lie in the blade. But in all the bridges we've made, that is the promise to glade, the hill we climb. If only we dare. It's because being American is more than a pride we inherit, it's the past we step into and how we repair it. We've seen a force that would shatter our nation rather than share it. Would destroy our country if it meant delaying democracy. And this effort very nearly succeeded. But while democracy can be periodically delayed, it can never be permanently defeated. In this truth, in this faith we trust. For while we have our eyes on the future, history has its eyes on us. This is the era of just redemption we feared at its inception. We did not feel prepared to be the heirs of such a terrifying hour but within it we found the power to author a new chapter. To offer hope and laughter to ourselves. So while once we asked, how could we possibly prevail over catastrophe? Now we assert, How could catastrophe possibly prevail over us? We will not march back to what was, but move to what shall be. A country that is bruised but whole, benevolent but bold, fierce and free. We will not be turned around or interrupted by intimidation, because we know our inaction and inertia will be the inheritance of the next generation. Our blunders become their burdens. But one thing is certain, If we merge mercy with might, and might with right, then love becomes our legacy, and change our children's birthright. So let us leave behind a country better than the one we were left with. Every breath from my bronze-pounded chest, we will raise this wounded world into a wondrous one. We will rise from the gold-limbed hills of the west. We will rise from the windswept northeast, where our forefathers first realized revolution. We will rise from the lake-rimmed cities of the midwestern states. We will rise from the sunbaked south. We will rebuild, reconcile and recover. And every known nook of our nation and every corner called our country, our people diverse and beautiful will emerge, battered and beautiful. When day comes we step out of the shade, aflame and unafraid, the new dawn blooms as we free it. For there is always light, if only we're brave enough to see it. If only we're brave enough to be it.

articles.text: Dear Jim: I recently had a home inspector give me a list of projects I should focus on. A high priority was my drainage system. Can you tell me why this would be important? And more importantly, how should I approach these issues? Dear Neighbor: While it’s always a bummer to have to pay for work you can’t tangibly see, like a beautiful new kitchen or bath, a homeowner’s value of a properly designed and constructed drainage system is highly underrated. Without proper drainage your house is subject to settlement problems, foundation and slab damage, moisture and mold problems. This is particularly relevant for most of our older homes, where 100-year-old concrete is subject to long-term moisture damage. The cracks you see inside or outside your house may or may not indicate issues with your foundation, but it all starts with drainage. Some common issues are discussed here to help you figure out how drainage may be affecting your home and how to go about fixing it. Unfortunately, drainage is poorly understood. It’s not just about the surface; underground water can be an insidious problem and more difficult and expensive to control. Simply put, you have to deal with water above and below, and they are each approached differently. Surface water is more obvious – water coming from your roof through downspouts and on patios, walkways and driveways needs to be channeled into solid piping and typically brought to the street (or occasionally to your back yard if you have a large lot). Water also flows underground, sometimes very deeply, especially when you are on a hillside with basements or lower levels. This is when and where French drains are needed to control underground water. In order to keep water out of basements or garages with tall foundations, the general concept is to dig the drains below the lowest interior level, which unfortunately can be 8 or 9’ deep with taller fully excavated basement areas. This can be expensive and time-consuming work, requiring the removal of huge amounts of soil and the replacement with similar amounts of gravel backfill. Deeper trenches require procedures to safely dig down deep (shoring) and sometimes material needs to be moved manually by wheelbarrow or buckets through small side-yards, up many stairs, etc. The differences can be night and day between simple downspout projects and deep French drains for highly sloped hillside lots with basements. Costs can vary dramatically. What is supposed to be never was. Most older homes were designed and built without drainage, or with old systems that fail over time. Lacking modern membranes and plastic piping, old clay pipes were used about 50 years ago for French drains, and they were laid in small sections with gaps in between, guaranteeing they were filled with dirt. Many downspouts drain directly on the ground next to the house Proper drainage is cheaper than a new foundation. articles.text: Like a number of concepts in the planning world, open space seems to lack a consistent definition among the various organizations that deal with it. In my experience, simply stated, it most often refers to open land, generally public, without (or with very few) buildings. Parks constitute the main and obvious category of open space, in fact “parks” and “open space” are often used interchangeably. One of the best parts of walking through Piedmont is to come upon our well used and well-maintained parks. They are clearly an invaluable and essential part of any city. The universal appreciation of open space is of course due to the many benefits. Recreational uses immediately come to mind – from more active uses like sports that require large fields of lawn or paved courts, to more passive uses like hiking and picnics. Protecting and enhancing natural resources is another benefit: The 15-acre Piedmont Park is the city’s only “Community Park”. It is an incredibly beautiful and functional amenity, located in the geographical heart of the city and would be a wonderful and appropriate park for even a much larger city. Considered a Neighborhood Park, popular Dracena is the city’s third largest at 7.8 acres. It includes a number of swings and play structures in addition to large grass areas and a dog run. Berkeley Photos by Will Adams There are a number of public streets in Piedmont that are a pleasure for strolling, with mature street trees, plus beautiful bosques and planting in people’s yards. This is not technically considered “open space”, but it has almost all the qualities of open space (except access to people’s private property). I call this common valuable amenity “borrowed open space”. Crocker Park is a delightful place with a large lawn area, mature pine trees and understory beds of rhododendrons, camellias, azaleas, and ferns. Punctuated with a granite sculpture of a mother bear and cubs by the noted sculptor Benny Bufano – the City’s best known public art – it is considered a mini-park (less than 1acre). ecological issues like air quality and animal, bird and insect habitat are inevitable beneficiaries of green open spaces. Open space can provide a wonderful aesthetic amenity for all of us, and even a partial view of a park’s vegetation can improve property values in a neighborhood. Like any successful public space, open spaces also foster community, bringing people together for both interaction and simple people watching. Maybe the most important advantage of open space is the most abstract and difficult to define. I’ll call it the spiritual advantage. In our world of extensive development, our ability to interact with a bit of the natural world (the opposite of the built environment I am always referencing) can raise our spirits, give us a chance to slow down and reflect, to experience our connection to nature—just a little of what the naturalist Henry Thoreau wrote about at Walden Pond in the 1800’s. I suspect the activity of simply strolling through or sitting and resting to enjoy trees, lawns, plants and benches is the most common, and important, See Open Space on page 32 The redwood bosque at Wildwood and Magnolia is a beautiful example of open space that has been created in a typically neglected area. It is one of a number of landscaped traffic islands and medians scattered throughout the city that have been put to good use.

articles.text: I just sort of stumbled on it. I was vacationing in Mendocino for a week and had done the usual tourist things – the Fern Canyon and Headlands walks, strolling through the town shops and bookstore. I remembered seeing an ad for a winery on the coast about 11 miles north of Mendocino and decided to check it out. It’s hard to describe the experience of rounding the bend on this remote, desolate portion of Hwy 1 and seeing this beautiful, rustic winery perched on the very edge of a cliff overlooking the pounding waves of the Pacific. It is the most stunning setting for a winery I have ever seen – and I have seen a lot of them. The first thing I thought of was “How the heck did this happen? How did this get approved by the California Coastal Commission?” Luckily, we had a chance to meet Sally Ottoson, the owner, who told us the story. Sally is a North Coast native, with roots in Comptche and Ft. Bragg. Because she was a “local”, she was able to talk the property owner into selling to her. Then she set about the long, arduous task of getting approval from the Coastal Commission. Every winery on the coast is required to have a vineyard. So she planted Pinot Noir grapes knowing they would never be any good. It’s far too cold there to grow grapes. The winery imports their grapes from the warmer side of Mendocino county – the Ukiah region on the other side of the coast range. With much perseverance she finally got approval to build the winery. I’m glad she did. We tasted outside socially distanced at a picnic table overlooking the stunning coast. Pacific Star Winery is now open Thursday to Sunday from 12 to 5 p.m., and is closed when it’s raining. Pacific Star Winery sits on the edge of a cliff just south of Westport and north of Fort Bragg. It is the most stunning setting for a winery I have ever seen – and I have seen a lot of them. The first thing I thought of was “How the heck did this happen? How did this get approved by the California Coastal Commission?” Luckily, we had a chance to meet Sally Ottoson, the owner, who told us the story. Sally is a North Coast native, with roots in Comptche and Ft. Bragg. Because she was a “local”, she was able to talk the property owner into selling to her. Then she set about the long, arduous task of getting approval from the Coastal Commission. Every winery on the coast is required to have a vineyard. So she planted Pinot Noir grapes knowing they would never be any good. It’s far too cold there to grow grapes. The winery imports their grapes from the warmer side of Mendocino county – the Ukiah region on the other side of the coast range. With much perseverance she finally got approval to build the winery. I’m glad she did. We tasted outside socially distanced at a picnic table overlooking the stunning coast. Pacific Star Winery is now open Thursday to Sunday from 12 to 5 p.m., and is closed when it’s raining. WINE NOTES 2016 Charbono Pacific Star’s best wine, this is an Italian grape that nearly went extinct. It is still rare with less than 100 acres planted in the world and some of the best is found in Mendocino County. Dark purple colored with an earthy, spicy, gorgeously pure nose, this wine offers blueberry and blackberry flavors as well as copious amounts of earthy richness, with a long, full-bodied powerful finish. It should drink well for two decades. Charbonno is the flagship grape at Pacific Star Winery. Pacific Star Winery sits on the edge of a cliff just south of Westport and north of Fort Bragg. NV It’s Not My Fault Named after the fault the winery sits on this is a blend of Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Chenin Blanc. It is medium weight and satisfying – a spicy fruit filled trattoria red to enjoy over the next 5 years. 2015 Tempranillo The Tempranillo grape originally from Spain, also does well in California. This is a concentrated, rich, yet streamlined and focused red that has earth, anise and black fruit aromas. It is deep and concentrated, pure and elegant with good acidity and structure. This blockbuster Is delicious now but will age for decades.

articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Frankie Rhodes, a loving wife, mother, grandmother and historic preservationist, passed away peacefully on January 15, 2021 at Alta Bates Hospital in Berkeley surrounded by her loved ones after a long illness. She was known throughout the Bay Area’s historic preservation community, having served more than five decades as a founding member of the Camron-Stanford House Preservation Association (CSHPA). It was charged with the restoration of the last of the 19th-century Victorian mansions that once surrounded Lake Merritt in Oakland. Frankie helped raise more than $800,000 in capital and gifts-in-kind to restore the city-owned building for the community in the early 1970s. The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972 and is cited by the Historic American Building Survey, the California Landmarks Committee and is a City of Oakland landmark. Camron-Stanford House opened to the public in May 1978 and has remained a teaching institution serving Oakland and the greater Bay Area. In addition to her work with Camron-Stanford House, she was active in the Junior League of the East Bay, Decorative Arts Forum, Art League of the East Bay, Oakland Museum docent program, Victorian Alliance and Victorian Society. Born Frances Hayden on August 28, 1939 at UCSF on San Francisco’s Parnassus Hill, she was the daughter of Dr. Charles Thomas Hayden and Margaret Nichols Hayden. She grew up in III and Blake Francis Rhodes. In addition to her work with Camron-Stanford House, she played an instrumental role in beginning a baseball program at her alma mater, the now coed Head-Royce School in Oakland. Both of her sons played on the team during their high school years. For her contributions to the school, she was honored with the Head-Royce School Alumni Association’s Founders Award in 2008. With her mother being born and raised in Hilo, Hawaii, she also was a member of the Daughters of Hawai’i, one of the first organizations in Hawaii to recognize the importance of historic preservation. Locally she was also a member of the Dirt Daubers Garden Club. Frankie is survived by Skip, her husband of 58 years, and by sons Jay and wife Dianne, and Blake and wife Carin. She is also survived by four grandchildren, Hayden, Brody, McKenzie and Addison. She is additionally survived by a nephew, Eric Rhodes, nieces Cheryl Thomas and Nance Weber, and numerous cousins. She is predeceased by her parents, a brother, Charles Thomas (Skip) Hayden, Jr., and a sister, Rhoda Jean Robinson. COVID-19 restrictions make planning for a celebration of life service difficult at this time. In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial gifts be made to the Camron-Stanford House Preservation Association, 1418 Lakeside Drive, Oakland, CA, 94612, or to the Head-Royce School, 4315 Lincoln Ave., Oakland, CA 94602. Frankie Rhodes, a resident of Piedmont for 55 years, passed away on January 15. She was 81. San Francisco, Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, Oakland and Piedmont. An accomplished diver, swimmer and horseback rider, she attended the Anna Head School in Berkeley, graduating in 1958 before matriculating to the University of Colorado, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in Fine Arts in 1962. After graduation she returned to San Francisco and married John Willett (Skip) Rhodes, Jr., on June 30, 1962 at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland. The next day, the couple moved to Anchorage, Alaska followed by a stint in Seattle, Wash. while Skip was on assignment with Chevron. Following those assignments, Frankie and Skip returned to San Francisco where she began her work with the interior design firm, Stroheim & Roman. articles.text: This letter was sent to Piedmont City Council. Editor: Please renew the lease of Piedmont Center for the Arts which is a vibrant center that enhances our community. articles.text: This letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: I am writing to urge you to renew the lease for the Piedmont Center for the Arts. In a community that prides itself on promoting culture and the arts in our school curriculum, it seems inconceivable that the city council might not renew the Center’s lease. Over the years and with countless numbers of tireless volunteers, the Piedmont Center for the Arts has become a venue for world-class musical events. It has enabled our residents to enjoy outstanding concerts without fighting the traffic and parking in San Francisco and Berkeley. Celebrated musicians from renowned companies have spoken of the venue’s lovely space, its stellar acoustics, and the magnificent Steinway piano. The Center has become a jewel in the crown that is Piedmont, and it saddens me to think of this almost sacred space being used as a community center. Do not let this cultural treasure slip away. Please renew their lease. –Freddi Robertson Jerome Ave. scared for our lives and those of our staff members,” Swalwell told Livermore’s The Independent. “Failing to prosecute and failing to hold everyone accountable will embolden domestic terrorists even more, just as Donald Trump was emboldened by the Senate’s craven failure to convict him in the impeachment trial [in 2020]. Editor: I am writing to urge you to renew the lease for the Piedmont Center for the Arts. In a community that prides itself on promoting culture and the arts in our school curriculum, it seems inconceivable that the city council might not renew the Center’s lease. Over the years and with countless numbers of tireless volunteers, the Piedmont Center for the Arts has become a venue for world-class musical events. It has enabled our residents to enjoy outstanding concerts without fighting the traffic and parking in San Francisco and Berkeley. Celebrated musicians from renowned companies have spoken of the venue’s lovely space, its stellar acoustics, and the magnificent Steinway piano. The Center has become a jewel in the crown that is Piedmont, and it saddens me to think of this almost sacred space being used as a community center. Do not let this cultural treasure slip away. Newsom’s plan includes a financial incentive. School districts can receive $450 per student if they open by February 15. With roughly 2500 total students, Piedmont School District would receive approximately $1,000,000. The biggest impediment to reopening with Newsom’s plan is a new requirement for testing of all students and staff. Testing must be done weekly or twice monthly depending on new case rates. School staff members in Piedmont are already being tested once a month and the district was able to increase testing frequency with the outside firm doing the testing. For student testing, School Board President Cory Smegal said, “We are working on it and should have that secured before our plan’s submission.” The district is also still working on a “Walkthrough [of the] COVID Safety Plan with Teachers and Staff Leaders,” which is being conducted this week. The previous Memorandum of Understanding with teachers is still valid and does not need to be negotiated. When said Person came back on the line, she repeated her instructions to go to the closed branch and play “knock knock” on the aforementioned closed door despite the fact that there was no one there to ask, “Who’s there?” Well, at that point the situation started going downhill. More accurately, it continued going downhill at an accelerating pace. When The LW used the Seven Word Magic Spell of Customer Service – “I’d like to speak to a supervisor” – she received this curt response: “Speaking to a supervisor will not help. Since I opened a file in your name and address, there is nothing else she’ll be able to do. It would be better to hang up, call back this number, speak to someone else, and open a new inquiry.” For those of you that don’t speak Big Bankalese, here’s the translation: “Don’t bother me anymore, I’m at my limit, I don’t want you talking to my boss. Try calling back again and speaking to one of my equally incompetent colleagues.” It’s a good thing it was not Wiley on the phone, because he probably would have said something that The LW considered rude (remember, Wiley has already picked out the opening words of his epitaph: “He didn’t suffer fools gladly”). After all, when was the last time you wasted fifteen minutes on a customer service call, only to be told it would be more efficient to call back and start over? It’s probably the last time you talked to a Big Bank. However, it was The LW, so she managed to get through to a supervisor, get a clue to the next piece of the puzzle, and state that said supervisor needed to be doing a bit more supervising. But the puzzle is not yet solved, and Sherlock Wiley has been gathering additional clues. The LW continues to plow ahead like a stubborn golden retriever (okay, retrievers are not stubborn, but we absolutely adore them), and she hopes to solve the mystery eventually. As they say, to be continued ….. By the way, you may be wondering which Big Bank operates like this. Unfortunately for you, Wiley isn’t telling. All he will say is “Well, Well, Well.” If you count them, that’s three “Wells”. Wiley Hoag is the Post’s Consumer Affairs correspondent. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, January 27, 2021 Open Space Continued from page 21 use of our open space. There are a number of other sites within Piedmont that contribute to the open space total. These include various EBMUD properties, landscaped medians and traffic islands, various wooded hillsides and ravines, part of the Rose Garden, and even part of the Mountain View Cemetery. Schools, with their large green playfields, seem to be burdened with the inconsistent open space definition mentioned earlier. In Piedmont however, the ongoing joint use of City and School District facilities realistically puts them in the open space category. In addition, because of our proximity and easy access to various nearby regional amenities such as Redwood Park, Temescal Recreational Area, or Joaquin Miller Park, these too can be considered as a part of Piedmont’s useable open space. Next: Density and Walkability Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. Teens4Biden Continued from page 7 Universally, members of the club used one word to describe the inauguration “relief.” A consensus has also formed about the National Youth Poet Laureate Amanda Gorman; she stole the show. “Gorman was brilliant. She was the runaway star,” said Edel with excitement. “I feel like she really resonated with everyone – young people, old people, and everyone in between. Children saw someone who is young, beautiful and a person of color speaking to all of America. I think that was one of the more meaningful moments,” said Edel, also a poet. Another active member of the club, senior Laney Tellegen, summed up the inauguration as being unlike any other. “My family took the morning off so we could watch it together because U.S. politics and the current administration affect all of our lives so greatly at this time in our history,” Tellegen said. “Administrations need to be held accountable to ensure they are working with the people’s benefit in mind,” she added. This is the most undisturbed, natural part of our Piedmont Park. The many beautiful redwood trees located here consume more CO2 and release more oxygen than any other tree on earth. Bushy Dell Creek comes to life On Friday morning last week, bracing the elements, a solitary walker explored Piedmont Park during a bit of rain that broke the spell of months of drought. As he gazed at the water flowing down Bushy Dell Creek, he realized that perhaps it was merely a mirage. Yes, he decided, it’s not water flowing, it’s all vodka. People have been driven to drink by the pandemic, the drought, the wildfires and the tumult in D.C. on January 6. Nonetheless, it was a relief for all to see the creek come alive after three-quarters of a year of mere gurgling. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved an employment agreement appointing former City Administrator Paul Benoit as a retired annuitant to provide consulting services on the design and construction of a new community pool. Funding will be provided by Measure UU, a bond approved by voters on November 3, 2020. Benoit will be assisting current City Administrator Sara Lillevand on the project. The passage of Measure UU marks the first successful capital bond measure in the city’s history, Lillevand explained. Given the size and scope of the project (estimated at $19,000,000), she recommended at last night’s meeting. that city council add Benoit as a Special Assistant to this effort. “Paul is well known to the community, as he served as City Administrator from 2014-2019. During his time in this position, Paul shepherded the community process to develop the Aquatics Master Plan Conceptual Design, which was accepted by the City Council in 2016 and will be refined and implemented with the Measure UU funds,” Lillevand explained. “In addition to his familiarity with Piedmont and the Community Pool project, Paul has overseen large capital projects in Alameda, California and Astoria, Oregon,” she added. Benoit will be an invaluable addition to the internal city team, she added. His initial tasks will include leading the efforts to hire project management services, as well as the architectural design team. As a retired annuitant, the former city administrator can work a maximum of 960 hours in a fiscal year. Retired annuitants cannot be employed in any regular staff position. The maximum annual cost of the agreement is $106,000. These expenses are directly related to the construction of a new community pool, so Measure UU bond proceeds will be utilized, and there will be no adverse impact on the city’s general fund budget.
articles.title: City Council appoints Paul Benoit as consultant on pool project

articles.text: On Monday, January 18, Alameda County officials announced they would pause administering doses from one batch of COVID-19 vaccines produced by Moderna linked to an unusual increase of allergic reactions elsewhere in California until an investigation is completed. Dr. Erica Pan, California State Epidemiologist, said on Sunday, January 17 that a batch of Moderna vaccines were connected to reports of “higher-than-usual” numbers of people suffering from allergic reactions at one vaccination clinic in San Diego. Alameda County Department of Public Health said they were halting distribution from this batch of Moderna vaccine until the matter is investigated. While no county points of dispensing received doses from this lot, other local providers had distributed some doses from the lot before the pause. No unusual vaccine responses from these doses had been reported as of press time. “Our goal is to provide the COVID vaccine safely, swiftly and equitably,” Pan said in a statement, adding “out of an extreme abundance of caution and also recognizing the extremely limited supply of vaccine, we are recommending that providers use other available vaccine inventory and pause the administration

articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board convened for a meeting on January 13 with a discussion mainly on Governor Newsom’s “Safe Schools for All Plan.” The plan, if approved by legislators, would change the requirements for TK-5 classes to reopen and pay districts to have in-person classes. Piedmont Superintendent Randy Booker and the school board reviewed the implications and associated complications. School reopening remains just as cloudy, if not more so, than before. The plan, announced December 30, has received much criticism from school superintendents across the state. A main benefit of Newsom’s plan is an incentive of $2 billion to school districts that reopen. Districts that submit their application by February 1 and get approved would receive $450 per student, plus an additional amount up to $250 per low-income student. Piedmont would stand to receive $1 million in funding with this plan. Approved applications would let TK-2nd grade start February 15, and grades 3-5 on March 15. A later application deadline of March 1, for a March 15 opening, would give districts $337 per student. Another benefit is that the criteria for districts to reopen schools would change to an “adjusted value” of fewer than 25 new COVID-19 cases per day (per 100,000 population). This level (an unadjusted value of around 500 Alameda County cases per day) would have to be maintained for a five consecutive days. The previous red-tier requirement for reopening was 7 new cases per day per 100,000, and it needed to hold there for two weeks. On January 17, Alameda County’s case rate was 37.7. Newsom highlighted those positives to his plan but many superintendents and school boards across the state vehemently object to the newly imposed mandatory impediments to reopening. articles.text: Transcript by Allyson Aleksey COVID risk, but that’s really only half of the equation. The other KCBS News Anchor and half is the measurable ongoing Piedmont resident Lisa Chan Carnazzo interviewed Dr. Jeanne Noble, UCSF Director of COVID-19 Response, on January 17, in a discussion about Bay Area schools, which have been closed since March of last year. It is the longest school closure due to COVID-19 in the world. A group of 30 UCSF medical professionals published an open letter calling for California schools to reopen by February 1. The following is a verbatim transcript from that interview. LC: Tell us, what did you write in this letter? JN: The purpose of the letter is really to refocus public dialogue. The majority of public dialogue about when to reopen public schools has been focused on cation. Our letter was designed to broaden this discussion. Keeping our kids safe at home is really a misnomer. Our national data shows increases in depression and anxiety among adolescents. Children’s Hospital of Oakland, for example, has seen [the rate of] 17 year-olds with recent suicidal thoughts increase from six percent to 16 percent between March and September of 2020. LC: You now have data from schools that have reopened. What does that data tell us? JN: We have very strong data that schools can operate safely even when COVID is widespread in the community. Locally, in Marin County, we’ve had 40,000 students, and 5,000 teachers back on campus since September, with a total of just seven cases of school-based transmission, – Dr. Jeanne Noble, UCSF Director of COVID-19 Response harm to children and adolescents from missing what is soon going to be a full year of in-person edu-
articles.title: UCSF Director of COVID Response says schools should open now

articles.text: As the Piedmont Post moves through its 23rd year of publication, some kind words have been received from our readers. A sampling is printed below. Editor: With fun news and challenging news, you keep the Piedmont community informed and connected. Thank you. –Robert Jolda and Nancy McKee-Jolda Editor: We can’t thank you enough for the wonderful service you have provided to both the city and our family over the years. The Hill roots in Piedmont go back over a century. The Post has been a mainstay in our lives during that time, and your willingness to take on the task years ago has benefited all of us. Sincerely, –George and Kay Hill Tiburon Editor: Thank you for the wonderful coverage for PBF highlighting both the tree lighting and the $100,000 donation for the Linda-Beach project. I love seeing the paper on my iPad with all of the photos in color. –Gayle Lambert Editor: The longer I live in Piedmont, the more I appreciate the Post, our own newspaper. It is the glue that holds this unique community together. –Tom Gandesbery San Carlos Avenue Editor: I appreciated your article about the union agreement and certainly spurred lots of conversations about the different options for reopening the schools. articles.text: The following article was written on March 7, one week before everything came to a screeching halt in Piedmont and throughout Alameda County. This article was first published in The New York Review of Books as part of its dispatches from around the world documenting the coronavirus outbreak. town San Francisco, already void of tourists, had turned ghostlier still. From behind the glass door of a shuttered Illy café on Battery Street, the Italian manager waved at me, his hand in a blue disposable glove, with an apologetic smile. For days, his parents, quarantined in Florence over the coronavirus epidemic, had been imploring him to stay away from people. It seemed as if they got their wish granted. weaving our way toward the Oakland maze. My neighbor’s parents had been on that ship; they were now at Travis Air Force Base, awaiting the results of their testing. I spent the weekend oscillating between “this can’t be real” and asking myself myriad odd questions, such as whether to explain to the kids, at least to the sixteenyear-old, how to claim our life insurance. I raided the rapidly depleting grocery aisles, picking up things I never thought I’d need, like pinto beans or soap in a 12-pack, all the while feeling the futility of the effort. If growing up in the shortage-ridden Soviet economy taught me anything, it’s that you can’t outsmart malfunctioning lines of supply and demand. We never knew what would disappear next, and even when we guessed right, the supply would eventually run out. The one thing that’s worth stockpiling is decency, that silver lining of our lives back in the USSR, with its near-permanent state of national emergency. Today, in America, where decency has taken a beating over the past four years, it might mean something as straightforward as not buying both of the last two loaves of bread, not forwarding that doomsday chain e-mail, and not going out even if you are healthy. Tomorrow, our challenges might not be so simple. Since I started writing this, a shelterin-place order for six Bay Area counties, including mine, has been issued. Decency won’t save us, but it will make our altered lives more tolerable, come what may. Anastasia Edek is a Piedmont writer author and lecturer. This article was first published in The New York Review of Books. The full series of writers reading their contributions is available at: nybooks.com/pandemic. articles.text: As the City Council considers approval of an extension of a 10-year lease with the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, letters sent to the city and the Center continue to be received. A sampling follows. Now is the time to put negativity and falsehoods aside, have a civil dialogue and find ways for the City and the Center to work together for the benefit for all citizens of Piedmont. I believe that members of the PCA Board are more than ready to work with the City to create policy and accessibility to the building to support the needs of interested groups. PCA has been a good tenant and is willing to continue to be a good team player with the City. The arts are an important part of our society and add an important dimension to our lives. Please renew the PCA lease. –Valerie Corvin
articles.title: Center for the Arts lease up for renewal

articles.text: This letter was sent to members of Piedmont City Council. Editor: I am a co-founder of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. I recently stepped down from the PCA Board to pursue other endeavors, but I served 9 years as program director, visual art program director, and juried art show administrator. As a board member and with no paid staff, I have put in countless hours at all hours of the day and night to help PCA grow into the City of Piedmont treasure that it is. The people of Piedmont love PCA. I have been thanked probably a thousand times by people who have attended events at the Center. Residents truly appreciate having an arts center as part the offerings of the City of the Piedmont. It ranks up there along with the school system and our well-run town. I have been told the PCA is one of the top 5 selling points of Piedmont cited by realtors. The Center for the Arts is now part of the fabric of this town. In this divided time, it is easy to allow a couple of disgruntled voices to overshadow all the good work that PCA has done in the last nine years. I have heard about false and unsubstantiated claims being made. I believe that the claims are being put forth for personal reasons or grudges. Other claims are for personal gain if PCA should be disbanded.
articles.title: PCA co-founder urges support by Council

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: I’d like to express my deep appreciation for everything the Piedmont Center for the Arts has done over the years for my organization, and for the supportive and welcoming way in which they foster our creative collaborations. I’m a founding member of the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco. Of all the venues we have performed in over eight years the Piedmont Center for the Arts has easily been the most enjoyable to play in. That is thanks to its excellent and thoughtfully designed acoustics. It has become a regular home for our East Bay concerts, and many of our concertgoers now prefer to come hear us in Piedmont though they may live in San Francisco, Marin or the Peninsula. The PCA board members have consistently made it easy for us to set up the space for each concert, even if it means trying new seat-
articles.title: Chamber Music Society of SF grateful for PCA

articles.text: Editor: We can’t think of a good reason not to extend the lease of 801 Magnolia Avenue to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. We have attended many events there and can state from direct observation that it is a positive asset for the City. Since its creation nearly 10 years ago, it has provided an outstanding range of events in music – from classical to jazz – and art and theater. Its board of volunteers has done a terrific job of managing and caring for the facility. We feel confident that the City Council knows the history and value the Center, and that it will renew a long-term lease extension for this treasure. –Pat and Mike Ruffolo
articles.title: Local music lovers urge lease extension for PCA

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV) and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) will co-host a virtual panel discussion on January 28, titled “Reimagining Public Safety: Can Surveillance be a Fair and Effective Tool?” The panel will include individuals in the public safety sector and is a follow-up to a similar panel discussion the League held in 2017. Panelists will include Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers; Brian Hofer, Chair of the Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission; Jennifer Jones, Technology and Civil Liberties Fellow at ACLU Northern California; and Mathew Guariglia, a Policy Analyst for Electronic Frontier Foundation. The discussion, via Zoom, is intended to focus on how surveillance impacts racial justice and public safety in Piedmont and the broader community. New surveillance technologies monitor, track, and predict the actions of citizens, and are becoming increasingly popular in public safety. The discussion will explore whether new technologies can help create unbiased, inexpensive public safety and justice, or if they are inherently problematic. Brian Hofer, Chair of City of Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission, will join a discussion panel on Public Safety co-hosted by the League of Women Voters and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. Featured speakers will delve into whether or not such surveillance systems can be used fairly and effectively. The panel discussion will begin at 7 p.m. and is expected to end at 8:30 p.m. To register for the event visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1363151.
articles.title: LWV, PREC to co-host public safety panel Jan. 28

articles.text: Oakland Congresswoman Barbara Lee Piedmont and East Bay residents gathered virtually for the City of Piedmont’s 24th annual Martin Luther King, Jr. Day celebration, held on Monday, January 18. The intersection of power, love and justice was the theme of this year’s event. Due to the ongoing health pandemic, the celebration, which usually draws hundreds to Piedmont’s Veterans Hall, was held virtually this year in observance of shelter-in-place regulations. Jodi Biskup, a moderator for the event, said that over 300 people registered via Eventbrite, making it one of the most well-attended MLK celebrations in Piedmont’s history, albeit virtually. The city historically draws a large crowd during this celebration, due in large part to the talent and broad reach of speakers and performers. This year was no different; featured speakers included Congresswoman Barbara Lee, California State Senator Nancy Skinner, Stanford Professor and King Institute Director Clayborne Carson, Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, and filmmaker and World Trust Founder Shakti Butler. Congresswoman Lee recalled the events of the January 6 domestic attack on the capitol in her observance of Martin Luther King, Jr. Day. “Racism is alive and well in America. Just two weeks ago, the U.S. Capitol was stormed in a violent attempted coup by white supremacists,” she said. “A confederate flag was brought into the Capitol, a noose was hung outside and Black Capitol Hill police officers – while defending our democracy, the Capitol building, members of Congress and staff – had to fight in combat to defend themselves.” Lee added that the murders of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and so many more at the hands of police officers, combined with the disproportionate impact of COVID-19 on people of color, prove that inequities in our country continue. “Dr. King passed the baton to us and gave us his marching orders,” she said. These events also host unique, local talent, especially from East Bay youth. This year featured traditional Native America flutist Vince Rehouse and Destiny Arts Youth Performance Company. The event closed at 12:30 p.m. with a brief video of late U.S Representative John Lewis, a champion of the Civil Rights era. King Institute Director Clayborne Carson A wide range of non-profit organizations and other groups hosted well-attended workshops following this year’s virtual event, a first for any Piedmont Martin Luther King, Jr. celebration. The Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) presented a book club discussion on the New York Times podcast “Nice White Parents,” hosted by Serial reporter Chana Joffe-Walt. The podcast focuses on a middle and high school that was formerly known as the School for International Studies (SIS) in Brooklyn’s gentrified Cobble Hill neighborhood. Participants discussed whether there were found parallels between Piedmont Schools and SIS. The Piedmont for Oakland Public Schools (POPS) hosted a discussion on the broader picture, and whether segregation is still alive in school across the United States education system. The organization supplemented the event with excerpts from Coretta Scott King. Piedmont youth were also involved in the virtual celebration. Piedmont High and Middle School’s Black Student Union (BSU) shared a brief video in which students addressed current events, and PHS 2009 graduate Aksumawi Turner hosted a podcast entitled “Perspectives on Power and Love: An MLK Roundtable.” For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Daniel Gonzales began his first day as Piedmont’s Public Works Director on Monday, January 11, and the beginning of his second week on the job proved eventful. High winds throughout the Bay Area toppled trees in Piedmont and created some damage. “We did have a few downed trees, including one on Oakland Avenue,” Gonzales confirmed. Fortunately, he added, the city’s Public Works crews already “knew the routine” and got in touch with PG&E quickly. There was no major damage, but crews were still hard at work clearing debris and monitoring strong winds yesterday afternoon. “Any time you have wind at that velocity, there’s a chance that it will wreak havoc,” he said. That is just a small sample of the scope of integral services Public Works provides. While Gonzales will be tasked with leading the department through large, ongoing projects, there is always work to be done “behindthe-scenes.” Piedmont’s Public Works Department oversees all maintenance to city infrastructure services, and the director is expected to guide the department through these major and minor tasks. Gonzales said one of his first priorities in the new position was getting to know his field staff. “Day one was getting set up and just getting oriented,” he said. “But for me, getting to know staff right away is a priority. [They] want to put a face to the name, and [I wanted to] have some interaction with them so they know what to expect.” Much of the support work in the department is conducted virpanel of city staff and residents. The interview process was virtual. Final candidates were interviewed on November 6, 2020, and the City Council formally announced on December 21 that Gonzales would be the department’s new director. Gonzales recognized the high expectations placed on him because of the efficacy of his two predecessors, Nakahara and Larry Rosenberg. “[Nakahara] had been in Piedmont for a quite a long time and certainly left his mark, not just on the department, but on the entire community,” Gonzales said. “That’s a tough act to follow, and you hope that you will be able to carry on that legacy.” Gonzales added that he is looking forward to connecting with the Piedmont community at large and “continue [Nakahara’s] relationship” with Piedmonters. A registered civil engineer, Gonzales earned a Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering from San Jose State University. From 2017 to 2020, he served as the Deputy Director of Public Works in the town of Hillsborough in San Mateo County, a city comparable to Piedmont in geography and demographics. “Hillsborough is a community of about 11,000 and is almost entirely residential. It’s a community in the hills with a number of canyons and beautiful trees. In terms of demographics, it’s very similar,” he said. “There’s also an expectation of a high level of service, that I prided myself on providing to the residents there. I expect to provide that level of service to Piedmont.” Gonzales also worked as a Senior Engineer with CSG Consultants in Foster City, and has Daniel Gonzales tually, just as most city departments have been conducting business virtually due to shelterin-place regulations. Department head meetings are all remote at this point, which means new hires are not able to meet city staff the way they normally would. Gonzales said that because of this impediment, he has made a point to go to the city’s Corporation Yard and meet with the DPW crew in person. “One of the fears I had on Day One – and may continue to have – is that there could be a disconnect between me and field staff” due to the unique circumstances surrounding COVID, he said. “Of course, physical distance is a barrier to any connection, so I made it a point to go to the Corporation Yard to meet them, to see what they are working on, what their needs are. articles.text: Nate Redinbo The City of Piedmont is currently considering the adoption of Reach Codes to help the City meet Climate Action goals set by the City Council. Natural gas emissions from residential homes are one of the leading causes of greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont, and the proposed reach codes will reduce natural gas emissions. On July 20, 2020, the Council considered a package of proposed local amendments to the California Electrical Code, Residential Code, and Building Energy Efficiency Standards. The amendments – collectively referred to as “Reach Codes” – would alter the requirements for home construction and renovation in Piedmont to facilitate building insulation, electrification, and solar panel installation. Council approved the first reading of the proposed codes and directed staff to conduct additional research and public engagement leading up to a second reading. Part of those engagement efforts included a random sample representative survey of Piedmont registered voters on the proposed codes. In November and December 2020, the research firm FM3 conducted an additional city-wide voter survey to supplement the public opinion survey that was completed in June 2020. The latest survey asked 384 Pied- • mont residents their opinions on the proposed reach codes and how the codes would affect them. On January 19, City Staff and FM3 researchers will present the results and analysis of this survey to the City Council. Here are some of the key takeaways from the survey: • Most residents are concerned about climate change, with nine in ten saying that climate change will harm future generations. Seven in ten say that climate change is a serious problem and immediate action is necessary. • Of those familiar with the City’s Climate Action Plan, half say that meeting the plan’s objectives is very or extremely important. • Two thirds (66%) of Piedmont voters say they support revising building codes to reduce natural gas in city buildings. This percentage has remained consistent between the two surveys that have been conducted (66% supported this proposal in June). • Three in four say the most convincing reason to support adopting the Reach Codes is the impact of greenhouse gas emissions reductions generated by homes. When presented messages opposing the Reach Codes: 87% are concerned about being vulnerable during power outages; 81% are concerned that the proposed reach codes are unfair to those who have already taken energy efficiency actions; and 79% of residents are concerned about costs related to renovations. Staff has worked to address these concerns in resources on the City’s website, as well as in the staff reports to City Council. To learn more about exceptions to the solar panel requirements, what the proposed reach codes include, and expected costs of the upgrades, please visit the reach codes webpage at https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city _news_ _ _notif ications/ reach_codes. Unless otherwise directed by City Council, City staff intends to bring forward a second reading of the Reach Codes at the February 1st City Council meeting. Alyssa Dykman is a Sustainability Program Manager for the City, and Nate Redinbo is Piedmont’s Civic Spark Fellow.
