articles.text: I recently had the opportunity to visit for the second time the Jura region of France. It is located in Eastern France, south of Alsace and north of Burgundy. The Jura is one of the least known wine regions in France and the smallest, producing only one percent of the country’s wine. It however has some of the most interesting and distinctive wines I have ever tasted. If you are ready for something a little different, this is the place to look. For red wine lovers there are two grapes produced that are grown almost nowhere else in the world. Ploussard and Trousseau grapes produce light, ethereal, perfumed wines of considerable charm. The color is so light it could almost be a rose’, and they are usually soft and light on the palate and finish. The nose has notes of strawberries and cherries and both have become darlings of today’s sommeliers. While the red wines of the Jura are interesting and different, it is their white wines that I find truly stunning. This is the only wine region I know where in the tasting room they first serve the red wines, followed by the whites. The two major grapes are Chardonnay and Savagnin. (Note that this is not Sauvignon Blanc.) They are made in two different styles – modern and traditional. In the modern style, they are made like most white wines from around the world: protected from oxygen and made to be fresh and fruity. The other traditional style is unique to the area. The barrels are not topped up but are only two-thirds full. The air space allows yeast to form on the surface of the wine, which eventually forms a film which begins to protect the wine. Domaine Dugois Sous Voile. The wine is left in barrels untouched for 4 to 6 years – that’s right, 4 to 6 years of patient waiting. This style is called “Sous voile” or “under the veil” and the only other wine where it is widely used is Sherry. If the wine is taken out at 4 years it can be called Tradition or sometimes just the name of the grape. If it is aged 6 years the wine is called Vin Jaune or Yellow wine and is bottled in little squat 62 ml bottles called clavelin. Only the Savagnin grape can be used to make Vin Jaune. For me, it is one of the greatest white grapes in the world. Tasting a sous voile Savagnin or a Vin Jaune is an otherworldly experience. There is nothing else like it in the wine world. When I have served them to friends I get this puzzled stare…what is this stuff? We are not used to wine with no fruit where the normal fruit flavors have been replaced by minerals and earth, baked bread and walnuts with a touch of bitterness. They are amazingly complex with tons of aromas and flavors and a long lingering finish. Winemaker Daniel Dugois So here is the good news: Because it takes 4 to 6 years to make these wines they are expensive. Not crazy Burgundy expensive, but a good Vin Jaune can set you back $80. I was happy to find the Daniel Dugois domaine whose wines are outstanding but much less expenDaniel Dugois of Domaine Dugois in Les Arsures, France.

Domaine Dugois Sous Voile. The wine is left in barrels untouched for 4 to 6 years – that’s right, 4 to 6 years of patient waiting. When I have served them to friends I get this puzzled stare…what is this stuff? We are not used to wine with no fruit where the normal fruit flavors have been replaced by minerals and earth, baked bread and walnuts with a touch of bitterness. They are amazingly complex with tons of aromas and flavors and a long lingering finish. Winemaker Daniel Dugois So here is the good news: Because it takes 4 to 6 years to make these wines they are expensive. Not crazy Burgundy expensive, but a good Vin Jaune can set you back $80. I was happy to find the Daniel Dugois domaine whose wines are outstanding but much less expenDaniel Dugois of Domaine Dugois in Les Arsures, France. sive. Part of that is that they are directly imported by K&L Wines in San Francisco, thus eliminating the middleman and his cut. Daniel Dugois bought an old winery in the tiny village of Les Arsures near Arbois in 1973. At age 23 he started producing his own wines and buying additional land. Today Daniel’s son, Phillipe, has taken over much of the work and has kept the quality of these wines extremely high. It was thrilling to visit the small stone building that held the tiny tasting room. Daniel poured for us every wine he makes. The reds were good, but what I remember are the whites. He poured a Chardonnay from 1996 that was stunningly still alive and vibrant. (Because of their great acidity, the Jura whites can age for an amazingly long amount of time. On my last trip to Domaine Jean Boudry, I was served a 1958 Chardonnay that was astounding.) The following wines are my favorites and I urge you to search them out and give them a try. Available at K&L Wines in SF or on the internet. • 2014 Dugois Savagnin (Sous Voile), $25 Light yellow tinge in the glass with a nose of grapefruit and minerals and walnuts. In the mouth it is amazingly complex with layers of flavors and great structure and acidity. It finishes bone dry, almost bitter, but clean and pleasant. • 2011 Dugois Vin Jaune, $45 Beautiful golden color in the glass with time (decanting recommended) the nose opens up to fresh baked bread, roasted chestnuts and walnuts. It is richer and fuller than the wine above and the 6 years in barrel have rounded off a bit of the acidity. Amazingly complex and profound. Drink by the fire on a cold night with some walnuts or toasted almonds. • 2013 Dugois Vin de Paille (375ml), $30 At the end of the tasting Daniel poured this dark golden nectar that was absolutely heavenly. Grapes, both red and white are left to dry on straw mats (paille) until they become raisins as the water evaporates and sugars intensify. Yet luckily there is still enough acid to keep the unctuous nectar from being cloying. Candied orange, honey, and baked apple flavors make their appearance and linger long on the palate. articles.text: Stagebridge returns for a new 8-week digital session with classes starting the week of January 25. This shortened schedule of classes is an accessible way to stay active while fighting social distancing in the new year. As a premiere arts education company for older adults, Stagebridge offers five introductory classes to escape into the magic of performance. “It may sound cliché, but we have really crafted our Winter 2021 session with a ‘New Year, New You’ attitude,” explained program director Lily Nguyen. “Even digitally, students have been able to start their journeys as performance artists at any age.” In renowned storyteller MaryGay Ducey’s Dip your Toe, a class available in Storytelling, anyone feeling the confidence to find their own voice will emerge from this class with a beautiful story mined from their lives— ready to share with the world. Ely Sonny Orquiza’s Beginning Acting and Bruce Bierman’s Making Theatre Move invite Stagebridge instructors April Axé Charmaine (left), Ely Sonny Orquiza, and Bruce Bierman return to offer fun classes for students new to performing arts and those looking to reignite some magic. skeptics to digital art. Participants will explore the bounds of online performance in fun and playful environments with longtime Stagebridge instructors. April Axé Charmaine’s Mind, Body & SOL and Bruce Bierman’s Joy of Dance provides radically inclusive spaces for movers and shakers. While Bierman celebrates improvisation inside traditional and world dance, Charmaine’s class welcomes students interested in using dance as a healing practice. “Before the first class had ended, I discovered that this class would really complement my singing, and all other dance forms,” said Stagebridge student Maxine Williams about an earlier movement class by Charmaine. “I have discovered so many ways to move. I like the idea of classes connecting that way, by accident or on purpose.” Students have until January 29 to sign up for Winter 2021 classes. Stagebridge continues to open the door for older adults with dreams of performing with socially-distanced programs. To learn more about the Performing Arts Institute and the range of classes being offered, visit https:// www.stagebridge.org/pai.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I am a therapist and am trying to switch to Zoom, Skype or Facetime to meet with my patients. I keep getting freezes and also one of my patients asked me if there are privacy protocols in place for Zoom. Is Zoom, SKYPE and Facetime HIPPA compliant? -Jessica G., Oakland Dear Jessica: Video conferencing, once a tool for only the very tech savvy is becoming the default for doctors, therapists, schools, private teachers, and any professionals who depend on face-to-face experiences with their clients and students. articles.text: Residents of The Lake Merritt out for a walk. After the first of the year many of us look at our physical selves and realize that the previous holiday season has resulted in a few extra pounds. This observation often jumpstarts the idea that we need to start exercising. In addition to the holiday gain, living in the COVID-19 world means many of us are staying at home and sitting down more than we usually do. It’s hard for a lot of us to do the sort of exercise we normally enjoy. It’s even harder for people who don’t usually do a lot of physical exercise. It is widely agreed that exercise and physical activity are important as we age. Staying active can help us remain independent by preventing loss of physical mobility. Besides keeping your body healthy, research has shown that physical activity also helps the brain and may slow age-related cognitive decline. We’ve heard it all before, but it bears repeating. The World Health Organization, and many others tell us that “regular physical activity benefits both the body and mind. It can reduce high blood pressure, help manage weight and reduce the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and various cancers - all conditions that can increase susceptibility to COVID-19.” Regular, moderate-intensity exercise has immune-boosting benefits that may help your body fight off infections and many viruses. How can we start? Walking is a great way for older adults to exercise. Frequent walking can build endurance helping each of us walk farther, faster, or even uphill with greater ease. The pandemic has also made it very difficult to exercise in other ways we have become accustomed to. With gyms closed, many exercise classes are unavailable. Yet, virtual fitness classes have sprung up online. These allow you to interact with other people in a fun way, which may be just the motivation we need to keep up with our fitness regime. Program Director Ryan Wilcox has set up The Lake Merritt’s exercise program online through Zoom. This allows residents to exercise in their own apartment, or join the group where they can exercise in a way that is socially distanced while wearing masks. Regular physical activity is essential for everyone under normal circumstances. It is especially important during the COVID-19 Pandemic. Although many things feel beyond our control right now, we do have the ability to be creative and to build physical activity and exercise into each of our days. We may even look back on this difficult time as the turning point when we learned new ways to build our physical health and resilience. articles.text: Dale Rogers Marshall, a resident of Piedmont starting in 1970, died from complications of COVID on January 14, 2021. A political scientist and academic administrator dedicated to equal opportunity for all, Dr. Marshall was 83. As president of Wheaton College in Norton, Massachusetts, from 1992-2004, Dr. Marshall oversaw the Campaign for Wheaton, a $90 million fund supporting student scholarships and academic inclusiveness. At Wheaton, Dr. Marshall pushed to find and hire academics from under-represented groups, as she had at Wellesley College where she was Dean of the College from 1986-1992 and Acting President from 1987-1988, and at UC Davis before that as Associate Dean in the College of Letters and Science. Her own research underlined the importance of equal representation – of the poor, of people or color, of women – in positions of power. In Protest Is Not Enough: The Struggle of Blacks and Hispanics for Equality in Urban Politics (UC Press, 1984), the winner of the 1985 Ralph J. Bunche Award for best book on ethnic relations and the 1985 Gladys Kammerer Award for best book on US national policy, which she co-authored with Rufus P. Browning and David H. Tabb, and her other works, Dr. Marshall documented the importance of diversity in government to securing progressive change. Dr. Marshall attributed her interest in equity to her years as a teenager in segregated Washington, D.C. Born on March 22, 1937, in Ithaca, New York, where her parents were students at Cornell Law School, her family moved often while her father, William P. Rogers, served in the Navy. The family settled in Bethesda, Maryland, in 1950, when Mr. Rogers took a position as counsel to the United States Congress. Mr. Rogers would go on to serve as Deputy Attorney General and Attorney General under President Dwight Eisenhower, and Secretary of State under President Richard Nixon. Following the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board of Education decision, Dr. Marshall, a high school student at the then all-white Sidwell Friends School in Washington, D.C., demanded that the school accept students of color. As she recalled in her privately published memoir, the head Dr. Dale Rogers Marshall, a longtime resident of Piedmont, died on January 14 from complications of COVID-19. She was 83. of school refused, explaining that if Sidwell Friends did that, families from southern states would withdraw. She left for Cornell University shortly after, but, she said, for years “when I saw a W on a restroom, indicating women, I mentally read it as ‘whites.’” Through work on freshman orientation at Cornell, Dr. Marshall met her future husband, engineer Donald J. Marshall. In 1959, shortly after Dr. Marshall’s graduation with a degree in Government and a Woodrow Wilson Fellowship to pursue graduate study, they married, and drove their two-door Ford station wagon from Washington, D. C., to San Francisco, California. There and, later, in Los Angeles, her husband worked for Standard Oil of California and she held multiple teaching positions. Dr. Marshall received her Ph.D. in political science from UCLA in 1969 for her work on the implementation of affirmative action policies in Los Angeles. As she documented in her dissertation, published as The Politics of Participation in Poverty (UC Press, 1971), equitable representation in government was the only way to fight co-optation by wealthier forces and to secure “equal access to political power and the resulting benefits of meaningful participation in the changing political system.” While a professor at UC Davis, she served on multiple committees addressing the unequal status of women in higher education, winning accolades for her contributions to equity as well as her teaching. She would later observe that her climb up the academic ladder – which included the presidency of the Western Political Science Association and vice presidency of the American Political Science Association – was made possible by the women who went before her. Dr Marshall served on numerous public and private boards and, like her mother Adele Langston Rogers before her, was a member of the Cornell University Board of Trustees. After her retirement from academia, she was an irrepressible volunteer, working as, among other roles, a mentor for the East Bay College Fund, a writing coach with WriterCoach Connection, a volunteer with Girls, Inc., and a docent and board member at the Berkeley Repertory Theatre. She is survived by her husband, Donald Marshall, three children – Jessica, Cynthia, and Clayton Marshall, and six grandchildren – William and Helena Belhumeur, and Maia, Dominik, Nina, and Robert Marshall. Memorial contributions may be made to Wheaton College, Massachusetts, to support either the Dale Rogers Marshall Fund for Global Education or the Dale Rogers Marshall Wheaton Fund Scholarship, both of which support programs Dr. Marshall created. articles.text: including four high schools with zero transmissions. A much larger amount of data was just released from North Carolina where 90,000 students and 10,000 teachers went back to school when COVID case rates were up to four times higher than our “purple tier” here in California. Nevertheless, there were only 32 school-based transmissions between September and November. These are tiny, incredibly reassuring numbers. The North Carolina schools are not well-resourced private schools, but public schools, where half of the students are students of color. The success is not based on intensive resource investments, but rather on wearing masks and social distancing. It’s also important to note that the limited outbreaks in these schools were not among middle or high school students, but pre-k and special needs children. LC: So, is it safe to open now, even while we are in the purple tier? JN: Yes. The state has already allowed open schools to stay open during our stay-at-home orders. And under the newest guidelines, all K through 6 schools can open when the daily case rate is below 25 per 100,000. This means that all elementary schools have permission to open very soon, likely by February 1. But the tragedy with these new guidelines is that 7 through 12 graders are completely left out, awaiting return to the red tier before their schools can open. LC: Let’s talk about middle and high school students. We mostly only hear about plans to bring back elementary school kids. I heard you say on a panel this week that they should go back to in-person learning, too. JN: Absolutely. Our adolescents are developmentally driven to be increasing those important social and emotional connections outside of the family. They are particularly hard-hit by these closures. No one has ever characterized adolescence as an easy time in life, and California’s policy of school closures has made it considerably harder. Even though transmission rates are higher among adolescents than younger children, data shows that high schools can operate safely, and therefore, they should be allowed to do so. LC: To open schools now, and safely, what precautions need to be in place? JN: Masks and social distancing, which together, block about 90 percent of transmissions – on par with vaccines. In addition, schools need to be symptom screening, and classroom doors need to be kept open to increase airflow. LC: Many schools are making plans to reopen, but it’s a hybrid model versus an all-day in-person. Is a hybrid model safer? JN: No, not necessarily. The bulk of evidence no longer supports the theory that fewer school hours means less COVID transmission. Students are more closely supervised at school than during remote learning. So reduced school often translates to more time in higher risk environments. LC: Do we need to wait until all teachers are vaccinated, and what about until students are vaccinated? JN: No, studies have already shown that schools can be operated safely, because masks and distancing block transmission. Data from Marin, North Carolina, and elsewhere demonstrate that we can keep both teachers and students safe, even before vaccines. LC: Is it safe though to open schools, even with this new strain? We keep hearing that it is more contagious. JN: Yes, it is safe, even when the new variant becomes dominant here, which could be as soon as March. The likelihood of getting COVID when you’re exposed is 11 percent. New contact tracing data from the UK shows that transmissability has increased to 14.7 percent with the new variant. Although that 11 to 14.7 percent change represents a large relative increase, it’s an absolute increase of only 3.7 percent, which does not fundamentally change whether schools can operate safely. LC: You said on a panel discussion that if you knew now what you knew in March, you would have never recommended closing schools as a safety precaution. Why is that? JN: We closed schools in March because we thought that children would be the primary drivers of COVID, like they are for the flu. Now we know that we were wrong. Kids are less likely to get COVID and transmit COVID than adults. Of the more than 30,000 COVID deaths in California, there have been only six deaths among people under age 15. If we had these numbers back in March, we never would have closed our schools. LC: If we know that schools can open now and open safely, and we know what to do to keep kids and teachers safe, why aren’t schools reopening? JN: The reason the Bay Area is living through the longest school closures on the planet is mired in politics. The California Teacher’s Association is one of the most powerful unions in the country, and has provided key support to Gavin Newsom. If the CTA does not want to open schools, Gavin Newsom is not going to mandate reopening. We need to get the safety data to union leaders so that we can move forward in a climate of trust and meet as many of their needs as quickly as possible, so that all of our kids, regardless of income, can be back in school by February. Our children have a right to in-person education, and we know how to do this. It’s time to get moving.

articles.text: Editor: I would like to add my voice to those speaking up about the wonderful things that have happened at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, and the bright future we hope to partner in building at the center. We presented a recital featuring Renée Rapier and Robert Mollicone to a full audience from both sides of the tunnel and San Francisco. Perhaps the most challenging and frustrating aspect of the plan is the requirement for all students and staff to receive testing once a week or twice a month depending on county case numbers. “I am most nervous around student testing. It’s not impossible, but it is going to take some effort,” Booker said. He stated that he was confident an increase in teacher testing would not be a problem (currently once a month). “It feels like [another] bait and switch. We play by the rules and the rules shift all the time, which is incredibly frustrating,” said board member Amal Smith. “While the plan has good intentions, the time and requirements of the plan are untenable for many districts. It sets superintendents and school boards up for failure. To give us two weeks to do all this, and bargain with teachers, and get students tests... Maybe we can do it in Piedmont with 2,500 students. But how are big districts with 50,000-300,000 students going to be ready in that time? It is not right,” Booker lamented. “When things seem hopeless we have to move forward with things that we can try to influence,” encouraged Board President Cory Smegal. “I know that it is going to be challenging to figure out, but maybe we can. I ask personally that we do try student testing to the extent we can. Anyone that has ideas on how we can facilitate testing can reach out to me [at csmegal@piedmont.k12.ca.us],” she said. Since the board meeting, California has announced resources for schools on their website site schools.covid19.ca.gov and ways to sign up. The site does seem to have many answers that were raised during the Piedmont School Board meeting. A school guidance checklist is also now available. Booker and the entire board are favoring reopening schools. Whether they can sort through state and county obstacles remains to be seen. Piedmont is dependant upon Alameda County’s COVID numbers to drop from the high values in the last month to drop below 500 per day. On January 14, 1049 cases of COVID were recorded. As a comparison, Piedmont had 65 new cases from December 17-January 17 or 2.1 cases per day. With a population of 11,317, Piedmont’s unadjusted case rate would (unofficially) be around 18.5 new cases per day, per 100,000, well below Newsom’s threshold of 25 per day. The Board will receive updates on Tuesday when Karen Monroe, Alameda County Office of Education Superintendent, hosts a meeting for school board members.

I am a concert pianist, educator, founder and artistic director of the San Francisco International Piano Festival, and active member of arts organization boards throughout the Bay Area. Having performed throughout the country and internationally in addition to dozens of venues throughout the Bay Area, I am particularly grateful for the experiences I have had at the PCA since I first became acquainted with it in 2016. I was invited to attend the inaugural season of Piedmont Chamber Music Festival led by the Formosa String Quartet. The level of musicianship was truly first rate, international, and satisfying. It became clear to me that this venue was at the level of the music, and I tucked that experience away in my memory. One year later I launched the San Francisco International Piano Festival with support from Piedmont Community members Craig and Letitia Casebeer. The structure of our festival features a different program each night in a different venue performed by musicians from all around the world. After establishing ourselves as the only international piano festival in the Bay Area, we chose PCA as the venue for our opening night program in 2018 and 2019. [This year’s opening was online due to Covid-19.] These evenings were great successes on every level, and the setting of the PCA was ideal. Soldout crowds, open air atmosphere, visual art, and world class piano playing in a warm and approachable environment. I have performed at the PCA myself on a number of occasions and have always found it to be a gratifying experience. As a guest artists with Gold Coast Chamber Players, I played most recently an all-Mozart concert that featured the Alexander String Quartet. The house Steinway is a warm and appropriately sized piano for the space, making it a perfect setting for chamber music both vocal and instrumental, solo piano, and masterclasses. The Center’s programming both visually, musically, and theatrically has contributed enormously to the community, and I look forward to seeing what they will do in their next decade of tenure. articles.text: 2020 presidential election was rigged. This is a racist lie that is a direct attack on the communities of color of Philadelphia, Atlanta, Detroit Milwaukee, Atlanta and elsewhere that showed up, sometimes at great risk to themselves, to exercise their right to vote. It is a lie that says, “If we white citizens don’t get our way, the system is, by definition, flawed.” We live in a time in which a presidential “patriotic education” commission releases a report, on MLK Day itself, attacking truth telling in regard to American history. Instead of honesty about the ways in which structural racism and unchecked whiteness have shaped, and continue to shape, our nation, the report calls for the parroting of the lie of American exceptionalism. This is a lie supported by prominent and powerful Christians. It is a lie that runs counter to our call to be the conscience of the state. As the celebration of Martin Luther King Jr. Remembrance Day 2021 fades into history, as Inauguration Day 2021 dawns, we would all do well to recommit ourselves to a tradition of truth-telling, a tradition that will ensure that not only the church, but all the citizens and residents of these United States, serve together as the conscience of the state. It is the truth that will keep us free. Rev. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue in Oakland.
articles.title: Religion Corner

articles.text: worked with both public and private sector clients. His experience includes project and construction management, as well as the preparation of long-term plans for capital improvements. A few of the major projects that will appear under Gonzales’ scope are the Linda Beach Playfield project, City Hall improvements, and public safety buildings improvements. “It’s clear to me that I’ll be working with the Police Department and Fire Department to assist them [in these improvements,]” he said. Gonzales guided Hillsborough’s Public Works Department through a similar project with their Police Department structures. “The [Police Department] building in Hillsborough is over 100 years old as well, so I have some experience with this. I know it’s a process – writing an RFP [Request for Proposal], bringing someone in to evaluate it, informing the public, and ultimately letting the public be the drivers of what the best solution is for the community,” he said. Another similarity between the two cities’ Public Works departments is a commitment to doing the “difficult work that puts them in a place where they do not have the same types of ongoing maintenance issues,” explained Gonzales, pointing to Piedmont’s commitment to replace and replenish its aging sewer lines as an example. “It really is the responsible, and the intelligent way to go,” he said. “There’s a responsibility to maintain your system and keep it in good shape. I think great communities don’t back down from doing that, even if it’s challenging,” Gonzales added.
articles.title: Daniel Gonzales

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host another virtual forum with internationally renowned epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford today, Wednesday, January 13 at 4 p.m. Rutherford last spoke at a LWV forum in May and answered questions on the efficacy of mask-wearing and vaccine availability. Next week’s forum aims to explore the epidemiologist’s predictions for the course of the COVID-19 virus in 2021 and answer questions about availability and distribution of the vaccine. Rutherford, a Piedmont resident, has been instrumental in keeping the Bay Area abreast on COVID-19 related concerns and is quoted as an expert source in nationwide media outlets. The virtual forum is entitled “COVID-19 Update: Are We Any Closer to the End?” and will focus on when life can return to “normal” after nearly a year of lockdowns. There will be a question-and-answer portion of the forum after a presentation. Viewers can submit their own questions directly in the forum. Rutherford leads the Global Strategic Information group within University of California (UCSF), San Francisco’s InstiUCSF epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford. tute for Global Health Sciences. He is the Salvatore Pablo Lucia Professor of Epidemiology, Preventive Medicine, Pediatrics and History; Head of the Division of Infectious Disease and Global Epidemiology in the Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics in the School of Medicine at UCSF and Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration in the School of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley. Registration is not required for the event. You can join the Zoom forum at 4 p.m. on January 13 online by clicking: https://us02web.zoom. us/j/87327219707?pwd=TlVxQVN5cGFIczFqcU.
articles.title: Dr. George Rutherford returns for COVID discussion today

articles.text: With all the hype surrounding elections, the Murphy family created a simple message of hope nearly two months prior to the November 3 Presidential election. Their message on a blue handmade sign on their front lawn read: “Make America Respectable Again.” Created by dad, Zach Murphy, and younger daughter Ella, 14, they installed the sign in front of their house on Oakland Avenue. Ella explained that the message simply calls for political decency. “We’re not really there right now,” she said this week. The message was an obvious twist on President Trump’s 2016 campaign slogan to Make America Great Again, and was painted in a bright blue rather than Trump’s red. Explaining the sign’s history, Zach said that both daughters, Ella and older sister Claire, walked around Piedmont in September, trying to count lawn signs for presidential candidates to see how Piedmonters would be voting in November. While there were many signs showing support for School Board and City Council candidates, there were far fewer signs showing support for either presidential candidate. “They were surprised to see very few national [campaign] signs. We started talking about what message we could put out there that would hopefully encourage people to aim for something attainable,” Zach said with a smile. Since the sign went up, both Ella and Zach have confirmed a neighborhood interest in the message and have noticed people taking photos of it and people walking by taking “selfies” with the sign. Given the negative advertising that accompanies most elections, their message was seen as one of optimism. It was the only one of its type in the city.
articles.title: Make America Respectable Again sign resonates with residents

articles.text: It’s been nearly one year since Piedmont residents became aware of the coronavirus, but with little knowledge of what might happen by the middle of March. This year, 2021, began with a sense of hope, A vaccine for the novel coronavirus, which plagued the majority of 2020, has been created and Is now being distributed. This time last year, the Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta confirmed California’s first reported COVID-19 case in Orange County. What transpired over the course of the next twelve months were feelings of isolation, confusion, and heartache in the Piedmont and global community. Here’s a brief synopsis of the previous year, and a look at how COVID-19 has changed our communities: January 26, 2020 The Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta confirm California’s first reported COVID-19 case in Orange County. The patient had recently traveled to Wuhan, China, where the virus originated. It was the third coronavirus case in the United States. January 31, 2020 Santa Clara country reports its first coronavirus case – the first in the Bay Area. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Alex Azar declares a national public health emergency due to the virus. articles.text: Last week, the Post published an article on the Mental Health Screener, a survey sent to all Piedmont students on September 30. Results were not released until mid-December to the public. This week, parents weighed in on the results, the screener itself and what they have noticed about the mental health of Piedmont students. They expressed an urgent need for School Superintendent Randy Booker and Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak to clarify the survey results in a comprehensible way and to address the current stress level of students at most grade levels. Alisa Crovetti, the Clinical Supervisor Psychologist at the school district’s Wellness Center and a Piedmont mom, was a consultant in the early stages before the mental health survey was sent out. She later became involved again when the data was made available. Crovetti wants to use a criterion-referenced screener rather than a norm-referenced screener on surveys in the future. She made that recommendation to the team of 18 that designed the screener once the initial results came back in October. “No screener can be diagnostic, but a criterion referenced screener may feel a lot more intuitive for the community. It would allow us to identify kids who fall into ‘extreme’ or ‘severe’ categories of symptomology. It’s very challenging to find a criterion-referenced tool that is appropriate for all age levels,” she added. Piedmont parent Laura Maestrelli took action on the mental health topic in October by conducting an informal anonymous survey of Piedmont students. The comments received from students after only two months of distance learning were harrowing, and she read the student comments aloud at a School Board meeting on October 26. They can be heard at the 50:00-minute mark at: www.piedmont.granicus.com/ MediaPlayer.php?view_id=3&- clip_id=2250. “Because of distance learning my depression has severely worsened and I have lost all motivation to do literally anything,” said one high school student. “I am constantly anxious and stopped talking to a lot of people because of it. I barely leave my house, so I get very little exercise and I don’t have the motivation to work out. I also overeat because I’m bored
articles.title: Parents weigh in on district’s inaction, slow response to students’ mental health

Results were not released until mid-December to the public. This week, parents weighed in on the results, the screener itself and what they have noticed about the mental health of Piedmont students. They expressed an urgent need for School Superintendent Randy Booker and Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak to clarify the survey results in a comprehensible way and to address the current stress level of students at most grade levels. Alisa Crovetti, the Clinical Supervisor Psychologist at the school district’s Wellness Center and a Piedmont mom, was a consultant in the early stages before the mental health survey was sent out. She later became involved again when the data was made available. Crovetti wants to use a criterion-referenced screener rather than a norm-referenced screener on surveys in the future. She made that recommendation to the team of 18 that designed the screener once the initial results came back in October. “No screener can be diagnostic, but a criterion referenced screener may feel a lot more intuitive for the community. It would allow us to identify kids who fall into ‘extreme’ or ‘severe’ categories of symptomology. It’s very challenging to find a criterion-referenced tool that is appropriate for all age levels,” she added. Piedmont parent Laura Maestrelli took action on the mental health topic in October by conducting an informal anonymous survey of Piedmont students. The comments received from students after only two months of distance learning were harrowing, and she read the student comments aloud at a School Board meeting on October 26. They can be heard at the 50:00-minute mark at: www.piedmont.granicus.com/ MediaPlayer.php?view_id=3&- clip_id=2250. “Because of distance learning my depression has severely worsened and I have lost all motivation to do literally anything,” said one high school student. “I am constantly anxious and stopped talking to a lot of people because of it. articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: I have been a Piedmont resident for 22 years. My wife and I have raised our 2 children here. I also am a professional musician beginning my 30th season with the San Francisco Symphony. Having an arts center here in Piedmont has been vital to our quality of life and to the cultural enrichment of our city and its citizens. With such a huge emphasis being put these days on technology and its accompanying short attention spans, it is a welcome respite to have a place in our city where one can come and experience music unfolding over a longer period of time than 3 1/2 minutes, take the time to sit and ponder a piece of visual art, or reflect on a theatre performance which confronts important issues of the human condition and of society. This exercise of looking inward and reflecting is one we don’t wish to be lost with our children’s generation. It is the meaning of truly being human, and our arts center is a vital provider of this most important commodity to our city. articles.text: One of the biggest understatements in the Bible might well be the statement of Jesus in the Gospel of John when He said: “In the world you will have tribulation.” It’s pretty hard to argue the truth of that statement. A quick look at local, national, and world events, not to mention taking stock of our own personal challenges, reminds us that in the world we have tribulation – and plenty of it. But Jesus put His statement about tribulation in the world into the context of the promises of His grace. He prefaced His statement by saying: “I have said these things to you, that in Me you may have peace.” Jesus was saying: “I know that tribulation is rampant. And I know it causes anxiety, discouragement, frustration, and stress of all kinds. But I am giving you My promises so that You may have My peace!” Jesus said: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart!” Literally that means to be confidant, to be courageous, and to be strong. It doesn’t imply the absence of fear, but it limits the power of fear by pointing to a rock-solid reason for confidence, for hope, and for victory. Jesus continued, “I have overcome the world.” Jesus overcame the world by conquering sin and guilt through His own death and by rising again in glorious victory over all the forces of evil in this life and in the life to come. The victory Christ won is our victory by God’s grace. There is a story about a little boy playing in his sandbox. He was busy building roads and digging trenches. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council. Editor: I have lived in Piedmont for over 30 years and am so appreciative of our beautiful parks, tennis courts, children’s playgrounds as well as our exceptional services. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is such a gift to our city and is part of the reason that our city is such a special place to live. As a lover of the arts, I was thrilled when the center opened nearly 10 years ago. From art shows, to concerts, to the numerous special events, the Center truly enhances our sense of community and importantly supports our local artists. Please join with supporters of the Center to ensure that the lease is approved and the Center can continue as an important community resource.

articles.text: Cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont increased by almost 25 percent over the past two weeks, mirroring a terrible surge across Alameda County linked to travel during the holiday season. articles.text: A screen shot of participants in the announcement by Piedmont Education Foundation that its Giving Campaign had raised over $3 million in the recent fundraiser. Amelie Kappes, Colleen Allan, and Teebie Saunders, Co-Chairs of this year’s Piedmont Education Foundation Giving Campaign, announced that the Giving Campaign’s $3,000,000 fundraising goal has been exceeded. The Giving Campaign is the largest annual fundraiser supporting the students and schools of Piedmont. This success came amidst a year of multiple challenges. “We set this lofty goal during a year of distance learning with no reopening timeline amid a coronavirus surge in the country, and when our district was facing issues of unprecedented scale and complexity,” said Allan. “This is a true testament to the value that our community places on the importance of a strong public school district and a topnotch education for Piedmont students.” The campaign, launched on September 21, went for 15 weeks. Kappes credits the work of the community for the strength of this year’s campaign. “It reflects untold hours of volunteer support and a team of thoughtful, strategic, dedicated and engaged staff at the PEF office. PUSD will benefit across all campuses as a result of this generosity, involvement and hard work.” More than 75 volunteers and staff members engaged in this effort, which included multiple forms of outreach as part of the overall strategy of personally reaching out to as many prospective donors as possible. This year’s total of $3,014,210 is an amount surpassed only once in the Campaign’s long history. The number of participants, however, was down. The participation rate among parents, which has been at about 68% for the past few years, dropped to 57% this year. Saunders suggested there were multiple reasons, “We are truly grateful to the 1,140 families that contributed to this year’s Giving Campaign. I am overwhelmed especially by the generosity of those families that chose to give more this year to help make up for those who were unable to participate,” she said. Piedmont Education Foundation will continue to accept additional gifts in support of Piedmont’s schools at PiedmontEdFoundation.org. Funds raised through the Giving Campaign and other PEF fundraisers will be distributed to Piedmont School District for use in next school year’s budget, 2021-22. Piedmont mom Lisa Carnazzo is concerned about why it took months to analyze and provide results from a survey of only multiple choice questions. Like Edel, she wants to know, ‘What’s next?’ “It doesn’t seem helpful to conduct a survey in September and reveal the results three months later, especially when the results require swift action. Our kids are suffering; that is clear from the mental health survey. So now what? What action will be taken to help our children? More screeners will be done in January or February but that isn’t helpful unless we are using the information to address the problems our kids are facing immediately.” California continues to be the global hot spot of the pandemic and little has changed since the start of the new year. Meanwhile, Piedmont secondary students undergo their final exams this week, an acutely stressful ordeal in itself, due to a little-publicized shift from the student and parent-preferred schedule of the past few years when finals were given prior to the Christmas break. A new hope arises in the form of a vaccine for COVID-19, but how long will it take for it to be distributed? Will teachers be willing to get vaccinated and return to the classroom?
articles.title: Giving Campaign reaches goal of $3 Million

Overall, my mental and physical health has gone super far downhill.” Another student shared an anonymous comment in October. “Being a high school senior is already very stressful, but DL (distance learning) has raised my stress to unmanageable levels. I have been throwing up multiple times a week and have lost significant weight. I am seeing a cognitive behavioral therapist, but it isn’t working. I don’t know how much longer I can do this. Having no delineation between work and relaxation has meant that my anxiety never turns off. It would be one thing if there was a definitive date that we were going back [to school], but it feels like there is nothing to look forward to.” Maestrelli commented on the screener as well. “My biggest concern about the screener – especially at the middle school and high school level – is the non-confidential nature of it. We have so many high-achieving kids in this district who feel a lot of pressure to succeed and perform well, and they may not have wanted to seem ‘weak’ or look like ‘failures’ by fully admitting their mental struggles in the screener. I suspect the concerning numbers the screener revealed would actually be much higher if the district had asked students to complete the screener anonymously.” Piedmont dad Misha Edel has his focus on what will be done now that the results are in. “It is great to see an external confirmation of what we already know and observe. Our students are suffering mentally, and potentially more than adults, as pandemic and Zoom-based education drags on,” he said. “What does the district plan to do to alleviate the issue? As a parent of a high schooler, I feel that the stress of grades and exams is way too much during these trying times. Clearly, ‘students have nothing else to do, but study,’ but this misses the important point of constant, unrelenting stress that social isolation brings. That greatly amplifies worries and anxieties and creates a cumulative negative effect on well-being.” “I would like the district to shift to more learning and studies but less exams and stress in its instructional approach during this online school year,” he added.
articles.title: Mental Health

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s English Department has selected Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate for its 11th annual community read project, known as Readmont. Klein argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. A limited number of copies will be available for checkout at the PHS library when school reopens sometime in January. Interested readers can reserve a copy by contacting Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12. ca.us. Books are available for purchase at A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair Village, where a 20% discount is being offered. Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at the high school starting in February and continuing through April. For more information, contact Beth Black, PHS English Department Chair at bblack@piedmont. k12.ca.us.

articles.text: Local and state lawmakers, representatives, and political leaders have released statements following the insurrection that unfolded in Washington D.C. on the afternoon of January 6. On the morning of January 6, supporters of President Donald Trump gathered for a “Save America” rally. During his speech, Trump claimed again falsely that the 2020 general “election was rigged.” By that afternoon, Congress had convened at the Capitol Building in a joint session to certify President-elect Joe Biden’s win. Soon after Trump’s speech ended, an estimated thousands of protestors gathered in front of the Capitol building and began toppling barricades and pushing past Capitol Police officers. Once past police, the rioters ran up to the Capitol’s steps, banged on doors, and attempted to break in through windows, the Washington Post reported. A mob broke at least one window and breached the capitol at approximately 2:15 p.m. Once inside, rioters ran through halls, tried to push through doors, and fought with police. “Then they were pounding on the door, so they told us to lie down on the marble floors which we did, and then there was a shot,” reported Congresswoman Jackie Speier of Hillsborough. At 2:20 p.m. PST, Rep. Speier tweeted “the Capitol has been breeched [sic]. We are in lock down!” At that time, Capitol Police ordered all staff, reporters and nearby senators into the Senate Chamber, which was sealed off and put on lockdown. Five people died and police made at least 52 arrests. No elected officials were harmed. The senate reconvened to complete the confirmation of Biden’s win, which was completed early the following morning. Gov. Gavin Newsom called the mob violence an “outright assault to our democracy” immediately after the events on January 6. “The people of California have spoken, and our congressional delegation should never have to fear for their lives to represent Californians,” Newsom said. “We are concerned for the safety of California’s congressional delegation and U.S. Capitol staff, and are reaching out to offer support in every way possible. President Trump must call for an end to this escalating situation, acknowledge the will of the people to bring President-Elect Biden to the White House and move immediately to a peaceful transition of power.” The same day, Senator Dianne Feinstein used social media platform Twitter to urge President Trump to “stop inciting violence with false claims of election fraud.” Trump did later condemn the violent acts of January 6, but many said it was too late, and that irrevocable damage had already been done. California Rep. Ro Khanna, along with many other democratic leaders, are echoing House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s call to use the 25th Amendment to remove Trump from office. “I support the Speaker, whether it is impeachment or whether it’s the 25th Amendment, but what really needs to happen is a group of Republicans like Mitch McConnell need to go over to the White House and demand Trump’s immediate resignation and say the votes are there for an impeachment,” Khanna said. “That’s what happened in Richard Nixon’s case.” Congressman Eric Swalwell of Dublin, a member of the house Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and of the House Judiciary Committee, demanded Trump’s immediate removal from office. “For the guarantee of our Republic’s survival, President Trump must be removed from office – either by the 25th Amendment or impeachment and removal in the Congress. President Trump can no longer defend our country or her ideals,” Swalwell said, adding that there must be an extensive investigation of how the Capitol was violently breached. Pelosi addressed the situation on Wednesday evening, January 7. “To those who strove to deter us from our responsibility, you have failed. To those who engaged in the gleeful desecration of this, our temple of democracy, American democracy, justice will be done,” she said. Many drew parallels to the strong police force that convened on the capitol in response to Black Lives Matter protests last summer. Rep. Barbara Lee of Oakland, who spoke the next day to KGO’s Kristen Sze regarding the events, said, “You can’t tell me that there’s not some systemic racism that we saw yesterday (January 6) in the disparities in how Black Lives Matter protesters would have been pushed back and how these protesters [were treated] because they’re Donald Trump protesters.” Rep. Eric Swalwell of Dublin House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of San Francisco “They [rioters] were there by the orders of this President; they were told to come to the Capitol and they were primarily white. You can’t tell me the response was equitable, because it wasn’t,” Lee said. San Francisco Mayor London Breed called the event “an attempted coup encouraged by the President.” Oakland Mayor Libby Schaff urged the public to “not lose faith in American democracy” and to “continue to push leaders to be more responsive to the American people, but also to not cross the line. On Monday, Democrats in the House of Representative introduced a single article of impeachment against the President, formally charging him with “incitement of insurrection” and making him the first president in American history to be charged with impeachment twice. The impeachment article states that Trump “willfully made statements that, in context, encouraged – and foreseeably resulted in – lawless action at the Capitol such as: ‘if you don’t fight like hell you’re not going to have a country anymore.” On Tuesday evening, January 12, Vice President Mike Pence said that he would not be invoking the 25th amendment to remove President Trump from office, and said “I will not now yield to efforts in the House of Representatives to play political games at a time so serious in the life of our nation.”

articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Cynthia Kane is offering a new course through the Adult School designed for grandparents of all ages. Gather virtually with other grandparents to explore how it feels to have a new baby in the family, and to navigate the joys and challenges of a role that’s completely new to you, yet remarkably familiar. What has changed and what hasn’t in the world of childrearing/ How does the pandemic affect your experience and your family’s daily routine? Discover ways to strengthen family ineractions through improved communication. We will review currnet child health and safety recommendations and have time to share gradnparenting experiences in a safe and confidential space. The course is onlien and is scheduled for two sessions, with four classes each. Session 1: Saturdays, January 23 to February 13; 11:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Seassion 2: Saturdays, February 27 to March 20, same time. The fee is $60 per session. To register, see: https://piedmontadultschool.asapconnected. com/#CourseID=238892. Instructor Bio Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. She has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership, and now works exclusively with grandparents and their families. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, education, and support for grandparents, particularly those providing care for grandchildren. Her website, https://itstheirturn. com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Sea Scout program received a major donation in September; a 27-foot 1983 Pacific Seacraft Orion 27. Piedmont boys and girls, and existing Scouts can now begin signing up for the Scout Council’s Sea Scouts program, with an opportunity for adventures from to McCovey Cove to Angel Island, and possibly the Delta. The new vessel, the third iteration of the SSS Revenge, elicited high praise from veteran Piedmont Scouter Javier Jerez, who will head up the revitalized Sea Scout program. Standing on the boat in its berth at Ballena Bay in Alameda, he recently said. “It is just built like a tank. The boat has really good bones. It is really exciting, ” The donor, Jonarde Raab, put $25,000 into the boat with the intent of sailing it around the world. Jerez says the boat is easily worth double that now and is in really good shape. Raab made the donation with the condition that it would be used by the Scouts and not sold to fundraise for another boat or another program. This caveat suited the Scouts and Jerez, as the newest Revenge increases the range and potential of the program exponentially. New Piedmont Scouting Director Kate Benson is strongly looking forward to the time when the Scouts will be able to invite people on the boat. Current Covid restrictions preclude that. “We have the utmost gratitude to Jonarde Raab for his generous donation of the boat for use in our Sea Scouts program. There are a lot of different program opportunities in scouts, but [Sea Scouts] really provides some special and unique opportunities.” Describing the boat, Jerez said, “This design was very well respected as a blue water cruiser back in the late 70’s and early 80’s. It was what you wanted to go around the world in; this was ‘it!’” More than a few people have accomplished the feat of sailing around the world in one of these. “The Bay is one of the best places in the world to learn to sail. You get consistent strong winds and currents,” Jerez explained. He will be teaching Scouts navigational skills with excursions on the Bay, to include some night sails. Jerez also envisions sailing past the Golden Gate and going north to Drake’s Bay at Point Reyes for a possible overnight, and later possibly a weeklong trip on the Delta. In a future year it’s likely they will be among the hundreds of boats on the Bay during Fleet Week when the Blue Angels fly over San Francisco and over the Bay. Jerez has taken friends and scouts to Angel Island for an overnight camping trip. In 2016 the Piedmont Sea Scouts joined 15 other Sea Scouts from Richmond and San Leandro on multiple sailboats for a twoweek cruise to Long Beach. The Piedmont Sea Scouts now have Since 2015 Javier Jerez has been the Piedmont Scouts’ head of the coed Sea Scouts program, and de factor Skipper of the SSS Revenge. The SSS Revenge, the newest sailboat owned by Piedmont Scout Council. the capability to do this on their own boat. “Wit h t h is boat, t he engine-propeller combination can actually push the boat really well, so I’m not as concerned about going out and having to time everything [currents and winds] perfectly to be able to make it back,” Jerez noted. Not many Sea Scout programs exist, although the national program started at the same time as the Boy Scouts – in 1910. Piedmont’s program will now be able to draw an interest from high school girls and boys ages 14-20. “We are kind of like the Swiss Navy, because we are completely landlocked,” Jerez said with a laugh. “’Piedmont has a boat?’ people ask me.” The vessel be a place of learning. “Sailing has a huge learning curve – gigantic, never ending. The scouts will be learning about sail-trim, weather, piloting, coastal navigation, off-shore navigation, and more weather.” Jerez explained. While the ocean breeze may make sailing a relatively low risk for COVID-19 transmission, the cockpit area of the Revenge is relatively small, the number of Scouts onboard at any one time will be limited. For more information on joining the Piedmont Sea Scouts, contact Jerez directly at: javier_ jerez@yahoo.com. The two fore sails of the 83 Pacific Seacraft Orion 27 make it as a cutter-rig. The SSS Revenge has all the amenities of home, and all the style of 1983. With the bowsprit, the Sea Scout’s new vessel measures 30 feet.

articles.text: Leaders in Europe and elsewhere expressed shock and horror over the violent mob attack on the U.S. Capitol. Universally, blame was laid upon Donald Trump. France’s Emmanuel Macron commented Thursday, “We believe in the strength of American democracy, What happened in Washington is not American.” U.S. allies made frank comments, such as from German Chancellor Angela Merkel whose relations with Trump were notoriously combative. She said she was “furious and saddened” by the events, and said Thursday, “I deeply regret that President Donald Trump has not conceded his defeat since November, and now this,” according to Deutsch World news service. British Prime Minister Boris Johnson termed the Capitol coup attempt a “disgrace” and called for “a peaceful and orderly transfer of power.” From Jerusalem, Israeli’s P.M. Benjamin Netanyahu spoke cautiously, saying the “rampage at the Capitol was a disgraceful act and it must be vigorously condemned.” EU leaders took to Twitter to “condemn the unrest” and “urge a peaceful transition of power.” Swedish P.M Stefan Löfven was more blunt: “President Trump and many members of Congress bear significant responsibility for what’s now taking place.” Closer to home, Canadian P.M. Justin Trudeau stated, “What we witnessed was an assault on democracy by violent rioters incited by the current president and other politicians.” Within the U.S., former leaders quickly condemmed the riots at the Capitol on January 6. Former President George Bush (2001- 2008) stated, “I am appalled by the reckless behavior of some political leaders” and blamed the riot on people “whose passions have been inflamed by falsehoods and false hopes.” Fore President Bill Clinton said, “the match was lit by Donald Trump.” Barack Obama in the Chicago Tribune called it a “moment of great dishonor and shame for our nation” and “called on Republican lawmakers to speak out against Trump.” high ground.” The Guardian quoted Iranian President Hassan Rouhani saying, “What we saw in the US last night and today really showed that first how brittle and weak western democracy is, and how weak its foundations are.” He called Trump an “unhealthy person” who “tainted his country’s reputation and credibility.” Russian lawmakers wasted no time jumping on the Capitol chaos as evidence of what thy described as the nation’s “moral bankruptcy,” and threw in a few scraps of support for th etheory of election fraud. The Chinese cited the chaos as proof of equivalency with their own violent crackdowns on Hong Kong’s democratic institutions. The Guardian wrote, “After four years of President Trump, the idea of the U.S. as a moral arbitrator has suffered repeated blows.” Europeans are following events in Washington about as anxiously as Americans are. “We are very much interested; the attack on the Capitol is frightening,” my landlady told me. Without prompting, she told me that the French strongly disliike Trump and see him as cruel. The French worry that Trump will “blow up something” on his way out.” She said she saw the bido posted by former california Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and said she like his remarks. I feel grateful for him having done nothing truly bad as Governor. Trump grievances about “disenfranchised voters” and “votes J. Scott Applewhite/AP House of Representatives Leader Nancy Pelosi addresses members on Capitol Hill after a pro-Trump mob attacked the Capitol last week. -Teddy Roosevelt 26th Preisdent of the U.S. Most leaders chose caution to stay out of the political fray that is fueling controversy. According to The Hill, leaders of hostile nations jumped on criticism of the President and democracy noting that “the insurrection capped four years of chaos, confusion and strife under Trump.” Adversaries in Moscow, Beijing and Tehran are reveling in broadcasts of “chaos and destroy” scenes” and gleeful about our “fall from the moral France’s President Emmanuel Macron stated, “We believe in the strength of American democracy, What happened in Washington is not American.” that didn’t count,” seem wildly inaccurate. The disenfranchisement tyranny cannot be what this is. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of legitimate voter registrations were thrown off the rolls quietly by an assortment of Republican tate lawmakers. The pro-Trump voters refer to ballots not winning as “votes that didn’t count,” a travesty of truth. We the people are the victims. Ballots were not dumped in a river, Looking to the horizon, I am calmed by the words of Joseph Biden, our elected leader who demonstrates care and concern Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said the “Trump-incited Capitol attack was shocking, deeply disturbing, and saddening.” for the country and all the people. My heart is lifting at how resourceful, gracious, and graceful a person he is. Regardless of politics, he is a person of character and a truthful human being, I believe. Covid-19 is still rampant and the vaccine distribution is slow to get out of the gate. articles.text: The Tule Elk State Natural Reserve can be found north of Tomales Bay State Park and the small town of Inverness in the Pt. Reyes National Seashore. Sunday’s High Surf Advisory along the California coast made for terrific wave-watching, while taking the near-five mile hike to Tomales Point put walkers next to herds of Tule Elk undisturbed by passersby. Taking the 9.7 out-and-back Tomales Point Trail heads to the northern most point on the Inverness side of Tomales Bay— overlooking remote stretches of beaches on the Pacific coast line to your left with Tomales Bay and The view of the remote Driftwood Beach along the Tomales Point Trail. You won’t find any tree cover on the Tomales Point Trail. Park officials advise to wear layered clothing to deal with the randomly changing weather on the coast. Staff Photos Herds of Tule Elk can be spotted at their reserve in the Pt. Reyes National Seashore on the Tomales Point Trail. the town of Dillon Beach to your right. The hike starts at Pierce Point Ranch, a historic farmstead of the Pt. Reyes Peninsula that has informative markers to describe the early dairy farming culture of the area. The near five mile walk to Tomales Point is in conjunction with the Tule Elk Reserve, there herds of male bulls, female cows, young male spikes, and baby calves. The ending is a bluff overlooking tide pools and a common array of birds: pelicans, cormorants, gulls, while red-tailed hawks and turkey vultures are often spotted looking for food as well. articles.text: Photo courtesy of the Brentwood Press NCS commissioner Pat Cruickshank mentioned that the Section is considering pushing sports into new seasons. North Coast Section commissioner Pat Cruickshank indicated on Tuesday, January 12 that the Section is considering changing the CIF sports calendar in an effort to fit more sports between January and May. “No decision has been made,” he said. “It’s a conversation we’re having, As fluid as this situation has been, we need to see what’s best for our schools, leagues, section, and the state. There are a lot of people having these conversations.” “The main goal is to get kids back into competition. That’s goal No. 1 at this point. Allow kids to have some semblance of normalcy is the goal,” added Central Coast commissioner Dave Grissom. Right now, only cross country would be given the green light to start competition once stay-athome orders are lifted. The possible changes would affect cross country, golf, tennis, swimming, and track and field, so-called Outdoor Non-Contact Sports deemed okay to play while in the Purple Tier. Of those, only cross country was planned to start in January. alongside football, water polo, and volleyball. The inherent dilemma with reshuffling the CIF’s individual sports’ schedules comes with their overall planning this far. Re-doing things, now in January, results in enormous problems with practice and field use schedules. “There are a lot of things to weigh when you’re looking at this,” Grissom explained. “It’s an oddly difficult thing to do. There’s quite a bit that goes into any season in any sport.” One solution is to allow schools to compete within their individual leagues, as suggested Photo courtesy of NCS The North Coast Section oversees schools from Alameda County to the Oregon border. Photo courtesy of Central Coast Section Central Coast Section commissioner Dave Grissom is also considering changes of sports schedules. by several Piedmont coaches. Te 12- school Western Alameda County Conference is one of the largest leagues in the state, making scheduling easier. But some leagues, schools, or counties may opt against joining in. Cruickshank, Grissom, and others have scheduled an executive meeting ahead of January 25 – the purported start date for competition. But with no answers, coaches and athletic directors remain close to the phone awaiting new information. Grissom said he is optimistic that the number of COVID- 19 cases drops by June. But that effectively wipes out an entire year of high school sports in 2020-21. “With vaccinations, I have to think things will get better,” he added.

articles.text: Last week’s announcement from the California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) that cross country could begin competing on January 25 caused more confusion than elation. Although the CIF deemed cross country as a Non-Contact Outdoor sport that is permissible for Purple Tier counties, Alameda County’s Public Heath Department must first give its approval “[We have] no official announcements, yet. It keeps getting pushed back, due in part to the State of California not releasing their expected guidelines on January 4,” said Piedmont High’s first- year Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “There’s a CIF North Coast Section meeting this week, which will hopefully give us more information, but it’s not set in stone. Everything is always up for delay,” explained Smet at Witter Field while overseeing cross country’s practice, checking in guests, and shooing away non-student visitors. In college, they run 3Ks, 5,000 meters, and 10,000 meters, so if they are going to run in college, its good experience,” said Homlund. All things considered, a January or February start is premature despite the CIF having had time since March last year to create a solid plan. “It’s just like in August [when all sports were shut down]. It really still feels like the offseason for us,” Holmlund said. “My hopes are that we will be returning to sports at some point this year and competition in some sort of form. It’ll be shorter seasons, but I do have high hopes. There’s a little more optimism with Purple Tier sports,” added Smet. Despite having no answers for the season, Holmlund said the athletes have been training hard “I would love to have cross country, just one competition. But do I think it’s going to happen? There are pods of 14 boys and girls having a great time and bonding.” A group of underclassmen on the cross-country team.

articles.text: It is a winter season like no other due to travel and health restrictions in California. Normally, residents of the Bay Area would be gearing up for trips to the mountains for cabin vacations. Piedmont’s annual Ski Week has less meaning this year. Here is an update on Yosemite and Lake Tahoe’s ski slopes and hiking trails. Yosemite National Park Yosemite National Park’s only ski resort, Badger Pass Ski Area, is closed for the entire 2020-2021 season due to COVID-19 concerns. Park officials announced that all downhill operations have been shut down and they are refunding season-pass holders or rolling over their credit to next winter. In addition, Ski huts at Glacier Point, Ostrander, Snow Creek, and Tuolumne Meadows are closed. Campgrounds and lodging is still closed through at least January 21 in conjunction with California’s Stay at Home orders. With Mariposa County having zero ICU capacity availability, that date will undoubtedly extend. Day trips to Yosemite are still permitted with advanced reservations through the winter but tracking current conditions are critical for would-be visitors. Yosemite’s most popular trail, Half Dome, has its cables down for the winter season and is subsequently closed. A permit is also required to hike when accessible. The Four Mile Trail is closed from Union Point to Glacier Point, a popular overlooking spot that views the Yosemite Valley, Half Dome, Yosemite Falls, and Yosemite’s high country. Other trails closed include the hike to Bridalveil Falls due to its rehabilitation project, and the Snow Creek Trail is shut down due to bear activity. All other trails are open. Lake Tahoe All mountain slopes are currently open for snow sports around Lake Tahoe, but lodging is still affected due to stay-athome orders for California since December 11. For the California side, including South Lake Tahoe in El Dorado County and Placer County’s Tahoe City and Kings Beach, lodging is still restricted due to each of El Dorado and Placer counties still below 15 percent ICU capacity. However, the Nevada side is still allowing lodging at its hotels but officials are still declaring that only essential travels are being welcomed to South Lake. This includes the casinos and hotels at Stateline of South Lake Tahoe given they reside in Nevada’s Douglas County and Carson City. Casinos and hotels open include Harrahs, Harveys, the Hard Rock, and Montebleu Resort. “Hotels and lodging cannot accept or honor in-state or out-ofstate reservations for non- essential travel, unless the reservation is for at least the minimum time period required for quarantine and the persons identified in the Photo courtesy of NPS.gov Yosemite National Park is still limited to day-use. It’s only ski area, Badger Pass, is closed this winter. Photo courtesy of SF Chronicle Yosemite’s Half Dome is currently closed for the season due to repairs on the cables on the way to the summit. reservation will quarantine in the hotel or lodging entity until after that time period has expired. When the Regional Stay Home Order is in effect in a region, hotels and lodging can only offer accommodation for COVID- 19 mitigation and containment measures, treatment measures, accommodation for essential workers, or providing housing solutions, including measures to protect homeless populations,” said South Lake Tahoe officials, via TahoeSouth.com. articles.text: These are dark, woeful, painful days (the pandemic, politics), but there’s a ray of sunshine if you’re a basketball fan, as I am. Jeremy Lin is a Golden State Warrior (again). You remember Jeremy Lin, right? Basketball fans certainly do, and many non-fans might. Eight years ago, there was no bigger star in professional basketball than Jeremy Lin. From obscurity, he became an international celebrity for what he did in February 2012, in New York City, the biggest American (and, arguably, world) stage of all. Really famous people (Barack Obama, Donald Trump, Spike Lee, et. al.) wanted to be his buddy. Documentary films were made of him. He gained fame and fortune. He was all of 23 years old. He created what became known as “Linsanity,” a phenomenon that dazzled the Big Apple and went stratospheric in the international world of sports and entertainment culture. For 12 games that month, Lin, a virtual nobody, became a sudden superstar, by leading the New York Knicks to many wins after the team had played terribly. Shortly thereafter, Lin came down to earth. He became injured and the Knicks didn’t exactly go overboard to try to retain his services after his Linsanity season ended. He bounced around with seven other NBA teams, never soaring to Linsanity levels again. Most recently, he played in China, where he was a star for a Beijing team. China, however, is where aging or underperforming NBA players go to try to revive their careers. Over the past weekend, the Warriors signed a deal with Lin and assigned him to their G-League team, the Santa Cruz Warriors. Frankly, it’s insulting that he’s being sent down to the G-League, which is like a training camp usually for marginal and inexperienced rookies. Lin has a lot of NBA experience and played well in China. Nonetheless, he’s going to have a chance to play for the Real Warriors again, his first NBA team after he wasn’t drafted by any team in 2010. The first time around with the Dubs, the 2010- 2011 season, he was mostly a benchwarmer and played very little. He eventually ended up with the New York Knicks in the Linsanity 2011-2012 season. We pro-Lin Warriors fans, however, can dream a little, can’t we? Already we hear some Dubs’ fans pooh-poohing the possibility of Lin becoming a Real Warrior again. Too old (32). Skills eroded. Too much competition on the Warriors’ roster. Can he really help the Warriors get back to elite status? That may all be true, but it’d be sweet if Lin became a Real Warrior again. The Bay Area, after all, is where he began his basketball career. He was a star on the Palo Alto High School team. It still puzzles me why Stanford, Cal, or UCLA never encouraged him to enroll. Palo Alto High is directly across the 101 freeway from Stanford. He had to “settle” for Harvard (yes, that Harvard, not exactly your typical collegiate basketball factory like Duke or Kentucky). H i s h o m e c o m i n g i s heart-warming to Warriors’ fans and the Bay Area’s large and diverse Chinese American/Asian American population. Born in Southern California to immigrant Taiwanese parents, he became the first Chinese American/Asian American in the NBA, a league dominated by African Americans. (There have been several other Chinese-from-China NBA players, the most famous being Yao Ming, who played for the Houston Rockets.) That’s one reason why I and other Chinese Americans and Asian Americans became Linsane. (Many nonAsians were also.) You know the stereotypes, don’t you? We folks of Asian descent are technological geeks, math and science wizards, conformist professionals, hard-working support staff, etc., but never a Superstar celebrity known practically worldwide! And never a professional basketball player, let alone one who for a month sucked up gobs of national and international attention. The racial-ethnic angle isn’t why Lin should play for the Real Warriors again. That decision should be made on the basis of his G-League performance, the team’s needs and the ultra-complicated financial and contractual protocols of the NBA and its teams. Call me sentimental, but given the racial-ethnic demographics of the Bay Area and of the Warriors’ fan base, his joining the Warriors would be a feel-good moment that we should all have right now, don’t you think? William Gee Wong, a Piedmont resident, is a retired syndicated journalist and author of Yellow Journalist: Dispatches from Asian America and Images of America: Oakland’s Chinatown.
