SKI REPORT Update on conditions for Yosemite & Lake Tahoe slopes and lodging By Jonathan Comeaux It is a winter season like no other due to travel and health restrictions in California. Normally, residents of the Bay Area would be gearing up for trips to the mountains for cabin vacations. Piedmont’s annual Ski Week has less meaning this year. Here is an update on Yosemite and Lake Tahoe’s ski slopes and hiking trails. Yosemite National Park Yosemite National Park’s only ski resort, Badger Pass Ski Area, is closed for the entire 2020-2021 season due to COVID-19 concerns. Park officials announced that all downhill operations have been shut down and they are refunding season-pass holders or rolling over their credit to next winter. In addition, Ski huts at Glacier Point, Ostrander, Snow Creek, and Tuolumne Meadows are closed. Campgrounds and lodging is still closed through at least January 21 in conjunction with California’s Stay at Home orders. With Mariposa County having zero ICU capacity availability, that date will undoubtedly extend. Day trips to Yosemite are still permitted with advanced reservations through the winter but tracking current conditions are critical for would-be visitors. Yosemite’s most popular trail, Half Dome, has its cables down for the winter season and is subsequently closed. A permit is also required to hike when accessible. The Four Mile Trail is closed from Union Point to Glacier Point, a popular overlooking spot that views the Yosemite Valley, Half Dome, Yosemite Falls, and Yosemite’s high country. Other trails closed include the hike to Bridalveil Falls due to its rehabilitation project, and the Snow Creek Trail is shut down due to bear activity. All other trails are open. Lake Tahoe All mountain slopes are currently open for snow sports around Lake Tahoe, but lodging is still affected due to stay-athome orders for California since December 11. For the California side, including South Lake Tahoe in El Dorado County and Placer County’s Tahoe City and Kings Beach, lodging is still restricted due to each of El Dorado and Placer counties still below 15 percent ICU capacity. However, the Nevada side is still allowing lodging at its hotels but officials are still declaring that only essential travels are being welcomed to South Lake. This includes the casinos and hotels at Stateline of South Lake Tahoe given they reside in Nevada’s Douglas County and Carson City. Casinos and hotels open include Harrahs, Harveys, the Hard Rock, and Montebleu Resort. “Hotels and lodging cannot accept or honor in-state or out-ofstate reservations for non- essential travel, unless the reservation is for at least the minimum time period required for quarantine and the persons identified in the Photo courtesy of NPS.gov Yosemite National Park is still limited to day-use. It’s only ski area, Badger Pass, is closed this winter. When the Regional Stay Home Order is in effect in a region, hotels and lodging can only offer accommodation for COVID- 19 mitigation and containment measures, treatment measures, accommodation for essential workers, or providing housing solutions, including measures to protect homeless populations,” said South Lake Tahoe officials, via TahoeSouth.com. articles.text: The San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers is closed to patrons due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, but the Conservatory’s horticulturists continue to add resources online during a time of sheltering-in-place. During the winter, the “best in bloom” have been added to the Conservatory’s website for patrons to browse. Included this season are aquatic plants, lowland tropics, potted plants, highland tropics, and glimpses of the West Gallery. Click on the website and learn about the unique Dracula plant, a native to Peru, and uncover some little-known history about the well-known San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers Hibiscus flower. Visit https://conservatoryofflowers.org/whats-in-bloom/ and click on “What’s in Bloom”. The San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers reopened to the public on October 1 following a seven-month closure; however, it is temporarily closed again, with no formal reopening date.
articles.title: SF Conservatory of Flowers: explore what’s in bloom online

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside. Filoli House and Garden, located in Woodside, is conducting a haiku contest to complement its “Winters at Filoli” calendar of events. Winter at Filoli is a time of quiet reflection in the garden. Interested participants can submit a haiku inspired by Filoli’s winter garden for a chance to win a Household Plus Membership, as well as a beautiful gift basket of Filoli-approved goodies. “Late December and early January tend to be a period of heavy rains, and with that rain comes a washing of the plants and hardscapes,” Director of Horticulture Jim Salyards said. “There is a vibrancy to the bare branches of the deciduous shrubs and dark green leaves of the evergreens during the winter months. The brick paths and walls, the balustrades, and even the gravel paths seem even more prominent in the cool and wet weather.” You may submit up to three original poems. Poems should be in the general haiku format of three short lines of 5-7-5 syllables, or free-form haiku. They must be inspired by nature, in this case by Filoli’s winter garden. Three prizes are being offered. Prizes • First Place: Filoli Household Plus Membership and Gift Basket • Second Place: Filoli Individual Plus Membership • Best Under 18: Filoli Household Membership All entries should be submitted by midnight, January 31. Finalists will be announced on Filoli’s website on February 10. Winners will also be announced via Zoom on Valentine’s Day, February 14. Special guest judge and San Mateo County Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto will read the winning poem online on Valentine’s Day. To submit your haiku, visit https://filoli.org/haiku/.
articles.title: All entries ae due by January 31

articles.text: Fort Mason’s Drive-In Theater will be hosting Sundance Film Festival satellite screenings, presented by San Francisco’s Roxie Theater. The special screenings will take place concurrent with the festival in Park City, Utah, with screenings from Thursday, January 28, through Tuesday, February 2. The opening film on January 28 at 5 p.m. will be Coda, directed by Sian Heder and produced by Philippe Rousselet, Fabrice Gianfermi and Patrick Wachsberger. The film follows the life of Ruby, a child of deaf adults who is the only hearing person in her family. When the family’s fishing business is threatened, Ruby finds herself torn between pursuing her love of music and her fear of abandoning her parents. The cast includes Emilia A rendering of Fort Mason drive-in theatre in San Francisco. Jones, Eugenio Derbez, Troy Kotsur, and Daniel Durant. All films are part of Fort Mason Flix and will be shown at Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture’s drive-through theater. It provides a socially distanced movie-going experience, with online ticket sales, contactless check-in, a limited capacity, safe physical distance between vehicles, expanded cleaning, and sanitation in restrooms, and PPE for all theater and security staff. Concessions are not available until San Francisco’s ShelterIn-Place rules are relaxed when COVID-19 pandemic conditions improve. To obtain tickets, visit https:// fortmason.org/event/flix/2021- sundance-film-festival-coda/.
articles.title: Movies to be shown Jan. 28 – Feb. 2 as satellite festival

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is presenting an archival production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream from Thursday, January 21 through February 10. The ballet, one of the company’s most well-known, is a Shakespearean favorite making its triumphant return to San Francisco after a cut-tooshort run in 2020. San Francisco Ballet presented one critically acclaimed performance of George Balanchine’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream last March before the War Memorial Opera House was forced to close due to COVID-19. This 1962 work by Choreographer George Balanchine, to music by Felix Mendelssohn, was his first original full-length ballet and quickly hailed as a masterpiece. Balanchine loved the original play – he could recite large parts of it in Russian – so the ballet sticks close to its inspiration. It tells the story of four lost lovers in the woods, as well as of a royal fairy court made up of Queen Titania, King Oberon, and mischievous Puck. Balanchine’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream is part of San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season and will be performed in Program 1. The magical comedy of errors is available through digital season subscriptions, which includes behind-the-scenes content. A Midsummer Night’s Dream is also available for 24-hour on-demand rental. To obtain tickets to this digital event, visit https://www.sfballet. org/tickets/2021-season/.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Midsummer Night’s Dream available to stream on January 21

articles.text: Toshi Reagon will perform in Living Jazz’s MLK Day tribute concert, January 17. Living Jazz will present its 19th annual musical tribute honoring Martin Luther King, Jr. on Sunday, January 17, the day prior to MLK Day, a national holiday. The lineup features locally and internationally known artists. Featured artists include Toshi Reagon, the Kronos Quartet, and Allison Miller. The event will be hosted by former KPIX News Anchor Dana King. Oakland Congresswoman Barbara Lee will present the Oakland Citizen Humanitarian Award to Dr. Noha Aboelata, Founder and CEO of Roots Clinic, during the event. The tribute is made possible through nonprofit organizations, including the California Arts Council, Alameda County Arts Commission, the William and Flora Hewlett Foundation and the City of Oakland Cultural Funding Program. The tribute will begin at 4 p.m. and will be presented online at https://www.livingjazz.org/mlktribute. Concert viewing will be on a “Pay What You Can” admission. All donations will benefit the Living Jazz Children’s Project, which provides free music education for low-income Oakland public elementary students.
articles.title: Living Jazz to present 19th annual MLK, Jr. tribute on January 17

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will stream its production of Samson and Delilah on Saturday, January 23, for 24 hours. The stream is made available through the company’s “Opera is On” series, which brings past productions and performances directly to audiences through digital platforms. Samson and Delilah is Camille Saint-Saen’s “most seductive opera,” and stars tenor Clifton Forbis in his company debut, and Grammy award-winning mezzo-soprano Olga Borodina in a performance that critics hailed as “lithe and lustrous.” The opera follows the biblical epic of Samson: blind, beaten, and his strength cut away from him. Samson has succumbed to the sins he vowed to vanquish, but when love is a trap, the only escape is to appeal to a higher power. San Francisco Chronicle noted that Forbis “had his best moments in the most demanding parts” of his role as Samson. Bass-baritone Juha Uusitalo is cast as the High Priest. He sings with what the Chronicle described as “both commanding Free delivery to Piedmont Clifton Forbis and Olga Borodina sing the lead roles in San Francisco Opera’s production of Samson and Delilah. breadth and a permanent sneer.” Bass Oren Gradus as the Old Hebrew and bass Eric Jordan as ill-fated Philistine Abimelech also make their company debuts in Samson and Delilah. The opera is directed by Sandra Bernhard and choreographed by Kenneth von Heidecke. This production will no longer be available after Sunday, January 24. More archival performances will be made available throughout shelter-in-place guidelines. To secure tickets for Samson and Delilah, visit https:// sfopera.com/opera-is-on/streaming/#comingupnext.
articles.title: SF Opera to perform Samson and Delilah January 23 and 24

articles.text: Dylan Walsh stars in The Stepfather. Movie review by Chris Honoré While The Stepfather is neither subtle nor shy, it does ratchet up serious tension as the film moves inexorably toward its predictable and harrowing conclusion. The story is familiar – a remake of the 1987 movie of the same name. It aims at that primordial fear that we don’t really know the people we’re close to until it may be too late. David Harris (Dylan Walsh), charming and smooth, inserts himself into the lives of a mother, Susan Harding (Sela Ward), and her three children. Susan is just coming off of a divorce and is vulnerable. The kids are teens and adjusting to a split family and weekends with dad. Suddenly they have a supportive guy around, someone who often insists that all he values in life is family. He tells them that his wife and daughter were killed in a car accident more than a year ago. The screenwriters do an interesting thing at the outset. They make it clear to the audience that Harris is a psychopath and pure evil in the guise of a wonderful guy. So, the first shoe is immediately dropped. What gives the film an unrelenting tension is that the audience is waiting for the second shoe to drop. The test of the film is how effective the filmmakers are in revealing to the unsuspecting family that Harris is a stone cold killer who is moving placidly among his victims with a wide smile and a loving, helpful persona. All the while small chinks – ever so subtle, ever so easily explained – in his behavior begin to appear. It’s chilling to watch. Walsh, as an actor, does a superb job in transforming his face from barely controlled rage to wide smiles in mere seconds. Susan, meanwhile, is oblivious. She’s in love. Her oldest son, Michael (Penn Bradley), however, begins to suspect that something is deeply wrong, though his girlfriend (Amber Heard) insists that it is all in his imagination. The audience knows he is right and it’s just a matter of time. The second shoe is about to fall. And it’s those minutes that make all the difference. As psych-horror films go, The Stepfather is well done. It’s a B-movie to be sure, one targeted at teens who unabashedly enjoy the genre and will surely turn out for this one. The Stepfather. Starring Dylan Walsh, Sela Ward, Penn Badgley and Amber Heard. Directed by Nelson McCormick. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13.

And so, Haller begins to peel layers of the onion, building his client’s defense, using his lead investigator, Frank Levin (William H. Macy). Levin is no rookie, his face deeply lined, his eyes tired, his hair touching his shoulders. What’s the adage? It’s not your age, it’s the mileage. And like Mick, he’s intuitive, knows the streets, and is bulldog tenacious. Macy, one of the best character actors working today, is exceptional, as are all of the actors in The Lincoln Lawyer, especially Marisa Tomei. Her face is now lined and even more attractive as her strength and character shine through. Mature, accomplished actresses like Tomei are a treasure and too often underused in Hollywood. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Nanny McPhee was last seen in 2005 arriving to set right a dysfunctional family needing more than an intervention. They needed the McPhee magic, delivered by a snaggletooth, starched, ominous and mysterious nanny who arrives with magic at her fingertips and a cane to put things right. McPhee is a wonderful character, played perfectly by the gifted Emma Thompson. In the recent incarnation, Nanny McPhee Returns, written by Thompson, McPhee arrives at a bucolic farm in northern England. It’s the middle of World War II and children from London, which is being subjected to Germany’s blitzkrieg bombing, are sent across England to wait out the war, most in the safety of the English countryside. And so we are introduced to the Green children and their mother, Isabel Green (Maggie Gyllenhaal). The family is hanging on by a thread, financially and emotionally, while waiting for the father to return from the war. What is a normal state of chaos on the farm turns chronic when cousins Cyril (Eros Vlahos) and Cella (Rosie Taylor-Ritson), arrive from upper crust London in a chauffer-driven limousine. Dressed to the nines, they refuse to step out of the car, holding their noses, insisting they’ve arrived at a “poo and mud” museum. Everything is icky. They want to go home, and dig in their snobbish custom made heels, refusing to help out. Things are dire. Isabel’s brother-in-law (Rhys Ifans), a weasel, is trying to sell the farm to pay off gambling debts, the barley needs to be harvested, and a new batch of piglets must be sold to keep the family afloat. What to do? Enter Nanny McPhee, and just in time to teach the kids five life-lessons that will transform them and the farm, to the delight of all. The film is enhanced by CGI – pigs can and do fly and even synchronize swim. But at its center is a wonderful cast of characters who are both charming and engaging. Kids and adults will enjoy without reservation this entertaining film that delivers a heart-tugging ending after Nanny McPhee does indeed put everything right. Nanny McPhee Returns, Starring Emma Thompson, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Rhys Ifans and Maggie Smith. Directed by Susanna White. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Emma Thompson as Nanny McPhee in Nanny McPhee Returns.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind is extraordinary, not only as a high adventure story but as a work of art, its visual, handdrawn aesthetics are well beyond the trope known as the cartoon. Its animation is lush, detailed, and gorgeous. This feature was Hayao Miyazaki’s first major film in what would become the renowned Studio Ghibli astonishingly deepbench catalogue of dozens and dozens of animated films highly regarded throughout the world. The Nausicaa narrative is based on Miyazaki’s manga series of the same name and tells a tale of a planet that was reduced to a toxic, desiccated wasteland and poisoned jungle, the result of an apocalyptic war that took place some 1,000 years in the past. In the midst of toxic plants and huge insects, humans have survived and live on small inhabitable islands where they have fashioned an agrarian life that does possess some advanced technology. One of those islands is called the Kingdom of the Valley of the Wind, nestled in a mountain gorge. It is home to Princess Nausicaa (Alison Lohan), a courageous, adventurous young woman who travels on a jet-propelled glider that she uses for exploration. She possesses an affinity for animals and plants and can communicate with the Ohmu, whale-sized intelligent isopods that are the dominant species on earth. The film opens with Nausicaa on a trip to gather needed supplies and it is then that she meets Lord Yupa (Patrick Stewart), a wandering sage who has brought peace and wisdom to the valley. Arriving back home, she encounters a princess from another country who tells Nausicaa that the advanced, war-like nation of Tolmekia is planning to revive the doomsday machines, called the Giant Warriors, which had originally destroyed the planet. It is at this point that the very dense plot begins. There are two threads that hold this remarkable story together. One is its environmental point of view, made manifest through the efforts by Nausicaa to co-exist with nature. As well there is the heroic archetype as embodied in the Princess who defends and helps her people, displaying a willingness to endure physical pain and take great risks to achieve her objectives. She is fearless and brave, yet reluctant to turn toward violence, though capable of doing so. The plot is complex, layered, and requires a level of attention that may make it difficult for younger viewers to fully comprehend the story. Nausicaa of the Valley of Wind (1984). Animé – written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Fantasy and adventure. With the voices of Alison Lohan, Patrick Stewart and Uma Thurman. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Nausicaa of the Valley of Wind – more magic from Studio Ghibli

It was noted that voters in California rejected affirmative action in the November election, and the question of what are other ways that inequality can be addressed was posed to the group. The problems of unequal law enforcement and crime sentencing were recognized. Additionally, the unequal funding of schools with the resulting disparity in the quality of education was also discussed. Swee Ling Chen provided some perspective based on her experience of living in Singapore, where it is composed of a set of different racial groups, but the government’s policies are designed to create societal integration, equality, and a level playing field for all its citizens. However, she stressed that benefits are not given away. People have to earn what is being provided. This orientation and policy are supported by the people and may have lessons for our country. It seems Kendi would consider them antiracist. With the book discussion complete, the group considered books to read in the future. The group previously selected two Olive Kitteridge novels by Elizabeth Strout for February. The books are the first Olive novel and also Olive Again. Drive Your Plow over the Bones of the Dead by Polish author Olga Tokarczuk was selected as the group’s March read. For April the readers decided on the non-fiction The Splendid and the Vile: A Saga of Churchill, Family, and Defiance During the Blitz by Erik Larson. The First Monday Reading Group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, February 1, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by contacting John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@piedmont. ca.gov). The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on January 4. Fourteen readers attended remotely to discuss the group’s January selection, How to be an Antiracist by Ibram X. Kendi. Participating in the discussion were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Jeri Lockhart, Margie Blodgett, Jen Cavenaugh, Swee Ling Chen, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. How to Be an Antiracist is a 2019 non-fiction book by American author and historian Ibram X. Kendi. The book presents concepts regarding racism and Kendi’s proposals for anti-racist individual actions and systemic policy changes. He defines a racist as anyone who supports “a racist policy through their actions or inaction.” He wants people who believe they are not racists to become “antiracists.” These are people who support ideas and policies affirming that “the racial groups are equals in all their apparent differences – that there is nothing right or wrong with any racial group.” For Kendi, there are no non-racists; there are only racists, people who allow racist ideas to proliferate without opposition, and antiracists, people who confront such ideas wherever they encounter them. Kendi presents ways of thinking about ourselves and others. Instead of working with the policies and system we have in place, he wants us to think about what an antiracist society would be, and how we can play an active role in creating it. For Kendi, “there is no such thing as a not-racist idea,” only “racist ideas and antiracist ideas.” Kendi tells the reader, “Every policy in How to Be an Antiracist, by Ibram Kendi, was the selection for January. every institution in every community in every nation is producing or sustaining either racial inequity or equity.” The former are racist policies and the latter are antiracist. The readers found the book to be a challenging read. Some found it to be like a textbook and its beginning to be somewhat dry and difficult to get through. However, the group felt the later chapters and the book overall provided an expanded understanding of how our society’s racial challenges can be viewed and addressed. Generally, the readers felt How to Be an Antiracist was an important and beneficial book to read. As a thought-provoking read, How to Be an Antiracist was the catalyst for a group discussion that expanded into personal experiences associated with privilege and injustice, as well as societal and local issues of inequality. The small number of educators of color in Piedmont schools was noted; as were the problems of recruiting them and the compensation provided to teachers in Piedmont. articles.text: Earl the Squirrel For the first time ever, I yield my column to a guest writer. He is a neighbor of mine who has a wealth of knowledge gained by perceptive experience and insight. He does not mince words, and will, therefore, say things that I never would. In sports, any outstanding player named Earl is knighted with the title “Earl the Pearl”. Please allow me to introduce my neighbor Earl the Squirrel. Q: Do you have any thoughts on the year 2020? Earl: Absolutely. I am glad you asked. 2020 began with every expectation of greatness. All the important musical organizations engaged the same shop – worn, completely predictable musical artistes. Those are the ones who bask in their own publicity but rarely live up to their press kits. The public appears to believe the publicity. Every performance gets a standing ovation. Q: How can you say this? Aren’t the top-notch performers better looking than ever before? Earl: Yep, that they are. The décolleté dresses women wear leave little to the imagination. Combined with leg-revealing skirts this makes their music more “all–encompassing“. Men simply can’t compete. So they eschew formal attire and stud their duds with safety pins or wear rabble-rousing shirts. It reminds me of the early days of the Russian revolution. Q: I try to avoid politics, but you opened the door. Isn’t revolution good? Earl: Mindless iconoclasm has its limits. Q: Well. I can see where this is going. Let me change the subject. Tell us about Michael Tilson Thomas, your friend from USC. Earl: Michael was the shining light in San Francisco for a long time. His final season was to be the best ever. The events of 2020 scuttled a beautiful season. But he won’t be forgotten. Q: And Beethoven and his 250th anniversary? Earl: He outlived his bad publicity. I read about him in the Piedmont Post of December 30. As soon as concerts begin again, we will hear more from him. Never fear. Q: Can you look into the future? Is our musical horizon a bright one? Earl: We need to get music education back in the schools big time. As I see it, the very existence of a healthy society depends on music education. The Greeks knew this. Why don’t our education administrators know the value of music? The cost is minimal but the societal rewards are great. I would even insist on music education in every prison. All humans have voices – so singing costs nothing. And I would call for community support. The Piedmont Center for the Arts has the right idea. Politicians could at least offer lip service – that would be a step in the right direction. I’d ask listeners to be enthusiastic, but also to listen critically. Sincere performers appreciate a standing ovation when it’s earned, not perfunctory. And finally, I’d encourage the audience to just come to concerts. It’s a lot of fun to be seen. Thanks, Earl. You have given me a lot to think about.
articles.title: Sidestepping controversy and a visit with Earl

articles.text: From Foolish Times My husband and I decided we didn’t want to have children. We’ll be telling them tonight at dinner. Ladies, there is a flea market event Saturday at the fairgrounds. It’s a good chance to get rid of those things not worth keeping. Bring your husbands. One of the greatest things about marriage is that, as both husband and father, I can say anything I want to around the house. Of course, no one pays the least bit of attention. My wife nudged me and said, “You weren’t even listening, were you?” I thought that was a strange way to start a conversation. I’ve been in a relationship with a guy for a couple of years, but I was never invited to his house. One time, I was in the area and decided to stop by. A girl answered the door. When I asked who she was, she said “You’re the one knocking on my door. Are you looking for my husband?” A husband is living proof that a wife can take a joke. I joined Bachelors Anonymous. Every time I feel like getting married they send a woman in curlers to my house to nag me. Drive Your Plow over the Bones of the Dead by Polish author Olga Tokarczuk was selected as the group’s March read. Earl the Squirrel By Joseph Gold For the first time ever, I yield my column to a guest writer. He is a neighbor of mine who has a wealth of knowledge gained by perceptive experience and insight. He does not mince words, and will, therefore, say things that I never would. In sports, any outstanding player named Earl is knighted with the title “Earl the Pearl”. Please allow me to introduce my neighbor Earl the Squirrel. Q: Do you have any thoughts on the year 2020? Earl: Absolutely. I am glad you asked. 2020 began with every expectation of greatness. All the important musical organizations engaged the same shop – worn, completely predictable musical artistes. Those are the ones who bask in their own publicity but rarely live up to their press kits. The public appears to believe the publicity. Every performance gets a standing ovation. Q: How can you say this? Aren’t the top-notch performers better looking than ever before? Earl: Yep, that they are. The décolleté dresses women wear leave little to the imagination. Combined with leg-revealing skirts this makes their music more “all–encompassing“. Men simply can’t compete. So they eschew formal attire and stud their duds with safety pins or wear rabble-rousing shirts. It reminds me of the early days of the Russian revolution. Q: I try to avoid politics, but you opened the door. Isn’t revolution good? Earl: Mindless iconoclasm has its limits. Q: Well. I can see where this is going. Let me change the subject. Tell us about Michael Tilson Thomas, your friend from USC. Earl: Michael was the shining light in San Francisco for a long time. His final season was to be the best ever. The events of 2020 scuttled a beautiful season. But he won’t be forgotten. Q: And Beethoven and his 250th anniversary? Earl: He outlived his bad publicity. I read about him in the Piedmont Post of December 30. As soon as concerts begin again, we will hear more from him. Never fear. Q: Can you look into the future? Is our musical horizon a bright one? Earl: We need to get music education back in the schools big time. As I see it, the very existence of a healthy society depends on music education. The Greeks knew this. Why don’t our education administrators know the value of music? The cost is minimal but the societal rewards are great. I would even insist on music education in every prison. All humans have voices – so singing costs nothing. And I would call for community support. The Piedmont Center for the Arts has the right idea. Politicians could at least offer lip service – that would be a step in the right direction. I’d ask listeners to be enthusiastic, but also to listen critically. Sincere performers appreciate a standing ovation when it’s earned, not perfunctory. And finally, I’d encourage the audience to just come to concerts. It’s a lot of fun to be seen. Thanks, Earl. You have given me a lot to think about. By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on January 4. Fourteen readers attended remotely to discuss the group’s January selection, How to be an Antiracist by Ibram X. Kendi. Participating in the discussion were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Jeri Lockhart, Margie Blodgett, Jen Cavenaugh, Swee Ling Chen, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. How to Be an Antiracist is a 2019 non-fiction book by American author and historian Ibram X. Kendi. The book presents concepts regarding racism and Kendi’s proposals for anti-racist individual actions and systemic policy changes. He defines a racist as anyone who supports “a racist policy through their actions or inaction.” He wants people who believe they are not racists to become “antiracists.” These are people who support ideas and policies affirming that “the racial groups are equals in all their apparent differences – that there is nothing right or wrong with any racial group.” For Kendi, there are no non-racists; there are only racists, people who allow racist ideas to proliferate without opposition, and antiracists, people who confront such ideas wherever they encounter them. Kendi presents ways of thinking about ourselves and others. Instead of working with the policies and system we have in place, he wants us to think about what an antiracist society would be, and how we can play an active role in creating it. For Kendi, “there is no such thing as a not-racist idea,” only “racist ideas and antiracist ideas.” Kendi tells the reader, “Every policy in How to Be an Antiracist, by Ibram Kendi, was the selection for January. every institution in every community in every nation is producing or sustaining either racial inequity or equity.” The former are racist policies and the latter are antiracist. The readers found the book to be a challenging read. Some found it to be like a textbook and its beginning to be somewhat dry and difficult to get through. However, the group felt the later chapters and the book overall provided an expanded understanding of how our society’s racial challenges can be viewed and addressed. Generally, the readers felt How to Be an Antiracist was an important and beneficial book to read. As a thought-provoking read, How to Be an Antiracist was the catalyst for a group discussion that expanded into personal experiences associated with privilege and injustice, as well as societal and local issues of inequality. The small number of educators of color in Piedmont schools was noted; as were the problems of recruiting them and the compensation provided to teachers in Piedmont. pages.text: Wednesday, January 13, 2021 21 Features Part 11 in a series By Will Adams Another important visual element of our built environment is signage. It is in many ways a lot like lighting, discussed in the last column. Both tend to stand out when done poorly and unrelated to their context. When designed well, both lighting and signage Signage seem to go unnoticed as they appear to fit right in, as if there were no other way they could have been designed. Besides providing necessary information to people on foot or in cars, appropriate signage can enhance and complement the architecture of a building or landscape of which it is a part. Walking around Piedmont, it is clear that the sensitive and understated use of signs pretty much everywhere contributes to the charm of the city. Like lighting, signage has both a functional requirement and an aesthetic character. Function is of course the first consideration: what is the sign’s purpose? And Photos by Will Adams The specific purpose of a sign and the people to whom it is directed should determine the design: the location, size, shape, text, images, and colors. There are usually numerous good alternatives. confirmation that the supposition was correct. Signage is often lighted. Internally illuminated signage has been done badly so often it is prohibited in many places because it is often coarse and annoying. Externally illuminated signage generally has a better opportunity for aesthetic success, provided that the signage is appropriate for the genre of architecture/site/ environs, and it is not over lit. In some cities very strict design review requirements for signs are problematic as they have resulted in a completely uniform, bland, lifeless array of signs, which are ironically hard to interpret or to decipher the required information. In my opinion, the best signs are those that are creative but restrained, and also reasonably varied. These seem to add life, interest and texture to the street and neighborhood. Clearly there is a huge difference in sign requirements for people walking around town versus those driving cars at various speeds. Unfortunately, often the size and use or purpose of signage is confused. articles.text: This might sound weird to some, but I believe that when we look back on 2020, at some point many of us will see what a gift that year was. It wouldn’t hurt to start looking for the gifts now. In life, we attract what we look for. What we pay attention to, is what we get more of, i.e.: where attention goes, energy flows. And that’s not to say we should bypass the very real, very scary, and very threatening situations so many are dealing with. I’m not suggesting that we turn a blind eye. It’s a both/and. We can look at this past year and we can feel the weight of it. A lot of us have deeply felt the grief and fear that so much threat and uncertainty have brought, not just because of Covid but also the impact we feel as a country and in our communities because of the political environment. The recent upheaval by extremists in our capitol, and the heartbreak over the social inequities of our country, with ongoing racism, and double standards that people of color continue to face, are awful and difficult things to contend with. So how do we also make space for the good when so much is going sideways? We can turn our attention toward what we do have control over and that is: Noticing what is good. This is the perspective I am choosing to look for when I reflect upon how 2020 impacted the world of interior design and construction. We can notice what has happened to us as we have slowed down, how things that seemed stressful, and inconvenient, like the supply chain breaking on various levels, forced us to get creative: to upcycle, recycle, and go local, to pivot. We were forced into a slowdown because the supply chain wasn’t gushing at full force as we have come to expect. There is a slowdown, and I am looking at it as a blessing of sorts. If you know me, you know I’ve been emphasizing thoughtful consumption all along, choosing local, choosing high quality, breaking our dependency on cheaply made products from far away. (I mean YOU, Amazon!) At the beginning of this world-wide slowing down, we all saw for the first time in a long time how there was clean air because the factories that pump out these quickly available, easily acquired, cheap products were forced to shut down. So now, after almost 12 months of slowing down, this is a good time to consider how this past year has changed our consuming habits. What if these changes are for the better? In the high-end design world, this trend towards artisanal, quality, and local was bypassed on a grand scale for decades by the quickfix model so many industries had adopted. But like the lessons taught for years by Alice Waters, food activist and one of my heroines, the Slow Food movement – the trend toward slow consumption – has taken a stronger foothold this past year. And not just with food. It’s happening in my industry too. I could not be more delighted. It is a political, ecological, economic, and community-supporting act to focus our buying habits in this way. In recent decades the Internet changed how we feel about instant gratification. Wanting things fast, wanting them now, next day free shipping, at the press of a button. I found myself having the responsibility to educate clients, set boundaries, and let them know it’s up to us to change the world. Every drop in the bucket counts. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. articles.text: An all-electric home is not as familiar as the increasingly popular electric car, but both innovations are important tools in the continued fight against climate change. Transportation is the No. 1 source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, followed closely by energy generation. Changing the way we use energy and drive can make a drastic change in emissions, both nationally and here in Piedmont. In an effort to reduce emissions stemming from energy usage, many California cities are advancing policies that encourage more electric appliances at home. In 2020, Berkeley banned natural gas in new buildings. Our other neighbor, Oakland, adopted a similar prohibition in December. Piedmont city staff introduced energy “reach codes” in 2020, which would reduce emissions coming from natural gas appliances over time. A second reading of the proposed reach codes will be brought to City Council in the future. Energy use in buildings is important because when a building is constructed, it generally remains standing for decades. A majority of Piedmont’s housing stock was constructed in the first half of the 20th century. Re-examining how we build and provide power in buildings and appliances can lead to big differences in emissions. Natural gas is less destructive than some other fossil fuels, but it still emits both carbon dioxide and methane when burned. Methane is more than 80 times more likely to trap heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, so policymakers are trying to reduce natural gas usage as much as possible. Having homeowners switch their natural gas appliances to electric would mean fewer methane emissions and more “clean” energy usage. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, January 13, 2021 Benefits of an all-electric home By Nate Redinbo An all-electric home is not as familiar as the increasingly popular electric car, but both innovations are important tools in the continued fight against climate change. Transportation is the No. 1 source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, followed closely by energy generation. Changing the way we use energy and drive can make a drastic change in emissions, both nationally and here in Piedmont. In an effort to reduce emissions stemming from energy usage, many California cities are advancing policies that encourage more electric appliances at home. In 2020, Berkeley banned natural gas in new buildings. Our other neighbor, Oakland, adopted a similar prohibition in December. Piedmont city staff introduced energy “reach codes” in 2020, which would reduce emissions coming from natural gas appliances over time. A second reading of the proposed reach codes will be brought to City Council in the future. Energy use in buildings is important because when a building is constructed, it generally remains standing for decades. A majority of Piedmont’s housing stock was constructed in the first half of the 20th century. Re-examining how we build and provide power in buildings and appliances can lead to big differences in emissions. Natural gas is less destructive than some other fossil fuels, but it still emits both carbon dioxide and methane when burned. Methane is more than 80 times more likely to trap heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, so policymakers are trying to reduce natural gas usage as much as possible. Having homeowners switch their natural gas appliances to electric would mean fewer methane emissions and more “clean” energy usage. As the electrical grid continues to get greener over time, it uses energy generated from “greener” sources, including solar and wind power. This means that when appliances are turned on, instead of using natural gas, they would be powered by increasingly “green” power plants. Not only are electric alternatives more efficient, they can also save energy in the long term in most climate zones, including Piedmont’s. One aspect of home electrification that confuses people is how to go about doing it. Because many people grew up with gas stoves and furnaces, fewer people have heard of electric heat pumps or induction cooktops. Fortunately, appliances are continuously improving and installing an electric appliance is easier than one might imagine. Electric cooktops were long considered inferior to gas stovetops, but now options like induction cooktops are safer, faster, and easier to control than their gas counterparts. Besides ease of use and cost, using electric appliances limits the dangers associated with natural gas use. Natural gas usage, especially in the kitchen, can release toxic gases such as formaldehyde and nitrogen dioxide, which generally can lead to poor indoor air quality. During a time of COVID, living in a healthy home and environment is especially important. Electrification is a key to achieving a healthy and safe environment. Nate Redinbo is with the Piedmont Planning and Building Department for one year as Piedmont’s Civic Spark fellow. He can be contacted at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: As California lags behind other states in COVID-19 vaccine distribution, Gov. Gavin Newsom has set a goal of administering 1 million doses by this weekend. To improve vaccination rates, mass drive-through vaccine distribution sites will be opening around the state, including one at the Oakland Coliseum. After discussions with the Oakland A’s and local healthcare providers, Alameda County officials will vote this week on opening a distribution site in the parking lot of the Coliseum. The date of the site’s opening has not been announced. The state is pushing to administer its stock of over 2.83 million doses of vaccine to healthcare workers and residents of longterm care facilities. “Those frontline workers — that’s why we want to vaccinate the vaccinators — so many of them are in those categories of vaccinators themselves, and those residents that are most vulnerable in these congregate facilities,” said Gov. Newsom in a press conference on Monday, January 11. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, California has administered 782,638 doses as of January 11. While California possesses the most doses in the nation, it is one of only eight states with a vaccine distribution rate below 2,000 doses per 100,000 residents. According to the state’s vaccine distribution framework, Alameda County is part of Region II, a grouping that includes a wide swath of coastal Northern California from Santa Clara County to Del Norte County at the Oregon border. In all of Region II, the narrowest dataset provided by California health officials right now, almost 199,000 vaccine doses have been administered as of Sunday, January 10. In mid-December, the Alameda County Department of Public Health began administering its first vaccine doses. California has prioritized vaccine distribution based on several broad categories. The people that are now receiving the vaccine are healthcare workers and residents of long-term care facilities, a category that counts an estimated 3 million people. Next in line are individuals 75 years of age or older as well as people working in education, childcare, emergency services, food, and agriculture. The state believes this tier will begin receiving doses later this month. After that, vaccines will be available to people aged 65 to 74 years and people working in fields including transportation, logistics, the industrial sector, the commercial sector and critical manufacturing. This tier also includes people living in congregate settings, like the homeless or those in prison. Next, probably in the spring, vaccines will be administered to people aged 50 to 64 as well as people aged 16 to 64 with underlying health conditions. People working in sectors like defense, energy, communications, finance, and government operations will also receive the vaccine. The state estimates that the vaccine will be widely available to the general public beyond these specific groups by the summer or fall, although health officials noted that the timeline is subject to change. California is administering two different vaccines for free, one manufactured by Pfizer and another by Moderna. Both vaccines were granted emergency use authorization by the Food and Drug Administration late last year. Importantly, both vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. As of now, there is no statewide registry to sign up to be vaccinated. Healthcare workers should contact their employers about when they will receive the vaccine, while residents in longterm care facilities should contact their caretaker.

articles.text: Piedmont Police officers parked in the Ace Hardware parking lot for traffic surveillance on Grand Avenue had a surprise visitor. At 7:34 p.m. on Thursday, January 7, in the nearly deserted parking lot, a white Hyundai Sonata entered the parking lot and parked behind the patrol vehicle. The Hyundai remained parked for about 15 minutes as the driver, Christopher Vargo, 32, a transient, got in and out of the vehicle several times. Vargo then took a backpack from the vehicle and started walking away. Unaware that the Hyundai had been stolen, the officers got out of their car and asked Vargo who he was, where he was going, and why he was leaving the vehicle in the lot. As the officers were talking with him, a black Toyota Prius pulled up and two people got out. The Prius driver said he was the owner of the Hyundai, which had been stolen 20 minutes earlier from 1800 Lakeshore Avenue. The police called for backup, and a third Piedmont police officer arrived. While one officer was questioning Vargo, he started walking away on Grand Avenue and onto Sunnyslope Avenue. As the officers told him to stop, he became non-compliant and began walking aggressively toward one officer, a female. Another officer tackled the suspect. Vargo was arrested and transported to Santa Rita jail for possession of a stolen vehicle and resisting arrest.
articles.title: Result: Tackled while running away; taken to jail

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, January 13, 2021 State pushes for mass COVID-19 vaccinations this weekend Oakland Coliseum parking lot likely to be used as one site By Barry Eitel As California lags behind other states in COVID-19 vaccine distribution, Gov. Gavin Newsom has set a goal of administering 1 million doses by this weekend. To improve vaccination rates, mass drive-through vaccine distribution sites will be opening around the state, including one at the Oakland Coliseum. After discussions with the Oakland A’s and local healthcare providers, Alameda County officials will vote this week on opening a distribution site in the parking lot of the Coliseum. The date of the site’s opening has not been announced. The state is pushing to administer its stock of over 2.83 million doses of vaccine to healthcare workers and residents of longterm care facilities. “Those frontline workers — that’s why we want to vaccinate the vaccinators — so many of them are in those categories of vaccinators themselves, and those residents that are most vulnerable in these congregate facilities,” said Gov. Newsom in a press conference on Monday, January 11. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, California has administered 782,638 doses as of January 11. While California possesses the most doses in the nation, it is one of only eight states with a vaccine distribution rate below 2,000 doses per 100,000 residents. According to the state’s vaccine distribution framework, Alameda County is part of Region II, a grouping that includes a wide swath of coastal Northern California from Santa Clara County to Del Norte County at the Oregon border. In all of Region II, the narrowest dataset provided by California health officials right now, almost 199,000 vaccine doses have been administered as of Sunday, January 10. In mid-December, the Alameda County Department of Public Health began administering its first vaccine doses. California has prioritized vaccine distribution based on several broad categories. The people that are now receiving the vaccine are healthcare workers and residents of long-term care facilities, a category that counts an estimated 3 million people. Next in line are individuals 75 years of age or older as well as people working in education, childcare, emergency services, food, and agriculture. The state believes this tier will begin receiving doses later this month. After that, vaccines will be available to people aged 65 to 74 years and people working in fields including transportation, logistics, the industrial sector, the commercial sector and critical manufacturing. This tier also includes people living in congregate settings, like the homeless or those in prison. Next, probably in the spring, vaccines will be administered to people aged 50 to 64 as well as people aged 16 to 64 with underlying health conditions. People working in sectors like defense, energy, communications, finance, and government operations will also receive the vaccine. The state estimates that the vaccine will be widely available to the general public beyond these specific groups by the summer or fall, although health officials noted that the timeline is subject to change. California is administering two different vaccines for free, one manufactured by Pfizer and another by Moderna. Both vaccines were granted emergency use authorization by the Food and Drug Administration late last year. Importantly, both vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. As of now, there is no statewide registry to sign up to be vaccinated. Healthcare workers should contact their employers about when they will receive the vaccine, while residents in longterm care facilities should contact their caretaker. articles.text: Editor: It is my pleasure to write in support of the Piedmont Center of the Arts and the renewal of their lease with the City. Having performed, presented, and attended performances at the PCA, I can say with emphatic certainty that it is a cultural gem in the heart of Piedmont, and I urge you to give them every consideration in this matter. I am a concert pianist, educator, founder and artistic director of the San Francisco International Piano Festival, and active member of arts organization boards throughout the Bay Area including Lieder Alive! and the San Francisco Conservatory’s Presidential Alumni Council. Having performed throughout the country and internationally in addition to dozens of venues throughout the Bay Area, I am particularly grateful for the experiences I have had at the PCA since I first became acquainted with it in 2016. I was invited by Harry Howe, whom I knew through Oakland Symphony, to attend the inaugural season of Piedmont Chamber Music Festival led by the Formosa String Quartet. The level of musicianship was truly first rate, international, and satisfying. It became clear to me that this venue was at the level of the music, and I tucked that experience away in my memory. In 2017, I launched the San Francisco International Piano Festival with support from Piedmont residents Craig and Letitia Casebeer. After establishing ourselves as the only international piano festival in the Bay Area, we chose PCA as the venue for our opening night program in 2018 and 2019. These evenings were great successes on every level, and the setting of the PCA was ideal. Sold-out crowds, open air atmosphere, visual art, and world class piano playing in a warm and approachable environment. I have performed at the PCA myself on a number of occasions and have always found it to be a gratifying experience. As a guest artist with Gold Coast Chamber Players, I played an all-Mozart concert that featured the Alexander String Quartet. The house Steinway is a warm and appropriately sized piano for the space, making it a perfect setting for chamber music both vocal and instrumental, solo piano, and masterclasses. The Center’s programming both visually, musically, and theatrically has contributed enormously to the community, and I look forward to seeing what they will do in their next decade of tenure. I recommend them without hesitation for renewal of their lease and am happy to speak with you directly if I can offer anything further to the process. –Jeffrey LaDeur, Founder, San Francisco Piano Festival
articles.title: In support of PCA lease extension with City

articles.text: St. Francis is known for that famous saying “preach the gospel, and if you have to, use words.” God is probably less concerned about what we believe and more concerned about the way we act. When we get right down to it, there are simply too many words flying around and not enough meaningful action. As Christians approach Easter, the celebration of Jesus’ resurrection, it is easy for us to get sidetracked by words in the form of creeds, liturgies and theologies. These provide enough words to suffocate the real story that was all about meaningful action. It’s in that context that I share what I consider to be an Easter Story. A few years ago, Elizabeth Gilbert, author of “Eat, Pray, Love”, wrote about an incident that changed her life. She was riding the midtown bus in New York City in evening rush hour traffic. The weather was the worst January had to offer, complete with sleet and gusting wind. To quote her, “It sucked”. The bus was moving at a crawl, tempting her to get out and walk, but the cold icy world she was staring at through the window paralyzed her. The depression in that mobile metal tomb was palpable. Then something happened. When they arrived at 10th Street, the bus driver turned to address his gathered congregation in the bus. He said: For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.
articles.title: When meaningful action trumps words

The bus was moving at a crawl, tempting her to get out and walk, but the cold icy world she was staring at through the window paralyzed her. The depression in that mobile metal tomb was palpable. Then something happened. When they arrived at 10th Street, the bus driver turned to address his gathered congregation in the bus. He said: Sheltering in place? Where in the World are You? articles.text: A program that lets California residents know if they have been exposed to COVID-19 was made available statewide on December 10. The smartphone application, CA Notify, is available on all iPhones and Android devices. G av i n Ne w s o m announced the launch of CA Notify during a press conference last week when the application officially went live across the “Throughout this pandemic we have tapped California’s talent pool to fight this virus, and that includes working with tech innovators like Apple and Google,” said Gov. Newsom. “CA Notify will help slow the spread by alerting those who opt in to receive an alert if they’ve come into contact with someone who has tested positive. The process is private, anonymous and secure, and is one of the many tools in the state’s data-driven approach to help reduce the spread.” The program is voluntary and is not defined as contact tracing. It notifies users who have been in close contact with another user who has opted into the system and tested positive for the virus. When individuals voluntarily activate CA Notify, the tool uses Bluetooth technology to exchange random codes between phones without revealing the user’s idenIf a CA Notify user tests positive for COVID-19, they will receive a verification code to plug into the app, if they choose. Any other CA Notify users who have been within six feet for 15 minutes or more of the COVID-19 positive individual will get an anonymous notification of possiA new iPhone application alerts users of possible COVID-19 exposure. ble exposure. Users who have tested positive will get a text from the California Department of Public Health with a code, which they can enter into the CA Notify application, triggering an alert to phones of people who may have been exposed in the previous 14 days. Android users can download CA Notify through the application store. Apple iPhone users simply need to activate the built-in feature. It is accessible by enabling “exposure notifications” in the settings area of the device. “When combined with other actions like wearing masks and physical distancing, CA Notify can help curb the transmission of COVID-19,” said Dr. Mark Gahly, California Health and Human Services Secretary. “Every day that is saved in alerting others of a possible exposure, is a day that a possibly infectious person can begin self-quarantine and reduce the spread. This technology is another way for Californians to take proactive steps to keep themselves, their loved ones and their communities safe.” California launched a pilot of CA Notify in September for university students, staff and faculty at UC San Diego and UC San Francisco, and then later to other UC campuses in mid-November. The university system estimates that more than 250,000 people are now utilizing the application and technology. “Our pilot experience starting at UC San Diego and expanding to other UC campuses showed this technology was effective in identifying exposed individuals early for quarantine and testing, and helping keep our communities as safe as possible,” said Christopher Longhurst, MD, chief information officer of UC San Diego Health. “This free and reliable smartphone technology can help all Californians. As we enter a new, and hopefully final, surge in the pandemic, now more than ever is the time to put every possible tool to use to slow the spread of the virus.” For more information, see: CaNotify.ca.gov and Covid19. ca.gov.
articles.title: COVID exposure app, CA Notify, now available

articles.text: UCSF epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford. The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host another virtual forum with internationally renowned epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford on Wednesday, January 13 at 4 p.m. Rutherford last spoke at a LWV forum in May and answered questions on the efficacy of mask-wearing and vaccine availability. Next week’s forum aims to explore the epidemiologist’s predictions for the course of the COVID-19 virus in 2021 and answer questions about availability and distribution of the vaccine. Rutherford, a Piedmont resident, has been instrumental in keeping the Bay Area abreast on COVID-19 related concerns and is quoted as an expert source in nationwide media outlets. The virtual forum is entitled “COVID-19 Update: Are We Any Closer to the End?” and will focus on when life can return to “normal” after nearly a year of lockdowns. There will be a question-and-answer portion of the forum after a presentation. Viewers can submit their own questions directly in the forum. Rutherford leads the Global Strategic Information group within University of California (UCSF), San Francisco’s Institute for Global Health Sciences. He is the Salvatore Pablo Lucia Professor of Epidemiology, Preventive Medicine, Pediatrics and History; Head of the Division of Infectious Disease and Global Epidemiology in the Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics in School of Medicine at UCSF and Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration in the School of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley. Registration is not required for the event. You can join the Zoom forum at 4 p.m. on January 13 online by clicking: https:// us02web.zoom.us/j/87327219707? pwd=TlVxQVN5cGFIczFqcU. “That’s when we retained Dude’s grammar school to tackle our programing.”
articles.title: Dr. George Rutherford returns for COVID discussion on Jan. 13

articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved a renewal of the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the city and the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office for mutual aid services, specifically for critical incident response and forensic services. The renewal was approved at a December 21 city council meeting. Piedmont Police Department (PPD) engaged the County to renew both the forensic services and critical incident MOUs. The city has maintained multi-year agreements for the sheriff’s office to provide forensic services for major crime scenes and mutual aid response for critical incidents in the city of Piedmont. The services are provided as needed. The prior agreement expired on March 2, 2020. A staff report, authored by City Administrator Sara Lillevand, explained that the addition of the investigative services for officer-involved shootings and in-custody deaths “is important to ensure such investigations are objective, thorough and fair. Officer-involved shootings and in-custody deaths are typically investigated by investigators of the jurisdiction within which the event occurred and by investigators with the local district attorney’s office.” Due to the small size of the city’s police department, resources for conducting these investigations are limited and could be further impacted if the investigators responsible for conducting such investigations are the involved officers. The criminal investigation of an officer’s actions in an officer-involved shooting or in-custody death conducted by the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office provides for independent investigations, which leverages the expertise, experience, and resources of both offices: county and municipal. Both the Piedmont Police Department and Alameda County Sheriff’s Office have agreed to a two-year renewal, which will expire on December 31, 2022, with possible extensions based

articles.text: The California Office of the Small Business Advocate has announced that the deadline to submit applications for the first round of Small Business COVID- 19 Relief Grant Program funding has been extended from January 8 to Wednesday, January 13. The program opened on December 30, and thousands of applications have been received since then. The high volume of applications has caused problems for some small business owners who are trying to access the program. Officials said the program “is not first-come, first-served, nor a rolling approval process,” and that “all applications will be reviewed following the now-extended application deadline.” Through the Alameda County CARES Grant Program, more than 1,900 grants have been issued to small, local businesses. In the last month, the Alameda County Board of Supervisors redirected up to $8 million in CARES Act funds to assist small businesses in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. To learn more about grant requirements and eligibility, visit carereliefgrant.com.
articles.title: State extends deadline for COVID relief grant applications

articles.text: Film directors Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht. No one at Camp Jened could’ve imagined that those summers in the woods together would be the beginnings of a revolution. Just down the road from Woodstock, Camp Jened was a camp for disabled teens. Directors Nicole Newnham, a local resident who lives near Piedmont Avenue, and Jim LeBrecht deliver a rousing film about a group of campers turned activists who shaped the future of the disability rights movement and changed accessibility legislation for everyone. Filled with the spirit, music, and humor of the era, Newnham and LeBrecht speak firsthand to the seeds of empowerment that were planted at Camp Jened. Footage from 1971 captures how the campers were finally seen beyond their disabilities. Milestones in the disability-rights movement intersect with LeBrecht’s personal story and the stories of several Camp Jened alums, including then-counselor Judy Heumann. She went on to play an indispensable role in historic protests leading to the Americans with Disabilities Act. Crip Camp shines a bright light on an overlooked civil-rights battle. Crip Camp acquires breadth and seriousness that neither its early scenes nor its playfully confrontational title suggest. As we follow campers into direct actions, occupations and unsparing encounters with government officials, the film’s approach remains anecdotal and emotional. Footage of a twenty-something Judy Heumann reproaching Eugene Eidenberg from the U.S. Department of Health is a master class in focused, righteous rage. Heumann went on to advise Presidents Clinton and Obama. Crip Camp opened the Sundance Film Festival and took home the Audience Award as Best Documentary. The film was produced by Barack and Michelle Obama under their production company Higher Ground. Join he Piedmont Appreciating Diversity film series on Zoom on January 7 from 5-6 p.m. with a screening and moderated discussion followed by a discussion with the co-directors, LeBrecht and Newnham. For more information see the website www.diversityfilmseries. org for the January 7 event Zoom link. Or contact Julie at 510 599- 9227 (julie@diversityfilmseries. org). The Appreciating Film Series is co-sponsored by the Piedmont City Council, Piedmont Adult School, Piedmont Anti-Racism Diversity Committee, and the League of Women Voters Piedmont.
articles.title: Diversity Film Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution to be shown January 7

articles.text: Samples of questions asked on a mental health survey sent to all Piedmont students in September last year. Results were not flattering and were discussed publicly only on December 15. which they were asked to identify one of four pictures depicting their mood. For example, in school connectedness, one question was “I am treated with respect at my school.” Students in grades 6-12 were able to respond by selecting: Almost always, Often, Sometimes, or Never. Student responses were scored by Piedmont school psychologists and “normed” at UC Berkeley. Students scoring in the highest one-sixth of responses were defined as “at-risk,” and the top one percentile were deemed “clinically significant.” The Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire found that approximately 14 percent of elementary school students registered in the at-risk category, and less than 1 percent of responses were deemed clinically significant. At Piedmont Middle School, approximately 13 percent of the student responses fell into the category of at-risk, but four percent showed the very troubling results defined as clinically significant. At Millennium High where 46 students took the survey, 14 percent were deemed at-risk and 2 percent were clinically significant. PHS found 13 percent of students tested as at-risk while 3 percent scoring as clinically significant. Joy of Learning and School Connectedness showed up as the biggest concerns at both Havens and Wildwood Elementary schools. Part Two The second part of the survey used a different surveying instrument, called Youth Internalizing and Externalizing Problems Screener (YIEPS). Its goal was to help understand how students are processing and expressing stress caused by: Pandemic Online classes Altered social lives Externalizing Externalizing was defined as externally-focused behavioral symptoms including aggression, problems of conduct, something called “oppositionality,” hyper activity, and problems of attention. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s English Department has selected Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate for its 11th annual community read project, known as Readmont. Klein argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. A limited number of copies will be available for checkout at the PHS library when school reopens sometime in January. Interested readers can reserve a copy by contacting Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Books are available for purchase at A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair Village, where a 20% discount is being offered. Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at the high school starting in February and continuing through April. For more information, contact Beth Black, PHS English Department Chair at bblack@piedmont. k12.ca.us.
articles.title: Readmont selects book on climate change

Samples of questions asked on a mental health survey sent to all Piedmont students in September last year. Results were not flattering and were discussed publicly only on December 15. which they were asked to identify one of four pictures depicting their mood. For example, in school connectedness, one question was “I am treated with respect at my school.” Students in grades 6-12 were able to respond by selecting: Almost always, Often, Sometimes, or Never. Student responses were scored by Piedmont school psychologists and “normed” at UC Berkeley. Students scoring in the highest one-sixth of responses were defined as “at-risk,” and the top one percentile were deemed “clinically significant.” The Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire found that approximately 14 percent of elementary school students registered in the at-risk category, and less than 1 percent of responses were deemed clinically significant. At Piedmont Middle School, approximately 13 percent of the student responses fell into the category of at-risk, but four percent showed the very troubling results defined as clinically significant. At Millennium High where 46 students took the survey, 14 percent were deemed at-risk and 2 percent were clinically significant. PHS found 13 percent of students tested as at-risk while 3 percent scoring as clinically significant. Joy of Learning and School Connectedness showed up as the biggest concerns at both Havens and Wildwood Elementary schools. Part Two The second part of the survey used a different surveying instrument, called Youth Internalizing and Externalizing Problems Screener (YIEPS). Its goal was to help understand how students are processing and expressing stress caused by: Pandemic Online classes Altered social lives Externalizing Externalizing was defined as externally-focused behavioral symptoms including aggression, problems of conduct, something called “oppositionality,” hyper activity, and problems of attention. Ten questions were asked to calculate the degree to which students are acting out their struggles. Among elementary students, 15 percent fell into the at-risk category for externalizing but with no clinically significant results. At the middle school (grades 6-8) externalizing surveys found 12 percent to be at-risk and 6 percent of students falling into the clinically significant category. Millennium’s externalizing survey showed that 17 percent were at-risk and 4 percent were clinically significant. Results among Piedmont High School students indicated that 10 percent of all students were at-risk, and 5 percent were clinically significant. Internalizing Ten more questions were designed to understand internally-focused behavior, such as: • being nervous or irritable • being withdrawn • eating more or less than usual • feeling sad, lonely or afraid These questions were not asked of elementary school students. Results from the middle school showed that 15 percent were at-risk, and 5 percent were clinically significant. Millennium results recorded a total of 22 percent of its students internalizing at an at-risk level and 4 percent clinically significant. Piedmont High had 14 percent of its student in the at-risk category for internalizing, and 4 percent classified as clinically significant. “There are definitely more students in the at-risk category than had been expected,” said Curriculum Director Wozniak. The most concerning item and biggest takeaway from the screener was the acknowledgement of the levels of “clinically significant” results, which the district had anticipated to only be 1 percent. The initial presentation to school board members on December 15 was murky and lacked clarity. Wozniak apologized at the end of the presentation. “It was late afternoon that I found out I was going to be the one explaining the data points. I of course had looked at [them], but not at any way close to the level the school psychologists had been studying these. I apologize for the lack of clarity in some of these explanations,” she said. “[The screener results are] exactly what we have been afraid of. I don’t know how it is going to unfold, but what we definitely need to do is find creative ways to bring our kids together in some kind of in-person communities in some way, even if it is not necessarily in a classroom,” said board member Amal Smith. Since the survey was non-confidential, counselors and teachers have been able to contact students and parents about the troubling responses. The counselors at each school have their hands full. “The truth is, [with] these numbers and only 40 percent FTE [full-time employees] at Beach and Wildwood [for counselors], you just cannot service and meet with students one on one every week,” she said. Board Vice-President Megan Pillsbury brought up a caveat to the non-confidential nature of the screener. “I was curious how it was framed, to the high school students especially. What were students told in regards to how and what questions were going to be used? I am just thinking with high school students, they would be savvy about ‘what are you trying to get at here?’,” Pillsbury said. Because students’ names were recorded on the surveys, a question to be asked could be if students “internalized” their stress on the screener itself and did not report it. MHS principal Shannon Fierro, who has been reviewing and coding the raw data for her students, said she does not see the lack of anonymity as a concern, but as a strength. “I do not get the sense that because students knew the data was connected to them, that broadly they shied away from being honest about it. There were quite a few students that were endorsing high levels of stress, anxiety and depression. It seems they were kind of saying, ‘Yeah, thanks for asking, come talk to me about it’,” Fierro said. Overall, a major concern is the delay in reporting the numbers to the public and to students and parents. Why did it take more than two months to tally, analyze and report the data? The school board specifically made a priority of social-emotional and mental health when they revised the Learning Continuity Plan for this year. Now January, over three months after the survey was sent and with California now the epicenter of the pandemic, Piedmont families are still waiting for a comprehensive explanation from the School Superintendent and Curriculum Director on the depth of the mental health problems affecting students throughout the district. The screener will be given out again in January or February, and another time in the spring. READ IT IN THE POST
