On December 31, Chabot Space and Science Center continued its 20-year tradition of a New Year’s Eve Balloon Drop. This time however, the festivities took place on Zoom. In prior years balloons would fall from Chabot’s entry way atrium every hour celebrating January 1 across the globe. Kids would line up and count down until the top of each hour inundated them with balloons cascading from above. This year 160 families tuned into the event, which took place from 11 a.m. to 12 noon on Thursday, December 31. The celebration culminated as a half world away, people in Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan were celebrating the first day of 2021. When the clock struck 12:00 hundreds of colorful, biodegradable balloons rained down from above for participants to watch on their screens. To spice up the event, noise makers, bubbles and a STEM Activity Kit was shipped to registered participants. Virtual Activity Guides were also included with all tickets purchased. Chabot New Year’s Eve revelers got to participate in many activities on the final day of 2020. Chabot’s High School Galaxy Explorers led a Solar Modeling activity, a Mars Lander activity and a Build your own Catapult activity. Nano@Stanford also conducted a magnet activity. Fun was had by all and time flew by, so much so that a couple of activities needed to be saved for the new year. The activity

articles.text: OTR/L January marks the midway point for the 2020-2021 school calendar. This is a perfect time to revisit your student’s home workspace as the continuation of some form of distance learning is highly likely. Setting up the best workspace both from an ergonomic and sensory framework will support participation and success. Dedicated work space First and foremost, does your student have a dedicated workspace? From my observations during classroom synchronized lessons, the majority of students have a dedicated and appropriate workspace. However, popups of couches and coffee tables as workspaces are occasionally seen. Best practice is to always work at a desk, folding table or kitchen/dining table as this alerts the brain that it is “work time” and not “chill time.” Furniture Second, how does the chair and desk/table fit? Poor posture as a result of an ill fit can lead to fatigue and discomfort which ultimately adversely impacts attention and focus. Remember hips, knees and elbows at 90-90-90. When seated, feet should be flat on the floor with knees and hips at 90 degrees. If feet are dangling, posture is compromised. A footstool or stacked books can do the trick. Forearms should rest on the tabletop with elbows at or slightly near a 90-degree angle. And ideally, the computer screen should be at eye level to prevent neck strain. Students can elevate their Chromebooks on a cardboard box when viewing a class. Investing in an external keyboard will allow the Chromebook to remain at eye level while working. Finding the best chair Third, students are now sitting for prolonged periods of time. Finding the right seating option for support and comfort is a must. Office chairs are an easy answer. They offer an adjustable height, cushion and back support and they swivel and rock for those that need more movement for self-regulation. For a regular straight back chair, consider purchasing a seat cushion designed to address both improved posture and comfort. Examples include the highly rated grid seat cushion by Purple and the Tempur-Pedic Memory Foam seat. However, regular straightbacked chairs are easily outfitted with pillows for comfort and height adjustment. Finally, take time to examine the sensory environment that your student is working in by completing an Environmental Sensory Scan. This will help to identify and remedy any sensory challenges that may be present. Environmental sensory stimuli, such as visual or auditory input, can be overwhelming, making your student work harder to process, organize and adapt to the external sensory input before they can even attempt to attend a synchronized class lesson. With your student, sit in the space and notice by looking and listening. What do they hear in the room, a nearby room or outside? What do they notice visually? For example, lighting, clutter or the level of activity in the room? Identify what is distracting and/or bothersome and make changes to the sensory environment. Examples of simple environmental auditory and visual sensory strategies include: external headphones; set Chromebook volume to preferred level; close windows or adjacent door; adjust natural and/or artificial lighting sources; use a cardboard trifold barrier; face the desk toward a wall; reduce visual clutter on and around workspace. With these tips and strategies, let’s welcome 2021 with renewed spirits and an ergonomic and sensory smart workspace that supports participation and success! Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Thinking Outside The Classroom Time to revisit your student’s home workspace

articles.text: I can’t wait till I have kids and they start learning about 2020 and ask me all kind of questions. That’s when I’ll just stare off into the distance and begin my story, while my husband sits in the back nodding slowly and occasionally adding a random fact. They’ll have to read an entire textbook on 2020, because we all know that a section isn’t going to cover everything about the historic year. I can imagine some of the questions on tests: What happened in 2020? 1) Murder hornets 2) California and Australia nearly burned to the ground 3) A pandemic halted the world 4) An American president tried to overturn election results 5) All of the above. At least that god-awful year is over. Going into 2021 isn’t going to fix our problems, but the way I look at it, we have a clean slate – a chance to start over. Thanks to the power of the people we got Joseph Biden as our 46th president. Now with a new federal government we at least have a renewed hope for a solid COVID task force that relies on science and experience. But no matter how good he might be, the president alone can’t make all our problems go away. Everyone needs to do their part to help bring the U.S. back to the stature it used to have in the world. First of all, we need to face the oncoming climate crisis that could potentially be devastating to the planet and the human race. Look around you. It’s December in California and you can walk around in lightweight clothing and not be cold. Right now, we should be having rain all the time, but it’s only rained three times since summer. We can do our part to reverse climate change by making small changes in our everyday lives. For example, we can stop buying fast fashion because it uses huge amounts of fossil fuel to make the clothes, and it generates hundreds of thousands of pounds of trash. You can support local businesses because they don’t need to transport their goods from halfway across the world, generating massive amounts of pollution. You can refuse to buy goods from companies that are known to be hurting our environment. Just google and the list will come up. You can also support an environmental cause like Saving the Arctic. The Arctic is in danger of being one of the last safe havens for animals as it is exploited for oil. You can help by signing a petition to help stop this. Go to protectthearctic.org and do your part to help. Another thing that you can do is take action for a cause you believe in. For instance, if you have a cause, you can start a club at school. No drastic measures are required for there to be an impact. You could even make posters and hang them around your school to show your support. Even the smallest change can help. Although 2020 seemed like a year without any good moments, it showed us that there are so many things that need to be fixed. It showed us how bad things had gotten over the last decade in terms of the climate, racial issues, and political controversies. But as Gen Z, it’s up to us to step up and take charge of our future. I believe we have everything it takes to make a world that is safe and stable. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.
articles.title: Look out, 2021 – here we come

Laurel Sarfan earns PhD at Miami University Laurel Sarfan, a Piedmont High graduate, was among more than 500 students from Miami University who received degrees during the summer semester of 2020. Sarfan, graduated with a Doctor of Philosophy in Psychology. Nationally recognized as one of the most outstanding undergraduate institutions, Miami University is a public university located in Oxford, Ohio. With a student body of nearly 19,000, Miami effectively combines a wide range of strong academic programs with faculty who love to teach and the personal attention ordinarily found only at much smaller institutions. 3 Piedmont alums on Dean’s List at Vermont Piedmont High School alums Rachel Elliott, Clara Feldman, and Maggie Lucas were named to the Dean’s List at the University of Vermont To be named to the Dean’s List, students must have a gradepoint average of 3.0 or better and rank in the top 20 percent of their class in their respective college or school. Located in Burlington, the University of Vermont has worked since its founding in 1791 to move humankind forward. It is one of the nation’s most vibrant small cities and top college towns. It is a Public Ivy and top 100 national research university with 10,700 undergraduate students and 1,627 graduate students. 4 from Piedmont on Colgate Dean’s List Four Piedmont students were named to the Dean’s List at Colgate University for the spring semester in 2020. Students who received a term grade point average of 3.6 or higher while completing at least three courses for a conventional letter grade earned the Dean’s Award with Distinction. Tucke Backer, Political Science major Colin Dixon, Physics major Emily Yu, Social Sciences major Katherine Yu, Sociology major Located in upstate New York in Hamilton, Colgate is a leading university for students who want classes with rigor, faculty with passion, and confidence in knowing they will learn how to thrive in work and life. Colgate offers 56 majors and supports 25 Division I athletic teams on a campus of about 3,000 students in central New York. Mueller, Pehanick on Oregon State honor roll Piedmont alums Sebastian Mueller and Madison Pehanick were named to the Scholastic Honor Roll for the Fall term at Oregon State University. Mueller is a senior majoring in Environmental Sciences. Pehanick, also a senior, is majoring in Digital Communication Arts. They were among 8400 students earning at least a 3.50 GPA. To be on the Honor Roll, students must carry at least 12 graded hours of course work. Located in Corvallis, Oregon State University has more than 31,000 students from across the globe, with programs operating in every Oregon county. Oregon State receives more research funding than all of the state’s comprehensive public universities combined. OSU has a main campus in Corvallis, a second campus in Bend, and a marine research center in Newport. Gilliland on Dean’s List at Belmont Chelsea Gilliland qualified for the Fall 2020 Dean’s List at Belmont University in Nashville, Tennessee. Eligibility is based on a minimum course load of 12 hours and a quality grade point average of 3.5. Belmont University has an enrollment of 8,200 students from every state and 28 countries. Nationally ranked and consistently recognized by U.S. News & World Report for its innovation and commitment to teaching, Belmont brings together the best of liberal arts and professional education in a Christian community of learning and service. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Cynthia Kane is offering a new course through the Adult School designed for grandparents of all ages. Gather virtually with other grandparents to explore how it feels to have a new baby in the family, and to navigate the joys and challenges of a role that’s completely new to you, yet remarkably familiar. What has changed and what hasn’t in the world of childrearing? How does the pandemic affect your experience and your family’s daily routine? Discover ways to strengthen family ineractions through improved communication. We will review current child health and safety recommendations and have time to share gradnparenting experiences in a safe and confidential space.. The course is online and is scheduled for two sessions, with four classes each. Session 1: Saturdays, January 23 to February 13; 11:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Session 2: Saturdays, February 27 to March 20, same time The fee is $60 per session. To register, see: https://piedmontadultschool.asapconnected.com/#CourseID=238892. Instructor Bio Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. She has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership, and now works exclusively with grandparents and their families. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, education, and support for grandparents, particularly those providing care for grandchildren. Her website, https://itstheirturn. com, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

Right now, Lins is only eligible to race in 25-meter pools. With the global pandemic, it’s been a matter of finding time to just put his skills into use. “To get an Olympic Trials cut, it must be earned in long-course meter pools. We’re racing in 25-yard pools during the winter season, and the only way to race in a sanctioned 50-meter pool is to qualify for Junior Nationals in Texas. articles.text: Photo courtesy of NY Post But Niners’ fans’ minds are likely less focused on who will command its talented young group of defenders and more concentrated on how coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch will approach the freeagent market and 2021 NFL Draft. As we had said throughout the season, the elephant in the room is quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo. We’re not doubting Shanahan, who already declared Jimmy G his starter for next season, but the draft is certainly a high likeliGaroppolo’s $25 million salary in 2021 makes him an obvious restructure candidate given the 49ers’ only have $20 million in cap space and have several pricey free-agents set to hit the market, like left tackle Trent Williams, cornerback Richard Sherman, defensive end Solomon Thomas, safety Jaquiski Tartt, and running backs Tevin Coleman and Jeff Wilson. The 49ers are likely to only sign Williams, and possibly one more of their impending freeagents, like Thomas. Signing a free-agent quarterback to compete with Garoppolo doesn’t make sense. Sitting at No. 12 overall in the 2021 NFL Draft doesn’t do San Francisco many favors when considering their options at quarterback. The top three college quarterbacks – Clemson’s Trevor Lawrence, Ohio State’s Justin Fields, and BYU’s Zach Wilson – should be off the board by the time the 49ers have their pick at No. 12. That leaves North Dakota State’s Trey Lance as the logical suit for the 49ers, but it could require Lynch trading up into the top-10 to grab him. The 49ers only have one second-round pick and none in the third round, meaning not much capital is available at this moment. However, SF will gain a thirdround pick for Sherman once he signs with a new team on the open market, while Thomas and Tartt could land contracts that would award third-round compensatory selections as well—which could become trade-bait for the 49ers’ front office. A wildcard option? The Jets may listen to lowball offers for quarterback Sam Darnold, who has a year left on his rookie contract. Over to the Raiders The Raiders’ biggest task is starting its offseason with a strong hire at defensive coordinator. They have already requested interviews with Chargers DC Will Las Vegas part ways with quarterback Derek Carr this offseason to start to rebuild their offense? Gus Bradley, Falcons’ interim HC Raheem Morris, and Rams’ assistant Joe Barry. Coach Jon Gruden showed he’s still an offensive guru. However, there was something so average about the Raiders this year, and they squandered their playoff chances against the Falcons, Dolphins, and Colts. Raiders QB Derek Carr had his best statistical year in the league with 4,103 passing yards, 27 touchdowns, and nine interceptions. But could he become trade bait, once again? The odds are currently favoring Carr returning as the team’s starting quarterback, but you can never count out Gruden and GM Mike Mayock pulling off an unexpected move. Carr’s been an offseason trade rumor for the past two years, and with two years and $40 million left on his deal, Las Vegas will have to answer this question: start its rebuild now and trade him, or ride out Carr’s contract.

The announcement was not accompanied by any definitive plan. All high school spors in California has been discontiued since August due to COVID-19. The State declared that some sports can start as planned for counties in the widespread Purple Tier. Those sports would include Cross Country, Tennis, Golf, Swimming, and Track & Field. This means that the cross country program will be the first sport to return. It currently is the only sport given clearance. Tennis, golf, swimming, and track are scheduled for Season 2, from March to June. Under the current CIF framework, cross country would behin competition on January 27 and the season would run until March 27. However, both the North Coast section championship meet at Haywards High and th eState Meet in Fresno have been canceled. “Everyone in California wants students to be able to return to in-person learning, sports, and all other co-curricular activities that are so important for their physical and mental wellbeing,” wrote CIF executive director Ronald Nocetti in a press release. “As COVID-19 transmission rates are rising significantly in California, communities across the state must continue to take measures to limit the spread of the virus. This is the way to ensure the best chance for CIF competition to commence by January 25, as allowed by the guidance from the California Department of Public Health. State agencies will continue to monitor epidemiological trends.” The CIF gave its first indication since March 2020 that inter-scholastic competition will be permitted. For Cross Country, that means events between schools will be allowed if both teams are located in Alameda County or on bordering counties—meaning PHS should be eligible to compete with schools from Contra Costa County, San Mateo County, Marin County, and Santa Clara County if they gain clearance. “Competitions, meets, races, or similar events are authorized only if (a) both teams are located in the same county and the sport is authorized, or (b) teams are located in immediately bordering counties and the sport is authorized in both counties,” wrote the CIF. The CIF also intends on amending rules for cross country, swimming, and golf to allow events with more than two schools. “Any tournaments or events that involve more than two teams are not currently permitted in California. Exceptions may be made, with authorization from the local health department, for the following sports where individual competitors from multiple teams are routine: track and field; cross-country; golf; skiing and snowboarding; tennis; and swimming/diving,” announced the CIF.
articles.title: CIF announces proposed plan for sports by Jan. 25

articles.text: Big Basin State Park’s relief efforts were given a big boost with Sempervirens Fund and Save the Redwoods League announcing that they have raised $543,000 in donations to help the park’s restoration following the devastating CZU Complex fire in August. Both organizations have supported Big Basin, California’s oldest state park, since its founding in 1902. On Decemer 26 they jointly announced that $200,000 will be directed toward staffing and equipment costs for removing trees deemed hazardous. “State Parks is grateful for this outpouring of support and the ongoing partnership with people who care so deeply about Big Basin,” said Chris Spohrer, Santa Cruz District Superintendent for California State Parks. “This initial funding will allow us to access the backcountry, inventory damages, continue hazard mitigation and take the first steps toward recovery.” Park officials added that the first phase of their recovery operation will allow them to prepare for winter storms, and allow deeper access to evaluate the total damage caused by the wildfire. “We are eager to visit Big Basin again, and that begins with clearing the way for a safe park to emerge from the wildfire’s aftermath,” said Sempervirens Fund executive director Sara Barth. “State parks can be lighter on the land, have more resilient infrastructure and be Photo courtesy of Los Angeles Times An initial $200,000 endowment will go toward removing hazardous trees in Big Basin State Park. Photo courtesy of San Mateo County The CZU Complex fire covered 86,509 acres of the San Mateo and Santa Cruz mountains. Photo courtesy of Sempervirens.org The Sempervirens Fund and Save the Redwoods League raised $543,000 for the restoration of Big Basin State Park which was severely damaged during the CZU Complex fire in August. welcoming and inclusive for all, and Big Basin can lead the way. We are grateful for the generosity of our donors, and to Save the Redwoods League for joining us in this effort and to California State Parks for their thoughtful approach to recovery,” she said. The 86,509-acre wildfire destroyed nearly all the buildings and campgrounds in Big Basin State Park, including its historic Ranger Station and Visitor Center. The funding will help rebuild facilities and operations. In November, park officials stated that it will take at least one year merely to determine the full scope of damage and plan for cleanup projects. “Bridges are out, trees are down across trails, hazard trees are being identified. Access is extremely difficult,” said California State Parks senior environmental scientist Joanne Kerbavaz. Specialists have mentioned time and again that the fire will enable heat-sensitive pine cones to sprout seeds. Although some redwood trees have been destroyed, the bark provided a natural resilience to the blaze. Save the Redwoods League CEO Sam Hodder said that given the larger picture, Big Basin’s trees are doing well. “We are encouraged by the resilience that the redwood forest in Big Basin is already showing,” he said. “We look forward to working closely with our longtime partners Sempervirens Fund and California State Parks to reimagine and rebuild the state’s original redwood park for a 21st-century California – to create a visitor experience that will be welcoming and resonant to our full community.” For more information on the Big Basin State Park recovery fund, visit www.Sempervirens. org/redwoods-recovery.
articles.title: $543,000 raised for Big Basin State Park recovery

pages.text: Wednesday, January 6, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON Five Bay Area rainy day hikes available to all By Jonathan Comeaux With some rain forecast for the week ahead, looking out the window might be discouraging for some hikers. But luckily for us in the Bay Area, there is a wealth of parks to choose from where hiking is highly enjoyable, and hikers are kept nearly dry thanks to large canopies of trees lining the hiking trails. So, grab your rain gear, hiking boots, and consider this group of five areas where you can enjoy the wet weather. • Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve was our No. 9 ranked hike in 2020. We visited it on a rainy day last May, and a canopy of California Bay Laurels, Redwood trees, and Manzanitas made it an ideal, brief 3.4-mile loop. East Bay Regional Parks District calls Huckleberry an “ecological gem” with its year-round display of blossoming plants. Manzanita trees, with their vibrant red burls, are currently on Joaquin Miller Park also has towering redwood trees to help provide overhead cover during rain. Purisima Creek Redwood Preserve has a vast amount of redwood trees, some much older than those in the East Bay Hills. full winter display. To see a list of all plants currently blooming in East Bay Regional Parks, see their website at: ebparks.org. • Redwood Regional Park A local favorite, Redwood Regional Park in the Oakland hills, part of the East Bay Regional Park system, is a default location for residents in Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley. Several trails provide extensive tree coverage. Consider the French Trail, Chown Trail, Madrone Trail, Fern Trail, and Redwood Peak Trail as hikes beneath a canopy of trees. The West Ridge Trail provides access to each of the trailheads. The Redwood Bowl Staging Area is the primary parking location. Another connecting trail with a tree canopy is the Stream Trail, with parking available at Canyon Meadow Staging Area. • Joaquin Miller Park Located adjacent to Redwood Regional Park on Skyline Boulevard, Joaquin Miller Park is popular for day hikers, so be prepared for more foot traffic. It has almost an entire tree canopy on the Big Trees Trail, Sequoia Bayview Trail, Palos Colorados Trail, and the Sunset Trail. • Purisima Creek Redwoods Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve is part of the Peninsula Open Space Trust in San Mateo County. Its hike on Harkins Ridge was among our Top 10 Trails in 2020. The trails beneath a canopy of trees are ideally suited for hiking during the rainy season. The Purisima Creek Trail follows Purisima Creek, an active waterway, and is home to large stumps of old growth trees with some second-growth trees scattered throughout the area. • Cataract Falls On the north end of Mt. Tamalpais State Park you will find Cataract Falls Trail, one of its most popular trails, with redwood trees towering over you. Rain will further enable the cascade of waterfalls along Cataract Creek, which the trail follows. Although slightly less than four miles in length, you’ll gain over 1,000 feet in elevation over steep steps and tree roots. The walk on Purisima Creek Trail is partially protected by a canopy of trees. The creek currently is flowing during the winter months. Staff Photos Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills is considered an “ecological gem” with its year-round display of blossoming plants. It has an ideal canopy for rain cover. A winter favorite, the Manzanita trees in Huckleberry Preserve, are currently in bloom. Redwood Regional Park has many trails that can be explored during rainy days without getting drenched. French Trail in Redwood Regional Park has an abundant canopy which provides some protection on rainy days.

articles.text: Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will offer a virtual concert on Friday and Sunday, January 15 and 17. Pictured are: Natasha Makhijani (left) Jory Fankuchen, Clio Tilton, and Samsun van Loon. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, comprised of musicians Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Clio Tilton, and Samsun van Loon, will present two virtual concerts on Friday. January 15 and Sunday, January 17. “Composers at the Keyboard” explores the world of composer-pianists from Johann Sebastian Bach to Carlos Simon. Audiences can expect a diverse sampling of Hungarian folk music, Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet, jazz idioms, and more. Pianist Stephen Prutsman will join the Chamber musicians for a performance featuring Bach, Brahms, and an original piece for solo piano. A pre-concert discussion and question-and-answer will be held with Steve Prutsman. The concert on January 15 will begin at 7:30 p.m., and the concert on January 17 begins at 6 p.m. Both are virtual and can be viewed from a smartphone, tablet, or desktop. To view the concerts, click on https://chambermusicsocietysf. org/events.
articles.title: Chamber Music Society of SF presents virtual concert on January 15 & 17

articles.text: Songs for a New World, filmed on stage at San Francisco Playhouse and presented as an on-demand video stream, will be available only through January 15. The play is about “hitting the wall and having to make a choice, or take a stand, or turn around and go back.” It is the first musical from Tony award-winning playwright Jason Robert Brown and is a moving collection of powerful songs that examine life, love, and the choices people make. Brown has been hailed as “one of Broadway’s smartest and most sophisticated songwriters since Stephen Sondheim” (Philadelphia Inquirer), and his “extraordinary, jubilant theater music” (Chicago Tribune) has been heard all over the world, whether in one of the hundreds of productions of his musicals every year or in his own live performances. The New York Times described Brown as “a leading member of a new generation of composers who embody high hopes for the American musical.” The play is directed by Bill English, with choreography by Nicole Helfer. Songs for a New World features cast members John Paul Gonzalez, Cate Hayman, Rodney Earl Jackson Jr., and Katrina Lauren McGraw. The play premiered on December 12. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2020-2021-season/songs-for-a-new-world/ for program information and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Playhouse’s Songs for a New World ends on January 15

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will be featuring six of the choirs from its Kinder & Training Department, and two touring choirs from, Concert Choir and Ensemble, in its annual winter concert, to be performed virtually on Saturday, January 23 at 4 p.m. A total of 130 singers will be performing. This will mark the first concert of the year for the choirs. All recitals have taken place virtually, due to the novel coronavirus and shelter-in-place restrictions. Visit the choir’s Youtube page to watch the premiere at https:// www.youtube.com/user/PiedmontChoirs.
articles.title: Piedmont Children’s Choir winter concert on January 23

articles.text: Edwin Outwater, Music Director of San Francisco Conservatory of Music, is the subject of a documentary film to be shown on Friday, January 8 at 7:30 p.m. What We Do on the Stage, a documentary concert film envisioned by San Francisco Conservatory of Music and its Music Director Edwin Outwater, will premiere this Friday, January 8 at 7:30 p.m. The documentary follows Outwater and his students as they explore what it means to perform on a stage for an audience and how that paradigm has evolved during the pandemic. The program includes works by Pauline Oliveros (Sonic Meditation VII), Samuel Barber (Mutations on Bach), Mozart (Gran Partita), Morton Feldman (Madame Press Died Last Week at Ninety) and more. The documentary will allow audiences to experience firsthand the advantages of playing in a large ensemble. You will also get a complete overview of orchestral repertoire, beginning with masterworks and then delving into lesser-known pieces of every era. To reserve a spot to view the film, visit https://sfcm.edu/performance-calendar/event/sfcmorchestra-conducted-edwin-outwater-1.
articles.title: SF Conservatory documentary concert film this Friday

articles.text: Gunchild Carling Piedmont Piano Company will host a virtual concert tomorrow, January 7, featuring Swedish artist Gunchild Carling. Carling is a well-versed Jazz “internationally acclaimed superstar.” The award-winning, multi-instrumentalist has been featured on Scott Bradlee’s Post Modern Jukebox, a rotating musical collective known for reworking popular modern music into vintage genres. She draws heavy influence from Bix Beiderbecke, Louis Armstrong, and Billie Holiday. Some of her extraordinary musical skills include playing trumpet and trombone with vaudeville stunts, such as playing three trumpets at once. In tomorrow’s concert she will put a 1920’s twist on popular 1980’s tunes, including “Material Girl,” “Never Gonna Give You Up,” and “Happy.” The live-stream concert will begin at 5 p.m. on Thursday, January 7. Visit https://www. piedmontpiano.com/concerts to secure tickets.
articles.title: Piedmont Piano Co. streaming Gunchild Carling concert tomorrow

articles.text: Cal Performances will host trumpeter and vocalist Bria Skonberg’s premiere concert tomorrow evening, Thursday, January 7, at 7 p.m. The event is part of the “Cal Performances at Home” series, which brings original, full-length performances streamed direct to your home screen. The premiere will be available on demand until April 7. Skonberg’s musical style combines the energy of New Orleans swing with the dreamy vocals of a radio crooner. Elements of bebop and jazz will be heard as well. Skonberg last performed at Cal Performances in April 2019, inally recorded from the historic Louis Armstrong House in Queens, New York, where Skonberg and her quintet performed selections from her latest album, Nothing Never Happens. The album is a mix of hot jazz classics, vintage vocal tunes, original compositions, and fresh new takes on pop songs by the Beatles, Queen, and Sonny Bono. Join the pre-concert conversation with Skonberg and Cal Performances Executive and Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen at 6:30 p.m. before the premiere concert at 7 p.m. For access and more information, visit https://calperformances.org/events/2020-21/ at-home/bria-skonberg/. articles.text: SF Jazz will feature Grammy-winning trumpeter Chris Botti in a pre-recorded concert this Friday, January 8 at 5 p.m. It will be part of SF Jazz’s Fridays at Five series, a new series of weekly pre-recorded concerts that aspire to connect audience members with music during shelter-in-place restrictions. Botti has made his sumptuous clarion sound, fluent phrasing, and evocative sense of space into a distinct signature. For this Friday’s performance, recorded during his sold-out run in January 2020, Botti brought his hugely entertaining 9-piece band featuring saxophonist Andy Snitzer, violin virtuoso Anastasiia Mazurok, and the show-stopping vocalist Sy Smith. Botti has recorded over a dozen albums and collaborated Trumpeter Chris Botti fronts a 9-piece band. with well-known musicians, ranging from Yo-Yo Ma and Herbie Hancock to Paul Simon, Joni Mitchell, and Sting. His most recent release, Impressions, won a Grammy Award as Best Instrumental Pop Album. To view the concert, click on https://www.sfjazz.org/fridaysatfive/. For more information about this Friday’s event, visit https:// www.sfjazz.org/fridaysatfive/.
articles.title: Chris Botti concert at SF Jazz to be shown this Friday

articles.text: Photo by Ruth Hartnup (Flicker – CC 2.0) Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall, home of the San Francisco Symphony. San Francisco Symphony has announced the cancellation of all concerts and performances through June 30 of this year. “While it is deeply disappointing to have to cancel the remainder of the planned concerts in our 2020–21 season, the ongoing impacts of COVID-19 make it clear that this is the best course of action for the Symphony at this time,” said CEO Mark Hanson. “By canceling these performances, we are able to turn our full attention to investing in the creation of compelling and timely digital content and experiences that both fit within required safety guidelines and take advantage of them as a catalyst for innovation.” San Francisco Symphony will continue to offer archival concerts and digital resources online. To learn more about specific show cancellations, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Calendar/ COVID-19.
articles.title: SF Symphony cancels performances through June 30

articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players will host its first concert of the year, “2LOW+,” on Sunday, January 24 at 4 p.m. and will feature cellist Amos Yang, Assistant Principal of San Francisco Symphony, accompanied by SF Symphony colleague Charles Chandler on double bass. Special guests include soprano Isabel Yang and Keisuke Nakagoshi, pianist-in-residence at San Francisco Conservatory of Music and Opera Parallele. The concert will be streamed via YouTube Live. Yang studied with Irene Sharp at the San Francisco Conservatory and played with the SFS Youth Orchestra in its early days. He has earned degrees from the Juilliard School before landing a post with the Seattle Symphony and performing as a member of the Maia String Quartet. Winning a position with the SFS in 2006 offered a rare and prized opportunity to join his hometown orchestra. This special event includes his daughter, Isabel, a budding violinist who sings with the San Francisco Girls Chorus. To reserve tickets, visit https:// www.gccpmusic.com/concert1. articles.text: Joon-ho Bong’s highly satirical movie, Parasite, is the first non-english language film to win the Academy Award for best picture. Movie review by Chris Honoré Winner of the Best Feature at the 2019 Academy Awards, Parasite is many things – a satire, a dark comedy, ambiguous to a fault, ever enigmatic, and a sendup of social inequality. It’s also persistently perplexing. Even when the narrative seems clearly framed it abruptly shifts in tone and direction, forcing the audience to pause and reconsider the meaning of the latest reveal. What Parasite is not is a horror film, its title referring to larger social norms and values, focusing on the differences between classes. In this case it is two families, each living in Seoul, in starkly different circumstances. The story opens with the Kim family: father, Ki-woo (Song Kang-ho), mother, Chung-sook (Jang Hye-jin), son, Ki-woo (Choi Woo-shik) and daughter, Ki-jung (Park So-dam). They live in a small rabbit-warren apartment below street level, bug infested, where they are able to get wi-fi only by using a neighbor’s signal while sitting on an elevated toilet in their one bathroom. Their meager income is derived from folding pizza boxes for a local business. It’s at this point that the story subtly shifts. The Kim son, Ki-woo, meets a friend who asks for a favor: while he is away, would he tutor the teenage daughter of the Park family, Da-hye (Jung Ji-so)? Ki-woo agrees. The following day he finds himself being interviewed by the mother, Yeon-kyo (Jo Yeo-jeong), who is desperate to find someone to help Da-hye with her lessons. Ki-woo is astonished by the house, a walled-in contemporary, spacious, elegant. It is clear that the Park family is affluent. The father, Dong-ik (Lee Sunkyun), is the owner of a successful IT firm. The Parks have a much younger son, Da-song (Jung Hyun-jun) who Yeon-kyo indulges in all ways and is convinced he could benefit from art lessons. Hired on the spot, Ki-woo meets Da-hye and supervises her first lesson and soon leaves. Later he sits with his own family and explains his good fortune. He mentions that the mother wants art lessons for the small boy and he has told the mother that his sister is schooled in art and perhaps she might be willing to instruct Da-song. Eager to have the boy occupied, the mother is grateful. And when Ki-woo returns for another lesson, he brings Ki-jung with him. It becomes apparent that the Kims are small-time grifters and they see an opportunity. Dong-ik has a driver. Get rid of him and Ki-woo can recommend Ki-taek for the position. The Parks also have a housekeeper (Lee Jeongeun). Cause her to be released and recommend the Kim mother, Chung–sook (Jang Hye-jin). And within a week or two, the entire Kim family is working for the Parks who are unaaware of the familial connections. It’s at this point that the story takes another turn. The Kims are astonished at their luck, realizing that their sudden wealth and positions are, as Chung-sook says, akin to an iron, which can smooth out all the wrinkles that once plagued them. But of course this is just the middle of act two and when the Parks leave for a long camping weekend, the Kims, of course, take up residence, feeling very much at home, lounging in the living room, food covering the furniture. What could go wrong? Can this charade end well? Writer/director Boon Jong-ho is eager to answer that question, and so the story takes yet another turn that is completely unanticipated. While the family is relaxing, the hour late, the house theirs to enjoy, the doorbell rings. They quickly learn that it’s the recently released housekeeper who has come to retrieve something she insists she left behind when she so hurriedly departed. Beyond this point that it’s best to drop any discussion of plot, for the story again changes, while a strange new twist is introduced. What Parasite does not do is cast either the Kims or the Parks as stereotypes. Each family is in its own way likable and in its own ways insulated by their social and economic situations. Either could have been foils and Joon-ho avoids that trap. How this all unfolds and resolves itself – its startling climax and quiet denouement – represent the true pleasure of watching what proves to be a truly unique and entertaining film. Parasite. Directed by Joon-ho Bong. Starring Song Kang-ho, Jo Jeo-jong and So-dam Park, With subtitles. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Parasite – Academy Award- winner as best film

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré While waiting for the moment when I can walk into a theater and spend two hours watching a movie with strangers, I wait. In the interim, I watch movies on a much smaller screen. Many, if not most, I have seen before. I’ve come to realize that seeing a film twice, maybe three times, can be more than interesting. Good movies are layered, can be deeply subtle, with small moments missed on the first viewing. That was my experience with The Book of Henry, which I first watched when it was released in 2017. The critics were almost unanimously harsh in their reviews. I recalled genuinely liking it. I just didn’t remember why. So, I watched with interest, trying to understand what there was about Henry that caused it to be so stridently judged. I watched it again the next day, and the day after that. My reaction to Henry was that I found it for many reasons to be extraordinary. Put simply, I loved it. The characters were beautifully rendered, beginning with Henry (Jaeden Lieberher), his younger brother, Peter (Jacob Tremblay, and his mother, Susan (Naomi Watts). Their individual performances were remarkable, inspired, with moments that bordered on the wondrous. (I’m thinking of one scene when Henry is in the hospital and Peter sits at the foot of his bed and they discuss what lies ahead). After three viewings I came to understand that Henry is a meditation on the remarkable connections that can define family. This film is magical realism; what takes place, especially in the second half, requires a willing suspension of disbelief. What the movie does is submerge the audience in a deeply moving story which is an aggregate of wonderful moments that resonate. They are filled with a tenderness and honesty that are both magical and clearly beyond that cranky cohort of critics bound by literalism. The character who gives the film its narrative structure is, of course, Henry. Introduced in the first act of the film we see that he is deeply smart (with a shrug he says he prefers precocious). That he is the family’s anchor is soon made manifest. He pays the bills, makes investments, admonishes his mother who is addicted to a video game, protects Peter at school, and carries the weight of concern for a young girl, Christina (Maddie Ziegler), living next door, who he discovers is being abused by her single parent stepfather, Glen (Dean Norris). There’s a scene in the film when he is grocery shopping with Peter and Susan and he sees a man raging at and pushing a young woman. Henry begins to walk toward them, intending to intervene. Susan stops him, saying it’s none of their business. Later the two discuss that moment, and Susan says that had Henry gotten involved there could have been violence. Henry responds, saying, “There are worse things than violence.” Susan asks, “What is worse?” Henry answers, “Apathy.” It’s a wonderful word, for the entire film is a repudiation of apathy and indifference; rather, it is framed and guided by empathy. Henry insists that his mother must rescue Christina, and so he brings all of his genius to bear, constructing a plan that is described and diagramed in his red book, the book of Henry. Its pages are saturated with his resilient joy and commitment and enthusiasm, as well as his single-minded detachment. As well, he leaves Susan a cassette tape, locked in a safe in the basement, with specific instructions regarding how to carry out his plan. Susan, book in hand, buds in her ears, listening to Henry’s voice, sets out to fulfill his wish which indeed does touch on the softly surreal. I assume that director Colin Trevorrow, who chose this story to tell, must have ultimately regarded it as an expression of the role that family plays in our lives – that fragile, resilient sanctuary, enmeshed with cross currents of emotion and memory. I remain puzzled, still, how the critics could have missed the breadth and depth of this wonderful film, which is magical in premise but profoundly real. The Book of Henry. Directed by Colin Trevorrow. Staring Naomi Watts, Jaeden Lieberher, Jacob Tremblay Maddie Ziegler, and Sarah Silverman. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13. Jaeden Martell (Lieberher) as Henry Carpenter in The Book of Henry.
articles.title: The Book of Henry – a magical film

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s My Neighbors the Yamadas, directed by Isao Takahara. Movie review by Chris Honoré My Neighbors the Yamadas, written and directed by Isao Takahara and based on a Japanese manga comic strip by Hisachi Ishi, titled Nono-chan, uses an unusual format. It resembles a four or five panel, episodic strip that is told in a series of vignettes which vary in length; each has its own title and deals with a singular issue, such as losing a child in a department store, the relationship between a father and son, the wisdom brought about by age and experience, and the uncertainty of meeting a girlfriend for the first time. The vignettes cover a spectrum of emotions from humor to frustration to heartbreak, demonstrating life’s small conflicts, problems, and joys, all offering an honest picture of the daily routines of a typical middle class Japanese family that resides in urban Tokyo. The family, the Yamadas, consists of a father, Takahashi (James Belushi); mother, Matsuko (Molly Shannon); grandmother, Shige (Tress MacNeille); son, Noboru (Daryl Sabara); and daughter, Nonoko (Lilliana Mumy). Providing a voice-over is David Ogden Stiers. The relationship between Takahashi and Matsuko is the primary focus of the vignettes, the two often disagreeing about the mundane, such as who gets to operate the television remote. Grandma Shige offers the family her wisdom and insights and helpful proverbs, and the children are typical children with their own issues (Noboru is 13; Nonoko is 5). While we see that all of the family members are in some ways flawed, the theme that holds the narrative together is one of familial love and affection. These are kind, decent people. The animation is atypical for a Ghibli feature film. The colors, instead of a vivid and rich palette typical of most of the work produced by the Studio, are soft watercolors that seem closer to simple line drawings. This film offers a nicely crafted window into Japanese family life and culture, which only enriches the story for the western audience. My Neighbors the Yamadas (1999). Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahara. With voices of James Belushi, Molly Shannon, Daryl with Sabara, Lilliana Mumy, Tress MacNeille and David Ogden Stiers. Rated PG. 1 hr., 40 min.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré In an article in the New York Times Magazine, director Spike Jonze, when discussing his film, Where the Wild Things Are, said, “Everything we did, all the decisions that we made, were to try to capture the feeling of what it is to be nine.” While it is true that a movie targeting young filmgoers must engage their imaginations and emotions, it shouldn’t necessarily mirror what it feels like to be 9-years-old. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, this type of film will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb on board – which, of course, they are fully prepared to do. Most likely at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, 10 million in the U.S. Its success begs the question what is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. Max, dressed in his wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Where the Wild Things Are is an elegant and simple story, wonderfully illustrated by Sendak, and one that appeals to any youngster who feels conflicted and perhaps frustrated at being buffeted by the whims of family, school and siblings, who wishes only for a magic place where he can be king. In the first act of the film, Jonze captures with pitch-perfect insight the existential pain of any kid who feels overwhelmed by life. Max (Max Records) is coping with the divorce of his parents, and with a sense of isolation so complete that he talks to fences as if they could talk back. When Max discovers his mother has invited a strange man over for dinner, and sees the nuzzling on the couch, he acts out, argues with his mother and runs from the house, angry and conflicted. It’s at this point that Sendak’s fable begins. This is the real challenge for Jonze as a screenwriter. The difficulty of adapting Sendak’s story to the screen is that it lacks even a semblance of a strong narrative arc. There is only a paper-thin plot, there is no real conflict and there is no resolution. For Sendak’s book to be adapted to the screen as a 98-minute feature, Jonze had to embellish considerably. But by deviating too far from the fable template (and from Sendak’s book), he does so at his peril. Kids wish to be swept up in a story that involves, in some fashion, a journey akin to that found in Shrek or Harry Potter or Spy Kids, one in which the protagonist struggles to overcome adversity, achieves a specific goal, is victorious, and the tale ends with a nice moral. Jonze’s film draws very little from that recipe. The film is imaginative, and the photography superb, with sepia tones in contrast to the crisp, bright colors of most kids’ movies. It could be argued that Where the Wild Things Are is not a film intended for children but for adults who enjoy watching movies that remind them of their childhood. The monsters, which Jonze develops, have names and speak, though they don’t in the book. They are somber and dysfunctional, and Carol (James Gandolfini), the wild thing Max comes to know best, is given to bouts of scary temper, threatening to hurt Max. It’s even suggested that they should eat Max and they’re surprised that they haven’t. Surprisingly, there is no emotional center to the film. Even the relationships between the wild things seem too subtle and strange, something likely to be missed by a younger audience. It’s clear that Jonze made an astonishing effort to adapt a children’s book, but the story simply did not have enough substance to be made into feature film. It was a high-risk gamble by the studio and Jonze. Where the Wild Things Are. Starring Catherine Keener, Max Records, James Gandolfini, Catherine O’Hara, Forest Whitaker and Chris Cooper. Directed by Spike Jonze. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Max Records stars in Where the Wild Things Are.
articles.title: Sendak’s beloved book, Where the Wild Things Are, now a film

Even the relationships between the wild things seem too subtle and strange, something likely to be missed by a younger audience. It’s clear that Jonze made an astonishing effort to adapt a children’s book, but the story simply did not have enough substance to be made into feature film. It was a high-risk gamble by the studio and Jonze. Where the Wild Things Are. Starring Catherine Keener, Max Records, James Gandolfini, Catherine O’Hara, Forest Whitaker and Chris Cooper. Directed by Spike Jonze. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s My Neighbors the Yamadas, directed by Isao Takahara. Movie review by Chris Honoré My Neighbors the Yamadas, written and directed by Isao Takahara and based on a Japanese manga comic strip by Hisachi Ishi, titled Nono-chan, uses an unusual format. It resembles a four or five panel, episodic strip that is told in a series of vignettes which vary in length; each has its own title and deals with a singular issue, such as losing a child in a department store, the relationship between a father and son, the wisdom brought about by age and experience, and the uncertainty of meeting a girlfriend for the first time. The vignettes cover a spectrum of emotions from humor to frustration to heartbreak, demonstrating life’s small conflicts, problems, and joys, all offering an honest picture of the daily routines of a typical middle class Japanese family that resides in urban Tokyo. The family, the Yamadas, consists of a father, Takahashi (James Belushi); mother, Matsuko (Molly Shannon); grandmother, Shige (Tress MacNeille); son, Noboru (Daryl Sabara); and daughter, Nonoko (Lilliana Mumy). Providing a voice-over is David Ogden Stiers. The relationship between Takahashi and Matsuko is the primary focus of the vignettes, the two often disagreeing about the mundane, such as who gets to operate the television remote. Grandma Shige offers the family her wisdom and insights and helpful proverbs, and the children are typical children with their own issues (Noboru is 13; Nonoko is 5). While we see that all of the family members are in some ways flawed, the theme that holds the narrative together is one of familial love and affection. These are kind, decent people. The animation is atypical for a Ghibli feature film. The colors, instead of a vivid and rich palette typical of most of the work produced by the Studio, are soft watercolors that seem closer to simple line drawings. This film offers a nicely crafted window into Japanese family life and culture, which only enriches the story for the western audience. My Neighbors the Yamadas (1999). Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahara. With voices of James Belushi, Molly Shannon, Daryl with Sabara, Lilliana Mumy, Tress MacNeille and David Ogden Stiers. Rated PG. 1 hr., 40 min. Max Records stars in Where the Wild Things Are.

articles.text: Boris Godunov ruled the Tsardom of Russia from 1585 to 1598 and then as the first non-Rurikid tsar from 1598 to 1605. An opera, Boris Godunov, was written about him 200 years later by Modest Mussorgsky. Once upon a time there was a man who thought a lot of himself. He was born to wealth. But that was not enough. He had dreams of greater achievements. As he achieved them, his fame grew also. But that only increased his thirst for power and fame. The young man was clever financially and used his wealth to increase his fame - which also increased his wealth and increased his thirst for power. As his fame and wealth and power increased, they served to feed his ego which also grew and grew. As happens with people like this, fame is not enough by itself. Nor is wealth. It is power that they want. There is a formula that goes something like this: great wealth + ego + the quest for fame = power–hungry megalomania. Our young man set his sights on the highest position of the land. Nothing would stop him. Through a series of manipulations, some legal, he became the leader of his land. He praised himself to the world and knew how to control the media. He gathered around him only those who would feed his ego in a worshipful way. He craved that. Those who didn’t pledge absolute obedience to him were “fired“. He enjoyed doing that. Corruption in his administration was ubiquitous. He feuded with the Congress. There were those in the land who loved him. But there was growing opposition. Abnormal weather catastrophes around the world indicated a very real problem – climate change. As if that was not enough, a global pandemic was killing people at an alarming rate. It would be called “the time of troubles“. Things were so bad that the government sent money to the people. But the leader was in denial; all the while touting his brilliance and success. He was, after all, “the greatest.” In the end, everyone had had enough of his administration. He must go. He screamed “I am the ultimate power“ to the bitter end. But his fate was sealed. And out he went. That’s the way it actually happened. And on Friday, the 13th of April in 1605, Czar Boris Godunov died.

February 26 – Augie Grahn, 26 (1994-2020). A graduate of Millennium High School, he was a creative, expressive, and deeply passionate person. He was a member of the lacrosse and water polo teams and became interested in acting through Drama Club. As a senior he had the starring role in Streetcar Named Desire, which was selected for a performance at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in Scotland in 2012. He developed a passion for photography at CalArts. March 1 – Joe Sullivan, 62 (1956-2020) A Piedmont High graduate, he opened a bookstore, Book Tree, in Montclair Village, and shared space with Montclair Pharmacy, operated by his father, Bill Sullivan. A Boy Scout with Troop 6 at Corpus Christi Church, he later became a troop leader when his son was in Scouts. He was a volunteer fireman in Auburn and was President of the Oakland-Montclair Lions Club. March 22 – Jan Towler, 96 (1923-2020). A third generation Californian, she was a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years. A founding member of Lincoln Child Center Foundation, she also served the Junior Center for Arts and Science and earned their Lifetime of Giving Award in 2008. She created the Cal Band Foundation in honor of her late husband, Herb. April 14 – Darryl Henley, 81 (1939-2020). A Piedmont native with a career of more than 30 years in hospital administration, he served as General Manager of Los Banos Cemetery District for 10 years. An active member of The Family, a man’s social organization, he was best known as a pianist who could play any song from any era in any key. April 23 – Sharon Banker, 96 (1923-2020), A native Piedmonter whose parents settled in town in 1926, she graduated from Piedmont High and UC Berkeley and had a 30-year career as a Congressional staff member in Washington, DC. Sharon was active in the Town & Country Club of San Francisco, the Sulgrave Club in Washington, DC, and the Colonial Dames of America. She was a member of the Junior League, Claremont Country Club, and remained an active volunteer at Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale in her 90s. She married William Banker and enjoyed traveling through the world, sharing time between Piedmont and Carmel. May 7 – Neil Guiney, 75 (1945-2020). As a builder he created beautiful homes, remodeling each house to his exacting taste and specifications. A Renaissance man, he enjoyed playing many instruments from piano to the fiddle. He loved literature, music and art, and spent many hours in museums throughout the world. Proud of his heritage, he obtained dual citizenship in Ireland and the U.S. June 7 – Leslie Haydel, 75 (1944-2020). The mother of four daughters, Leslie’s generous spirit made her home a popular after-school gathering spot for her daughters’ friends, including back-to-school spaghetti dinners. Leslie’s home was also a welcoming place for foreign exchange students from Japan, Switzerland, Germany, the Dominican Republic, and Denmark. June 16 – Dr. Jon Sigurdson, 86 (1933-2020). Born and raised in Winnipeg, Manitoba, he moved to the U.S. after medical school and became an orthopedic surgeon with Kaiser. He and his wife formed a successful practice in Oakland and lived in Piedmont for 50 years. They were longtime patrons of San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera, and avid hikers, with extended hikes in Scotland, England, and Australia. July 12 – Dr. J. Harper Gaston, 88 (1931-2020). A dedicated, talented cardiologist, he was Chief of Medicine with Kaiser Permanente Medical Group of Northern California for over 20 years, and later founded and served as the first Medical Director and Physician-in-Chief of the Kaiser Permanente Southeastern Medical Group in Atlanta, Georgia. July 18 – Richard “Dick” Brooks, 92 (1928-2020). A 22-year resident of Piedmont through 1987, he was a long-time resident of Ketchum, Idaho where he died. While in Piedmont he was a member of the executive council of the Boy Scout Council and helped to maintain the independence of the Piedmont Council. August 5 – Rob Bond, 79 (1941-2020). Founder of World Franchising Network with annual directories, websites, databases and franchise analytical services. He also published numerous art books under the brand name Half Full Press. His love of travel and adventure took him to 94 countries and 49 states, with numerous trips involving hiking and climbing. He actively coached youth sports when his two sons were in school. A resident of Piedmont for 43 years, he died in Orinda, where he and his wife Leslie resided for the past six years. August 28 – Linda Trowbridge, 65 (1965-2020). A Piedmont resident for 37 years, she had a 35-year career as a health care executive, culminating with seven years as founder and CEO of the Center for Elders Independence in Oakland. She was an active volunteer with the Piedmont Scout Council, and winner of the Sidney C. Singer Service to Youth Award in 2018. She also co-led a Girl Scout troop in Piedmont, with members obtaining the Gold Award. She was an active member of College Avenue Presbyterian Church, where she served on its Board of Elders. September 19 – Barbara Borsuk, 97 (1922-2020). A resident of Piedmont for more than 60 years, she and her husband Sydney were philanthropists supporting Oakland Ballet, Oakland Symphony, the Jewish Welfare Fund and the Jewish Home for the Aged in Danville. She was a volunteer for 26 years at the Cancer Society’s Discovery retail shop on Piedmont Avenue, and as a docent at Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale. October 10 – William V Hassenzahl Jr., 53 (1964-2020). A Piedmont High graduate in 1983, he was an active member of the Piedmont Boy Scouts, and an Eagle Scout in Troop 4. Professionally he was an engineer with a love of outdoor activities. He was an avid skier and a ski patrol member, a skydiver and skydive instructor, and a bicyclist. He enjoyed and meticulously cared for his Viper and Kawasaki racing bikes and loved family getaways in the Utah mountains. October 11 – Stuart Schneck, 77 (1942-2020). Founder of the largest US-based manufacturer of macrame, he later invented a hydroponic garden product, used to grow plants without soil. He sold the company and became the parent company’s General Counsel. He later served as General Counsel at a number of other companies before retiring. October 13 – Alpha Mae Beamer, 100 (1920-2020). Alpha Mae Beamer, acknowledged by most as Piedmont’s unofficial matriarch, died at home. She was born during the Spanish Flu Epidemic and died at home during the COVID-19 worldwide epidemic. She lived to be 100 years and 8 months. In Piedmont she served on the PTA and other organizations at Havens School, and later was a member of the School Board. She was actively involved with Piedmont Community Church, Piedmont Boy Scouts, Children’s Hospital, Merritt Hospital, Lincoln Child Center, Oakland Museum of California and its White Elephant Sale. October 14 – Lucretia Wieking, 87 (1933-2020). A longtime former Piedmont resident, she died in Chico, where she and her husband have lived for several years. She was the sister of Piedmont resident Sheldon Crandall. With her husband Jim she enjoyed. traveling to Europe, Tahiti, and Fiji, but her favorite destination was Napili Kai on Maui. She also loved the mountains, and spent time at vacation homes in Twain Harte, Graeagle, Bethel Island, and Whitehawk Ranch. October 14 – David Perez, 68 (1952-2020). A father, coach and friend to all, David Perez, owner of quality Auto Body in Oakland, died at age 68. He was Piedmont’s first reported fatality as a result of the worldwide COVID-19 pandemic. He knew that the key to a fulfilling life was to make the people around him happy, and he practiced that every day. He was known to walk into a room and announce, “Hoy comienza la fiesta” (Now the party begins). Unable to have a traditional funeral ceremony due to COVID, the auto dealers on Oakland’s Automobile Row, most of whom were his customers, participated in a car caravan on Broadway, with car alarms blaring in the showrooms. He was named Man of the year by the California Hispanic Chamber of Commerce. October 16 – David Maglaty, FAIA, 70 (1950-2020). A talented architect, his work received numerous awards, including the prestigious AIA National Honor Award in 2008 for work at UC
