pages.text: Wednesday, January 6, 2021 21 VITAL STATISTICS – 2020 IN REVIEW Members of the community marked milestones both joyful and sad during 2020. Piedmont lost many friends during the year, including the city’s first death resulting from the coronavirus epidemic. FRIENDS LOST November 20, 2019 – Bonnie Bell, 74 (1945-2019). Co-owner of Bell Investment Advisors in Oakland, she was a well-respected career counselor and, with her husband Jim, a patron of the arts, including major support for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir and Oakland Symphony. January 5, 2020 – Mary Maes, 106 (1913-2020). Piedmont’s oldest resident, she was a shipyard worker during World War II, and became a nurse at Peralta Hospital. February 8, 2020 – Paul Manolis, 92 (1928-2020). A Piedmont resident for 55 years, he was the family patriarch. He served as executive aide to U.S. Senate Majority Leader William Knowland in Washington, DC, and became Executive Editor of the Oakland Tribune. He served on dozens of boards and committees of civic, business, religious and fraternal organizations, including Vice Chairman of the California Arts Commission, and board member of Children’s Hospital and Oakland Museum. He was co-creator with Father Tom Paris of Greek Week at Ascension Cathedral in Oakland. He was a major supporter of Greek Orthodoxy and the Greek diaspora worldwide and led many initiatives for more than 70 years. He was an advisor to numerous archbishops, was the Orthodox representative to the World Council of Churches. February 15 – Beverly Schmidt, 80 (1939-2020). A Piedmont resident for 44 years, she enjoyed a long career as a fourth-grade teacher at Wildwood School. Prior to becoming a classroom teacher, she was the first person to teach students at Piedmont’s three elementary schools about computers. February 19 – Keith Tollas, 76 (1943-2020). A Piedmont resident for 39 years, he had a successful career in banking and wealth management with Bankers Trust and Solomon Brothers. He was known for his values of integrity and frugality, and of being unfailingly dapper. A member of the Board of Deacons at Piedmont Community Church, he was a faithful supporter of and volunteer at George Mark Children’s House, a children’s hospice. February 25 – Bruce H. Wolfe, 65 (1954-2020). A distinguished member of the State Water Resources Control Board for more than 40 years, he served as Executive Officer of the San Francisco Bay Regional Board for the past 15 years. A lifelong Piedmont resident, he was an active member of Piedmont Community Church for more than 40 years, and part of the infamous Piedmont Fourth of July Parade Band. A member of the U.S. Orienteering Team in international competition three times, he later served as coach of the team and as the U.S. representative of the International Orienteering Federation. He was North American Masters Champion from 1994 to 2000. February 26 – Augie Grahn, 26 (1994-2020). A graduate of Millennium High School, he was a creative, expressive, and deeply passionate person. He was a member of the lacrosse and water polo teams and became interested in acting through Drama Club. As a senior he had the starring role in Streetcar Named Desire, which was selected for a performance at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in Scotland in 2012. He developed a passion for photography at CalArts. March 1 – Joe Sullivan, 62 (1956-2020) A Piedmont High graduate, he opened a bookstore, Book Tree, in Montclair Village, and shared space with Montclair Pharmacy, operated by his father, Bill Sullivan. A Boy Scout with Troop 6 at Corpus Christi Church, he later became a troop leader when his son was in Scouts. He was a volunteer fireman in Auburn and was President of the Oakland-Montclair Lions Club. March 22 – Jan Towler, 96 (1923-2020). A third generation Californian, she was a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years. A founding member of Lincoln Child Center Foundation, she also served the Junior Center for Arts and Science and earned their Lifetime of Giving Award in 2008. She created the Cal Band Foundation in honor of her late husband, Herb. April 14 – Darryl Henley, 81 (1939-2020). A Piedmont native with a career of more than 30 years in hospital administration, he served as General Manager of Los Banos Cemetery District for 10 years. An active member of The Family, a man’s social organization, he was best known as a pianist who could play any song from any era in any key. April 23 – Sharon Banker, 96 (1923-2020), A native Piedmonter whose parents settled in town in 1926, she graduated from Piedmont High and UC Berkeley and had a 30-year career as a Congressional staff member in Washington, DC. Sharon was active in the Town & Country Club of San Francisco, the Sulgrave Club in Washington, DC, and the Colonial Dames of America. She was a member of the Junior League, Claremont Country Club, and remained an active volunteer at Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale in her 90s. She married William Banker and enjoyed traveling through the world, sharing time between Piedmont and Carmel. May 7 – Neil Guiney, 75 (1945-2020). As a builder he created beautiful homes, remodeling each house to his exacting taste and specifications. A Renaissance man, he enjoyed playing many instruments from piano to the fiddle. He loved literature, music and art, and spent many hours in museums throughout the world. Proud of his heritage, he obtained dual citizenship in Ireland and the U.S. June 7 – Leslie Haydel, 75 (1944-2020). The mother of four daughters, Leslie’s generous spirit made her home a popular after-school gathering spot for her daughters’ friends, including back-to-school spaghetti dinners. Leslie’s home was also a welcoming place for foreign exchange students from Japan, Switzerland, Germany, the Dominican Republic, and Denmark. June 16 – Dr. Jon Sigurdson, 86 (1933-2020). Born and raised in Winnipeg, Manitoba, he moved to the U.S. after medical school and became an orthopedic surgeon with Kaiser. He and his wife formed a successful practice in Oakland and lived in Piedmont for 50 years. They were longtime patrons of San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera, and avid hikers, with extended hikes in Scotland, England, and Australia. July 12 – Dr. J. Harper Gaston, 88 (1931-2020). A dedicated, talented cardiologist, he was Chief of Medicine with Kaiser Permanente Medical Group of Northern California for over 20 years, and later founded and served as the first Medical Director and Physician-in-Chief of the Kaiser Permanente Southeastern Medical Group in Atlanta, Georgia. July 18 – Richard “Dick” Brooks, 92 (1928-2020). A 22-year resident of Piedmont through 1987, he was a long-time resident of Ketchum, Idaho where he died. While in Piedmont he was a member of the executive council of the Boy Scout Council and helped to maintain the independence of the Piedmont Council. August 5 – Rob Bond, 79 (1941-2020). Founder of World Franchising Network with annual directories, websites, databases and franchise analytical services. He also published numerous art books under the brand name Half Full Press. His love of travel and adventure took him to 94 countries and 49 states, with numerous trips involving hiking and climbing. He actively coached youth sports when his two sons were in school. A resident of Piedmont for 43 years, he died in Orinda, where he and his wife Leslie resided for the past six years. August 28 – Linda Trowbridge, 65 (1965-2020). A Piedmont resident for 37 years, she had a 35-year career as a health care executive, culminating with seven years as founder and CEO of the Center for Elders Independence in Oakland. She was an active volunteer with the Piedmont Scout Council, and winner of the Sidney C. Singer Service to Youth Award in 2018. She also co-led a Girl Scout troop in Piedmont, with members obtaining the Gold Award. She was an active member of College Avenue Presbyterian Church, where she served on its Board of Elders. September 19 – Barbara Borsuk, 97 (1922-2020). A resident of Piedmont for more than 60 years, she and her husband Sydney were philanthropists supporting Oakland Ballet, Oakland Symphony, the Jewish Welfare Fund and the Jewish Home for the Aged in Danville. She was a volunteer for 26 years at the Cancer Society’s Discovery retail shop on Piedmont Avenue, and as a docent at Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale. October 10 – William V Hassenzahl Jr., 53 (1964-2020). A Piedmont High graduate in 1983, he was an active member of the Piedmont Boy Scouts, and an Eagle Scout in Troop 4. Professionally he was an engineer with a love of outdoor activities. He was an avid skier and a ski patrol member, a skydiver and skydive instructor, and a bicyclist. He enjoyed and meticulously cared for his Viper and Kawasaki racing bikes and loved family getaways in the Utah mountains. October 11 – Stuart Schneck, 77 (1942-2020). Founder of the largest US-based manufacturer of macrame, he later invented a hydroponic garden product, used to grow plants without soil. He sold the company and became the parent company’s General Counsel. He later served as General Counsel at a number of other companies before retiring. October 13 – Alpha Mae Beamer, 100 (1920-2020). Alpha Mae Beamer, acknowledged by most as Piedmont’s unofficial matriarch, died at home. She was born during the Spanish Flu Epidemic and died at home during the COVID-19 worldwide epidemic. She lived to be 100 years and 8 months. In Piedmont she served on the PTA and other organizations at Havens School, and later was a member of the School Board. She was actively involved with Piedmont Community Church, Piedmont Boy Scouts, Children’s Hospital, Merritt Hospital, Lincoln Child Center, Oakland Museum of California and its White Elephant Sale. October 14 – Lucretia Wieking, 87 (1933-2020). A longtime former Piedmont resident, she died in Chico, where she and her husband have lived for several years. She was the sister of Piedmont resident Sheldon Crandall. With her husband Jim she enjoyed. traveling to Europe, Tahiti, and Fiji, but her favorite destination was Napili Kai on Maui. She also loved the mountains, and spent time at vacation homes in Twain Harte, Graeagle, Bethel Island, and Whitehawk Ranch. October 14 – David Perez, 68 (1952-2020). A father, coach and friend to all, David Perez, owner of quality Auto Body in Oakland, died at age 68. He was Piedmont’s first reported fatality as a result of the worldwide COVID-19 pandemic. He knew that the key to a fulfilling life was to make the people around him happy, and he practiced that every day. He was known to walk into a room and announce, “Hoy comienza la fiesta” (Now the party begins). Unable to have a traditional funeral ceremony due to COVID, the auto dealers on Oakland’s Automobile Row, most of whom were his customers, participated in a car caravan on Broadway, with car alarms blaring in the showrooms. He was named Man of the year by the California Hispanic Chamber of Commerce. October 16 – David Maglaty, FAIA, 70 (1950-2020). A talented architect, his work received numerous awards, including the prestigious AIA National Honor Award in 2008 for work at UC Berkeley, and honor awards by the AIA in Santa Clara and in San Francisco. He was named a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects in 2014. An avid, lifelong runner and biker, his days began with a 5-7 mile run. He competed in triathlons and ran in many 5K races. October 23 – Elizabeth “Betty” Smith, 100 (1920-2020). The mother of Dorinda Woodley of Piedmont, she was a longtime member of the Berkeley Hiking Club, with fond memories of hiking Half Dome in Yosemite. She enjoyed sharing her love of nature with others and always knew the names of wildflowers, birds, trees and butterflies. In later years she became a docent at the John Muir Home Museum in Martinez, and at the Oakland Museum of California. October 23 – Jim Adams, 58 (1962-2020). A Piedmont high graduate in 1980, he earned a journalism degree from San Francisco State and began a career as a stock broker with Dean Witter. Jim immensely enjoyed traveling, including a cruise with his parents and years later an African safari with the entire family. Jim enjoyed all things outdoors – from fly fishing to duck hunting and especially scuba diving. He was a member of the Bohemian Club and the St. Francis Yacht Club He died at his home in San Francisco. November 3 –Burch Fitzpatrick, 82 (1938-2020). After working as a deputy attorney general for the State of California, he spent 20 years with the real estate law firm of Miller, Starr and Regalia where he was managing partner. He finished his career with the San Francisco law firm of Graham and James. He was a co-founder of Piedmonters for Peace and helped organize marches to protest the Iraq war. He was a longtime supporter of the George Mark House, a children’s pediatric hospice. November 3 – Pete LaChapelle, 84 (1936-2020). A former Piedmont resident, he was a youth baseball coach and volunteer assistant high school varsity coach for many years. A native of Webster Groves outside Denver, he was inducted into the East High School Sports Hall of Fame as a basketball player. He had a 30-year career as a Deputy District Attorney for the Alameda County Counsel’s office. November 16 – Susan Freeman, 70 (1950-2020). A college placement counselor by profession, she was a prodigious supporter of the arts. In Piedmont, she was a big part of the success of the Piedmont Center for the Arts, including theater productions and the annual weeklong Piedmont Chamber Music Festival. For many years she was part of the group of volunteers organizing the annual Turkey Trot. November 26 – Marella Guigou, 89 (1931-2020). A resident of Piedmont for 55 years, she was well-known for her daily walks at Witter Field in her crimson Stanford sweatshirt. Marella passed away on Thanksgiving morning, in Northbrook, Illinois. She was a passionate supporter of public education. See Vital Statistics on page 32

articles.text: While I know there are folks who have not yet discovered Beaujolais, I have yet to meet someone who dislikes it. It is a charming, fruity, refreshing, early drinking, easy-going wine that goes with tons of foods and is inexpensive. What’s not to like? In many ways it is the opposite of its closest neighbor Burgundy, whose wines are complex, scarce, require serious aging, and cost an arm and a leg. Burgundy was once planted with Pinot Noir and Gamay in roughly the same amounts. In 1395 the Duke of Burgundy decided he didn’t like Gamay and banished it from being planted in Burgundy. So, the Gamay grape migrated to an area just north of Burgundy near the town of Villefranche sur Saone, where it has flourished ever since. The Beaujolais area now produces hundreds of millions of bottles of wine a year and is also, with its green rolling hills, one of the most scenic wine areas to visit. Unlike Burgundy where you have to have an appointment at most places, the Beaujolais vintners have their doors open and welcome drop-in visitors. The two major wine producers in Beaujolais are Louis Jadot and Georges Duboeuf. They are “negociants” who work with hundreds of small farmers to blend and sell their wines. There are 10 villages that make up the heart of Beaujolais – Brouilly, Regnie, Chiroubles, Cote de Brouilly, Fleurie, Saint-Amour, Chenas, Julienas, Morgon, and Moulina-Vent. It is often these names rather than Beaujolais that you will see on the bottle and the name of the Village connotes a step up in quality than regular 2017 Jean-Ernest Descombes Morgon Cote du Py Beaujolais. As mentioned above, Beaujolais goes with a wide variety of foods and is the perfect picnic wine. It is very important to chill the bottle for a half hour in the fridge as its’ not as good at room temperature. I had the opportunity to taste some of the wines of the great Georges Duboeuf. From humble beginnings he has built an empire that sends 30 million bottles of wine all around the world each year. What is stunning about the Duboeuf wines is that even though they are mass produced he retains a very high level of quality. The following wines are ones chosen by Duboeuf from small growers. The wines are imported by Quintessential (www.quintessentialwines.com) of Napa and are widely available locally and on the internet at Wine.com. • 2017 Domaine de Quatre Vents Fleurie, $24 This is a lovely Fleurie, bursting from the glass with aromas

articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club, in conjunction with five other Bay Area garden clubs, is sponsoring a webinar that discusses the unique ecological system of the San Francisco Bay. The free webinar will be available on Wednesday, January 13, and will host four Bay Area professors who will discuss flooding, the importance of seaweed, restoration of marshlands, and the need to plant native plants. The event will begin at 9:30 a.m. with an opening slide show. The main program will run from 10 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. Titled “The Power of Plants Will Protect the Bay,” the webinar will describe how scientists are collaborating on ways to protect and restore the Bay shoreline by utilizing plants underwater, in the wetlands, and along the shores. The webinar will feature speakers Karina Nielson, Director of the Estuary and Ocean Science Center, SF State; Dr. Katharyn Boyer, professor of Biology and Wetlands Ecology; Josie Iselin, author of The Curious World of Seaweed; and Diana Benner and Laura Hanson, co-owners of The Watershed Nursery in Richmond. Karina Nielsen, Director of Estuary and Ocean Science Center at San Francisco State University Co-sponsors include Piedmont Garden Club, Woodside-Atherton Garden Club, Marin Garden Club, Hillsborough Garden Club, Orinda Garden Club, and Carmel-By-the-Sea Garden Club. These six organizations are affiliates of the Garden Club of America, whose mission is to “restore, improve and protect the quality of the environment through educational programs and action in the fields of conservation and civic improvement.” Pre-registration for the event is required. Register at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/bay-visions-tickets-127648342629.
articles.title: Piedmont Garden Club to co-sponsor Jan. 13 webinar on SF Bay ecological system

articles.text: There are two major types of quality port – Vintage and Tawny. Vintage port is bottled early and left to mature in the bottles, something that takes a long time. If you buy a bottle of the current vintage port (2017) it may not be ready to drink for 10 years. For those of us who are getting up in years, this can be a problem. There is a solution however: tawny port. Tawny port is left in the barrels at the winery to age anywhere from 10 to 40 years. So, when it is released it is totally ready to drink with no further aging required. Its time in barrel turns the wine from dark purple to a tawny golden brown, hence the name. This beautiful wine starts slow and builds to a nice crescendo, with the acidity emerging to cut the fruit. This elegant wine has a semi-sweet finish to go with its vibrancy and energy. It’s a pretty picture overall with caramel, molasses and hints of chocolate on the finish. This wine cries out for a bowl of cashews, a nice pipe and a roaring fire.
articles.title: Dow’s Tawny Porto 10 Years Old, $37

Charming and subtle, it has a long clean finish. • 2017 Jean-Ernest Descombes Morgon Cote du Py, $24 Morgon is one of the biggest bodied of the Beaujolais and can last surprisingly well in the cellar. Aromas of raspberries, plums and sweet spices introduce the wine and leads to a full-bodied, layered wine with a rich, dep core or fruit, fine but firm structuring tannins and a long stony finish. 2017 Chateau de Saint-Amour Saint-Amour • 2017 Chateau des Capitans Julienas, $22 The village was named for Julius Cesar and they produce one of the most complex wines in Beaulojais. The palate is medium bodied with silky smooth tannins and well -judged acidity. There is plenty of velvety black fruit here, almost sumptuous toward the finish that is very well-balanced. • 2017 Domaine de la Vigne Romaine Moulin-A-Vent, $25 This charmer has an opulent bouquet with dark cherries and cassis, quite voluminous with fine delineation. The event will begin at 9:30 a.m. with an opening slide show. The main program will run from 10 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. Titled “The Power of Plants Will Protect the Bay,” the webinar will describe how scientists are collaborating on ways to protect and restore the Bay shoreline by utilizing plants underwater, in the wetlands, and along the shores. The webinar will feature speakers Karina Nielson, Director of the Estuary and Ocean Science Center, SF State; Dr. Katharyn Boyer, professor of Biology and Wetlands Ecology; Josie Iselin, author of The Curious World of Seaweed; and Diana Benner and Laura Hanson, co-owners of The Watershed Nursery in Richmond. Karina Nielsen, Director of Estuary and Ocean Science Center at San Francisco State University Co-sponsors include Piedmont Garden Club, Woodside-Atherton Garden Club, Marin Garden Club, Hillsborough Garden Club, Orinda Garden Club, and Carmel-By-the-Sea Garden Club. These six organizations are affiliates of the Garden Club of America, whose mission is to “restore, improve and protect the quality of the environment through educational programs and action in the fields of conservation and civic improvement.” Pre-registration for the event is required. Register at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/bay-visions-tickets-127648342629.

articles.text: Even in these unprecedented times, the Piedmont Avenue Branch is running smoothly. That it is even open in the face of the daunting challenge of COVID-19 is testimony to the spirit, ingenuity, persistence, and commitment of the four people who make it happen – Emily, Hana, Nikki and Colette. Three of them work inside and one is at the outside table from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. five days a week, Tuesday through Saturday. Inside the library they collect the books that are returned to the Echo Avenue receptacles, take them inside and spread them out on a table where the books stay for at least 24 hours before being put on shelves. They also receive books delivered by Oakland Public Library’s van, and process those books immediately. The books were held in quarantine before OPL delivered them to the branch. Inside workers check email requests, find the right books and package them in a bag with the patron’s name. When the patron arrives outside, a worker calls the inside desk on a walkie-talkie and the bag with the order is brought outside. On a recent day, Jenera Burton, the branch librarian a few years ago and now the Supervising Librarian for West and North Oakland, was visiting the Piedmont Avenue library to see how things are going. She said that the librarians in all the branches miss having regular contact with patrons. Ruby Long is a neighbor whose work has appeared in local and national publications. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

On March 5, 2018, the city entered into a contract with Callander & Associates to develop a master plan for Coaches Field. The firm utilized the Blackwell and Oraftik plan as a base plan. Proposed improvements to the field include a new picnic area, a new wood deck and walkway in the southwest corner of the field, re-grading of the field topography, and re-configuration and expansion of the existing parking and enhancement of the vehicle entrance from Moraga Avenue. As the concepts for the new plan came into more focus, former City Administrator Paul Benoit and former Recreation Director Sara Lillevand conducted meetings with residents living in the vicinity of Coaches Field. Meetings occurred on Linda Beach Field, between Beach School and the Oakland Avenue Bridge.

articles.text: 3. People age 65-74, and people working in transportation, logistics, industrial sector, commercial sector and critical manufacturing. This tier also includes people living in congregate settings, including homeless and people in prison. 4. People age 50-64, as well as people age 16-64 with underlying health conditions. People working in sectors like defense, energy, communications, finance, and government operations will also receive the vaccine. The state estimates that the vaccine will be widely available to the general public beyond these specific groups by the spring, although health officials noted that the timeline is subject to change. California is administering two different vaccines for free, one manufactured by Pfizer and another by Moderna. Both vaccines were granted emergency use authorization by the Food and Drug Administration in late 2020. Importantly, both vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. As of now, there is no statewide registry to sign up to be vaccinated. Healthcare workers should contact their employers about when they will receive the vaccine, while residents in longterm care facilities should contact their caretaker. All others are encouraged by the state to coordinate with their healthcare provider. Newsom said it wasn’t clear why vaccine distribution in California is lagging. He noted that he will propose a $300 million plan to improve vaccination efforts in the coming days. “It’s like a flywheel,” he said at a press conference this week. “In the first 10 [to] 15 days, we’re going to slowly start building pace, going to start building up, and you’re going to start seeing more rapid distribution of this vaccine. I can assure you of that. But [with] that said, it’s gone too slowly.” With cases of COVID-19 skyrocketing throughout December in Alameda County and California, many residents want to be vaccinated as soon as possible. On March 5, 2018, the city entered into a contract with Callander & Associates to develop a master plan for Coaches Field. The firm utilized the Blackwell and Oraftik plan as a base plan. Proposed improvements to the field include a new picnic area, a new wood deck and walkway in the southwest corner of the field, re-grading of the field topography, and re-configuration and expansion of the existing parking and enhancement of the vehicle entrance from Moraga Avenue. As the concepts for the new plan came into more focus, former City Administrator Paul Benoit and former Recreation Director Sara Lillevand conducted meetings with residents living in the vicinity of Coaches Field. Meetings occurred on October 21, 2018, and January 28, 2018, both at the home of William and Marge Blackwell. In June of last year, city council voted unanimously to send out requests for proposals for hiring a consultant to ensure the upgrades comply with CEQA, and to determine if further environmental reporting is needed. At that meeting, neighbors in the vicinity of Coaches Field griped at the possibility of light installations on the field. “We are currently finishing the lighting stimulation study,” Nakahara explained, which should be completed by the end of this month. Linda Beach A master plan was adopted by city council in 2017 to redesign parts of Linda Beach Playfield, adjacent to Beach Elementary School, and to install a new “playscape” in the park. The new “California Nature Playscape” redesigns an area that is paved with asphalt into an outdoor recreation area for children, and will take full advantage of the topography of the site to allow for free-form exploration. Nakahara explained that Parks Projects Manager Nancy Kent and Recreation Director Chelle Putzer are working to secure a Proposition 68 grant to help fund the ongoing project. “It is a competitive grant, with lots of stipulations,” he said. The city was able to secure another Proposition 68, non-competitive grant, where the city has been allocated $168,000 for any park project. “Linda Beach is certainly on that list, so we are slowly starting to assemble the funds necessary to complete a portion of the master plan,” Nakahara said. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) also donated $100,000 to help assist with the project, with a particular emphasis on the Tot Lot. “These funds help the city really start thinking seriously about [moving forward] with the master plan,” Nakahara said. A ceremonial check was presented by former PBF president Patty Siskind to Lillevand at the city’s Tree Lighting ceremony on December 2. Lillevand was instrumental in helping with the master plan for the project when she was the city’s Recreation Director. “$100,000 will go a long way to help us move forward with the Linda Beach master plan,” Lillevand commented on December 2. “The inspiration for the whole [project], was a wonderful community process, which several Piedmont Beautification Foundation members participated in. The county health order is connected to a supplemental state health order that went into effect this month due to coronavirus cases spiking across California. The orders are based on intensive care unit availability in a region – the state order is mandatory for any region where ICU capacity dips below 15 percent. Alameda County issued its order before ICU capacity dropped below the state’s threshold, but Bay Area ICU capacity is currently around 6 percent. The stayat-home orders will not be lifted in Alameda County until the availability of ICU beds is at 15 percent or more. The rising case rate caused the state to put Alameda County into the Purple Tier on November 18. The Purple Tier, or Widespread Tier, is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system. Currently all but four Californian counties are in the Purple Tier. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 2,452,334 total cases of COVID- 19 in California, making it the hardest hit state by the virus. There have been 27,003 deaths due to the disease statewide. As of Monday, December 28, the state had allocated 47,375 doses of COVID-19 vaccine to Alameda County. articles.text: What can you do to fill time while you’re responsibly sheltering in place? Write poetry Yes, poetry. And here’s a famous example to get you started: A tutor who tooted the flute Tried to tutor two tooters to toot. Said the two to the tutor, “Is it harder to toot or To tutor two tooters to toot?” Yep, it’s a limerick, that unique five-line form that will never challenge the sonnet for versatility, but which can make us smile. It can also provide plenty of chances for writers to show what they can do. Here’s one I did yesterday: A limerick is a big cinch to write. No problem, no poetic fright. Only pen lines one and two. Just three more to do Ogden Nash it’s not, but I had fun putting it together, so in the spirit of fun I challenge all Piedmonters to have fun, too—to fashion their own limericks and to submit them to the Post. The challenge is a friendly one, with no winners or losers. In a way you’ll be challenging yourself, and you’ll be doing your part to cheer up your town. So, give it a try. Here are three more from me to get you started: A fussy food critic named Willy Thought that noshing sushi was silly Raw fish on a plate Was nothing he ate But he scarfed steak tartare willy-nilly. A virus named Vern hit the air. An explosive sneeze blew him there. But with no host around, He fell to the ground, Crying, “Darn it all, life isn’t fair!” A plucky newspaper, the Post Refused to give up the ghost. It showed up online Doing fantastically fine, Giving folks not just more but the most. Let’s hear from you! To submit your limericks, send them by e-mail to: news@peidmontpost.org. Be sure to read the Post each week online at: piedmontpost.org. Bob Hall is the Piedmont Post’s theater reviewer and a member of the Bay Area Critics Circle. With all theaters temporarily closed, he has turned his sights to a project to keep his creative juices flowing, and to help lift the spirits of a community in lockdown mode.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, January 6, 2021 VITAL STATISTICS – 2020 IN REVIEW Continued from page 21 MARRIAGES September 9, 2020 – Ben Gandesbery, a 2011 Piedmont High graduate, married Julie Ivy of Guilford, Connecticut on September 9 at Sunflower Hill Farm near St. Louis, Missouri. The groom and bride were classmates at Case Western Reserve University Medical School and now are doctors at Washington University in St. Louis. September 12 – In an all-Piedmont wedding, Libby Faughnan (Piedmont High class of 2008), the daughter of Vince and Claire Faughnan, and Daniel Davis (PHS 2006), the son of Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado, were married among the redwoods at the Sonoma County property that has been in Libby’s family for over 50 years. Both are graduates of UC Davis and Samuel Merritt University, where they completed the Accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing. She is now at San Francisco General Hospital’s Family Birth Center, and he is an ICU nurse at Alta Bates Summit in Oakland. Write poetry Yes, poetry. And here’s a famous example to get you started: A tutor who tooted the flute Tried to tutor two tooters to toot. Said the two to the tutor, “Is it harder to toot or To tutor two tooters to toot?” Yep, it’s a limerick, that unique five-line form that will never challenge the sonnet for versatility, but which can make us smile. It can also provide plenty of chances for writers to show what they can do. Here’s one I did yesterday: A limerick is a big cinch to write. No problem, no poetic fright. Only pen lines one and two. Just three more to do By line five the end is in sight. Ogden Nash it’s not, but I had fun putting it together, so in the spirit of fun I challenge all Piedmonters to have fun, too—to fashion their own limericks and to submit them to the Post. The challenge is a friendly one, with no winners or losers. In a way you’ll be challenging yourself, and you’ll be doing your part to cheer up your town. So, give it a try. Here are three more from me to get you started: A fussy food critic named Willy Thought that noshing sushi was silly Raw fish on a plate Was nothing he ate But he scarfed steak tartare willy-nilly. A virus named Vern hit the air. An explosive sneeze blew him there. But with no host around, He fell to the ground, Crying, “Darn it all, life isn’t fair!” A plucky newspaper, the Post Refused to give up the ghost. It showed up online Doing fantastically fine, Giving folks not just more but the most. Let’s hear from you! To submit your limericks, send them by e-mail to: news@peidmontpost.org. Be sure to read the Post each week online at: piedmontpost.org. Bob Hall is the Piedmont Post’s theater reviewer and a member of the Bay Area Critics Circle. With all theaters temporarily closed, he has turned his sights to a project to keep his creative juices flowing, and to help lift the spirits of a community in lockdown mode. School Board meeting...................................Virtual meeting via Zoom On an extended trip to Chile, Argentina and Tierra del Fuego in January, Paul and Flo Raskin went on a kayaking expedition on Enterprise Island along the Antarctic Peninsula. While in Antarctica they couldn’t resist reaching in their rucksack for a copy of the Piedmont Post and a glimpse of some news back home. Send your photos of the Post in the far corners of the world, or of other communities named Piedmont, to: WITWAW, 1139 Oakland Ave., Piedmont, 94611.
